articles.text: The city will not pursue an appeal to decrease the number of housing units mandated by state housing law. Instead, city staff were directed to move forward with plans to create over 500 new and fairly-priced units by the end of 2031. On Monday, June 21, City Council considered an appeal of the Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) that has been assigned to Piedmont. RHNA quantifies the need for housing within each jurisdiction across the state during specified planning periods. The next mandated RHNA requires that Piedmont produce 587 new homes and apartments at fair pricing by the year 2031, the end of the next RHNA cycle. The expected allocation includes 163 very low-income units, 94 low-income units, 92 moderate income units, and 238 above-moderate income units. “Instead of appealing [the city’s mandated] RHNA, Piedmont can show leadership by embracing the effort to meet the housing needs of the Bay Area,” Planning Director Kevin Jackson told councilmembers. Piedmont is challenged by its built-out quality; with very little space to create new housing units, the city and its residents have largely considered accessory dwelling units (ADUs) as a way to fulfill the current RHNA. The city is close to meeting, and surpassing, the amount of housing units mandated by the current RHNA 2015-2023, or 5th RHNA cycle, according to a 2020 annual progress report. Piedmont has issued building permits for the construction of over 70 new units out of a mandated 60 units by the end of next year, 2022. On May 3, city council approved a proposal from Lisa Wise Consulting, Inc., (LWC) to prepare updates to the city’s housing element. LWC submitted the only proposal received. In addition, City Attorney Michelle Kenyon advised councilmembers that an appeal would likely not succeed and that the expense of pursing an appeal of the 2023 - 2031 RHNA is not worth it. According to Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell, appeals by cities in Southern California were only partially successful in reducing their allocations. “I’m all for ambitious goals, and I fully appreciate that appealing our RHNA allocation is not a good use of our time and resources, that can be better spent thinking about how we will meet those ambitious goals,” Councilmember Betsy Andersen said.
articles.title: Staff moves forward with plans to create 587 new housing units by 2031

articles.text: The Piedmont Community Hall is back to offering accommodations for full-capacity events, including wedding receptions. Event planners may also choose an al fresco reception on the Community Hall Patio. Covid health guidelines remain in place for those who are not vaccinated. articles.text: Editor: Recent letters to the Piedmont Post from Shirley Hooi voicing concerns over education content in the public schools show her to be a responsible, concerned parent that wants the best education for her children. The phrase “critical race theory” has appeared in the media as it relates to public education, and it has her worried. A simple media search that you can do will provide, as it did for me, a clear explanation of this phrase and how it is being used. Here is what I found. You should be able to easily find the same in the media and on the internet: 1. Critical race theory (CRT) is an intellectual “framework” used by university and graduate schools as a “tool” to aid in discussions revolving around the role that race has in a culture. These discussions have been going on since the mid- 1990’s. 2. CRT is not the title of a curriculum or a class (like History or English). 3. CRT cannot by its nature as a “framework” be taught in public schools in California. 4. It seems that Ms. Hooi has been told an alternate definition of CRT that is false. 5. This false definition is another dangerous example of a type of propaganda that distorts a word or phrase or slogan and creates a new false meaning that aligns with the false belief system of a group or political party that does the distortioning. In this case it is a simple matter to go on the internet and satisfy yourself of the truth (or falsehood) of what I have said. Beyond CRT, she indicates concern that guilt over racial issues come down on her children. This is understandable and brings up the recurring issue of what and when do we expose our children to difficult issues in the real world. I believe our children are tougher than we think. School presents in its best form a neutral, non-threatening environment to present issues and facts to students. The creation of fully functioning future citizens of our country requires that they receive the knowledge to be active members of our society. History, Social studies, Government, Environment must be taught in the schools. Reading, Writing and Arithmetic are not enough. I admire Ms. Hooi for taking the trouble to express her concerns in this forum. It is parents like her that create the excellent school district in Piedmont. –Alan Rudy
articles.title: Observations of Critical Race Theory

articles.text: A colleague and I were recently called upon to minister to a family after the tragic death of their child. I do not know of a pain greater than the death of a child. I do not know of a loss more heartbreaking. The family’s counselor had recommended the book Bearing the Unbearable: Love, Loss and the Heartbreaking Path of Grief by Joanne Cacciatore to them. The title accurately describes what they are being asked to do, to bear the unbearable. Tragedies like the death of a child bring questions like “Why?”, “Where was God?”, and “Is this truly God’s will?” to the fore. One could spend a lifetime reasoning, researching, praying, studying, discerning in an attempt to answer these questions, and still fall short of any semblance of understanding. I know that, for me, satisfactory answers have yet to present themselves. Rather than answers, what I find are promises like this from I Corinthians 13. Now faith, hope and love remain – these three things – and the greatest of these is love. The Bible Points from this year’s Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church Vacation Bible Camp are in the same vein. God knows us. God hears us. God comforts us. God forgives us. God chooses us. While these lessons do not eliminate unanswerable questions, they do point us to promises beyond the questions. The Bible Camp lesson “God comforts us” is drawn from the story of Hezekiah, king of Judah. Hezekiah is receiving written and verbal threats from the Assyrian army which is threatening to overrun Jerusalem. In response to these lies, threats and insults, the king clothes himself in sackcloth and heads to the temple where he literally lays the written threats before God. articles.text: Piedmont Police officer Jason Germano assisted Oakland police officers in rescuing a man and dog from a burning car on the city border on June 15. Officer Germano was on patrol when he heard on his radio that Oakland police needed help from someone with a fire extinguisher. A car was engulfed in flames at the intersection of Park Boulevard and Estates Drive on the Oakland-Piedmont border, and someone was still inside the vehicle. Germano arrived at the scene at about 11:20 p.m. “I grabbed my extinguisher from my vehicle and sprayed the front of the [crashed] car but wasn’t able to put the fire out,” he explained. Germano, an auto mechanic for over 20 years prior to joining the Police Department in 2019, said he understood that he had “limited time to act.” The driver initially refused to come out of the vehicle and appeared incoherent. Body camera footage shows Germano pulling the man out with the help of Oakland police officers. An OakBody camera footage shows the hood of the car engulfed in flames. Officer Jason Germano land officer then safely pulled the dog out of the burning vehicle. The scene was turned over to the Oakland Police Department for further investigation, and alcohol impairment is a suspected factor in the collision. It is unclear how the fire started, but body camera footage shows the vehicle facing the wrong way on Park Boulevard adjacent to yellow safety poles along the street. “The driver was transported to a local hospital for medical treatment,” Oakland Police Department confirmed in a statement. “The quick actions of all the officers saved the life of the driver and dog.”
articles.title: PPD Officer Jason Germano saves man, dog from burning car

articles.text: Constantly adapting and finding ways to make things happen, the Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) will continue hosting the city’s traditional July 4 Pancake Breakfast. Instead of having it at the Veterans Hall, it will be held outdoors on Waldo Avenue from 9 a.m. to 12 noon this Sunday, July 4. Each year the coed teen crew cooks and serves a sumptuous pancake breakfast to hundreds of residents as a fundraiser that helps support the extensive community volunteer work by the crew. The outdoor event is open to the public and will be a bona fide block party on the block-long street, located just off Highland Avenue. Pancakes, Aidells sausages, fresh fruit, coffee and juice will be served, courtesy of donated products from Piedmont Grocery, Starbucks, and Village Market. Cooks and servers will be fully vaccinated and wearing masks and gloves. Arts and crafts and other kid-friendly games will be provided. Families may order tickets for the whole family ahead of time or buy on Sunday on Waldo Avenue. Tickets are $15 for people age 14 and older, and $10 for children. Advance tickets may be purchased at: https://forms.gle/1LwsoZK3peDycnZq5.
articles.title: Community Service Crew to host annual July 4th Pancake Breakfast

articles.text: Editor: I have worked with our Superintendent for the last several years as part of the Steering Committee for the new STEM and performing arts building projects funded by the Measure H1 bond program. Reporting to the School Board, he has the ultimate charge of ensuring that the bond delivers what was promised to our community. I am a retired high-tech executive. From my experience he is an outstanding administrator, very skilled and knowledgeable within the California Public Education System. I am very impressed with the quality of the PUSD staff that he was able to attract to the project. By the way he delegated responsibilities and leveraged their domain knowledge while still keeping the helm. He has outstanding communication skills adapted to the many constituents within the District and the community. His decisions were always guided by consulting teachers and students, the future customers of these new facilities. He is a clear thinker able to synthesize problems to their core, thereby setting paths for solution. The “four scandals” mentioned by Jodi Biskup in her opinion published in last week’s edition of the Post raise two questions: Who has primary responsibility for the moral education of our children: parents or the School District? To what extent is the power of the Superintendent constrained by law and the California Education Code? As a Piedmont homeowner since 1984 and having lived through several school administrations, I encourage you to support our Superintendent. We have a great school district that serves our many constituents well. –Bernard Pech For 22 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send us photos still on your camera or in a scrapbook for publication in the Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. Otherwise we are left to ask, “Where in the World Are They?” Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmontpost.org, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.
articles.title: Support our Superintendent

pages.text: Wednesday, June 30, 2021 3 PPD Officer Jason Germano saves man, dog from burning car By Allyson Aleksey Piedmont Police officer Jason Germano assisted Oakland police officers in rescuing a man and dog from a burning car on the city border on June 15. Officer Germano was on patrol when he heard on his radio that Oakland police needed help from someone with a fire extinguisher. A car was engulfed in flames at the intersection of Park Boulevard and Estates Drive on the Oakland-Piedmont border, and someone was still inside the vehicle. Germano arrived at the scene at about 11:20 p.m. “I grabbed my extinguisher from my vehicle and sprayed the front of the [crashed] car but wasn’t able to put the fire out,” he explained. Germano, an auto mechanic for over 20 years prior to joining the Police Department in 2019, said he understood that he had “limited time to act.” The driver initially refused to come out of the vehicle and appeared incoherent. Body camera footage shows Germano pulling the man out with the help of Oakland police officers. An OakBody camera footage shows the hood of the car engulfed in flames. Officer Jason Germano land officer then safely pulled the dog out of the burning vehicle. The scene was turned over to the Oakland Police Department for further investigation, and alcohol impairment is a suspected factor in the collision. It is unclear how the fire started, but body camera footage shows the vehicle facing the wrong way on Park Boulevard adjacent to yellow safety poles along the street. “The driver was transported to a local hospital for medical treatment,” Oakland Police Department confirmed in a statement. “The quick actions of all the officers saved the life of the driver and dog.” City seeks recycling volunteers Applications due by July 9 By Allyson Aleksey The city is seeking volunteers to help complete a recycling audit of waste bins. Volunteers will conduct field and desk research and deliver a final report of their research to City staff. It is an ideal position for college students aged 18 or older, or anyone interested in local government and environmental work. The Piedmont Evergreen Program aims to increase recycling and composting throughout the city and reduce waste to the landfill. In the last several years, the city installed a three-can series of receptacles (waste, organics, and recyclables) to improve garbage diversion in public parks. Piedmont currently has a diversion rate of 75%, meaning that 75% of waste is composted or recycled, while 25% goes to the landfill, explained Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman. The City’s Climate Action Plan 2.0 outlines the City’s goal to divert 85% of waste going to the landfill by 2030. To reach this goal and encourage further diversion, the City purchased additional waste, organic, and recycling receptacles for use in public areas throughout Piedmont. Responsibilities Volunteers will be expected to complete the following during the course of the project: • Bin Inventory: Complete a walking audit of Piedmont parks and other public places to locate and inventory all of the trash, recycling, and compost bins in the City. This information will be used in future decision-making processes, so accurate information gathering is key. Volunteers will use this information and compile a map and/or database of all bin locations. • Gathering Usage Data: Volunteers will keep track of usage of various bins, and track data over time. Volunteers may also offer assistance with sorting into bins. This task may include sitting by a bin location for a period of time and keeping track of how many people use the bin, what they put in the bin, etc. Volunteers may be asked to complete a waste characterization of different public bins to see how residents are sorting their waste. • Education and Engagement: Volunteers will meet with the Sustainability Program Manager weekly and will have a chance to ask questions about solid waste, compost, and recycling and learn more about the industry. Reporting to the School Board, he has the ultimate charge of ensuring that the bond delivers what was promised to our community. I am a retired high-tech executive. From my experience he is an outstanding administrator, very skilled and knowledgeable within the California Public Education System. I am very impressed with the quality of the PUSD staff that he was able to attract to the project. By the way he delegated responsibilities and leveraged their domain knowledge while still keeping the helm. He has outstanding communication skills adapted to the many constituents within the District and the community. articles.text: Can you remember catching your young child in a lie? For most of us, this experience strikes fear: am I raising a deceitful person? Is this the first step down a dangerous path of dishonesty? Actually, lying is a normal part of cognitive-linguistic development which typically occurs during the preschool years. Studies show that up to 80% of 4-yearolds lie. This milestone indicates that the child has learned that other people have their own and often differing opinions. It signifies that the child has learned that they can use words in a more abstract way than simply to express their needs and wants, namely that words can get someone to think something that is not actually true. The child now understands that what we say does not always correspond with what we are thinking and sometimes we hide what we are really thinking and feeling. To make matters worse, this is often the age at which parents may start to encourage lying in certain situations, such as when they receive a present they already have or do not like. Fortunately, many positive traits are associated with this period of language development as well, such as increased communication related to conflict resolution, increased social competence and relationship building. The concomitant emergence of these skills will help parents when attempting to discuss this complicated topic with their little language learners. There are positive ways to talk to your toddler about lying. So, if we view the early appearance of lying as an important developmental milestone, rather than a morality issue, how can we best react to it? First, it is important to determine the function of the lie. Common functions include: to get something the child wants, to avoid embarrassment, to gain approval or attention, to remove the spotlight form themselves, to spare someone’s feelings, to avoid a consequence or conflict, or poor impulse control. Keeping the truth hidden or creating a “story” often makes the child feel better. Once we have determined the function of the lie, we can discuss it. Resist the impulse to ask, “why did you do that?” It is the first question parents go to, and unfortunately it does nothing to increase awareness or insight and adds the negative element of shame. Instead, stick to “what” and “how” questions to review what happened in a supportive and positive way. For example, you can ask what happened first, second, last. You can ask the child how they worked it out. You can discuss what the options were. You can talk about what the child can do differently next time. You can model what you would or would not have done in the situation. And lastly, postponing this kind of a discussion to a later time can allow for a more effective exchange and successful learning opportunity. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C .

articles.text: Piedmont Boy Scouts Joseph Haggerty and Seamus Meagher of Troop 1 were presented with the rank of Eagle at a National Court of Honor on May 29 in the gardens at 212 Bonita Avenue among a crowd of family, friends, and fellow scouters. They were the 217th and 218th Scouts from Troop 1 to attain Scouting’s highest honor. Begun in 1920, Troop 1 is the Scouting unit in Piedmont. Both Haggerty and Meagher began their scouting journey in elementary school. They celebrated their Arrow of Light Ceremony together in March 2014. pages.text: Wednesday, June 30, 2021 7 SUMMER THOUGHTS Does lying come naturally? By Katie Penguilly Can you remember catching your young child in a lie? For most of us, this experience strikes fear: am I raising a deceitful person? Is this the first step down a dangerous path of dishonesty? Actually, lying is a normal part of cognitive-linguistic development which typically occurs during the preschool years. Studies show that up to 80% of 4-yearolds lie. This milestone indicates that the child has learned that other people have their own and often differing opinions. It signifies that the child has learned that they can use words in a more abstract way than simply to express their needs and wants, namely that words can get someone to think something that is not actually true. The child now understands that what we say does not always correspond with what we are thinking and sometimes we hide what we are really thinking and feeling. To make matters worse, this is often the age at which parents may start to encourage lying in certain situations, such as when they receive a present they already have or do not like. Fortunately, many positive traits are associated with this period of language development as well, such as increased communication related to conflict resolution, increased social competence and relationship building. The concomitant emergence of these skills will help parents when attempting to discuss this complicated topic with their little language learners. There are positive ways to talk to your toddler about lying. So, if we view the early appearance of lying as an important developmental milestone, rather than a morality issue, how can we best react to it? First, it is important to determine the function of the lie. Common functions include: to get something the child wants, to avoid embarrassment, to gain approval or attention, to remove the spotlight form themselves, to spare someone’s feelings, to avoid a consequence or conflict, or poor impulse control. Keeping the truth hidden or creating a “story” often makes the child feel better. Once we have determined the function of the lie, we can discuss it. Resist the impulse to ask, “why did you do that?” It is the first question parents go to, and unfortunately it does nothing to increase awareness or insight and adds the negative element of shame. Instead, stick to “what” and “how” questions to review what happened in a supportive and positive way. For example, you can ask what happened first, second, last. You can ask the child how they worked it out. You can discuss what the options were. You can talk about what the child can do differently next time. You can model what you would or would not have done in the situation. And lastly, postponing this kind of a discussion to a later time can allow for a more effective exchange and successful learning opportunity. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C . articles.text: The journey to this point in our life has been a long, ever twisting, roller coaster ride. Throughout the three years students have spent at Piedmont Middle School, we have gone through a great calamity that has forced us from the physical world, to the online world for our learning. And today we have gathered, undeterred. Despite every curve ball, every hurdle, every crazy thing thrown at us through these times, we are able to stand here today, permanently united, teacher and student alike. And as we close off this chapter for students, and move onto the next one, we only have one way to go from here, forward. With this, a new horizon has taken shape. Where, for the most part, the clouds have cleared, and the sun shines bright. The road ahead of us, all of us, is windy, and warped, with no clear sense of direction. It’s filled with potholes and road bumps. But alas, we cannot take a single step back. As deranged as this new coming world ahead of us may be, we have nowhere to go but permanently forward. We must keep our heads high; our will’s shining; to hold the eternal flame of life with us, as we continue down the road. Now, I want to bring out a single term popularized by Salvador Allende of Chile that I feel is related to this speech: Venceremos. What does this mean? “Let Us Triumph.” For as we move along with the infinite march of time, that is all we can strive for. The triumph of yourself, your friends, your community as a whole, triumph in the face of adversity. And with that, I wish all students and faculty of Piedmont Middle School a happy graduation. Let us triumph.
articles.title: 8th grader gives rousing speech at PMS graduation

articles.text: School is out and summer is here. While kids are enjoying a well-deserved respite from “busy work,” it’s important to have a few summer activities that engage their senses and test their skills. Here is a great activity for elementary school-aged children, from kindergarten to 4th grade, that takes only minimal work by parents while still keeping them busy. Summer sensory station (ages 2 - 8) Sensory stations are easy to create and are tons of fun. They help develop vital skills in little ones, including fine motor skills, creativity, imagination and exploration. By adding items that encourage toddlers to stir, scoop, dig, and pour, you are providing opportunities to increase hand strength in your child. For older kids, about age 5, you can introduce items like tweezers, spoons, and funnels, tools that help them grasp patterns needed for handwriting and managing utensils. Sensory bins are also a quiet activity which allows children to calm down and play independently - the perfect “wind-down-before-nap time” activity. You can change your sensory bin however you’d like. First, grab a big plastic bin that will not leak. Then, choose your ‘base’ appropriately for your child’s age. Sand and water in a Choose an appropriate base for your bin. Water is a popular base for young, elementary aged children. Sensory bins are not just independent activities. Young kids will learn how to cooperate and take turns when playing together. shallow bin are perfect for toddler-aged kids. Don’t forget to add some food coloring or glitter in the water! For older kids, you can use aquarium rocks, twigs and leaves found outside, dry rice, pasta, or beans. Add in items like spoons, paper clips, tongs, mini spatulas, or any other tools children can use for play. Hiding dice, Scrabble pieces, or other number and letter shapes in the bin will provide children the opportunity to learn the alphabet, their numbers, and gain practice counting and spelling; talking with your child about the hidden items allows them to expand their vocabulary. articles.text: Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) is a coed youth-led organization that inspires teens to actively uplift the broader community through service events. It is the largest of the Venturing Crews with the Piedmont Scout Council with Approximately 150 members. Recent 8th grade graduates are now eligible to become members and start volunteering. A companion club, Piedmont Service Club, is for 6th-8th graders who can volunteer with their parents and develop connections with older teens in the Community Service Crew. In PSC members are able to choose how much time they can put in and when. “Events are optional and there are plenty to choose from”, said previous PSC co-president Bruno Banuelos. During the past year and the Covid quarantine, PCSC remained active and completed more hours of service than the previous year. It worked with Youth Spirit Artworks on their Tiny House Village for homeless youth and built three Tiny Houses, as well as helped construct the village itself and prepare it for the move-in. For 16 years members of PCSC have partnered with Rebuilding Together Oakland, an organization that repairs homes of low-income. It will be renovating the home of a woman with seven children and a 102-year-old mother. The crew will be patching and repainting the exterior of the home and installing new kitchen cabinets and flooring. PCSC will have building events on weekends through mid-July and will be looking for more volunteers. The Community Service Crew also has weekly cooking events St. Mary’s Center, College Presbyterian Church, and Harbor House Summer Camp. The crew also has nature events such as Sausal Creek clean-ups. Youth and parents interested in participating can learn more on the website www.pcservicecrew.org/new-member, or by contacting Crew Advisor Ken Li at ken.i.li@sbcglobal.net. Shelby Cavenaugh & Lauren Quick, PCSC co-VPs Administration, contributed to this article.

articles.text: The Post is publishing installments of The Best Books for Your Summer Reading List from the New York Times. Each list covers a handful of selections in genres such as Romance, Historical Fiction, Audio Books, and Thrillers. This assemblage includes Science Fiction, from a collection of short stories in translation, to a debut about a single consciousness in multiple bodies, to an Antarctic ghost story. The descriptions and reviews are edited for length. to do with the personalities of the individuals involved. Chaos on Catnet by Naomi Kritzer (Tor Teen, 292 pp.) Chaos introduces new characters and a dark mirror to Cheshire Cat, the friendly sentient artificial intelligence who loves pictures of cats and helping people make friends on the internet. This young-adult novel managed to be both a fantastic thriller and a phenomenally warm and kind bildungsroman. Kritzer’s author’s note at the end is well worth reading, both in its own right and as context for the book’s truncation. “One of the interesting things about near-future science fiction is that sometimes you catch up to the future while you’re still writing it,” she says, before addressing the reality of revising a book in the Twin Cities while Minneapolis was on fire during mass protests and a pandemic. Sorrowland by Rivers Solomon (MCD/Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 355 pp.) Sorrowland is a tremendous, riveting work, sinking long, deep roots into the nightmare soil of American history in order to grow and feed something new. It is concerned with the haunting weight of history and its effects on queer Black bodies; it reckons, through a fantastical lens, with inherited traumas and the consolations and difficulties of building community. Sorrowland’s patient, roiling intensity is as defiant and devastating as its heroine. Unity by Elly Bangs (Tachyon, 289 pp.) Unity f lings us hundreds of years into a future that has weathered multiple apocalypses and is on the brink of an extinction-level war between political powers that operate from metropolises beneath the much-warmed Pacific. Danae and her lover, Naoto, decide to risk heading for the blasted, inhospitable remnants of Arizona in search of the power and absolution of her whole, multiplied self. “Unity” is an astonishing debut, twisty and startling, demonstrating both the disciplined development of a long-gestated project and the raw, dynamic flashes of an author’s early work. Folklorn by Angela Mi Young Hur was published earlier this year. Rivers Solomon’s Sorrowland is a tremendous, riveting work. I’m Waiting for You: And Other Stories by Elizabeth Lippman (Harper Voyager, 316 pp.) A collection of four stories (two pairs of linked stories) translated from the Korean by Sophie Bowman and Sung Ryu. In the opening story a groom and a bride’s struggle to meet each other at the correct time and place in order to marry, despite the vagaries of interstellar travel and relativity. The iterations take place in a cosmic Dark Realm that contains our universe, and is populated by entities that regard Earth as a school in which to experience embodiment. This is a book as much about the process of translation as it is about science fiction, Buddhism and how to live among people. articles.text: Folklorn by Angela Mi Young Hur (Erewhon Books, 408 pp.) In many way Folklorn is also about translation: translation as physical movement, from Korea to the United States to Sweden to Antarctica; secret knowledge translated across languages and time; and translation as interpretation across genres, from folk tales and family history to experimental physics and poetry. Elsa is determined to choose science over superstition, but while researching neutrinos – so-called ghost particles – in Antarctica, she succumbs to an old hallucination of ringing bells and a lovely, mysterious woman with red ribbons trailing from her long black braid. Folklorn loops in and out of itself like a ghost’s red-ribboned braids, like a woman’s voice harmonizing with its own echoes. It’s beautiful and hard and hungry, full of sharp, painful observations, slicing clichés open like prickly pears and devouring their hearts. articles.title: SCIENCE FICTION

pages.text: Wednesday, June 30, 2021 9 New York Times Summer Reading Lists New Science Fiction and Fantasy – a sense of belonging The Post is publishing installments of The Best Books for Your Summer Reading List from the New York Times. Each list covers a handful of selections in genres such as Romance, Historical Fiction, Audio Books, and Thrillers. This assemblage includes Science Fiction, from a collection of short stories in translation, to a debut about a single consciousness in multiple bodies, to an Antarctic ghost story. The descriptions and reviews are edited for length. SCIENCE FICTION Folklorn by Angela Mi Young Hur (Erewhon Books, 408 pp.) In many way Folklorn is also about translation: translation as physical movement, from Korea to the United States to Sweden to Antarctica; secret knowledge translated across languages and time; and translation as interpretation across genres, from folk tales and family history to experimental physics and poetry. Elsa is determined to choose science over superstition, but while researching neutrinos – so-called ghost particles – in Antarctica, she succumbs to an old hallucination of ringing bells and a lovely, mysterious woman with red ribbons trailing from her long black braid. Folklorn loops in and out of itself like a ghost’s red-ribboned braids, like a woman’s voice harmonizing with its own echoes. It’s beautiful and hard and hungry, full of sharp, painful observations, slicing clichés open like prickly pears and devouring their hearts. We are Satellites by Sarah Pinsker (Berkley, 381 pp.) Explores the far-reaching social implications of a new technology while staying deeply rooted in the day-to-day dynamics of a single family. In the novel, students show up at school with small blue lights embedded in their temples; they’ve chosen to have a productivity-boosting device called a Pilot installed in their brains, allowing them to achieve a state “as close to actual multitasking as a person can currently get.” The faultlines along which the family fractures have nothing to do with the presence or absence of shared DNA, and everything to do with the personalities of the individuals involved. Chaos on Catnet by Naomi Kritzer (Tor Teen, 292 pp.) Chaos introduces new characters and a dark mirror to Cheshire Cat, the friendly sentient artificial intelligence who loves pictures of cats and helping people make friends on the internet. This young-adult novel managed to be both a fantastic thriller and a phenomenally warm and kind bildungsroman. Kritzer’s author’s note at the end is well worth reading, both in its own right and as context for the book’s truncation. “One of the interesting things about near-future science fiction is that sometimes you catch up to the future while you’re still writing it,” she says, before addressing the reality of revising a book in the Twin Cities while Minneapolis was on fire during mass protests and a pandemic. Sorrowland by Rivers Solomon (MCD/Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 355 pp.) Sorrowland is a tremendous, riveting work, sinking long, deep roots into the nightmare soil of American history in order to grow and feed something new. It is concerned with the haunting weight of history and its effects on queer Black bodies; it reckons, through a fantastical lens, with inherited traumas and the consolations and difficulties of building community. Sorrowland’s patient, roiling intensity is as defiant and devastating as its heroine. Unity by Elly Bangs (Tachyon, 289 pp.) Unity f lings us hundreds of years into a future that has weathered multiple apocalypses and is on the brink of an extinction-level war between political powers that operate from metropolises beneath the much-warmed Pacific. Danae and her lover, Naoto, decide to risk heading for the blasted, inhospitable remnants of Arizona in search of the power and absolution of her whole, multiplied self. “Unity” is an astonishing debut, twisty and startling, demonstrating both the disciplined development of a long-gestated project and the raw, dynamic flashes of an author’s early work. Folklorn by Angela Mi Young Hur was published earlier this year. Rivers Solomon’s Sorrowland is a tremendous, riveting work. I’m Waiting for You: And Other Stories by Elizabeth Lippman (Harper Voyager, 316 pp.) A collection of four stories (two pairs of linked stories) translated from the Korean by Sophie Bowman and Sung Ryu. In the opening story a groom and a bride’s struggle to meet each other at the correct time and place in order to marry, despite the vagaries of interstellar travel and relativity. The iterations take place in a cosmic Dark Realm that contains our universe, and is populated by entities that regard Earth as a school in which to experience embodiment. This is a book as much about the process of translation as it is about science fiction, Buddhism and how to live among people. The lovers’ stories are as powerful and clear as the middle stories are difficult and woolly. ADVERTISE IN THE POST You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. 10 Wednesday, June 30, 2021 Postcards from Camp Postcards from Camp Letters to home by kids at Camp Augusta Throughout the summer the Post will print a sampling of letters written by kids attending Camp Augusta, Piedmont’s residential camp at Lake Vera outside Nevada City in the Sierra foothills. Founded in 1931, the camp remains a vital part of the life of hundreds of children each summer. For a local view of the summer ritual, residents will see large groups of families waiting each weekend for the arrival of busses with kids returning from camp, and a fresh group ready to head to Camp Augusta for one or two weeks of pure fun. articles.text: Coach Bryan Gardere’s 2021 girls’ basketball team earned two more post-season honors after finishing 15-3 overall. The San Jose Mercury News recently named senior Kai Johnson and sophomore Trinity Zamora to its “Fab 25” players from last season. Darren Sabedra and Evan Webeck of the Mercury News credited Johnson for helping Piedmont dispatch Bishop O’Dowd for the second time in three years, a 66-55 victory on June 4. They also noted that Zamora is drawing “national recruiting interest” as a sophomore, as often reiterated by Gardere. “Bound for Weber State after averaging 22 points, 12 rebounds and four steals a game for Piedmont. Knocked off Bishop O’Dowd for the second time in three years in her final high school game,” the news article described Johnson. “Drawing national recruiting interest from the top programs in the country. Averaged 23 points, 18 rebounds and seven assists per game for 15-2 Piedmont,” noted the Mercury News about Zamora. Johnson was named by the Post as its Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year in 2021, and Zamora was named as its SophStaff Photos Kai Johnson, who recently graduated from Piedmont, will join Weber State’s basketball program this fall. omore of the Year. She was also named Freshman of the Year in 2020. Recently, Johnson was named as the school’s Outstanding Female Athlete at the Senior Awards ceremony. Johnson was a four-year varsity starter from 2017-2021 and a team captain for the past two seasons. She was the only senior on this year’s roster and was a major part of a strong four-year run for the girls’ basketball program at Piedmont, finishing with records of 23-7 in 2017/2018, 20-11 in 2018/2019, 21-7 in 2019/2020, and 15-3 here in 2021. “We’re going to miss Kai. She’s been amazing, not just as Trinity Zamora was the Post’s Sophomore of the Year. She will be a major contributor to Piedmont’s basketball team heading into her junior year. a player but as a teammate,” said Gardere. She’s had 1,000 points, 700 rebounds and all the accolades. She always stayed positive. When we were not doing well, she always responded with. ‘All right, ladies, let’s pick it up, We’re okay!’ She was always trying to build up her teammates.” Zamora is no longer a secret in the Bay Area basketball world and has drawn some interest from several Division 1 schools. She is a double-double machine for the Highlanders, logging seven consecutive double figures in wins over St. Joseph, Hayward, Cal High, Alameda, San Leandro, San Marin, and Marin Catholic. In a 73-67 win over Oakland Tech on May 22, she pulled down 22 rebounds, the most for PHS since Kelea Pickeral-Dennis had 38 in 2015. Zamora already does it all for Piedmont High as a shooter, finisher at the rim, rebounder on both ends of the floor, and a marquee defender. She will inherit john’s role as team leader next year. “The talent we have is a correlation of how hard Trinity works. She’s poised to have a big summer, and as a junior [next season], I’m expecting a lot of college coaches watching our open gyms. She’s that type of player she is. The word is out,” said Gardere. articles.text: Photos courtesy of ATPTour.com Mackie McDonald reached the first round of Wimbledon after winning three rounds in the qualifiers but lost in the opening round to Karen Khachanov in four sets. Former Piedmont resident Mackie McDonald suffered a first-round loss at the Wimbledon Championships on Monday, June 28, falling in four sets to No. 25 seeded Karen Khachanov of Russia, 3-6, 6-3, 6-4, 7-6 (7-3). McDonald, No. 108, entered the first round as the heavy underdog to the 6-foot, 6-inch Khachanov, who is ranked No. 29 in the world. To reach the first round, McDonald entered as the No. 2 seeded player for the qualifiers at Wimbledon Park after beating Belgium’s Kimmer Coppejans 6-7 (7-5), 7-5, 6-2 on June 22, Ukraine’s Illya Marchenko 6-1, 3-6, 6-4 on June 23, and beating his former UCLA teammate, Maxime Cressy (ranked 152) in a five-set thunderous comeback on June 24, 3-6, 4-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4. The loss to Khachanov, in the first round marked his third consecutive loss to a Top-25 opponent at a Grand Slam tournament since defeating Borna Coric in the Australian Open in February, Coric was ranked No. 24 when McDonald beat him 6-4, 6-2, 4-6, 6-4. Against Khachanov, McDonald opened strongly with a 6-3 victory in the first set but struggled to close out winnable games throughout, converting just three of 17 break point opportunities. In the three wins leading up to his match with Khachanov, McDonald was able to successfully hit his first serves to over 70 percent success rates. However, he had 61 percent of his first attempts in against the Russian. 5-Set win vs. Cressy The match with Cressy was UCLA teammates’ first match on the ATP tour. It featured Mackie rallying back from down two sets after losing 6-3, 6-4 to open before closing out with wins of 6-3, 6-4, 6-4, taking advantage of Cressy’s nine double faults while converting 71 percent of his first serves.
articles.title: Mackie McDonald battles to first-round of Wimbledon

pages.text: Wednesday, June 30, 2021 13 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 14th year in the Post. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. Luke Barrett, a 2020 Piedmont grad, recently completed his freshman year at St. Mary’s College in Moraga. LUKE BARRETT Basketball My goals for the summer are to build lower body and core strength. How are you measuring your development? I am tracking my weight, quickness, and overall strength in each workout. For shooting drills, our numbers are recorded so I can track progress and consistency. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working with my coaches at Saint Mary’s and with the strength and conditioning staff. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? I’ve gained 20 pounds in muscle over a few months’ time and feel much, much stronger. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? Work on your game and body outside of Middle School and High School. There is always so much you can do to improve; just going to practices is not enough. If you build basic skills, strength, and good habits from a young age, you won’t have to catch up later and you will be ahead of most of your peers. Piedmont High Class of 2020 St. Mary’s College Class of 2024 Moraga, CA Luke Barrett, Class of 2020, originally declared for Pitzer College before transferring to Saint Mary’s College, a Div. 1 program in Moraga. He was named Athlete of the Year by the Piedmont Post last year after leading Piedmont High to the Div. 4 North Coast Section Championship and scoring more than 1,000 points in his career. He played in one game for the Gaels against South Dakota State on November 27. Barrett etched his name into Piedmont High history as a junior in the 2018-2019 season when the team reached the North Coast Section Semifinals for the first time and then advanced to Regional Semifinals in the State Championships. He scored 24 points in the NCS Finals, a 77-67 victory over No. 3 St. Mary’s, including 17 points in the second half and two thunderous blocks in the final minutes of the game. Barrett was named to the AllBay Area Preps third team by the San Jose Mercury News. What is your workout program this summer? I am lifting three times a week and conditioning twice per week, in addition to daily basketball workouts. What are your fitness goals for this summer? We then traveled to the Arctic What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? It is important to always stay fit, even when you are exhausted from eight hours of duty. What is your workout program this summer? I’m doing a workout plan with my brother, Owen, where we try to work out each of the major groups (legs, push, and pull) a few times a week. I’ll be on a new workout plan when I get to school. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My main goal for the summer is just to get stronger for when I get to school. That’s been a goal of mine for a while, to get stronger. How are you measuring your development? I can measure my development by weighing myself and seeing how much I’ve grown. Another way is just monitoring how my body is feeling. Usually, I can notice that I’ve gotten stronger in certain muscle groups when I’m pitching. For example, because legs are so important for pitching, if I feel really strong and stable through my legs when I’m on the mound. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am primarily training with my bother before traveling to school, which will have a workout structured by its staff. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I’ve recently been able to reach my highest pitching velocity. The workouts and training that I’ve done have definitely helped me achieve that goal, so it’s nice to see results. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? My biggest piece of advice for younger athletes is: learn to be disciplined. It’s not always easy to stay motivated, so it’s really important to be able to set goals for yourself and focus on working toward achieving them. articles.text: The 108th edition of the Tour de France is underway with Dutchman Mathieu van der Poel leading the general classification standings with an eight second advantage over Julian Alaphilippe of France through Stage 4. This year’s Grand Tour started at Brest in northeast France on June 26, the first day of a 3,417-kilometer route ending at the Avenue des Champs-Élysées on July 18. The Grand Départ from Brest The Netherlands’ Mathieu van der Poel holds the Yellow Jersey through Stage 4. Four-time Tour de France champion Chris Froome was caught up in the Stage 1 crash. France’s Julian Alaphilippe won Stage 1 but is second in the general classification. A detailed list and description of the 21 Stages of the race.

articles.text: started in a big way, but not for reasons typically expected. The race went viral during Stage 1 when a woman held out a sign as a greeting for her grandparents. It read “ALLEZ OPIOMI!” But standing too far onto the course with her back turned to the approaching peloton, she obstructed German cyclist Tony Martin, who collided with the fan and set off a domino effect of crashing riders. A total of 21 riders were caught in the crash, including four-time champion winner Chris The Grand Depart. Stage 1 of the Tour d’France made headlines for all the wrong reasons. During the pandemic, we went up high peaks to cover over 170 miles of trails, some more strenuous than others. In this week’s issue, we highlight two short trails that have been in the news: Oakland’s Bridgeview Trail with its hand-crafted Trolls, and Big Sur’s recently re-opened Pfeiffer Falls Trail after a 13-year closure. The Bridgeview Trail has a collection of over 20 “Trolls” on the 0.7 mile out-and-back trail. Pictured is Bebe, one of the original trolls. “Arthur” sits underneath some brush. “The Braided Maiden” greets you as you walk along a ravine above the Montclair Golf Course. A map of the Bridgeview Trolls Trail. Bridgeview Trail A 1.4 mile round trip hike in the Oakland Hills provides whimsical thrills for kids, dog walkers, and those young at heart with its collection of hand-crafted rustic trolls hiding along the trail for visitors to find. The trend unofficially began in fall of 2020 and grew in popularity during the pandemic. Located with trailheads on Bridgeview Drive or Monterey Boulevard near the Montclair Golf Course, the walk is great for all ages. You will see more than 20 trolls, some more elaborate than others. There are also some rope swings. You’ll pass by the Montclair Golf Course driving range about midway through the hike, while the trail leads down four switchback turns heading to Sausal Creek. Look for two more trolls in the area. The walk will provide less than 200 feet of elevation gain, making it perfect for seniors and families with children. Due to the trolls and swings expect to see plenty of people. Hiking on a Monday at 10 a.m., we saw 34 hikers on the brief trek. See our collection of photos from our favorite trolls found on the Bridgeview Trail. Follow The Bridgeview Trolls updates on social media; Facebook: The Bridgeview Trolls. Instagram: @Bridgeviewtrolls. Pfeiffer Falls Trail The conservation group Save The Redwoods League recently announced the completion of a $2 million renovation of Pfeiffer Staff Photos “Frank and Filbert” sit in the ivy. They are two original Bridgeview Trail Trolls. “Quincy” dangles on a wire above a small creek. Falls Trail in Big Sur, including a 70-foot pedestrian bridge above Redwood Creek ravine. The trail was closed in 2008 due to the Basin Complex Fire which burned 162,818 acres including the bridges, railings, steps, signs, and retaining walls of the Pfeiffer Falls Trail. A 1.5 mile hike, the trail leads under redwoods and over a gorge to a 60-foot tall waterfall, Pfeiffer Falls. The rail has been reopened after a 13-year closure to one of the park’s most popular hikes. To find this trail, punch in “Pfeiffer Falls Trailhead” to your GPS device. Save The Redwoods League announced that the popular Pfeiffer Falls Trail has re-opened after a 13-year closure. Pictured is the newly renovated 70-foot pedestrian bridge. The Pfeiffer Falls Trail underwent a $2 million renovation after being damaged in the Basin Complex Fire in 2008.

articles.text: Diego Rivera’s colossal mural, “Pan American Unity”, was moved from City College (pictured) to SFMOMA, where it was officially unveiled on June 28. On June 17, Diego Rivera’s colossal fresco, “Pan American Unity”, was carefully moved from San Francisco’s City College to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. The priceless 4,000-pound series of panels, created in 1940, is arguably one of San Francisco’s greatest art pieces of the 20th century. Rivera’s mural was the centerpiece of the Art in Action exhibit, which featured different artists engaged in creating art pieces while the public watched. The fresco on plaster is 670 by 2,260 centimeters and was created on 10 steel-framed panels bolted together. The entire mural weighs nearly 21 tons. It was designed to be portable and was moved to the college campus from Treasure Island after the World Exposition ended. It is the largest of the artists’ works and completely spanned the narrow lobby of the college’s theater, which is named for the artist. A four-year, multimillion dollar undertaking resulted in its careful removal and transport across the city to SF MOMA, where it officially went on display on June 28. “Diego was building a metamorphic bridge between the Mexican culture and the tech culture of the United States,” said Will Maynez, the former physics lab manager at City College. Maynez became a de facto guardian of the piece and “long dreamed of finding a way to allow more people to experience it.” He has spent 25 years researching and promoting “Pan American Unity.” Neal Benezra, SFMOMA Director, said, “This is one of the most ambitious things the museum has ever done — to move something this large, this fragile, and this important.” “We’re living in a time of tremendous resurgent nationalism around the world, and this is an anti-nationalist way of looking at things,” Benezra told The New York Times.
articles.title: Diego Rivera’s giant “Pan American Unity” mural unveiled at SFMOMA

articles.text: SF Playhouse’s Hold These Truths is being performed live at San Francisco Playhouse through July 3. This is the last chance to catch San Francisco Playhouse’s production of Hold These Truths in person through Saturday, July 3. Directed by Jeanne Sakata and Jeffrey Lo, “Hold These Truths” is based on the true story of Japanese American Gordon Hirabyashi, whose defiance of President Roosevelt’s Executive Order authorizing the incarceration of thousands of Japanese Americans, led him into a 50-year journey of advocacy. The play was inspired by many hours of interviews conducted by Sakata with Hirabayashi, as well as anecdotes and primary sources from his life. The New York Times called the play a “gripping story about a shameful chapter of our country’s history,” in its re-telling of the American internment order of 1942. This is the first on-stage play presented by San Francisco Playhouse since COVID-19 prohibited live entertainment in March 2020. All COVID guidelines and protocols will be enforced. The play will also stream on-demand starting July 4. To obtain tickets, visit: https:// w w w.sf playhouse.org /sf ph / upcoming-plays/. articles.text: Classical music station KDFC will launch a new, hour-long opera broadcast the first Sunday of every month at 8 p.m. Entitled “The Opera Hour,” the broadcast is created and hosted by KDFC’s President Bill Lueth and San Francisco Opera’s General Director Matthew Shilvock. “The Opera Hour” includes opera’s most “intriguing performances” curated by Shilvock. Each month, Shilvock and Lueth share new opera recordings they’re enjoying and some of their favorite singers and performances of the past. The radio show will also highlight great opera singing being performed locally and will dig into the archives of San Francisco Opera for stellar events recorded live at the War Memorial Opera House. “Opera has some of the most beautiful and dramatic moments General Director of San Francisco Opera Matthew Shilvock in all of classical music. Matthew and I want to share this music with a larger audience and invite more people to discover what makes opera so wonderful,” Leuth said. This Independence Day, Sunday, July 4, tune in at 8 p.m. on 90.3 FM for a discussion and slew of performances. articles.text: St. Lawrence String Quartet (Geoff Nuttall, violin, Owen Dalby, violin, Lesley Robertson, viola, and Christopher Costanza, cello) will highlight the Cabrillo Festival this summer. The Cabrillo Festival of Contemporary Music, America’s longest-running festival of new orchestral music and located in Santa Cruz, returns this summer with an all-virtual season over two weekends. Festival highlights include world premieres by composers Gabriela Lena Frank, Sean Shepherd, and Jake Heggie. The festival’s virtual season is completely free to the public and features dance, photography, videography, animation, and other art forms. Guest artists include the St. Lawrence String Quartet, mezzo-soprano Sasha Cooke, violinist Benjamin Beilman. This year, the award-winning Cabrillo Festival Orchestra will be led Cristian Macelaru. The virtual festival will take place over two weekends in the summer, July 31 and August 1, and August 7 and 8. Visit https://cabrillomusic.org/ to learn more about how to stream performances.
articles.title: Cabrillo Festival returns virtually July 31 to August 8

articles.text: Festival Opera’s 2021 season will continue at Piedmont Center for the Arts with a live-audience event on Sunday afternoon, July 11. “Un raggio di speme,” (“A Ray of Hope”) will be performed by Syrian-American coloratura soprano Lila Khazoum with celebrated pianist Alexander Katsman. The collection of songs is a celebration of the beauty of hope, even as it relates to loss and longing – a timely performance as we begin to gather again. The program also features virtuoso arias by Antonio Vivaldi, the tender storytelling in Sei ariette by Vincenzo Bellini, as well as the songs of George Bizet, Reynaldo Hahn, and Henri Duparc. This special event is the first concert presented at Piedmont Center for the Arts with a live audience since the onset of the COVID pandemic in March 2020. “I am thrilled by the opportunity to highlight this exciting new voice in the opera world with a live performance, and that we are making this performance available online to our friends around the globe,” said Festival Opera General Director, Zachary Gordin said. “Festival Opera maintains our commitment to seeking out and nurturing exceptionally talented artists and highlighting diverse voices. I look forward to this event with great excitement, and hope that you’ll join us either in person, or in the digital concert space.” The concert will begin at 5 p.m. Following the concert, a video interview with Khazoum and Gordin will be hosted on the organization’s YouTube channel. All ticket buyers will automatically receive a link to this companion offering. Soprano Lila Khazoum will appear at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on July 11. To purchase tickets, visit: https://www.festivalopera.org/ artist-recital-series
articles.title: Festival Opera comes to Piedmont Center for the Arts July 11

articles.text: As part of Cal Performances “Illuminations - Music and the Mind” programming, legendary soprano singer Renee Fleming presents a discussion and performance that is available to stream through July 28. Fleming performs with guest musicians and UC Berkeley Professor of Neuroscience Ehud Isacoff, as part of her own ongoing collaboration with educators and researchers. Fleming has explored the relationship between music and human psychology in her most recent work, and recently launched a live-streamed series of conversations and podcasts with leaders and practitioners working at the intersection of music, neuroscience, and healthcare. During next Thursday’s Soprano Renee Fleming performance, Fleming will offer insights into music’s potential for healing the mind, as well as perform illuminating selections from her repertoire with piano. Fleming is well-known for her performances in opera, concerts, recordings, theatre, and film around the world. Her signature roles include Countess Almaviva in Mozart’s Le nozze di Figaro, Desdemona in Verdi’s Otello, Violetta in Verdi’s La traviata, the title role in Dvorak’s Rusalka, and the title role in Massenet’s Manon. She is a recipient of the National Medal of Arts, and has been nominated for 17 Grammy awards throughout the span of her lengthy career. Beyond opera, she has recorded songs in jazz, musical theatre and independent rock. The stream is archived as part of Cal Performances “Performances at Home” series, which was created in response to the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent venue closures. The video is available on demand until July 28. Visit https://secure.calperformances.org/15181/15820 for streaming information.
articles.title: Cal Performances features soprano Renee Fleming

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Capital punishment, when combined with a deeply flawed system of justice that mirrors an entrenched racism toward those charged with a crime, is not only unsettling but can be forever irretrievable. Therein is the essence and power of Just Mercy, a devastatingly good film that is understated while offering exceptional portrayals. The film is set in Alabama. The year is 1989. Walter McMillan (Jamie Foxx) is a black man on death row for a murder he could not possibly have committed. His conviction, as we learn, was based on the extorted testimony of a man (Tim Blake Nelson) who was known to be profoundly unreliable. And yet, as the record shows, there was no other physical evidence or witnesses produced by the prosecution that place McMillan at the scene. As we learn, there were multiple alibi witnesses who were ignored by the police and the D.A. And still McMillan was found guilty and sentenced by a judge who overturned the jury’s decision of life in prison and sentenced him to death by electrocution. When McMillan meets newly minted Harvard lawyer Bryan Stevenson (Michael B. Jordan), he has been on death row for six years and has exhausted countless avenues of appeal. He has lost all hope and concluded that he will die for a murder he did not commit. He initially rejects Stevenson’s offer of help. Undeterred, Stevenson begins to peel the evidentiary onion and is astonished to find that the state went ahead with what seems a prima facie case of an innocent man falsely accused, choosing instead to prosecute. Nevertheless, regardless of where Stevenson turns, he is met with a malevolent resistance by both the sheriff’s department and the local prosecutor. It’s at this point that Just Mercy becomes a legal procedural and a courtroom drama as Stevenson explores all alternatives open to him in an attempt to have all charges dropped, or, in the alternative, secure a new trial for McMillan. It is a harrowing process for Stevenson. He, like McMillan, is a black man who feels increasingly vulnerable and even threatened with harm. In one scene he is pulled over in the dead of night by the local police, a gun placed to the back of his head. He asks repeatedly why he was stopped and is braced, legs wide apart, against his car. The only words offered by the police are when he is told to get out of the car and called “boy” with a dripping malignancy. And yet both Stevenson and McMillan both refuse to abandon their belief that ultimately we are a nation of laws and that justice can prevail. The audience is not so certain. Just Mercy. Directed by Destin Daniel Cretton. Starring Michael B. Jordan, Jamie Foxx, Brie Larson. 2 hrs., 16 min. Rated PG-13. Jamie Foxx plays Walter McMillian in Just Mercy.

By Chris Honoré Call it a staple of Hollywood screenwriting: girl meets damaged boy. She is moved to reach out and care for him, perhaps rescue him in some fashion. Ditto for boy meets damaged girl. Incrementally and inextricably, both scenarios become matters of the heart and love is soon entangled with the impulse to help. As stories go, it’s instantly familiar but also ripe with new and interesting permutations. Adam, written and directed by Max Mayer, is such a narrative. Beth (Rose Byrne), twenty-something, an aspiring writer of children’s books, having just escaped a disastrous love affair, moves into an Upper West Side brownstone. Living in the building is Adam (Hugh Dancy), an electrical engineer who designs toys and is also consumed with origins of the universe. When they first meet, in the laundry room, it is inescapable that Adam’s affect and responses are different. He doesn’t respond to the normal cues of conversation. Beth is intrigued for Adam is also bright and direct and sincere. What she soon learns is that his quirkiness is caused by Aspergers Syndrome, a form of high functioning autism. Though she comes to understand how Adam’s Aspergers presents itself, she also recognizes a lovely human being. In slow motion she falls in love with him and he with her. Beth also comes to understand that an aspect of the syndrome (at least in Adam’s case) is an inability to feel empathy, or make straightforward contact, such as looking her in the eyes. Adam hears what others say, but he is unable to feel the subtext behind the words or detect humor or irony. What is said, he takes at face value, even if a sentence ends with a question mark. Still, Beth moves forward, slowly involving Adam in her life, introducing him to her parents and to her friends. It’s not easy for her or for Adam. Adam is a sweet movie, wonderfully acted, and, to Mayer’s credit, explores both characters. Clearly, it was tempting to make this Adam’s story; Mayer resisted. Hence, Beth’s ambivalence and personal qualities are nicely balanced with Adam’s struggles. As well, there’s a tangential story concerning Beth’s affluent parents (Amy Irving and Peter Gallagher): her father is on trial for embezzlement, the family uncertain if he will go to prison. Adam is a small nugget when compared to the decidedly shallow fare that is offered up during the summer. Mayer takes a decidedly obscure condition and treats it with insight and genuine humanity and creates a touching film that’s worth seeing. Adam, Starring Hugh Dancy, Rose Byrne, Frankie Felson, Peter Gallagher and Amy Irving. Directed by Max Mayer. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG-13. Jamie Foxx plays Walter McMillian in Just Mercy. articles.text: Rose Byrn plays Beatrix Potter in Peter Rabbit. Peter Rabbit is loosely based on the iconic book by Beatrix Potter. This incarnation is a fast-paced, frenetic comedy starring, Peter (James Corden), dressed in his familiar blue coat. Always mischievous, he resides on a bucolic farm in the English countryside. He lives a relatively carefree life along with his siblings Flopsy (Margot Robbie), Mopsy (Elizabeth Debicki), and Cotton-tail (Daisey Ridley). This cohort also includes cousin Benjamin Bunny (Colin Moody) and is looked after by the kindly painter, Bea (Rose Byrn). Meanwhile the denizens of the warren clash with farmer McGregor (Sam Neil) whenever they raid his vegetable garden. But in one veggie raid, with Mr. McGregor in hot pursuit, he unexpectedly collapses and fails to get up. Now in the absence of old Mr. McG, the clan discovers it has the run of the farm, all happily gorging on rows and rows of vegetables. That is until Mr. McGregor’s great-nephew, Thomas (Domhnall Gleeson), moves from London to take over the farm, rehab the aging cottage, all in preparation for a quick sale. Feeling out of his element, he plans a quick return to the city and there opens a toy store. But Peter, of course, has other plans and so he and his rabbit tribe set out to obstruct Thomas at every turn, intending to sabotage this city slicker’s efforts. Unexpectedly, for Peter and crew, Thomas doesn’t retreat but decides that he’s all-in and the battle is joined, despite the reality that he doesn’t know a rake from a hoe. And thus begins the rabbit vs. city boy scrum over the rights to feed on the veggie garden whenever they please. As it turns out it was old man McGregor who had captured Peter’s father and turned him into a stew. So with a score to settle, and a carrot in hand, Peter, becomes a committed rebel, leaning into battle against another McGregor. Meanwhile, Thomas confides in Bea, telling her he has a “rabbit problem.” Bea in contrast is on the side of the rabbits insisting they are harmless and just part of the local color. No matter their viewpoints, Thomas does find Bea to be very charming. And so the story goes, riotous at times, and rarely slowing down. Kids will definitely be entertained. Peter Rabbit. Directed by Will Glick. Using live action and CGI with voices/performances by James Corden, Faysai Bazzi,Rose Byrn and Doomhnall Gleeson. 1 hr., 35 min. Rated PG. articles.text: Luca, the 24th animated feature from Pixar, opened absent a wide theater release, and is now streaming on Disney+. It is a coming-of-age story set in the Italian seaside village of Portorosso, on the sun-washed Riviera, a place of dreamy blues, soft oranges, and inviting yellows. The time is somewhere between the 50s and 60s. At the center of the tale is Luca Paguro (Jacob Tremblay), a restless tween-teen who is a sea monster. He lives with his extended sea monster family in an underwater world. There’s Daniela, his mom (Maya Rudolph); Lorenzo Paguro, his dad (Jim Gaffigan); Grandma Paguro (Sandy Martin); and Uncle Ugo (Sacha Baron Cohen). Plus Luca’s new best friend, also a sea monster, Alberto Scorfario (Jack Dylan Grazer). The interesting twist is that when Luca and Alberto venture on shore they turn into regular boys who look like everyone else. And it’s on land where they discover that though they were warned by their families that the town of Portorosso could be dangerous, the boys find it filled with interesting, eye-widening possibilities. The two set off on an irresistible adventure. They meet a cast of interesting characters to include a feisty girl, Giulia Marcovaldo (Emma Berman), and her good-hearted fisherman/cook father, Massimo Marcovaldo (Marco Barricelli). They enter an annual Vespa race, take countless Vespa rides around town, meet and confront the previous winner of the Vespa race medal, the town bully, Saverio Raimondo (Ercole Visconti). Along the way, they learn the meaning of true friendship. The animation is delightful, the palette of detail and colors extraordinary. And the filmmakers acknowledge the influence of the iconic Japanese Studio Ghibli and the creative genius of animator and storyteller Hayao Miyazaki. Luca is a wonderful, imaginative story that should engage a wide audience of kids who will find Luca, both the sea monster and the boy, compelling.
articles.title: Luca, Pixar’s new animation with sea monsters

articles.text: Violinist Mischa Elman There are many cynical pundits these days. That type of thinking isn’t new. More than 100 years ago Ambrose Bierce and his “Devil’s Dictionary” reigned supreme. He observed that the phonograph restores life to dead noises. Do not believe him. There is more to life than negativity. Some years ago, I was walking along Haight Street in San Francisco. A perfume shop had its door open, and I could hear some very beautiful violin music from within. As soon as I went in, the owner said to me, “The violinist is my grandfather, Mischa Elman.” Stream of consciousness overwhelmed me. I had heard Mischa Elman play his last concert in Los Angeles. The memories remained as vivid as the concert. And now I was standing with the granddaughter of one of the greatest musicians of all time. Elman was the first great Jewish violinist to emerge from the pale of settlement in Czarist Russia. As such, he single-handedly

articles.text: The Bookmark Bookstore, operated by the nonprofit Friends of the Oakland Public Library, launched new hours for in-store browsing on June 16. Located in Old Oakland at 721 Washington Street, The Bookmark is open from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Wednesday through Sunday. Providing a safe environment for everyone (customers and the mostly volunteer staff) is the Bookmark’s top priority. The store will follow these guidelines: • Masks are required for entry into the store. • Use of hand sanitizer is required upon entering the store. • Capacity will be managed to maintain distance of 6 feet from others. To prepare for reopening, the store manager and volunteer staff have received, sorted, priced and shelved thousands of donated books, CDs, DVDs, and puzzles. All inventory is donated by the public (no library discards). The Bookmark continues to accept donations of books. Guidelines for materials accepted are posted on the website at www. fopl.org/the-bookmark. Members of the Friends of the Oakland Public Library always receive a 20% discount on their in-store purchases. Memberships are $25 per year ($15 for full-time students and seniors 65 or over). Learn more about membership at www.fopl.org/get-involved. Shopping online supports the Friends The Friends joined Bookshop, an online bookstore formed to support independent bookstores, such as the Bookmark. Visit https://bookshop.org/shop/theBookmarkBookstore where you can browse booklists curated by the Friends with suggestions from Oakland librarians, then shop for new books, puzzles, notecards and more. Bookshop digital gift cards make great gifts. And your gift keeps giving: The Friends receives 25- 30% of each sale. All purchases support the Oakland Public Library.

The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet Even though his violin professor, Leopold Auer, was highly regarded in Russia, it was Elman who changed the course of violin playing. The youthful violinist’s tone was likened to the eruption of a volcano. It was absolutely lascivious. There is more to life All the other young violinists in the class tried to emulate that than negativity sound, something that caused Jewish families to alter their thinking. Music became the passport out of oppression. But Elman possessed much more than musical talent. He had a great work ethic and practiced the violin every day of his lifeexcept on Yom Kippur. He was a well-spoken linguist in at least four languages. In addition, he was a perfect gentleman in every respect. Strangely, despite his great sense of humor, historians remember when the joke was on him. He was seated in Carnegie Hall on that memorable afternoon, October 27, 1917, when Jascha Heifetz made his debut. It was hot in Carnegie Hall and Elman wiped his brow and said to the musician next to him: “sure is hot in here.“ His neighbor responded with the memorable line: “not for pianists.“ Just recently I became reacquainted with another granddaughter of the great Mischa Elman. I learned that Terry Magnin and her sister, Dana Mack Prinz, made a significant contribution to Keshet Eilon in the western Galilee in Israel. This is a magnificent music center with concert halls, music studios, a music library, violin shop and a lively concert season. The library was named in honor of Mischa Elman. Space limitations prevent me from going into greater detail. There is so much more to say. I urge my readers to take the cynics with a grain of salt. Sure, Ambrose Bierce was partially correct when he said that the phonograph restores life to dead noises. Rest assured, there is much more to life than negativity. Put on a recording of the beautiful song “There is no death“ sung by John Charles Thomas. Then put on some of the recordings by Mischa Elman. Prepare to be amazed. articles.text: Jeanine and Guy Saperstein in front of the Picasso Museum in Paris. Guy and Jeanine Saperstein, longtime residents of Piedmont, have decided to sell their home on Glen Alpine Road and relocate permanently to France. The 12,000-square-foot house, the most expensive listing in Piedmont, was constructed in 1930 by renowned architects Williams and Wastell. The English Country Tudor-style home has been impeccably maintained throughout the years and features a hand-carved floating staircase against a two-story leaded glass window in a dramatic foyer. The home also boasts an elevator, attic game room, ballroom, home theatre, separate carriage house, and three-car garage. Why the move? The life-altering decision to move permanently across the globe is the result of what the couple sees as the stark inequality in this country. “There are tremendous inequalities [in America] racewise and class-wise. Two senators per state means there will never be a real democracy, and I don’t see that changing in a long time,” Guy confessed. Both are longtime civil rights workers and philanthropists. Guy has been named one of “the 100 most influential lawyers in America” by the National Law Journal. In 2006, he helped write the “Real Security” plank of the Democratic Party’s New Directions for America, and in 2007, helped found the National Security and Foreign Policy New Ideas Fund, with funding from the Democracy Alliance. He also has been Co-Chair of the Democracy Alliance’s Strategy Group and was active in its National Security/Foreign Policy Group. “We’re perched on the edge of potential fascism,” Guy said of members of the Republican party questioning the legitimacy of the 2020 election. “Added to that, I’m not enamored by the constant threat of wildfires, earthquakes… Even if we weren’t going to Paris, I needed to rethink living in California altogether.” Jeanine offered that, as a lifelong educator and philanthropist, she “wanted to make the world a better place.” “But we tried with his career, and my work in education; we tried to do what we could. In Europe, countries don’t have a big philanthropic movement, because people support [one another.] For a long time [in America,] people told us ‘either love it or leave it,’ and now we’re leaving it,” she said with sadness. “National healthcare, parental leave… many of the things we’ve fought for, they already have [in France].” Guy explained that the couple is relocating to Paris for a number of positive reasons. “Every country has social problems, but France has 19 times fewer crimes of violence than America. It’s safe to walk the streets at night,” he said. “France has a real middle class, and far less disparities than the truly wealthy. There’s virtually no homelessness.” “And Paris is basically a socialist province,” he added. The travel opportunities from Paris are also a draw, Jeanine noted. Being “smack-in-the-middle” of Europe allows for quick trips anywhere across the continent. The couple is looking forward to “lingering in Paris cafes, visiting world-class museums, meeting new people and bumping into old friends.” Their son, Leon, a fashion photographer who lives in Piedmont with his wife and son, lived in Paris for 10 years. “They always wanted to go back,” Jeanine said with a smile, and explained their plan to move several family members piecemeal to Europe.
