articles.text: Jules Leyhe is the headliner at the Sound Room in downtown Oakland this Saturday, July 3. Jules Leyhe, a 2008 Piedmont High graduate, has worked professionally since graduating from Berklee College of Music. He and his Family Jules Band are playing back-to-back concerts at The Sound Room in downtown Oakland this Saturday night, July 3. The 8 p.m. show is sold out, but tickets are available for a show at 10:15 p.m. Leyhe’s band is a high energy blues quartet consisting of some of Oakland’s greatest blues and jazz musicians, including vocalist Libby Labella, Isaac Schwartz on drums, Ian McArdle on keyboard, and Matt Roads on bass. The ensemble’s blend of funky, blues and soul inspired improvisation makes for a highly entertaining performance. Leyhe combines classic blues guitar with modern electronic instrumentation and creates a sonic mesh you’ll feel in your core. Named one of Guitar Player Magazine’s top 12 players in 2014 as well as the Bay Area Blues Foundation’s All Stars in 2015, Leyhe has already shared the stage with many of Blues greatest talents including Buddy Guy, Charlie Musselwhite, Chris Cain, Jimmy Vivino, Barry Goldberg, Fantastic Negrito, Nick Gravenites, Elvin Bishop, and Maria Muldaur. Both with his band and on his own, Leyhe has been taking over the San Francisco Bay Area one venue at a time, playing everywhere from the seminal Boom Boom Room to the Sweetwater Music Hall, the Great American Music Hall, and Slims Tickets for the 10:15 p.m. show are available at: https://www. eventbrite.com/e/the-familyjules-band-tickets-160230819695.

articles.text: Part 23 in a biweekly series After reviewing the last column, I thought readers might be interested in a little more information on the relationship between building materials, engineering, and architectural expression, especially on roofs, one of the most visually prominent surfaces of a building. Architects want their roof designs to look good, but also not to leak! This is not always as easy as it seems. Complicated building forms and leak-risky layouts like decks over living spaces can make a dry building a challenge. In fact, the number one litigation issue architects and engineers face is water intrusion, i.e., leaks. The roof design process is therefore multi-faceted with structural and waterproofing considerations closely tied to aesthetics. In the roofing world, there are basically two kinds of roofs: sloped roofs and “flat” roofs, each with its own requirements and limitations. Sloped roofs are finished with shingles: asphalt, wood, clay, slate etc. For waterproofing integrity, all types of shingles require a minimum roof slope of at least 3:12. Otherwise water can creep or be blown back under the shingles. Shingles are indeed used on slopes as low as 2:12, but with special underlayment. How effective these applications are I’m not sure. Generally, the steeper the roof slope, the better. Getting water off the roof quickly is best for water intrusion prevention as well as the durability of the shingles. “Flat” roofs aren’t really flat, but almost always have a low slope that directs water to drains. This system only works with low slope roofing materials like membranes or built-up roofs such as tar and gravel. To complicate things, these low slope roofing materials are the opposite of shingles—they don’t work if the roof slope is too steep. articles.text: Pictured in front of the main Masoleum at Mountain View Cemetery in Oakland are members of the Walking on Wednesdays group: Albert Chen, Alicia Rivera, Emma Sangil, Winston Lee, Pat McSwain, Iris Hudis, Elain Rehr, Susan Martin, Helen Dong, Quincy Dong, Alan Goldhammer, Nadine Guffanti, Judee Lee, Phil Witte, Jim Kuo, Sarah Johnson, Adrienne Hamlin, Nancy Lenahan, John Lenahan, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Sherry Jacobs, Susan Huppert, Andree Greenberg, Mark Greenberg, Larry Olsen, Nancy Olsen, Stella Houston, Charlene Louie, Noemi Alvarado, Haybert Houston, Gavin Hughes, Priscilla Wanerus, Eric Hughes, Harriette Louie, Toni Sevans, Dick Carter, and Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had tours of the Mountain View Cemetery in 2018 and 2019, but missed their visit last year because of the pandemic. With Dr. Ron Bachman as their tour guide, the walkers turned out in force on Wednesday, June 23, with 40 people on the tour. The cemetery had been closed to the public until recently because of the pandemic, and is now still only open on Wednesdays and Saturdays. This was Dr. Bachman’s first docent tour in over a year too, so he was pleased to see so many people. The walkers met in front of the entrance to the main Mausoleum which is just beyond the fountain in front of the cemetery’s main office. Dr. Bachman is a retired Kaiser pediatrician with an additional area of expertise in epidemiology. His knowledge of Mountain View Cemetery and California history is that of a professor. After a brief introduction, he told the group that if they were fully vaccinated he was comfortable with them not wearing masks during the tour. He also explained the Messenger RNA science behind the vaccines which made the walkers all the more comfortable. Dr. Bachman told the group that Mountain View is a 226- acre cemetery established in 1863 by a group of East Bay pioneers led by Samuel Merritt. At that time there were a few local cemeteries, but Merritt’s group wanted to create a truly beautiful space for the final resting places of the area’s growing and prosperous population. The association they formed still operates the cemetery today. They bought 200 acers of land for $3,000, and an additional 26 acres were later purchased from the original Blair Park. Mountain View was designed in 1864 by Frederick Law Olmsted, the landscape architect of New York City’s Central Park and much of the University of California in Berkeley and Stanford University. Many of California’s important historical figures are buried at the cemetery, including five California governors. Early California senators and many UC Berkeley presidents and professors are also buried at Mountain View. Its first burial was in 1865, and there is a section with Civil War veterans whose remains were moved to the cemetery after their deaths. Currently there are between 175,000 and 200,000 people buried at Mountain View, which has room for an additional 200,000 graves. Dr. Bachman took the group to the back of the Mausoleum. To show them the Strangers Plot that was established in 1870 for people who could not afford burials. This included many Chinese immigrants who helped build the railroads and worked in the California gold mines. Dr. Bachman took some time to tell the story behind a large Egyptian pyramid that the walkers came to. See the also attached photo of Dr. Bachman and members of the group. It is the mausoleum of U.S. Senator William Gwin. He was a medical doctor, politician, and a senator from Mississippi and later California. He and John Frémont were California’s first US senators. He died in 1885 at a time when Egyptian archeology and motifs were very popular. The histories of prominent architects Bernard Mayfield and Julia Morgan, as well as many other notable people and cemetery events, were also shared by Dr. Bachman. There are many grandiose crypts in tribute to the wealthy at Mountain View. Dr. Bachman concluded his tour by pointing out a ridge section of the cemetery with a set of large, tall buildings and a view of the Bay and San Francisco. It is known as “Millionaires’ Row,” and houses the mausoleums of the early California “Big Four,” the influential businessmen who funded the Central Pacific Railroad – Leland Stanford, Collis Potter Huntington, Mark Hopkins, and Charles Crocker. They built the western portion of the transcontinental railroad during the middle and late 1860s, creating routes that crossed both the Rocky Mountains and the Sierra Nevada range. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Recreation Department is required by contacting John Wilk at jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: History of 158-year old historic cemetery revealed

articles.text: If you are a grandparent of a young child today, there’s a good chance that your now-adult child watched many episodes of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood when they were growing up. As Mister Rogers zipped up his cardigan and donned his house sneakers, he sang “It’s a beautiful day in the neighborhood...” while a little piano riff played in the background. Next, Mister Rogers fed the fish and then sat down, looked directly into the camera lens, and spoke directly to each individual young viewer, usually about feelings. He told each child: “I like you just the way you are.” Mister Rogers tackled the current events of the day by seeing the world through the eyes of a child and addressing the scary parts with the reassurance of a wise elder. The renewed interest in the teachings and the biography of Fred Rogers nearly two decades after his death in 2003 is extraordinary. It has spawned documentaries, biopics, podcasts, books, educational seminars, magazine articles, blogs, Facebook pages, and countless academic essays on the profound impact that he had on children’s educational television, and more importantly, on educating and guiding the adults who interact with small children. What can grandparents of young children learn from the legacy of Mister Rogers? Most grandparents have the luxury of not being in the role of primary guardian of small children with the requisite responsibilities for their education, health, nutrition, etc. This leaves room for possibly the most important role anyone (apart from a parent) may play in a child’s life: the person who can love the child just the way they are. “Knowing that we can be loved exactly as we are gives us all the best opportunity for growing into the healthiest of people.” Mister Rogers wanted adults to understand that ideally, we love others not because they are particularly good or particularly special, but rather, because we are all special and deserving of love, understanding, acceptance, and kindness. And he hoped that this lesson could be communicated to children. Mister Rogers taught us that we can love another person even if they are imperfect, or very different from ourselves, or even if we don’t really know them very well. Because the main part of loving is the kindness part. Being presumptively kind to another person is simply a way to love. As a grandparent, your abiding interest in your grandchild helps them to realize that they are worthy of love and do not need to perform or achieve anything in particular to receive and feel that love. articles.text: One year ago in April, while driving across the Bay Bridge it was hard to miss seeing the Grand Princess, the enormous white cruise ship docked in Oakland. The local news reported the story, but seeing it hit me hard. It was a ship full of vacationers, many of whom had COVID. It was international news. My phone started ringing with friends and family calling and texting who imagined the ship disembarking onto my neighborhood streets. None of us knew what was ahead. We hadn’t yet learned what we now know. And so, 2020 began a year of near-daily panic. A long, slow year marked by never-ending news stories of COVID, George Floyd’s death, homelessness, and the election. My spring birthday typically is marked by the usual seasonal changes, lush green California hills, the buzz of bees, and pretty, blooming trees. This year, spring has hit me with a jolt of self-reflection, digesting what I’ve been through, what we’ve all been through. It was not entirely traumatic; I never got COVID. I remember being in disbelief when at Safeway seeing only potatoes and onions in the produce section after Governor Newsom ordered the shelter in place. I drove home, sat down, and had my first panic attack. I often thought this past year about my parents who talked about the Depression during their lives. It stayed with them, as I’m pretty sure the pandemic will stay with all of us regardless of our ages. Today I’m more resilient than I ever imagined. I understand how to pivot. I’ve become a better bird watcher, gardener, wife, mother, and cook. I’ve learned how to stay in the moment. My life, along with everyone’s on the planet, slowed and returning to “normal” feels scary. I’m out of practice on almost all things. I wonder I we all could move forward getting back our lives slowly and rethinking almost everything. The pandemic put a spotlight on so many things, cracks in our society. How we treat our citizens. Who is in our safety net? It’s a question I keep asking myself. I’m weary, resilient, but finally fully vaccinated. Joanne Devereaux is a freelance writer and owner of Mindful Transitions, serving the needs of seniors and their families throughout the downsizing and home moving process. She can be reached at 510-757-7340 or at jmk.devereaux@gmail.com

articles.text: The American Red Cross continues to experience a severe blood shortage. Blood and platelet donors are needed now to help ensure hospital shelves are stocked with blood products over the Fourth of July holiday and beyond. As a thank-you, all those who come to give July 1-6 will receive a Red Cross embroidered hat by mail. And donors who donate blood between July 7-31 will receive a $10 Amazon.com gift card by email, plus a chance to win gas for one year (a $5,000 value). Donors of all blood types – especially type O and those giving platelets – are urged to make an appointment to give now by using the Red Cross Blood Donor App, visiting RedCrossBlood. org, or calling 1-800-RED CROSS (1-800-733-2767). The Red Cross is working around the clock to provide blood products to hospitals responding to an unusually high number of traumas and emergency room visits, as well as overdoses and resulting transplants. As a result of the blood shortage, some hospitals are being forced to slow the pace of elective surgeries until the blood supply stabilizes, delaying crucial patient care. To donate blood, call the Oakland Blood Bank, 6230 Claremont Avenue, at 800-733-2767. The blood bank is open from 7:45 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. most days, and until 6:45 p.m. on June 30 and July 6. To donate blood, individuals need to bring a driver’s license or their blood donor card. Individuals aged 17 who weigh at least 110 pounds and are in good health may be eligible to donate blood.

articles.text: When someone needs assistance with daily activities in the home, it can appear that they never leave home. In some cases, due to a chronic illness, infection concerns, or mobility issues, a person may not be able to go out much. However, a professionally trained caregiver can become a companion outside of the home too and help with activities when away from home. Traveling by plane, car, or train can be complicated and require many stops along the way that require the assistance of a caregiver. Simply pausing for a bathroom break safely may necessitate help from someone else, while handling luggage and important papers too. Before embarking on a trip, stop to consider all of the little ways in which a caregiver helps around the house – daily or weekly. Then, weigh the risks of not having the caregiver along for a trip. Will there be walking and inherent fall risks? Are all bathrooms accessible with grab bars? Are medication reminders needed daily? A trusted caregiver with the proper training can be of help in these new settings and make a big trip more enjoyable as well as safe. Maybe taking a big trip is out of the question, but it is possible to leave the home for a short time with the help of a caregiver. This variety in the day can be meaningful for someone who’s activities have become limited as a result of age or illness. Not every outing with a caregiver has to be a chore, such as a trip to the grocery store or a visit to the doctor’s office. A caregiver can be there for a favorite neighborhood visit, a scenic drive, or a walk in a park – a time to be there when catching up with an old friend so that things go smoothly with food preparation or light housekeeping. Each of these experiences can be an opportunity to make new memories and break up mundane routines. This summer – or any time of year for that matter – consider doing something new outside the home with the support of a caregiver for yourself or a loved one who could benefit from new surroundings. Homewatch CareGivers is located at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and is owned and operated by Piedmonters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www.CarePiedmont.com.

pages.text: Wednesday, June 30, 2021 25 By Cookie Segelstein Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear Readers: Buyer beware! Today’s article is about a situation I came across last week with a customer (whom I will call Andrew) who bought a new 21.5 inch iMac in January. Since he and his family are now fully vaccinated (as am I), I did a house call to set up this new machine. When I looked at the specs of the machine, we realized that this iMac was from 2017. I was not aware that these 21.5 inch iMacs have not been updated since then. Of course, Andrew was not happy, having bought this machine new from Apple. So, we called Apple’s sales department and were transferred to a representative in “post sales”. The agent declared that although the model has not been updated since 2017, the machine was built new in January. I told him that my client had not been informed of the age of the model he was purchasing. And that he had spent a long time talking to the sales representative, and indicated over and over again that he wanted a new machine. He explained that he was replacing an eight-year-old machine and wanted something that would last him for another eight years. They discussed the 21.5 inch versus the 27 inch, and because of space requirements my client chose the smaller. This client is an expert in many things, but technology is not one of them. He indicated to the sales person that he was really just concerned with getting something that would have the same longevity as his previous machine. Never in the conversation, did the sales person tell him that the iMac model he was buying, although new, was made up of components from 2017. So, thinking he would have another seven or eight years on this machine, Andrew ended up buying a fouryear old machine. I requested that my client be allowed to return this computer for a newer model, and of course the answer was this: “I’m so sorry, but you were outside the two week return window”. I said to the agent, of course we are, but with the pandemic, this was the first chance we have had to be together to do the set up. And I strongly suggested that the sales person was remiss in providing all the information necessary for my client to make a good decision. With sales in technology, it’s up to the sales person to explain to the consumer what in fact they are buying. The representative promised to send this to a higher tier, and someone in this mysterious department called Andrew later that day. The bottom line in the conversation with this representative was, “we are so sorry, there’s really nothing we can do.” Andrew called me and gave me the number of this mysterious department, and I called them the next morning. After being disconnected once, I finally spoke to a representative named Dawn. At first, she gave me the same company line, that this was outside the two-week return window. I stressed that those requirements should not be enforced during these times, when clients have not been able to get in-home support until now. I also stated to her many instances of what I would call “age-ism” with previous clients and with Andrew. And I stressed that with computer sales, it is up to the salesperson to explain to the consumer exactly what they are getting. I reminded her that Andrew was never told that he was getting a new build of a four-year old machine, and that had he been informed, he would have chosen a different model. I told her about a previous instance where a client went into one of the local Apple stores to buy a new machine. This client was a retired professor, who had had a stroke. His IQ was off the charts, a very bright man. His speech was affected by the stroke, and he had a little card printed up to give to salespeople to explain his situation. The last sentence on this card, which was just brilliant, was “I’m not stupid, I just talk funny.” This client was treated like a five-year-old child, and although he explained in writing on a note pad he kept that he takes a lot of photos, he was sold a laptop with a small hard drive with the lowest amount of RAM. When I was called to set it up, I promptly recommended he exchange it for a larger and faster machine. Again, had the representative listened to his needs, he would have recommended the appropriate machine. After talking for more than an hour, Dawn promised she would advocate for us and call me back. I explained to Dawn that we would not let this go if the response was in the negative and that we would call some consumer advocates, possibly the newspaper, possibly AARP. About 20 minutes later, she called me back and said that they would take this machine for a refund. She also indicated that the sales person was no longer working for Apple. I thanked her profusely and recommended that she tell her higher ups that they need to train their salespeople better to deal with customers of all ages. Here is a list of what Apple has for sale right now on their website and the release dates: • MacBook Air: Nov 2020 • 13-inch MacBook Pro Intel Model: May 2020 • 13-inch MacBook Pro Apple M1 Model: Nov 2020 • 16-inch MacBook Pro Intel Model: Nov 2019 • MacMini: Nov 2020 • 21.5-inch iMac (no longer on their site): June 2017 • 24-inch iMac: April 2021 • 27-inch iMac: Aug 2020 What can we take from this? When it is time to upgrade your computer, please remember to ask questions. If you are an artist, musician or photographer, you need processing speed and power as well as storage space if you want to store your media on the computer. If you are just emailing and surfing the web, you need a simpler setup. Remember to ask the production date of the model that is being recommended. And if you need buying advice, contact me. I’ll be happy to help. Cookie Segelstein is the Macmama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com and themacmama.blogspot.com. As a thank-you, all those who come to give July 1-6 will receive a Red Cross embroidered hat by mail. And donors who donate blood between July 7-31 will receive a $10 Amazon.com gift card by email, plus a chance to win gas for one year (a $5,000 value). Donors of all blood types – especially type O and those giving platelets – are urged to make an appointment to give now by using the Red Cross Blood Donor App, visiting RedCrossBlood. org, or calling 1-800-RED CROSS (1-800-733-2767). The Red Cross is working around the clock to provide blood products to hospitals responding to an unusually high number of traumas and emergency room visits, as well as overdoses and resulting transplants. As a result of the blood shortage, some hospitals are being forced to slow the pace of elective surgeries until the blood supply stabilizes, delaying crucial patient care. To donate blood, call the Oakland Blood Bank, 6230 Claremont Avenue, at 800-733-2767. The blood bank is open from 7:45 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. most days, and until 6:45 p.m. on June 30 and July 6. To donate blood, individuals need to bring a driver’s license or their blood donor card. Individuals aged 17 who weigh at least 110 pounds and are in good health may be eligible to donate blood. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. articles.text: In a match lasting 3 hours and 12 minutes, McDonald limited mistakes with just 18 unforced errors and allowed just one break point to Cressy in the final three sets. McDonald, 26, reached the Round of 16 of the 2018 Wimbledon before losing to Canada’s Milos Raonic in four sets, 6-3, 6-4, 7-6 (7-5), 6-2, it was his longest Mackie’s current ranking marks his highest since being No. 57 when he sustained a torn hamstring tendon in April of 2019 and underwent an extensive surgery. He dropped to No. 132 when he returned in January 2020 and fell out of the Top 250 to No. 272 as he recovered. Prior to Wimbledon, McDonald reached the semifinals of the ATP Challenger Nottingham II in England on June 19 with wins over Antoine Hoang (6-4, 6-2), Zhang Zhizen (6-4, 7-6 (7-3), 6-4), and Anton Matusevich (6-2, 6-3) in the quarterfinals before losing to Australia’s Alex Bolt, 6-3, 6-4. Park Commissioner Jim Horner’s 1953 Ford convertible will serve as a backup vehicle. A police motorcycle will follow. “We know what a great tradition the July 4 parade [in Piedmont] is, and we’re happy to be able to do a small part in having everyone enjoy the celebrations,” said Dan Pitcock, owner of the W.A Rose Company. “I’m happy that we’ve finally arrived at a place where a parade of whatever size can actually happen.” Barrelhouse Jazz Band The Barrelhouse Jazz Band will lead the flotilla on the W.A Rose flatbed truck this year, the first year the truck has led the parade. The band started at Montclair Presbyterian Church in 1969 and has played in the Piedmont Parade ever since. The band is led by Al Flood (clarinet, saxophone), and includes Chuck McLain (trombone), pianist Margaret McElwain, Jim Lockie-Brown (banjo), Viki Jacobsen (bass saxophone) and trumpeters Art Wood and Joel Jacobsen. The band’s focus remains the West Coast brand of New Orleans-style Dixieland jazz. Unlike traditional Mardi Gras strutting and strolling bands, Barrelhouse always plays on the back of a truck. “We are all looking forward to playing this year,” Flood said. pages.text: 32 Wednesday, June 30, 2021 Goats Continued from page 5 fires can grow in intensity and speed the more vegetation they have to burn as fuel. The goats are a natural and rugged way to clear grasses and brush ‘ladder fuels’ which could carry fire from the ground into the trees,” explained Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “The goats can get to hardto-reach areas, work efficiently, and don’t use any fossil fuels once delivered to the location. “In addition, they are fun to watch,” he added with a grin. Annual vegetation management helps firefighters control a grass fire before it becomes a conflagration, Brannigan added, like the 1991 Oakland-Berkeley hills fire, or the more recent Tubbs Fire in Santa Rosa. The length of time the goats will be here depends entirely on the herd’s appetite, although they will need to be moved out of urban areas before Independence Day, because the sound of fireworks spooks them. The herd will eat their way around the open space surrounding the Corporation Yard. Once that area is cleared of dry brush, they will cross Moraga Avenue and eat the vegetation at Blair Park. “This could take a week, it could take two – we’ll see how fast the goats chew,” Brannigan said. The Piedmont Fire Department asks that residents who want to see the herd keep in mind not to park on dry grasses or block traffic. And although it may be tempting, do not try to touch the goats. articles.text: All fully vaccinated city staff members will be welcomed back to the workplace on Tuesday, July 6. A report was provided to councilmembers by Fire Chief Dave Brannigan at a June 21 meeting. Brannigan explained that July 6 was chosen as a tentative “re-opening date” because of the nature of changing Cal/ OSHA regulations, and lack of certainty. The governor, and the California department of Public Health, has lifted most major restrictions regarding COVID. In addition, based on Alameda County’s reported statistics, Piedmont is the first and only city in the county to reach 100% of the available population over the age of 12 to receive their first vaccine, and over 80% are fully vaccinated. “This gives [city staff] a few weeks to make sure our interpretations are accurate, and that employees have the opportunity to adjust their lives,” Brannigan said following the June 21 staff meeting. Re-opening the city would begin with City Hall. Vaccinated members of the public will be allowed into city hall for services. This would be done through an “honor system,” keeping in mind that nearly all residents are now fully vaccinated. Anyone who is fully vaccinated will not be City staff has set a target re-opening date of July 6. required to wear a mask. Brannigan noted, however, that “there are still many businesses that ask [employees and patrons] to wear a mask, and it is up to the individual regardless of vaccination status if they would like to continue wearing a mask.” Social distancing rules have been lifted if employees are fully vaccinated. Unvaccinated workers, or people who decline to report their vaccination status, will still have to wear masks indoors according to Cal/OSHA. Public Works Department staff is working on phasing in services around the city before the July 6 target date. “Our message to the public is, please be patient - we’ll have as much information as possible as we re-open. We are getting very granular with our plan on how we do this safely,” Brannigan added. “We believe this is a more upbeat report on COVID than you have received in the past year and a half. By all accounts, we are coming out on the other side of the pandemic,” said Paul Benoit, Special Assistant to City Administrator.
articles.title: 100% of eligible Piedmonters have received dose of vaccine

articles.text: Editor: As someone who has lived in Piedmont for 15 years, one thing that has been a constant is the 4th of July parade. I can recall being very young and watching the marching bands and the old cars drive by. It was always a source of joy during the summertime for me and many others. As we all know, the parade was cancelled last year due to the pandemic, and I believe that was the best choice. But now things are different. Things are re-opening. And I think that it is safe and possible for us to have a parade. Here’s why: 82.5% of eligible people are fully vaccinated for COVID-19 in Piedmont, the highest rate in Alameda County. Fully vaccinated people are able to be with each other without masks, so this makes the parade much safer than last year. Also, the parade is an outdoor activity. As many of us know, outdoor activities are far safer than indoor activities with regards to COVID-19. But above all other reasons, we as a community need a big activity like this to bring us together again. Over the course of more than a year we have had to adapt to online meetings and social distancing, and it has been extremely tough. We have all had moments of hardship during lockdown, but I think a 4th of July parade would be the perfect thing to lift the community’s spirits. articles.text: A change of school leadership is overdue. Leading in education, especially in this era, requires more than just reacting in crisis mode and apologizing for failures and harm once public recognition demands it. Piedmont Unified School District has received national and local media attention for several scandals involving discriminatory conduct of racial, sexual, and anti-Semitic nature: Football Fantasy Slut League, the Cowherd incident, student dance formations of a swastika, hate speech on lockers, and recently the white support circle. Superintendent Booker’s responses to these incidents have been defensive, lacking in transparency, and have failed to fix the damage to our female and BIPOC students. We have been made to accept and absorb the effects of egregious behavior and dismissive apologies from the city’s highest paid administrator. Even if well meaning, responses that are tone deaf to the needs of minorities and the less privileged protect offenders and discount the victims’ experience. To chastise instead of supporting students of color and female students for bringing up harassment experienced at school has far-reaching, lifelong consequences. articles.text: A report of the 2019 greenhouse gas emissions inventory, and goals accomplished related to Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan, was provided to City Council on Monday evening, June 21. The report was produced by Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman and CivicSpark Fellow Nate Redinbo. The report found that natural gas and personal transportation are now the primary sources of emissions in Piedmont. In 2016, Councilmembers joined the Compact of Mayors, a global coalition of city officials with the common goal of reducing their local greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The initial three-year commitment has led to the adoption of the Climate Action Plan (CAP), which sets an ambitious goal of reducing GHG emissions 40% below 2005 levels by 2030, and 80% below those levels by 2050. The goal is considered met if the city does not emit more than 29,291 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent in a single year. The report garnered information on the city’s GHG emissions through 2019. Compiling data annually allows the city to track its progress toward meeting its climate action plan. The 2019 GHG emissions inventory was completed in spring of this year and shows that Piedmont’s emissions were approximately 34,197 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalents. This shows a large reduction of 30% below 2005 levels, but a slight reduction of less than 1% from the year before, 2018. The large reductions in 2005 can be attributed to decreases in emissions from building appliances, Dykman explained. “To achieve these reductions, it is critical to understand the main contributors to emissions,” she said. “The two main contributors (to GHG) in Piedmont have been, and continue to be, residential energy and transportation.” Dykman added that, if Piedmont residents do not reduce emissions from gas vehicles and natural gas use, the city will not meet its CAP goals. “Together, these two sources account for nearly 90% of greenhouse gas emissions,” Dykman said. Redinbo noted that although there was a 30% reduction in emissions between 2005 and 2019, there has been “less than 1% of a reduction in emissions since 2018.” “The main thing to take away from that [statistic] is that residential activities and buildings emit an overwhelming majority of Piedmont’s emissions. While reducing all emissions is important, spending more of our attention on our residential actions will have a larger impact,” he said. Redinbo noted that Piedmont is close to meeting its 2030 emissions goal of reducing GHG emissions 40% below 2005 levels, but at this current pace, the city will not meet the 2050 goal without significant changes, mostly in the residential sector. What’s next? The city programs that have contributed to progress toward CAP include newly implemented reach codes, which require that new residential buildings and accessory dwelling units (ADUs) be outfitted with all-electric appliances, and a Home Energy Assessment Policy, now required when listing a property for sale, which helps buyers decide how to best improve a home’s energy use. The Induction Cooktop Lending program will loan residents an electric cooktop for free and provides education to residents about the benefits of electrifying your kitchen. “Actions considered to be the low-hanging fruit have already been taken, further action is needed in order for the city to be on track in meeting its CAP goals. It will require ongoing commitment that builds upon, and surpasses, the city’s past successes,” Dykman told city councilmembers. The city staff recommended that city council consider a permanent funding source for electrification incentives for homeowners. This includes reducing building permit fees for installation of photovoltaic systems, heat pump water heaters, and heat pump furnaces. The city can also pursue increases in gas user taxes or establish a carbon tax on natural gas. The staff also recommend the creation of a climate action committee, and to create a resolution committing Piedmont’s municipal facilities and activites to be zero-carbon by 2050.
articles.title: Natural gas, vehicles are primary sources of emissions in Piedmont

articles.text: According to Alameda County Public Health Department data, 100 percent of eligible Piedmonters have received at least one dose of COVID-19 vaccine as of Sunday, June 20. The news comes days after California widely reopened its economy on Tuesday, June 15 after 15 months of pandemic restrictions. articles.text: At its meeting on June 21, the Piedmont City Council delayed final approval of the installation of electric vehicle (EV) charging station in the center of town. East Bay Community Energy (EBCE) and city staff have worked together to plan the installation of EV charging stations and proposed locations by the Piedmont tennis courts on Bonita Avenue. A 10-year agreement would allow EBCE to install two dual-port, fast-charging stations at the location, which would be able to charge up to four vehicles at one time. The stations would be maintained and operated by EBCE at no cost to the city. CivicSpark Fellow Nate Redinbo called the proposal a “win-win” for the city in terms of reaching its ambitious Climate Action Plan goals of reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Jessie Denver, a representative of East Bay Community Energy at the meeting, confirmed that Bonita Avenue was the most desirable location because it is adjacent to commercial retail, and that a one-hour charging limit and 24-hour accessibility would encourage turnover. “We want those chargers to be highly utilized, and turnover to happen rapidly,” Denver said, and added that there seemed to be “ample parking space in the Civic Center area” of Piedmont, adjacent to the tennis courts. Mayor Teddy Gray King disagreed, noting that the area is “next to city hall, a high school, middle school, and lots of residences. To suggest it’s easy to find parking [there] is just never the case,” she said. Councilmembers agreed that having EV charging stations in the city would be ideal but discussed other locations and configurations. They also noted that a one-hour turnaround is not ideal in that location, where educators, school, and Recreation Department employees often park. City Planner Kevin Jackson confirmed that other potential locations are being considered. Special Assistant to City Administrator Paul Benoit, acting as city administrator in interim, suggested to delay the vote with EBCE until other options are explored. He noted that it could return to city council in a month. “This is a 10-year contract. We’d like to better understand the flexibility of both parties built in to the contract,” Councilmember Betsy Andersen said. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. pages.text: Wednesday, June 23, 2021 3 Climate Action Plan successes noted by Council Natural gas, vehicles are primary sources of emissions in Piedmont By Allyson Aleksey A report of the 2019 greenhouse gas emissions inventory, and goals accomplished related to Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan, was provided to City Council on Monday evening, June 21. The report was produced by Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman and CivicSpark Fellow Nate Redinbo. The report found that natural gas and personal transportation are now the primary sources of emissions in Piedmont. In 2016, Councilmembers joined the Compact of Mayors, a global coalition of city officials with the common goal of reducing their local greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The initial three-year commitment has led to the adoption of the Climate Action Plan (CAP), which sets an ambitious goal of reducing GHG emissions 40% below 2005 levels by 2030, and 80% below those levels by 2050. The goal is considered met if the city does not emit more than 29,291 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent in a single year. The report garnered information on the city’s GHG emissions through 2019. Compiling data annually allows the city to track its progress toward meeting its climate action plan. The 2019 GHG emissions inventory was completed in spring of this year and shows that Piedmont’s emissions were approximately 34,197 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalents. This shows a large reduction of 30% below 2005 levels, but a slight reduction of less than 1% from the year before, 2018. The large reductions in 2005 can be attributed to decreases in emissions from building appliances, Dykman explained. “To achieve these reductions, it is critical to understand the main contributors to emissions,” she said. “The two main contributors (to GHG) in Piedmont have been, and continue to be, residential energy and transportation.” Dykman added that, if Piedmont residents do not reduce emissions from gas vehicles and natural gas use, the city will not meet its CAP goals. “Together, these two sources account for nearly 90% of greenhouse gas emissions,” Dykman said. Redinbo noted that although there was a 30% reduction in emissions between 2005 and 2019, there has been “less than 1% of a reduction in emissions since 2018.” “The main thing to take away from that [statistic] is that residential activities and buildings emit an overwhelming majority of Piedmont’s emissions. While reducing all emissions is important, spending more of our attention on our residential actions will have a larger impact,” he said. Redinbo noted that Piedmont is close to meeting its 2030 emissions goal of reducing GHG emissions 40% below 2005 levels, but at this current pace, the city will not meet the 2050 goal without significant changes, mostly in the residential sector. What’s next? The city programs that have contributed to progress toward CAP include newly implemented reach codes, which require that new residential buildings and accessory dwelling units (ADUs) be outfitted with all-electric appliances, and a Home Energy Assessment Policy, now required when listing a property for sale, which helps buyers decide how to best improve a home’s energy use. The Induction Cooktop Lending program will loan residents an electric cooktop for free and provides education to residents about the benefits of electrifying your kitchen. “Actions considered to be the low-hanging fruit have already been taken, further action is needed in order for the city to be on track in meeting its CAP goals. It will require ongoing commitment that builds upon, and surpasses, the city’s past successes,” Dykman told city councilmembers. The city staff recommended that city council consider a permanent funding source for electrification incentives for homeowners. This includes reducing building permit fees for installation of photovoltaic systems, heat pump water heaters, and heat pump furnaces. The city can also pursue increases in gas user taxes or establish a carbon tax on natural gas. The staff also recommend the creation of a climate action committee, and to create a resolution committing Piedmont’s municipal facilities and activites to be zero-carbon by 2050. articles.text: On Saturday morning, June 19, a group of Piedmonters installed another “Flower Flash” in the city, this time in honor of Pride month. The idea was conceptualized by Piedmont High School sophomore Eve Tellegen, and was made possible with help from members of the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, the Public Works Department, and other city staff. Mini, colorful floral arrangements appeared in two of the city’s most recognizable venues – City Hall and the Exedra – as well as Blair Park, Dracena Park, the Recreation Center, and Highland Avenue in front of the Community Hall. Park Commission Chair Patty Dunlap and Pam McBain propped up bouquets against the Exedra with red, orange, yellow, green, blue and purple bamboo, representing colors on the LGBTQ+ pride flag, which also flies in front of public buildings throughout Piedmont. The two also arranged a caper of flowers with matching vases at City Hall. Gayle Lambert, Lili Bassett, and Molly Ashford designed an arrangement in Dracena Park and in front of the Community Center, and Tellegen, with help from family members and friends, displayed a vivid bouquet at the Recreation Center. The arrangements were on display through Monday, June 21. Former City Administrator Paul Benoit and Assistant City Clerk Lisa Argue. Park Commission Chair Patty Dunalp (left) with Pam McBain

Scouts paddle through a rapid in synchronization. The night before beginning their rafting trip, Troop 15 Scouts enjoy time with each other around a campfire. On the weekend of June 12-13, a group of 56 Piedmont Scouts and parents from Troop 15 rafted 26 miles on the South Fork of the American River. Scouts had an awesome time rafting across raging river rapids and even swimming in the river. In some parts of the river the Scouts could leap out of their rafts to be carried down the river a brief way by the currents. For regular rapids, Scouts paddled down the water, maneuvering around rocks, with their paddles in sync. The weekend on the water was exciting and a new experience for many of the younger Scouts. “Our entire patrol attended, all 10 of us,” said Caleb Canada. “Nobody wanted to miss this trip. All of us had a fantastic time rafting down the river. We were constantly laughing and enjoying ourselves. Everyone agreed that it was an awesome trip.” Scouts also got to admire the beautiful surroundings of the river. The hills, trees, and fields of green and yellow complemented the dark waters of the American River. The guides on the raft helped ensure that the Scouts had fun by adding unique twists to the journey. One raft guide had her entire raft paddle against each other, so their raft spun around in circles as they went down one section of the river. articles.text: There is an art to listening. For parents, an important challenge right now is to teach our children how to listen. As our country tunes into the pain caused by generations of social injustice and brutality, our children need to understand what it means to listen, to truly listen. Each year, in my psychology class, I teach students about listening. To begin, I pair them up and give them a simple task: listen to your partner talk about something that’s troubling them, for one minute, without interruption, and then trade places. Invariably, this exercise causes a lot of discomfort. Sure, it can be hard to hear about another person’s troubles, but the discomfort arises mostly because students don’t understand what listening is all about. They don’t know how to simply focus on someone else’s experience, full stop, without inserting themselves into it. Most students are inclined to jump in and problem solve, or share their own experience as a way to connect, but these tactics serve to circumvent the listening process, not to advance it. Also, many students don’t realize that listening takes practice and some feel guilty or embarrassed that they don’t know how to do it well right away. I explain to them that if they want to be good listeners, they need to exercise their listening muscles, so to speak, and there are some basic guidelines that can help. articles.text: Hillary Crissinger was the Director of Special Education for PUSD for the last three years. She will retire on June 30. A total of 11 teachers and staff in Piedmont School District’s Special Education Department have either retired, resigned or requested a leave of absence after the 2020-2021 school year. The list of departures includes Director of Special Education and Student Services Hillary Crissinger and 18 year veteran Occupational Therapist Kimberly Bonacum, both of whom are retiring. Superintendent Randy Booker gave accolades to the retiring Crissinger at the June 9 school board meeting for her three years of service in the district. “Hillary Crissinger is authentic, honest and unbelievably knowledgeable in her field,” Booker said. “It has just been great to be a part of this community,” Crissinger said. “I truly feel like I was contributing in a really positive way to the community and to Special Ed. I had the honor of working with a really solid team that takes a thoughtful and caring approach.” Crissinger spearheaded the Counselor Enrich program in the Special Education Department. In explaining her impact, Booker said, “Hillary brought together all the resources and did all the research through SELPA to help our students in need stay here on campus and have an alternative program. By Susan Eva Porter, Ph.D. For parents, an important challenge right now is to teach our children how to listen. As our country tunes into the pain caused by generations of social injustice and brutality, our children need to understand what it means to listen, to truly listen. Each year, in my psychology class, I teach students about listening. To begin, I pair them up and give them a simple task: listen to your partner talk about something that’s troubling them, for one minute, without interruption, and then trade places. Invariably, this exercise causes a lot of discomfort. Sure, it can be hard to hear about another person’s troubles, but the discomfort arises mostly because students don’t understand what listening is all about. They don’t know how to simply focus on someone else’s experience, full stop, without inserting themselves into it. Most students are inclined to jump in and problem solve, or share their own experience as a way to connect, but these tactics serve to circumvent the listening process, not to advance it. Also, many students don’t realize that listening takes practice and some feel guilty or embarrassed that they don’t know how to do it well right away. I explain to them that if they want to be good listeners, they need to exercise their listening muscles, so to speak, and there are some basic guidelines that can help. To be an effective listener, begin with the following assumptions: • The person you’re listening to has something important to say. • That something is not about you (even if the topic is about you, the person you’re listening to is sharing their experience, which is different than • • yours, and therefore it’s not really about you). It is not your job to fix the situation, at least not while you’re listening. Doing nothing is doing something. This last assumption can be tough for students to swallow. In almost every other area of their lives they are taught to act, to do something, but when it comes to listening, doing nothing is doing something. In fact, it’s doing a lot. Then I instruct my students to do the following, once their partner has finished speaking: • Thank them for sharing. • Ask relevant follow up questions, if you have them. • Ask if there’s anything you can do to help. • Listen some more. The best way to help children develop good listening skills is to practice them yourself. Take time to listen to your child, parenting partner, family and friends and watch your relationships deepen and transform. It’s what the world needs right now. Dr. Susan Eva Porter is the Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. She can be reached at sue@orindaacademy.org. This article originally appeared in the Piedmont Post on June 24, 2020. articles.text: Crew members check their topo map before starting the hike. Four new members of the Piedmont High Adventure Crew went camping in China Camp State Park in San Rafael. Pictured are Jamie Schwartz (left), Anne Reardon, Jessica Liu, and Annabel Horvath. Piedmont’s High Adventure Crew is looking for enthusiastic teens to join its summer backpacking trip July 22-27 in the Sierras. We’ll camp at lakes each day and enjoy the beauty of the mountain wilderness. Beginners are welcome. Anyone interested should join as soon as possible and meet with Crew Advisor Ken Li to develop a plan on how to prepare for the trip. The coed crew is part of the Piedmont Scout Venturing program. The HAC experience is typically very social, allowing teens to meet new friends and develop confidence through the challenges of being self sufficient in the wilderness. The crew loves members who want to help plan and run events, select event dates, and plan the outings with the guidance of the Crew Advisor. Many young adults who were members of the Crew look back fondly on their time in the crew where they were first introduced to hiking, camping, and backpacking. These experiences whet their appetite for doing more during their college years and beyond. We also seek local adults who want to share a love of the outdoors with teens and help mentor youth as they grow. Crew members have access to leadership training and recognition for their contributions to crew leadership and personal growth through a Venturing Award series. Our mission is to provide our members with a fun and rewarding experience, with emphasis on teens taking control of what they do. For more information, contact Crew Advisor Ken Li at: Ken.i.Li@sbcglobal.net. Each day’s travel ended at a lake where the group rested and often swam in mountain water. Dinner on backpacking trips is a high point of each day with creative and satisfying meals. Pictured is Valerie Xiong (near right, wearing a bug net over her head), serving Clare Murphy, while Toshi Troyer waits his turn. Aya Troyer, at near left serves trip leader Mike Bandrowski.

Pictured are: Haybert Houston, Stella Houston, Cat Gustafson, Bob Gustafson, Priscilla Wanerus, Helen Dong, Emma Sangil, Noemi Alvarado, Jim Kuo, Alan Goldhammer, Cheryl Coleman Jones, Fia Hsu, Pat McSwain, Melba Yee, Sherry Jacobs, Nancy Olsen, Swee Ling Chen, Larry Olsen, Adrienne Hamlin, Nancy Henn, Albert Chen, Alicia Rivera, Sarah Johnson, Harriette Louie, Brenda Ferrero, and Susan Martin. Not pictured: Quincy Dong A record 28 walkers showed up last Wednesday for the weekly outing of the Piedmont Recreation department-sponsored Walking on Wednesdays group. On hand were Albert Chen, Swee Ling Chen, Jim Kuo, Harriette Louie, Cheryl Coleman Jones, Alicia Rivera, Adrienne Hamlin, Melba Yee, Nancy Henn, Brenda Ferrero, Nancy Olsen, Sherry Jacobs, Larry Olsen, Cat Gustafson, Bob Gustafson, Haybert Houston, Alan Goldhammer, Pat Mc Swain, Susan Martin, and Dick Carter. The group was especially pleased to welcome first time walkers Stella Houston, Emma Sangil, and Fia Hsu. Drawing from Gail Lombardi’s Piedmont Historical Society articles, the walkers learned more about early Piedmont developer Frank C. Havens. Havens created and opened the Piedmont Park with its mineral springs attraction in 1898 to promote his land sales. Havens also built a new Piedmont Springs Clubhouse in 1898 at the top of the park across from today’s Wells Fargo bank. The clubhouse overlooked a wooden ravine. Additionally, Havens built a landscaped Maze in 1904 in the current location of Witter Field. A Japanese Tea House was installed in 1907 at its current location in Piedmont Park, and an art gallery at the site of the Park Tennis Courts. He also added a bandstand for Sunday concerts, with rustic park benches, and exotic plants. Havens was a major developer, but around 1915 he experienced financial difficulties. The Oakland Tribune reported that lawsuits totaling $90,000 were filed against him. Havens auctioned his art collection, and by 1916 he was planning on developing the park into residential home sites to raise money. A mortgage on his Piedmont Park of $172,000 had not been paid and the park was to be sold at a foreclosure action in 1917. The Piedmont School Board wanted 13 acres of the park land for a new high school, but Havens would not sell less than its total 27 acres. The land was still available in 1921 when Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander and others offered to buy 14 acres for a city park, if the City would reimburse them. The School District could also buy the 13 acres it wanted. One year later in 1921 the voters passed a bond issue, and the City reimbursed Alexander and his partners. Prior to this Havens built a large home for himself. His estate, which he called “Wildwood,” was on land that today is the Wildwood Gardens neighborhood. His mansion is the current residence at 101 Wildwood Gardens. Havens initially lived in a house at 801 Magnolia which was built by the Wetmore family for their daughter. The house was later converted to the Christian Science Church and Reading Room, and now is the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The location was convenient for Havens while developing Piedmont Park. He later moved to the Randall house at the corner of Highland and Hazel, which was closer to the construction of his Wildwood estate. The Randall house was originally Miss Ransom’s School for Girls and was demolished around 1930. In 1908 Havens hired Bernard Maybeck to design his grand mansion. It was five stories tall and was stepped down the canyon. It took two years to build and more years to finish the interior. Havens’ wife Lila was a student of Eastern religions, You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: The Smithsonian’s Hope Diamond has long been suspected of being directly connected to 17th century French king Louis XIV, but no proof existed until 2009 when technology and an unfathomably lucky find by the Musée of National d’Histoire Naturelle’s curator unearthed a lead cast created by the royal jeweler that carried the precise contours of the 69-carat diamond. The Hope Diamond is the Français Blue. Cubic Zirconia A cubic zirconia replica of the Hope Diamond was featured in Precious Stones when the exhibit opened last September and soon closed due to Covid-19. Making a manufactured zirconia diamond in the color of blue is an incredibly complex process that laboratory scientists took years of work, until 2017. The original Français Blue and the original 112-carat diamond from India are now near-perfect replicas. The Hope Diamond as a cubic zirconia replica had to be pulled from the expo due to scheduling; however, other jewelry made of zirconia, a natural element, are available in the show’s exhibits. articles.text: The past year and a half sure hasn’t been easy. Describing it as unconventional would be a vast understatement. Students across the globe endured the closure of schools for more than one year due to the COVID-19 pandemic. For student-athletes, the Class of 2020 and 2021 endured and overcame severe obstacles, requiring a mighty amount of patience and careful planning and quick adapting by the coaches and Piedmont’s new Athletic Director, Bradley Smet. Historically the Post honors a Coach of the Year in our school year-ending issue. The whirlwind of sports compressed from 9 months into three required diligent involvement of Piedmont coaches, players, and their parents and volunteers, With the late-August start of school, teams weren’t allowed to practice until the California Interscholastic Federation gave clearance on February 19, 2021. Despite everything working Staff Photos Piedmont football coach Jerome Johnson (left), assistant coach Scott Kail, and offensive coordinator Jarmar Julian helped lead the program to a perfect 5-0 season. against them, Piedmont High finished with high rankings and achievements in nearly every sport. Football was perfect at 5-0. The boys’ soccer team also was undefeated in league at 10-0. Baseball, similarly, was undefeated at 8-0 in the Shoreline Division The girls’ cross-country team won the WACC Title. Ryan Price’s boys’ lacrosse team and Carlton Chan’s girls’ team each had dramatic wins over rival Bishop O’Dowd. At a time when many schools in the area struggled to even have teams ready to compete, Piedmont’s success in the pandemic year is paramount for the growing student-athletes in the community. The school didn’t drop any sports and even added one, boys’ volleyball team, for the first in 20 years. pages.text: Wednesday, June 23, 2021 13 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 14th year in the Post. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. Photo courtesy of USCTrojans.com Henry Saunders, Class of 2019, completed his redshirt-freshman season on the USC water polo team, a 10-time National Championship program. and off the pool deck to achieve and maintain my physical and mental readiness regarding the water polo. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? Being a member of the USC water polo program. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? Set individual as well as team goals. These goals will help you track your development, as well as demonstrate accountability in the face of your coaches and peers. I would also suggest pushing your peers to achieve group aspirations. HENRY SAUNDERS Water Polo How are you measuring your development? I’m measuring my development by how much I can lift and by my weight. I’ll also be timing my swim training. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working out in our garage. We have a series of weights, bench, pull-up bar, and a Peloton. Last year at school when we couldn’t use the pool, I helped bring a gym inside our fraternity, so we were able to stay in shape during the pandemic. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I’ve been working on my upper body strength. Surfing has really helped with the upper body, and the time in the weight room has been paying off. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Stay up on the academics, and to work hard at a sport that you love. Doing your best is what matters and making friends and feeling good about yourself is the reward. I would recommend to Piedmont water polo players swimming as training. Piedmont High Class of 2019 University of Southern California (USC) Class of 2023 Henry Saunders recently completed his sophomore year at USC and redshirt-freshman debut season on the water polo team. The Trojans went 8-9 in 2021 but fought their way to the NCAA Championship game on March 21, narrowly losing 7-6 to crosstown rival UCLA. It was the 15th year in the past 16 that USC played in the NCAA title game. Saunders graduated from Piedmont High with a long list of accomplishments. He won first-team All-League honors for four years, received honorable mention as an All-American, was a two-time All-North Coast Section player, and a two-time academic All-American. Saunders is Piedmont’s alltime leading player on assists with 57 as a senior, 50 as a junior, 16 as a sophomore, and 21 as a freshman. He helped the team reach four consecutive NCS playoffs, twice advancing to the semifinals. What is your workout program this summer? This summer I will be training on campus at the University of Southern California with many of my teammates in preparation for the upcoming season. Our program for the two summer sessions consists of considerable pool time coupled with strength conditioning in our weight room. What are your fitness goals for this summer? Similar to many summers prior, I plan to best prepare myself physically for the upcoming season and challenges to come. How are you measuring your development? I set goals during the beginning of my summer training to improve specific strengths or eliminate specific weaknesses I have identified. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? Currently I am working with a variety of coaching staff both on Photo courtesy of University of Toronto Patrick Conn, PHS Class of 2019, is Piedmont’s all-time leading scorer. PATRICK CONN Water Polo Piedmont High Class of 2019 University of Toronto Class of 2023 Piedmont High’s all-time leading scorer, Patrick Conn, completed his sophomore year at the University of Toronto. He helped Toronto achieve its fourth consecutive League championship in 2019 with a 20-2 overall record. The 2020 season was not played due to the global pandemic. A four-year varsity player at Piedmont, Conn was a two-time All-NCS recipient, two-time second-team All-League recipient, and a two-time first-team honoree. He scored 146 goals his senior year, 128 goals his junior year, and 95 as a sophomore. Alongside Henry Saunders, Conn helped his team reach four consecutive NCS playoffs and two semifinals. After a year away from water polo, Conn admits he’s eager to get back in the pool. “I have missed a whole year of water polo because of COVID- 19. I am really looking forward to playing again this fall and getting back to the pool,” he said. What is your workout program this summer? This summer my workouts consist of surfing, swimming and weight training. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My fitness goals for the summer are to continue to add muscle mass, and to be ready for my water polo season when I go back to school. Teitelbaum was among the Banana Slugs’ top finishers in the 2019 Division 3 NCAA West Region Cross Country Championship, helping his team to finished 3rd of 15 teams. He was also named All-West Region after helping Santa Cruz to qualify for NCAA Championships. He graduated from Piedmont High in 2018 and earned a firstteam All-League selection in 2017 after helping lead the boys’ cross-country team to the CIF State Championship berth. Below he details his extensive training regimen for his senior season in college. What is your workout program this summer? My training this summer is has some modifications from last year and added cross-training. My coaching staff at UC Santa Cruz distribute our training plans at the beginning of June. I am expected to arrive in Santa Cruz in mid-August for our summer training camp fit, healthy, and ready to take on some harder workouts and races for the cross-country season (August-November). This year, my summer training has an emphasis on increasing weekly running volume, cross-training, building ankle strength, and injury prevention. Monday: Easy 30-50min jog or bike, maybe take the day as an off day Tuesday: 10min warmup jog, drills+speed development, 40-65min training run Wednesday: Pre-Meet warmup (20min jog, drills, strides), Aerobic Tempo (4 -8mi depending on assigned pace, anywhere between 5:25-5:55), Cooldown, 15-30min shakeout or bike ride later in the day, Core + Lift in the afternoon Thursday: Mid-Week Long Run (60-80min), if I’m feeling beat up I’ll switch this with a 1-2.5 hour bike ride, Stretching + Rehab in the afternoon Friday: Pre-Meet (20min jog, drills, strides), 10-30min Cooldown Saturday: Either Progression (50-60min cutting down every mile to about 5:30) or just a 50-75min training run, Core + Lift in the afternoon Sunday: Long Run! (80-100min) What are your fitness goals for the summer? To stay strong and happy. It is likely that I will be making our travel roster for the NCAA Regional and National Cross-Country Championship in November. Because of this, I don’t want to start tiring myself out and putting additional stress on my body until a bit later in my training block. How are you measuring your development? In running, it is very easy to measure fitness. My ability to handle a fast tempo pace for a longer duration each week on Wednesday workouts is generally a great indicator. I also use Strava to compare my training with my teammates and competitors. Using a GPS watch with a heart rate monitor is also an absolute necessity for me. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am training on my own in the Bay Area this summer. Starting in August, I will start training with the cross-country team (20 men, 20 women) in Santa Cruz. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Despite running about 15 percent of my usual training volume, I’ve actually been able to stay very fit from just biking and a couple of running workouts. I raced at the C2C Conference Championship in Maryland in May, placing 5th overall in the 5K. I raced one other 5K this season, surprising myself with a new personal best, 15:27. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? As a runner, it’s much more important to be the healthiest than it is to be the most fit. A growth mindset and a willingness to succeed will take you far in this sport. Give the gift of trusted news Send your high school graduate off with 50 weeks of the Piedmont Post. articles.text: The Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame has announced that six high school alums will be inducted in a ceremony in February 2022. The new members of the Hall of Fame are Lauren Barbieri 2001 (Cross Country and Track); Devin Brown 2009 (Football, Basketball and Baseball); James Danielson 1981 (Football, Track and Soccer); Georgia Hill 2013 (Softball and Basketball); Jon Minor 1983 (Basketball); Kerri Roemer 1999 (Tennis, Basketball, Softball and Track). They will be enshrined at a ceremony at the Claremont Country Club on Saturday, February 26, 2022. Details for the event, including how to purchase tickets, may be found on the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame website: www.PSHOF.org. Georgia Hill, 2013 – Softball, Basketball A 2013 graduate, Georgia lettered in softball and basketball. A standout softball player, she earned 1st Team All-League honors four times, team MVP three times and was named West Alameda County Conference (WACC) League MVP, 3rd Team All-East Bay (East Bay Times) and 1st Team All-State (Cal-Hi Sports) her senior year. Georgia played two years at The College of Wooster, where she broke four team records her freshman year, including home runs in a single season. Jon Minor, 1983 – Basketball Jon earned three varsity letters in basketball. He was a dominant 6’6” starting center his junior and senior years, earning 1st Team All-League honors and Alameda County Athletic Conference (ACAL) Player of the Year both seasons. He also received the Optimo Award his senior season as the team’s Most Valuable Player. Jon continued his basketball career at UC Davis. Kerri Roemer 1998 – Tennis Kerri led the girls’ tennis team to North Coast Section all 4 years, highlighted by winning the NCS team championship in 1998. Kerri played doubles with Meghan Wardlaw and reached the semi-finals one year and finals another year. As PHS team captain (‘98) she won the CIF sportsmanship/citizenship award. Kerri was ranked in the top 20 USTA NorCal juniors and was nationally ranked her senior year. At UC Davis, she was named the Western Conference Rookie of the Year for 1999-2000. Devin Brown, 2009 – Football, Basketball, Baseball Devin was a dynamic athlete in football, basketball, and baseball for the Highlanders. On the gridiron, he was a threeyear starter on offense and defense. As a senior, he led the State with 13 interceptions and earned 1st Team All-League honors, All-Bay Area by both the San Francisco Chronicle and Contra Costa Times, and was named to the All-State 1st Team Defense by MaxPreps. Additionally, he received All-League honors in basketball in 2008 & 2009. After graduation, Devin attended the University of Massachusetts where he was a Scholar Athlete of the Year on the football team. Lauren Barbieri, 2001 – Cross-Country, Track Lauren was a Track and Cross-country standout. She was the recipient of the Track MVP award all 4 years at PHS, qualified 4 years for the North Coast Section championships, and set school records in the Triple Jump, 4x400 relay and 100 Hurdles. She qualified for the California State Meet. At UC Berkeley, she competed in both Cross Country (2 years) and Track (4 years) where she was named Academic All-Pac 10 for Track and Field. Jim Danielson, 1981 – Football, Soccer, Track Jim was a 3-sport star in football, soccer, and track. In soccer, after his MVP year, he led the Piedmont team to its first North Coast Section Championship, while earning Piedmont’s first NCS Individual Player honor in 1981. In track he set a school record in the Triple Jump and was the 1981 track Optimo winner. He was team captain and a 1st Team All-League recipient in all 3 sports, and earned 10 total varsity letters at Piedmont High.

articles.text: Former Piedmont resident Mackie McDonald is competing for another Grand Slam Tournament this week, the Wimbledon Classic from June 21 to July 12. McDonald is currently in the qualifiers with the No. 2 seed, defeating Belgium’s Kimmer Coppejans 6-7 (7-5), 7-5, 6-2 on Tuesday, June 22. McDonald faces Ukraine’s Illya Marchenko today, Wednesday, June 26 and will likely be completed with his match by the time you pick up today’s Post. The singles final round of qualifiers is on Thursday, June 27 before the main draw on June 28. To win Tuesday’s match over Coppejans, McDonald was mighty at the service line with 10 aces, winning 75 percent of his first serves, gaining five break points in the process. It marked McDonald’s third victory over the Belgian in his career. He last defeated Coppejans in three sets, 6-4, 4-6, 6-3 on May 12 at a Challenger in Heilbronn, Denmark. Mackie also beat Coppejans in straight sets at a San Francisco ATP Challenger event in 2017, 6-2, 6-2. McDonald, ranked No. 108 on the world chart, walks into today’s match with Ukranian Piedmont’s Mackie McDonald is competing at the Wimbledon qualifiers this week. Illya Marchenko, No. 155, and is considered the favorite. Marchenko’s furthest appearance in a Grand Slam was the 2016 U.S. Open. He hasn’t qualified for a Grand Slam since 2017. Prior to the Wimbledon, McDonald reached the semifinal of the Challenger Nottingham II in England on June 19, losing to Australia’s Alex Bolt 6-3, 6-4. Mackie also reached the second round of the French Open on June 2, falling in five sets to No. 20 Cristian Garin of Chile after opening with wins in the first two sets and a heated thirdset super breaker, 4-6, 4-6, 7-6 (9-7), 6-3, 8-6. McDonald, 26, made one of his longest Grand Slam appearance of his career at the 2018 Wimbledon when he reached the Round of 16 before losing to Canada’s Milos Raonic in four sets, 6-3, 6-4, 7-6 (7-5), 6-2. Mackie’s current ranking of No. 108 marks his highest since holding the No. 57 spot at the time of a torn hamstring tendon injury in April 2019. Now climbing back up the world rankings, McDonald’s matches will air on ESPN+ and The Tennis Channel. Match time is not yet confirmed.

articles.text: This writer is pleased to announce that he’s teaming up with OaklandRootsBlog over the summer to provide coverage and reporting of the Oakland Roots Sports Club, getting on the ground floor of an up-and-coming soccer league in the Bay Area. The Roots postponed their home-opening game last Saturday, June 19, after officials with the USL Championship professional men’s soccer league deemed the pitch unplayable just 20 minutes prior to kickoff. The surface itself is a pieced together surface of 3’ x 4’ turf rectangles. According to Sacramento-based reporter Evan Ream, a player on the Sac Republic squad complained to the USL Players’ Union on Friday, June 18 but the Roots nor league officials addressed the matter until referees inspected the pitch on Saturday. articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) reopened on Friday, June 18, after a 15-month closure. The highlight of the museum’s reopening is its renovated seven-acre campus, including a new entrance from Lake Merritt and redesigned gardens. The museum opened its first weekend to press and museum members. After a seven-month closure, these groups caught the first glimpse of a re-landscaped garden complete with native trees and plantings. A new stage by the main lawn will be used for outdoor programs and performances. articles.text: The musical Hamilton returns to the Orpheum Theatre this summer in August. Li n -M a nuel M i r a nd a’s acclaimed musical Hamilton returns to San Francisco’s Orpheum Theatre for a limited four-week run August 10 through September 5. The sung-and-rapped musical tells the story of one of America’s Founding Fathers, Alexander Hamilton. Miranda said he was inspired to write the musical after reading Ron Chernow’s 2004 biography about Hamilton. The show draws heavily from pop, soul, hiphop, and traditional-style show tunes. It received Tony Awards for Best Musical and Best Original Score, and a Pulitzer Prize for Drama. The show is 2 hours and 45 minutes with one intermission. The show is produced by Jeffrey Seller, Sander Jacobs, and Jill Furman, with scenic designs by David Korins and costumes designed by Paul Tazewell. articles.text: “In Between Art and Science,” an art exhibit by local artist Nina Reeves, will be on display at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this weekend, Saturday and Sunday June 27-28 from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. “My paintings strive to merge abstraction, figurative elements and the origin of culture and its influence,” Reeves said. “Each component translates in the work through layering, color, and depth, seeking a unique perspective to approach art practice. The exhibit is the most recent body of work that explores figurative elements to elaborate the development of culture.” The artist intends the viewer to be hovered over the painting, looking into scientific structures through an abstract composition, layering, texture, and color. She uses digitized tissue samples as a base for an abstract composition. “I create a visual language that dissects abstraction through the means of science. articles.text: Jules Leyhe is the headliner at the Sound Room in downtown Oakland on July 3. Jules Leyhe, a 2008 Piedmont High graduate, has worked professionally as a guitarist since graduating from Berklee College of Music. He and his Family Jules Band are playing back-to-back concerts at The Sound Room in downtown Oakland on Saturday night, July 3. Leyhe’s band is a high energy blues quartet consisting of some of Oakland’s greatest blues and jazz musicians.
