articles.text: Music@Menlo returns this summer with a mix of in-person and digital performances, opening on July 16. Tickets are on sale now and can be purchased by visiting https://musicatmenlo.org/. Music at Menlo is an internationally acclaimed chamber music festival founded by David Finckel and his wife Wu Han. Begun in 2003 at Menlo School, the festival features concerts, lectures, and a training program for aspiring professional musicians. This year’s events will be smaller in size than its 18 previous seasons but will continue to include a star-studded lineup of musicians. The festival will include a mix of live and digitally-streamed performances between July 16 and August 1. Titled “Gather,” the festival will take place in and around the for approximately an hour without intermission. Nine main concerts have been scheduled over three weekends: The season-opening concert, on July 16, begins with the world premiere of Patrick Castillo’s Gather, commissioned for the opening of Spieker Center. Castillo has held a variety of positions with the festival since its inception and was recently named the New York Philharmonic’s Vice President of Artistic Planning. “I was honored to be asked by David and Wu Han to create a new piece to celebrate the opening of Music at Menlo’s new concert hall. For the occasion, I composed a paean to our sacred ritual of coming together around a shared love of music,” Castillo said. “Little did I know at the time how starved we would be for that ritual by the time of the piece’s first hearing.” Patrick Castillo, New York Philharmonic’s Vice President of Artistic Planning, composed a piece that will open the Music@ Menlo Festival this summer. festival’s new home, the $40 million 384-seat Spieker Center for the Arts on the campus of the Menlo School. articles.text: Bobi Cespedes kicks off this year’s Yerba Buena Gardens Festival with a concert on Friday, June 26. The Yerba Buena Gardens Festival returns this summer, kicking off this Friday, June 26. Live music and performance is free to the public. The festival runs through August 28. For more than two decades Yerba Buena Gardens Festival has presented free outdoor music, circus, dance, poetry, theatre, and youth programs by artists from the Bay Area and around the world. The festival was not held last year due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The festival kicks off this year with a June 26 concert by Bobi Cespedes, the “matriarch of Cuban roots in the Bay Area.” July highlights include the first of a three-part series of dance events by the Yerba Buena Gardens ChoreoFest, music by Zydeco musician Andre Thierry, and Oakland-based hip-hop orchestra Ensemble Mik Nawooj. Children’s programs in July include Pi Clowns and Red Panda Acrobats. “I could not be more thrilled to announce this special Festival season of free performances and concerts this summer,” said Festival Artistic Director Linda Lucero. “I am excited to welcome everyone back to the beautiful Gardens to experience our region’s rich cultural diversity and the immense fortitude of our local artists and performers after a long period of isolation. Yerba Buena Gardens Festival remains a space for art and joy, welcoming people from all walks of life.” Yerba Buena Gardens is located on Mission Street between 3rd and 4th streets in San Francisco. Visit www.ybgfestival.org for a full schedule.
articles.title: Music at Yerba Buena Gardens returns on Friday

articles.text: Pianist Jeremy Denk’s spring performance in Berkeley is now streaming through July 14 as part of Cal Performances’ “At Home” digital season. An insightful pianist and music essayist, Denk is a MacArthur Fellow whom the New York Times called a “mesmerizing musician with a profound affinity with Bach.” He will perform Book I of the composer’s Well-Tempered Clavier, the 1722 collection of 24 fugues and preludes in every major and minor key that Beethoven had referred to as his musical bible. Denk has also written about Bach as a great humanist, and described how the composer’s music represents an “intoxicating combination of the divine balanced with the earthy beauty of Pianist Jeremy Denk logic and discipline.” Visit https://secure.calperformances.org/15177/15818 to obtain streaming access. Tickets purchased for each digital event are limited to the account holder. The mission of Cal Performances, part of UC Berkeley, is to produce and present performances of high artistic quality that explore intersections of education and performance art. The Cal Performances “At Home” series makes digital performances available during shelterin-place restrictions.
articles.title: Jeremy Denk concert streaming through July 14

articles.text: American composer John Alden Carpenter D-Day came and went with hardly a mention. But June 15… That’s a different story. It was declared the official day when states could allow public gatherings after more than a year of restrictions due to the COVID pandemic. The implications (ramifications, if you will) cause the mind to race. What was will be again. The checkered flag is poised at the starting gate. But will imagination take flight? It depends on how you interpret it. The word “flight” is the key. Many of us were fortunate to have grown up in the heyday of radio. There were live concerts of all sorts. News was presented at the top of the hour; if at all, and only briefly. Radio was the dominion of imagination. Many popular radio programs were devoted to drama and comedy. Even the advertisements were imaginative. Composers wrote catchy jingles so that the ads lingered in our minds for years. Today, all you get is speed talk and a machine-generated drum track. But it was the theater of the mind that made the overwhelming impact. We were limited only by our imagination. That was the miracle of radio. Just about every program had its own orchestra. Some programs were pre-recorded, but most had live music which was conceived and performed on the spot. The musical selections were vivid and were chosen to enhance
articles.title: Imagination takes flight

articles.text: By Allyson Aleksey Visit Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside any Thursday evening through September to celebrate “Summer Nights.” The historic house is open until 7 p.m., and the Gardens are open until 8 p.m. Summer Nights are a tradition at Filoli, and serve as a time to gather with family and friends and enjoy the sunset and summer blooms. Every Thursday night throughout the summer, the Grove Bar is serving wine and beer in the garden, nestled under the shade of the Olive Grove. The Georgian-style terraces around the historic house offer sweeping views of the Santa Cruz Mountains, a contrast to the 16-acre formal English Renaissance-style garden. All admission, including for Summer Nights, must be reserved in advance. Masks will be required for those not yet fully vaccinated. For tickets and more information, see: https://filoli.org/summer-nights/. Reservations for “Summer Nights” at Filoli House and Garden can now be made.
articles.title: Summer nights at Filoli Gardens every Thursday

pages.text: Wednesday, June 23, 2021 19 The Musical Gourmet Imagination takes flight the program. Listeners gained a The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet wide knowledge of music simply by listening to the programs – even the jingles used in the commercials. Composers’ minds ran wild. If you were John Alden Carpenter, you might start out with “Adventures in a perambulator.” Cartoons were drawn by hand by imaginative artists. And then the producer came in and selected the music that was most appropriate to enhance the story. Composers and arrangers created music performed by brilliant Hollywood orchestras. It was live, and it was exciting. The compositions were really inspired. Beethoven enjoyed nature so he wrote his Pastoral Symphony. The storm sequence had an effect on Rossini, and that music was used as the theme for the Lone Ranger series of radio shows. And then Rossini parodied life and inheritance with his Little Pleasure Train. Space travel was not neglected, because there were trips to the moon. And there was music of the spheres long before men walked on the moon. My neighbor Ferde Grofe composed the pictorial Grand Canyon Suite and the Mississippi Suite. The music told you everything. You didn’t even need to be there. That was – and is – the miracle of imagination. Composers of genius continue to write pieces for flights of imagination. Spanish guitarist and composer Jaume Torrent went back to his childhood when he wrote Journey to a Magical World. Most recently, Cristiana Pegoraro took us on a musical and aerial adventure. While she performs the Italian patriotic hymn on the piano, an airplane is flying around the citadel of the picturesque town of Narnia. The photography is spectacular. Those of you who read the C.S. Lewis classic, The Chronicles of Narnia, will want to see Cristiana Pegoraro’s production. Political wisdom has declared June 15 as the reopening date after 15 months of isolation. But think of all the music that broke the “dominion of nightfall”. June 15 is a date. The dominion of the mind is without limit. articles.text: Last month I wrote about some wonderful wines created by Dr. Loosen winery in the Mosel River Valley of Germany. Mosel wines are known for the or featherlight weight and extreme finesse. For German wines with a little more power and weight we need to turn to two other famous wine regions – Rheingau and Rheinhessen. These two regions border the mighty Rhine River and contain some of Germany’s oldest wine growing regions. I remember visiting the Rheingau winery Langwirth von Simmern and asking when they started making wine. The answer was 1175 – now that’s some history. This month I want to introduce you to two outstanding German wine producers – Robert Weil and Wittman. Robert Weil The town of Kiedrich, home of Weingut Robert Weil, was first mentioned in 950, so the Weil winery. started in 1875. is a relative newcomer. Today the wines are made by William Weil, the great grandson of the founder. The dramatic slopes leading to the Rhine River can have inclines of up to 60% and are some of the steepest vineyards in the world. One of the characteristics of Rheingau wines and Robert Weil in particular is the power and weight of the wines. That is not to say they are heavy or ponderous but compared to the Mosel River Valley wines they have more depth and power. The wines of Robert Weil are built to last and can be cellared for decades. • 2019 Robert Weil Riesling Tradition This is an off-dry wine made from a blend of various vineyards. The bouquet is cooling, clear, fresh and flinty-aromatic. On the palate is a very juicy, round and seductive wine with piquant acidity and stimulating salinity. It is gorgeously lush and sensual. Could last for a decade. • 2019 Robert Weil Kiedricher Riesling Trocken This Trocken offers lovely aromatic peach and apricot fruit. It’s a lush and fruity Riesling with a certain power, good acidity and mineral grip. It boasts a long, clean and satisfying finish. Try this food friendly wine with fresh fish or shellfish. • 2019 Robert Weil Kiedrich Grafenberg Riesling Auslese (375ml) As mentioned last month, I don’t really think of Auslese as a table wine. To me the level of sweetness makes it more appropriate as an after-dinner wine. This lovely example displays a light, delicate bouquet of white peaches, crushed stones and mango fruits. Sweet, clean and piquant on the palate with a lingering salinity, this young and mouth-watering Auslese is stuffed with passion fruit, honeydew melon as well as honey flavors in the aromatic aftertaste. Serve by itself as dessert. Wittmann The Rhinehessen region is not as famous as the Rheingau or Mosel, but it has some truly fine wine producers of which Wittmann is one. The family has been producing wine in the village of Westhofen since 1663. They are fully onboard the organic wine movement and their vineyards were certified biodynamic in 2004. One of the lovely things about the Rhienhessen region is that you see more grapes than just Riesling. Wittman also produces Robert Weil is one of the premier producers in the Rheingau region. • 2019 Robert Weil Kiedrich Grafenberg Riesling Trocken GG Aromas of honeysuckle vie with peach and lime. On the palate it is quite expansive, juicy, and totally refreshing, with its zesty bitter aspects not overdone and a lovely interplay between fruit savory and mineral notes on the finish. The Wittmann Weisser Burgunder is my favorite wine.

articles.text: If you don’t have a spouse or children, you might think you don’t need to do much estate planning. But if you have any assets, any familial connections, any interest in supporting charitable groups – not to mention a desire to control your own future – you do need to establish an estate plan. In evaluating your needs for this type of planning, let’s start with what might happen if you die intestate – that is, without a last will and testament. In this scenario, your assets will likely have to go through the probate process, which means they’ll be distributed by the court according to your state’s intestate succession laws, essentially without regard to your wishes. Even if you don’t have children yourself, you may have nephews or nieces, or even children of cousins or friends, to whom you would like to leave some of your assets, which can include not just money but also cars, collectibles, family memorabilia and so on. But if everything you own goes through probate, there’s no guarantee that these individuals will end up with what you wanted them to have. If you want to leave something to family members or close friends, you will need to indicate this in your last will and testament or other estate planning documents. But you also may want to provide support to one or more charitable organizations. Of course, you can simply name these charities in your will, but there may be options that could provide you with more benefits. One such possibility is a charitable remainder trust. Under this arrangement, you’d transfer appreciated assets – such as stocks, mutual funds or other securities – into an irrevocable trust. The trustee, whom you’ve named – in fact, you could serve as trustee yourself – can then sell the assets at full market value, avoiding the capital gains taxes you’d have to pay if you sold them yourself, outside a trust. Plus, if you itemize, you may be able to claim a charitable deduction on your taxes. With the proceeds, the trust can purchase income-producing assets and provide you with an income stream for the rest of your life. Upon your death, the remaining trust assets will go the charities you’ve named. Aside from family members and charitable groups, there’s a third entity that’s central to your estate plans: yourself. Everyone should make arrangements to protect their interests, but, in the absence of an immediate family, you need to be especially vigilant about your financial and health care decisions. And that’s why, as part of your estate planning, you may want to include these two documents: durable power of attorney and a health care proxy. A durable power of attorney lets you name someone to manage your finances should you become incapacitated. This arrangement is especially important for anyone who doesn’t have a spouse to step in. And if you become incapacitated, your health care proxy – also known as a health care surrogate or medical power of attorney – lets you name another person to legally make health care decisions for you if you can’t do so yourself. Estate planning moves can be complex, so you’ll need help from a legal professional and possibly your tax and financial advisors. You may not have an immediate family, but you still need to take steps to protect your legacy. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. TK Stevko is a Financial advisor with Edward Jones, 370 Highland Avenue in Piedmont. Tel. (510) 547-4589

Today the wines are made by William Weil, the great grandson of the founder. The dramatic slopes leading to the Rhine River can have inclines of up to 60% and are some of the steepest vineyards in the world. One of the characteristics of Rheingau wines and Robert Weil in particular is the power and weight of the wines. That is not to say they are heavy or ponderous but compared to the Mosel River Valley wines they have more depth and power. The wines of Robert Weil are built to last and can be cellared for decades. • 2019 Robert Weil Riesling Tradition This is an off-dry wine made from a blend of various vineyards. The bouquet is cooling, clear, fresh and flinty-aromatic. On the palate is a very juicy, round and seductive wine with piquant acidity and stimulating salinity. It is gorgeously lush and sensual. Could last for a decade. • 2019 Robert Weil Kiedricher Riesling Trocken This Trocken offers lovely aromatic peach and apricot fruit. It’s a lush and fruity Riesling with a certain power, good acidity and mineral grip. It boasts a long, clean and satisfying finish. Try this food friendly wine with fresh fish or shellfish. • 2019 Robert Weil Kiedrich Grafenberg Riesling Auslese (375ml) As mentioned last month, I don’t really think of Auslese as a table wine. To me the level of sweetness makes it more appropriate as an after-dinner wine. This lovely example displays a light, delicate bouquet of white peaches, crushed stones and mango fruits. Sweet, clean and piquant on the palate with a lingering salinity, this young and mouth-watering Auslese is stuffed with passion fruit, honeydew melon as well as honey flavors in the aromatic aftertaste. Serve by itself as dessert. Wittmann The Rhinehessen region is not as famous as the Rheingau or Mosel, but it has some truly fine wine producers of which Wittmann is one. The family has been producing wine in the village of Westhofen since 1663. They are fully onboard the organic wine movement and their vineyards were certified biodynamic in 2004. One of the lovely things about the Rhienhessen region is that you see more grapes than just Riesling. Wittman also produces Robert Weil is one of the premier producers in the Rheingau region. • 2019 Robert Weil Kiedrich Grafenberg Riesling Trocken GG Aromas of honeysuckle vie with peach and lime. On the palate it is quite expansive, juicy, and totally refreshing, with its zesty bitter aspects not overdone and a lovely interplay between fruit savory and mineral notes on the finish. The Wittmann Weisser Burgunder is my favorite wine. The 2019 Wittmann Riesling Dry 100 Hills is rated as Best Value. • 2019 Wittmann Riesling Dry 100 Hills (Best Value) Bursting with citrus and apple aromas, the Wittmann dry Riesling is a light to medium-bodied offering. Its dry mineral-dominated personality exhibits excellent levels of extract and concentration. This bright, focused wine will be at its best consumed within the next 5 years. • 2019 Wittmann Riesling Trocken This is a step up in quality from the 100 Hills Riesling. It starts deep, cooling and intense on the nose showing aromas of ripe pineapples and pears. Full, rich, broad, and elegant, this well-structured and spicy Riesling reveals a very juicy and meaty palate of good concentration. Very long in the finish, this Riesling should age very well. • 2019 Wittmann Riesling Westhofener This is from a specific vineyard in the village that Wittmann calls home. The Westhofener is a medium-bodied wine that explodes on the palate with layer after layer of pear, apple, spice, mineral and jasmine whose flavors linger long. It is extremely rich, well-balanced and elegant. • 2019 Wittmann Weisser Burgunder Trocken This is a step up from the 100 Hills Weisser Burgunder and was my favorite wine in the Wittmann portfolio. It shows a perfectly ripe and concentrated nose of white stone fruit. The wine is round and elegant, with a dry, lean palate. Really refined, well-structured, pure and fresh, this is a Pinot Blanc that has a nice tartness in the finish with refreshing citrus in the aftertaste. A formidable wine to have with fish or white meat. Even “singles” need estate plans If you don’t have a spouse or children, you might think you don’t need to do much estate planning. But if you have any assets, any familial connections, any interest in supporting charitable groups – not to mention a desire to control your own future – you do need to establish an estate plan. In evaluating your needs for this type of planning, let’s start with what might happen if you die intestate – that is, without a last will and testament. In this scenario, your assets will likely have to go through the probate process, which means they’ll be distributed by the court according to your state’s intestate succession laws, essentially without regard to your wishes. Even if you don’t have children yourself, you may have nephews or nieces, or even children of cousins or friends, to whom you would like to leave some of your assets, which can include not just money but also cars, collectibles, family memorabilia and so on. But if everything you own goes through probate, there’s no guarantee that these individuals will end up with what you wanted them to have. If you want to leave something to family members or close friends, you will need to indicate this in your last will and testament or other estate planning documents. But you also may want to provide support to one or more charitable organizations. Of course, you can simply name these charities in your will, but there may be options that could provide you with more benefits. One such possibility is a charitable remainder trust. Under this arrangement, you’d transfer appreciated assets – such as stocks, mutual funds or other securities – into an irrevocable trust. The trustee, whom you’ve named – in fact, you could serve as trustee yourself – can then sell the assets at full market value, avoiding the capital gains taxes you’d have to pay if you sold them yourself, outside a trust. Plus, if you itemize, you may be able to claim a charitable deduction on your taxes. With the proceeds, the trust can purchase income-producing assets and provide you with an income stream for the rest of your life. Upon your death, the remaining trust assets will go the charities you’ve named. Aside from family members and charitable groups, there’s a third entity that’s central to your estate plans: yourself. Everyone should make arrangements to protect their interests, but, in the absence of an immediate family, you need to be especially vigilant about your financial and health care decisions. And that’s why, as part of your estate planning, you may want to include these two documents: durable power of attorney and a health care proxy. A durable power of attorney lets you name someone to manage your finances should you become incapacitated. This arrangement is especially important for anyone who doesn’t have a spouse to step in. And if you become incapacitated, your health care proxy – also known as a health care surrogate or medical power of attorney – lets you name another person to legally make health care decisions for you if you can’t do so yourself. Estate planning moves can be complex, so you’ll need help from a legal professional and possibly your tax and financial advisors. You may not have an immediate family, but you still need to take steps to protect your legacy. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. articles.text: 4 servings 5 japanese eggplants or 2 medium purple globe eggplants (about 16 ounces total) 8 ounces beef tenderloin (or your favorite boneless steak) 1 teaspoon sunflower oil, or other neutral oil ¼ teaspoon salt Marinade 3 tablespoons soy sauce 2 tablespoons mirin (sweet Japanese rice wine) 1 teaspoon toasted sesame oil 1 green onion, very thinly sliced 1 tablespoon golden brown sugar 1 tablespoon fresh lemon juice 1 tablespoon minced peeled fresh ginger 1 large garlic clove, smashed with a knife and peel removed Crunchy vegetables ½ cup julienne or shredded daikon ½ cups julienne or shredded carrots 8 green onions, cut into 1” sections Pickled ginger (as for sushi) 1 cup shiso or watercress leaves, stems removed Lemon-soy dipping sauce 1/2 cup soy sauce 1/4 cup fresh lemon juice 2 tablespoons mirin (sweet Japanese rice wine) (or sake/white wine mixed with 2 teaspoons sugar) 2 tablespoons water Instructions: 1. Preheat a grill or grill pan over low heat. 2. Peel the eggplants, then rub the beef and eggplants all over with the sunflower oil and salt, until they are well and evenly coated. 3. Cook the eggplants slowly, about 5 minutes per side for the thinner japanese eggplants, and 10 minutes per side for the plumper globe eggplants, until they are covered in grill marks and tender but not mushy. Remove the eggplants from the grill and allow them to cool slightly. 4. Raise the heat under the grill to high. Sear the steak for about 1 minute on all sides, keeping it rare in the center. Remove from heat and allow to cool slightly. 5. Place the eggplants and steak in a large lidded bowl (or two) which just fits them, and add the marinade. Marinate for at least 12 hours and up to 24 hours, rotating the eggplants and steak so they marinate evenly. 6. A few hours before serving, prepare the crunchy vegetables and the dipping sauce (for the dipping sauce, whisk all of the ingredients together until well-combined). 7. Remove the eggplant and steak from the marinade. Use a sharp knife to slice them very thinly lengthwise on the diagonal (you can also freeze the beef for an hour or so to make it easier to slice thinly). The goal is for each slice to contain some of the outer marinated layer and tender interior, and be long enough to be rolled around the vegetables and dipped using chopsticks (or fingers!). Arrange everything artfully on individual plates or a serving platter, and serve with individual bowls of the dipping sauce, allowing each guest to assemble their own rolls. Steamed rice or soba noodles and a salad of Asian greens like tatsoi.

articles.text: Susan Miller-Davis Could what we eat be part of the solution to a more sustainable future? The answer is a resounding “yes!” The cultivation and transport of food causes one third of global emissions, and half of all habitable land is currently being used to produce food. In the US, about 80% of all drinkable water is used for agriculture. As both populations and incomes rise around the world, climate-warming emissions are also growing. Animal products have a higher carbon impact than grains, pulses, vegetables and fruits. Beef, lamb and dairy have the highest carbon impacts of all, for two reasons: ruminants like cattle and sheep create large amounts of methane (a potent greenhouse gas) from their digestive systems; they also require large amounts of grazing and cropland, which contributes significantly to global deforestation. While the connection between fossil fuel extraction and emissions can be clear, the effect our diet has on the environment can be more difficult to see. Compared to even 10 years ago, attitudes about diet have shifted in the U.S. More and more people are embracing “flexitarianism”, eating more vegetables and less red meat, or going even further to adopt vegetarian or vegan diets. More plant-based food products are appearing on shelves and restaurant menus all the time. Despite this, we collectively have a long way to go, and systemic changes matter as much as personal ones. Right now, the federal government encourages meat consumption, giving over $35 billion in subsidies to meat and dairy producers annually, compared with less than 0.5% of that to fruit and vegetable production subsidies. Prices and affordability matter a lot. Large-scale food system change will be needed to make sustainable diets accessible and desirable. That said, change can happen right in our homes, right now. Here are two examples of the change. Susan: the omnivore I work at the intersection of food and climate. My two current projects are conducting research on food waste and plant-rich diets for Project Drawdown and co-authoring a climate-friendly cookbook. I want to help recontextualize how people think about “sustainable” diets, ones that are good for our health and the health of the planet. Spoiler alert: they don’t have to be vegan. Practically speaking, many of us love the flavor of meat, and many of our food traditions and rituals involve meat, from burgers on the grill to a Sunday roast chicken. Animal products also provide important nutrients and minerals that can be harder to come by in vegan diets. For subsistence farmers in many parts of the developing world, livestock provides an important source of income and food security, converting non-arable land into valuable protein and calories. Model diets that can nourish an expected global population of 10 billion people in 2050, lower diet-related disease and mortality, and reduce environmental impacts, all at the same time are being developed by groups like the EAT-Lancet Commission. These diets boil down to balancing calories from a range of foods, and reducing the amount of animal products we consume in affluent countries like the US. So, for example, what does the EAT-Lancet diet look like for a beef-lover? Sticking to about two juicy burgers or a single 14-ounce rib-eye per month. Yup, per month. But there are more creative ways to enjoy beef more often, like this recipe I created which uses beef sparingly but to great effect. You could enjoy a dish like this, which really allows the beef flavor to shine, as often as twice per week without a hint of climate guilt. The Japanese preparation known as tataki flips the conventional marinate-then-cook equation on its head, creating an ultimate make-ahead dish. Serve the flavorful slices of tender beef and silky eggplant at room temperature, to wrap around fresh shredded vegetables and dunk in a savory dipping sauce...it’s a hands-on yet elegant meal to share with friends for a foray back into summer entertaining as California opens up. Nate: the vegan I initially made the switch to a plant-based diet as an environmental decision. Red meat, poultry, and fishing have significant environmental impacts, and changing my diet seemed like a small way to make the world a better place. However, food is complicated. Our personal choices take place against the larger backdrop of our food system and food economy, which undoubtedly will need to shift as well in order to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Fixing the larger, systemic issues that plague our food economy will require large-scale changes that individual diets are unlikely to accomplish on their own. This is not a reason to give up on plant-based eating -- in fact, I highly recommend it. Although this isn’t the diet for everyone, even occasional plantbased eating can add concrete benefits to anyone’s life. Vegans are often portrayed as out of touch, preachy, and difficult to please. While these characteristics are true of certain people, it isn’t true for the vegan community as a whole. Although numbers are hard to come by, it is often estimated that 5% of Americans eat a vegetarian diet, and some smaller portion of that eschew all eggs and dairy to eat a completely plant-based diet. That means there are millions of vegans walking among us. People have many different reasons for trying plant-based eating. Some religions, such as Buddhism, promote vegetarianism, and numerous countries, primarily in Africa and Asia, have very plant heavy diets. In India, where over 80% of the population practices Hinduism or Jainism, vegetarianism is the norm. Ethiopia boasts delicious vegetarian fare, including injera bread (a personal favorite of mine). Living in America, vegetarianism is less widespread, but there are vegetarian-friendly areas. California and the West Coast as a whole are largely vegan friendly, which can probably be linked to the history of social movements, large supply of fruits and vegetables, and varied cultures that have taken root here. Speaking from first hand experience, everywhere from supermarkets to farmer’s markets offer vegan wares in abundance that would have seemed ludicrous 5-10 years ago. Despite the growing acceptance of vegetarian diets, there is still a deeply entrenched resistance to trying plant-based foods. People have a range of reasons why they are skeptical: “Where would I get my protein?” “I wouldn’t know what recipes to make.” “It seems hard to eat out.” Vegetarianism, like running or learning the flute, can be intimidating, but rewarding. There are hundreds of blogs, social media accounts, Youtube channels, and physical cookbooks you can turn to start putting together recipes. There has never been a better time in the US to try a different diet. Here are a few tips that I humbly offer as a way to attempt something new: • Start small. Try eating one meal a day without meat and see how you feel. Switching to a new style of eating is a gradual effort. Nobody expects you to ditch all meat in a day. Avoid substitutes. I personally try to avoid plant products that fake meat. Make meals that embrace vegetables instead of emulating meat products. Don’t limit yourself to just veggie burgers, veggie dogs, or fake crab cakes. There is a wide world of vegetarian dishes that just focus on vegetables. You may find your new favorite recipe. Try something new. Never had indian food? Give it a shot. Use this as a learning experience and a chance to talk to new people about foods you don’t know much about. Meal plan. it’s easier to make changes when you have a plan. Go to the store with a shopping list; it’s easier to stick to vegetables. The internet is your friend-- there are so many resources out there. Google “how to vegetarian” and do some reading. There are schedules, options for recipes, and groups you can join. Finally, make sure you know why you want to try it. Some of the main reasons people attempt it are for health reasons, to lose weight, or just try and add some variety to their diet. Don’t let plant-based eating be something you dread – approach it as a fun thing to add to post-pandemic life. Please reach out to me at nredinbo@piedmont.ca.gov if you have any questions or need recipes. • • • •

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: Dear Jim: We are about to start a remodel and are debating about whether to hire a designer and then a contractor, or whether we should do design-build with a single firm. Your thoughts? –Austin H. Know yourself A decision about how you want the design aspects of your project to occur should be made and stuck to. Will you be hands-on, making the bulk of the selections and design decisions? Or will you want the contractor or designer to make choices and provide you with selections to choose from? This may seem simple, but in our experience the matter of how you want to work is decided early on to avoid mistakes. Know your designer Finding and sourcing compatible fixtures, cabinets, tile, flooring, paint colors, etc. are all skills that most designers possess. However, some lack the construction knowledge needed to integrate their choices into architectural drawings and construction work. In a recent project, our client’s designer didn’t read our architect’s drawing properly Installing a narrow tub and vanity improved the space in this bathroom. Recessing appliances and closets into the crawlspace of this basement second unit created much needed working space. and ordered a vanity that was too wide, had to be returned, and reordered, causing project delays and high return shipping and restocking fees. Get to know your project First, decide on your level of involvement. Often clients tell us they are hands-off, then change their minds and want to be more involved later in the game. Understand that any changes in the design-build process, including increasing your involvement can significantly affect timelines, budget and choices. Next, make sure your contractor or design-builder has clear expectations on the decision-making process for items being selected and ordered, and the time frames for delivery and budget. Keep in mind that the current supply chains are erratic. Having to return and reorder supplies may sideline a project. Finally, in addition to your designer and contractor being a good fit for you, be sure your selections properly fit the space and are reviewed by the contractor, designer and you before being ordered. Measure twice and cut once applies to the design process, too. Conversations with Your Local Contractor is a feature by Jim Gardner of Jim Gardner Construction Inc., who is a long-time Piedmont resident and has been doing structural repair and basement renovation in your neighborhood since 1983. To schedule an estimate or for more information please go to our website at jimgardnerconstruction.com. 3820 Broadway, Oakland Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03

pages.text: Wednesday, June 23, 2021 25 Conversations with Your Local Contractor Why proper design decisions are crucial By Jim Gardner Dear Jim: We are about to start a remodel and are debating about whether to hire a designer and then a contractor, or whether we should do design-build with a single firm. Your thoughts? –Austin H. Know yourself A decision about how you want the design aspects of your project to occur should be made and stuck to. Will you be hands-on, making the bulk of the selections and design decisions? Or will you want the contractor or designer to make choices and provide you with selections to choose from? This may seem simple, but in our experience the matter of how you want to work is decided early on to avoid mistakes. Know your designer Finding and sourcing compatible fixtures, cabinets, tile, flooring, paint colors, etc. are all skills that most designers possess. However, some lack the construction knowledge needed to integrate their choices into architectural drawings and construction work. In a recent project, our client’s designer didn’t read our architect’s drawing properly Installing a narrow tub and vanity improved the space in this bathroom. Recessing appliances and closets into the crawlspace of this basement second unit created much needed working space. and ordered a vanity that was too wide, had to be returned, and reordered, causing project delays and high return shipping and restocking fees. Get to know your project First, decide on your level of involvement. Often clients tell us they are hands-off, then change their minds and want to be more involved later in the game. Understand that any changes in the design-build process, including increasing your involvement can significantly affect timelines, budget and choices. Next, make sure your contractor or design-builder has clear expectations on the decision-making process for items being selected and ordered, and the time frames for delivery and budget. Keep in mind that the current supply chains are erratic. Having to return and reorder supplies may sideline a project. Finally, in addition to your designer and contractor being a good fit for you, be sure your selections properly fit the space and are reviewed by the contractor, designer and you before being ordered. Measure twice and cut once applies to the design process, too. Conversations with Your Local Contractor is a feature by Jim Gardner of Jim Gardner Construction Inc., who is a long-time Piedmont resident and has been doing structural repair and basement renovation in your neighborhood since 1983. To schedule an estimate or for more information please go to our website at jimgardnerconstruction.com. Mom can have her independence back. We can help. articles.text: According to 2020 statistics, the Oakland-Berkeley area office of Guaranteed Rate, a fiercely independent mortgage originator led by area manager Dianne Crosby, closed more than $747 million in home loans while serving the financial needs of more than 1,200 California families. “It’s so gratifying to see clients achieve their dreams of home ownership or to improve their lives with a money-saving refinance,” commented Guaranteed Rate area manager Dianne Crosby, who accounted for $384 million in volume. Despite the challenges brought on by the pandemic, the Oakland-Berkeley office doubled its productivity to become one of the fastest growing mortgage origination offices in the United States. To learn more about the factors contributing to its growth, I recently interviewed each of its vice presidents. Sam Krueger, VP of Mortgage Lending Sam Krueger has been in the mortgage business for 18 years and with six different companies over that time. He joined Guaranteed Rate’s Berkeley Office in December 2019 and was still ramping up with Guaranteed Rate’s team-based approach to processing loans when the pandemic shut everything down. Krueger began working from home, which allowed him to be close to his wife and two teenaged daughters and reconsider his daily habits. The disruption proved not to be a setback. “I trusted Dianne, I trusted the technology, and the efficiency of a team approach,” Krueger stated. “And that’s a good thing because Guaranteed Rate is the No. 1 provider of jumbo loans. It offers the most products at the best rates – the clear winner.” Previously, Krueger was accustomed to annual volumes ranging from $40-$50 million. Last year, after moving to Guaranteed Rate, he surpassed $100 million, far exceeding his expectations and giving him great satisfaction. “It’s a joy working with my clients,” he said about his work. “I enjoy getting to know them well while assisting them with one of the biggest transactions of their lifetime.” But that’s not all. “This is a good time to get financing,” Krueger noted in conclusion. “Operational capacity has never been greater.” Evelyn Freitas, VP of Mortgage Lending Evelyn Freitas has been originating mortgages since 2004. She joined the Berkeley Office of Guaranteed Rate in February 2019; since then, she has learned the benefits of the team-based processing and thrived. “I feel very different about my work nowadays,” Freitas stated before explaining. “Now I can be future forward…I spend more time reaching out to future clients.” And that’s important to Freitas, because in her words: “There’s a lot of information out there that is perhaps applicable to someone, but rarely everyone. It’s my job to hear clients, to weed out the misinformation, and then present a financing package that it tailor-made to them.” Providing long term value to the client is of paramount importance to her. “People are working so hard these days. They deserve the help we can provide.” Since joining Guaranteed Rate, Freitas’s annual production has doubled each year. This year, she’s on target to accomplish $40 million, which would put her in the President’s Circle for the first time. Leonard Briones, SVP of Mortgage Lending Leonard Briones has been originating mortgages for 18 years. He joined Guaranteed Rate in December 2017, and he remembers the transition well, The decision to leave his previous company was a difficult one. At that point in his career, he was comfortable with his income and pleased that he was earning a living while still putting “family first.” Before taking a leap of faith, he braced his wife for the possibility of lower income. articles.text: non-contact drill in November only to be cut short after a couple of weeks. The team returned to the practice field in early March ahead of a five-game season from March 19-April 16. The team was undefeated in its five games in the Western Alameda County Conference’s newly formed Mission Division. “It goes all the way back to the summer, getting together virtually, really learning and quickly putting it together when we got back on the field. We finished as the No. 1 team in Division 4 of NCS,” said football coach Jerome Johnson after Piedmont beat Kennedy 14-12 to cap its perfect season. Piedmont’s football team took big hits to its roster when California had overlapping football and baseball schedules. The baseball team went out to finish 12-4 and would have had a high raking in the NCS postseason playoffs. Both the League and North Coast Section decided not to have post-season championships for baseball, a great disappointment after coach Eric Olson’s teams contended in the last two league title games. “We only had a week of practice before our first game. We had a very casual inter-squad but that was it,” said Olson at the end of the season on April 20.

articles.text: ing becomes open to a natural flow,” Ayofemi said. “My installation responds to the Museum’s distinctive pavilions as portals to activate the senses and expresses Black and Indigenous spaces through regenerative power and Oakland’s built environment.” Oakland Museum brings together a vast collection of art, history, and natural sciences that tell the stories of California and its residents. The museum’s collection of nearly two million art works and artifacts often draw on first-person accounts and anecdotes over decades of the state’s history. On display currently is “You Are Here: California Stories on the Map,” which opened just before the pandemic shuttered the museum in March 2020. The exhibit showcases a diverse range of maps from the East Bay, the entire Bay Area, and the state. It focuses on environmental surroundings, health conditions, community perspectives and creative artworks, weaved together to display the importance of location and cartography. Also on display are the ongoing exhibitions “Dorothea Lange: Photography as Activism,” and “Black Power.” The museum currently is open Friday through Sunday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Full reopening is expected later this summer. For more information on reopening, parking and capacity information, and safety protocol, visit https://museumca.org/reopening. A couple enjoys the view from the museum’s rooftop gardens, which offers unrivaled views of Oakland’s Lake Merritt. The museum will operate under a tentative schedule, Friday through Sunday, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.

articles.text: On a beautiful summer day, 219 seniors at Piedmont High School and Millennium High School graduated in a traditional ceremony at Witter Field. The event, held Friday June 11, was historic. It marked the first time in 15 months classmates and parents were together in one place after the COVID-19 pandemic caused the elimination of all public gatherings. The grandstands were full, the gowns were purple, and the sun shone brightly through a tapestry of high clouds in an undulating, rippling pattern. Seniors were seated in long rows on the field facing their families in the bleachers as the PHS band played Elgar’s “Pomp and Circumstance” to officially begin the ceremony. With a beaming smile, PHS Principal Adam Littlefield welcomed the graduates and their families on a day some thought might never happen. After more than a year of isolation, anxiety and change, everyone was there – teachers, students, family, and friends – collectively celebrating a most difficult year. Speakers emphasized the resilience of the students and the strength and adaptability of the parents. Salutatorian Anthony Wong said, “What has changed most are our perspectives. We think about life, ourselves, and others differently now. We’ve toughened up, we’ve found ourselves.” Co-Valedictorian Thomas Chu got everyone’s attention when he said, “All of my own greatest accomplishments in high school have been built upon failure. Life is not a steady vertical climb to the top, it is a vertical oscillating spring, where you have to go down to go up,” he said. His Co-Valedictorian Sam Eisenbach delivered a rousing speech that was partially a graduate seminar on physics, dealing with the relativity of time and the importance of community and shared experiences. “For the past fifteen months, our perception of time has been at the mercy of our isolation. But now, we have a unique opportunity to take time into our own hands. It’s about time that we un-pause our lives,” Eisenbach said. (To read his speech, see page 8.) As Senior Speakers, thespians and comics Seth Elkins and Sadie Tschider did a playful skit that captivated the audience. Elkins walked up to the podium in “tears.” Tschider asked if he was okay, “No.” he responded. “Do you need to let it out?” she asked. And then the pair screamed away from the microphones and invited the rest of the class and audience to participate in their own cathartic screams. The final student speaker was Audrey Edel, senior class President. In a polished and calculated speech she announced the Senior Class Gift – the installation of water bottle fillers at Witter Field and Binks Rawlings Gym. articles.text: Piedmont was recently given an award from the office of Gov. Gavin Newsom acknowledging the city’s efforts in accelerating the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) market. The governor’s office created the award series, entitled ZEV Permitting Olympics, to honor counties that streamline permitting for electric vehicle charging stations that accelerate economic recovery. Alameda County received “gold” recognition, meaning that 100% of its jurisdictions have streamlined permitting for ZEV infrastructure. Alpine, San Francisco, Napa, and Tuolumne Counties also received gold status. In September 2020, Gov. Newsom signed an executive order to set a target that 100% of in-state sales of new passenger vehicles will be zero-emission by 2035. To help meet the challenge, the ZEV Permitting Olympics competition focuses solely on the creation and maintenance of electric vehicle charging stations. Piedmont supports residents in their effort to buy, lease, and drive electric vehicles. An online building permit application procedure allows residents to obtain a charger permit within three days. The City is also working with East Bay Community Energy in order to expand EV charging opportunities in public spaces around Piedmont. Currently, 26% of Piedmonters own an electric vehicle. More information on EV charger permits can be found on the city’s website at https://piedmont. ca.gov/services___departments/ planning _ _ _building/about_ building_/electric_vehicles.

articles.text: St. Francis is known for that famous saying “preach the gospel, and if you have to, use words.” God is probably less concerned about what we believe and more concerned about the way we act. When we get right down to it, there are simply too many words flying around and not enough meaningful action. And as Christians approach Easter, the celebration of Jesus’ resurrection, it is easy for us to get sidetracked by words in the form of creeds, liturgies and theologies. These provide enough words to suffocate the real story that was all about meaningful action. It’s in that context that I share what I consider to be an Easter Story. When meaningful action trumps words By the Rev. Scott L. Denman St. Francis is known for that famous saying “preach the gospel, and if you have to, use words.” God is probably less concerned about what we believe and more concerned about the way we act. When we get right down to it, there are simply too many words flying around and not enough meaningful action. And as Christians approach Easter, the celebration of Jesus’ resurrection, it is easy for us to get sidetracked by words in the form of creeds, liturgies and theologies. These provide enough words to suffocate the real story that was all about meaningful action. It’s in that context that I share what I consider to be an Easter Story. A few years ago, Elizabeth Gilbert, author of “Eat, Pray, Love”, wrote about an incident that changed her life. She was riding the midtown bus in New York City in evening rush hour traffic. The weather was the worst January had to offer, complete with sleet and gusting wind. To quote her, “It sucked”. The bus was moving at a crawl, tempting her to get out and walk, but the cold icy world she was staring at through the window paralyzed her. The depression in that mobile metal tomb was palpable. Then something happened. When they arrived at 10th Street, the bus driver turned to address his gathered congregation in the bus. He said: “Ladies and Gentleman, we are now nearing the Hudson River. I’m going to ask you to do me a favor. When you get off the bus, I’m going to hold out my hand. As you walk past me, I want you to drop your troubles into the palm of my hand. I’ll take your troubles for you, and when I drive past the river, I’ll throw them in. The reason I want to do this is because you all seem like you’ve had a bad day, and I don’t want you taking all your worries and sorrows home to your friends and families now, because they deserve better than that, don’t they? So you just leave your troubles here with me to dispose of, and you all go have a wonderful night, OK?” Gilbert recounts: “The whole bus – the whole grumpy lot of us – broke into laughter. (Some of us, myself included, might have even shed a tear or two.) And one by one, as we filed off the bus, we dropped our troubles into the palm of this good man’s hand, and we stepped off the bus with smiles on our faces.” The resurrection stories of Christianity emerge in the context of darkness, struggle and despair, but proceed to inspire a radical shift of energy towards love, hope, justice, peace and kindness. Just as this man changed the energy in his mobile office, we too, might be inspired to embrace our power to positively change the energy in the contexts where we live. Maybe then we will know what it’s like to preach some good news, and – only if we have to – use words. The Rev. Scott Denman is Rector of St. John’s Episcopal Church, 1707 Gouldin Road in Montclair. articles.text: City Council will consider the adoption of a housing item at its regularly scheduled meeting on Monday, June 21. Councilmembers will also consider an appeal of the state-mandated Regional Housing Needs Allocation, which requires that Piedmont produce over 500 new housing units within eight years. Residents are invited to attend and provide public comment during the meeting, which will be held via Zoom. Councilmembers will consider the adoption of Guiding Principles for implementing state-mandated Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) programs, as well as objective design standards for the construction of apartment buildings. At the same meeting the city council will consider an appeal of the Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) that has been assigned to Piedmont. The mandated RHNA requires that Piedmont produce 587 new homes and apartments at fair pricing by the year 2031, the end of the next RHNA cycle. articles.text: “One hundred years later, the Negro lives on a lonely island of poverty in the midst of a vast ocean of material prosperity.” Dr. Martin Luther King – Aug 28th, 1963 – “I Have A Dream” I want to thank Ms. Hooi in her recent OpEd for highlighting the growing reaction, mostly from conservatives, to critical The meaning and intent of Critical Race Theory is being distorted for political purposes. As introduced by Richard Delgado, Charles Lawrence, Mari Matsuda, Patricia Williams and others in the 1970’s, CRT is not an ideology. It is an evolving body of research into systemic racism. CRT explores the causes of income and wealth disparity, inequities in the criminal justice system, ongoing perpetuation of segregation, and the stubborn racial bias that permeates our legal system and societal norms. I presume we all agree that, despite some very visible wins — end of slavery, Civil Rights Act, our first African American president — we remain saddled with a legacy of racism that is seemingly intractable and systemic in nature. As I grew up, white and privileged, in the Oakland-Berkeley area, I could not help but notice racial disparities such as our segregated neighborhoods and how wealth correlates so directly to skin color. Unfortunately, the topic was avoided in school and not understood among my family and friends. The result is that I was left vulnerable to being infected by non-objective, often racist, opinions and ideologies. Today in the era of social media, the problem is magnified. Our kids are influenced 24-7 by the loudest, most charismatic, most opinionated voices on the internet. Contrary to your assertion, teaching our children using the latest research -- at an age-appropriate level, of course – about how and why things are the way they are is essential in order to combat the very “poisoning their minds with ideological race rhetoric” that you fear. Critical race theory offers key insights into this intractable problem. CRT is not about assigning guilt. It is about understanding truth. Our kids can handle it. articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department (PPD) has become the first law enforcement agency to launch a public Automatic License Plate Reader (ALPR) Transparency Portal, which will serve as a hub for the department’s ALPR usage, data retention, and access policies. The portal is a new offering from Flock Safety, the provider of the department’s ALPR camera system. “The opportunity to be the launching agency partner on this first-of-its-kind program underscores our deep commitment to openness, accountability, and integrity,” said Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. “The Piedmont Police Department strives to provide transparency on all police activities, policies, and practices, and Flock Safety’s Transparency Portal is another positive step in that direction,” Police Chief Jeremy Bowers said. “We recognize that the public has a right and responsibility to understand how the officers who are sworn to protect and serve them do their jobs.” The system provides Piedmont residents with anonymized audit logs of all police usage of ALPR technology. The portal displays usage statistics, to include the number of cameras the department owns and operates throughout the city and the other law enforcement agencies PPD shares data with. It also displays specific statistics on number of vehicles captured, as well as “Hot List” alerts - when neighborhood ALPR cameras capture a vehicle that is on the FBI’s National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a computerized index of criminal justice information available to Federal, state, and local law enforcement, the alert will be posted to the portal. “Flock Safety was founded four years ago based on the principle that it is possible to improve safety while protecting the critical right of citizen privacy,” Matt Feury, Flock Safety Co-Founder and CTO, said. “We place privacy, transparency, and bias mitigation at the forefront of our product development and are constantly engineering new features that encourage and align with our ethical principles. We’re excited for the Transparency Portal to serve as another tool that our law enforcement partners can use to strengthen ties with their communities.” To view the ALPR transparency portal, visit https:// transparency.flocksafety.com/ piedmont-ca-pd. The police department’s full ALPR policy can be found at https://www. ci.piedmont.ca.us/UserFiles/ Servers/Server_13659739/File/ Gove r n me nt / De pa r t me nt s / Police%20Department/Automated_License_Plate_Readers__ ALPRs_%20(5).pdf. articles.text: Piedmont High School seniors Bridget Bentley and Helena Lowe were presented with the Gail Dryden Community Service Award at the school’s awards ceremony on June 1. The perpetual award is presented each year to deserving seniors demonstrating selfless service. The plaque is named for former School Board member Gail Dryden. Bentley has been a leader in Piedmont Scouting and was named winner of the William J Peterson Youth Leadership Award earlier in the year. Bentley co-founded the Repurpose Runway club in 2019 which upcycles clothing and donates the proceeds from a fashion show. Bentley served as president of the Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) this year and was in charge of the Cub Scout summer camp last year. She worked Bridget Bentley Helena Lowe extensively on helping renovate low-income homes with the program Rebuilding Together Oakland (RTO). She also participated in Youth Educators at school. She will be attending UC Berkeley in the fall next year with plans to major in Environmental Science. Lowe started off volunteering at the Chabot Space and Science Center as a Galaxy Explorer Volunteer, giving scientific demonstrations for the public. “I really loved teaching kids about science and being a source of inspiration for them.” said Lowe. She now interns at Chabot, participating in rocketry, telescope engineering and astronomy via machine learning. Lowe will attend Tufts University next year to study Computer Science.
articles.title: Bentley, Lowe win Gail Dryden Award

articles.text: Jay Russell Piedmont High School seniors Lynnea Boa, Athene La Jeunesse, and Emma Moorhead were awarded the Susan Kawaichi Diversity Plaque at the school’s awards ceremony on June 1. The award is named for Susan Kawaichi, co-founder of the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee, a former president of the Piedmont League of Women Voters, and a former member of the Piedmont School Board. During the summer of 2020, Moorhead, Boa and La Jeunesse worked toward passing the Racial Equity School Board policy following civil unrest and subsequent anti-racism movements. articles.text: The time is 5:25 on June 11, 2021, 15 months after the World Health Organization first declared COVID-19 a pandemic. Has it really been that long? For many of us, it feels like our life has been on pause. For such a fundamental idea, the concept of time is inscrutable. What does it mean for time to pass? To truly understand time, we need a conceptual approach. We often think of time as an arrow, linear and rigid, projecting ever forward into the future. Physicists have formulated many arrows of time, but only the psychological arrow, the one we all experience collectively, is germane to our day-to-day lives. In a sense, we are all time travelers, proceeding forward at the constant rate of one second per second. However, our perception of time is anything but constant. When we look back on our experiences, certain periods of time feel as though they lasted longer than others. Think back to, say, the Homecoming Dance in freshman year. Remember the anticipation as you waited in line for a breathalyzer test [outside] Alan Harvey Theater, walking down to the quad to meet friends in the central tent, dipping Oreos in the chocolate fondue fountain, posing in sunglasses and frilly pink scarves in the photo booth, and dancing, ears ringing, as loud music blasted from the speakers in the student center. Despite it only happening over the course of a few hours, I have countless memories from the dance, and it feels like it lasted for days. Now think about a random day during quarantine, say November 16, 2020. Do you remember anything about that day? It barely feels like it even happened. Our perception of time is not static, but dynamic; not rigid, but malleable. It is not an individual experience, but a collective one. the pandemic made our lives less memorable, and as a result, it feels like the time passed in the blink of an eye. Community is essential for not only our memories, but for our sense of time itself. For the past 15 months, our perception of time has been at the mercy of our isolation. But now, we have a unique opportunity to take time into our own hands. It’s about time that we un-pause our lives. By connecting with others, we can appreciate our time and have more to remember. Let’s go out into the world and make our lives memorable. The speech of Valedictorian Sam Eisenbach was given at Piedmont High School’s graduation ceremony on June 11, 2021.
articles.title: Valedictorian speech: “It’s about time”

articles.text: Piedmont residents Pamela Schwartz and Dr. Steve Sidney are creating a summer program of talks by Kaiser Permanente community health leaders and preventive health researchers targeted primarily to high school students. Examples of community health topics that are being considered are Kaiser Permanente’s efforts to address housing and food security. Possible health topics includes research-based guidelines for lifelong health and the health effects of vaping and of marijuana use. Schwartz and Sidney are planning a weekly series of talks over 6-8 weeks in July and August. Schwartz serves as the Executive Director of Community Health for Kaiser Permanente and leads Kaiser Permanente’s effort to address crucial social factors that affect people’s health. Those include food security, housing, social isolation, digital divide, and financial security aimed at transforming health care. Dr. Sidney is a senior research scientist and Director of Research Clinics at the Kaiser Permanente Division of Research. His research has focused on understanding the development of cardiovascular disease. Interested parents and students are encouraged to contact Schwartz at Pamela.M.Schwartz@ kp.org, or Dr. Sidney at Steve.Sidney@kp.org, stating a preference of in-person or virtual meetings, and preference of days and times of meetings. The museum has hand painted murals, vintage jukeboxes and rotating exhibits. No reservation is required. It is open Tuesday through Sunday 11:00 a.m. until 9:00 p.m. and until 10:00 p.m. on Friday and Saturday. Tilden Park Steam Train 2481 Grizzly Peak Blvd, Orinda 548-6100 Redwood-valley-railway.business.site Put the conductor hats on and head for the hills. Tilden’s Steam Trains are back. Kids will love hopping on the miniature steam train chugging along on 15 inch gauge tracks. Sit in an open-air cabin, ride the caboose or sit inside the luxurious miniature dining car. The Tilden Steam train has been in operation since 1952 and is now open weekends from 11:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Grab a $3 ticket for views of the bay and even traverse through dark tunnels while riding a real life Thomas the Tank Engine. Oakland Zoo 9777 Golf Links Rd, Oakland 632-9525 Oaklandzoo.org The Oakland Zoo continues to reopen exhibits and attractions that kids will love. The crowd favorite Petting Zoo area is now open for kids to feed goats with ice cream cones full of goat kibble. The Children’s California Wilds! Playground just reopened, where children can slide, spin, soar, and build in the five play zones inspired by the different native habitats of the zoo’s animals in its California Trail area. Make sure to stop by the giraffe exhibit to see the new 4-year old male giraffe Tsavo and the rest of the reticulate giraffe herd. Advanced ticketing is required. Celebrating 100 years of Scouting in Piedmont Piedmont’s Scout Council BSA is 100 years old and will be celebrating its Centennial throughout the year. Pick up a free yard sign at the council office at 10 Highland Way during business hours and join in the fun. For more information, call the Scout office at 547-4493. #ScoutMeIn

Ultimately, Ride gave up a potential career as a professional tennis player to follow what she loved: science. When NASA opened up their selection to women for the first time in 1978, Ride applied as a doctoral candidate at Stanford. She ultimately became one of the five female candidates selected, and she began her astronaut training the same year she received her PhD in astrophysics. Five years of NASA training and ground crew positions later, she boarded the Challenger and was hailed as the first American woman in space. As the expert with the shuttle’s robotic arm, she helped launch crucial satellites into orbit. Five months after her first mission she returned for a second mission to continue her work. However, following the 1986 Challenger disaster, Ride’s third flight was put on hold and she instead served on the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident. Later, she retired from NASA to teach and uplift women in STEM. After she came back to the ground from her second mission, Ride also fell in love with Tamara O’Shaughnessy, a docPhoto by Ron Sachs Astronaut Sally Ride carrying out a number of tasks simultaneously on the Challenger flight deck. Ride and O’Shaughnessy were strong advocates of science, writing children’s books together and founding Sally Ride Science to encourage girls in STEM. It was only after Ride’s death that it was revealed that they also had a successful and long-lasting relationship together. Ride was able to rise up despite the obstacles of sexism. articles.text: Piedmont Middle School’s graduation celebration, held on June 10, honored the 230 students in 8th grade. The ceremony featured four student speakers, a presentation from ASB members and congratulatory words from PMS administrators. The ceremony opened with 17 students welcoming the crowd in 17 different languages, a representation of the diverse background of the class. After welcoming remarks by Principal Ryan Fletcher, Dahlia Saffouri gave a speech as the first student speaker. “The past three years have been strenuous, and to some extent, a blur,” she said. “This has been the ultimate test, of not only our resilience, but also the strengths of our Wi-Fi networks, and the capacity of Schoology. As well as our own dilemmas, the country was in the middle of a polarizing election, California battled severe wildfires, and many of us partook in the Black Lives Matter marches to protest racial injustice. “With our newfound resilience and confidence, we are more than ready for the challenges ahead,” she said. Eighth grade speaker Inaya Majid said, “If this year has taught us anything, it is to look for the silver lining. As we slowly log off, whenever you come across a struggle, look back and remember this odd yet resilient year where we, students, teachers, families, all persevered. As we progress to high school and the future, we should go out into the world, face our unique challenges, and make no apologies for who we are.” The third student speaker, Faizan Kashmiri, described the journey to graduation as “a long, ever-twisting, roller-coaster ride. Despite every curve ball, every hurdle, every crazy thing thrown at us through these times, we are able to stand here today, permanently united, teacher and student Piedmont Middle School 8th grades students walk up the Witter Field stairs after receiving their graduation certificates. Luella Helmy celebrates receiving her 8th grade diploma and Sophie Hess (right) waits for her name to be called. Principal Ryan Fletcher reflects on the soon-to-be-freshmen, the PHS class of 2025. Benjamin Sachs takes a bow after receiving his credentials from Principal Fletcher. Claire Weiss gives the final speech at the 8th grade graduation celebration on June 10 at Witter Field. ASB representatives (left) Genevieve Hiller and Juliana DeYoung address the crowd after the presentations of certificates. Emmett Asulin (left) followed by Bruno Banuelos lead their class down the Witter Field stairs past the large crowd on hand June 10, for 8th grade graduation.

articles.text: Millennium High honored the 23 graduates of the 2021 class on Thursday, June 10 with a live ceremony at Witter Field. Normally, the ceremony is an intimate event at the Veterans Hall, but the event the last two years have been outdoors at Witter Field. The ceremony began with a welcoming address by Principal Shannon Fierro. Nick Safir, a MHS Paraeducator and high school baseball coach followed with remarks on the recent graduates. “I cannot thank this place and the class of 2021 enough for the amazing memories it has given me,” said Safir. MHS Student Body President Blaise Harrison gave a lively speech, thanking her peers and the Millennium staff. “We’ve had a wild run of high school, but this adventure could not have been completed without each and every staff member,” she said. She then listed off every staff member and called them, “Important, unforgettable and incredibly impactful.” Perpetual school awards, presented at graduation each year, were presented to Ken Yale Leadership Award Blaise Harrison Millennium Spirit Award Victoria Houston Personal Achievement Award Samson Bhatti Seth Marason-Banquer Community Contribution Award Harmonee Ross Alyssa Ultreras Also congratulated for their excellence were: Nakilah Johnson, who was named Piedmont High School’s Outstanding Female Athlete. Honors Society members included: Nakilah Johnson, Asa Goldberg-Berman, Ang Lee and Alyssa Ulteras. Millennium Student Body President Blaise Harrison receives her diploma from Principal Shannon Fierro before heading to Lewis and Clark University in Portland. Millennium Principal Shannon Fierro with graduate Samson Bhatti and his parents. Nakilah Johnson approaches the podium to receive her diploma. She won PUSD’s Female Athlete of the Year Award, and in the fall will be attending Weber State in Ogden, Utah, to play Div. 1 basketball. articles.text: After the sports year was reduced from nine months to three due to pandemic-related closures and schedule changes, school is now out for the summer. Piedmont’s Class of 2021 now prepares for the next chapter its academic and athletic career. Without league championships, North Coast Section playoffs or CIF State tournaments, all sports had severely truncated seasons, making our selection of top athletic performances all the more difficult. In an unusual topsy-turvy year, each athlete and coach at PHS deserves additional praise. As California drops most restrictions yesterday, June 15, this is a time to celebrate the accomplishments of individual athletes and Piedmont sports teams. It is a time to honor all of them for making the most out of all situations and overcoming nearly all obstacles. Without further ado, the Post is pleased to announce that Makenna Thiel of tennis, and Luke Harris of basketball have been named Athletes of the Year, with basketball star Kai Johnson of two-sport athlete Brian Cain as Honorable Mention. Makenna Thiel, Tennis Makenna Thiel graduates from Piedmont High as one of the most dominant tennis players in school history. In 30 appearances during her three years on the varsity, she lost one match. She was named Athlete of the Year as a sophomore. She will be playing for the University of California’s Pac-12 Championship program in the fall. In 2021, Thiel won the WestStaff Photo Staff Photo sport athlete with baseball as a sophomore and junior. He’s been the workhorse of coach Jerome Johnson’s offense, defense, and special teams for the past two years, helping lead the program to a perfect 5-0 finish in its shortened season after the team went 3-7 in 2019. In 2021, Cain recorded 721 rushing yards on 122 attempts to average 5.91 yards per carry with 14 touchdowns. He averaged an Staff Photo
articles.title: The Piedmont Post’s Athletes of the Year: Makenna Thiel & Luke Harris

Her teams went 20-2 as a freshman and 21-2-2 as a sophomore. She returned to her schedule of outside Tournaments during junior year. This year Thiel never lost a set was the No. 1 seed in the WACC Singles Championship. During the WACC Tournament April 16-17, Thiel opened with a 6-0, 6-1 win over Bishop O’Dowd’s Marianne Taner 6-0, 6-1, shut out Berkeley’s Estelle Handa 6-0, 6-0 in the semifinals, and handled Kyra Yee of Alameda 6-0, 6-1 in the finals. Aside from her success on the PHS team, Thiel earned her rank as a premier U.S. tennis recruit by competing in prestigious tournaments throughout the country. She won third place at the Premier Tennis Tour Las Vegas Hard 2 on May 30, and advanced to the semifinals of the PTT Newport Beach Women’s Hard 5 on May 8. Luke Harris, Basketball Luke Harris concluded his career at Piedmont High with over 1,200 points scored. He’s now the second consecutive basketball player to be named Athlete of the Year. Luke Barrett was last year’s winner. Harris finished the year with 383 points with a sterling 55 percent shooting, 85 free throws made, 46 assists, and 33 steals. In 2021, he improved his career-high in scoring to 35 points in two separate games, a season-opening 88-82 win over Northgate on April 20 and against Castro Valley on April 30. Makenna Thiel is the Post’s two-time Athlete of the Year after concluding her varsity career with a Div. 1 NCS Double title, and WACC Singles title. A three-year starter, he’s part of three highly successful teams. The team was 21-11 when he was a sophomore. Last year he was the leading scorer on Piedmont’s NCS Championship team, the only time the school has won the North Coast Section title. That team finished 24-6, and this year in a pandemic-shortened season, it was 11-5. As a sophomore, Harris led PHS to NCS Semifinals for the first time, making the school’s debut in the CIF State Tournament. They reached the D4 Regional Semifinals. In his junior year, Harris led the team in scoring with 538 points. He was electric in their NCS Championship victory over St. Mary’s with a game-high 29 points and 14-of-15 free throws. On their way to the section finals, Harris scored 14 against No. 4 University and 22 against No. 6 Eureka. He also set a career high of 33 points against El Cerrito. Prior to the pandemic, Harris was a two-sport athlete, batting on the baseball team, batting .370 with 10 hits, five RBIs and seven runs scored as an outfielder. He will be playing basketball at Carlton College in Minnesota next year. Luke Harris becomes the Post’s second consecutive basketball star to win Athlete of the Year.
