pages.text: 12 Wednesday, June 16, 2021 Sports The Piedmont Post’s Athletes of the Year: Makenna Thiel & Luke Harris Honorable Mention: Kai Johnson, Brian Cain By Jonathan Comeaux After the sports year was reduced from nine months to three due to pandemic-related closures and schedule changes, school is now out for the summer. Piedmont’s Class of 2021 now prepares for the next chapter its academic and athletic career. Without league championships, North Coast Section playoffs or CIF State tournaments, all sports had severely truncated seasons, making our selection of top athletic performances all the more difficult. In an unusual topsy-turvy year, each athlete and coach at PHS deserves additional praise. As California drops most restrictions yesterday, June 15, this is a time to celebrate the accomplishments of individual athletes and Piedmont sports teams. It is a time to honor all of them for making the most out of all situations and overcoming nearly all obstacles. Without further ado, the Post is pleased to announce that Makenna Thiel of tennis, and Luke Harris of basketball have been named Athletes of the Year, with basketball star Kai Johnson of two-sport athlete Brian Cain as Honorable Mention. Makenna Thiel, Tennis Makenna Thiel graduates from Piedmont High as one of the most dominant tennis players in school history. In 30 appearances during her three years on the varsity, she lost one match. She was named Athlete of the Year as a sophomore. She will be playing for the University of California’s Pac-12 Championship program in the fall. In 2021, Thiel won the Western Alameda County Conference (League) singles championship. She also won the North Coast Section Div. 1 doubles championship in 2019 with Lauren Young. Her teams went 20-2 as a freshman and 21-2-2 as a sophomore. She returned to her schedule of outside Tournaments during junior year. This year Thiel never lost a set was the No. 1 seed in the WACC Singles Championship. During the WACC Tournament April 16-17, Thiel opened with a 6-0, 6-1 win over Bishop O’Dowd’s Marianne Taner 6-0, 6-1, shut out Berkeley’s Estelle Handa 6-0, 6-0 in the semifinals, and handled Kyra Yee of Alameda 6-0, 6-1 in the finals. Aside from her success on the PHS team, Thiel earned her rank as a premier U.S. tennis recruit by competing in prestigious tournaments throughout the country. She won third place at the Premier Tennis Tour Las Vegas Hard 2 on May 30, and advanced to the semifinals of the PTT Newport Beach Women’s Hard 5 on May 8. Luke Harris, Basketball Luke Harris concluded his career at Piedmont High with over 1,200 points scored. He’s now the second consecutive basketball player to be named Athlete of the Year. Luke Barrett was last year’s winner. Harris finished the year with 383 points with a sterling 55 percent shooting, 85 free throws made, 46 assists, and 33 steals. In 2021, he improved his career-high in scoring to 35 points in two separate games, a season-opening 88-82 win over Northgate on April 20 and against Castro Valley on April 30. Makenna Thiel is the Post’s two-time Athlete of the Year after concluding her varsity career with a Div. 1 NCS Double title, and WACC Singles title. A three-year starter, he’s part of three highly successful teams. The team was 21-11 when he was a sophomore. Last year he was the leading scorer on Piedmont’s NCS Championship team, the only time the school has won the North Coast Section title. That team finished 24-6, and this year in a pandemic-shortened season, it was 11-5. As a sophomore, Harris led PHS to NCS Semifinals for the first time, making the school’s debut in the CIF State Tournament. They reached the D4 Regional Semifinals. In his junior year, Harris led the team in scoring with 538 points. He was electric in their NCS Championship victory over St. Mary’s with a game-high 29 points and 14-of-15 free throws. On their way to the section finals, Harris scored 14 against No. 4 University and 22 against No. 6 Eureka. He also set a career high of 33 points against El Cerrito. Prior to the pandemic, Harris was a two-sport athlete, batting on the baseball team, batting .370 with 10 hits, five RBIs and seven runs scored as an outfielder. He will be playing basketball at Carlton College in Minnesota next year. HONORABLE MENTION Kai Johnson, Basketball Kai Johnson is a four-year starter under coach Bryan Gardere, bursting onto the scene in 2017. She’s been the team captain for the past two seasons and was the only senior on this year’s roster. Johnson has been a major part of a strong four-year run for the girls’ basketball team, with season records of 23-7 in 2017/2018, 20-11 in 2018/2019, 21-7 in 2019/2020. This year in a shortened season, the posted a 15-3 record. This year’s team undoubtedly would’ve received a top seeding in NCS and CIF tournaments. Luke Harris becomes the Post’s second consecutive basketball star to win Athlete of the Year. She is the only female basketball player at Piedmont High to hold two victories over Bishop O’Dowd since PHS joined the Western Alameda County Conference in 2012. She will be joini9ing the Div. 1 Weber State team in Ogden, Utah later this year. Brian Cain, Football Brian Cain is a two-year starter for the varsity football team. He’s also a former twosport athlete with baseball as a sophomore and junior. He’s been the workhorse of coach Jerome Johnson’s offense, defense, and special teams for the past two years, helping lead the program to a perfect 5-0 finish in its shortened season after the team went 3-7 in 2019. In 2021, Cain recorded 721 rushing yards on 122 attempts to average 5.91 yards per carry with 14 touchdowns. articles.text: Loud and Proud, a virtual concert sponsored by the San Francisco Lesbian/Gay Freedom Band, will showcase performances by thirteen LGBTQIA+ bands and will stream for free. The bands will cover musical genres from pop, symphonic, classical, modern, soundtrack, and more. There will also be a joint shared performance by musicians across all featured bands. The San Francisco Lesbian/ Gay Freedom Band, the first openly-gay musical organization in the world, is organizing the logistics for the event. The concert will feature musical groups across the country, including the Mid America Freedom Band of Kansas City, Triangle Pride Band, Queen City Freedom Band, Mile High Freedom Band, South Florida Pride Wind Ensemble, and more. Loud and Proud is a free streaming event, but you need to register to watch. There will be two showings on Saturday, June 26, at 4 p.m. and again at 7 p.m. Visit https://loudandproudconcert.sflgfb.org/ to register.

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre has announced a return to live theatre this fall with a robust program of performances, including world premieres. Seven productions are slated to begin this fall. A full list of productions is available at https://www.berkeleyrep. org/season/, with descriptions from directors. Berkeley Rep Theatre released a theatrical experiment in six movements, The Waves in Quarantine, inspired by a stage adaption of Virginia Woolf’s The Waves. Written and directed by Lisa Peterson, the show invites audiences into the creative process. that meditate on themes from the musical adaption of the novel. The play builds on Woolf’s prose to reveal an intimate look at the marriage of art and isolation. The play circles around themes of music in unexpected places, the intimacy of strangers, and metaphor in the ordinary. The episodic movements include “Memory,” “Those We Love,” “The Female Gaze,” “Absence,” “The Sun Cycle,” and “Reunion.” Music and lyrics are by David Bucknam, and additional music and lyrics are provided by Adam Gwon. The play is being streamed now through June 30. Visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/season/2021/15964.asp to stream. Lisa Peterson is directing The Waves in Quarantine at Berkeley Rep now through June 30. Woolf’s novel, which the play is adapted from, is considered her most experimental work. The book consists of soliloquies spoken by six characters; similarly, the play is told in six movements

articles.text: West Edge Opera will perform outside this summer with a series of performances at Bruns Amphitheater in Orinda from July 24 through August 8. West Edge Opera, originally the Berkeley Opera, was created in 1979 by Cal professor Richard Goodman. The company, under music director Jonathan Khuner and general director Mark Streshinsky, focuses primarily on lesser-known, contemporary, and avant-garde operas. West Edge Opera’s summer productions are titled West Edge Festival with three programs of music. The festival has been conducted in unconventional performance spaces, including the abandoned 16th street train station, the Pacific Pipe warehouse, and in 2019, in Oakland’s Bridge Yard under the Bay Bridge. Bruns Amphitheater became the festival’s home for its 2021 season through a partnership with California Shakespeare Theater (Cal Shakes). Cal Shakes announced that it will be sharing the Bruns Amphitheater in Orinda this summer with other arts organizations. Berkeley Symphony, West Edge Opera, Destiny Arts and Bandloop are among the organizations who will perform or host events there. “What gives us our proverbial edge is that our venue at the Bruns is in the open air, which makes a big difference. Even if everyone has the vaccine, it is likely that we’ll all be sporting fabulous West Edge Opera masks, and distancing,” said Streshinsky. Visit https://www.westedgeopera.org/festival-2021 to obtain tickets. Series tickets are now available, and single-day tickets go on sale on Friday, June 18.
articles.title: West Edge Opera to perform at Bruns Amphitheater

articles.text: San Francisco’s American Conservatory Theater will present a special online screening of Armistead Maupin’s Tales of the City: The Musical, to stream on Broadway on Demand’s National Theater Network during San Francisco’s Pride Week, June 25-27. “As San Francisco returns and we celebrate Pride anew this month, I’m thrilled to have ACT’s beloved musical and Armistead Maupin’s characters be part of the celebration,” Director Pam MacKinnon said. “This is a show that deserved a longer life. We’re grateful to have this simple but beautiful archival capture that represents the city, where we were, and who we can be.” A week prior to the musical release affords you enough time to introduce, or re-introduce, yourself to Maupin’s series of novels chronicling the lives of fictional San Franciscans in the late 1970’s. Portions of the novels, which were adapted as a miniseries with Olympia Dukakis and Laura Linney, and again as a Netflix series in 2019 starring Elliot Page, were published as a newspaper serial in 1974 in Marin County’s The Pacific Sun, the longest running alternative weekly in the nation. The success of Maupin’s serial prompted the San Francisco Chronicle to pick it up two years later, and HarperCollins published it as a book two years after that in 1978. Tales of the City is a series of nine novels. They are binge-worthy and excellent beach, park, or overall-summer reads. The series begins with protagonist Mary Anne Singleton, a “naive young woman from Cleveland” who is visiting San Francisco for vacaLaura Linney (left) and Olympia Dukakis as Mary Anne Singleton and Anna Madrigal in the first television adaption of Armistead Maupin’s Tales of the City. tion and impulsively decides to stay after falling in love with the culture and “scene.” “The worst of times in San Francisco was still better than the best of times anywhere else,” was Mary Ann’s rationale to her mother for not returning to Ohio. San Francisco in the 1970’s becomes a character in itself in the series of novels and Maupin does a stellar job narrating and observing through the wide eyes of a Midwestern transplant. He was born in Washington D.C. and attended college at University of North Carolina in Chapel Hill but has always said that San Francisco is where he feels most at home. Tales of the City covers a group of misfits, 20-and-30- somethings in one house located at the fictional 28 Barbary Lane, headed by Anna Madrigal. Maupin is widely accepted in the literary community as one of the first writers to address the subject of the AIDS epidemic in his 1983 novel Babycakes, a continuation of the “Tales” series. Of the autobiographical nature of his characters, he said, “I’ve always been all of the characters in one way or another.” The book series in the 70’s and 80’s served as a sparkling, semi-soap opera. Reviewers on GoodReads.com affectionately call it a “time capsule” and “an indelible portrait of an era that changed forever the way we live.” The series evolved into a Netflix drama and addressed, 40 years later, gentrification and how the “dot-com boom” rattled native San Franciscans. Maupin’s laughout-loud narration is all, clearly, an homage to the city he loves - he wrote in his first in the series, “if [Mary Anne Singleton] ever had a child, she would want him to grow up in San Francisco - where Mardi Gras was celebrated five times a year.” Netflix’s Tales of the City was released one year before Olympia Dukakis passed away. For information on how to watch ACT’s musical adaption, visit www.act-sf.org/whatson/20202122-season/tales-of-thecity.
articles.title: ACT to present screening of Tales of the City: The Musical on June 27

articles.text: Let the royal family of England enjoy the crown jewels. Simple pleasures are often the best. This philosophy was driven home to me on Saturday afternoon, and it came as an unexpected surprise. My wife suggested an early dinner at Anaviv in Richmond. Surprisingly, it isn’t in downtown Richmond. Quite the opposite. It is situated just off Highway 580 near the entrance to the San Rafael bridge and appears to be more a parking lot than a restaurant. But don’t let that bother you. The restaurant itself has a Spartan ambience. Everything is outdoors. There is a woodfired oven, simple tables and chairs, and a few umbrellas. What Anaviv lacks in ambience, they compensate with enthusiasm. Service is good and so is the food. The menu is modest. There are a few starters and snacks. We chose charcoal roasted asparagus ($12). The slender spears of asparagus were charcoal roasted to perfection and served with an elegant sauce. For our main dish, we chose a pizza margarita ($20) and added some hen of the woods mushrooms. You could imagine that you were in a simple outdoor restaurant in Naples, enjoying a soft crust pizza while the hot sun beats down. (Remember to wear a hat on sunny days.) For dessert we ordered a beautiful combination of ube and avocado ice cream with a jellied coconut panna cotta. Curiously, the waitress brought the panna cotta at the same time as the pizza. Upon request, they brought it back at the end of the meal. Anaviv has live musical entertainment three days a week. The food in the restaurant is well worth the price. But when you add in the entertainment, it is an amazing bargain. The show began with a few flamenco guitar solos. It was apparent from the beginning that the show would be memorable. The guitarist’s stage name is Keni el Lebrijano. Close your eyes when you listen and you’ll be transported to a gypsy cave in Seville or Granada. It was obvious to me from the first notes that Keni lives and breathes flamenco. In a few minutes he was joined by two women and a man. The entire audience became energized with excitement. The man began to sing in authentic canto hondo style. He looked the part and sang with the passion that is so characteristic of a great flamenco singers. The two women took turns on the dance floor. You could tell that the audience was really appreciating the music. A woman from the audience got up and started to dance. She was every bit a professional dancer, but her performance was impromptu. I spoke with her during the break, and she told me that she is a professional dancer. It turns out that she was the dance partner of one of my school classmates. She is Andrea la Canela. They say that people are beginning to travel internationally once again. Travel is still a hassle. Do yourself a favor. You don’t need to go to the Gypsy caves in Seville. Anaviv will do just fine.
articles.title: Flamenco and pizza in Richmond

articles.text: Opera San Jose has announced its 2021-22 season, to include in-person performances beginning this November in the California Theatre. The season launches with a production of Rimsky-Korsakov’s Mozart and Salieri, followed by Purcell’s Dido and Aeneas, Bizet’s Carmen, and Bernstein’s West Side Story to close. “This season, we explore the necessity of human connection. We explore love—and love interrupted. We witness people who are confronted by a world incompatible with who they are or who they wish to be,” General Director Khori Dastoor said. Mozart and Salieri, a Heiman Digital Media Studio production, will begin as a live-streamed capture in September. Subscribers will receive access to the production. Based on Alexander Pushkin’s play of the same name, the psychological drama follows the Italian composer Antonio Salieri and his envy of Mozart’s musical genius. Conducted by Donato Cabrera and directed by Fenlon Lamb, the play incorporates quotations from Mozart’s Requiem and Don Giovanni; Baritone Sidney Outlaw stars as Salieri. Dido and Aeneas will launch Opera San Jose’s return to live performances, beginning on November 13. Starting in November, patrons will enjoy earlier performance times. Evening performances will begin at 7:30 p.m., and matinees will begin at 2 p.m. For more information on COVID protocols and to obtain tickets to upcoming live performances, visit https:// www.operasj.org/subscriptions/. Patrons of Opera San Jose will return for live performances in California Theatre in November.
articles.title: 2021-22 season opens with Mozart and Salieri

articles.text: Oakland Symphony recently announced a return to live performances for its 2021-22 season, to begin on October 15 at the Paramount Theatre. For its upcoming season, Oakland Symphony will be following the developing recommendations and regulations of the Alameda County Public Health Department, which may include social distancing, mask wearing, and proof of vaccination or negative COVID testing. Subscriptions are not yet available for online purchase at this time, but for renewing subscribers, seats will be held until October 1 to allow patrons to monitor the county’s re-opening. All seven concerts will be available for the price of five. The return to live performances begins on Friday, October 15, with Music Maestro Michael Morgan conducting and to Oakland Symphony Artistic Director Michael Morgan include violinist Natasha Makhijani. Samuel Coleridge-Taylor’s “Ballade,” Mozart’s Violin Concerto No. 5 and Antonin Dvorak’s Symphony No. 8 are included in the first program. All performances will take place at Oakland’s Paramount Theatre. Call 510-444-0802 or visit https://www.oaklandsymphony. org/tickets/subscriptions/ for ticketing information.
articles.title: Oakland Symphony announces live concerts in fall

Oakland Symphony announces live concerts in fall An excellent flamenco show is part on the allure at Anaviv in Richmond. Flamenco and pizza in Richmond By Joseph Gold Let the royal family of England enjoy the crown jewels. Simple pleasures are often the best. This philosophy was driven home to me on Saturday afternoon, and it came as an unexpected surprise. My wife suggested an early dinner at Anaviv in Richmond. Surprisingly, it isn’t in downtown Richmond. Quite the opposite. It is situated just off Highway 580 near the entrance to the San Rafael bridge and appears to be more a parking lot than a restaurant. But don’t let that bother you. The restaurant itself has a Spartan ambience. Everything is outdoors. There is a woodfired oven, simple tables and chairs, and a few umbrellas. What Anaviv lacks in ambience, they compensate with enthusiasm. Service is good and so is the food. The menu is modest. There are a few starters and snacks. We chose charcoal roasted asparagus ($12). The slender spears of asparagus were charcoal roasted to perfection and served with an elegant sauce. For our main dish, we chose a pizza margarita ($20) and added some hen of the woods mushrooms. You could imagine that you were in a simple outdoor restaurant in Naples, enjoying a soft crust pizza while the hot sun beats down. (Remember to wear a hat on sunny days.) For dessert we ordered a beautiful combination of ube and avocado ice cream with a jellied coconut panna cotta. Curiously, the waitress brought the panna cotta at the same time as the pizza. Upon request, they brought it back at the end of the meal. Anaviv has live musical entertainment three days a week. The food in the restaurant is well worth the price. But when you add in the entertainment, it is an amazing bargain. The show began with a few flamenco guitar solos. It was apparent from the beginning that the show would be memorable. The guitarist’s stage name is Keni el Lebrijano. Close your eyes when you listen and you’ll be transported to a gypsy cave in Seville or Granada. It was obvious to me from the first notes that Keni lives and breathes flamenco. In a few minutes he was joined by two women and a man. The entire audience became energized with excitement. The man began to sing in authentic canto hondo style. He looked the part and sang with the passion that is so characteristic of a great flamenco singers. The two women took turns on the dance floor. You could tell that the audience was really appreciating the music. A woman from the audience got up and started to dance. She was every bit a professional dancer, but her performance was impromptu. I spoke with her during the break, and she told me that she is a professional dancer. It turns out that she was the dance partner of one of my school classmates. She is Andrea la Canela. They say that people are beginning to travel internationally once again. Travel is still a hassle. Do yourself a favor. You don’t need to go to the Gypsy caves in Seville. Anaviv will do just fine. Francis Ford Coppola’s The Outsiders will be shown at Fort Mason’s Drive-In Theater this Saturday. Coppola’s film is based on the S.E. Hinton novel of the same name. It focuses on class struggles experienced by two groups of Oklahoma teenagers in the 1960s and captures the feelings of being caught between childhood and adulthood. It was released in 1983 and has a runtime of 90 minutes. The cast includes C. Thomas Howell, Matt Dillon, Diane Lane, Ralph Macchio, Patrick Swayze, Rob Lowe, Emilio Estevez, Tom Cruise, and Tom Waits. The film inspired the Brat Pack genre of the 1980s. articles.text: By Allyson Aleksey “In Between Art and Science,” an art exhibit by Piedmont artist Nina Reeves, will be on display at the Piedmont Center for the Arts the weekend of June 26-27. “My paintings strive to merge abstraction, figurative elements and the origin of culture and its influence,” Reeves said. “Each component translates in the work through layering, color, and depth, seeking a unique perspective to approach art practice. The exhibit is the most recent body of work that explores figurative elements to elaborate the development of culture.” The artist intends the viewer to be hovered over the painting, looking into scientific structures through an abstract composition, layering, texture, and color. She uses digitized tissue samples as a base for an abstract composition. “I direct the viewer by creating a visual language that dissects abstraction through the means of science. The visual language is articulated with different layers Artist Nina Reeves of strokes and color, revealing the nature of my practice. The colors create an energy that mirrors the brushstrokes and creates a sense of depth,” Reeves said. Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday, June 26-June 27. The Piedmont Center for the Arts is at 801 Magnolia Avenue. “Cellular Division Two,” acrylic, oil, medium on MDF 48” x 48”
articles.title: Nina Reeves art exhibit at PCA next weekend

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony, under the guidance of consulting firm Elevated Diversity, will host a series of listening sessions that will provide “a crucial foundation for [the] work ahead,” said symphony Executive Director Jim Tibbs. It is one aspect of the symphony’s Inclusion, Equity, Diversity, and Access (IDEA) project, to begin this summer. “The sessions are intended to provide an opportunity for you to share your perspectives and insights relating to inclusion, diversity, equity, and access at Berkeley Symphony,” Tibbs said. The symphony was awarded a $19,500 grant from the League of American Orchestras, with the purpose of strengthening their understanding of diversity, equity and inclusion. Berkeley Symphony has engaged Elevated Diversity, a diversity, equity and inclusion consultancy and training organization based in California, to assist in engagement projects this summer. The organization’s mission is to help other organizations “create workplaces where diversity is viewed as a competitive strength and where inclusion is woven into the very fabric of our culture.” “We are beyond thrilled to have been selected to work with the Berkeley Symphony on this incredibly important initiative,” Founder of Elevated Diversity Rhonda Moret said. “Being arts lovers ourselves, we find the project to be highly engaging and without experience and expertise working with other organizations in the arts space, we feel like we are the perfect group to ensure the effort a successful one.” A listening session is similar to a “focus group” in which participants are asked to candidly share their experiences and answers on-topic questions. The goal of these sessions is to better understand the opportunities, and challenges, surrounding a topic as each individual perceives them. Sessions will be conducted via Zoom, and are designed as a set-structured roundtable discussion. Those who wish to participate in a listening session may register your interest via a Google form at https://docs.google.com/ forms/d/e/1FAIpQLScg9-6l5r7BpqWcNXyHIXmmRtoMFxA6wgm-HBZUpawriOv8lw/viewform. Berkeley staff will reach out to interested participants about next steps. These sessions will last approximately one hour.
articles.title: Berkeley Symphony hosts listening sessions in diversity project

articles.text: Piedmont High School seniors enjoyed a last evening together as the class of 2021 on Wednesday, June 6, prior to their official graduation ceremony that Friday. The Senior Spirit Committee created a “Senior Sunset,” a modified version of Day on the Green, held two nights before graduation at Witter Field. The event included the Mr. Softee ice cream truck sponsored by Debbi DiMaggio and Adam Betta, a noodle food truck, and a plethora of jubilant high school seniors. “The Senior Spirit Committee was formed earlier in the academic year when there was still no in-person attendance,” Committee Chair Anne Callahan explained. Students faced a few obstacles in the planning process due to the restraints brought by the COVID-19 pandemic, but nothing was too large to deter them from creating an appropriate send-off for their peers. “Our goal had always been bringing the student body together in a safe manner. Throughout the year, we worked closely with district administraCouncilmember Betsy Andersen and Anne Callahan. Students line up at the California Garlic Noodle truck. tion and finally got the go-ahead to create an event for seniors,” Callahan said. Senior Class Parent Representatives Michele Helm, Laura Katter, Susan Ormond and Teela Shine “worked around the clock” to make the event happen, Callahan said. “It took a lot of planning, many Zoom calls, and working with [restrictions] that change almost daily,” she said. It proved to be a great success, with almost all of the 230 students from Piedmont High and Millennium High School attending. The event was free for all seniors. articles.text: As we walk through the city at a pace slow enough to appreciate the many fine structures in town, it is clear that the building materials used are one of the major components of both the style and quality of the architecture. In fact, all the architectural styles we have been discussing are built of certain materials that have long been developed, along with the building forms, to define the different styles. There are many overlapping and intertwined considerations in the selection of building materials, including aesthetics, cost, durability, and structural qualities. But maybe local availability was, and still is, the driving force. The ancient Egyptians didn’t build extensively with wood because they didn’t have much of it. articles.text: The First Mondays Reading Group, sponsored by the Recreation Department, welcomed Piedmont author Shanti Brien at its June 7 meeting for a discussion about her recently released book Almost Innocent. Fifteen readers called in to talk with her. Participating were: Mike Bandrowski, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Margie Blodgett, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Albert Chen, Pat McSwain, Alicia Rivera, Sally Arney, Jamie Forsythe, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. Brien is a criminal defense attorney and the wife of a former NFL player. In Almost Innocent, she writes about our criminal justice system based upon her own experience and the stories of nine of her previously convicted felon clients. The conversation took place before the group’s regular June discussion of President Obama’s new memoir, A Promised Land. Brien did a brief reading from her book, made some comments, and then opened the talk to accept questions. She said that her clients were happy to be included in the book so that their stories would be told. Her hope is that these and other, similar situations will create “radical empathy” for injustice in the system; and that some reform will result. Shanti said that everyone can do something. One of the most basic things is for voters to make informed choices about district attorneys, who have great control in the system. She also talked about the process of writing a book. It took nearly three years to initially write the book, and another two to three years of editing, plus five years to find an agent. Publishers are hesitant about first time authors because the financial uncertainty associated with them. The profit margins associated with publishing are thin. Publishers prefer proven authors or established “personalities.” She encouraged anyone with a desire to write a book to “just start writing chunks” of content. The 40-minute conversation was highly enjoyable and informative. For more information, visit: https://www.shantibrien.com/. A Promised Land This memoir by former President Barack Obama (2009-2017) was published in November 2020 and is the first of a planned two-volume series. The book covers Obama’s life from his early years through the events surrounding the killing of Osama bin Laden in May 2011. The book has received good reviews from the New York Times, The Washington Post, and The Guardian. Commercially, it has been extremely successful and was on the New York Times best-seller list in non-fiction for eight weeks. It is 768 pages long, has been translated into two dozen languages, and is also available as a 28-hour audiobook with Obama reading it in its entirety. The book is a unique, thoughtful, intimate, and revealing exploration of Obama’s personal and family lives. There are insights into the people and leaders with whom he interacted, as well as the impact pf presidential power. The readers agreed that Obama is a masterful writer and his prose is enjoyable to read. It was noted that he writes the way he talks, eloquently and expansively. The group especially enjoyed the details about Obama’s life and personal anecdotes. He describes his relationship and interactions with his wife, Michelle, shows her strength and importance during his presidency. The candid impressions of world leaders are fascinating, including the events leading up to the killing of Osama bin Laden. While the positive aspects of the book are undeniable, some readers had issues. Obama’s writing covers all facets of an issue, action, or event. All the details can be a challenge, especially with situations that are most appealing to politicians and public policy makers. The book’s length can also be a challenge, and some readers found it tedious at times. Some found it more of a history book than a memoir. The group said it was pleased to have selected and read A Promised Land. Additionally, the book reminded many of what it was like just a short time ago in our nation, and candidly in a happier time. With their book conversations complete, the group discussed future books to read. For July they had previously selected the timely fiction Interior Chinatown by Charles Yu. For August, September, and October respectively, they picked The Fire Next Time by James Baldwin, Deacon King Kong by James McBride, and Nomadland by Jessica Bruder. The group will meet next in a Zoom call on Monday, July 5, at 1:30 p.m. New members are always welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required by contacting John Wilk at jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov.

New hours are 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Wednesday through Sunday. The Bookmark Bookstore is located in Old Oakland, at 721 Washington Street. The store will follow Alameda County Public Health protocols and CDC guidelines. Masks are required for entry into the store, use of hand sanitizer is required upon entering the store, and capacity will be managed to maintain distance of 6 feet from others. To prepare for reopening, the store manager and volunteer staff have received, sorted, priced and shelved thousands of donated books, CDs, DVDs, and puzzles. All inventory is donated by the public. The Bookmark Bookstore continues to accept donations of books by appointment. Guidelines for materials accepted are posted on the website at www. fopl.org/the-bookmark. Members of the Friends of the Oakland Public Library receive a 20% discount on their in-store purchases. Learn more about membership at www.fopl.org/ get-involved. “We look forward to welcoming everyone back,” said store manager Phyllis Couillard. Shopping online still available The Friends of Oakland Public Library (FPL) has a mission to financially support independent bookstores. Browse booklists curated by the Friends with suggestions from Oakland librarians, then shop for new books, puzzles, notecards and more. Bookshop digital gift cards make great gifts. And your gift keeps giving: The Friends receives 25- 30% of each sale through this website: https:// bookshop.org/shop/theBookmarkBookstore. All purchases support the Oakland Public Library. The Bookmark Bookstore is located in Old Oakland at 721 Washington Street.

articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will present a Zoom-based discussion on criminal justice reform with Piedmont resident Shanti Brien as guest speaker on June 22. An attorney and reform advocate, Brien will speak on what individuals and organizations do for criminal justice reform and racial justice. She will take questions from audience members. The forum will be online through Zoom on Tuesday, June 22 at 4 p.m. Brien’s book Almost Innocent: From searching to saved in America’s criminal justice system was published last month. It chronicles her experiences growing up in the central valley, becoming an attorney, and representing convicted individuals. Brien said that she “reimagines the current criminal justice system as smaller, fairer, and more humane.” Brien is a member of the Muscogee Creek Nation, and a graduate of UC Berkeley and Stanford Law School. As a former criminal defense lawyer, she co-founded Fogbreak Justice, an organization that collaborates with criminal justice professionals to reduce bias and build community trust to create equitable outcomes. She is also a writer and speaker on social justice issues in criminal law and policy. As a Piedmont resident, she has served on the Public Safety Committee, is a member of the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC), and participates in the Piedmont Race and Equity Campaign (PREC). To join in the discussion, register at: https://www. lw v pied mont.org /content. aspx?page_id=4002&club_ id=601389&item_id=1441599. Registrants will receive an email with the Zoom link. This event is free and open to all. The talk will be recorded and can be viewed later on the League of Women Voters Piedmont YouTube Channel: https:// www.youtube.com/channel/ UC3v 6 0XG m r13V_ 9WaYj6qUJg/featured.

articles.text: East Bay Republican Women gathered for its first in-person event on June 10. The speaker was Jonathan Madison, Bay Area Regional Vice Chair of the GOP. He is a trial attorney, former policy analyst for the House of Representatives, and a media contributor. He discussed ways that everyone can contribute to good government, sharing some personal experiences that led to his political convictions. Pizza and wine was served, and the opportunity to mingle was greatly appreciated by all.

pages.text: Wednesday, June 16, 2021 23 FIRST MONDAYS READING GROUP First Monday book group discusses Brien book By Dick Carter The First Mondays Reading Group, sponsored by the Recreation Department, welcomed Piedmont author Shanti Brien at its June 7 meeting for a discussion about her recently released book Almost Innocent. Fifteen readers called in to talk with her. Participating were: Mike Bandrowski, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Margie Blodgett, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Albert Chen, Pat McSwain, Alicia Rivera, Sally Arney, Jamie Forsythe, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. Brien is a criminal defense attorney and the wife of a former NFL player. In Almost Innocent, she writes about our criminal justice system based upon her own experience and the stories of nine of her previously convicted felon clients. The conversation took place before the group’s regular June discussion of President Obama’s new memoir, A Promised Land. Brien did a brief reading from her book, made some comments, and then opened the talk to accept questions. She said that her clients were happy to be included in the book so that their stories would be told. Her hope is that these and other, similar situations will create “radical empathy” for injustice in the system; and that some reform will result. Shanti said that everyone can do something. One of the most basic things is for voters to make informed choices about district attorneys, who have great control in the system. She also talked about the process of writing a book. It took nearly three years to initially write the book, and another two to three years of editing, plus five years to find an agent. Publishers are hesitant about first time authors because the financial uncertainty associated with them. The profit margins associated with publishing are thin. Publishers prefer proven authors or established “personalities.” She encouraged anyone with a desire to write a book to “just start writing chunks” of content. The 40-minute conversation was highly enjoyable and informative. For more information, visit: https://www.shantibrien.com/. A Promised Land This memoir by former President Barack Obama (2009-2017) was published in November 2020 and is the first of a planned two-volume series. The book covers Obama’s life from his early years through the events surrounding the killing of Osama bin Laden in May 2011. The book has received good reviews from the New York Times, The Washington Post, and The Guardian. Commercially, it has been extremely successful and was on the New York Times best-seller list in non-fiction for eight weeks. It is 768 pages long, has been translated into two dozen languages, and is also available as a 28-hour audiobook with Obama reading it in its entirety. The book is a unique, thoughtful, intimate, and revealing exploration of Obama’s personal and family lives. There are insights into the people and leaders with whom he interacted, as well as the impact pf presidential power. The readers agreed that Obama is a masterful writer and his prose is enjoyable to read. It was noted that he writes the way he talks, eloquently and expansively. The group especially enjoyed the details about Obama’s life and personal anecdotes. He describes his relationship and interactions with his wife, Michelle, shows her strength and importance during his presidency. The candid impressions of world leaders are fascinating, including the events leading up to the killing of Osama bin Laden. While the positive aspects of the book are undeniable, some readers had issues. Obama’s writing covers all facets of an issue, action, or event. All the details can be a challenge, especially with situations that are most appealing to politicians and public policy makers. The book’s length can also be a challenge, and some readers found it tedious at times. Some found it more of a history book than a memoir. The group said it was pleased to have selected and read A Promised Land. Additionally, the book reminded many of what it was like just a short time ago in our nation, and candidly in a happier time. With their book conversations complete, the group discussed future books to read. For July they had previously selected the timely fiction Interior Chinatown by Charles Yu. For August, September, and October respectively, they picked The Fire Next Time by James Baldwin, Deacon King Kong by James McBride, and Nomadland by Jessica Bruder. The group will meet next in a Zoom call on Monday, July 5, at 1:30 p.m. New members are always welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required by contacting John Wilk at jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: The Number 11 streetcar on the right-of-way between Linda and Sunnyside Avenues in 1948. was what then was the newly built Transbay Terminal in San Francisco. Cars travelled east and west on the top level of the bridge. Electric trains served other parts of the East Bay. The A Train covered downtown Oakland, and the B Train travelled through the Lakeshore and Trestle Glen neighborhoods. The E Train went to Berkeley to the Claremont Hotel. In Berkeley, the F Train travelled on Shattuck to Solano, the G Train served Westbrae, the H Train travelled on Monterey Avenue, and the K Train ran on College Avenue. Today, some AC Transit buses use the same letters to identify their routes. End of the Line The last Piedmont streetcar operated until 1948. With the proliferation of automobiles after World War II, electric streetcars were no longer considered efficient. Buses, later run by AC Transit District, took over the streetcar routes. The C Train continued to run to San Francisco until 1958 when streetcars on the Bay Bridge were discontinued. The Oakland Tribune described this poignant time as “sad, exuberant, quiet, noisy, confused and orderly.” That last ride was standing room only. Homeowners along the train’s route came out to wave goodbye, as the motorman saluted back. The C Train at the small Oakland Avenue station at Latham that provided shelter to waiting passengers in 1940. Legacy The Number 11 and 12 streetcar lines and the C Train also left a legacy of vacant right-ofway land. The right-of-way for the Number 11 between Sunnyside and Linda became the beautifully landscaped Linda Park and the energetic Linda Avenue Dog Park across from Beach School. The Number 12 streetcar on Fairview Avenue had no dedicated right-of-way. When the C Train stopped running, its right-of-ways were filled with houses. Today, three narrow houses occupy the right-of-way along Latham. The land between Ricardo and York became more back yard space for adjacent houses. New houses were built on York near Arroyo. The C Train also shared the right-of-way on Arroyo with the Number 10 streetcar before it As the C Train curves to the right toward its route to Latham and Oakland, the Number 10 streetcar descends Arroyo toward Piedmont Avenue.

It was the longest Key Route line in Piedmont and ran from Piedmont Avenue and 41st to Crocker Park. There were two other streetcar lines and an electric train in Piedmont that provided convenient, reliable and inexpensive transportation to other neighborhood cities, downtown Oakland and San Francisco. The Number 11 streetcar ran from 7th and Broadway in Oakland up Oakland Avenue into Piedmont. At the Oakland Avenue Bridge it turned left and continued onto the rightof-way that ran between Linda and Sunnyside Avenues. At Lake Avenue, the streetcar ran on Linda Avenue to Piedmont Avenue and to the end of its line at the Piedmont Avenue Station. (The route up Oakland Avenue from Grand Ave. was too steep for electric streetcars.) The Number 12 streetcar also traveled from downtown Oakland, but it served another part of Piedmont. It ran up Grand Avenue and up Fairview Avenue beside the strip park. It ended at Oakland and Jerome Avenues. From there, passengers could cross Oakland Avenue to board the C Train to San Francisco. Taking the C Train to San Francisco When the Bay Bridge was completed in 1936, the Key System added electric train service to San Francisco. (The Key Route had became the Key System in 1923.) The electric C Train began service to Piedmont in 1939 and offered direct transportation from Piedmont to San Francisco every 20 minutes. Each train had a smoking section and “card tables were provided for commuters used to such diversions when they rode the ferries.” Many Piedmont commuters caught the C Train from the small Spanish-style waiting station at Oakland Avenue and Latham Street. From there the train travelled along Latham, then between the houses on Ricardo and York. Two stops allowed more passengers to board before the train left Piedmont for the station at 41st Street and Piedmont Ave. and on to the Bay Bridge. The lower level of the new Bay Bridge was reserved for trucks and trains. The electric trains ran on parallel tracks on the south side of the bridge, and trucks used the north side. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: Wednesday Walkers pause for a group photo on Palm Drive on June 9. Pictured are: Albert Chen (left), Jim Kuo, Harriette Louie, Cheryl Coleman Jones, Alicia Rivera, Haybert Houston, Adrienne Hamlin, Melba Yee, Nancy Henn, Andree Greenberg, Brenda Ferrero, Nancy Olsen, Mark Greenberg, Sherry Jacobs, Larry Olsen, Cat Gustafson, and Bob Gustafson. With nearly perfect weather, the Walking on Wednesdays group had its biggest turnout so far this year with 18 people. The group was especially pleased to welcome first time walker Haybert Houston. The walkers enjoy local history and find it is often helpful to put what they see into a historical context. So, drawing once again on information provided by Gail Lombardi of the Piedmont Historical Society, an account of Piedmont’s early development was told. Gold was discovered in California at Sutter’s Mill in 1848 and the 49ers soon followed, many coming to San Francisco. Trees in the East Bay were cut to satisfy the construction needs. This opened large areas in the Oakland foothills, and what is now Piedmont, for ranches with livestock and grain. The Reed Ranch covered much of what is now Piedmont. In the 1860s a person bought part of the ranch and “rediscovered” a mineral spring that a Mr. Holmes had discovered years before. After Holmes died the springs were forgotten. However, as they were only three miles from the Oakland railroad station, the new owner thought a mineral spring with perceived health benefits was a big business opportunity. He recruited San Francisco investors and they built the Piedmont Springs Hotel in 1876 on the very spot where the Exedra stands today. The hotel burned down in 1892, but this created a new business opportunity. Frank C. Havens, a developer, bought the land and opened Piedmont Park in 1898 with the mineral springs and two grottos as attractions. Another attraction was a large hedge maze where Witter Field is today. The main entrance to the park was at the current bus stop across from the Wells Fargo bank, but visitors could also access the park by a path from Grand Avenue on what is now Palm Drive. The walkers decided to walk through Piedmont Park, see the site of the mineral springs with Havens’ grottos, and on to Palm Drive. They saw children playing near the upper grotto, and one exploring the drought-depleted water flow of Bushy Dell Creek. They took the lower path through the park to the site of the lower grotto, where they read a historical maker about Mark Twain’s visit to this location in 1868 when he was on a lecture tour in Oakland. On the marker there is a picture of the event with Twain identified. The group continued to another marker that showed the “Eucalyptus Amphitheater” that Havens built in 1908. The marker has a picture with a large group of the Sons of Norway holding annual meeting in 1915. They noted the location of Piedmont Play School for preschoolers. The school was moved to Hampton Field when Witter field and track were expanded in 1998. The walkers emerged from the park and read about Havens’ “Maze” on another historical marker. They entered Park View Avenue at the base of Witter Field, and followed Palm Drive, noting some unique, colorful homes and gardens. The majestic palm trees are over 125 years old, and are the last remaining trees that lined the path from Grand Avenue to the lower entrance of Piedmont Park and the Maze. The palms are in the front yards of the homes, not on city property. Sherry Jacobs, who lives nearby, told the group that some trees have been removed over the last few years. It had been a beautiful morning with lots of Piedmont history and good conversations with friends. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues). The gathering time is 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge, and new walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required by contacting jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov. The palms are in the front yards of the homes, not on city property. Sherry Jacobs, who lives nearby, told the group that some trees have been removed over the last few years. It had been a beautiful morning with lots of Piedmont history and good conversations with friends. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues). The gathering time is 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge, and new walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required by contacting jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. Although most of the headlines go to the offense, the Highlanders were well known for their strong defense. articles.text: Almost all eligible Piedmonters have received at least one dose of COVID-19 vaccine as of Sunday, June 13. The Alameda County Public Health Department reported that 9,234 Piedmonters, amounting to 99.4 percent of the City’s population ages 12 and older, are now at least partially vaccinated. An estimated 68 percent of the eligible population, some 7,558 people, are fully vaccinated. Over 1.94 million doses of vaccine have been administered in Alameda County. Almost 79 percent of the county’s population ages 12 and older, more than 1.11 million people, are partially vaccinated. Almost 65 percent of eligible people in the county, nearly 914,000 people, are fully vaccinated. In Oakland, almost 77 percent of the population is partially vaccinated and about 61 percent is fully vaccinated. “Nearly 80 percent of Alameda County residents, 12 and older, have received at least one dose of a safe and effective COVID-19 vaccine, which has directly resulted in reduced case rates,” proclaimed ACPHD public information manager Neetu Balram in a statement this week. Three vaccines are available in the United States. Pfizer and Moderna vaccines require two doses administered several weeks apart. A vaccine produced by Johnson & Johnson requires only one dose. Pfizer is approved for children as young as 12, while the other two vaccines are approved for those age 18 and older. The vaccination effort across the state is an essential part of California’s reopening strategy that went into effect yesterday, Tuesday, June 15. As part of the reopening plan, fully vaccinated people do not have to wear a face mask in most situations. An earlier decree from the state’s workplace safety agency Cal/OSHA said that masks would have to be worn in Californian workplaces unless everyone in a room is fully vaccinated, but Gov. Gavin Newsom is expected to eliminate mask rules for fully vaccinated workers via an executive order tomorrow, Thursday, June 17. Yesterday, Newsom gave 10 vaccinated Californians $1.5 million each in a drawing as part of his “Vax for the Win” program. About 2 million doses have been administered statewide since the $116.5 million initiative program began, including about 840,000 Californians getting their first doses. COVID-19 vaccines are available for free to all Alameda County residents ages 12 and older. Appointments are not required at many vaccination locations in Oakland and elsewhere in the county. As of press time, same-day appointments were available at several locations in Oakland and Berkeley. Alameda County links to available vaccine appointments at covid-19.acgov.org/vaccines Across California, 39.8 total doses of vaccine have been administered. Almost 18.9 million Californians are fully vaccinated, amounting to about 56 percent of the population ages 12 and older. COVID-19 is low in the area, it is concerned that outbreaks could occur amongst unvaccinated people. The county is urging everyone to get vaccinated as soon as possible. Vaccines are free and many pharmacies in the area have walk-in appointments available. “The decline in cases and mortality shows that the best protection against COVID-19 is vaccination,” Neetu Balram, the public information manager for ACPHD, said in a release posted Monday, June 14. “All currently available vaccines are safe, effective, free, and widely available. When you are ready, get vaccinated.” As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,697,927 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 62,515 deaths due to the disease statewide. The state positivity rate is 0.7 percent, the same as one week ago.

In addition to aesthetic considerations, material selection always is a balancing act between quality and cost. More durable, longer-lasting materials generally cost more initially. Factoring in the true building-life costs, however, mitigates the differences. If, for example more expensive copper flashing and gutters are used, they are probably going to last the life of the building, whereas less expensive gutters of less durable materials will have to be replaced after a certain number of years. As any home remodeler knows, the decision-making required around material selection can be overwhelming. The process often has just begun with the actual selection of a material or product. The next decision may be size, then the choice of an available texture (the tactile surface) and then the colors. Most of the time selections are made from manufacturers’ standards, but often for a premium they can be custom made to the architects’ unique specifications. And finally, in the case of materials like masonry or brick, the laying pattern and coursing has to be decided. articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council unanimously approved on June 7 an agreement with Griffin Structures as the project manager for the new Piedmont Pool, a $19.5 million bond approved by voters in November 2020 as Measure UU. A contract of $612,700, which includes a 10% contingency, was awarded. A Request for Proposal (RFP) was issued by the city on February 16 seeking a project management firm, or owner’s representative services, that would be solely dedicated to oversight of the $19.5 million bond from design development through construction. By March 19, four proposals were received, and all were reviewed independently by city staff and Howard Fuchs, an independent consultant. City staff reviewers included Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, Recreation Director Chelle Putzer, Planning Director Kevin Jackson, City Engineer John Wanger, and Special Assistant to City Administrator Paul Benoit. The cost of the proposals ranged between $500,000 to $1 million. “Of the four firms, it was the unanimous opinion of the reviewers that Griffin Structures stood out. They seemed the most capable of meeting everything we’ve addressed in the RFP. Unlike the other firms, they have extensive experience in managing public aquatic design and construction,” explained Benoit, Piedmont former City Administrator. Griffin Structures, headquartered in Irvine in Southern California and with offices in Santa Clara, has managed design and construction for 15 aquatics facilities out of more than 50 recreation projects in the state. One of its local projects is the renovation of the pool at nearby Roberts Regional Park in the Oakland hills. Other projects include the Marguerite Aquatics Complex in Mission Viejo (pictured), the Rengstorff Park Aquatic Center in Mountain View, the San Bruno Recreation and Aquatics Center, the San Clemente Aquatics Center, and the Sports Park in Vista Hermosa. Benoit noted that the company also has a qualified, full-time staff with in-house capabilities, and has communicated an understanding of the detriments of climate change. It is both knowledgeable and experienced in implementing “green technologies” in the design of facilities. “One of the key aspects of [the Project Manager’s] work will be to keep the project moving, on schedule and on budget,” Benoit said. “Another aspect is community engagement. The project manager will work with [city staff] to provide regular updates that we can post online.” George Sanen will serve as Project Manager for Griffin Structures. Sanen has 34 years of experience in program and construction management of multi-million dollar recreational, aquatic, and community centers. He received a B.A. Public Administration from University of San Francisco. He also holds diplomas in Interior Architectural Design, Airport Planning and Design, Hotel Planning and Development, and Courthouse Design, all from Harvard University’s Graduate School of Design. Piedmont’s city staff expects to host a series of public meetings throughout the implementation of the project to review the progress of the design and to solicit feedback from the community. Sanen will assist in communicating public comments, concerns and suggestions to the design team.
articles.title: City Council hires construction manager for $19 million pool

articles.text: One week before most restrictions due to the COVID-19 pandemic are eliminated in California, Alameda County was moved into the Yellow Tier yesterday, Tuesday, June 8. The yellow tier is the least restrictive tier for reopening its economy. Since March 30, Alameda County was in the orange tier, or moderate tier, the second-least restrictive tier. Due to decreasing case counts, the county was moved into the yellow tier, or minimal tier. In the yellow tier, almost all indoor and outdoor operations can resume with modifications, usually involving capacity restrictions and face coverings. Alameda and Napa this week joined Marin, Monterey, Santa Clara, Santa Cruz, San Francisco and San Mateo counties in the yellow tier. The positivity rate in Alameda County is 0.6 percent, a historic low for the pandemic. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas is 1.3 percent. The number of cases per 100,000 people is 1.5, a decrease from last week. “The increasing number of residents who are fully vaccinated is directly reducing case rates and helping Alameda County to move into the Yellow Tier ahead of the June 15 transition,” Alameda County Health Officer Dr. Nicholas Moss said in a statement. Next Tuesday, June 15, California will lift most COVID-19 restrictions, including capacity limits and physical distancing. The four-tier color-coded reopening system will be abandoned. Fully vaccinated people will not have to wear masks in most situations unless they are on public transit, an airplane, in a healthcare setting or working indoors around unvaccinated people, according to current state rules. The masking guidance is based off guidelines updated in May by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
articles.title: County positivity rate drops to 0.6 percent

articles.text: Editor: “I will permit no man to narrow and degrade my soul by making me hate him.” - Booker T. Washington As the school year comes to a close and Piedmont families begin their summer break routines, school is an afterthought to most. During this upcoming summer break, a growing group of Piedmont parents, grandparents, residents and teachers will ponder what our children will face when returning to the classroom in a mere eight weeks. Will our children continue to be made to feel guilty or beneath themselves because of their skin color? Will our children be indoctrinated into Marxist-based race ideology? We hope that this is not the case. Although I have had to deal with my children pondering whether or not their White father is a racist (while simultaneously straddling the line of being Chinese), it is shocking to hear stories from Bay Area public and private school parents of the effect that school honed race-based ideology has had on their families. From Asian families who feel that their children’s academic successes will be in vain because of the color of their skin, to a White child accusing her White parents of being racists and the cause of societal breakdown. As I continue to study Critical Race Theory (CRT), it frightens me that school leaders across the country would allow the demise of our future generation of children. As the rest of the world surpasses the US in K-12 educational achievements, the U.S. continues its downward spiral. The Oregon Department of Education recently sent a newsletter to math educators in their state regarding a course associating math to white supremacy. The course highlights include links to white supremacy when the teacher has a greater focus on the student getting the math answer “right”; when students are required to show their work. “Good” math teaching is considered inequity to non-White students. As a parent, this is unfathomable that a U.S. school district would advocate teachers to partake in a course that dumbs down U.S. students even further. Our children are at a formative age, and we look to our school leaders to be guiding lights for them to be constructive members of society. Please teach our children to read, write and perform math. Please teach history as history should be taught. And please do not psychologically abuse our children by poisoning their minds with ideological race rhetoric. articles.text: In her book, No Joke, Ruth Wisse, a professor at Harvard University, speaks to the development of humor in the Jewish tradition. As a Jew she admitted to having great pride in telling a joke that “even made other Jews laugh”. “Four Europeans go hiking together and get terribly lost. First, they run out of food, then out of water. ‘I’m so thirsty,’ says the Englishman. ‘I must have tea’. ‘I’m so thirsty’, says the Frenchman. ‘I must have wine’. ‘I’m so thirsty’, says the German. ‘I must have beer’. ‘I’m so thirsty’, says the Jew, ‘I must have diabetes’.” Wisse argues that humor, in the Jewish tradition, was used to embrace their humanity, acknowledge their quirks but also to point to their strengths even to the point of defiance. She cites a quotation found in the Warsaw Ghetto during the holocaust. It read, “God forbid that this war should last as long as we are able to endure it.” The statement is both humorous and also defiant. articles.text: Allyson Aleksey, the Piedmont Post’s city reporter, has been named its new City Editor as of June 1. Since February 2020 she has been the principal reporter, covering City Hall, feature stories and a wide range of performing arts. “We are pleased to welcome Allyson to a position offering more responsibility for the overall content of the paper each week. She has proven to be an excellent reporter and writer and has a wonderful appreciation and understanding of the community – what makes Piedmont unique,” said publisher Gray Cathrall. Aleksey grew up in Brooklyn, New York, and attended Dominican Academy on the Upper East Side of Manhattan. Upon graduating in 2012, she moved to New Orleans, Louisiana to pursue a Journalism degree at Loyola University, obtaining a B.A in Mass Communication with a minor in film studies in 2016. While working toward her degree, she was an intern with New Orleans’ then-only daily newspaper, the Times-Picayune. In 2016 she earned the Best in News Reporting award from the Society of Professional Journalists for her coverage of Covenant House’s efforts in preventing homelessness and promoting community stewardship in New Orleans’ 9th ward. She also shadowed and covered the efforts of the Plessy & Ferguson Foundation in unveiling historic markers of closed public schools throughout Orleans Parish due to budget cuts and redirection of municipal funds. Both stories were published on Nola. com and printed in editions of the Times-Picayune. After graduating she accepted an offer to teach 4th grade at Ridgewood Preparatory School, a private, non-denominational K-12 school in Metairie, a suburb of New Orleans. While stepping aside from journalism, she taught for three years and developed a Photo by Jay Russell Allyson Aleksey has been named City Editor of the Piedmont Post. love for the field of education and an intense appreciation for educators. Before joining the Piedmont Post in 2020 she was the lead reporter and assistant editor of Beverly Hills Weekly. During her time there she covered everything from the crime beat, most notably the litigation of Police Chief Sandra Spagnoli and officers’ accusations of sexual misconduct and racial bias, to the Metro purple line’s extension onto Rodeo Drive and the many CEQA, public meetings, town halls and the litigation that followed. Aleksey grew up in a home that consumed media daily in all its forms. Early mornings were dedicated to radio news, oftentimes New York City’s 1010 WINS. In the evenings it was television news. In between, she was often spotted by professors and colleagues on the Lexington Avenue local 6 train with a newspaper on her way to class. When her father forgot to leave her the scraps of Daily News, New York Post, and New York Times issues, she would pick up a free Metro paper that was passed out at the Hunters College train station daily. To reach Allyson Aleksey, e-mail allysonaaleksey@gmail. com. “It’s serious... his wife’s credit cards are maxed out.”
articles.title: Allyson Aleksey named City Editor at Piedmont Post

articles.text: About 40% of car trips last less than 2 miles. This shocking statistic helps explain why improving transportation, especially the “last mile” even slightly, could make a drastic difference in how we choose to move ourselves. Transit isn’t only an opportunity to reduce our car use, it is also a climate issue. Transportation is one of the largest causes of greenhouse gas emissions in California and the country as a whole. Making it easier to get from one place to another can make communities more enjoyable to travel, while at the same time improving air quality, safety, and health outcomes for all travelers. California, home of some of the most recognizable highways in the country, has been pushing for ways to “green” state transportation options for years. In 2020, Governor Newsom finalized an executive order that mandates that all new vehicles sold in the state be electric by 2035. California is the fifth largest economy in the world, meaning this executive action may accelerate electric vehicle sales. Since 2008, the federal government has offered tax credits or rebates for electric vehicles, and California drivers are currently eligible for thousands of dollars in rebates, depending on eligibility. President Biden repeatedly talked about the need for more electric vehicles and chargers during his campaign. Transportation is increasingly being linked to other issues such as housing. When more housing is built close to urban centers, people generally have shorter commutes, meaning that building affordable housing can have a real effect on transportation. Although the shift from gas powered cars to electric will reduce tailpipe emissions, it will require multiple transit solutions to significantly reduce emissions. Bicycling, walking, and public transit continue to offer some of the largest benefits to communities, especially lower income communities. Every $1 invested in public transit generates $5 in economic returns. Public transit is also markedly safer than driving-- taking public transit instead of driving reduces risk of a road accident by 90%. Despite all this, driving infrastructure improvements continue to receive a majority of public funding. The unfortunate reality is that cars take up the most space on roadways while transporting the smallest number of people. Cars emit more pollution, harm more people, and lead to worse health outcomes than the alternatives. Regardless of whether a car is electric, or even autonomous, it still takes up the same space on a roadway. pages.text: Wednesday, June 9, 2021 3 Making transit bike-friendly By Nate Redinbo About 40% of car trips last less than 2 miles. This shocking statistic helps explain why improving transportation, especially the “last mile” even slightly, could make a drastic difference in how we choose to move ourselves. Transit isn’t only an opportunity to reduce our car use, it is also a climate issue. Transportation is one of the largest causes of greenhouse gas emissions in California and the country as a whole. Making it easier to get from one place to another can make communities more enjoyable to travel, while at the same time improving air quality, safety, and health outcomes for all travelers. California, home of some of the most recognizable highways in the country, has been pushing for ways to “green” state transportation options for years. In 2020, Governor Newsom finalized an executive order that mandates that all new vehicles sold in the state be electric by 2035. California is the fifth largest economy in the world, meaning this executive action may accelerate electric vehicle sales. Since 2008, the federal government has offered tax credits or rebates for electric vehicles, and California drivers are currently eligible for thousands of dollars in rebates, depending on eligibility. President Biden repeatedly talked about the need for more electric vehicles and chargers during his campaign. Transportation is increasingly being linked to other issues such as housing. When more housing is built close to urban centers, people generally have shorter commutes, meaning that building affordable housing can have a real effect on transportation. Although the shift from gas powered cars to electric will reduce tailpipe emissions, it will require multiple transit solutions to significantly reduce emissions. Bicycling, walking, and public transit continue to offer some of the largest benefits to communities, especially lower income communities. Every $1 invested in public transit generates $5 in economic returns. Public transit is also markedly safer than driving-- taking public transit instead of driving reduces risk of a road accident by 90%. Allyson Aleksey named City Editor at Piedmont Post Allyson Aleksey, the Piedmont Post’s city reporter, has been named its new City Editor as of June 1. Since February 2020 she has been the principal reporter, covering City Hall, feature stories and a wide range of performing arts. “We are pleased to welcome Allyson to a position offering more responsibility for the overall content of the paper each week. She has proven to be an excellent reporter and writer and has a wonderful appreciation and understanding of the community – what makes Piedmont unique,” said publisher Gray Cathrall. Aleksey grew up in Brooklyn, New York, and attended Dominican Academy on the Upper East Side of Manhattan. Upon graduating in 2012, she moved to New Orleans, Louisiana to pursue a Journalism degree at Loyola University, obtaining a B.A in Mass Communication with a minor in film studies in 2016. While working toward her degree, she was an intern with New Orleans’ then-only daily newspaper, the Times-Picayune. In 2016 she earned the Best in News Reporting award from the Society of Professional Journalists for her coverage of Covenant House’s efforts in preventing homelessness and promoting community stewardship in New Orleans’ 9th ward. She also shadowed and covered the efforts of the Plessy & Ferguson Foundation in unveiling historic markers of closed public schools throughout Orleans Parish due to budget cuts and redirection of municipal funds. Both stories were published on Nola. com and printed in editions of the Times-Picayune. After graduating she accepted an offer to teach 4th grade at Ridgewood Preparatory School, a private, non-denominational K-12 school in Metairie, a suburb of New Orleans. Before joining the Piedmont Post in 2020 she was the lead reporter and assistant editor of Beverly Hills Weekly. During her time there she covered everything from the crime beat, most notably the litigation of Police Chief Sandra Spagnoli and officers’ accusations of sexual misconduct and racial bias, to the Metro purple line’s extension onto Rodeo Drive and the many CEQA, public meetings, town halls and the litigation that followed. articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will present a Zoom-based discussion on criminal justice reform with Piedmont resident Shanti Brien as guest speaker on June 22. An attorney and reform advocate, Brien will speak on what individuals and organizations do for criminal justice reform and racial justice. She will take questions from audience members. The forum will be online through Zoom on Tuesday, June 22 at 4 p.m. Brien’s book Almost Innocent: From searching to saved in America’s criminal justice system was published last month. It chronicles her experiences growing up in the central valley, becoming an attorney, and representing convicted individuals. Brien said that she “reimagines the current criminal justice system as smaller, fairer, and more humane.” Brien is a member of the Muscogee Creek Nation, and a graduate of UC Berkeley and Stanford Law School. As a former criminal defense lawyer, she co-founded Fogbreak Justice, an organization that collaborates with criminal justice professionals to reduce bias and build community trust to create equitable outcomes. She is also a writer and speaker on social justice issues in criminal law and policy. As a Piedmont resident, she has served on the Public Safety Committee, is a member of the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC), and participates in the Piedmont Race and Equity Campaign (PREC). To join in the discussion, register at: https://www. l w v p ie d m o n t .o r g /c o n t e n t . a spx?page_id= 40 02&club_ id=601389&item_id=1441599. Registrants will receive an email with the Zoom link. This event is free and open to all. The talk will be recorded and can be viewed later on the League of Women Voters Piedmont YouTube Channel: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC3v60XGmr13V_9WaYj6qUJg/featured.

The job description includes the following responsibilities, “Creating a strategic communications plan and infrastructure; researching, writing and disseminating information about district news, schools, current events and issues affecting Piedmont students, staff and parents; and for providing multiple pathways for the community to provide feedback to District leaders.” In prior years Piedmont School District has had individuals working as independent contractors doing public relations writing. It was understood that the individual was being paid approximately $50,000 for year-round work on an as-needed basis. For more information contact Kim Randlett in the District office at 594-2618.
