articles.text: This time last year, we were trying to figure out how we were going to survive a summer of COVID and all of the social restrictions. And then, like a breath of fresh air, the Piedmont Recreation Department came to our rescue. They announced they’d be hosting a modified in-person day camp, Camp (Almost) Everything, starting June 1, 2020. This was literally the first summer camp in the Bay Area that gave children a chance to be together again since schools abruptly closed in March. While school districts around the country continued to debate about the best path forward for kids, PRD quietly and quickly got to work and figured out how to safely meet the social and emotional needs of Piedmont kids. As Erin Rivera recently noted at the City Council meeting, “We were on the cutting edge, keeping kids happy. We followed the science, we followed the safety. We did really amazing things.” On behalf of so many grateful Piedmont parents, I would like to thank Erin and the rest of the Recreation Department team for the many amazing things they accomplished for our families over the last year. The wonderful staff showed up every day for our kids, helping them thrive and feel normal in this very abnormal year. They helped keep our kids healthy from the devastating emotional effects of isolation. Here are a few words of gratitude from local families. were really missing their teachers and coaches. articles.text: A friend of mine who belongs to the Greek Orthodox church reminded me that the faithful of that denomination greet one another in the Easter season with, “Christ is risen” and the other replies, “He is risen indeed!” What a beautiful way to connect our ordinary daily speech with our faith in the basic reality of Christianity. But something else is in play here: the sense of community, in which people are conscious that there is something important they have to share. The Christian scriptures, beginning with the letters of St. Paul and later with the gospel accounts, clearly indicate that the followers of Jesus were acutely aware of belonging together, that togetherness was a hallmark of their existence. It was in gathering together with the common purpose of remembering the Lord’s words and deeds that they would fulfill his command to love one another. That in turn would reveal the substance of the one great commandment to love God and one’s neighbor as oneself. The practical outcome of this is found in the Lord’s declaration: As long as you did it to one of the least of my people, you did it to me. This expansiveness is different from an attitude so prevalent today in which the narrow approach of personal autonomy and social restrictiveness result not only in pain and suffering but in downright injustice. It is important to distinguish patriotism – the love of country – from the nationalism which sees all others as the enemy or the adversary. The end result is separation where there should be the aim of union. As Pope Francis has so well said: Christians do not build walls; we build bridges. New York Times columnist David Brooks recently distinguished between what he calls “weavers” and “rippers.” The latter spend their time and efforts dividing people, while the weavers do their best to knit people together. The Easter season especially is a time of knitting people together. This is based on the belief that Christ died for all, regardless of religious or national or racial diversity. In the Catholic liturgy of Good Friday, we pray for everyone, even atheists, because, as St. Paul says, All have sinned and all need the glory of God. Partly due to the coastline and inland mountain ranges, California has some of the most variable patterns of rain of any state. Northern California is currently in one of the largest rainfall deficits in modern history. The paltry rainfall can be partly attributed to a La Niña year. Drier conditions are to be expected, but this year is atypical. Humans continue to release greenhouse gases, which can exacerbate naturally occurring weather events such as La In addition to weather patterns and water infrastructure issues, there are often conflicts over the best way to secure water. The Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta, an important source of drinking water for over 20 million Californians, is currently under court ordered mandates to reduce pumping, and is the cause of a spirited debate (and litigation) among stakeholders. Based on its series of levees, scientists have raised the alarm that the current method of managing water in the Delta cannot be sustained in the long term. Other concerns over native fish populations have made the Delta a contentious location. Some regions are trying to solve these issues using alternate methods. In order to maintain crop yields, Central Valley groundwater has been over-pumped, meaning that underground reserves of water are being depleted without a consistent way to refill them. Parts of the landscape are sinking, in some areas by up to two feet per year. Although the state legislature has attempted to prevent this practice, there are still no firm rules about how much water can be pumped. If farmers don’t have water from other sources, they will continue pumping, which can lead to less water for the future. California produces two-thirds of all American fruits and over onethird of all American vegetables, meaning that agricultural issues here affect huge swaths of the country. Usage and payment are one area that most consumers are most familiar with. There has long been underlying tension regarding payment for water. California cities often pay more than agricultural users, meaning that cities essentially subsidize water usage for farming purposes. Some say that this makes sense, as agriculture is predictably a large user of water, using about 80% of all water that goes to businesses and homes. Use in urban areas such as the Bay Area are also a large drain on resources, but as populations have increased, per capita usage has decreased, showing that it is feasible to use water conservation practices. During the last drought, the agriculture industry lost a lot of revenue. Wells dried up and cities implemented water-saving measures. Thousands of trees died, helping to fuel the historic fires of 2020. As the effects from climate change grow more extreme, droughts are going to become more common, and water shortages are likely. These conditions raise questions, such as: who should get to pump groundwater? What do we do when the aquifers run dry? How involved should the state government be? These are all difficult questions, but they need to be answered soon, before the water crisis gets worse. In order to maintain water levels and prepare for the future, state and regional partners must make plans now in order to manage future droughts. This only gives a brief glimpse into the complicated topic that is California water. I encourage you to conduct your own research on the subject, which is as engrossing as it is complex. In Piedmont, there are some things that can be done to reduce individual water usage. • Consumption What you purchase can impact water usage. One cotton t-shirt requires 2,700 liters of water to produce, which is equivalent to about two years of an individual’s drinking water. One pair of jeans can take 7,500 liters of water to produce. In addition to clothing, certain food staples such as wheat and soy that are used to feed cattle and livestock are particularly water intensive. • Indoors Over half of indoor water use comes from the bathroom. Toilets are the highest water user inside the home. Fix leaky toilets and install low-flow. Take shorter showers. • Outdoors Watering landscaping is a huge water user. Use drought-resistant native plants in your yard, and carefully plan the best time to water. Install a rain barrel and use it to water outdoors when possible. This is just a beginning guide to how to save water. There are further resources online to learn more about saving water. You can also use Piedmont’s Climate Challenge website to learn more and work with friends to reduce your water consumption. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Piedmont’s newly-formed Housing Advisory Committee held its first public meeting on May 19. An informational report on the community outreach effort was provided by Lisa Wise Consulting within the results of interviews in November 2020 and the citywide fair housing community survey conducted this year. ADUs and alternatives Interviews were conducted over the course of two days in November with 34 individuals. Respondents brainstormed strategies to increase housing production in the city beyond the development of Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs), to include rezoning to allow for more multi-family homes, conversion of houses into duplexes or multi-family structures, and deed restrictions to ensure long-term affordability, among others. Respondents in the November interviews listed Blair Park, the city’s tennis courts, Bank of America, Ace Hardware, and deep lots along the Moraga Canyon as opportunity areas where housing production would be feasible. A community survey was open to residents from March 12 to April 15, and a total of 877 responses were received. Survey results found that the majority of residents support the acquisition and rehabilitation of existing buildings for affordable housing, and would like to prioritize housing for Piedmont’s teachers, first responders, seniors and service providers. Residents were also in favor of more streamlined permit approvals. Those who responded to the survey mostly opposed city-sponsored rent subsidies and are not in favor of developing land owned by the city, school district, or religious organizations. The meeting also included a digital poll, where representatives from Lisa Wise Consulting asked participants to choose their preferred architectural style, street frontage and facade among a sampling of multi-family and mixed-use buildings. Funding The survey found that participants support a proposed Transient Occupancy Tax, but oppose a parcel tax. Transient Occupancy Taxes are paid on temporary lodging at hotels, motels, Airbnbs and vacation rentals. Residents also suggested that the city might issue bonds to create more housing, seek grant opportunities, and explore state, federal, or joint-municipal funding. Respondents also supported an increase in sales tax revenue. The next Housing Advisory Committee meeting will be held on June 15 and will serve as another public outreach workshop. The city welcomes residents to participate in upcoming Housing Advisory Committee meetings. Meeting materials are posted at https://www.piedmontishome. org/event/housing-advisory-committee-meeting-sb-2-workshop. The June 15 meeting will be televised on KCOM-TV, the City’s government television station (Channel 27), and will be available to stream on the city’s website.

articles.text: Rodney Wong, Piedmont’s UPS (United Parcel Service) driver for 22 years, has taken a new job with UPS and will no longer be seen driving his regular delivery route in the familiar big brown truck. A familiar face throughout the city, he now works nights in his new position. Wong explained that Piedmont was his favorite route to cover when he was a “floater” for UPS but joked that his colleagues often passed it up when given the opportunity. “It was too much work, they said,” Wong laughed. “But their loss was my gain. I’ve always considered Piedmont a lovely, peaceful space.” Wong said that, although the work could be strenuous and difficult, that he does miss being a driver. He said he will miss the Piedmont community, the many friendly faces and wagging tails that he’s encountered through the years working here. “In all those years, I’ve never missed more than a few days [of work on the route]. I didn’t get a chance to say a permanent goodbye to people in town. I wanted to write a farewell letter, but it was hard,” Wong said. He will continue with his new assignment until the end of next year, when he likely will retire at age 60. Many residents are more familiar with him due to his active participation each year in the AIDS/LifeCycle event, a 545- mile bike ride from San Francisco to Los Angeles. In 2003 he rode for the first time in the cycling event, a fundraiser in the first week of June for the AIDS FounWong has switched positions to a nightly inside assignment. Oakland resident Rodney Wong served as Piedmont’s UPS driver for 22 years. dation. For one week, cyclists pass through communities largely on less-traveled roads, averaging about 80 miles a day. At the end of each day of riding, cyclists arrive at a camp to eat, shower, and rest before riding out again the next morning. Participants - riders and “roadies” - raise money throughout the year prior to the start of the ride. Wong participated in the event for 14 consecutive years and was well known as one of the top fundraisers in Northern California. Wong’s secret of success – raising over $400,000 over the years – was doing it the old-fashioned way. “I liked writing personal fundraising letters, with a donation form and pre-addressed envelopes. I would leave them with my deliveries, and over a few years I was leaving over a thousand with my deliveries,” Wong said with a smile. The response he received from the Piedmont community was immense - leading to an avalanche of donations and sponsorships. “Some ‘regulars’ would contribute every year,” Wong said. “I’m definitely proud of the community for the support they gave me, and that will be one characteristic I will always remember about this city – how giving it is,” he said. Wong made a point each year to publish in the newspaper an invitation for people to donate to the AIDS/LifeCycle organization. At the conclusion of each ride, he also wrote a letter of thanks to the community, letting everyone know how much money they had raised.
articles.title: Rodney Wong, Piedmont’s UPS driver, moves to job inside

articles.text: a wastewater increase of $1.87 per month, after both proposed The East Bay Municipal Utility District (EDMUD) will hold a virtual public hearing on proposed rate increases to water and wastewater service charges on Tuesday, June 8 at 1:15 p.m. A notice was sent by EBMUD to their customers in Piedmont, Alameda, Albany, Berkeley, El Cerrito, Emeryville, Kensington, and Oakland last week. EDMUD is proposing to increase the rates for both its water and wastewater service charges based on its most recent rate models and cost of service studies. Rates would increase over a two-year period, by approximately 4 percent overall on July 1, 2021, followed by another 4 percent increase the next year, July 1, 2022. This is an approximate increase, individual bills may increase by slightly more or less that amount depending on the specific rates and charges that apply to you and how much water you use. The notice mailed to residents provides the example of an average single family customer, who could expect a water rate increase of $5.19 per month, and annual increases have taken effect. A temporary “Drought Surcharge” may be assessed on all potable water use during a declared drought or water shortage. At the date of the mailed notice, EDMUD had not declared a drought; but in the event that a drought occurs, EDMUD will activate the surcharge in addition to other charges. Drought surcharges are calculated to recover costs of providing supplemental water, cost of water-shortage related customer service, and losses of revenue. How to participate in the hearing The public hearing on June 8 will be conducted via Zoom. To participate in the hearing, enter www.edmud.com/rates on your computer, then enter the Zoom Meeting ID (958-6681-4531) and passcode (810650). To participate telephonically, call 1-699-900- 6833 and enter both numbers, Written comments may be mailed before the hearing date to EDMUD, MS 218, PO Box 24055, Oakland, CA 94623-1055.

Rodney Wong, Piedmont’s UPS driver, moves to job inside By Allyson Aleksey Rodney Wong, Piedmont’s UPS (United Parcel Service) driver for 22 years, has taken a new job with UPS and will no longer be seen driving his regular delivery route in the familiar big brown truck. A familiar face throughout the city, he now works nights in his new position. Wong explained that Piedmont was his favorite route to cover when he was a “floater” for UPS but joked that his colleagues often passed it up when given the opportunity. “It was too much work, they said,” Wong laughed. “But their loss was my gain. I’ve always considered Piedmont a lovely, peaceful space.” Wong said that, although the work could be strenuous and difficult, that he does miss being a driver. He said he will miss the Piedmont community, the many friendly faces and wagging tails that he’s encountered through the years working here. “In all those years, I’ve never missed more than a few days [of work on the route]. I didn’t get a chance to say a permanent goodbye to people in town. I wanted to write a farewell letter, but it was hard,” Wong said. He will continue with his new assignment until the end of next year, when he likely will retire at age 60. Many residents are more familiar with him due to his active participation each year in the AIDS/LifeCycle event, a 545- mile bike ride from San Francisco to Los Angeles. articles.text: Each spring the Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) welcomes new members to its Board of Directors who will help fulfil the 45-year-old organization’s mission to provide sustained financial support to Piedmont schools through fundraising and community engagement. New members on the board this year are: Colleen Allan, Tonya Antonucci, Amber Brumfiel, Francis Hoang, and Jean Takazawa. Colleen Allan co-chaired this year’s Giving Campaign and is looking forward to leading it again next year. She is a brand marketing professional with nearly 20 years of experience at LinkedIn, Clorox and General Mills. She and her husband Brian Payne have three daughters and they moved to Piedmont for the public schools. “The schools are the cornerstone of the Piedmont community,” said Allan. “I am honored to join the PEF Board to help support and strengthen our schools, especially as we navigate the return to school post-pandemic, through academic programming, enrichment offerings and the Wellness Center to help all of our children to flourish.” Tonya Antonucci is an entrepreneur and marketing professional, with leadership stints at Yahoo!, Women’s Professional Soccer, and the Oakland A’s. Tonya and her partner, Tasha Cupp, moved to Piedmont from San Francisco to raise their daughter and son. Antonucci shares “PEF’s mission-based approach and engagement to support Piedmont schools and the broader community is absolutely crucial for sustaining quality public education for every child.” Amber Brumfiel and her husband, Chris, have lived in Piedmont since 2001, and Amber is a member of the City’s Park Commission. Before becoming the mother of three sons (age 8 and 6-year-old twins), she was a commercial real estate litigator in San Francisco. “I feel strongly about PEF’s emphasis on community engagement in its fundraising efforts,” said Brumfiel. “I want to help make people feel excited about supporting our schools and about the sense of community that our schools provide.” Brumfiel’s commitment to Piedmont is illustrated by her past leadership with Spring Fling and the city’s Harvest Festival. Francis Hoang is a Software Engineer at Salesforce and a California native. Francis and his wife, Kim Dao, have been in Piedmont for over 10 years and have three children. Hoang is strongly supportive of the school district’s holistic approach to education. “[It] is not only focused on academics, but also emotional health. The curriculum fosters the love and understanding of music, the arts, and social issues,” he said. “The foundation’s work in the community is what sets us apart and makes Piedmont a truly special place to raise a family.” Jean Takazawa is a professional educator with over 15 years of experience. She is the creator of the Piedmont Affinity Mentoring program that reaches elementary students as well as offering guidance to high school students. Jean and her husband, Tadashi, have two children in Piedmont schools. “We are fortunate to have so many educators in the district focused not only on learning, but on the social-emotional wellbeing of our children. PEF has a fundamental part in supporting and funding our schools. It is an honor to be part of that,” she said. The Educational Foundation extends its thanks to outgoing board members, Abby Scott, for five years of service, including as Board Secretary, and Linda Song Wendel for four years, including Vice Chair. Sara Davison DeVries will take a sabbatical from the Board while she serves as the Piedmont High School Parents Club Co-President during the 2021-2022 school year. The leadership of the 2021- 2022 PEF Board of Directors includes Nicki Gilbert (Chair), Cortney Allen (Co-Vice Chair), Amelie Kappes (Co-Vice Chair), Charlotte Ero (Treasurer), Dana Lung (Secretary), and Emily Harrold (Communications). Heather Frank is the Executive Director. The foundation is already working on the fall fundraising efforts. More than $3 million was raised to support Piedmont schools during the 2020-2021 Giving Campaign. Learn more about the Piedmont Education Foundation at www.piedmontedfoundation.org. Colleen Allan Tonya Antonucci Amber Brumfiel Francis Hoang Jean Takazawa

articles.text: The only total lunar eclipse of the year hid a full moon in total shadow early Wednesday morning, May 26. The ideal viewing position was the center of the Pacific Ocean, but Piedmont and the West Coast still experienced full eclipse conditions for 14 minutes, between 4:11 and 4:25 a.m. Night owl Piedmont residents and amateur astronomers took to the streets early in the morning to view the rare occurrence. In the peak eclipse a deep shade of red enveloped the moon. An interesting phenomenon occurs when staring at an unlit moon: the stars directly behind it become visible. As the moon orbits around the night sky, different stars are behind it, but the glare of the moon usually outshines the stars immediately behind it, This glimpse behind the moon is a rarity. The eclipse was classified as a “Super Flower Blood Moon.” A Blood Moon is another name for an eclipses. A Super Moon, or perigean full Moon, happens when a full moon is closest to the earth. A Flower Moon is the full moon when flowers are at their peak bloom. From any one location a total lunar eclipse is only visible every 2.5 years. The last lunar eclipse visible from the Pacific Northwest zone was on January 20, 2019. The next partial eclipse for the Pacific Northwest will be November 18-19 this year, and then not until May 15, 2022. Solar eclipses are even more rare and occur only when the moon obscures the view of the sun. The next one will be an “Annular Solar Eclipse,” where only the outer circle of the sun is visible creating a “ring of fire.” This will occur next week when the sun passes directly over the north pole on June 10. It will not be visible from the Western United States however. The East Coast of North America will have a partial view of the phenomenon, but the best viewing will be from western Europe. articles.text: Educators tell us that there is no more important activity for preparing our children for success as a reader than reading aloud together. And the earlier the better. Research reveals that the benefits of shared reading include: facilitating language-rich exposure and vocabulary development, fostering the development of listening skills, boosting comprehension, and establishing essential foundational literacy skills which will be critical for reading and spelling eventually. Not to mention the fact that story time is a bonding family ritual that can bring closeness, joy and momentary peace to hectic family life. Many children love books and all related activities from the start. However, throughout the past three decades, I have had many parents of toddlers in my office concerned about the child who is not interested in books, despite parents’ repeated efforts. Often these parents are avid readers themselves, which adds to their dismay. My suggestion is this: let’s apply modern principles of neuroscience to maximize the ageold storytime experience. How do we do this? Recent research points to certain neurotransmitters (chemical messengers in the brain) which are particularly involved in learning. Increasing production of these brain chemicals will improve the story time experience. Let’s consider two of these, and how we can maximize them during book reading. Seratonin is the mood regulator. Taking the time to set the mood will increase the serotonin level in the brain, thereby increasing engagement in the activity which follows. Specifically, increased serotonin enhances memory and learning speed. Consider setting the mood by playing some music before jumping in. We may need to focus on increasing the comforting, ritual aspect of storytime. Think about a special, comfortable space, (diming lights, special reading spot, staying up a few minutes later than usual at bedtime), and aesthetically pleasing illustrations. Creating opportunities for back and forth interactions such as line completion (rather than passively listening) can boost the mood by promoting the relationship/emotional and shared elements of the activity. Increased dopamine levels in the brain is related to increased learning and retention. Dopamine is increased when we find an activity rewarding or pleasurable. To increase the rewarding aspect of book reading, praise your toddler (“I like the way you looked at the pictures/listened/ pointed to the pictures/closed the book”). Encouraging and celebrating attempts is your first hurdle in getting a child engaged in the learning activity you have planned. Eventually learning something new is the reward. Choosing high interest books also boosts the pleasure and reward factors. Novelty has also been shown to increase dopamine. Maybe read in the dark with a flashlight once in a while? Maybe sing, whisper or shout certain words? Make up a surprise twist or ending. Read expressively, read slowly, read quickly. Change character voices. So, for the child who does not relish book time, lets boost the mood as well as the positive feedback. I will follow up in April to look at two other important neurotransmitters, and how we can maximize their production to enhance story time in other ways. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at pengilly.katie@gmail.com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C .

articles.text: Piedmont High School held its annual Senior Awards ceremony last night, June 1. Although reduced to a virtual event, the same bounty of awards was presented to members of the Class of 2021. In addition to the perpetual awards (see list below), the school handed out 35 departmental awards, ranging from certificates to trophies and plaques. Students are not told which award(s) they will be receiving in advance to heighten the excitement of being surprised by the administrators, teachers, and counselors with the presentation of each award. Each award winner’s distinguishing accomplishments are expounded upon by the faculty presenters. PERPETUAL AWARDS • Susan Kawaichi Diversity Award Presented to Lynnea Bao, Athene La Jeunesse, and Emma Moorhead The award is named for Kawaichi, a former school board member who co-founded the Appreciating Diversity Committee in Piedmont. The award honors students who promote diversity, tolerance, and progress in the school. Athene La Jeunesse worked with Youth Anti-Racism Project and spoke publicly at numerous events promoting diversity. Lynnea Bao worked for equity throughout the community and also excelled in dance and as a choreographer. Emma Moorhead also won the Outstanding Senior in Dance Plaque. • Gail Dryden Community Service Award The award was won by Bridget Bentley and Helena Lowe At the Piedmont senior awards ceremony, Bridget Bentley and Helena Lowe won the Gail Dryden Community Service Award, a perpetual award presented each year to deserving seniors. The plaque is named for former School Board member Gail Dryden. Bridget Bentley has been a staple in the Scouting Community, winning the William J Peterson Youth Leadership Award earlier in the year. Helena Lowe’s accolades span many sectors as well. She volunteered at the Chabot Space and Science Center, and also competed in Robotics. • League of Women Voters Civics in Action Award Piedmont senior Audrey Edel was named winner of the 2021 League of Women Voters Civics in Action award on June 1. Edel, the Senior Class president, demonstrated a commitment to improving the Piedmont and larger communities throughout her four years in school. Edel founded the Teens for Biden Club (now Teens for Democracy) to get the students involved in campaigning for the November elections. She also spearheaded the immensely successful mentorship program between elementary students and high schoolers during the pandemic. • Eric Swart Rachesky Memorial Certificate Piedmont senior Seamus Meagher won the annual Eric Swart Rachesky Award at the Senior Awards ceremony on June 1. Named after the late Eric Swart Rachesky, a Piedmont High School graduate, the memorial award is presented each year to students who make significant academic leaps, overcoming obstacles and hardships along the way. Meagher excelled in both academia and in sports. He was a multi-sport athlete, playing on the football and basketball teams. • Daughters of the American Revolution Good Citizen Award Jenna Kim was announced as the recipient of the DAR Good Citizen Award last night. Kim competed at the national level as a Piedmont Police Explorer, tutored Havens students through the Advocacy for Asian Americans (AAA) club, all while maintaining a high GPA. • Dean Faberman Memorial Prize (Mock Trial) Piedmont senior Anthony Wong was named the recipient of the annual Dean Faberman Memorial Prize. The plaque is awarded to a graduating senior who excels in public speaking and debate. It was created by the Faberman family in memory of their son, a 1979 graduate of Piedmont High who excelled in public speaking. While attending UC Berkeley he was killed by a drunk driver. Wong participated in Mock Trial all four years in high school. As a junior he became the Lead Prosecuting Attorney for the team. As a senior he was Co-captain, prosecution pretrial attorney, and defense attorney, leading the team to first place in the county and advancing to state competition. Wong was also named the class Salutatorian for having the second highest GPA in his class. • Valedictorian Thomas Chu and Samuel Eisenbach will share the award presented the student with the highest grade point average, each a 4.50 weighted GPA. Chu is an AP National Scholar and completed five AP courses and four Honors courses at PHS. Although reduced to a virtual event, the same bounty of awards was presented to members of the Class of 2021. In addition to the perpetual awards (see list below), the school handed out 35 departmental awards, ranging from certificates to trophies and plaques. Students are not told which award(s) they will be receiving in advance to heighten the excitement of being surprised by the administrators, teachers, and counselors with the presentation of each award. Each award winner’s distinguishing accomplishments are expounded upon by the faculty presenters. The award honors students who promote diversity, tolerance, and progress in the school. Athene La Jeunesse worked with Youth Anti-Racism Project and spoke publicly at numerous events promoting diversity. Lynnea Bao worked for equity throughout the community and also excelled in dance and as a choreographer. articles.text: As the end of the year is fast approaching, the senior class of 2021 is frantically getting ready for the prom, getting graduation outfits – and trying not to let their In contrast, those in the 8th grade, also the Class of 2021, get nothing besides a graduation. Let me tell you. Being the sister of a senior is a full-time job. I have to make sure that her prom dress looks good on her and approve an after-party outfit. And that’s only the beginning. Let’s just say if I ever have to look at another pair of six-dollar earBut all I need is a dress. My mother insists that I get better shoes for my dress, but I would much rather just wear a pair of white Converse and When I’m with my sister these days, it’s like watching a reality TV show. The level of drama in the two weeks before prom is huge (the Kardashians are probably jealous). There have been endless hours of scrolling to find the right dress that would make my sister look like a queen, years taken off my life to find the perfect necklace that would fit with her outfit, and too many close calls when her boyfriend almost saw the dress (a secret), so I had to turn into a speedster and steer Not that I’m complaining, it’s just that I think that I have gotten wrinkles from all the stress I’ve been going through. I can’t wait for the day of prom when I get to see my sister and her boyfriend see each other for the first time all dolled up and ready I’ll admit that we stalked other girls on social media to see what prom and graduation dresses they would be wearing so that we would know what my sister is up against. For eighth grade girls it’s just a bunch of texting “have you got your dress yet?” or “Do you want to go dress shopping together?” Really, our dress could be anything. But for seniors, the tradition is to wear white. I think that’s not the best idea because white gets dirty way too quickly. Mi hermana is yet to get a dress so the energy surrounding the house is getting more and more frantic. But in a worst case scenario, my mom has a dress she can borrow. But let’s get to the important items. What about the middle school graduation? First of all, we don’t get to have a dance. Eighth graders used to have a boat dance at graduation, but not for class of 2021 because of Covid. (There is rumor that the 8th grade class might have a boat dance in August, but that’s a little late.) So, no worries about a dress for me. All I will do this June is walk across a stage, get a diploma, and listen to my classmates talk. As tradition goes, people get asked to the prom. The prom asks can range anywhere from standing at a locker with a flower and asking the person when they get there or making a sign and surprising your (hopeful) date to the prom, or if you have extra money laying around, renting a plane and attaching in big letters “Go to prom with me”. I helped my sister with her prom ask: we went to Michael’s together and bought all the supplies. It was the cutest thing watching her worry over the poster’s every detail and making sure it was perfect. In the long run we should have used more glue, because we did lose a “u.” Instead of “Will you?” we had “Will yo?,” which was kind of funny, in my opinion. It doesn’t feel real that I’m graduating from middle school, because I still remember the first day of sixth grade when I thought that I was the coolest person ever. But I wish we could have had a real in-person eighth grade year, so my friends and I could have ruled the school. Somehow, the seventh graders took over that role, though no one knows how. But I wouldn’t want to repeat this year – a year spent couped up at home, making unforgettable memories, and the constant threat of a global pandemic looming. I made amazing friends this year that I hope to keep all through high school. The teachers I had this year managed to make online school not terrible, if not exactly enjoyable, but there’s only so much they could do given the circumstances. I am extremely excited to go to high school, no matter how much it scares me. I still can’t comprehend that my role model, idol, and partner in crime (also known is my sister) is going to college in the fall. Because I remember she held my hand when I walked to kindergarten, when she went to middle school, when she played water balloon volleyball in 5th grade, and when she went on her first date. And now she is going to be walking across a stage and getting a diploma that says “Congrats. Get ready to start your life as an adult.” As a younger sister, that’s really hard. I will miss her not being around 24/7 no matter how many times I fight with her. I can’t wait for her to go chase her dreams and hopefully one day catch them. She deserves the world. And I can’t wait for the day she finishes college. I can’t wait for the day she says, “I do”. I can’t wait for the day I become an aunt. So, this is a thank you to an Anonymous Older Sister. Thank you for being the best big sister I could have ever asked for. It truly is the end of an era that I will never forget. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, June 2, 2021 By Jay Russell The music blared, and water balloons flew Thursday May 27 on the PHS campus, as seniors in the Class of 2021 celebrated their last few days on campus with snacks, trinkets, and, of course, water balloons. During lunch break, ASB seniors gave their classmates Krispy Kreme, Otter Pops and Top Dogs to eat, along with reusable straws, wrist bands, and carabiners. Seniors celebrate last days on campus with water balloons “We were celebrating the seniors. It was a free and fun get together to celebrate the end of the year,” said organizer and Senior Class president Audrey Edel Two buckets of water balloons provided the entertainment on a sunny, beautiful day. English teacher Beth Black and ASB Advisor Aaron Barlin stopped by to catch a couple of balloons. Other teachers playfully requested a ceasefire as they walked by with stacks of papers in their arms. Joy resonated on the high school campus, and deservedly so. Seniors had to wait over a year to return to campus this spring and were the last grade to return. Screams of laughter resonated through Piedmont High and the face masks could hardly contain the smiles. The class of 2021 will have its final get together at the graduation ceremony on Friday June 11 at 5:00 p.m. at Witter Field. ASB seniors staff a table of goodies: Anjuli Turner (left), Grace Davies, Sophie Jorcino, Ang Lee, Audrey Edel and Bella Kjellen. Seamus Meagher “catches” a water balloon and is rewarded with a refreshing spritz of water on a sunny May afternoon at PHS. Senior Malia Lee reacts to getting soaked by an errant water balloon. ASB Advisor and English teacher Aaron Barlin stops by the quad for a little research on the poetic flight of water balloons. English teacher Beth Black joins the water balloon toss with Senior Class president Audrey Edel. Sophie Eng points out what tasty treat she would like from the ASB table.

articles.text: Photos by Abe Katz More than two dozen Scouts and Scout Advisors from Piedmont Troop 6 installed flags in Mountain View Cemetery on Saturday in advance of Memorial Day, May 31. More than 20 Scouts and 7 adult leaders from Piedmont Council’s Troop 6 participated in the installation of nearly 1000 flags at Mountain View Cemetery two days in advance of Memorial Day, May 31. Troop 6, based at Corpus Christi Church, has taken responsibility for many years for placing flags in the sections of the cemetery that are of a military significance. Tobias Guzman helps Scouts from Troop 6 install flags at Mountain View Cemetery. Troop 6 Scout Jack Gros installs flags on the upper part of Mountain View Cemetery. Lenny Gustavson, a member of Piedmont Scout Troop 6, installs flags in Mountain View Cemetery in advance of Memorial Day. Troop 6 Scout JD Sellman places flags along the main drive into Mountain View Cemetery. Aiden Velasco helps Mountain View Cemetery prepare for Memorial Day by installing flags.
articles.title: Troop 6 Scouts honor Memorial Day with flags at cemetery

articles.text: Photos by Todd Marshburn Piedmont’s soccer team plays its final match of the season tomorrow, June 3. The Highlanders are currently 8-0-1 with no league losses. Care to take a guess as to which the hottest team in Piedmont is? With a convincing 5-1 win on the road against rivals San Lorenzo last Tuesday, May 25, Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team remains undefeated in league play with an 8-0-1 record. Their final match of the season is tomorrow, June 3 at Hayward. The victory over the Grizzlies last Tuesday came just one day after suffering its only loss of the season to non-league Bishop O’Dowd 2-0 on May 24. “We scheduled O’Dowd and SLZ a day after each other because we wanted to challenge ourselves. San Lorenzo is a massively tough opponent who you can never take lightly,” said PHS coach Todd Sullivan. Against SLZ, the Highlanders led 2-0 in the first 15 minutes of action with quick goals from Andre Stankiewicz and William Daniel. The Grizzlies went into halftime within striking distance after scoring from a penalty kick in the 27th minute—it marked the first PHS goal allowed to a Shoreline Division team this season. Stankiewicz nearly had a second goal in the 29th minute, but his shot trailed narrowly wide of the left post. Piedmont’s next goal came around five minutes into the second half after being awarded a free kick from 40 yards, where a lob was headed in by Andrew Szerdy – who started the year on Junior Varsity – putting PHS ahead 3-1. Andre Stankiewicz scored an early goal against San Lorenzo for Piedmont’s first score in a 5-1 win. Center back Sawyer Collins scored a goal against San Lorenzo.
articles.title: Highlanders remain undefeated in league at 8-0-1

articles.text: Greg Gately, generally a quiet kid at school, bellowed in exuberance, a sound that could be heard by spectators at Witter Field on Friday night, and probably by neighbors within a two-block radius. Gately, one of 13 seniors on the lacrosse team and its offensive leader on faceoffs, had just scored the winning goal barely one minute into overtime to lead his team to a thrilling 9-8 victory over rival Bishop O’Dowd. When looking for the best lacrosse in the East Bay, you’d be hard pressed to find a better rivalry than the one between Piedmont and O’Dowd. Piedmont head coach Ryan Price came from O’Dowd three years ago, and he has not lost to his former school since then. Friday’s win came exactly two weeks after a 7-6 victory at O’Dowd – also in overtime – on May 12. Gately’s goal put an exclamation point on a night dedicated to PHS seniors. Running on adrenalin, he was determined to score. Describing the play, Gately explained, “Everyone was gassed. We just had to get it up the field. We got so lucky they messed it up on their possession. I saw the matchup, I saw the lane, the ball got around, and what happened, Greg Gately scored the game-winning goal against O’Dowd 1 minute into overtime. happened,” he added, beaming from ear-to-ear. “You never know with this rivalry; it’s a fun one,’ said coach Price. “Hats off to O’Dowd, they were really well coached and had us figured out. We just stuck with it. We’ve been preaching heart and attitude, and the heart came through.” In a typical season, PHS and O’Dowd play each other twice before the league championship tournament for the title in early May. Without a post-season tournament and a bonafide championship this year (due to a Covid-related shortened season), the two games in May provided all the emotions of playoffs. Friday’s recap O’Dowd jumped out to a 3-0 lead before the end of the first quarter, and PHS fans appropriately looked nervous. After an early goal by Jack Nelson and assist by Gately, Luke Biehn scored with 1.5 seconds left in the quarter to inch closer, though still trailing 3-2. But O’Dowd seemed up to the task and scored twice more to lead 5-2 with 7:58 left before halftime. Price called a timeout, rallied the Highlanders, and soon the momentum of the game changed. Gately scored with 7:40 to go, and Nate Guzdar scored on a long shot three minutes later. PHS tied the game at 5-5 on a man advantage on a shot from Soren Dixon. With 2:22 left before halftime, J.D. Harrison, the hero of Piedmont’s May 12 overtime win with O’Dowd, scored to give the Highlanders a 6-5 lead at the half. Piedmont fans came to life, as the possibilities began looking a bit brighter. Piedmont went up 7-5 with a slick goal from Nate Fredericks while driving through traffic. However, O’Dowd tied the match at 7-7 with 5:48 left in the quarter, then regained the lead at 8-7 with 38 seconds remaining. In the fourth quarter, the Highlanders tied the match 8-8 with 5:18 left. They had several chances on net which were saved, including one from Gately with

pages.text: Wednesday, June 2, 2021 13 By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team finished its 2021 season with a third-place finish in the Western Alameda County Conference tournament after defeating Alameda on Saturday, May 29 at the Encinal Pool in Alameda. In the semifinals on Thursday, May 27, the Highlanders suffered a heartbreaking 8-7 loss in overtime to Bishop O’Dowd. “We knew Alameda would use the same defense that Bishop O’Dowd ran on us. The kids have put in a lot of work [this season]. I’m very grateful for the everyone to help make this happen. They’ve been working since December,” said coach John Savage. The high school water polo Staff Photos Max Wagener scored five goals against Alameda and had a goal against Bishop O’Dowd. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team finished its season with a third-place finish at the Western Alameda County Conference (league) tournament at Encinal in Alameda. They defeated Castro Valley 9-3 on Saturday, May 29, and lost 16-6 to Encinal in the semifinals on Thursday, May 27. “We played great defense against Castro Valley. They are good at driving, and we had to play our best. Our girls stepped up and played as a team on defense. Offensively, we had to think outside the box and start driving more. It’s something I’ve wanted to see all season,” said coach Sarah Mooney. It marks a turnaround for the girls’ program, achieving their top performance in the WACC Tournament since Mooney’s senior year at Piedmont High in the fall of 2014 when they finished with a 16-6 record and runner up to Alameda. With a 5-4 overall record in Rosie Feldman scored a careerhigh six goals against Castro Valley to help Piedmont win third place at the WACC Tournament. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team is wrapping up a busy end to the 2021 season, winning three of their last five games in as many days starting with a critical 94-88 win over Dublin on Tuesday, May 25 at Binks. In a scheduling nightmare, they played Bishop O’Dowd the next day and lost 82-73. They beat Oakland High 75-72 in the Rawlings Gym on May 27, defeated San Leandro 77-66 on Friday, May 28, and lost 75-56 to University in San Francisco on Saturday. May 29. Whew. What a week. The group of games featured matches against top-ranked schools in the area. Currently, MaxPreps.com ranks Dublin as the No. 3 team in North Coast Section, and WestCoastPreps. com listed them as No. 5 in the Bay Area prior to May 25. University and O’Dowd are ranked in the top 10 by both of the online sports groups. Piedmont clearly is in the mix, ranked No. 9 by both MaxPreps and WestCoastPreps. And the Luke Harris has scored 106 points over the five-game stretch. He makes his final appearance at Binks Rawlings Gym this Friday, June 4, against O’Dowd. season isn’t quite over, with three more games in three days starting tonight, Wednesday, June 2. Tonight’s game against Berkeley brings back former Highlanders’ and current Yellowjackets’ coach Mike Hudson to Piedmont. On June 3, PHS travels to Alameda High before closing the season at Binks Rawling’s Gym against Bishop O’Dowd on Friday night, June 4. 94-88 win over Dublin Dublin, a Division 1 program and last year’s runner up in the NCS Open Division, came into Piedmont heralding its high ranking and looking to conclude its season on a high-note. But the Highlanders quickly dashed the Gaels’ hopes. Piedmont led 28-20 at the end of the first period and nearly put the game out of reach at halftime, leading 52-38. Dublin battled back in the second half and cut the deficit to 75-66 by the start of the fourth quarter. They came within one point, but the Highlanders closed out strong to win the high-scoring game, 94-88. PHS players were on fire from 3-point land, hitting 19 of 30 attempts. JoJo Murphy finished with 25 points and six 3-pointers. Standout sophomore A.J. Harris bagged a career-high 24 points, hitting six-of-seven 3-pointers along the way, and older brother Luke Harris had 21 points and two 3-pointers. “We had a big-time win against Dublin. We had contributions from the starters and the bench guys; we shot the lights out. We were 19 of 30 from three; we just couldn’t miss,” said am ecstatic coach Ben Spencer. 82-73 loss to Bishop O’Dowd Piedmont visited Bishop O’Dowd the next day on Wednesday, May 26, and battled to an 82-73 loss. PHS led 25-22 at the end of the first quarter but trailed 42-39 by halftime. O’Dowd extended its advantage to 60-54 by the start of the fourth and finished with an 82-73 victory. The Dragons’ Jarin Edwards was the catalyst with 27 points, all of which came in the paint. “It was a tough game; it was our third game in three days, but no excuses. articles.text: Piedmont’s badminton team finished the abbreviated 2021 season with a 4-1 record. The squad opened its season with a 10-4 loss to San Lorenzo on April 29 before reeling off four straight wins – against Hayward 9-6 on Saturday, May 1, Encinal 6-5 on Thursday, May 6, Hayward 9-5 on Saturday, May 8, before a 4-2 win over Tennyson to end the season on Thursday, May 20. The Piedmont High badminton team gathered for a team photo after the end of its season. The Highlanders were forced to suspend activities for two weeks following a positive COVID-19 case on the roster on May 12. It effectively put an end to their once promising season. There was no season-ending league tournament. “The coaches tried [for a league tournament] but the logistics were too difficult. Many of the schools did not have enough players this year. Piedmont was the only team with a full roster,” explained coach David Siu. 4-2 win over Tennyson In its most recent match, Piedmont took nine eligible athletes to Tennyson and came away with a 4-2 win. Linus Lee won at boys’ singles, Jonathan Wu and Dylan Ong won at mixed doubles, Anne-Marie Gibbs won at girls’ singles but Cameryn Kwong lost. At girls’ doubles, August Thigpen and Sally Post won, while Kira Ma and Truc Le lost. Final set scores were not recorded. 9-5 win over Hayward On Saturday, May 8, Piedmont swept boys’ singles, mixed doubles, and took two of three boys’ doubles matches. At boys’ singles, No. 1 starter Collin Mortimer won 21-10, 21-10; Linus Lee won in three sets, 9-21, 21-18, 21-17 at No. 2; Ethan Tran won 21-5, 21-18 at No. 3. To mixed doubles, No. 1 pair of Thomas Yu and Isa Griffis won 21-11, 21-9; No. 2 Jerry Liu and Sam Lee won in three sets, 9-21, 21-19, 21-14; No. 3 Jonathan Wu and Dylan Ong won 21-9, 17-21, 21-7. In doubles, Jeremy Yiu and Niko Rapport won 21-6, 21-8 at No. 1; No. 2 brother pairing of David and Gary Zhou won 21-13, 21-11. 6-5 win against Encinal Piedmont won narrowly 6-5 on May 6 with help of a clean sweep by the three boys’ singles matches in straight sets. At No. 1 Mortimer won 21-7, 21-7; No. 2 Tran won 21-10, 21-8; No. 3 Lee won 21-2, 21-4. In boys’ doubles, No. 1 Yiu and Rapport won 21-6, 21-6; No. 2 the Zhou brothers won 21-1, 21-5; No. 3 Wu and Roman Reyes lost 21-1, 21-5. In mixed doubles, No. 1 Yu and Griffis were the only victorious team 21-5, 21-5. No. 2 and No. 3 scores were not recorded. Encinal lost two girls’ singles and two girls’ doubles matches. In singles, Kwong lost 21-4, 21-6 at No. 1; No. 2 Katie Wen lost 21-5, 21-6. articles.text: Staff Photos Natalie Martinez had 19 points San Leandro, including the gamewinning baskets. Piedmont’s girls’ basketball hit a rocky patch last week, losing to Bishop O’Dowd in regulation and Marin Catholic in overtime. They also beat San Leandro for the second time this season. They have two games left in the shortened season and have an 11-3 record. The squad lost to O’Dowd on the road 60-49 on Wednesday, May 26, neat San Leandro by three points, 60-57, on Friday, May 28 at home, and lost a 41-40 nail-biter in overtime to Marin Catholic on May 29. The Highlanders’ final home games are against Berkeley tonight, Wednesday, June 2 and Bishop O’Dowd on Friday, June 4. Berkeley and O’Dowd hold two of PHS’ losses. Marin Catholic, meanwhile, avenged its 49-44 loss to Piedmont on May 10. “We faced some tough teams. Overall we want to see the competitive-greatness show up and match that every night. These teams are good, and they are good for a reason,” said coach Bryan Gardere. The girls’ basketball team currently is ranked by MaxPreps’ as No. 4 among Fic. 4 schools in the North Coast Section and No. 12 in the Bay Area. 60-49 loss to O’Dowd The Highlanders led 13-12 by the end of the first quarter but fell behind 27-21 prior to halftime after being held to eight points in the second quarter. The Dragons extended the lead to 43-31 in the third before closing out their win, 60-49. Trinity Zamora finished with 23 points, six rebounds, four assists, and a steal. Kai Johnson had six points eight rebounds, and an assist. Natalie Martinez had 12 points, three boards, and one assist. Brie Sotelo had two points and four rebounds. Hannah Govert and Maddie Hill had three points. Senior Kai Johnson makes her final appearance at Binks Rawlings Gym on Friday, June 4 against Bishop O’Dowd. Trinity Zamora had 23 points in Piedmont’s loss to Bishop O’Dowd. 3-point win vs San Leandro Piedmont led 18-10 at the end of the first quarter and took a 32-20 lead by halftime. The Pirates made a major comeback, and led 44-43 at the start of the final quarter. PHS was held to 11 points in the third quarter. The fourth quarter featured Martinez, a freshman, who scored 11 of the team’s 17 points in the final quarter to help Piedmont win, 60-57. “It was a crazy fourth quarter. Natalie made two huge 3-pointers, a layup and free throws to ice the game,” said Gardere with a big smile. Zamora had 13 points, 20 rebounds, six assists. Johnson scored 16 points, eight rebounds. Martinez had 19 points, eight rebounds, four steals. Hill had four points, Govert scored three. Sotelo had five points and six rebounds. OT loss at Marin Catholic Piedmont traveled to Kentfield to play Marin Catholic on Saturday, May 29, and lost a low-scoring overtime battle, 41-40. The game was tied 11-11 at the end of the first quarter, while MC held a 25-21 lead at halftime. The Highlanders held the Wildcats to five points in the third period to tie the game at 30-30 before ending the fourth quarter in a 39-39 deadlock. In the two-minute overtime, PHS hit one of three free throw attempts but relinquished two free throws to the Wildcats in the final minute to lose, 41-40. Johnson had 11 points, Martinez scored 10, Zamora had nine, Hill scored eight, and Sotelo had two. NEXT UP Piedmont (11-3) has a big game at Binks Rawlings Gym with Berkeley tonight, Wednesday, June 2 at 5:30 p.m. The team hosts its season-finale against Bishop O’Dowd on Friday, June 4, also at 5:30 p.m. Piedmont will honor its one senior, Kai Johnson, a four year starter who is headed to play at Weber State nest year.

articles.text: The Highlanders fell to Berkeley 2-0 on Tuesday, May 25 in Berkeley, then had their Senior Night at Witter Field derailed in a 3-0 loss to San Leandro last night, June 1. The team honored its four seniors on the roster yesterday prior to playing San Leandro: Sophie Allen-Goix, Paxton Grimmer, Charlotte Hubbell, and Abby Gallagher. “We had the seniors all play most of the game. Sophie has been injured, she took the kickoff and came out. It’s a fun occasion, Senior Night is always fun, but San Leandro came to play. We were probably the stronger team in the second half, but they killed the game with a close counter-attack,” said coach Dan Chubbock. Piedmont plays its final game of the season tomorrow night in Castro Valley. In the 2-0 loss to Berkeley, the game was tied at 0-0 before the Yellowjackets added the go-ahead in the early minutes of the second half. They scored later for an insurance goal. But San Leandro caught the Highlanders’ sleeping, pouncing quickly for two goals by the 30-minute mark, for a 2-0 lead at halftime. articles.text: The Girls Academy League hosted a Talent Identification event in Northern California on May 24, featuring the top talent in the League’s Northwest conference from the 2004, 2005, 2006, and 2007 age groups. The Girls Academy advertised these events as scouting opportunities for the U.S. Soccer youth national teams. This was the fourth regional event for the 2020- 21 season. Lamorinda led the way among the clubs with 29 players called into the event between the four age groups. FC Bay Area and San Francisco Elite Academy (SFEA) each had 21 players called into the event. Piedmont soccer players on the Lamorinda team selected for the Girls Academy Talent ID Event included Sadie Lahey-Teare (defense) and Audrey Lam (midfield) in the age 2005 division, and defenders Amy Derr and Rina Higashi in the 2006 age division.

articles.text: The Piedmont Spartans won the Bronco league championship (age 11-12) in an 18-10 victory over the Orinda Vipers on Sunday, May 23 in a back-and-forth affair. In the top of the fourth inning, the Spartans rallied to tie the game at 5-5 after Tsukasa Sano singled and drove in 2 runs. In the top of the fifth inning, the Spartans took a 6-5 lead scored on a stolen base and a double by Aiden Morgan. Orinda kept the game within reach with a grand slam home run in the sixth inning, but a big seventh inning by the Spartans, led by Morgan, Ragones, Declan Bair, and Milo Chipman, all with RBIs, put the game away. On the mound, Sammy Ragones went five innings, allowing six runs on five hits, striking out seven and no walks.

articles.text: The entire Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir student body will perform in their annual “Spring Sing!” concert. Watch the entire Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir student body perform in their annual “Spring Sing!” concert, which will stream live this Saturday, June 5, at 4 p.m. The performance will be available to watch after the live-stream. The Kinder, Training, and Performing Department choirs join together for this musical celebration of community. It will include 200 singers from all 10 of the choir’s ensembles. The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir is able to offer its 2020-21 virtual concert season free to the public due to the generosity of donors. articles.text: Berkeley Symphony Music Director Joseph Young will lead the San Francisco Symphony in live concerts Thursday and Friday this week, June 3 and June 4. The performances mark a return to live performances at Davies Symphony Hall after a 14-month closure due the current health crisis. Young will lead music from the contemporary American experience, to include Jessie Montgomery’s Banner and Carlos Simon’s reflective An Elegy: A Cry from the Grace. The program will be topped off with Georges Bizet’s Carmen. The symphony’s live concert reopening was developed in accordance with San Francisco County and city guidelines; masks and physical distancing will be observed, and all attendees must provide proof of vaccination or a negative COVID-19 test. As part of a series of six concerts, the June 3 and 4 concerts will be approximately 75 minutes in length and will be performed without intermissions. For tickets, visit: https://www. sfsymphony.org. Tickets are also available for the following future performances: • June 10 and 11: Guest conductor Joshua Weilerstein • June 17 and 18: San Francisco Symphony conductor EsaPekka Salonen • June 24 and 25: Esa-Pekka Salonen Visit https://www.sfsymphony. org/calendar for a full calendar of events, to include live and digital performances. Berkeley Symphony Music Director Joseph Young

articles.text: Lily Tomlin and Julie Garner in a scene from Grandma. Don’t be misled by the trailer or the posters for the just-released film, Grandma. This is not a road trip across Nebraska with Lily Tomlin as Elle, the snarky/wise, playing-it-for-laughs grandma. She is accompanied by her clueless, teenage granddaughter, Sage, portrayed by Julia Garner, as the story explores the generational chasm that defines and separates them. As example, when Elle mentions The Feminine Mystique, Sage assumes she’s referring to a character in the X-Men series. But this is a wonderful, character-driven film that was written by director Paul Weitz for Tomlin. Without question her Oscar-worthy performance is a tour-de-force. There is nothing about Elle that is shallow or casually flippant; rather, she is a 70-something woman who is still grieving for the loss of her partner of 38 years, Violet. Elle is also a no-compromise feminist, a poet, and a retired college professor who feels herself falling, incrementally, into a misanthropic well of emptiness. After a hurtful scene at the opening of the film in which she breaks up with a younger woman, Olivia (Judy Greer), calling her a mere footnote in her life, she weeps for all that is now absent. What’s left? Feeling angry and maudlin, dressed in her scholarly cap and gown, she is going through old photographs when the doorbell rings. It’s her granddaughter, Sage, who has turned to her grandmother for help and money. She’s a senior in high school and pregnant and needs $600 for an abortion scheduled for later that day. Sage can’t turn to her mother, Judy (Marcia Gay Harden), who will shower her with rage and criticism. Elle, as it turns out, is also broke (she’s recently sold wind chimes she made out of her credit cards to pay off all of her debts.) Grandmother and granddaughter set out on a kind of L.A. road trip, going to Elle’s old friends and acquaintances to raise the money by that afternoon. The ride? Violet’s vintage Dodge. At every stop, Elle, with Sage in tow, demonstrates that her irascible, foul-mouthed, shortfuse temper may stand her in good stead in keeping the world at bay, but it doesn’t help when it comes to getting cash from those she knows. For those she drops in on, she’s a splinter under a fingernail, a fact demonstrated eloquently in one scene with a longago flame, Karl (Sam Elliot), who has the cash but can’t let go of the hurt Elle caused him 40 years earlier. There is a patina of humor in many of the scenes, including one that is especially funny – a confrontation Elle and Sage have with Sage’s irresponsible, “not my problem” boyfriend. In the main, however, the issues involved, to include the decision to have an abortion, are serious and sad and touching. So many of the films released today merely circle the drain of farce. Grandma is the antidote, and the antithesis. It is filled with honesty and doesn’t back away from the pain felt by Elle as she struggles to come to terms with the hole left in her life by Violet’s illness and death. To spend 38 years with another person, creating a quilt of experiences, stitching days and years into a familiar pattern and then have that person suddenly gone involves regret that can seem insurmountable. Make no mistake, this is a very special film, one that is heartfelt from the first frame until the last. Grandma. Directed by Paul Weitz. Starring Lily Tomlin, Julie Garner, and Marcia Gay Harden. 1 hr., 18 min. Rated R.
articles.title: Grandma a gem of a film with Lily Tomlin

articles.text: Film review by Chris Honoré The power of fine filmmaking can be extraordinary. Take the issue of illegal immigration, generally regarded in the abstract – our borders are porous, hence there are 11 million undocumented workers in America. It is a problem that is distant, political, a conundrum and one from which we are often insulated. But create an irresistible story about a gardener, Carlos Galindo (Demian Bichir), living in East Los Angeles, without documents, a single parent raising a 16-yearold boy, Luis (Jose Julian), and suddenly the problem becomes real, even personal. At the center of this wonderful film is a principled man, cutting and trimming the grounds of the wealthy, while struggling to keep himself and Luis above water. His goal, his dream, is to have his own truck, his own tools and mower, and so create a life that has at its center, family and stability. A Better Life is a moving portrait of Carlos, who leaves his one-bedroom bungalow each morning at dawn and returns long after dark, falling exhausted onto the hard-used sofa in the living room. He is unaware that his son is drifting away and is finding the faux family security of gangs more inviting than the home offered by his father. Luis, who was born in America, stands with one foot in the culture of his parent and one foot in the culture he finds at school and on the street. His connection to Mexico is tentative, the language and customs seeming ever more strange. Each day Carlos copes with a shroud of anxiety because of his illegal status, ever fearful that he will be stopped by “la migra” and asked for some form of identification. The gardener he works for offers to sell his truck to Carlos and include his client list. He is returning to Mexico. But Carlos, who has no license, no I.D., decides to take the risk. He views the truck as the path to the American dream. Filled with pride, he drives through Los Angeles, looking out the window of the truck. We see parts of the city that are hidden from the usual traveler. There is a diversity created by immigrants that is rich with color and vitality. These are not the mean streets; they are, however, the hardscrabble streets. Sadly, many of the inhabitants, though they contribute to America, are part of a shadow population that is seen but not seen, residing in a place apart, living in immigration ghettos filled with doss-apartments, the drapes tightly closed. But just as Carlos senses that life is about to turn around, events occur that put him and his son in jeopardy. The film is not a political tract or a polemic about immigration. It is a deeply human story, both touching and compelling, about a father and his son who learn about one another as they set about recovering something they have lost. Their journey is transformative. A Better Life. Directed by Chris Weitz. Starring Demian Bichir, Dolores Heredia, Jose Julian, Joaquin Cosio and Tim Griffin. 1 hr., 38 min. Rated PG-13
articles.title: A Better Life a lovely film about an immigrant father and son

articles.text: A scene from the Dreamworks animation movie, The Croods. Movie review by Chris Honoré The Croods is a comedy of sorts, set in prehistoric times (the Pilocene era). The Croods are a dysfunctional family of five who live in a cave and only venture out to collect food. Otherwise they obey the pater familia, Grug (Nicolas Cage), and remain safely inside, living by his motto, “Never not be afraid.” They are prey and their world is filled with predators. The Croods – mother, Ugga (Catherine Keener), Gran (Cloris Leachman), and brother Thunk (Clark Duke) – are introduced to us in voice over by teenage daughter Eeep (Emma Stone), who is rebelliously curious about what there is to discover beyond the cave. One night, with everyone asleep, she sneaks out, and seeing a strange light in the distance, she investigates. Holding a torch is an evolved Sapien named Guy (Ryan Reynolds), who has discovered fire. He is adventurous, a bit dashing, and relies on intelligence rather than brute force. He looks down on the Neanderthals. Guy warns Eep that an apocalypse is about to happen, likely in the form of lava producing earthquakes, and she and her family should leave their cave for higher ground. When Guy and Eep share this prediction with Grug, he is doubtful and resistant – until their cave is destroyed by a quake. The family is now forced to head out in search of new shelter. Guy leads them into new environs where they encounter a surprising number of critters. He invents things along the way, such as, well, footwear. The plot involves a series of adventurous detours, kind of a Paleolithic road trip in which they discover a bucolic jungle and animals such as saber toothed housecats and a flock of razor-toothed birds. Eventually they do find a cave that is suitable for the family, but by now they have unexpectedly discovered that they prefer to live outside. The Croods, released eight years ago in 2013, was nominated for an Oscar for Best Animated Feature film and was also nominated for a Golden Globe for its dazzling animation. The Croods. Directed by Kirk DeMarco, Chris Sanders. Dreamworks animation. With voices of Nicolas Cage, Emma Stone, & Ryan Reynolds. 1 hr., 31 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: The Croods – welcome to a Paleolithic road trip

articles.text: In an article in the New York Times Magazine, director Spike Jonze, when discussing his film, Where the Wild Things Are, said, “Everything we did, all the decisions that we made, were to try to capture the feeling of what it is to be 9.” While it is true that a movie targeting young filmgoers must engage their imaginations and emotions, it shouldn’t necessarily mirror what it feels like to be 9 years old. At least not completely. There must also be magic and surprise. In other words, a film of this type will find more success if it’s a fable that asks young audiences to suspend their disbelief and climb onboard. It’s something they are fully prepared to do – say, at the drop of a hat. But first, consider the book. Written by Maurice Sendak and published in 1963, it has sold 19 million copies worldwide, including 10 million in the U.S. Its success begs the question, what is there about this story that young readers so completely embrace? The story, after all, comprises only 338 words; 41 lines of text; and is only 37 pages long. Perhaps it’s the fact that story is a seamless melding of reality and fantasy. A boy, Max, dressed in a wolf costume, consumed with a riptide of emotion, rebels, causing mischief, and is sent to his room. And that’s when the magic begins. His room grows into a forest, and he finds a boat and sails to a distant shore where he discovers a band of feral monsters – large, furry, exotic, all strange hybrid animals. He becomes the king of the monsters, wears a crown, carries a scepter, and is empowered. It’s an overwhelming feeling for Max. He stands and yells to the monsters that it’s time to howl and experience their inner wildness. Eventually, however, he decides to return to his family, to those who love him most. Where the Wild Things Are is an elegant and simple story, wonderfully illustrated by Sendak, and one that would appeal to any youngster who feels conflicted and perhaps frustrated at being buffeted by the whims of family, school and siblings, wishing only for a magic place where he or she can be king. In the first act of the film, Jonze captures, with pitch-perfect insight, the existential pain of any kid who feels overwhelmed by life. Max (Max Records) is coping with the divorce of his parents. His sense of isolation is so complete that he talks to fences as if they could talk back. When Max discovers his mother has invited a strange man over for dinner, and sees then nuzzling on the couch, he acts out, argues with his mother and runs from the house, angry and conflicted. It’s at this point that Sendak’s fable begins. And therein is the real challenge for Jonze as a screenwriter. The difficulty of adapting Sendak’s story to the screen is that it lacks even a semblance of a strong narrative arc. There is only a paper-thin plot; there is no real conflict and no resolution. Hence, for Sendak’s book to be adapted to the screen as a 98-minute feature, Jonze had to embellish considerably. But if he deviated too far from the fable template (and from Sendak’s book), he would do so at his peril. Kids wish to be swept up in a story that involves a journey akin to that found in Shrek or Harry Potter or Spy Kids, one in which the protagonist struggles to overcome adversity, achieves a specific goal, is victorious, and in a tale that ends with a nice moral. Jonze’s film draws very little from that recipe. Though the film is imaginative, and the photography superb, the tones are sepia and dark in contrast to the crisp, bright colors of most kids’ movies. In fact, it could be argued that Where the Wild Things Are is not a film intended for children, but for adults who enjoy watching movies that remind them of their childhood. The monsters, which Jonze develops, have names and speak, something they don’t do in the book. They are somber and dysfunctional, and Carol (James Gandolfini), the wild thing Max comes to know best, is given to bouts of scary temper, threatening to hurt Max – even suggesting that Max should be eaten. In the end, there is no emotional center to the film. Even the relationships between the wild things seem too subtle and strange, something that will be missed by the younger audience. It’s clear that Jonze made an astonishing effort to adapt a book that simply did not have enough substance to be made into a feature film. It was a high-risk gamble by the studio and Jonze and is laudable. But is it high gain? Where the Wild Things Are. Starring Catherine Keener, Max Records, James Gandolfini, Catherine O’Hara, Forest Whitaker and Chris Cooper. Directed by Spike Jonze. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG. Max Records stars in Where the Wild Things Are.
articles.title: Where the Wild Things Are – Sendak’s book on the big screen

articles.text: Live theater returned to Piedmont High School from May 21 to 23 with four sold-out performances of the musical Mamma Mia! The performances were held in the amphitheater on the high school campus, with standard Covid health precautions in place. Virtual auditions were held last September, and the cast rehearsed 100% remotely for six months. In-person rehearsals began less than one month before the show’s opening. In a curtain speech before each performance, Director and choreographer Amy Moorhead expressed gratitude to the cast and crew for their “trust in each other, and their trust in the process of putting on a musical in extremely uncertain times.” The show included 22 students: Ellie Andersen, Aaron Belikoff, Lucca Carr-Veramo, Nellie Daniels, Sophia Ethington, Cole Garcia, Alex Guevara, Shari Lynn Halden, Maya Hollingsworth, Charlie Lucas, Scott McKenzie, Graham McWeeny, Photos by Julie Reichle Shari Lynn Halden in the lead role in Mamma Mia. Molly McWeeny, Emma Moorhead, Payton Morell, Quincy Munyan, Corinn Richards, Zoe Saldanha, Katherine Stormer, Gabe Symkowick, Holden Temple, and Aidan Weiss. The production was directed by Moorhead, with vocal direction by Jon Gallo, and PHS vocal music teacher Jorell Chavez. Zoe Saldanha (left), Emma Moorhead, and Payton Morell in Mamma Mia. Quincy Munyan (left), Cole Garcia, and Lucca Carr-Veramo in Piedmont High School’s production of the musical Mamma Mia.
articles.title: PHS produces musical Mamma Mia in amphitheater

articles.text: Henry Fisher, a dapper Hollywood violinist, with his luxurious and speedy Auburn automobile, a purchase influenced by a friend, famous racecar driver Barney Oldfield. The Indianapolis 500 was celebrated last Sunday. The Bay Bridge on Tuesday evening seemed like a warm-up to the race. The posted speed limit on the Bay Bridge is 50 miles an hour. Cars going 60 miles an hour were cowering in the right lane. All around them, people were driving like lunatics, weaving in and out and going between 75 and 80 miles an hour. It was a very harrowing experience. Was it, perhaps, the lunar eclipse? Speaking of speed demons, I am reminded of one of the most interesting characters in the history of automobile racing. He was a cigar-chomping former bicycle racer named Barney Oldfield. In his day, Oldfield was synonymous with speed itself. Cops would pull over speeders and say to them: “Who do you think you are, Barney Oldfield?” I don’t know if Barney Oldfield played the violin or was even interested in music. But I do know that he had a big influence on my first violin teacher. It was because of Oldfield that my first violin teacher fell in love with fancy cars. Included among these were cars by Stutz, Auburn, and Cord. The great Italian opera composer Giacomo Puccini was also in love with fast cars. His passion for speed almost resulted in his death in a serious car crash. Puccini wasn’t the only one. Immortal violinist Jascha Heifetz also had a passion for cars. He wasn’t addicted to speed in the same way that Puccini was, but he used to drive his Bentley like a parking lot attendant. Heifetz was concerned about the air that we breathe, and he commissioned the father of a friend of mine to build a special electric car which he publicized in every way. He was also responsible, in large part, for the emergency number 911. Thank you, Jascha. Another violinist interested in fancy cars was the Jan Kubelik, a Czech. He used to drive around in a Duesenburg. For effect, he strapped his famous Stradivarius to the side of the car where the spare tire usually went. Kubelik loved California so much that he bought a house in Los Gatos and was a frequent guest at the Bohemian Grove. Kubelik’s successor was a guy named Vasa Prihoda. His passion was big and powerful Mercedes-Benz convertibles. He was equally adept in virtuoso violin playing and virtuoso driving. There was even talk that he might become a racecar driver. The old days certainly had some interesting characters. They were great musical personalities and they knew how to enjoy life. It has been my great pleasure to write about music education and to advocate music as core curriculum. One of the best examples of making music fun is the song “When the Saints Go Marching In. “See if you can find the duet version as sung by Louis Armstrong and comedian Danny Kaye. In about three minutes you get an introduction to music and learn the names of almost every famous composer. Armstrong and Kaye are having a great time and so will every listener. It has my highest recommendations.
articles.title: Lunatics, speed demons, and musicians
