articles.text: The American Booksellers Association fights to keep independently owned bookstores alive and thriving. At the start of each month ABA publishes a list of 25 inspired recommendations, the “Indie Next List,” from independent booksellers. The titles below are accompanied by reviews from bookstore owners from across the country. For full book reviews, and ways to support small bookstores, visit: www.indiebound.org/indienext-list Morningside Heights, by Joshua Henkin was named one of 2021’s most highly anticipated new books by Newsweek Morningside Heights Fiction “I loved this book! The writing is beautiful, and the character development is phenomenal. I was moved by all of the characters in the story, but quirky Arlo stands out as a favorite. I also shed a few tears, so this book has it all. It’s a winner with so much heart! I highly recommend it.” —Sarah Fox, Titcomb’s Bookshop, East Sandwich, MA Malibu Rising lantine Books, Fiction “This ode to Malibu in the 1980s is the perfect beach read. Four famous siblings throw a star-studded party and over the course of 24 hours find their lives changed forever. It’s enthralling and layered and so vivid it could be a memory. Perfectly paced and suspenseful from page one!” —Meagan Dallner, Books Are Awesome, Parker, CO The Other Black Girl Books, Fiction “This is the tale of two Black women coworkers in the cutthroat publishing industry trying to determine if they are friends or enemies. A literary fiction tale with a side of suspense, this expertly woven critique on society is bound to keep readers on the edge of their seats.” —Kirsten Wilson, The Snail on the Wall, Huntsville, AL One Last Stop tin’s Griffin, Fiction/Romance “What a magical and creative tale; an addictive read that I did not want to put down. A fun and diverse cast of characters took this story to the next level. With such wide appeal, I know I will be able to put One Last Stop into the hands of almost any customer this summer.” —Cori Cusker, Bright Side Bookshop, Flagstaff, AZ Animal Press, Simon & Schuster, Fiction “Much like Taddeo’s Three Women, this novel is not for the prudish or for people who like their women to be silent or demure. If you are looking for originality, sexiness, or fearlessness in your next read, this is the book for you. Grab the reins and be prepared for a ride!” —Shane Mullen, Left Bank Books, St. Louis, MO Legends of the North Cascades quin Books, Fiction “A sad, sweet, and ultimately hopeful novel of loss, family, and wilderness. Even while maneuvering through two very different story lines, Legends of the North Cascades is imaginative, endearing, and poignant. This is my new favorite of Evison’s novels.” —Stephen Sharpe, A Book for All Seasons, Leavenworth, WA The Maidens Books, Fiction/Thriller “Alex Michaelides approaches The Maidens with a skillful hand and an eye for the mystery/thriller novel while expertly intertwining dark academia and psychological influences. This is one that will keep you invested until the very end.” —Maxwell Leaning, Paragraphs Bookstore, Mount Vernon, OH Unsettled Ground Books, Fiction “Another fantastic story from Claire Fuller, whose novels are full of depth and insight. Unsettled Ground reveals a complex relationship between a mother and her twin adult children, and the secrets that push them to the very edge of existence. I can’t recommend her enough!” —Julie Slavinsky, Warwick’s, La Jolla, CA The Soulmate Equation Books, Fiction “I finished this in one sitting and my neck is killing me. I loved this new story from Christina Lauren, from the third-person point-of-view to the mix of science and romance! It was perfect, from every last side character to the sexual tension between the mains.” —Blair Boles, Beausoleil Books, Lafayette, LA The Thousand Crimes of Ming Tsu Company, Fiction “A raucous romp through a nearly lawless post-Civil War American West. Ming Tsu’s story is captivating and impossible to put down; the cast of characters is just too unique to forget or dismiss. A blood-crusted gem of a tale.” — Jamie Fiocco, Flyleaf Books, Chapel Hill, NC House of Sticks “This timely book follows the life of a young woman whose family immigrates to New York from Vietnam. It is a heartbreaking look at the challenges in overcoming PTSD, poverty, and mental illness. Ultimately, Ly Tran’s story is one of hope, one that is much-needed today.” —Alecia Diane Castro, Sweet Home Books, Wetumpka, AL The Chosen and the Beautiful tion/Fantasy “What would you give up to have it all? Magical and queer as hell, Jordan Baker takes readers through Jazz Age New York as her snark, rage, and feelings for Daisy keep us turning pages until early morning. Like one of Gatsby’s cursed parties, this book was one I wanted to never end.” —Abby Rice, The Briar Patch, Bangor, ME Heaven Editions, Fiction “I loved this book. Its portrayal of bullying is moving and intelligent. Kawakami gives us characters who speak to the heart and illustrate in one form or another the dilemma facing everyone in adolescence. Hopeful but chilling in equal measures.” —Don Luckham, The Toadstool Bookshop, Keene, NH The Kingdoms bury Publishing, Fiction/Fantasy “What a strange, unputdownable book. The Kingdoms weaves characters freed from time and space and memory, rebuilding our world as we know it and inviting us into a delicious story of love and loss.” —Hannah Oxley, Mystery to Me, Madison, WI One Two Three and Co., Fiction “I absolutely loved this heartwarming story of three courageous sisters fighting for justice in their town. It’s a modern David and Goliath tale of small-town America told with wit and heart. Frankel is a superb storyteller, and I did not want my time with this wise and endearing family to end.” —Shannon Burgess, The Bookstore of Glen Ellyn, Glen Ellyn, IL Our Woman in Moscow Morrow, Fiction/Historical “Ruth Macallister runs a New York modeling agency, while twin Iris Digby chooses marriage and motherhood, but her diplomat husband turns out to be a spy. Can Ruth extricate Iris from exile in Moscow? A wonderful plot weaves around Red Scare events of the early 1950s.” —Clay Belcher, Signs of Life, Lawrence, KS Palace of the Drowned Books, Fiction/Thriller “Bridging the gap between genre and literary fiction with enormous skill and agility, Mangan has again given us an electrifying yarn full of menace and atmosphere. With a mesmeric sense of place, Palace of the Drowned is a fully transportive experience.” —Wesley Minter, Third Place Books, Lake Forest Park, WA

articles.text: Come join your friends at the Piedmont Center as it begins to reopen for public events after a year of closure due to COVID-19. LAST WEEKEND - SPRING CREATIVE This is the last weekend to view Spring Creative, an art exhibit by five Piedmont artists at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The gallery will be open from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday, June 5 and 6. The artists exhibiting are Mike Welch, Paula Valenzuela, Valerie Corvin, John Schleuning, and Brian Molyneaux. Artists will be on-site during the final weekend hours to answer questions. Advance reservations are not required. Entry to the exhibition will be through the front doors of the Center at 801 Magnolia Avenue. • • • • • Mike Welch – Large scale oil and mixed media paintings (mikewelchfineart.com) Paula Valenzuela – Mixed media (www.paulavalenzuelaart.com) Valerie Corvin – Painting and mixed media (www.valeriecorvin.com) Jon Schleuning – Watercolor and handmade inks (jonschleuningart.com) Brian Molyneaux – Photography (www.BrianMolyneaux.com) To view a sampling of past exhibits and performances, click on https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d3q9otV5emI

articles.text: Mountain Music, a music store on Piedmont Avenue owned by Piedmont resident and musician Adam Lipansky, never got to hold its grand opening due to the pandemic. Now that many restrictions have been lifted, it will be having its official Grand Opening on Sunday, June 20. The celebration will be a block party, with live music, raffles, food, and vendors. Come join the fun and festivities on Sunday June 20 from 12:00 to 4:00 p.m. Mountain Music is located at 4444 Piedmont Avenue, between J. Miller Flowers and Mountain View Cemetery. For more information call 655-2263 (mountainmusicstore.com).

Part 21: Design disciplines that shape the built environment By Will Adams The various design issues we have been discussing these last months are all layered and interrelated and maybe at times somewhat confusing. It might therefore be helpful to summarize the work of the various design professions that shape our surroundings to better understand how things fit together and function. Basically, there are six main interrelated design disciplines involved. This work is done by hired professionals on projects like large new homes or the new Piedmont high school buildings, or in the case of small remodel jobs, by contractors or homeowners themselves many times, following the standardized building code requirements, as well as city regulations. All development starts with the field of Planning, which involves design and regulatory requirements at the broadest scale. This work ends up in documents like general plans, zoning documents or design guidelines and forms the basis of the design process for all participating professions. When we submit for building permits, applications are first reviewed by the planning department for compliance and then passed on to the building department for more detailed engineering and code checking. Next is Urban Design, which we have addressed in previous columns. It is a narrower scale consideration, somewhere between Planning and Architecture. Difficult to codify, design guidelines come closest to setting the requirements for this invaluable work. There are urban design specialists but architects and landscape architects also support and contribute to this field. Architecture, of course, is the work of buildings themselves – the scale and discipline with which most people are familiar. Architects, usually known for the design of buildings, have traditionally also led, managed, and coordinated the team of professionals from these disciplines whose expertise is needed to deal with all the different specialty issues involved. Landscape Architecture is a discipline whose scope of work is essential and connected to everything, from huge master plans through Urban Design, and down to individual small homes. Like Urban Design, good Landscape Architecture is critical to the success of any project. but unfortunately is not always given the importance required. Interior Design is the discipline most personal to all of us because we see this work up close. Every day we reach out and touch and use the furniture, fixtures, equipment –everything on the inside of the building – that interior designers specify and design. Engineering is a separate layer coordinated with everything that architects, landscape architects and planners design. For retaining walls to not tip over, or sewage systems to have the required capacity, they must be engineered. Unlike small residential projects, the list of engineers involved on larger projects can be long and comprehensive, including those in less known fields like life safety, telecommunications and energy systems. Next: The Aesthetic of Materials Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com LANDSCAPE ARCHITECTURE: In addition to planting, landscape architects’ work includes hardscape (paving) irrigation, monuments, plazas, fountains, fences, trellises – in short, everything outside the building. INTERIOR DESIGN: Besides furniture selection or design, artwork, and surface coverings, interior designers work closely with architects to design and/or specify the materials, textures, colors and finishes of everything from light fixtures to building hardware. ENGINEERING: Engineers’ drawings are the most detailed and specific since they are responsible for the “nuts and bolts” of construction. They form a coordinated part of virtually all project documentation, alongside the work of all the other professions. ® R&S OVERHEAD R&S OVERHEAD GARAGE DOOR, INC. GARAGE DOOR, INC. articles.text: Chicken Curry Stir-Fry an easy, casual dinner for summer nights. This quick stir-fry is inspired by a recent dinner with friends. I prepared a veggie-only side dish of stir-fried zucchini and cherry tomatoes for our alfresco gathering. It made an easy switch to a weeknight dinner by adding chicken for an all-in-one skillet meal. The “weeknight” in the recipe title translates to fast and easy. Using a prepared curry powder blend provides most of the flavor and marinating the chicken pieces beforehand is purely optional. I keep a few varieties of curry powder blends on hand; each has a distinct flavor profile. There are common ingredients – cumin, coriander, turmeric – but each blend brings a nuance to the part of the world that inspired the blend. Stir fry dishes are easily adapted with substitutions. Any combination of meat and vegetables will work. For best results, remember the idea is to slice the meat and vegetables so they will be of similar size for even cooking. Weeknight Chicken Curry Stir-Fry INGREDIENTS • 1-1/2 pounds boneless chicken, sliced into 1-inch pieces • 1 pound tender zucchini, about 5 - 6 young squash, sliced into 1-inch pieces • 15 cherry tomatoes • 1/2 white onion, diced in 1/2” - 3/4” pieces • 2 - 3 teaspoons curry powder • Salt and cayenne pepper, to taste • 2 - 3 teaspoons ghee or vegetable oil that will withstand high heat, divided • Cilantro to garnish INSTRUCTIONS Use a heavy, 12-inch frying pan. Heat the pan over medium-high heat for about one minute. Add 1 teaspoon of ghee or oil and distribute it evenly using a spatula. Add the zucchini in a single-layer, cut-side facing down. Allow to brown slightly, then turn the pieces over to cook on both cut sides. Take care to just barely cook through; this should take only 4-5 minutes. Remove the zucchini to a plate and set aside. With the heat still set at medium-high, add the onion and spread into one even layer. Add a bit of ghee or oil if needed, but there should be enough in the pan so they will not stick. Cook the onion until brown at the edges but are still barely cooked through, then remove from the pan to the plate along with the zucchini. Return the pan to the medium-high heat and wait about one minute to assure the pan is hot. Add the chicken pieces all at once to the hot pan and begin spreading into one layer as quickly as possible. Once the chicken is in one layer, leave it alone to brown; about 5 minutes. Flip the pieces of chicken over and spread them back into a single layer. Add the curry powder and cook another 5 minutes until the chicken is nearly done. Add the cherry tomatoes, cooked zucchini, and onions to the pan with the chicken and stir to combine everything. Cook another 3 or 4 minutes to ensure the chicken is thoroughly cooked and the vegetables are hot. Ideally the zucchini will retain a bit of crunch when bitten. Remove to a serving dish. Sprinkle liberally with chopped cilantro and/or sliced green onions. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com.

Add the curry powder and cook another 5 minutes until the chicken is nearly done. Add the cherry tomatoes, cooked zucchini, and onions to the pan with the chicken and stir to combine everything. Cook another 3 or 4 minutes to ensure the chicken is thoroughly cooked and the vegetables are hot. Ideally the zucchini will retain a bit of crunch when bitten. Remove to a serving dish. Sprinkle liberally with chopped cilantro and/or sliced green onions. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com. READ IT IN THE POST

articles.text: Michèle Stone of Oakland, the life partner of Harry Howe, passed away peacefully in her sleep early in the morning of Saturday, May 15, 2021, at Kaiser Oakland Medical Center. She was 78. Born Michèle Dee Hyman in Santa Monica on July 14, 1942, she was the daughter of Frank and Yetta Hyman. Frank was an engineer and moved to various major jobs in Southern California, so she spent her early years in Los Angeles, Mojave, Twenty-nine Palms, Van Nuys, and Pomona before moving to a home in Claremont that her father had designed. After graduating from Claremont High School in 1960, she moved to the Bay Area, where she earned a Bachelor’s degree with a Decorative Arts major at UC Berkeley in 1964. She earned a lifetime teaching credential and first taught with Oakland Unified School District in 1966. She taught first- and second-grade classes in several different schools and managed to earn a Master’s in Education degree from Cal State Hayward. She taught at Crocker Highlands Elementary School for the last 34 years of a 42-year teaching career. The wonderful, full life that Michèle was able to build and enjoy in Oakland included a deep and constant commitment to the community and its future growth and well-being, as evidenced by her influence on the hundreds of children she taught with such dedication and satisfaction. Her membership for many years at Oakland’s Temple Sinai resulted in many lasting friendships spanning all walks of life, while providing her with emotional security and support whenever needed. She spent many years also as an active member of Women’s American ORT, helping The Piedmont Center for the Arts and other performing arts organizations lost one of the principal cheerleaders and supporters with the passing of Michèle Stone on May 15. to support a world-wide network of schools for both children and adults, and was instrumental in the establishment and operation of a local thrift store supporting both her temple and ORT. Michèle also had a deep love of the arts and performing arts and recognized the singular value they provide to communities. She was a collector of books and objects of visual and creative arts of all kinds. She was a supporter and subscriber of Oakland Symphony since the days when Calvin Simmons was its director, and was a moving force supporting the Symphony’s educational and outreach programs, donating hundreds of hours every season. She also was a strong supporter and constant volunteer with Piedmont Center for the Arts, where she typically was the first person in the front row for nearly all concerts. She and Harry were also longtime supporters of and regular attendees at concerts of the New Century Chamber Orchestra, San Francisco Chamber Orchestra, the Philharmonia Baroque, Berkeley Symphony, and the SFJazz Center. Michèle loved the excitement of exploring new places and new ideas, traveling extensively and frequently throughout the United States, and throughout Western Europe and the Mediterranean and Aegean Sea areas. She always came home with new friends with whom she stayed in touch over the years. Wherever she went she would be greeted by young adults who had at one time been her students in their first years of elementary school, or adults whose children she had taught. When she was at home, she loved to explore new recipes, to cook for and entertain her many circles of friends, to work on and cherish her rose garden and extensive collection of orchids, and to play mah-jongg and socialize with those with whom she was closest. After all these years of giving, her final gift was to donate her remains to the UCSF Willed Body program, with the hope that she might thus contribute one day to a better outcome for another person, and at the same time relieving her surviving family members from the tasks involved with a funeral or burial. This final gift also relieves all who knew her from any obligation to travel to a specific location in order to visit her spirit, which will instead always be with all those she knew wherever you are. Gifts in memory of Michèle Stone may be made to Oakland Symphony, George Mark Children’s House, or Temple Sinai in Oakland. Michèle is survived by her life partner Harry Howe, her younger brother Steven Hyman, her son Adam, his wife Eran and daughter Emma, and her son Erik Stone and his wife Erin. An opportunity to celebrate Michèle’s life and share memories together will be planned for late summer.
articles.title: Longtime arts champion Michèle Stone dies on May 15

articles.text: William T. (Bill) Ruth, passed away on March 15, 2021 in Piedmont, He was 82. Born in Newport, Rhode Island during a hurricane in 1938, Bill was the son of Col. Harold S. Ruth and Ruth T. Ruth. As an “army brat”, as he would call it, he was raised in the Philippines, and lived in Virginia, Boston, and in Tokyo from 1946-1950 during the occupation. His parents moved to Piedmont in 1953 and he graduated from Piedmont High School in 1956. He went on to UC Berkeley, where he was a part of the Phi Kappa Sigma fraternity. He was drafted into the military and served in Vietnam as the skipper of a Swift Boat. After returning to California, he graduated from UC Berkeley with a Master’s degree in Business Administration. He became a successful financial consultant for more than 30 years, including many development projects in San Francisco, Richmond and Stockton. He also was on the Phi Kappa Sigma Alumni Board and helped rebuild the Phi Kap house after a fire in 1990. He re-financed and became the manager of what became Barrows House, helping provide young students with affordable housing at UC Berkeley for almost 30 years. Bill had a passion for restoring classic cars and boats and loved sharing his interests with others. Most of all, he enjoyed spending time with his family and his community. He could always be seen on his walks around Piedmont, chatting with all his neighbors. Bill Ruth is survived by his wife Light Ruth and his two daughters, Kerry Connors and husband John of Peabody, Massachusetts, and Erin Fell and Bill Ruth, a resident of Piedmont since 1953, passed away on March 15. He was 82. her husband Blake of Honolulu, Hawaii. He is additionally survived by grandsons Lucas Fell (5) and Alex Fell (4).
articles.title: Piedmont native Bill Ruth dies March 15 at age 82

Shanti is a practicing defense attorney and wife of a former NFL player. In her book she writes about our criminal justice system seen through her life experience and the stories of nine of her previously convicted felon clients. The conversation will be about a half hour before the reading group discusses its previously planned June selection. Those interested in learning more about Shanti and Almost Innocent can go to https://www.shantibrien. com/. Those interested in joining the First Monday Reading Group may contact John Wilk at the Piedmont Recreation Department (jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov).

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.
articles.title: Wednesday Evening Meditation Group is online

articles.text: Mountain View Cemetery recently reopened to the general public two days a week for limited recreational activities. The historic 226-acre cemetery has a long history of welcoming the public to enjoy its park-like space. It has been closed for more than a year due to the Covid pandemic. People may now visit on Saturdays and Wednesdays between 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. Enter at the Piedmont Avenue gate. Center for Disease Control guidelines are in place and masks are required. All visitors are asked to be respectful of plots. Founded in 1863 and designed by Frederick Law Olmsted, the architect of Central Park in New York City, Mountain View Cemetery is a private, non-profit cemetery providing mortuary services to the public; unlike other open spaces in Oakland, it does not receive any public funding. Costs to host the public are borne by plot owners. Dogs must be on leash and are not allowed on plots. No alcohol, loud vehicles and music, skateboards, or scooters are allowed in the cemetery. For more information, call 658-2588 Millionaires Row in historic Mountain View Cemetery at the end of Piedmont Avenue in Oakland
articles.title: Mountain View Cemetery reopens to the public – 2 days a week

articles.text: Even as most Bay Area counties are now in the least restrictive tier for reopening their economy, the number of daily COVID- 19 cases in Alameda County remains too high for the county to move up tiers. However, in less than two weeks, most COVID-19 restrictions across the state will be eliminated. Until June 15, counties are still subject to the state’s color-coded four-tier reopening system. Yesterday, Tuesday, June 1, Marin and Monterey counties joined Santa Clara, Santa Cruz, San Francisco and San Mateo counties in the least-restrictive yellow tier, or minimal tier. Alameda County, along with Contra Costa, Napa, Solano and Sonoma counties, is in the second-least restrictive orange tier, or moderate tier. Alameda County has been in the orange tier since March 30. While most businesses can reopen with modifications in the orange tier, capacity limits and other restrictions are further reduced in the yellow tier. COVID-19 positivity in Alameda County is at 0.7 percent, its lowest level since the coronavirus pandemic began 14 months ago, according to Alameda County Public Health Department data on May 31. To move into the yellow tier, the positivity rate in Alameda County needs to stay below 2 percent. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to remain below 2.2 percent – it is currently 1.4 percent in Alameda County. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to be below 1, but right now there are 1.6 cases per 100,000, although this represents a decrease from last week. The new reopening guidelines that go into effect everywhere in California on June 15 abolish all COVID-19 capacity restrictions and physical distancing rules. For large outdoor events with over 10,000 participants, the state recommends that venues ask attendees for vaccination proof or a negative COVID-19 test. For large indoor events with over 5,000 participants, venues must require attendees to provide proof of vaccination or a negative test. Along with the wide reopening of the state’s economy, mask mandates will be mostly eliminated for fully vaccinated people on June 15. The new mask rules follow guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention released last month, which said fully vaccinated people can go without masks and social distancing in most situations. The CDC said that masks are only required for the vaccinated in certain instances, like on airplanes or buses. Instead of an immediate mandate change, California opted to wait several weeks to adopt the CDC guidance, a move applauded by Alameda County health officials. Masking guidelines are ultimately up to local and state governments, the CDC said. People are considered fully vaccinated if it has been two weeks since their second dose of Pfizer or Moderna vaccine or their one dose of Johnson & Johnson vaccine. Across Alameda County, the total caseload is 88,955, an increase of roughly 290 in the past seven days. There have been 27,741 cases recorded in Oakland and 13,750 cases in Hayward. Tragically, the total number of COVID-19 fatalities countywide is now 1,693. One new case of COVID-19 was reported in Piedmont across the past seven days. The total number of Piedmont cases since the pandemic began is 185. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,685,455 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 62,021 deaths due to the disease statewide. The state positivity rate is 0.7 percent, the same rate as Alameda County and a record low for California. read.” —Mary Salazar, The Country Bookshop, Southern Pines, NC A Ghost in the Throat lioasis, Memoir “This is a literary mystery explored with white-hot intensity. articles.text: California announced on Monday, May 31 that it had reached a goal set by President Joe Biden to inoculate 70 percent of the adult population with at least one dose of COVID-19 vaccine by July 4. Alameda County surpassed the goal by reaching the 70 percent benchmark on May 10. California became the 11th state to reach the goal of 70 percent of the population with at least one dose. The state joined Pennsylvania, Vermont, Hawaii, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Maine, New Jersey, Rhode Island, and New Mexico. Soon after the declaration from Gov. Gavin Newsom, Maryland announced that it had become the 12th state to reach Biden’s goal. California has the biggest population of any of the 12 states by a large margin. The White House set its vaccination goal for the nation on May 4. Three vaccines are available in the United States. Pfizer and Moderna vaccines require two doses administered several weeks apart. A vaccine produced by Johnson & Johnson requires only one dose. To incentivize Californians toward total vaccination, Newsom last week unveiled the “Vax for the Win” program that will award millions of dollars to vaccinated Californians in a lottery. Any California resident, including those under the age of 18, who has received at least one dose will be eligible to win $50,000 or $1.5 million. This Friday, June 4, 15 people will win $50,000. Another 15 will win $50,000 on June 11 and 10 people will be awarded $1.5 million on June 15. The next 2 million Californians to get fully vaccinated will receive a $50 gift card. “California has already made incredible progress in the fight against COVID-19, with the lowest case rates in the country while administering millions more vaccines than any other state,” Newsom said in a statement last week. “But we aren’t stopping there, we’re doing everything it takes to get Californians vaccinated as we approach June 15 to help us fully reopen safely.” As of Sunday, May 30, 1.83 million doses of vaccine have been administered in Alameda County. Almost 76 percent of the county’s population ages 12 and older, over 1 million people, are partially vaccinated. Almost 60 percent of eligible people in the county, about 847,000 people, are fully vaccinated. Piedmont continues to be the most vaccinated municipality in the county. Nearly 97 percent of residents ages 12 and older, an estimated 8,983 people, have received at least one dose of vaccine. Almost 74 percent of City residents ages 12 and older, some 6,862 people, have been fully vaccinated. In Oakland, 74 percent of the eligible population is partially vaccinated, and 57 percent is fully vaccinated. Pfizer received emergency approval for children ages 12 to 15 on May 13. Since then, over 33,300 kids in this age group have received their first dose of vaccine. This amounts to over 40 percent of this demographic in the county. Both Pfizer and Moderna are currently conducting vaccine trials in children as young as 6 months old. Dr. Anthony Fauci, the Chief Medical Advisor to the White House, has said that he expects all children will be eligible for vaccination by the end of the year. All three vaccine manufacturers have received emergency use authorization to produce vaccines, but Moderna yesterday, Tuesday, June 1, began applying for a full license from the Food and Drug Administration. Pfizer applied for full approval for their vaccine for people ages 16 and older in early May. Additionally, health officers for all Bay Area counties announced on Friday, May 28 that children and adults can receive other vaccinations along with their COVID-19 vaccine. “We know a lot of people have delayed getting care and regular immunizations during the pandemic,” Dr. Chris Farnitano, health officer for Contra Costa County, said in a statement. “This new guidance will make it easier for people to catch up on any immunizations they’re due for when they get a COVID- 19 vaccine at their provider’s office.” COVID-19 vaccines are available for free to all Alameda County residents ages 12 and older. Appointments are not required at many vaccination locations in Oakland and elsewhere in the county. As of press time, same-day appointments were available at several locations in Oakland and Berkeley. Alameda County links to available vaccine appointments at covid-19.acgov.org/vaccines

articles.text: Pursuant to Section 4.04(A) of the Piedmont City Charter, residents are hereby notified that at 6:00 p.m. on June 7, 2021 the Piedmont City Council will hold a public hearing regarding the proposed City budget and fee schedule for fiscal year 2021-2022. The Council will hold an additional meeting at 6:00 p.m. on June 21, 2021. Consistent with Executive Orders No. N-25-20 and No. N-29- 20 from the Executive Department of the State of California and the Alameda County Health Official’s Shelter in Place Orders, the City Council meeting will not be physically open to the public and City Council members will be teleconferencing into each meeting via Zoom Teleconference. The specific teleconference details will be available on the agenda for each meeting. At the same meetings, the City Council will hold public hearings regarding the Municipal Services Tax and Municipal Sewer Tax and will set the tax rates for the fiscal year 2021-2022. Copies of the proposed budget are available for public inspection on the City’s web site at https://piedmont.ca.gov. A limited number of paper copies of the budget are available from the City Clerk’s office. You can email cityclerk@piedmont.ca.gov or telephone (510) 420-3040, between the hours of 8:30 a.m. and 12:00 noon, and 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. to request a copy. John O. articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council approved a lease agreement with Gulf South Towers to construct a 95-foot-tall telecommunications tower in the City’s Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue. The new tower will be used by up to four wireless providers. The tower, base station, and other improvements were unanimously approved by City Council on April 19. The new “monopole” will replace an existing 31-foottall pole in the same location, currently with only one provider, T-Mobile. The city’s General Plan includes guidelines related to wireless communication facilities (WCF), and states that city staff must ensure “that the siting and design of infrastructure facilities mitigate the potential for adverse visual impacts.” The city’s Corporation Yard, located at 898 Red Rock Road, is located in a zone where telecommunications facilities are permitted without height restriction. The selected location was chosen because of natural “buffers” to the south, north, east, and west of the monopole. The visual impact and sight line analysis indicated that there may be minimal impacts to Bay views of some residences located directly to the east of the site, in Moraga Canyon, but that the impact is low. The lease agreement was approved by City Council in a second reading, following an approval by the city’s Planning Commission earlier this year. articles.text: COVID-19 positivity in Alameda County is at 0.8 percent, its lowest point since the coronavirus pandemic began 14 months ago, according to Alameda County Public Health Department data from Monday, May 24. Even though positivity is declining, new cases of COVID- 19 are reported every day. Across Alameda County, the total caseload is 88,665, an increase of several hundred in the past seven days. There have been 27,653 cases recorded in Oakland and 13,708 cases in Hayward. The total number of COVID- 19 fatalities in Alameda County is 1,679. Two new cases of COVID- 19 were reported in Piedmont in the past week. The total number of Piedmont cases since the pandemic began is 184. California officials recently confirmed plans to lift most COVID-19 restrictions in three weeks. “We’re at a point where we can actually move beyond saying we expect to open on June 15, to confirming that we’re opening up June 15,” Dee Dee Myers, senior adviser to Gov. Gavin Newsom, said in a briefing to the media on Friday, May 21. Along with a wide reopening of the state’s economy, mask mandates will be mostly eliminated for fully vaccinated people. The new mask rules will follow guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention released on May 13, which said fully vaccinated people can go without masks and social distancing in most indoor and outdoor situations. articles.text: Editor: I must take a contrarian’s view to the opinions in the May 12th Post of my friend of 40 years, Dr. Marvin Engel. Greta Thunberg is an enormously successful “climate provocateur.” The world is a far, better place because of her and her message. “Systemic racism” in my opinion is with us. I cite a few facts from the 2017 book by Richard Rothstein, The Color of Law - A forgotten history of how our government segregated America. When the WWII shipyards were built in Richmond the Federal government needed all the labor it could recruit to build those ships and get them launched. They thought nothing of putting black workers side by side with white workers. However, when they faced the need to build housing for all those workers, they decided they didn’t want blacks living with whites. So, the Feds deliberately segregated the housing. I know because my family and I lived in one of the whites-only units. In 1953 Ford Motor Company announced a new plant in Milpitas and the closing of the Richmond plant. The union negotiated an agreement that would allow the 1400 employees (about 250 of whom were African American) to keep their jobs if they transferred. The civic leaders of Milpitas quickly said there could be no new construction of multi-unit buildings – no apartments, no rentals. They also said only single-family homes could be built in the city. The union tried to intervene by building their own integrated subdivision for their members, but it was thwarted at every turn and was ultimately unsuccessful. Milpitas remained white. And let’s not forget the role of “red-lining”, that silent and nefarious practice to keep minorities from buying homes outside their segregated neighborhoods. Then there was the even more recent “reverse red-lining” in the form of predatory lending. It was at its worst during the run-up to the real estate crash of 2008 and included “excessive marketing of exploitative loans in African America communities”. These loans turned out to be disastrous for black homeowners. The Federal government gathered data from financial institutions that revealed this abuse but did nothing to protect minority borrowers. It was not until the Fair Housing Act of 1968 that decent homes started to open to black buyers. I have to believe all the unfair treatment and discrimination they have been subject to during my lifetime would lead them to agree that systemic racism is still with us. White young people and white adults need to better understand this so we can effectively remedy our history.
articles.title: Another history lesson of the Bay Area

articles.text: Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church was founded as the First Baptist Church of Brooklyn on the shores of Oakland’s Lake Merritt in 1860. Over the 161 years of our history, we have changed names (FBC Brooklyn, Tenth Avenue Baptist Church, Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church). We also have changed buildings and have changed from being an almost exclusively white congregation to being one of Oakland’s most diverse congregations. In terms of race, we are approximately 45% African-American, 45% Euro-American, 7% Asian American, 2% Latino/a American and 1% Native-American. Our diversity is not accidental. It is a gift of the Spirit. It is the result of decisions made over many years. It is the result of making-mistakes and being willing to learn from them. It is the result of vision, courage, determination, resilience and repentance. It is the result of believing that, as we see in the eighth chapter of the book of Acts, Phillip from Judea and the Eunuch from Ethiopia belong in the same chariot, the same Bible class and the same waters of baptism. At this point I need to be very clear. We have not arrived. Many of the decisions listed above remain aspirational. We have much work to do. If we want to move from being diverse to being inter-connected, we have a training or two to participate in. If we want to move from being interracial to being anti-racist, we have some baggage we need to get rid of. If we want to move from being mono-cultural to being truly multicultural, there is some truth we need to hear and changes we need to make. These things can happen, but they won’t “just happen.” As we move forward, we have much to learn from the Bible. Biblical scholar N.T. Wright says it well. “The church was the original multicultural project, with Jesus as its only point of identity. It was known, and was for this reason seen as both attractive and dangerous, as a worship-based, spiritually renewed, multi-ethnic, polychrome, mutually supportive, outward-facing, culturally creative, chastity-celebrating, socially responsible fictive kinship group, gender-blind in leadership, generous to the poor and courageous in speaking up for the voiceless.”
articles.title: A word to a Church in formation

Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.’s dream is also that of Shirley Hooi, as expressed in last week’s Piedmont Post. I was stunned by her naivete, confused by her assertions, and perplexed by her selective thinking. She said today’s “mainstream” ideology posits that “Whiteness” equals oppression and non-Whiteness as the oppressed. Certainly, such an ideology exists in today’s America. Rather than being “mainstream,” it competes with other ideologies in our hyper-polarized political culture, including Trump’s right-wing Big Lie and disharmonies among the many non-White, non-male communities. Remember, America was founded by wealthy White men, some of them slave owners. America has indeed progressed from those oppressive times, and it has been a land of opportunity for immigrants, despite institutional barriers. But as our population is becoming less White, portions of White America feel threatened. (See Trump’s insurrectionist supporters.) America’s racial-ethnic history isn’t glorious -- slavery, genocide of Native peoples, conquests of LatinX territories, the Chinese Exclusion Act, the Japanese American internment, and, today, anti-Islamic and anti-Central American hostilities. Ms. Hooi’s litany about America being the “land of the free, the land of opportunity” was muddled and confusing. She wrote, “…this is the land my ancestors fought to travel to and from during the Chinese Exclusion Act, this is the land that contained my ancestors on Angel Island…” Are these really “good” things about America? My parents and three older sisters, detained at Angel Island, felt imprisoned. She holds America “dear to my heart because of the freedom and opportunities that have been afforded my ancestors…” Her forbears must have been luckier than my immigrant father, who lived and worked in Oakland’s Chinatown, barred from “freedom and opportunities” because systemic racism kept him socially segregated, socioeconomically oppressed, and politically disenfranchised. Ms. Hooi worries that schools may implement Critical Race Theory (CRT) because, she says, “CRT promotes Whiteness as oppressive…” The CRT process will surely be politically volatile, but American schools must do better teaching all children the truth about America, the good, bad, ugly, and beautiful. Ms. Hooi urged people to speak out against her idea of “mainstream” ideology that, according to her, censures, ostracizes, and categorizes as racists or sell-outs those who go against “the tide.” That happens, as racial-ethnic issues persist as difficult, divisive, and daunting. Even so, many Americans can’t or won’t engage in rational, dignified, and respectful conversations about these issues without fear, paranoia, defensiveness, and insincere platitudes. creativity and innovation, of caring for and nurturing literally thousands of children. In 1994, fresh-faced Erin Mulligan (soon to be Erin Rivera) showed up at the Piedmont Recreation Department. And so began the Erin Rivera Era. Not familiar with the Erin Rivera Era? If you raised children in Piedmont in the 90’s, 00’s, 10’s or early 20’s – indeed you very much are. Think back to those crazy years when your kids were little and every day seemed like a relentless mountain to climb. How hard did you cling to the Rec Department as a lifeline? Did you send your children to Tiddlywinks, or Tot Zone, or First Step? Did they go to the Bunny Hop every year to search for that golden egg? Did they spend their summers in Huckleberry, or Camp ISHI, or Summer Stock, or any of hundreds of other magical day camps? Did you ever have breakfast with Santa, or hang out at Dreidels and Donuts? Any of your kids play middle school volleyball? How about Schoolmates – was it your absolute savior before school, after school, or both? Remember those Halloween visits to the Haunted House? Ever take in the Movies-in-the Park? When they got older, did any of your kids pull on a green shirt and pass the fun on to a new generation of summer campers as Jr. CITs? You did and they did. And you have Erin Rivera to thank. And she did it all with a magical smile and an uncanny ability to remember not only every single Piedmonter’s name, but who their friends are, and their favorite color, and what they wore to their first day of Schoolmates. articles.text: Crime is down slightly overall in Piedmont, according to the Police Department’s quarterly report on May 17. The city experienced a decrease in reportable offenses through the first quarter of 2021, compared to the same period in 2020, Police Chief Jeremy Bowers explained. A total of 78 reportable offenses in the first quarter of 2020 decreased to 73 reportable offenses in 2021. Motor vehicle thefts were steady both years, with 10 total reported offenses in the first quarter of 2020 and 2021. Burglaries, which the department defines as the unlawful entry into a dwelling with the intent to commit theft, decreased from 17 incidents in the first quarter of 2020 to six incidents this year so far. Robberies, which involve an individual stealing another’s belongings through means of force, increased from zero last year to two incidents in 2021. Larceny and theft, which includes breaking into locked vehicles, was up from 47 incidents in the first quarter of 2020 to 54 incidents in the first quarter of this year. Chief Bowers noted that there have been numerous reported incidents of vehicle break-ins throughout the city, which would be reflected in the second quarter crime report. The department continues to utilize Automated License Plate Reader cameras (ALPR) to address crime; Bowers explained that officers have made 13 arrests and have recovered 15 stolen vehicles in events directly related to ALPR cameras through the first quarter of 2021, compared to one arrest and two recovered stolen vehicles in the first quarter of 2020. A Request for Proposal (RFP) has been completed for the Public Safety Camera program. A recommendation will be made in the near future. Traffic safety The city continues to expand and maintain safe roadways for motorists, pedestrians and cyclists, with help from the Pedestrian and Bicycle Safety Committee. The Piedmont Police Department assists by conducting selective traffic enforcement targeted in areas throughout the city known for speeding and other violations, as well as in areas of high pedestrian traffic. Also, a traffic safety group of police officers works closely with the Public Works Department and city engineer to address safety concerns on roadways and at intersections throughout the city. Bowers noted that accidents doubled from last year, with 18 collision reports in the first three months of 2021, and nine the year prior. Of the 18 accidents, 12 were categorized as hit-and-run. articles.text: A mountain lion that was captured and removed from a tree in San Francisco’s Bernal Heights neighborhood was brought to Oakland Zoo on May 20. It immediately received a complete exam, bloodwork, and preventative care vaccines. The two-year-old male nicknamed “Mr. Handsome” by zoo veterinary staff, and weighing 98 pounds, was released the following day into a rural area of Santa Clara County. San Francisco Animal Care and Control (SFACC) was the first agency to issue a notice post about the lion having been seen on May 19. At about 10:30 p.m., SFACC posted a photo on their twitter page of a mountain lion that was perched in a tree on Santa Marina near Mission Street. California Fish and Wildlife arrived at the scene and removed the animal from the tree after tranquilizing it with a dart. Data collected from the big cat’s radio collar revealed it was the same animal that Bernal Heights residents spotted roaming the streets in the two days leading up to his capture. KCBS radio reported that, after being shot with a tranquilizer in the hindquarters, the lion “got woozy and fell asleep on the front porch of a nearby home” before being tagged and caged, and then transported to the Oakland Zoo. “I felt frightened, but also somewhat giddy to have the worlds collide in this fashion, a beautiful beast like that living in the wild, yet wandering the city at night, looking for something to do and possibly a bite to eat - just like the rest of us,” said resident Ken Shelf who sent a photo to be shared with SF Animal Control. Veterinarians at Oakland Zoo explained that “long-range travel” into urban neighborhoods isn’t out of the ordinary for mountain lions. The species is known to travel long distances in search of food, shelter, and a mate. Luckily, the big cat received a total clean bill of health by the Oakland Zoo – strong, hydrated, and a healthy weight of 98.5 pounds. He was treated for internal and external parasites, which are common in wildlife, and was given preventative vaccinations during his exam. Mr. Handsome is the 16th mountain lion rescue for the Oakland Zoo through their Bay Area Cougar Action Team (BACAT) alliance. While this big cat’s journey has a happy ending, not all mountain lions are as lucky. They face numerous threats in California, often struck by cars, killed with depredation permits, and by illegal poaching. Oakland Zoo’s partnership with conservation organizations aims to educate the The two-year-old mountain lion awaits examination by Oakland Zoo staff before being re-released in rural Santa Clara County. Dr. Alex Herman, Vice President of Veterinary Services at Oakland Zoo, performs a complete examination of ‘Mr. Handsome,” the 2-year-old mountain lion found in San Francisco’s Bernal Heights neighborhood. public on this issue. “We take pride in doing our part to help rescue and protect animals in the wild, through our partnerships and collaboration with CDFW, Bay Area Puma Project, and the San Francisco Police Department” said Dr. Alex Herman, Vice President of Veterinary Services at Oakland Zoo.

articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will present a Zoom-based discussion on criminal justice reform with Piedmont resident Shanti Brien as guest speaker on June 22. An attorney and reform advocate, Brien will speak on what individuals and organizations do for criminal justice reform and racial justice. She will take questions from audience members. The forum will be online through Zoom on Tuesday, June 22 at 4 p.m. Brien’s book Almost Innocent: From searching to saved in America’s criminal justice system was published last month. It chronicles her experiences growing up in the central valley, becoming an attorney, and representing convicted individuals. Brien said that she “reimagines the current criminal justice system as smaller, fairer, and more humane.” Brien is a member of the Muscogee Creek Nation, and a graduate of UC Berkeley and Stanford Law School. As a former criminal defense lawyer, she co-founded Fogbreak Justice, an organization that collaborates with criminal justice professionals to reduce bias and build community trust to create equitable outcomes. She is also a writer and speaker on Attorney Shanti Brien social justice issues in criminal law and policy. As a Piedmont resident, she has served on the Public Safety Committee, is a member of the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC), and participates in the Piedmont Race and Equity Campaign (PREC). To join in the discussion, register at: https://www. l w v p ie d m o n t .o r g /c o n t e n t . a spx?page_id= 40 02&club_ id=601389&item_id=1441599. Registrants will receive an email with the Zoom link. This event is free and open to all. The talk will be recorded and can be viewed later on the League of Women Voters Piedmont YouTube Channel: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC3v60XGmr13V_9WaYj6qUJg/featured.
articles.title: Piedmont resident, attorney Shanti Brien featured June 22

articles.text: Haydn Wolfers, a senior at Piedmont High School, has earned the Gold Award from the Girl Scouts USA. The Gold Award is the highest award in Girl Scouts and requires a minimum of 80 hours devoted to identifying, designing, and implementing an action project to address a significant community need. The project must be sustainable, measurable, and connect with a national and/ or global issue with relevance beyond the community. When Haydn was in 10th grade, PHS alum Susan Reynolds visited Haydn’s classroom to share information about her new non-profit organization, Lookup. live, which was created to help youth take action to challenge the digital ecosystem and improve mental health. Haydn became interested in teaching others to develop healthy habits with technology, and it became the topic of her Girl Scout Gold Project. Her initial plan was to teach digital wellness to local 5th graders, but after two lessons, the lockdown due to the COVID pandemic occurred. Haydn was able to adapt her plan to a virtual format, and created online lessons, resources, PHS Senior Haydn Wolfers receives her Gold Award patch. and speakers on national panels to spread the message of digital wellness. It is a message perhaps even more important as students navigate isolation and distance learning. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department is inviting teens to apply for summer jobs as Counselors-in-Training (CIT). Before they begin working with camps, they will receive a two-week training, learning professional development. The Junior CIT and CIT programs are now combined. Each day CITs will spend their mornings working directly with Camp Everything campers – playing games, singing songs, and helping make sure they have a fantastic day of camp. Then in the afternoon CIT’s will hone their skills in first aid, group management, resume writing, and interview techniques. Enrollments costs $382 and runs Monday through Friday from 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. The first session runs from June 21 to July 1 and is for students from 6th to 9th grade. Registration is at: Register. communitypass.net/reg/cat_program_class_detail.cfm?s=&t=&- season_id=24069&program_ id=1432270&family_mbr_str= For more information, contact Jackson Stearns, at 420-3070 (jstearns@piedmont.ca.gov). Outdoor Explorers Schoolmate’s David Hopkins will lead a new iteration of the Outdoor Explorer program this year. It is at a new locale, closer to home – in town, in Piedmont parks. “In years past we usually went to the east bay regional parks, but now we are going to meet in the park and explore all the different parks we have in the city, because they are so wonderful. It is going to be great,” Hopkins said with a smile. Outdoor Explorers will have a special visit from a beekeeper this year for demonstrations and a Q & A. “We are going to talk about ecology and talk about how important all the local trees, flowers and insects are, and we have bug catchers so we can catch and release. It will be fun, everything should be fantastic,” Hopkins explained. Outdoor Explorers Summer Session III runs from July 12 - July 23 and is for kids in grades 1-5. Explorers takes place Monday to Friday from 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. The camp cost is $700. This summer – as it emerges from more than one year of lockdown due to COVID-19, the Recreation Department is offering more than 70 camps, classes, and sport leagues this year. Online registration has been open since May 7. Sign up for your first pick of camps, art and dance classes, martial arts, and music. Most camps run from June 14 to August 6. For more information, call the Recreation Department at 420- 3070.
articles.title: Summer CIT jobs return to Recreation Dept.

articles.text: Early this morning, from 4:11 a.m. to 4:25 a.m., a lunar eclipse occurred, hiding the full moon in total shadow. The May 26 ultra-rare “Super Flower Blood Moon” turned a shade of red as it passed through the Earth’s umbral shadow. Blood Moons are not overly rare in themselves, but the combination of Blood Moon, Super Moon, and Flower Moon on the same night is exceedingly rare. A Super Moon is the point of the moon’s orbit when it’s at its closest to Earth and it appears up to 14% larger and 30% brighter than normal. A Flower Moon happens during springtime when the flowers are hitting their peak bloom. A Blood Moon is another name for a lunar eclipse. The celestial phenomenon was most visible from the middle of the Pacific Ocean, and Australia. Much of North and South America, AntPictured is the lunar eclipse on January 20, 2019. arctica, South and East Asia, and Antarctica had visibility too. For an animation showing global visibility, click on: https://c. tadst.com/gfx/eclipses2/20210526/ anim2d-380.mp4. Two more total lunar eclipses will occur next year, on May 16 and November 8, 2022. articles.text: Kids have had to forgo many important rites and rituals this year. In-person learning, social activities, sports, prom – you name it. When I think about how completely abnormal this year has been for children, it is mind blowing. As a Head of School I am searching for ways to help them recover. Horrible, challenging, lonely, frustrating, sad – there are a million emotions to describe it. Take your pick. When we focus on our feelings and help our kids do the same, we embark on a dynamic journey. Going with the emotional flow inevitably allows us to move through the experience rather than being stuck in it. And this is what our children need right now. This past year was a whole bunch of things, but it wasn’t lost. Encouraging our kids to express their feelings about the experience, rather than writing it off, will allow them to come out the other side feeling empowered. Now that they’re back in school, my students are confronting their feelings about the past year, and it’s hard. But with our encouragement, they are doing it. And as they do it, little by little, they are reclaiming their former selves. Dr. Susan Eva Porter is the Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. She can be reached at sue@orindaacademy.org. As we start to see the light at the end of the tunnel, and as students return to school, I see glimmers of hope. But I also see the lingering struggle, and I anticipate it will take a while before things return to normal. “It’s been a lost year,” a parent said to me recently. “And they’ll never get it back.” I’ve heard the term lost year a lot lately. It makes sense that peoThink about COVID in terms of how it felt rather than what it did or did not do to us. ple would see COVID this way after so much deprivation. But I think it’s a mistake to think about the past year as being lost, and an even bigger mistake to use this term with our kids, and here’s why. Losing a year implies nothing happened, which is untrue, and the phrase also leaves us feeling helpless. There’s literally nothing we can do to reverse the clock; there’s no option for a mulligan. The term lost also fixes the experience in our minds; it’s a definitive and static descriptor. Thinking of the past year as lost hinders our kids’ ability to process the experience because it keeps them focused on what happened, or what didn’t happen, or on what they can’t change. This breeds helplessness. Thinking about COVID in terms of how it felt is another story.

By Jay Russell Early this morning, from 4:11 a.m. to 4:25 a.m., a lunar eclipse occurred, hiding the full moon in total shadow. The May 26 ultra-rare “Super Flower Blood Moon” turned a shade of red as it passed through the Earth’s umbral shadow. Blood Moons are not overly rare in themselves, but the combination of Blood Moon, Super Moon, and Flower Moon on the same night is exceedingly rare. A Super Moon is the point of the moon’s orbit when it’s at its closest to Earth and it appears up to 14% larger and 30% brighter than normal. A Flower Moon happens during springtime when the flowers are hitting their peak bloom. A Blood Moon is another name for a lunar eclipse. The celestial phenomenon was most visible from the middle of the Pacific Ocean, and Australia. articles.text: Piedmont Community Church welcomed church-goers for in-person worship on May 16 for the first time in over a year. The church has been closed for in-person worship and has relied on digital, live-streamed services since March 2020 due to the global health pandemic and subsequent industry closures. Currently, the Piedmont Community Church is welcoming parishioners at about half capacity - or approximately 75 people total. It requires masks and social distancing. Still, pews were “at capacity,” and reservations filled up prior to the first in-person Sunday service. May 16 also marked the first in-person worship service for Transitional Minister Dr. Steve Schibsted, who joined the church in the midst of the global pandemic. In his sermon Dr. Schibsted described the theme as a “perfect storm,” referencing the Bible text of Jesus’ walk on water, and the 2001 George Clooney film of the same name. “We just experienced a perfect storm, or a confluence of storms. It’s easy to think of the pandemic as one [factor], but we’ve been through an economic downturn, social upheaval, racial injustices, and our country coming faceto-face with the racism that still exists,” Dr. Schibsted said. His first live sermon carried a theme of hope and of transition. Piedmont Community Church will continue with modified, in-person worship services for the next three weeks and will maintain virtual services. The state and county have not given guidance for how to operate in-person worship services beyond June 15, at which time the state’s color-coded “tier” system is expected to disappear. Gov. Gavin Newsom said that on June 15 California will fully open its economy if vaccine supply is sufficient and hospitalization rates are stable and low. Dr. Schibsted said that given the fluctuating nature of regulations, it is hard to say what worship services will look like past the current tier system. “We’re thinking that by June 15 things will be very different. What that means exactly, I Piedmont Community Church wouldn’t want to speculate,” he said. Sunday services begin at 10:30 a.m., and reservations are required. Services will include liturgical readings with response, music, and a sermon. Reservations can be made for May 30, June 6, and June 13 by visiting https://www.piedmontchurch.org/ reopening/. Michael Barber, Communications Director for Piedmont Community Church, explained that the church will continue live-streaming worship services. “We began live streaming services in 2018. Our online worship has been pre-produced since March of 2020. Going forward, we will continue to provide online worship for our parishioners, and the 30% of our online audience that live outside the state,” he said. “However, we are looking at ways to combine the live worship experience with the highly produced content to which our online audience has become accustomed.” Corpus Christi Catholic Church St. James Drive, Piedmont Indoor services are available. Saturday Vigil services at 6 p.m., weekday mass is at 9 a.m., and Sunday mass is at 9 a.m. and 11 a.m. Masks must be worn, and parishioners are asked to remain 6-feet apart from others in pews, unless accompanied by another member of your household. Once communion is received, you can lower your mask to consume the Eucharist. Zion Lutheran Church Park Blvd., Piedmont Indoor Worship is held every Sunday at 10 a.m., and is limited to 50% of capacity, with social distancing and face masks required. Drive-through Communion is every Sunday, from 10:45 to 11:15 am. Zion continues to Live Stream the Sunday Services every Sunday at 8:30 am and 11:00 am. St. John’s Episcopal Church Gouldin Road, Montclair The first in-person worship service was held on Pentecost, May 23. The outdoor service was held at 7:45 a.m. and was limited to 25 people. Worship services will continue on Sundays at 7:45 a.m. and a 10 a.m. virtual service including music. There are plans to move inside in August if restrictions will allow. Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church Lakeshore & Mandana, Oakland During shelter in place orders, all worship services are held online with plans to return in July if restrictions allow. Visit https:// www.labcoakland.org/home.php to view services. St. Clement’s Episcopal Church Claremont Blvd., Berkeley In-person worship services are being held on the lawn in front of the church on Sundays at 8 a.m. and 10 a.m. Everyone is welcome. The church asks people to call ahead so that enough chairs are placed outdoors. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community. tel: 510-658-2588 www.piedmontfuneralservices.com 5000 piedmont ave., oakland, ca (fd#2210)

articles.text: He persuaded a reluctant General Dwight Eisenhower to support the French Resistance and FreeFrance with troops and tanks. To reach his starting point at Montparnasse station, LeClerc fought off heavily armed enemy troops surrounding Paris. A Secret Command Center Liberation Museum sits atop a historical secret bunker. It is a featured exhibit, built as a command center meant to protect against air strikes. If under attack, the essential public services of Paris could be powered from this location. The government could manage vital communication systems that control water, electricity, telephone, and hospitals. The bunker’s private telephone exchange was independent of public access and equipped with 250 telephone numbers. It had its own air supply and capacity for recirculating air like a submarine. Its 1930s diesel-powered generator kept the lights on, and as a backup, a bicycle-built-for-two was converted for pedal-power. During the war, the Germans knew the bunker location with identity as an air raid shelter. They had no knowledge of its command-center features. It was a fear-obsessed era when the public grew panicky about poison-gas attacks. It was commonly known that poison-gas canisters of mustard-gas were in abundant supply, left-over from World War I. The populace knew that poison-gas injuries were severe and terrifying, and they feared imminent air-attacks of poison gas – attacks that never came. The command bunker’s fate was to sit idly in neglect for years. But the French Resistance discovered its value for clandestine activities such as a hideout, or trading post for messengers. Most significantly, Resistance leaders used the command center Exodus of the French fleeing before the German troops arrive. More than eight million French were displaced or fled the Nazi occupation during WWII to organize the Parisian military strike against the German occupiers. The start of World War II World War II started in Europe when Germany bombed Poland’s Danzig naval port, followed by a ground invasion on September 1, 1939. The Polish Army fought back hard, but the battle was lost when Russia invaded from the east. Joseph Stalin had signed a pact with Adolph Hitler for a surprise attack. Russia wanted the territory it lost at the Versailles Treaty after World War I. In a north-south boundary agreement, Germany took western Poland and Russia got the eastern half. Europe was frantic over the Polish invasion. France declared war on Germany and then waited and watched for the first strike during the next eight months. France’s war declaration devolved into ridicule with jokes about “the phony war.” Then, abruptly, German armies broke into a blitzkrieg, overrunning Belgium and the Netherlands, driving the British into the sea at Dunkirk; and defeating France. Upon defeat, Parisians gathered sadly to watch a stream of Reich motorcades speeding victoriously into the heart of the city. The City of Light had surrendered to avoid destruction. Paris would be flooded with German Army troops. The Supreme commandants selected the finest hotels, Le Meurice, Le Ritz, Lutetia, George V, Le Crillon – to set up shop. The Fuhrer’s objective was to neutralize France militarily, contain and source Paris with its industry-rich environs, and control the seaports. Calais, just 21 miles across the English Channel, was situated favorably for a ground strike against England. The North Atlantic coastline ports – Brest, Saint-Nazaire, and Bordeaux – were brought to heel. the Reich blocked vital war shipments to the Allies, especially from the United States. France suffers Allied Bombings Few Americans are familiar with the Western Allied bombings of civilian installations in German-occupied France during WWII. The Germans’ use of France’s coastline ports as bases for their U-boats made the cities an unintentional target where the Allies were forced to deliberate about the loss of civilian lives in their ongoing recalculations of essential military strategies to weaken the Germans. Collateral damage in terms of human lives during wartime is an uncomfortable debate and an unconscionable reality, but the museum exhibits do not shy away from the killings that caused severe hostilities between nations on the same side of the war. The Paris-La Chapelle marshalling yard is a critical example of an Anglo-U.S. bombing raid that killed 670 workers propagandized by the Germans to taunt the French about their very own military-partners attacking French P.M. Churchill (left) walking with General Charles de Gaulle to a WWII victory celebration in Paris.

They rise to a high note at the German expulsion on August 25, 1944, France’s Liberation Day. Le Musée de la Liberation de Paris on the Left Bank just south of Montparnasse was opened in 2019 – exactly 75 years to the day that Paris drove the Nazis out of the city. The museum’s intriguing mix of film, soundtrack, photography and artifacts create the Paris story from defeat and humiliation to liberation. A serious and somber experience, the visitor travels back to learn firsthand the fear and harsh realities inside an occupied city in a brutal war. From its depths, one is delivered to victory with a huge sigh of relief. The museum’s presentation is an intricate weave of the victors: the French Resistance and Free-France forces that mustered to fight and defeat the Germans in Paris. The week-long battle was hard-fought. The German retreat signaled a turning point in France’s liberation and the end of the war. The United States proudly enjoined in the French attack, and they shared the Paris victory. The full name of the Liberation Museum is Le Musée de la Libération de Paris - le Musée du Général LeClerc – Musée Jean Moulin to denote three collections of related artifacts now wrapped into one museum. Though its name is unnecessarily lengthy, it serves to spotlight two celebrated war heroes, General LeClerc of Free-France and Jean Moulin, the renowned chief architect of the French Resistance. articles.text: The PHS boys’ lacrosse team split its last two matches, losing to non-league Miramonte 11-7 on Saturday afternoon, May 22 in Orinda, while pounding Washington 19-1 at Witter Field one day earlier. The pair of games brings Piedmont’s record to 5-5 overall with three matches remaining: at Berkeley today, May 26; Senior Night against Bishop O’Dowd on Friday night, May 28; and the final game of the season on June 1 in Novato. “We have to be prepared against O’Dowd. It’s going to be an exciting and emotional game, especially after that last one,” said coach Ryan Price, citing Piedmont’s 9-8 overtime win over BOD on May 12. Friday’s game against O’Dowd will be the final home game of the season, and Piedmont will honor its 14 seniors on the roster: Nate Guzdar, Briggs Settlemier, Greg Gately, Tommy McNeil, Luke Biehn, Nicky Allen-Goix, Jake Alering, Alden Heske, Jake Richmond, Nate Seevak, Ryan Roos, J.D. Harrison, Andy Melian, and Alex Hilton. The community is invited to attend the game at Witter Field and to come early to honor the seniors at a recognition ceremony at 6:15 p.m. The game is a 7:00 p.m. game. 11-7 loss to Miramonte Piedmont trailed 3-1 by the end of the first quarter and fell behind 6-3 by halftime. Soren Dixon scored the game’s first goal to give PHS a 1-0 lead after nearly eight minutes of no scoring by either team. Miramonte, a North Coast Section power, rallied to score three goals before the end of the first quarter. Nate Guzdar scored to open the second quarter and Nate Fredericks made it 4-3 with 3:46 left in the half on an assist from Luke Biehn. But again, the Matadors added two clutch goals in the final three minutes to maintain a 6-3 lead. Biehn scored Piedmont’s only goal in the third period on a pass from Guzdar from behind the goal, Miramonte added two more goals for an 8-4 score. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team closed out its regular season in strong fashion, beating the San Leandro Pirates 12-5 on Thursday, May 20. The victory brings the team’s record to 7-1 heading into the Western Alameda County Conference league championship tournament. The Highlanders celebrated their six seniors on the roster on May 20: Max Wagener, Spencer Stein, Jack Dunlap, Jake Hart, Sam Corcoran, Dominic Ripley, and Grant Fisher. Without a Piedmont pool since last fall, the team made the most of its regular season throughout the pandemic. They trained extensively at Witter Field during the offseason, bounced around to pools in Berkeley for in-season practices. Senior Night was conducted by coach Savage in San Leandro High’s parking lot. “We started out the school year not knowing if we’d have sports, and then we got to have workouts down at Witter. [Athletic Director] Bradley Smet had to scramble to find a pool, and now we’re in a parking lot celebrating our seniors. If you want an image of the hard work they’ve put in; it’s us winning a game and then celebrating in a parking-lot in our towels,” said coach John Savage. Wagener, a four-year starter on the program, reiterated similar sentiments that the hard work throughout the offseason and regular season is paying off. “It’s a really good representation of our season. It shows the dedication of our guys. Whether it was at Witter or at some pool in Berkeley, we just showed up and tried to do our thing. This group is so hard working, it makes coming to practice enjoyable. Even if we were working out at Witter Field, it translated to when we were in the water,” added Wagener. The program now looks ahead to the WACC Tournament which started yesterday, Tuesday, May 25 at Encinal. The second round is set for tomorrow, Thursday, and the semi-finals and finals will be this weekend, on Saturday, May 29. PHS enters as the No. 2 seed behind Berkeley after losing 15-11 to the Yellowjackets on May 13. The water polo team is still looking for its first league championship since joining the WACC. It was the 2nd place team in 2017 and 2018, and third place team in 2019. Big win vs. San Leandro Piedmont blasted the Pirates out of the water in Thursday’s Staff Photos Max Wagener scores a goal in front of the San Leandro net. Jake Hart scores against the Pirates with a toss-in over the keeper’s head. Spencer Stein had a pair of goals against San Leandro. match, leading 8-0 by the end of the first quarter and enabling Savage to rotate in subs and put players into new positions. The Highlanders were up 11-1 by halftime, no goals were scored in the third, and PHS closed out the victory at 12-5. Corcoran scored the game’s first goal after a minute with Dunlap putting another in with 5:15 left in the first, 2-0. After a pair of saves by goalie Murray Davis, Dunlap hit Corcoran for the open shot with 3:28 to go, while Wagener assisted Stein to go ahead 4-0 a minute later. To close out the first quarter, Hart had a steal and score with 1:41 left, while Davis found Dariush Kashani on a fast break down the pool to make it 6-0 with a minute left. Kashani, the sophomore goalie, for to play in an attacking role on Thursday, scoring the sixth goal. Stein scored with 22 seconds left, while Wagener made it 8-0 on a shooting penalty in front of the net with 4.5 seconds left. In the second quarter, Wagener made it 9-1 with 3:58 left in the first half, while freshman George Stein scored with 59 seconds left, and Shane Miller with 20 seconds; 11-1. Following a scoreless third quarter by Piedmont, Stein got the game’s final goal. Final stats include Wagener, Corcoran, Spencer Stein, and George Stein with two goals, and Wagener with an assist. Individual goals were scored by Dunlap, Hart, Kashani, and Miller. WACC first-round vs. Castro Valley The Highlanders beat Castro Valley 19-4 in the opening round of the League Tournament at Encinal. See next week’s Post for tournament details. NEXT UP Piedmont (7-1) will play in the second round of the league tournament at Encinal on Thursday, May 27 at 4:00 p.m. The finals are on Saturday, May 29.
