articles.text: Staff Photos Macie Gard scored three goals against San Leandro in an 11-4 win. Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team closed out its regular season with a huge game, an 11-4 victory at San Leandro. The Highlanders finish the season with a 3-3 record. They will advance to the second round of the Western Alameda County Conference tournament at Encinal tomorrow, with the Finals set for Saturday, May 29. “We started the season off trying to figure out where we were good at. We improved everywhere, I couldn’t be prouder of what they accomplished so far. Everything has improved, they are playing like a team, they love each other and it is fun to watch,” said coach Sarah Mooney. “We want to focus on keeping up what we’ve shown to be an excellent team defense, keep looking for the open shot, and end the season on a positive note,” added assistant coach Hannah Mooney. At Thursday’s match, the Highlanders honored its two seniors on the roster, Ella Wright and Gwen Jones. San Leandro win Against the Pirates, after ending the first quarter in a 2-2 draw, the Highlanders scored four unanswered goals to go ahead 6-2 by halftime. The team put in one more in the third but allowed two, 7-4, but added four more unanswered to close out strong, 11-4. “The girls started shooting and began playing with a little more confidence. I think they figured out who was open and started executing. It’s something we have really pushed on every game,” said Sarah Mooney. Macie Gard and Odessa Dando had the first two goals of the game for Piedmont in the first quarter. The second-quarter drubbing started with Rosie Feldman scoring after 40 seconds, and Annika Nilsson netting one with 3:58 left. Gard scored quickly after the Highlanders drew an ejection, while Feldman made it 6-2 with 24 seconds left in the first half. articles.text: The Piedmont girls’ basketball team is on a hot streak, winning three games last week against St. Joseph 83-62 on Wednesday, May 19; obliterating Alameda 66-17 on Friday, May 21l and beating Oakland Tech 73-67 on Saturday, May 22. The string of games brings Piedmont’s record to 10-1 overall with five games left to play, including a critical game tonight against Bishop O’Dowd. “It’s always a big game against O’Dowd. We have a good team and we want to beat them, It will be a tough game,” said coach Bryan Gardere. It was a big run of games for senior captain Kai Johnson, who scored 28 points against Tech, 27 at Alameda, and 25 against St. Joseph. “Our senior, Nakilah [Kai], she does it all,” said Gardere. “She balances out the team. “She’s always confident and optimistic, telling her teammates, ‘We got this’.” 6-point win vs. Oakland Tech The Highlanders led 16-15 by the end of the first quarter and 36-29 at halftime. The lead extended to 54-45 at the end of the third before closing out strong 73-67. Johnson led the way with 28 points, 12 rebounds, and three steals, while Trinity Zamora piled on the stats with 15 points and 22 rebounds, and eight assists. Zamora’s 22 rebounds is a number Piedmont hasn’t seen since the days of the Paris twins under Gardere. Freshman Natalia Martinez had 20 points, three rebounds, and three assists. Maddie Hill had seven points. Lopsided win over Alameda In a blowout win against Alameda, PHS led 39-10 at halftime, 57-14 to start the fourth, and allowed just three points in the fourth, 66-17. articles.text: Piedmont High School welcomed back an official interscholastic sport in 2021 to Binks Rawlings Gym after a 20-year absence. The boys’ volleyball team, expansion team in the Western Alameda County Conference, beat Encinal 3-1 on Tuesday, May 25 by scores of 22-25, 25-20, 25-12, and 26-24. “The old boys’ volleyball team disbanded 20-some years ago. Interest in the sport picked up back in middle school. We were set to start last but we only played one match before the pandemic,” said a sophomore captain Wilson Wong. The school finished the 1999 season as the No. 3 seed in the NCS Tournament, falling to No. 2 Campolindo 3-0 in the semifinals on May 20, 1999, exactly 21 years ago. The volleyball team finished the 20th century with a successful 16-5 overall record, but was never heard from again. That was until Wong and the current members of the team began a middle school club that formed into a full-fledged team for the high school. They officially entering the WACC in 2020 prior to the pandemic. “It feels like we’re a part of something bigger by helping the sport grow at the school. We didn’t think we’d play volleyball again after middle school, but our group of guys wasn’t ready to stop. I got in contact with people, went to meetings and collected the players. Now we’re here, playing, and having fun,” explained Wong. The team has 11 players: Wong, sophomore Owen Kelly, sophomore Ryan McConathy, sophomore Brayden Day, junior Patrick Alexandre, sophomore Kai Lambert, sophomore Romen Meima, freshman Danny Allen, freshman Shunji Higashi, freshman John Champion, and sophomore Eric Olaru-Hagen. The Highlanders defeated Tennyson on Tuesday, May 18 in a narrow 3-2 contest by scores of 21-25, 25-19, 25-21, 22-25, and 16-14. “We lack experience, but we can swing momentum. We have a lot of fire. We know that we’re undersized [and less experienced], but if we really get going, we can bring out the skill,” explained Wong. In their first year with three wins and teetering on the edge of a .500 win percentage, the players have reason to be proud. 2021 has been a terrific start, and with a team of 11 potential returners for 2022, the future is certainly bright. “We have a lot of potential. Next year, we’ll have a longer season and a lot of experience playing together. We hope to push people to play for clubs outside of the school,” said Wong. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-4) play Bishop O’Dowd in Binks Rawlings Gym tonight, May 26 at 4:00 p.m. Sophomore outside hitter Ryan McConathy with a spike.

articles.text: Spring Creative, an art exhibition featuring work by five local artists, opened at the Piedmont Center for the Arts last weekend. It will be on view this weekend and next, Saturday and Sunday, May 29-30, and June 5-6 from 11 a.m. through 2 p.m. Featured artists include Paula Valenzuela, Jon Schleuning, Mike Welch, Valerie Corvin, and Brian Molyneaux. the surface. Textures, color and organic forms are layered into a complex visual weave that hints at the underlying feelings and complexity of our lives. Paula moved with her family from Santiago, Chile to Piedmont in 2013. She has a studio in the Industrial Center Building in Sausalito. www.Paulavalenzuelaart.com Paula Valenzuela Paula Valenzuela is a Chilean abstract artist based in Piedmont. Her work explores the connection of darkness and light within us, the complexity of layers that we show to others and to ourselves. As an artist and psychotherapist, Valenzuela is interested in the cycles of the human experience, specially the internal and spiritual transformations between the birthing and dying processes. articles.text: A scene from the documentary Maiden. Maiden is the name of a boat helmed by an all-female crew that entered what was then called the Whitbread Round the World Race, a sailing competition that began in September 1989 and would not finish until May 1990. This race (perhaps “ordeal” is a better word) departed from South Hampton, England, on the first leg to Punta Del Este, Uruguay; then on to Fremantle, Australia; next Aukland, New Zealand; back to Punta Del Este; then Ft. Lauderdale, Florida; and finally a long return to South Hampton. The distance covered was some 45,000 nautical miles across and through some of the most grueling and harrowing sailing conditions imaginable. It was a test of will and tenacity that challenges the edges of a sailor’s abilities and all but defies the imagination. At the center of this race was Tracy Edwards who, after being denied berths on boats slated to enter the competition, and coming to realize that yacht racing was viewed as a man’s world, decided to mortgage her home, find a second-hand boat, and assemble an all-female crew with a plan to enter the 1989 Whitbread – an effort viewed as being against all odds. The boat was a fixer-upper that needed stem to stern retrofitting. As well, Tracy was desperate to find sponsorship and funding. Ultimately, King Hussein of Jordan stepped forward and offered to underwrite the Maiden’s entry. To Tracy’s relief, her crew proved to be a startling resilient group of women who refused to yield. Ironically, Tracy herself, despite her patina of resolve and courage, proved, at times to be the most fragile. Clearly the yachting world in 1989 was male dominated. The Maiden’s entry was met with unvarnished skepticism, if not outright hostility from dry land experts, blue water sailors, and a nautical press that would follow closely every leg of the race. Nevertheless, Edwards and the women carried on. Initially, much of the press coverage bordered on the misogynistic. But eventually Maiden was given some faint praise, and finally awarded a grudging acknowledgment of what they were in the process of achieving. The crew and Edwards herself proved to be a committed group of fierce competitors. And a more apt name for their boat might have been Defiant, for that is what they were all about. Despite yachting’s glass ceiling, they never yielded. During the leg to Auckland, the boat began to take on water, due in part to a leak around the mast. The problem delayed them 18 hours. The most harrowing days were after leaving Punta Del Este and sailing around the tip of South America. The deck was covered in snow and ice and the ocean a spray of freezing water and pounding, surging waves. It was a test of their grit and steadfastness and ultimate determination as well as a test of endurance and survival for the women and the boat. Edwards does say, looking back, she didn’t realize she had entered a battle until she was in it, one against not just the ocean, but also the chauvinistic world of yachting. When asked if she was a feminist, she said “no.” She later clarified that she merely wanted to engage in a race that fully captured her spirit and desire. “I’d begun a fight I didn’t realize I was having,” she said upon reflection. Maiden is a sea tale that is both electric and riveting, yet it also feels incomplete. The 16mm film had the feel, in parts, of a home movie with voice-over and interviews with crew members and Edwards. But there was so much that could not be covered and that needed more time and description – something that can only be conveyed through a tightly written screenplay with actors at the helm. The Maiden won two legs of its race, a remarkable feat given the circumstances of its entry into the Whitbread. Also remarkable is this account of an unforgettable and compelling race, a race that reveals a most surprising and wonderful final return to South Hampton. Maiden . Documentar y. Directed by Alex Holmes. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: Director-Screenwriter Yorgos Lanthimos won the European Film Award for Best Screenwriter in 2015 for The Lobster. The Lobster dribbled into theaters in 2015 to an initial reception of dumbfoundedness and confusion. Filmed in Ireland, this surreal, black comedy loosely aims at satire. Greek Director Yorgos Lanthimos takes the viewer to a dystopian society where everyone must be married or else they are forced to be transfigured into an animal of their choice. Colin Farrell stars as the protagonist, David. After his wife leaves him, he is taken to a lastditch hotel designated for matching up singles. He chooses to be transformed into a lobster if he cannot find a suitable mate. In brutal, dead-pan fashion, he tells the hotel manager (Olivia Colman) that lobsters remain fertile for life, have blue blood like aristocrats, and that “he quite likes the sea.” The Lobster may be too weird for some. Though it’s a comedy, there may not be a single chuckle of laughter by any of the actors in the film. I recommend that you give it a go, maybe even watch it a second time with the subtitles on. It’s a head scratcher but also a movie that requires thought well outside the box office. In the story, adults who become single or have just graduated from high school are taken to the fancy resort to find a new companion within 45 days. The only way to extend your stay is to shoot and capture one of the “loners” in the woods with a tranquilizer dart. Each captured loner buys you one more day at the hotel and prolongs your dating misadventure. The single people doomed to become dogs, ponies, or peacocks preoccupy themselves with the notion that they must match themselves up with someone with similar physical flaws, like frequent nose bleeds or a limp. Such oddities riddle the movie, and “the bizarre” becomes the resounding motif. Some viewers may be frustrated by these “holes” in the plot line, but they serve as a commentary on dating society with poignancy. John C. Reily (Talladega Nights, Step Brothers) has a lisp and awaits for a woman also with a lisp to arrive at the hotel. The film offers no explanation for why the characters are convinced that physical deficiencies are the key to love. Other than suggesting there are no rules in love or war. If you’re looking for something different, check it out. It is available at Piedmont Avenue’s Video Room. In 2015 The Lobster had a slow opening weekend, grossing only $50,000. Since then, the film has all the elements of becoming a cult classic. The Lobster. Directed by Yorgos Lanthimos. Starring Colin Farrell, John C. Reily, Rachel Weisz and Olivia Coleman. 119 minutes. Rated R. Colin Farrell and Rachel Weisz in a scene from The Lobster.
articles.title: The Lobster – strange, but worth the viewing time

articles.text: A scene from Disney’s Zootopia. Zootopia is not your typical animated talking animals movie; rather, Disney created a family-friendly buddy cop comedy with a raft of subtle messages and teachable moments. The film is set in a world where predator and prey identities have been abolished, hence Zootopia (utopia). The story focuses on Judy Hopp (Ginnifer Goodwin), the first metropolitan bunny cop ever hired. She’s a perky go-getter and determined to prove herself. But on her first day on the force, to her surprise, she confronts some discouraging prejudices. Given her size, and given some thick-headed assumptions, officer Hopps is assigned parking ticket duty by her Cape Buffalo police chief, Bogo (Idris Elba). But then Judy learns that a family man, Mr. Otter, has disappeared and his wife, Mrs. Otter, is frantic, and appeals to Judy to help find him. Judy rises to the challenge and bets her career that she can. The problem is that in order to track down Mr. Otter she will have to partner up with slick and sly fox, Nick Wilde (Jason Bateman), which forces her to rethink her assumptions about foxes in general. The team’s search for the missing Mr. O. takes the pair in unexpected directions, while encountering a most extraordinary cast of characters, including an adorable lamb, a mafia-type polar bear, and a wonderful sloth who works for the Department of Motor Vehicles, guaranteeing extremely slow service and long, exasperating lines. Judy and Nick must also unravel an unanticipated conspiracy, one that tests their teamA scene from Disney’s Zootopia.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR KIDS Zootopia a lovely film with strong messages

articles.text: work, and tucks nicely into that thread of prejudice that stitches the narrative together at every turn. There are also moments of silly slapstick, exciting chases, all while taking them into fascinating enclaves of Zootopia known as Tundra Town, Sahara Square, and Little Rodentia. For all of the film’s asides, and some not too subtle references to Disney’s Frozen, the most significant are the scenes that touch on racism in everyday Zootopian life. Hopps, for example, makes the point that “cute” is a word used only by bunnies and considered offensive if used by other denizens of Zootopia. What Disney points out, often with the lightest of touches, is that we are all tempted to prejudge one another, even by the benign Judy Hopps. However, when Judy is confronted by her blind spots regarding Zootopians, she willingly steps up and apologizes to those she has offended and promises to do better. All of this takes place in the context of a fun, exiting movie with lots of laughs and energetic, fast-paced animation that pays close attention to detail and texture. Zootopia. Disney animation. Directed by Byron Howard & Rich Moore. Voices of Ginnifer Goodwin, Jason Bateman, & Idris Elba. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: Reading George Lang’s cookbook, Cuisine of Hungary, will bring a smile to your face. It reads more like an historical novel than a cookbook. Hungarian music is very communicative. Everyone knows Brahms’ Hungarian dances, and Liszt’s Hungarian rhapsodies. This music has entertained millions of people through cartoons for almost 100 years. But there is more to Hungary than Brahms’ Hungarian Dance No. 5 or Liszt’s Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2. When considering the cuisines of the world, Hungary is hardly ever mentioned. For sheer numbers, Chinese and Indian food must rank at the top. French cuisine is the touchstone for the rest of the world. The interesting thing is that French cuisine is the stepchild of Italian cuisine. When Catherine de Medici became the queen of France by marrying King Henry II in 1533, she brought her chefs from Florence. The French then did the thing which they do so well – take credit for whatever you can. The United States is famous for its international restaurants, but there are precious few Hungarian restaurants on the list. This is a shame because Hungarian cuisine is fabulous. By Chris Honore’ Zootopia is not your typical animated talking animals movie; rather, Disney created a family-friendly buddy cop comedy with a raft of subtle messages and teachable moments. The film is set in a world where predator and prey identities have been abolished, hence Zootopia (utopia). The story focuses on Judy Hopp (Ginnifer Goodwin), the first metropolitan bunny cop ever hired. She’s a perky go-getter and determined to prove herself. But on her first day on the force, to her surprise, she confronts some discouraging prejudices. Given her size, and given some thick-headed assumptions, officer Hopps is assigned parking ticket duty by her Cape Buffalo police chief, Bogo (Idris Elba). But then Judy learns that a family man, Mr. Otter, has disappeared and his wife, Mrs. Otter, is frantic, and appeals to Judy to help find him. Judy rises to the challenge and bets her career that she can. The problem is that in order to track down Mr. Otter she will have to partner up with slick and sly fox, Nick Wilde (Jason Bateman), which forces her to rethink her assumptions about foxes in general. The team’s search for the missing Mr. O. takes the pair in unexpected directions, while encountering a most extraordinary cast of characters, including an adorable lamb, a mafia-type polar bear, and a wonderful sloth who works for the Department of Motor Vehicles, guaranteeing extremely slow service and long, exasperating lines. Judy and Nick must also unravel an unanticipated conspiracy, one that tests their teamA scene from Disney’s Zootopia. work, and tucks nicely into that thread of prejudice that stitches the narrative together at every turn. There are also moments of silly slapstick, exciting chases, all while taking them into fascinating enclaves of Zootopia known as Tundra Town, Sahara Square, and Little Rodentia. For all of the film’s asides, and some not too subtle references to Disney’s Frozen, the most significant are the scenes that touch on racism in everyday Zootopian life. Hopps, for example, makes the point that “cute” is a word used only by bunnies and considered offensive if used by other denizens of Zootopia. What Disney points out, often with the lightest of touches, is that we are all tempted to prejudge one another, even by the benign Judy Hopps. However, when Judy is confronted by her blind spots regarding Zootopians, she willingly steps up and apologizes to those she has offended and promises to do better. All of this takes place in the context of a fun, exiting movie with lots of laughs and energetic, fast-paced animation that pays close attention to detail and texture. Zootopia. Disney animation. articles.text: Oakland Ballet Company’s dance film In Plain Sight, which premiered at the dance company’s gala on May 15, is available to watch on-demand now. In Plain Sight is based on the lives of Hannie Schaft, Truus Oversteegen, and Freddie Oversteegan, three courageous young women who lived in the Netherlands during the Nazi Occupation. Working with the Dutch resistance, these three women served as couriers, distributed illegal newspapers, transported weapons, committed sabotage, and carried out assassinations while hiding “in plain sight.” The dance film is choreoGraham Lustig, Director of Oakland Ballet. graphed by Oakland Ballet Company dancer Samantha Bell. Graham Lustig serves as the company’s Artistic Director. To view the film, visit: https:// oaklandballet.org/.
articles.title: Oakland Ballet film, In Plain Sight, available on demand now

articles.text: The San Jose Museum of Art (SJMA) is open to the public on weekends, Friday through Sunday. Currently on view are Do Ho Suh’s “Karma” and Pae White’s “Noisy Blushes.” White’s “Noisy Blushes” (2020) serves as a meditation on movement and time, light and color; as well as actual material presence and form. The artwork was commissioned by the San Jose Museum of Art; it fills the building’s 39-foot high atrium to transform the entrance for visitors. Another sculpture on display is Do Ho Suh’s “Karma,” a 23-foot tower of bronze male figures perched on top of each other’s shoulders and shielding that figure’s eyes with his hands. “Karma” will be on display through January 30, 2022. There are exhibitions for youth as well. The Koret Gallery and Art Learning Lab is an exhibition space inspired by sensory learning, and promotes creative exploration by children age 12 and younger. The museum’s multi-award winning STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Art and Math) education program features a diverse selection of artworks from the permanent collection. Through interactive play, young visitors are encouraged to draw their own connections between individual creative exploration using various tools and mediums. “We have been hard at work investing in a better SJMA for a stronger post-pandemic Museum,“ said Executive Director Sayre Batton. We continue internal work to become an anti-racist museum with allday trainings on building racial Art installation in the Atrium at the San Jose Museum of Art. equity that tie into our strategic goal to discuss issues and places for change.” The museum is restricting large groups and has temporarily cancelled group tours. Individuals, and small cohorts of visitors, are welcome to view exhibitions and artist highlights that are on gallery walls. All volunteers, docents, staff, and visitors must wear a mask or face covering and observe physical distancing guidelines. The museum is open Friday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., with the first hour dedicated to seniors, women who are pregnant, and those with underlying health concerns. SJMA offers free admission for youth, college students, and teachers. To obtain tickets, visit https:// sjmusart.org/.
articles.title: On view: Do Ho Suh’s “Karma” and Pae White’s “Noisy Blushes”

articles.text: The Oakland Symphony Youth Orchestra season finale. The Oakland Symphony Youth Orchestra presented its season finale in a two-part concert digital series on May 16 and May 23. The concert series is now available to watch online through the Oakland Symphony’s website. The program series features Youth Orchestra musicians performing pieces by Bizet, Dvorak, Mendelssohn, Mozart, and Shostakovich as well as woodwind ensembles. The series is hosted by Omid Zoufonoun. The May 16 concert was recorded at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Visit https://www. oaklandsymphony.org/osyo- 2020-21-season-finale-concerts/ to watch.
articles.title: Oakland Youth Orchestra season finale is online

articles.text: Filoli House and Garden is celebrating the LGBTQ community with a weekend of history and art on Saturday and Sunday, June 5 and 6. Visit the garden in Woodside any time between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m. Visitors can embark on a colorful journey on the iconic pride flag through Filoli’s Estate Trail. The trail is transformed into a rainbow walk; at each station, you will learn about the meaning of each color in the flag. A “soundscape” will be offered on the Garden House lawn, where visitors will have the opportunity to hear about the progress that has been made in the fight for equality, the people who have advocated for such, and what’s still left to be done. Stunning floral arrangements will take over the gardens, created by the Nigella botanical boutique team in San Francisco. Visitors will learn more about the company’s connection to the LGBTQ community. Specialty drinks and treats will be sold from Little Green Cycle under the shade of the olive groves between 11 a.m. and 3 p.m. Summer Nights at Filoli Pride weekend also coincides with Filoli’s “Summer Nights” series of events, which begin tomorrow, May 27, and run through the end of September. Come dressed in your most extravagant Dynasty lookalike outfit on Thursday, June 3 from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. Some will remember that Filoli House served as the mansion on the popular Dynasty TV show about the goings-on of a wealthy Denver family. The show spanned a decade in the 80s and helped pioneer compelling narratives around gender inequality and featured prime time’s first openly gay character and first Black female lead. Numerous scenes were filmed at Filoli, including the series pilot. Visit https://filoli.org/pride/ for ticketing information. Celebrate Pride month will be saluted by Filoli House and Garden the weekend of June 5-6.
articles.title: Celebrate Pride at Filoli Garden June 5 and 6

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Napa Valley Register Festival Napa Valley will return next month as an all-outdoor, 10-day celebration. Festival Napa Valley is returning live next month in an all-outdoor celebration, beginning July 16. The 10-day summer arts festival will take place in iconic Napa Valley locations. Festival Napa Valley kicks off at 6:30 p.m. on July 16 with soprano Lisette Oropesa who will perform in the picturesque outdoor stage at Charles Krug Winery. The Cuban-American soprano singer has been celebrated for a voice that is “brightly crystalline and arrestingly powerful,” the New York Times said. The concert will be followed by an outdoor patron dinner at Hall St. Helena, an artfilled estate. The Dallas Symphony Trio, Blackburn Music Academy musicians, Alexander Malofeev, Matt Haimovitz, Chad Hoopes, Audrey Vardanega and many other classically-trained musicians, trios, and groups are slated to perform outdoors, with a mix of donor luncheons and dinners served alfresco. To view a full list of concerts scheduled for this summer, visit https://festivalnapavalley. org/2021-summer-season/.
articles.title: Festival Napa Valley returns live July 16 - 25

articles.text: The San Francisco Jazz Festival will begin on June 3 as a virtual festival. First launched as a two-day festival in 1983, the San Francisco Jazz Festival is the foundational annual June concert event upon which the organization SF Jazz was built. The festival will present a virtual edition of programming, to include 18 exclusive broadcasts that will feature highlights from past performances, world premiere concerts, a rare film documentary on Thelonious Monk, events honoring Juneteenth, and more. SF Jazz utilizes its extensive archives and presents a hybrid of the annual June jazz festival, with virtual performances by vocalist Jazzmeia Horn, drummer Brian Blade, The Harold Lopez-Nussa Quartet saxophonist Melissa Aldana, and pianist Harold Lopez-Nussa from Havana. On T hu rsd ay, Ju ne 3, Lopez-Nussa’s quartet will perform live from Havana at 7 p.m. Visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ for information on how to reserve a spot for the live-stream performance. Through the month of June, SF Jazz will present a total of 18 concerts, both archival and live-streamed performances. For a full lineup, visit https:// www.sfjazz.org/sfjazz-digital/ virtual-san-francisco-jazz-festival-2021/.
articles.title: Archived SF Jazz performances available through June

articles.text: The Kronos Festival returns on June 11 after a one-year hiatus. This year’s virtual festival will expand the San Francisco-based event to include eight online presentations featuring 10 world premieres. The festival will showcase more than 20 guest performers, and will highlight the work of Kronos’ artistic collaborators and community partners. Art, activism, and the fight for civil rights are key themes in Kronos’ works, represented at the festival in pieces by Sahba Aminikia, John Coltrane, Nicole Lizée, Bill Morrison, Tongo Eisen-Martin, Eiko Otake, Pete Seeger, Valerie Soe, Vân-Ánh Võ, and Zachary James Watkins. articles.text: Stern Grove Festival will return to San Francisco to present its 84th season live on June 20. The festival will run for 10 weekends through August 29, with a range of free concerts. An official line-up will be announced soon and will be made available on https://www.sterngrove.org/. Founded in 1938, Stern Grove Festival Association is a nonprofit organization whose mission is “to make live musical experiences accessible to all.” The organization presents public, outdoor music events in an amphitheater in Sigmund Stern Grove at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. The amphitheater is owned and operated by the City of San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites. The festival has brought more than eight decades of opera, theatre, and music events completely free. Stern Grove Festival is one of San Francisco’s best loved and wellattended summer festivals.
articles.title: Full line-up to be announced soon

articles.text: The kitchen is often the hub of the home. It’s no wonder a kitchen remodel has some homeowners leaving their home until the work is done. But if that’s not part of the plan or budget, you can survive a kitchen remodel with a little preparation. You’ll want to work with a contractor who values your schedule to minimize disruptions to family routines. Here are a few of our sanity-saving tips to prepare any area of your home for construction. Create a “Safe Zone” – Designate a room to store temporarily displaced items. Pack fragile and valuable items like fine china, photos, artwork, electronics, etc. and move it to the “safe zone.” Define “Work Zone” – Define where workers are allowed, and not allowed in your home. We recommend ZipWalling these areas off from the rest of the house. Define “Time Zone” – Define when workers are allowed to work or visit before construction begins. Always wear shoes – Take precautions to protect yourself when walking around a construction zone. Keep a Positive Attitude – This too shall pass – and we hope the results are worth it. Construction is dusty work, but with a little preparation your home can stay relatively dustfree. Here are a few techniques any contractor should employ to minimize dust exposure: Dust barriers and ZipWalls – Install plastic sheets over doorways and openings to create a barrier to non-construction areas. Air filtration – Reduce dust by drawing in particulate laden air and filtering it, before venting outdoors. Power tools with dust extractors – Employ tools with built-in dust extractors to further minimize dust and debris. Sticky mats and floor paper – Place at entries to remove dirt from tracking in and out and to protect flooring and carpet. Now for the biggest concern: Cooking during a kitchen remodel Consider remodeling your kitchen during the summer or fall when the weather allows for outdoor cooking and grilling. Areas to set up a temporary kitchen can include: the garage, patio, deck, or even your front porch. Here are our tips for keeping you fed when your kitchen turns into a construction zone. Set up a temporary kitchen – Pack up your kitchen in advance, reserving minimal items for your temporary kitchen. Set up a wash station – Designate a room with a sink as the temporary wash station. Bring out your camp cook – Normalize camp food and prepare hot meals using your gas grill, electric skillet or propane stove, for a reliable heat source. ZipWall barrier will help to keep dust out of the rest of your home during construction. Get a mini-fridge – A minifridge gives you easy access to store perishables while construction is underway. You can ask your contractor to move your fridge to a temporary location and move it back when the job is done. Create a temporary countertop – Get a foldable table for countertop space to fit a microwave, electric kettle, or a cutting board. And lastly, factor in the costs of dining out in your overall budget, because you will have to eat out occasionally! Now, you’re all set for a successful kitchen remodeling project. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, May 26, 2021 Features By Kevin Mond The kitchen is often the hub of the home. It’s no wonder a kitchen remodel has some homeowners leaving their home until the work is done. But if that’s not part of the plan or budget, you can survive a kitchen remodel with a little preparation. You’ll want to work with a contractor who values your schedule to minimize disruptions to family routines. Here are a few of our sanity-saving tips to prepare any area of your home for construction. Create a “Safe Zone” – Designate a room to store temporarily displaced items. Pack fragile and valuable items like fine china, photos, artwork, electronics, etc. and move it to the “safe zone.” Define “Work Zone” – Define where workers are allowed, and not allowed in your home. We recommend ZipWalling these areas off from the rest of the house. Saving your sanity while preparing for a kitchen remodel Define “Time Zone” – Define when workers are allowed to work or visit before construction begins. Always wear shoes – Take precautions to protect yourself when walking around a construction zone. Keep a Positive Attitude – This too shall pass – and we hope the results are worth it. Construction is dusty work, but with a little preparation your home can stay relatively dustfree. Here are a few techniques any contractor should employ to minimize dust exposure: Dust barriers and ZipWalls – Install plastic sheets over doorways and openings to create a barrier to non-construction areas. Air filtration – Reduce dust by drawing in particulate laden air and filtering it, before venting outdoors. Power tools with dust extractors – Employ tools with built-in dust extractors to further minimize dust and debris. Sticky mats and floor paper – Place at entries to remove dirt from tracking in and out and to protect flooring and carpet. Now for the biggest concern: Cooking during a kitchen remodel Consider remodeling your kitchen during the summer or fall when the weather allows for outdoor cooking and grilling. Areas to set up a temporary kitchen can include: the garage, patio, deck, or even your front porch. Here are our tips for keeping you fed when your kitchen turns into a construction zone. Set up a temporary kitchen – Pack up your kitchen in advance, reserving minimal items for your temporary kitchen. Set up a wash station – Designate a room with a sink as the temporary wash station. Bring out your camp cook – Normalize camp food and prepare hot meals using your gas grill, electric skillet or propane stove, for a reliable heat source. ZipWall barrier will help to keep dust out of the rest of your home during construction. Get a mini-fridge – A minifridge gives you easy access to store perishables while construction is underway. You can ask your contractor to move your fridge to a temporary location and move it back when the job is done. Create a temporary countertop – Get a foldable table for countertop space to fit a microwave, electric kettle, or a cutting board. And lastly, factor in the costs of dining out in your overall budget, because you will have to eat out occasionally! Now, you’re all set for a successful kitchen remodeling project. articles.text: Wednesday Walkers stop for a group photo halfway up Scenic Avenue at the Eliassen Overlook. Pictured are (front): Cheryl Coleman Jones (left) and Sherry Jacobs; (back) Albert Chen, Nancy Henn, Kat Gustafson, Bob Gustafson, Brenda Ferrero, Melba Yee, Jim Kuo, and Dick Carter. The members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group enjoy walking to seldom seen places in Piedmont. The hidden pathways and stairs around the city provide this opportunity. On a recent walk, the group had experienced the short 89-foot path between Piedmont Court and Mountain Avenue. This past Wednesday, May 19, they were interested in seeing more similar paths. Twelve members of the group assembled at the Exedra on a mild morning. On hand were Brenda Ferrero, Jim Kuo, Adrienne Hamlin, Susan Martin, Albert Chen, Kat and Bob Gustafson, Nancy Henn, Melba Yee, Sherry Jacobs, and Dick Carter. The group was especially pleased to welcome first-time walker Cheryl Coleman Jones. The group was up for a bit of a challenge. They learned from a summary in a past issue of Gail Lombardi’s Piedmont Historical Society magazine that there are 21 paths in Piedmont, the longest of which is the 281-foot set of stairs that links Scenic and Blair Avenues. In fact, there are two other stair pathways on Scenic; two fewer than St. James which has the most in the city with four stairway paths. Strong winds the night before had helped clean the air, so the walkers thought the views of Oakland, the Bay, and San Francisco would be good from Scenic Avenue, an appropriate name. The group departed from the Exedra on Highland Avenue to Pala Avenue and up to Mesa Avenue. The group has an informal objective of walking every safe Piedmont street during the year. Going on Mesa to Moraga, then back on Monte Avenue one block away allowed the walkers to color in a set of streets on their Piedmont map. The route allowed them to see the lovely homes on these streets, and they particularly liked a beautiful Victorian on Mesa and what they believe is a Julia Morgan designed home on Pala. At the top of Pala they found the 161-foot set of stairs connecting the street with Scenic Avenue, a fairly steep climb, but the group took their time and emerged on Scenic. It was noted that Scenic is a historic Piedmont street. In the early 20th century it was a bit of a Piedmont bohemian district with artists and writers like early California painter Xavier Martinez and author Jack London. London wrote the classic Call of the Wild in 1903 in a house on Blair Avenue near Scenic. The group followed Scenic to a place where it turns 90 degrees and continues up the hill. An open spot affords a wonderful view of the Bay, Moraga Canyon, and Mountain View Cemetery far below. While stopping for a group photo, the walkers got to meet neighbor Roger Eliassen who had just arrived home. He and Dick Carter exchanged some friendly banter. Roger’s next door neighbor, Dara Birnbaum, who has joined the Wednesday group for several walks, came outside to greet the walkers. At the intersection of Scenic and Alta Avenues the group noted a large fir tree in the middle of the street, which creates a roundabout of sorts. They took Alta up to where it connects with Scenic. Along the hilly walk, everyone got to enjoy seeing rhododendrons, bottle brush, and other plants and flowers. The walkers then searched for the city’s longest set of stairs, and thanks to a neighbor, found the 281-foot set of steep stairs with no end in sight and were happy there was a handrail its entire length. The group came out on Blair Avenue, crossed over to Pacific Avenue and down to its intersection with Mountain and Craig Avenues. One of the very first homes built in Piedmont is on Craig Avenue, the former home of Hugh Craig, Piedmont’s first mayor. It was originally built in 1879 on Vernal Avenue (now Highland Avenue). The house was moved in 1912 using tree logs as a rolling cushion and pulled by horses to its current location. It was a beautiful home then and still is now. The walkers completed their walk going down Mountain past the Piedmont Community Church, returning to Highland Avenue and the Community Hall parking lot. It had been a leisurely, one-hour walk on a lovely morning with beautiful views from Scenic Avenue and a chance to learn more about Piedmont’s history. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are always welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required by contacting John Wilk at the Piedmont Recreation Department (jwilk@ piedmont.ca.gov),

articles.text: Michael Cavenaugh passed away peacefully on May 1, 2021, at his home in Walnut Creek with his family at his side. Up to his last days, he remained joyful and happy, always with his sense of humor. He was 88. Born Michael Frederick Cavenaugh on November 17, 1932, he was the son of Harry Taylor Cavenaugh and Ruth (Andrews) Cavenaugh of Yonkers, New York. His mother performed on Broadway before passing away at the age of 39 from pneumonia in 1941. After his mother’s death, Mike was sent to boarding school as his father struggled with the loss of his wife. Mike inherited her gift of music. As an organist he could play any song by ear. Years later, every day after work Mike would sit at his organ and play. He found joy in the music that warmed the house every evening. After high school, he joined the Air Force. One year later he earned admission to the U.S. Military Academy at West Point, New York. He graduated from West Point in 1956 as the fourth generation of the Cavenaugh family to do so. During his six years in the military, he was an expert marksman and served as a general’s aide while stationed in Panama, South America, and Korea. He also served in the Old Guard in Washington, D.C., and had the distinction of leading the Inaugural Parade for President John F. Kennedy. His time at West Point shaped his life, which was built on hard work, honesty and integrity. He was known as a true gentleman, kind to strangers, gentle, warm and always with a great sense of humor that he seemed to enjoy as much as anyone. He left the Army in 1962, and longed for a traditional family life which he had missed since age nine. He joined Merrill Lynch as a financial advisor in 1962 in Baltimore, Maryland. In September he answered an ad for a rental apartment, then occupied by Frances Glass from North Wilkesboro. There he met a charming Southern redhead full of energy and donning a big smile. She was making plans to move to New York. The two of them talked for three hours that day. Afterward, Fran called her friend and said she had met the man she was going to marry, despite not even knowing his name. He clearly felt the connection and knocked on her door one week later. Two years later, on September 5, 1964, they were married Mike was with Merrill Lynch for 35 years and he retired in 1997. He missed only one day of work in three decades due to illness. He worked with good friends Bob Sanford and Steve Griswold and almost daily had lunch with them while playing pinball. Watching Mike play pinball was a spectacle as he energetically made it an aerobic exercise. Mike was a loving husband and father. He and Fran lived most of their lives in Baltimore, where their children, Lisa and Dan, attended Roland Park Country School and Gilman, respectively. Mike was an avid tennis player and played five days a week until he was 84. He was also a great dancer, an occasional artist (including stained glass), a lifelong genealogist, a restorer of antique cars, and a regular handyman. Perhaps his greatest passion though was his family. It was rare to have a conversation with him when he was not fawning over Fran as the one and only love of his life. His lavish praise was also spent on his children, where he always saw the best in them. To talk of his life and leave out his warm sense of humor would be the grandest of oversights. He was a lover of Peter Seller’s movies and would often start laughing while telling jokes before others could even understand or appreciate the punchline. During his last moment of consciousness, he tried to tell a joke with a twinkle in his eye. Mike was also an incredibly patient man and full of great advice. He shouldered the role of the family patriarch in his 20s, providing both thoughtful counsel and financial support to his father and brothers. He did so out Michael Cavenaugh at West Point in 1956. Michael Cavenaugh died on May 1 at age 88. of love and his belief that there was nothing more important than family. His love of family expanded to embrace Fran’s mother and father in North Carolina. During their trips to North Wilkesboro, he would spend his days working on the home of his in-laws, Mansfield and Novel Glass. He could also be found at the local library investigating the family history, talking to cousins, aunts and uncles to soak up everything there was to know about his extended family. With family always a priority, Mike and Fran daringly moved to California in 2004 to be closer to their grandchildren. Mike helped his son fix up their new home in Piedmont, where he loved his house projects. In his last seven years as he dealt with dementia, he remained joyful and happy. Fran cared for him every step of the way, along with help from his daughter in their home in Rossmoor. Mike had a life of rich memories. His favorite saying was “Life is a Collection of Memories.” By that measure Michael Frederick Cavenaugh had a life better than he could have imagined as a young man…a family, a home, a love. His last words to Fran were, “I’m happy.” He is survived by his loving wife of over 56 years, Frances Rebecca (Glass) Cavenaugh; daughter Lisa; son Dan; daughter-in-law Jennifer (Smith); and grandchildren Jackson, Salem and Shelby. Michael is predeceased by his brothers, Alan and Harry Cavenaugh. The family will have a private memorial service in June at Mountain View Cemetery in Oakland. In lieu of flowers, the family requests that memorial donations be made to Hospice East Bay (hospiceeastbay.org). articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

He worked with good friends Bob Sanford and Steve Griswold and almost daily had lunch with them while playing pinball. Watching Mike play pinball was a spectacle as he energetically made it an aerobic exercise. Mike was a loving husband and father. He and Fran lived most of their lives in Baltimore, where their children, Lisa and Dan, attended Roland Park Country School and Gilman, respectively. Mike was an avid tennis player and played five days a week until he was 84. He was also a great dancer, an occasional artist (including stained glass), a lifelong genealogist, a restorer of antique cars, and a regular handyman. Perhaps his greatest passion though was his family. It was rare to have a conversation with him when he was not fawning over Fran as the one and only love of his life. His lavish praise was also spent on his children, where he always saw the best in them. To talk of his life and leave out his warm sense of humor would be the grandest of oversights. He was a lover of Peter Seller’s movies and would often start laughing while telling jokes before others could even understand or appreciate the punchline. During his last moment of consciousness, he tried to tell a joke with a twinkle in his eye. Mike was also an incredibly patient man and full of great advice. He shouldered the role of the family patriarch in his 20s, providing both thoughtful counsel and financial support to his father and brothers. He did so out Michael Cavenaugh at West Point in 1956. Michael Cavenaugh died on May 1 at age 88. of love and his belief that there was nothing more important than family. His love of family expanded to embrace Fran’s mother and father in North Carolina. During their trips to North Wilkesboro, he would spend his days working on the home of his in-laws, Mansfield and Novel Glass. He could also be found at the local library investigating the family history, talking to cousins, aunts and uncles to soak up everything there was to know about his extended family. With family always a priority, Mike and Fran daringly moved to California in 2004 to be closer to their grandchildren. Mike helped his son fix up their new home in Piedmont, where he loved his house projects. In his last seven years as he dealt with dementia, he remained joyful and happy. Fran cared for him every step of the way, along with help from his daughter in their home in Rossmoor. Mike had a life of rich memories. His favorite saying was “Life is a Collection of Memories.” By that measure Michael Frederick Cavenaugh had a life better than he could have imagined as a young man…a family, a home, a love. His last words to Fran were, “I’m happy.” He is survived by his loving wife of over 56 years, Frances Rebecca (Glass) Cavenaugh; daughter Lisa; son Dan; daughter-in-law Jennifer (Smith); and grandchildren Jackson, Salem and Shelby. Michael is predeceased by his brothers, Alan and Harry Cavenaugh. The family will have a private memorial service in June at Mountain View Cemetery in Oakland. In lieu of flowers, the family requests that memorial donations be made to Hospice East Bay (hospiceeastbay.org). Instead of an immediate mandate change, California opted to wait several weeks to adopt the CDC guidance, a move applauded by Alameda County health officials. Masking guidelines are ultimately up to local and state governments, the CDC said. People are considered fully vaccinated if it has been two weeks since their second dose of Pfizer or Moderna vaccine or their one dose of Johnson & Johnson vaccine. The new reopening guidelines that go into effect on June 15 include the elimination of capacity restrictions and physical distancing rules. For large outdoor events with over 10,000 participants, the state recommends that venues ask attendees for vaccination proof or a negative COVID- 19 test. For large indoor events with over 5,000 participants, venues must require attendees to provide proof of vaccination or a negative test. The June 15 guidelines will replace the state’s current color-coded four-tier system for reopening on a county-by-county basis. Alameda County has yet to meet state benchmarks to move into the least-restrictive tier for reopening. Since March 30, Alameda County has been in the orange tier, or moderate tier, the second-least restrictive tier. Santa Clara, Santa Cruz, San Francisco, and San Mateo counties are all now in the least-restrictive yellow tier. Most indoor activities can resume, with modification, in the yellow tier. The Council will hold an additional meeting at 6:00 p.m. on June 21, 2021. Consistent with Executive Orders No. N-25-20 and No. N-29- 20 from the Executive Department of the State of California and the Alameda County Health Official’s Shelter in Place Orders, the City Council meeting will not be physically open to the public and City Council members will be teleconferencing into each meeting via Zoom Teleconference. The specific teleconference details will be available on the agenda for each meeting. At the same meetings, the City Council will hold public hearings regarding the Municipal Services Tax and Municipal Sewer Tax and will set the tax rates for the fiscal year 2021-2022. Copies of the proposed budget are available for public inspection on the City’s web site at https://piedmont.ca.gov. A limited number of paper copies of the budget are available from the City Clerk’s office. You can email cityclerk@piedmont.ca.gov or telephone (510) 420-3040, between the hours of 8:30 a.m. and 12:00 noon, and 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. to request a copy. John O. Tulloch City Clerk City of Piedmont 120 Vista Avenue Piedmont CA 94611 Posted May 18, 2021

pages.text: 30 Wednesday, May 26, 2021 COVID NEWS Officials announce over 75 percent of Alameda County residents are at least partly vaccinated Nearly 8,900 Piedmonters have received at lease one dose of COVID-19 vaccine county’s residents ages 16 and older, are now fully vaccinated. Since a vaccine manufactured by Pfizer received emergency approval for children ages 12 to 15 on Thursday, May 13, over 27,000 kids in this age group have received their first dose countywide. Three vaccines are available in the United States, but only the Pfizer vaccine has been approved by the FDA for children under the age of 16. Pfizer and Moderna vaccines require two doses administered several weeks apart. A vaccine produced by Johnson & Johnson requires only one dose. In Piedmont, over 97 percent of residents ages 16 and older have received at least one dose of vaccine, according to the county. Almost 80 percent of residents age 16 and older have been fully vaccinated. In Oakland, 75 percent of the adult population is partially vaccinated, and 58 percent are fully vaccinated. Both Pfizer and Moderna are currently conducting vaccine trials in children as young as 6 months old. Dr. Anthony Fauci, the Chief Medical Advisor to the White House, has said that he expects all children will be eligible for vaccination by the end of By Barry Eitel Over 75 percent of residents in Alameda County have received at least one dose of COVID-19 vaccine, county health officials announced yesterday, Tuesday, May 25. Officers with the Alameda County Health Care Services Agency marked the milestone as a way to encourage unvaccinated residents to make an appointment as well as nudge those who are partly vaccinated to return for their second dose. Starting this month, even children as young as 12 can be vaccinated. “Our message is loud and clear,” said Alameda County Supervisor Wilma Chan. “Get vaccinated if you haven’t already. Get your second shot if you have a two-dose regimen and have only had your first. The vaccine is free and available to all Alameda County residents age 12 [and up] who want it, either from health care providers, local pharmacies or locations run by the county or its non-profit partners.” In total, Alameda County has administered 1.79 million doses of COVID-19 vaccine as of Sunday, May 23. Instead of an immediate mandate change, California opted to wait several weeks to adopt the CDC guidance, a move applauded by Alameda County health officials. Masking guidelines are ultimately up to local and state governments, the CDC said. People are considered fully vaccinated if it has been two weeks since their second dose of Pfizer or Moderna vaccine or their one dose of Johnson & Johnson vaccine. The new reopening guidelines that go into effect on June 15 include the elimination of capacity restrictions and physical distancing rules. Appointments are now not required at many vaccination locations in Oakland and elsewhere in the county. As of press time, same-day appointments were available at several locations in Oakland and Berkeley. Alameda County links to available vaccine appointments at covid-19.acgov.org/vaccines After more than 500,000 doses of vaccine were administered at the Oakland Coliseum Mass Vaccination Site since the middle of February, the county shuttered the Coliseum site this week. Over 18 percent of fully vaccinated Alameda County residents, including many Piedmonters, were vaccinated at this location or through one of the many mobile units the site sent throughout the area. The state has administered about 36.5 million vaccine doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. The state is vaccinating an average of over 221,000 people per day, a slight decrease from last week. Almost 16.8 million Californians, about 50 percent of the adult population, have been fully vaccinated. venues ask attendees for vaccination proof or a negative COVID- 19 test. For large indoor events with over 5,000 participants, venues must require attendees to provide proof of vaccination or a negative test. The June 15 guidelines will replace the state’s current color-coded four-tier system for reopening on a county-by-county basis. Alameda County has yet to meet state benchmarks to move into the least-restrictive tier for reopening. Since March 30, Alameda County has been in the orange tier, or moderate tier, the second-least restrictive tier. Santa Clara, Santa Cruz, San Francisco, and San Mateo counties are all now in the least-restrictive yellow tier. Most indoor activities can resume, with modification, in the yellow tier. To move into the yellow tier, the positivity rate in Alameda County needs to stay below 2 percent. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to stay below 2.2 percent – it is currently 1.8 percent in Alameda County. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to be below 1 – right now there are 2.6 cases per 100,000, a small decrease from last week. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,674,662 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 61,770 deaths due to the disease statewide. The state positivity rate is 0.8 percent, the same rate as Alameda County and a record low for California. On Sunday, May 23, the seven-day average for new cases in the United States dropped below 30,000 per day, the lowest level since June of 2020, the CDC reported. I’m continually impressed by Piedmont’s robust offerings and I am excited to bring my experience, creativity and passion for building community and family-focused programs to the city.” “I am looking forward to working with Eva and thrilled to have her join the Piedmont Recreation Department,” said Recreation Director Chelle Putzer, who was hired from Albany’s Recreation Department in October 2019. ”She brings a wealth of recreation experience to our team and will be able to hit the ground running on her first day in Piedmont.” lett. “Pear [as Dick Johnson was known] came up with the idea of a parade. articles.text: The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals’ decision in City of Portland v. United States (2020) significantly affects the ability of local governments to regulate the installation of “small cell” wireless facilities. On March 22, Piedmont joined a national coalition of dozens of cities, led by the City of Portland, to file a writ of certiorari to review the judgement of the Court of Appeals. A writ of certiorari is a request that the Supreme Court order a lower court to send up the record of the case for review. The Supreme Court decision is currently pending. The Federal Communication Commission issued the Third Order, or “Carr Order,” in September 2018, which limited Piedmont’s control over the applications filed by Crown Castle LLC in 2017 and 2019. Crown Castle first applied for Wireless Communications Facilities Permits (WCF Permits) in October of 2016. When Piedmont turned down an application by Crown Castle for cell towers, the company sued the city. In August 2020 the Ninth Circuit Court upheld most of the provisions of the Carr Order. The City of Piedmont filed an appeal of the order in federal court, citing that it was without precedent. Piedmont joined a coalition of much larger cities, including Atlanta, Boston, Philadelphia, Chicago, Los Angeles, San Jose, Santa Monica, and Monterey. The Federal Communication Commission (FCC) and the United States of America are the respondents in the court case. The consortium of cities is being represented by Best, Best & Krieger LLP, a law firm based in Walnut Creek. The firm maintains a strong presence in Washington, D.C., where lawyers regularly meet with key members of the FCC as well as members of Congress on issues related to telecommunications. The firm’s area of expertise includes cell tower siting, wireless communications, and interplay of federal and state regulations, among others. Firm partner Gerry Lederer participated in a recorded debate on 5G and its impact on cities’ right of way, as well as the challenges posed by ongoing conflicts between the wireless industry and local government agencies, and said that “the FCC has tilted the table too much in favor of industry and not enough for communities.” “It would be nice if industry would tell the truth about size. Small cells are not ‘small’. [They should] stop going to state legislatures and city councils with small boxes and saying ‘this is a small cell’, and forgetting about the other 28 cubic feet that [come along with it,]” he said. More information about the case is available at: https://www. supremecourt.gov/search.aspx- ?filename=/docket/DocketFiles/ html/Public/20-1354.html.
articles.title: Coalition of U.S. cities fighting for right to limit cell towers

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s graduating class of 2021 will have an in-person graduation ceremony on Friday afternoon, June 11 at Witter Field this year. articles.text: In your May 5 issue, Piedmont High School student Alexander Kibarian wrote a thoughtful essay on police violence, centered on an interview with Officer David Cutler of the Piedmont Police Department. Officer Cutler described the benefits of de-escalation training in reducing police violence. Kibarian concluded that when police departments fail to adopt de-escalation training they contribute to the problem of sysIn response to Kibarian’s essay, Dr. Marvin L. Engel wrote a letter published in your May 12 issue accusing Kibarian of “denigrating” our country. Engel claimed that President Biden and Vice President Harris have asserted that “the U.S. is not a systemic racist country.” This is a gross misstatement. On his first day in office President Biden signed an Executive Order addressing “the unbearable human costs of systemic racism.” What Biden did say is “I don’t think the American people are racist, but I think after 400 years, African Americans have been left in a position where they are so far behind the eight ball in terms of education and health, in terms of opportunity.” In other words, Black Americans are severely disadvantaged by systemic racism. Systemic racism is a system of interlocking and compounding disadvantages and disinvestments. Discrimination in housing, employment, banking and our criminal justice system intersect with lack of access to good schools, good health care, good food/nutrition, business opportunities, voting rights, public services and other benefits of American life. As Kibarian correctly noted, these connected disadvantages are exacerbated by inequities in policing. To recognize this social reality is not denigrating our country, it is holding us to a higher standard. Kibarian was right to applaud Officer Cutler for speaking in support of de-escalation. And Kibarian and President Biden should both be applauded for speaking out against systemic racism. –David Oppenheimer For 22 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some The Post invites families to send us photos still on your camera or in a scrapbook for publication in the Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. articles.text: Editor: We now know the elementary school day schedule will remain unchanged through June. Our youngest learners will see their teachers in-person for only 9 hours a week, instead of the 30 in-person hours a week offered by comparable, Bay Area school districts. In a letter to elementary school families, Superintendent Booker wrote that not adding more in-person instructional minutes “... may be a disappointment to some community members.” Let’s consider that “some” is actually “most” and “community members” are the “students we strive to serve,” especially since at this point, there is no scientific or safety restriction preventing every student from being in-person at school full-time. Our inability to move past these logistics is reflective of the results of the recent communication survey that demonstrated that both teachers and families alike don’t trust our leadership to hold our interests at heart. On May 5, 2021, the school board held a special closed-door session to review Superintendent Booker’s performance and to discuss the upcoming teacher negotiations. Despite many pleas for greater transparency from families, the board returned after the closed session to announce “no action was taken.” No further details were provided. And so, where do we go from here? After the challenges of this year, each group of stakeholders needs to ask themselves a series of questions: • Do you respect and look toward our superintendent, assistant superintendent and school board for honest leadership and expertise? • Would new leadership at all levels be the most efficient way forward? School board members should be asking themselves: • Can you effectively and objectively evaluate our superintendent and assistant superintendent? • Have you provided clear and consistent direction for the district with the wellbeing of the students at the center, guiding your decisions?
articles.title: Piedmont is behind. Here’s how we can move ahead

articles.text: On August 28, 1963, people gathered in Washington, D.C. to hear this powerful declaration: “I have a dream that my four little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the color of their skin, but by the content of their character.” This was beautifully spoken by Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. I am beyond sadden that society today is tearing apart Dr. King’s work that he painstakingly fought for. Dr. King’s legacy is being torn down by people who are demanding that you recognize your skin color as a determinate of your character. If you are White you are the oppressor; if you are non-White you are Recently President Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris agreed with South Carolina Senator Tim Scott (the only Black Republican in the U.S. Senate) that the U.S. is not a racist country. Yet, throughout the U.S., school districts are contemplating the implementation of Critical Race Theory (CRT) to their The basic ideological beliefs include “Whiteness” as oppression and propagation of racial stereotypes that the way people think and act are tied to their skin color. Decades ago in the segregated South, the emphasis upon skin color was deemed racist, but in today’s modern society, this is viewed as a progressive way of battling racism. The USA is the land of the free, the land of opportunity. This is the land that my ancestors fled to in order to feed their starving families left behind in their native land; this is the land that my ancestors fought to travel to and from during the Chinese Exclusion Act; this is the land that contained my ancestors on Angel Island; this is the land that my ancestors escaped to from Chinese Communist control; this is the land where my ancestors faced discrimination. And this is the land that I hold dear to my heart because of the freedom and opportunities that have been afforded to my ancestors, myself and, hopefully, to the next generations to come based on hard work and character – and not on race. As a parent I must do what I can to protect and educate my children. In today’s turbulent times, it is difficult for individuals to openly express their dissatisfaction with the mainstream. There is fear of being censured, ostracized, categorized a racist or sell-out when going against the tide. But there comes a time when one must set aside the fear of speaking out and go against that tide. The time is now.
articles.title: The time is now

articles.text: On May 10, Gov. Gavin Newsom added 39 counties to the state’s emergency drought proclamation, which include Alameda County and three others in the Bay Area. Alameda, Contra Costa, Napa and Solano counties were added to the proclamation. Newsom has proposed a $5.1 billion investment in water infrastructure and drought resilience in the state budget as California is confronted with critical water shortages. The allocation includes $1.3 billion for drinking and wastewater infrastructure, $60 million to assist the agriculture industry in reducing its water use and greenhouse gas emissions, and $200 million for habitat restoration. “This package of bold investments will equip the state with the tools we need to tackle the drought emergency head-on while addressing long-standing water challenges,” Gov. Newsom said. The 41 counties now under a drought state of emergency represents 30 percent of the state’s population. The state issued a “red flag” fire warning on May 2, the first time a red flag warning was issued in May since 2014. Red flag warnings are triggered by a combination of dry, hot conditions and strong winds. While temperatures around the Bay Area in the last week, have been unseasonably cold, when the warning was issued, temperatures were about 15 degrees Fahrenheit above average temperatures. EBMUD makes it official; drought is here The Board of Directors at East Bay Municipal Utility District, or EBMUD, voted to declare a Stage 1 drought shortage at its April 27 meeting based on projections that water runoff will fall below what is needed to refill reservoirs this year. The board also voted to purchase supplemental water supplies from the Sacramento River at the same meeting. Dr. King’s legacy is being torn down by people who are demanding that you recognize your skin color as a determinate of your character. If you are White you are the oppressor; if you are non-White you are oppressed. Recently President Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris agreed with South Carolina Senator Tim Scott (the only Black Republican in the U.S. Senate) that the U.S. is not a racist country. Yet, throughout the U.S., school districts are contemplating the implementation of Critical Race Theory (CRT) to their curriculums. The basic ideological beliefs include “Whiteness” as oppression and propagation of racial stereotypes that the way people think and act are tied to their skin color. Decades ago in the segregated South, the emphasis upon skin color was deemed racist, but in today’s modern society, this is viewed as a progressive way of battling racism. The USA is the land of the free, the land of opportunity. This is the land that my ancestors fled to in order to feed their starving families left behind in their native land; this is the land that my ancestors fought to travel to and from during the Chinese Exclusion Act; this is the land that contained my ancestors on Angel Island; this is the land that my ancestors escaped to from Chinese Communist control; this is the land where my ancestors faced discrimination. And this is the land that I hold dear to my heart because of the freedom and opportunities that have been afforded to my ancestors, myself and, hopefully, to the next generations to come based on hard work and character – and not on race. As a parent I must do what I can to protect and educate my children. In today’s turbulent times, it is difficult for individuals to openly express their dissatisfaction with the mainstream. There is fear of being censured, ostracized, categorized a racist or sell-out when going against the tide. But there comes a time when one must set aside the fear of speaking out and go against that tide. The time is now. articles.text: The Bay Area “Bike to Wherever Day,” which replaces the popular “Bike to Work Day” due to the COVID-19 pandemic, will take place this Friday, May 21. Bike East Bay coalition welcomes riders to nearly 80 “energizer stations” across Alameda and Contra Costa counties. “Bike to Work Day” is a celebration of cycling as a sustainable and healthy way to get to work and serves as an opportunity for those who don’t usually commute by bike to try it out. Many Piedmont residents and city staff participate in the event. Due to reduced number of people going to a work location outside their home, this year’s event has been renamed “Bike to Wherever Day” for the second year. “Thanks to the recent bike boom, bike trips in cities and towns across the country are sure to be high. In the East Bay alone, thousands will pedal to school, as a break from Zoom meetings, and wherever,” said Eileen Rice, Bike East Bay Communications Director.

articles.text: Ordinance 750 N.S., or “reach codes,” will go into effect on Tuesday, June 1. The amendment was adopted by Piedmont’s City Council on February 1 and will affect sales and transfers of real estate and the construction of new and existing residential buildings. Reach codes require certain home renovation projects to include energy efficiency measures or photovoltaic systems. For renovation projects that cost more than $25,000, at least one from a series of energy efficiency measures must be included in the project. For renovations costing more than $100,000, two energy efficient measures must be included. It is up to the homeowner which option or options to choose. Options range from less expensive options, such as switching out lightbulbs, to more expensive ones, like replacing water heaters. For reference, in 2019, 22% of building permits had a cost over $25,000, and 5% of building permits had a cost over $100,000. But more than threefourths of all projects had a value under $25,000 and would not be affected by these requirements. All new homes constructed in Piedmont, including new detached Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs), will be prohibited from having natural gas supplied to them. Building a new, all-electric home is expected to be less expensive than one with gas. Installing a new gas line can cost thousands of dollars, which all-electric homes will not need. Ordinance 750 N.S. was approved by the California Energy Commission on May 12. The ordinance is intended to reduce greenhouse gas emissions stemming from natural gas appliances. In staff reports related to the adoption of reach codes, city council found that “increasing levels of atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrates are expected to result in global temperature increases, and based on scientific literature and studies, are likely to cause a variety of local changes, including extreme weather conditions, sea level rise, more frequent heat waves, and extended period of drought.” We are currently feeling the effects of extreme weather caused by greenhouse gas concentrates. As more emissions enter the atmosphere, there is less precipitation and higher temperatures across California, leading to an increased likelihood of fires and drought. Even though Piedmont is small, it has the highest per capita emissions in the entire Bay Area, meaning that each citizen of Piedmont emits more greenhouse gases than average citizens anywhere else in the Bay. The majority of these emissions come from natural gas appliances. Home Energy Score (Home Energy Audit) Additionally, Ordinance 751 N.S., or the home energy assessment policy, went into effect on March 3 and affects homeowners and real estate agents. When selling a property or transferring the title, the seller must provide potential buyers with a Home Energy Score or Home Energy Audit prepared in the past five years, in addition to the normal disclosure information. Getting a Home Energy Score involves a few simple steps that can be accomplished while still living in the home. You can schedule a home energy assessment by contacting an authorized Home Energy Assessor before listing, or otherwise announcing your home for sale. The City maintains a list of authorized Assessors on its site: (https://piedmont.ca.gov/cms/ one.aspx?portalId=13659823&p ageId=17415806). Assessors also can be found by a Google search. Once you choose an assessment company, a Home Energy Assessor will visit your home to assess it. They will collect information about a home’s foundation, insulation, walls, and windows, as well as its heating, cooling, and water systems. CEC’s new Energy Code Draft Every three years, the California Energy Commission (CEC) approves a new Energy Code, which impacts how structures are built and renovated during that code cycle. Two weeks ago, the CEC released their proposed changes to the 2022 Energy Code, to take effect January 1, 2023. This is what’s called the “45-day language”, meaning that everyone has 45 days to review and provide comments, which are due June 21, 2021. If members of Piedmont want to comment on the proposed Energy Code, they can send them to the website: (https://efiling.energy.ca.gov/EComment/ EComment.aspx?docketnumber=21-BSTD-01). There will be three public hearings available on Zoom on May 24, 27, and 28. The Energy Code helps dictate the work that the Planning and Building Department completes in Piedmont. For instance, the reach codes came to pass because they “reach” above and beyond the minimum requirements in the Energy Code. The new Code will go into effect in 2023. For any questions about these ordinances, please visit the city’s website at: https:// piedmont.ca.gov/cms/one.aspx? portalId=13659823&pageId= 17415806 or email adykman@ piedmont.ca.gov or nredinbo@ piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: Energy Reach Code goes into effect June 1

Once you choose an assessment company, a Home Energy Assessor will visit your home to assess it. They will collect information about a home’s foundation, insulation, walls, and windows, as well as its heating, cooling, and water systems. CEC’s new Energy Code Draft Every three years, the California Energy Commission (CEC) approves a new Energy Code, which impacts how structures are built and renovated during that code cycle. Two weeks ago, the CEC released their proposed changes to the 2022 Energy Code, to take effect January 1, 2023. This is what’s called the “45-day language”, meaning that everyone has 45 days to review and provide comments, which are due June 21, 2021. If members of Piedmont want to comment on the proposed Energy Code, they can send them to the website: (https://efiling.energy.ca.gov/EComment/ EComment.aspx?docketnumber=21-BSTD-01). There will be three public hearings available on Zoom on May 24, 27, and 28. The Energy Code helps dictate the work that the Planning and Building Department completes in Piedmont. For instance, the reach codes came to pass because they “reach” above and beyond the minimum requirements in the Energy Code. The new Code will go into effect in 2023.
