Bike East Bay coalition welcomes riders to nearly 80 “energizer stations” across Alameda and Contra Costa counties. “Bike to Work Day” is a celebration of cycling as a sustainable and healthy way to get to work and serves as an opportunity for those who don’t usually commute by bike to try it out. Many Piedmont residents and city staff participate in the event. Due to reduced number of people going to a work location outside their home, this year’s event has been renamed “Bike to Wherever Day” for the second year. “Thanks to the recent bike boom, bike trips in cities and towns across the country are sure to be high. We are grateful for our stunning forest backdrop and all of the ways it helps the Center. The forests around Chabot reduce air pollution, filter rainwater and provide the perfect scenery for The Coastal Redwood, also known as the Pacific Redwood, is the California state tree. Towering at heights of up to 376 feet, widths of up to 30 feet and depths of up to 12 feet, coastal redwoods “The crown of a tall redwood has a towering, cloudy, irregular form. The crowns of the tallest redwoods can sometimes look like the plume of exhaust from a rocket taking off, ” said Richard Preston. If you have ever noticed that it looks like the trees are raining on a foggy day, they are. In the warm summer months the redwoods use fog to generate up to 500 gallons a day of muchneeded precipitation through transpiration. You may have also noticed that some redwoods grow in clusters around large round open spaces. Within these circles, sometimes called fairy rings, are the graveyards of the parent and grandparent trees, some of which stood for up to 2,000 years. What makes these majestic beauties so resilient? How have they been able to withstand the test of time? The durable fire-resistant wood is a desirable building material. Reclaimed redwood is permissible and highly sought-after. They benefit from the low vegetation clearing and the aid in seeding fire provides. An extremely thick spongy bark and thick massive trunk allows the coastal redwood to hold an extreme amount of water. Redwoods also contain anti-fungal and decay properties that contribute to their longevity. One of the oldest species of trees on the planet, the Coastal Redwoods goes back to the late Jurassic period, some 200 million years ago. The Coastal RedCoastal Redwoods woods in the Oakland hills stem from intricate root systems of older trees. They are still relatively young at 50-75 years, mere toddlers compared to their life expectancy, yet they reveal evidence of an ancient generation. The onset of the California Gold Rush and the subsequent population boom starting in 1849 led to the demise of the old growth trees due to extensive logging. You won’t see 2,000-year-old redwoods in the Oakland hills anymore, except for one, called the Old Survivor, preserved as a historical landmark. Coastal Redwoods provide significant benefit to the planet. They are climate champions. As the largest trees on earth, they convert more carbon dioxide into oxygen than any other tree. In addition to air quality, the redwoods are not alone in the forest. They are usually in the company of plants and trees and shrubs such several species of ferns, maples and bay. Together they sustain a delicate symbiotic ecosystem of plants, animals, streams and trees. Lisa Hoover is with Chabot Space and Science Center, located at 10000 Skyline Blvd., in Oakland. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department has revamped its summer camp and classes, to include bringing back its popular Counselor-In-Training (CIT) program for tweens and teens. Registration for summer programming is now open at: Register.communitypass.net/reg/cat_program_ list.cfm?season_id=24069 More than 70 camps, classes, and leagues are planned, including dozens of new activities to make this an unforgettable summer for kids. Online registration has been open since May 7. Sign up as soon as possible to get your first pick of sports camps, art and dance classes, martial arts, music and more. Most camps run from June 14 to August 6. The Summer Schoolmates program will be at Havens School for Afternoon Summer Fun. Schoolmates runs from June 21 to July 14, Monday through Friday from 1:00–5:00 p.m. Kids entering grades K-5 are invited. The fee is $836. Jobs available for teens Job opportunities are back this year for CITs and Jr. CITs. CITs will spend their mornings working with Rec. Dept. staff in summer camps and preschool programs. During afternoons CITs will hone their skills in supervision, first aid, resume writing, and interview preparation. The program runs Monday through Friday from 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. from June 21 to July 2 and is for girls and boys in grades 6–9. There’s fun for adults as well. Register for the adult softball and pickleball leagues. The adult softball league is $65 and goes from June 14 to August 6. Games are played at Coaches Field on Monday, Wednesday, or Friday evenings. For more information, call the Recreation Department at 420- 3081. Green - Normal Risk - Continue to monitor through other indicators (such as grades and attendance) and staff interactions - No parent contact necessary During public comment at the April 28 school board meeting, Piedmont parent Amy Vallerie, M.D., called in to discuss the survey. “I was well aware when the first student survey went out in the fall, but I don’t recall receiving information about the second survey being distributed. I don’t recall getting the results on either survey. I guess I have to assume they are fine, but I would still like my child’s results,” Vallerie said. PHS school psychologist Alisa Crovetti worked on details of the survey design and analysis of the results. She explained that results were not automatically given out to parents of students in the “normal risk” range. “There were parents that reached out asking about their child’s results. My recommendation for Piedmont High School, was to take a case-to-case approach. If it seems appropriate, we offer to sit down with parents, and go over the results. I rarely release the raw data to parents, even for parents paying for my services privately. It is my job to interpret, draw conclusions and make recommendations,” Crovetti said. The School District now plans to gauge students’ mental health through re-administering surveys several times a year. PUSD aims to use survey data to guide development and implement interventions with students and parents. To watch the survey results presentation visit: Piedmont. g ranicus.com / MediaPlayer. php?view_id=3&clip_id=2340 and skip ahead 2 hours and 10 minutes.

articles.text: The pandemic did not stop the Highlander Robotics team from building world-class robots. Their efforts paid off at the Northern California FIRST Robotics Competition (FRC) awards show on Saturday, May 15. The team won the Rookie Game Changer Award for their robot Whirlpool. The Highlanders competed against teams from Australia, India, Norway, Canada, plus teams from all over the U.S. This was a highly unusual and challenging robotics season due to Covid. Instead of competing in person at UC Davis or San Jose State, the team submitted photos and videos of Whirlpool performing various skills challenges. They also interviewed with judges around the world. The team was fortunate to still have access to the Lambert workshop on Dracena Avenue. Piedmont School District offered critical support, letting the team test their software code, practice driving Whirlpool, and film the virtual skills challenges in the Morrison Gym. The Highlanders were very ambitious this season and built an advanced robot. Team member Charlie Lambert advocated for the team to switch to a swerve drivetrain which allows the robot to spin while traveling along any path. It also makes it very easy for the driver to maneuver while still having good traction for defense. Veteran teams warned the Highlanders that the software was extremely complicated and not suitable for a rookie team. Undaunted, software team members Sebastien Combes and Jasper Zietlow got the job done with guidance of mentor Kevin Clark. Whirlpool features a shooter, which launches dodgeballs into an 8-foot tall target, and an innovative climbing mechHighland Robotics Team Photo. Whirlpool, the 2021 Robot. Assembling Whirlpool. Climber team (Alyssa Angsupanich, Basia Young and Alex Ware) with Piedmont resident mentor Klaus Zietlow working on a prototype of the climbing mechanism. Shooter team (Peter Stokes, Will Shields and Reece Beck) gets training on fabricating aluminum on the CNC Router with mentor, John Lambert. Whirlpool’s climbing mechanism in action. anism. Senior Will Shields led the shooter hardware team while Avery Chan and Robbie Sylvia wrote the software that allows it to shoot rapidly and accurately. Alyssa Angsupanich led the team that built Whirlpool’s climbing mechanism. The 100 plus pound robot sports a carbon fiber hook on an extendible cable track and uses a winch to pull itself off the ground. Piedmont resident software mentor, Kevin Clark, juggles questions from software team members virtually and in person. Jasper Zietlow, Sebastien Combes and Henry Lambert working on the code for swerve drive. John Lambert, the team’s fabrication mentor said, “The team made huge strides in the design process this season. Each subteam designed their mechanism in Solidworks (industry leading computer aided design software) and fit them together before any final parts were fabricated. The lab’s new laser cutter was also a huge benefit for prototyping mechanisms.” The Highlanders aim to become a world class team at Piedmont High School. Students and parents interested in getting involved by mentoring, sponsoring, or joining the team, are asked to contact frc8033@piedmontmakers.org. The team is sponsored by NASA, Zenni, Google, Apple, East Bay Community Energy and the Silicon Valley Community Foundation.

articles.text: Morgan Fjord, the Piedmont District Executive (Program Coordinator) has accepted a promotion with the Golden Gate Area Scout Council as District Director, effective May 16. articles.text: California’s health officers announced on Monday, May 17 that the state’s mask mandate will remain in place until June 15 after the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention put out guidance last week saying people vaccinated against COVID-19 do not have to wear masks inside in most situations. The CDC on Thursday, May 13 said that fully vaccinated Americans can go maskless and without social distancing indoors and outdoors in most cases. The CDC said that masks are only required for the vaccinated in certain instances, like on airplanes or buses. Masking guidelines are ultimately up to local and state governments, the CDC said. After discussing the issue for several days, California made the decision to continue its mask mandate until June 15. “This four-week period will give Californians time to prepare for this change while we continue the relentless focus on delivering vaccines, particularly to underserved communities and those that were hard hit throughout this pandemic,” Health and Human Services Secretary Mark Ghaly said on call with reporters. The CDC’s mask announcement came as a surprise to many across the nation, although several states began adopting the new guidelines within days of the announcement. Many national retailers have announced they will follow the CDC’s plan, although California’s guidelines would supersede any business’ policy. Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office said that the June 15 deadline would allows Californians to prepare for the mask rule change as well as increase the number of vaccinated residents. The state’s mask mandate last changed on May 3, when California adopted CDC guidance that that said fully vaccinated people do not need to wear masks outdoors unless they are in a crowd of strangers. People are considered fully vaccinated if it has been two weeks since either their second dose of Pfizer or Moderna vaccine or their one dose of Johnson & Johnson vaccine. As of Monday, May 18, the rolling seven-day COVID-19 positivity rate in Alameda County is now 1 percent, the lowest point since the pandemic began in March of 2020. Alameda County has yet to meet state benchmarks to move into a less-restrictive tier for reopening its economy, but metrics continue to movie in the right direction. Since March 30, Alameda County has been in the orange tier, or moderate tier, the second-least restrictive tier in California’s color-coded four-tier system. Yesterday, Tuesday, May 18, Santa Clara and Santa Cruz counties joined San Francisco and San Mateo counties in the least-restrictive yellow tier. All other Bay Area counties are in the orange tier, besides Solano County, which has remained in the red tier, or substantial tier, for weeks. Most indoor activities can resume, with modification, in the yellow tier. To move into the yellow tier, the positivity rate in Alameda County needs to stay below 2 percent. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to stay below 2.2 percent – it is currently 1.6 percent in Alameda County. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to be below 1 – right now there are 2.9 cases per 100,000. The entire color tier system will end the same day as the mask mandate for vaccinated Californians. Newsom announced plans several weeks ago to lift most COVID-19 restrictions statewide on June 15. It is expected that the reopening plan will continue if hospitalizations remain low and vaccination supply is not majorly disrupted. One new case of COVID-19 was reported in Piedmont across the past seven days. The total number of Piedmont cases since the pandemic began is 182. Across Alameda County, the total caseload is 88,157. There have been 27,459 cases recorded in Oakland and 13,670 cases in Hayward. Tragically, the total number of COVID-19 fatalities countywide is now 1,668. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,666,591 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 61,513 deaths due to the disease statewide. The state positivity rate is 0.9 percent, a record low for the pandemic.
articles.title: CDC: vaccinated people do not need to wear masks in most places

articles.text: Alameda County’s entry into the least restrictive Yellow Tier in the state’s blueprint for re-opening would mean loosened restrictions for music and performance venue operations and live entertainment. While Alameda County has yet to meet benchmarks to move into the Yellow Tier, metrics are currently moving in the right direction to do so. The county has been in the Orange Tier since March 30. To move into the least restrictive, or minimal “yellow tier,” positivity rates in the county need to stay below 2%. Yellow Tier restrictions would vary greatly depending on whether the event is held at an outdoor or indoor venue. Live events are permissible now in the Orange Tier, both in outdoor and indoor venues with restrictions. Indoor venues with a 1,500 capacity can open with a maximum of 25% or 300 people, or 50% if all guests provide proof of full vaccination or show a negative test result within 72 hours prior to attendance. For venues larger than 1,500 seats, there is a 2,000-person capacity, and no eating or drinking is allowed. The capacity goes up to 50% if all guests show proof of full vaccination or a negative test result within 72 hours prior to the event. An indoor venue’s capacity can go up with proof of negative test or vaccination card, but there is no current guideline that says an outdoor venue can increase capacity with proof of vaccination. However, for outdoor venues, according to the California Department of Public Health, only in-state spectators may be allowed; at the time a guest purchases tickets, the operator must obtain an attestation that the guest’s block of seat reservations contains no more than three households and that the guest, and all members of the guest’s party are “in-state visitors.” In April, the East Bay Venue Coalition, Oakland’s Cultural Affairs Commission, and the Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) hosted a virtual town hall meeting to discuss health and safety guidelines for in-person events. While county public health officials can allow for loosened restrictions regardless of state-wide status, the County Public Health Department has confirmed that it will be following the state’s “Blueprint for a Safer Economy,” which provides specific guidelines for industries, including the live entertainment industry. Note that, current rules are temporary and will not apply after June 15 if vaccine supply is sufficient and hospitalization rates remain low. Gov. Gavin Newsom said that California will move away from its color-coded tier system, and Blueprint for a Safer Economy, by that date. There are currently no county-wide rules for what venues and event organizers will be required to do after June 15.

articles.text: Photos by Todd Marshburn Piedmont moved to 3-1-2 after beating San Leandro and Castro Valley last week. Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team won twice more last week, beating San Leandro 3-1 on Tuesday, May 11 on the road, and 2-1 against Castro Valley at Witter Field on Thursday, May 13. On Saturday, the magic vanished in al 6-0 loss to Berkeley. “We’ve been running our 4-4-2 formation where we pack the midfield with width coming from the fullbacks. We want to try and possess the ball and control the game,” said coach Dan Chubbock. Due to some players taking the SAT test on Saturday, Piedmont had to call up several JV players for the game with Berkeley. PHS kept it close for the first half, trailing 1-0, but the more experienced Yellowjacket lineup pounced for five second-half goals. “We had to bring up several JV girls, who played earlier in the day, and move players to positions they never played. Audrey Harmon was fantastic but had to leave early for ACT testing, she looked like a varsity player,” said Chubbock. chance to tie, but their shot sailed over the net. “A lot of the girls know each other [from club soccer]. I used to coach in Castro Valley. It’s nice to see them come through; and obviously it’s nicer to beat them,” said Chubbock with a laugh. The win required some clutch work by sophomore goalkeeper Morgan Hunt, who made a critical save in the second half when she deflected a shot over the crossbar. 3-1 victory over Pirates The Highlanders beat the San Leandro Pirates 3-1 on the road Tuesday, May 11. Emily Fitzgerald scored an early goal to put Piedmont up 1-0, but the Pirates tied it 1-1 by halftime off a corner kick. Tucker Donahue put Piedmont ahead in the second half and Sophie Hebert added the insurance goal, 3-1. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team won two of its last three matches, beating Alhambra on Monday, May 17 in Martinez, 18-12, and obliterating Castro Valley 17-4 on Tuesday, May 18. They lost to league rivals Berkeley 15-11 on Thursday, May 13. It was a strong three games for senior captain Max Wagener, who netted five goals against Alhambra and Berkeley while putting in three against the Trojans. The Highlanders now have a 6-1 record with one match left before the league tournament. 11-4 win vs. Castro Valley The Highlanders jumped ahead 4-0 by the end of the first quarter and led 8-1 at halftime. They added three goals in the third quarter and six more in the final period. Piedmont got the show started early with five straight goals from senior hole set Spencer Stein. Max Wagener added two goals to make it 7-0 before the Trojans’ first score with 58 seconds left in the first half. Peter Krumins made the game 8-1 at halftime. Piedmont added goals from Davis, Wagener, and Sam Corcoran in the third quarter, 11-3. With Stein and Wagener resting the fourth quarter, PHS gained scores from Dunlap, two from Jake Hart, Antonio Rivera, Krumins, and George Stein. Final stats: Stein with five goals and one steal. Wagener had three goals, two assists, and four Staff Photos Max Wagener scored five goals against Alhambra and Berkeley, while adding three against Castro Valley. steals. Corcoran had a goal and three assists. Hart had a goal, two assists, and three steals. Rivera had a goal, two assists, and a steal. Goalie Dariush Kashani had 10 saves. Alhambra win In a closer contest on Monday, May 17, the match was tied 3-3 at the end of the first quarter and 6-6 at halftime. But Piedmont burst open the lead with a huge third quarter for a 14-8 lead, then tacked on four goals in the last quarter for the 18-12 final. Stein got the day started with a goal a minute, 45 seconds into the game, but the Martinez school quickly tied it. Shane Miller and Goalie Dariush Kashani had 10 saves against Castro Valley, and four each in games with Alhambra and Berkeley. Antonio Rivera scored in all three games last week. Wagener scored to make it 3-3 at the end of the first. In the second, Alhambra scored first after three minutes of back-and-forth action, but Wagener had the tying 4-4 goal with 4:46 left before half. After trailing 6-4, Piedmont tied it at 6-6 with scores from Dunlap and Hart. Alhambra went ahead 7-6 in the third quarter, but four unanswered goals by Miller and Wagener, two each, put the Highlanders in the lead to stay at 10-7. Rivera made it 11-8 with 2:38 left in the third quarter, followed by quick scores from Wagener, Miller, and Davis to make it 14-8 with 14 seconds left in the third. PHS received goals from Dunlap, Hart, Corcoran, and Declan Linnane in the fourth quarter. Final stats: Wagener with five goals, Miller with four goals, Hart and Dunlap had two goals, while Rivera, Corcoran, Linnane, Hart and Davis had one. Kashani had four saves and one steal. Loss to Berkeley The Highlanders trailed 6-2 by the end of the first quarter but narrowed the gap to 8-6 by halftime. Berkeley extended its lead to 12-7 by the start of the fourth and kept the advantage for the 15-11 win. Final stats: Wagener’s five goals, Miller had two, while individual scores include Stein, Hart, and Rivera. Kashani had four saves and one steal. NEXT UP Piedmont (6-1) plays at San Leandro tomorrow, Thursday, May 20 at 3:30 p.m. The WACC League Tournament is scheduled for Tuesday, May 25 at Encinal, with a second round on Thursday, May 27, and Finals on May 29.
articles.title: Highlanders swamp Alhambra, Castro Valley

articles.text: PHS water polo players are encouraged by their coach. The PHS girls’ water polo team had a thrilling group of matches last week, beating Berkeley 10-5 on Thursday, May 13, followed by a close 6-3 loss against Alhambra in Martinez on Monday, May 17, and a razorthin 7-6 loss last night to Castro Valley. “It was an exciting win against Berkeley. We pulled ourselves together late in the games against Alhambra and Castro Valley after allowing some early goals,” said coach Sarah Mooney. The Berkeley win featured Piedmont’s hole set Ella Wright scoring five goals. She also scored three against Castro Valley. Big win vs. Berkeley, 9-3 Piedmont led 3-2 by the end of the first quarter, jumped ahead 5-2 by halftime and put the game out of reach at 9-3 by the end of the third period. Wright opened the scoring with two goals in the first six minutes. Macie Gard made it 3-0 with 4:40 left in the first, but Berkeley scored twice to close the gap to 3-2 after the first period. Annika Nilsson scored two minutes into the 2nd quarter and Odessa Dando boosted Piedmont’s lead to 5-2 with 3:14 before halftime. The Highlanders added three more goals in the third quarter, from Gard with 5:53 left, Wright after a quick steal 30 seconds later, and another goal with 3:50 remaining in the third. After a Yellowjackets’ goal, Wright rocketed in her fifth and final goal, 9-3. Nillson scored Piedmont’s last goal with 6:37 left in the game, making it 10-3 before the Jackets’ tacked on two late goals for the 10-5 final. Final stats: Wright’s five goals, five ejections drawn, and one steal. Nillson had two goals, one assist and three steals. Gard also scored twice with one assist and a steal. 6-3 loss to Alhambra The Highlanders trailed 3-0 after the first three minutes but fought back to a 4-3 deficit by the start of the fourth quarter. However, the Highlanders were not able to find the goal another time in the later going. Frankie Broening, Dando and Nilsson were the goal scorers, official times were not recorded. One-goal loss to Castro Valley The Highlanders battled to a 7-6 loss against Castro Valley last night, May 18, after battling back from a 5-1 deficit at halftime. In fact, Piedmont took a 6-5 lead heading into the fourth quarter, but couldn’t sustain the advantage. Wright’s goal in the first quarter made it a 3-1 game. The Trojans tacked on two more goals in the second quarter before the Highlanders rallied for a 6-5 left with 22 seconds left in the third period. Bike team is recruiting more girls and plans to host clinics this summer. Piedmont’s Mountain Bike Team competed in league championship for NICA’s NorCal section at Six Rigma Ranch in Clearlake on Sunday, May 16. The Highlanders’ lone varsity rider, PHS senior Will Shields, finished fourth of nine athletes with a time of 43:01.11. “Riding outside three times per week has been a very positive and healthy outlet for our riders throughout the pandemic. We increased our numbers to 27 registered riders from Piedmont High, gained three girls to form a team, and another 25 riders from Piedmont Middle School,” said coach Sally Aldridge. The varsity limited size in 2021 was due to the lack of necessary qualifying by athletes after COVID-19 canceled their 2020 season. The Junior Varsity, sophomore, and freshman boys have crowded fields and thrilling racing. Will Shields placed fourth in the League Finals at Six Sigma Ranch in 43:01. In the JV event, Artun Duransoy finished eighth of 40 riders in 45:11, while Kurt Wilson clocked a 47:56 to place 12th and Nathan Willson timed a 49:17 in 15th. Andres Roberts placed third of 23 in the Sophomore Boys’ event with a time of 46:15. Behind him was Aleksi Valkonen in 13th in 52:57, Ethan Villareal times in at 54:53. “Andres’ goal was [to make] top-five and he trained very hard in between races to get there,” said Aldridge. Freshmen rider Schuyler Sawicki finished sixth with a time of 49:57, Matteo Scanu was seventh in 52:50, and Max Rivera was 11th in 57:45. Piedmont had two girls in the Sophomore event, Julia Caputo who timed in at 1:13:46, and Heather Stoneman in 1:29:05. The Mt. Bike Cub’s sponsors include Cycle Sports, JISEKI, MB Jessee, Bigge, ,Zesty.ai, and Tempo Endurance Coaching. The team plans to schedule some fun rides in October and will host girls’ clinics during the summer. For more information, contact piedmontbiking@gmail.com.

articles.title: HIKING WITH JON

articles.text: The Tule Elk State Natural Reserve can be found north of Tomales Bay State Park and the small town of Inverness by Pt. Reyes National Seashore. A High Surf Advisory along the California coast made for terrific wave-watching, and the near-five mile hike to Tomales Point put walkers next to herds of Tule Elk completely undisturbed by passersby. Taking the 9.7 mile out-andback Tomales Point Trail heads to the northern most point on the Inverness side of Tomales Bay – overlooking remote stretches of beaches on the Pacific to the south and Dillon Beach to the north. The hike starts at Pierce Point Two bulls rest, posing perfectly for the shot. A young spike grazes near the trail, undisturbed by hikers. The view toward Tomales Point during January’s High Surf Advisory. Ranch, a historic farmstead of the Pt. Reyes Peninsula that has informative markers to describe the early dairy farming culture of the area. The walk to Tomales Point is in conjunction with the Tule Elk Reserve, where herds of male bulls, female cows, young male spikes, and baby calves. The trail ends at a bluff overlooking tidepools and an array of pelicans, cormorants, gulls, while redtailed hawks and turkey vultures. The main attraction, the Tule Elk, are native to Central California and regarded as the smallest subspecies of elk. They were a big part of Pt. Reyes becoming a National Seashore in 1976. At that time, the species faced local extinction due to hunting in the 1850s. In the fall of 1978, the National Park Service released 17 elk into the area after converting decommissioned farmland into a reserve. Now the park has over 400 elk. The area is located along the wind-swept region of Bodega Bay on the ridgeline of the Pt. Reyes National Seashore. Without any tree coverage, visitors should wear proper attire given they can experience high-winds, fog, and rain at any random moment. Although officially considered a 9.7 mile, mostly flat round-trip, our odometer came out at 10.45 miles and an elevation gain of 1,336 feet. To locate this hike, punch in “Tomales Point Trailhead” or “Pierce Point Ranch” to your GPS device. Originally published in the Post on January 13, 2021.
articles.title: Tule Elk, Tomales Point, & Pt. Reyes Seashore

articles.text: “America, America, 2009” by Papo Colo; inkjet print with string; 30 ½ x 44 ½ in.; gift of Exit Art. The University of California, Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) is offering a look at the effects of colonialism on Latin American and Caribbean arts in a new exhibition entitled “Present Tense: Five Centuries of Colonialism.” “Present Tense” examines both historical and contemporary works that reveal how colonization has shaped life in the Latin Americas and Caribbean islands. The artists in this exhibition have experienced lingering injustices in the wake of colonialism. The exhibition was organized by History of Art Professor Todd Olson and Associate Professor of Spanish and Portuguese Ivonne del Valle. It is the fifth in a series of annual exhibitions called “Cal Conversations”. developed in collaboration with UC Berkeley classes. The exhibition opened on April 30, and will be open through June 20. To obtain timed tickets, visit https://bampfa.org/program/ virtual/present-tense-five-centuries-colonialism-latin-american-and-caribbean-art.
articles.title: BAMPFA: A look at the effects of colonialism in arts

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse is returning to live productions this summer beginning with the premiere of Hold These Truths, which will be performed from June 8 to July 3. Directed by Jeanne Sakata and Jeffrey Lo, Hold These Truths is based on the true story of Gordon Hirabayashi, whose defiance of President Roosevelt’s Executive Order authorizing the incarceration of thousands of Japanese Americans led him to a 50-year journey of advocacy. The play was inspired by many hours of interviews conducted by Sakata with Hirabayashi, as well as primary sources from his life. The New York Times called the play a “gripping story about a shameful chapter of our country’s history,” in its re-telling of the American internment order of 1942. This is the first live production of San Francisco Playhouse since COVID-19 restrictions in March 2020. All COVID guidelines and protocols will be enforced. Book tickets by visiting https://www.sfplayhouse.org/ sfph/upcoming-plays/. Choose seats you’d like and the system will automatically place at least two empty sides on both sides of each group after purchase. Masks must be worn at all times, regardless of vaccination status.
articles.title: SF Playhouse play, Hold These Truths, begins live on June 8

articles.text: Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery, located in Walnut Creek, is offering an in-person “garden iPhoneoragphy” workshop on Saturday morning, May 29. Led by photographers John Ricca and Richard Valenti, workshop students will learn how to elevate their smartphone skills, iPhone or Android, by exploring the photographic possibilities in the colorful spring setting of the gardens. You will learn about shooting techniques and strategies, while taking advantage of the early morning light. This is a two-part workshop: part one, on May 29, is an in-person workshop at the garden and includes a short, introductory lecture. Students will have the opportunity to have one-on-one time with instructors during this time. Part two will take place on June 5 at 10 a.m., and will be a Zoom session with the two instructors. Each student will have their photo critiqued, and will be able to submit up to three photos. Visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/event/garden-iphoneography-workshop/ to reserve your spot. Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery in Walnut Creek.
articles.title: Bancroft Garden offers “Garden iPhoneography” workshop May 29

articles.text: Berkeley Reparatory Theatre released a theatrical experiment in six movements inspired by a stage adaption of Virginia Woolf’s The Waves. The Waves in Quarantine, written and directed by Lisa Peterson, invites audiences into the creative process. (510) 652-1662 Office (510) 652-1690 Fax info@woodwindowswarehouse.com woodwindowswarehouse.com 1301 66th Street Emeryville, CA 94608 Wood Windows Warehouse Residential & Commercial Custom & Standard CA Contractors License No. 823258 Lisa Peterson, playwright and director of Waves in Quarantine at Berkeley Rep. Woolf’s novel, from which the play is adapted, is considered her most experimental work. The book consists of soliloquies spoken by six characters; similarly, the play is told in six movements that meditate on themes from the musical adaption of the novel. The play builds on Woolf’s prose to reveal an intimate look at the combination of art and isolation. The play circles through themes of music in unexpected places, and the intimacy of strangers. The episodic movements include “Memory,” “Those We Love,” “The Female Gaze,” “Absence,” “The Sun Cycle,” and “Reunion.” Music and lyrics are by David Bucknam, and additional music and lyrics are provided by Adam Gwon. The play will be available to stream free through May 28. Visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/season/2021/15964.asp to stream.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep’s Waves in Quarantine streaming through May 28

articles.text: A scene from San Francisco Ballet’s production of Helgi Tomasson’s Romeo & Juliet. San Francisco Ballet will stream Helgi Tomasson’s “Romeo & Juliet” through Wednesday, May 26. The multi-capture, cinematic production was performed on-stage at San Francisco’s War Memorial Opera House. The production was the last work that SF Ballet toured prior to 2020 COVID-19 closures. It was performed last in the fall of 2019 at the Royal Danish Opera House in Copenhagen, where it was noted for its “color rich” set design and interpretation of the classic Shakespeare story. The production premiered during SF Ballet’s 1994 Repertory Season and is considered a signature work of the San Francisco Ballet company and has been performed worldwide. Tomasson’s Romeo and Juliet is performed under the direction of SF Ballet music director Martin West, and includes former principal dancers Maria Kochetkova and Davit Karapetyan in the title roles. Pascal Molat, now on faculty at SF Ballet School, is cast as Mercutio. The opulent set is designed by Jens-Jacob Worsaae, with lighting design by Thomas Skelton. This was Worsaae’s final collaboration with Tomasson before he died shortly after the ballet’s premiere. “I think it was the most beautiful work he’d ever done, and yet he did not see it. That’s one reason why this production is very, very special to me,” Tomasson said. To purchase tickets to the streaming production, visit https://www.sfballet.org/productions/digital-program-06/. Swan Lake closes digital season June 9 San Francisco Ballet’s production of Swan Lake is now streaming and will continue through June 9. Tomasson’s Swan Lake will close out the company’s 2021 digital season. The archival performance from 2016 stars Yuan Yuan Tan as Odette-Odile and Tiit Helimets as Prince Siegfried. It features the corps of 30 swans and Odette, whose story is introduced in the prologue. The director showcases male dancers in the first act in his 2009 production. Set and costume designs for the production are by Tony Award-winner Jonathan Fensom. The streaming production is available to watch on-demand until June 9. Visit https://www.sfballet.org/ productions/digital-program-06/ for streaming access. By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Ballet will stream Helgi Tomasson’s “Romeo & Juliet” through Wednesday, May 26. The multi-capture, cinematic production was performed on-stage at San Francisco’s War Memorial Opera House. The production was the last work that SF Ballet toured prior to 2020 COVID-19 closures. It was performed last in the fall of 2019 at the Royal Danish Opera House in Copenhagen, where it was noted for its “color rich” set design and interpretation of the classic Shakespeare story. The production premiered during SF Ballet’s 1994 Repertory Season and is considered a signature work of the San Francisco Ballet company and has been performed worldwide. Tomasson’s Romeo and Juliet is performed under the direction of SF Ballet music director Martin West, and includes former principal dancers Maria Kochetkova and Davit Karapetyan in the title roles. Pascal Molat, now on faculty at SF Ballet School, is cast as Mercutio. The opulent set is designed by Jens-Jacob Worsaae, with lighting design by Thomas Skelton. This was Worsaae’s final collaboration with Tomasson before he died shortly after the ballet’s premiere. “I think it was the most beautiful work he’d ever done, and yet he did not see it. That’s one reason why this production is very, very special to me,” Tomasson said. To purchase tickets to the streaming production, visit https://www.sfballet.org/productions/digital-program-06/. Swan Lake closes digital season June 9 San Francisco Ballet’s production of Swan Lake is now streaming and will continue through June 9. Tomasson’s Swan Lake will close out the company’s 2021 digital season. The archival performance from 2016 stars Yuan Yuan Tan as Odette-Odile and Tiit Helimets as Prince Siegfried. It features the corps of 30 swans and Odette, whose story is introduced in the prologue. The director showcases male dancers in the first act in his 2009 production. Set and costume designs for the production are by Tony Award-winner Jonathan Fensom. The streaming production is available to watch on-demand until June 9. Visit https://www.sfballet.org/ productions/digital-program-06/ for streaming access. articles.text: George Clooney stars in Up in the Air. For so many reasons Up in the Air is a marvelous movie: stylish, intelligent, poignant and consistently comedic. And yet, beneath its patina of casual elegance and charm is a perpetual tragedy that mirrors the reality of millions of Americans today. The fact that this underlying reality, which is haunting, doesn’t overpower the film is testimony to the brilliance of writer-director Jason Reitman, and a superb acting ensemble led by George Clooney. Clooney portrays Ryan Bingham, a debonair corporate assassin who travels nonstop, from city to city, firing people. It’s a job that the companies themselves are loathe to do. And so he sits across a table and explains to long-time employees that they are being “let go,” as he prefers to say, instead of “fired.” Bingham embraces his life in the air. He has elegantly turned his entrance to and exit from airports into an art form. He packs with studied efficiency, breezes through lines, swipes his cards, flashes his ID and is soon ensconced on the next flight and on his way to the next series of firings. He brags that he spends 322 days on the road and is miserable the other 43 days. He has no home to speak of – his apartment looks like an impersonal hotel room – and no connections to anyone, though he has a sister. He turns the idea of the lonely crowd on its head and his solitary life into an enthusiastic preference absent even a hint of angst. What is so superb about the film is that Bingham is an executioner and the audience is completely beguiled by his smile and intelligence and wit. He never pauses to unpack his emotions or reflect on the impact of his task and for a good part of the film neither does the audience. But then two women enter his life, one a businesswoman, Alex (Vera Farmiga), and Natalie (Melanie Lyskey), a new hire at his company. He meets Alex in a hotel lounge. Natalie is sent on the road with him to learn the ropes, so to speak. Both challenge his view of life, his contented detachment, and his elaborate rationales for his choices. Incrementally, the audience begins to sense that Bingham’s carefully manicured existence may not be as tightly compacted as first assumed. Though the film focuses all but exclusively on Bingham, so likable, so nicely constructed, and perhaps so starkly alone, the real tragedy resides with those he fires. Reitman includes snapshots of non-actors who have been recently let go, asking them to look into the camera and share what it means to lose their jobs after a decade or more. We watch as their faces crumble and they run the gauntlet of emotions. They are the subtext of this film. Up in the Air was one of the best films of 2009, wonderfully written and acted, a quilt of themes, surprising and enjoyable in every way. Up in the Air. Directed by Jason Reitman. Starring George Clooney, Vera Farmiga and Melanie Lynskey. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated R. Vera Farmiga, George Clooney and Melanie Lynskey star in Up in the Air.
articles.title: Up in the Air one of Clooney’s best films

articles.text: Captain Fantastic, written and directed by Matt Ross, finds a complex and revelatory sweet spot and expands on it. In so many ways this film is sublimely poetic while remaining firmly grounded as it probes the many facets of what it means to be a parent. It is also an engaging and captivating character study. At the film’s center is Ben, portrayed by Viggo Mortensen, a gifted, nuanced actor who inhabits Ben completely as he grapples with all of the subtle and overt challenges of being a single parent to six very independent children. But their collective lives are not lived in a suburban two-story home somewhere on the west coast; rather, home is a camp or sorts, nestled in the verdant forest of the Pacific Northwest. They live in a place apart, off the grid, and their existence, that of the children, mirrors the values of their father. He strives to instill in them a fearlessness toward life, to think for themselves, to let their minds engage in the seminal questions of purpose and existence, questions that dominate their days and, with the urging of Ben, fill their evenings as they search for answers in books and more books, from literature to philosophy to biology and history; his oldest son, Bodevan (George McKay), has recently decided he is a Maoist, a declaration that prompts a smile from Ben. As well, they are schooled to be survivalists, to engage in extreme rock climbing, hunting, hand-to-hand combat, and they find together a harmony and web of support and concern that so often eludes families surrounded by the trappings and distractions of a consumer-driven pop culture saturated with electronics. What disrupts this harmony is the death of their mother in a hospital in New Mexico where she was taken for treatment. The children, at first devastated, argue strongly, against the wishes of Ben, that they not attend their mother’s funeral. Ben fears the journey could have unintended consequences; however, he finally relents. And suddenly these children of the forest, with all of their attendant skills, are confronted with a culture steeped in all that Ben has attempted to shield them from: television, Gameboy, Walmart and a funeral, organized by their grandparents (Frank Langella and Ann Dowd), a religious ceremony that they know is against the wishes of their mother. This immersion is both humorous and revealing and for most of the children jaw-dropping. These are not feral children, but neither for all of their resilience are they children of this century. Painfully, gradually, Ben is faced with a truth that he has tried to avoid: while his children are supremely prepared for a good part of life, they are also woefully lacking in so many other aspects of what it means to live in a complete world. His didacticism – embedded with his values and convictions and love – has been his gift to them. But the revelation that haunts him is that their lives have been unexpectedly truncated, their prism while wide and encompassing and rich has also been too narrow. Perhaps Ben has loved his children too much. Captain Fantastic is a beautifully crafted film, a story that is life-affirming and lovely, thanks in great part to exceptional writing by Ross and a fine ensemble of actors, all wonderful. Surprisingly, this story comes along at a time when so much of our lives can feel disjointed, and our values seemingly inadequate to the issues that confront us. In essence, our contemporary grid can sometimes seem frayed, at times empty and unfulfilling. And so, Thoreau’s simplicity beckons, the quiet voice that urges us to wander off the grid; it can feel so seductive, the vision/ fantasy seemingly idyllic. But there are larger truths involved than simply leaving the grid. And it is those truths that gradually begin to confront Ben and challenge his vision of the ideal. And it is those truths and their inherent cost that make up the thematic structure of this wonderful film. Captain Fantastic. Starring Viggo Mortensen, Frank Langella and Kathryn Hahn. Directed by Matt Ross. 2 hrs. Rated R.
articles.title: Captain Fantastic a wonderful story of a father and children living off the grid

articles.text: A scene from Pixar’s Brave.. One of Disney’s favorite tropes has been the adorable princess and the wicked stepmother. Recall Snow White and the spiked apple; Cinderella, forced to scrub and clean; or Rapunzel, locked away in a high tower. The movie Brave, directed by Piedmont resident Mark Andrew, does feature a strong-willed teenage princess, Merida (Kelly MacDonald), who rebels not against an unkind stepmother, but against her imperious mother, queen Elinor (Emma Thompson). The period is medieval Scotland, filled with crags and castles and rolling highlands. And there is, of course, Merida, with her massive ginger-colored tresses, a young royal who happens to identify with her father, onelegged, big lug King Fergus (Bill Connoly). She can ride like the wind, and is an expert archer (not unlike Katniss Everdeen of The Hunger Games), and would rather be racing horseback through the surrounding forests than spending time with the staid ladies of the court. Elinor, of course, has her own ideas of how a young princess should behave. But Merida, as wild as her red mane, snorts when she laughs, scoops up food from the pantry, and is a tomboyish, headstrong teenager who has her own ideas regarding gender equality. Queen Elinor is not to be deterred in her efforts to civilize Merida in the image of a domesticated princess, marriage being at the fore. She therefore invites three suitors to the yearly Highland Games, deciding that the best of the three will win her daughter’s hand. Merida, of course, has other plans, finding the three definitely unsuitable as prospective husbands, and defiantly declares to her mother that she’ll not marry, period, followed by an age-appropriate tantrum to make her point. To further drive home her wishes to be her own person, she dominates the archery contest with extraordinary skill and accuracy. But when her mother insists that she will accept the best suitor, Merida runs away into the forest. To her surprise she comes upon a cottage inhabited by an old witch, a crone with magical powers who tells the princess that she can, indeed, cast a spell on Elinor. Merida rashly, rebelliously, agrees. She realizes, too late, however, that her decision has some unintended consequences. In other words, be careful what you wish for when you say, “I want my freedom!” Brave, has more than a few Disneyesque life lessons that result in some tender moments between daughter and mother. This is a wonderfully animated tale that is easy to like. And it’s Pixar’s first female lead out of 13 feature films. Brave. Pixar animation. Directed by Mark Andrews, Brenda Chapman, Steve Purcell. With voices of Kelly MacDonald, Bill Connoly and Emma Thompson, 1 hr., 33 min. A scene from Pixar’s Brave..
articles.title: Pixar’s first release with female lead

articles.text: Abominable, a collaborative animation feature from Dreamworks and China’s Pearl Studios, is, in so many ways, kid-friendly and delightful. So, mom or dad, if you have any youngsters, say newbie tweens, take them to see a film about a spunky-scrappy girl named Yi (Chloe Bennet) who lives in an apartment in Shanghai with her mom (Michelle Wong) and grandmother, Nai Nai (Tsai Chin). Yi, sadly, just lost her dad and has created a small shrine to him on the roof, where she keeps her violin. Alone, after climbing up a precarious scaffolding, she plays solos into the night, music that soars above the city sounds and mournfully expresses her grief. It’s on such an evening that Yi, to her startled and then panicky surprise, discovers that hiding behind a curtain, deep in the shadows, is a young, furry Yeti (the size of a VW bug) with glacially blue eyes. Discovering that this Himalayan creature means her no harm, and seeing an enormous billboard advertising Mt. Everest in the distance, she decides to call him Everest. The audience already knows that Everest has just escaped from a high-tech lab and is now being pursued by a cranky old rich guy, Mr. Burnish (Eddie Lizzard), Dr. Zara (Sarah Paulson), a zoologist, and her mercenary crew. They are intent on recapturing Everest. And so begins a great adventure. Yi, realizing where this Yeti must have come from, decides he must be returned to his home and his family. She recruits two long-time friends who live in her building – Jin (Tenzing Norgay Trainor), a classmate, and Peng, who is obsessed with basketball. Together they head out with Everest on a road trip (to include river barges) making their way toward Mt. Everest. Of course, Burnish, Zara, and company are in hot pursuit, prepared to do whatever it takes to get Everest back to the Shanghai lab, for reasons never fully explained. As expected, while they travel cross-country, the crew have lots of close calls, keeping just barely ahead of the bad guys. Along the way there are also lyrical moments when Yi plays her muchloved violin. And there are those moments when the gang discovers that Everest isn’t just a Yeti but possesses magical powers that he calls forth when needed. In one beautiful scene, running from Burnish and Zara, Everest turns a field of flowers into an undulating cresting wave that they surf while riding in a small wooden boat, surrounded by a riot of pastel colors. It’s superb animation, filled with breathtaking imagination. What is done so well in Abominable is that the writers and animators nail not only the wonderful pastel panoramas, but they create, in Yi and Jin and Jeng, kids that seem truly authentic. Yi has just the right amount of courage and attitude. Jin is a perfect newbie teen who, like Yi, is goodhearted and kind. Peng is about the same age as Everest (ten, perhaps?), and they form a bro-bond that is always resilient and fun to watch. All of them are there not only for Everest, but committed to each other as they meet challenge after challenge on their way to getting Everest home. Of course, they learn some nifty life lessons along the way, especially about family and friendship. Is Abominable formulaic? Indeed. But in the best sense of the word. Does it have a right ending? Indeed. Kids dig stories that are accessible and comfortable and familiar with easydoes-it excitement. This movie gets all of that just right. So, mom and dad, no worries. Abominable . Animated. Voices of Chloe Bennet, Albert Tai, Tenzing Norgay Trainor. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: Abominable a lovely animation feature that gets it right

articles.text: Violinist Grisha Goluboff (left) with Henry Ford in the 1930s. Grisha Goluboff is the forgotten genius of the violin. The city of San Francisco in the 20th century can boast of four of the greatest violinists of all time. Three made it to everlasting fame. You know their names. In chronological order they were Yehudi Menuhin, Ruggiero Ricci and Isaac Stern. Perhaps the greatest of these is the one who is unknown. He was Grisha Goluboff, born to Russian immigrant parents in San Francisco in 1919. In order to make a successful career, talent is not the only thing. Luck and timing play an important part. Unlimited financial backing is absolutely necessary. Yehudi Menuhin had it for certain. Isaac Stern did also, but he also knew how to finesse the system. Ruggiero Ricci’s struggle to the top was more arduous. He made it and had probably the longest career of any concertizing musician. But what of Grisha Goluboff? From his debut at the age of six he was a sensation. Success followed success – even into his adolescence. And then, for a variety of reasons, his career ended. The “big three” violinists had many things going for them. They were great talents, they had important financial backing and they were lucky. Grisha Goluboff was a special talent. I got to know Grisha accidentally when I was in the 10th grade. His fame was a distant memory by the early 1960s, but his genius was readily apparent. He had uncanny insight. Every one of my lessons included listening. One example of his insight was that without knowing the name of the person playing, he could tell with certainty if the performer were a man or a woman. For several years, Grisha was a news sensation. Headline: Hitler becomes Reich chancellor August 2, 1934. Among his first edicts was that Grisha must return his Guarneri violin to Germany. Industrialist Henry Ford heard about this and delivered a Stradivarius violin to Grisha in an armored car, followed by a police escort and the entire press corps of New York City. He was thankful for the years that he was allowed to play on Henry Ford‘s Stradivarius violin. Grisha could have been a successful Hollywood photographer. His photographs of the actress Colleen Gray are artistic masterpieces. It is sad that an artist of this stature disappeared from the stages of the world. There are so many things he could have offered succeeding generations. There is no doubt we have arrived at some stupendous technical perfection. articles.text: Brown Gables, the Alexander home at Sea View and Hampton, was named for its prominent gables, painted brown. Their grand three-story mansion was completed in 1909, and they named it “Brown Gables” for its massive gabled dormers with bargeboards, painted brown. The first floor was faced in brick, and half timbering covered the upper stories. Two large porte cocheres were also trimmed in brown gables. Diamond paned leaded glass windows graced the entry, and large bay windows offered expansive views from every room in this most elegant early home in Piedmont. City records indicate that the Alexander house had three living rooms, five bedrooms and five bathrooms. Koa wood and other exotic woods enhanced the interior. It was an exceptional house in 1909 with 3240 square feet, and was the site of many festive balls. The gardens of the Alexander home also hosted many garden parties benefiting local charities. Mary Alexander was a strong supporter of the Ladies Relief Society, the Matilda Brown Home and the Women’s Guild of the Piedmont Church. She also organized the Bay Area chapter of the Red Cross at the onset of World War I and led it for over 30 years. Their beautiful gardens extended over nine of today’s lots on Sea View and King Avenues. A low brick wall with a subtle detail surrounded the property. The wall is visible in the photo of the house, and portions still stand today on Hampton. The Alexander carriage house, which still exists at 84 King, had servants’ quarters and an indoor swimming pool. Helen Wills Moody, the Wimbledon tennis star in the 1920s and 1930s, practiced on the tennis court there. The Alexander family formed a small community near Sea View and Hampton. In 1911, Wallace’s mother built her own home across the street at 92 Sea View, designed by Charles W. Dickey, and Mary’s mother built her home down the street at 236 Sea View. Wallace Alexander was president of the Alexander and Baldwin sugar firm, vice president of the Matson Navigation Company, director of several other Hawaiian companies and a trustee of Stanford University. Although he was active in many businesses, he found time for many civic and charitable organizations in Piedmont. In addition to constructing the stores and saving Piedmont Park, Alexander was also the moving force behind the construction of the Piedmont Interdenominational Church (now Piedmont Community Church), arranging for the purchase of the land and again hiring Albert Farr to design the church. Wallace Alexander also established the Piedmont Boy Scout Council. He arranged for the scouts to meet in the basement of the church, as they still do today. In 1929, he leased land from the Forest Service near Keddie, in Plumas County, and established Camp Wallace Alexander, a Piedmont scouting tradition fondly remembered by generations of Piedmont Boy Scouts. The land lease expired in 1982, and Camp Wallace Alexander was dismantled. In 1939, Wallace Alexander suffered a fatal stroke at his second home in Honolulu. He was eulogized as “Piedmont’s leading private citizen.” Wallace left a large bequest to the Piedmont Community Church and to the Piedmont Boy Scouts. His philosophy was that he “was but a trustee of the money that came to him.” Upon his death, Mary Alexander followed her husband’s wishes that the property be subdivided into 13 lots. The entire estate would not be sold to a single builder. She stated that the lots would be purchased by individuals who intended to build their own homes. The Alexanders wanted more families to live in Piedmont. Footnote on the Stores My previous column on Piedmont’s “stores” brought out a few comments by readers. One fondly remembers the steps leading up to the stores. They were a favorite place for students to hang out. “Kids with cars would ‘cruise by’ checking out the scene. articles.text: Wallace Alexander was Piedmont’s premier philanthropic citizen and a leader in establishing many of Piedmont’s institutions. In previous columns I have mentioned Wallace Alexander. He was instrumental in the 1913 construction of the Piedmont Commercial Center, Piedmont’s first stores, and in the 1921 purchase of the upper Piedmont Park land, saving it from development. Wallace Alexander, a profile Wallace McKinney Alexander was born on the island of Maui in 1869. His father, Samuel Alexander, was related to the Baldwin and Cooke families and was a pioneer in sugar planting and refining. When it was time for Wallace and his sisters, Juliette and Annie, to attend high school, the family moved to Oakland where Wallace attended Oakland High School. He later attended Andover and graduated from Yale University. He married Oakland classmate Mary Barker in 1904. In her memoir, Queen of the Hills, Evelyn Craig Pattiani tells the story of the Alexanders choosing their homesite at the prominent corner of Sea View and Hampton (then called Union Street). Illustrated here is work in the Caribbean where Dutch Colonial is adjusted with large windows for views and easy access to terraces. What is most important is preserving the sense and the feeling of the base style and place.

articles.text: In addition to the more prominent architectural styles we have been discussing during the last months, there are yet more to be seen walking through town. Some, like Victorian, are well known but not numerous here; others are hybrid, sometimes difficult to classify. But it also strikes me that every new building, or even every remodel, is necessarily advancing, albeit in small steps, the evolution of any and every base style employed. Looking back maybe 50 years from now, these incremental trends will probably be clearer and help describe how and why the future style came to be. To better understand the initial selection and continuing evolution of building styles it might be helpful to review the process architects normally employ in design. Based on my experience, there are three overriding considerations in the design of any building: the site, the building program, and the design style. 1. Any building site has a specific size, solar orientation, topography, along with existing amenities (like views, trees, rock outcroppings, or water features for example). Any site is also a part of a surrounding context – anything from vacant land to 2-story homes to 12-story office buildings. 2. The building program answers the questions: how big is the intended building? What types of uses and spaces are included? What service systems are included? While zoning regulations limit these options, there still are a wide range of choices based on user lifestyle preference, cost, and response to the site. 3. The design style chosen, no matter how closely or loosely followed, determines the aesthetic of both the building massing and details – inside and out. It influences materials, forms and siting. While the two long continuous slender columned porches on both levels suggest Monterey Colonial style architecture, this house ends up principally as a backdrop for the incredible front garden and brickwork. It is the kind of special personalized property that makes Piedmont wonderful.

All sales are final - so make sure to review all photos and descriptions carefully before purchasing. All merchandise for sale will be on a first-come, first-serve basis. Note that, while you can shop from home, no shipping or delivery of items will be availOakland Museum’s first-ever online White Elephant Sale began on May 1 able. articles.text: Back in the pre-Covid days when they actually had big, live wine tasting events, one of the perennial favorites was the Rhone Rangers tasting. It was held at varied venues in the Bay Area and featured about 100 wineries who specialize in Rhone grape varietals grown in California. They were raucous events filled with passionate wine producers and wine lovers. Every year when it came to selecting the 10 best wines of the tasting, Austin Hope always ended among the winners, whether it was their Grenache, Syrah or one of their blends. The Hope Family has been farming in Paso Robles for 30 years, getting their start with apple orchards. Today they have expanded to five brands – Austin Hope, Treana, Quest, Liberty School, and Troublemaker. I recently was able to taste the current releases of the Austin Hope wines and get caught up on how the winery is doing today. • 2020 Austin Hope Chenin Blanc There used to be a lot of Chenin Blanc planted in California, but much of it was converted to Cabernet or Chardonnay vineyards. Luckily a resurgence seems to be afoot as it truly is one of the finest white grapes on the planet. The Austin Hope Chenin Blanc is a brilliantly focused, vibrant, fresh and delicious dry wine that is bursting with fruit and seductive, flowery aromas. Crisp and fragrant, it is hard to imagine a better aperitif than a wine such as this. • 2019 Austin Hope Sauvignon Blanc The Hope Sauvignon Blanc has expressive green apple and fresh grass notes with hints of jasmine, lime and grapefruit. Medium-bodied, the palate has tons of freshness with loads of citrusy layers and a smooth, clean finish. Would be great with fish or shellfish. • 2019 Austin Hope Chardonnay This Chardonnay opens with notes of almonds, hay, and peach with nuances of yeast, bread and flowers. Medium-bodied, it fleshes out in the mouth to tropical-tinged fruits, with juicy freshness on the finish. Try with roast chicken. • 2020 Austin Hope Rose This is one of the lightest colored Roses I have seen, with just a glimmer of copper coloring. It has a nose of strawberries, currant jelly and baking spices plus a waft of dried herbs. articles.text: Photo by Katie Heatherington The Recreation Department-sponsored Walking on Wednesday group visited Hampton Park last week. Pictured are Harriette Louie (left), Nancy DeRoche and k-9 best friend Chili, Jim Kuo, Brenda Ferrero, Melba Yee and Albert Chen. Not pictured Andree and Mark Greenberg, and Susan Martin. The sun broke through the morning fog just as the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group departed from the Exedra for its walk on May 12th. Ten walkers were on hand: Harriette Louie, Brenda Ferrero, Jim Kuo, Adrienne Hamlin, Susan Martin, Albert Chen, Andree Greenberg, Mark Greenberg, Nancy DeRoche and Melba Yee. Since the group resumed its activities after the pandemic put them on hold for one year, the walkers have been visiting some of the area’s wonderful parks and recreational facilities. They have gone to Dracena Park, the Davie Tennis Stadium, and the Morcom Rose Garden. On May 12 it was decided that going to Piedmont’s Hampton Park with its Piedmont Sports Field, also as known as Hampton Field, would add to their park-seeing collection. Activity leader Dick Carter was out of town, so Harriette Louie and Melba Yee stepped in to lead the day’s walk. The walkers went up Highland Avenue to Sheridan Avenue, then to Wildwood Avenue, and through the Hall Fenway to Crocker and Hampton Avenues. They took a short side trip to Crocker Park to enjoy its flowers and the sculpture Mother Bear Nursing Her Two Cubs by noted San Francisco-base sculptor Beniamino “Benny” Bufano. It was gifted to the city and installed in Crocker Park in 1979. It is described by the City as granite, but described by the Smithsonian American Art Museum as black marble. The walkers closely examined the sculpture and all agreed the material was indeed granite. Three other copies of the Bear and Cubs sculpture, rendered in different materials, can be found outside the Oakland Museum, the Kaiser Hospital in Fremont, and near UC San Francisco. Crocker Park was gifted to the city in 1916 by Mary and Wallace Alexander, owners of a large home that covered the entire block between Crocker and Sea View Avenues. In addition to being one of the city’s founding fathers, Wallace Alexander’s civic contributions to the city were significant and enduring: he founded the Piedmont Boy Scouts in 1910; helped the city buy Piedmont Springs Park from Frank Havens; led a group of residents to purchase 2 acres of land across from Piedmont Park. He hired Albert Farr to design the town’s commercial center, and later to design the Piedmont Community Church. Despite his many contributions, most of the walkers had not heard of Wallace Alexander and the group wondered whether any honorary designations existed in town. The sole surviving structure from the Alexander estate is a residence across the street from the park on Crocker Avenue. Nancy DeRoche informed the group that this structure was originally the carriage house, and that it is probably representative of the architectural style of the now-destroyed main house. The group then left the park and went up Hampton past a set of huge eucalyptus trees where St. James Drive ends at Hampton. They continued up the street to Hampton Park. Hampton Park has evolved greatly over the years. Drawing on information from Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s research, the walkers learned that Hampton Park was part of 50 acres purchased in 1911 by Louis Titus, a Berkeley real estate developer. He intended to build a mansion on this large tract of land, but in 1912 the new city of Piedmont raised property taxes significantly, and Titus dropped his plans and left Piedmont. In 1914 James Tyson, a lumber and shipping businessman bought 30 acres of the land for his home. Tyson was also a strong supporter of Piedmont Boy Scouts, and in 1921 Tyson made a portion of the land available for the scouts to use as an outdoor camp. During the Great Depression in 1938 the Tysons also make the land available to the Piedmont schools. A WPA project leveled the land and it was intended to be the site of a future “East Piedmont” school. However, it was never built. In the 50s and 60s the space was a dusty, sometimes muddy baseball field for younger players. Later, when grass was planted on the field, youth soccer matches were played, sometimes on a soggy field. An underground water flow was an on-going problem. Hampton Park and the Piedmont Sports Field are much different today than what Piedmonters experienced 100, 50, and even 20 years ago. A building was constructed in 2000 to house children’s programs that is used by both the Piedmont Cooperative Playschool and the Recreation Department. Dramatic improvements were made to the field and park during 2017 with a $2 million public/private partnership that the Piedmont community generously supported. Drainage and artificial turf were installed that made the field much more serviceable during the year. In 2019 the baseball backstop was dedicated and named in honor of Oakland Police Officer John Raymond Hege. The 41-year-old Piedmont native was one of four officers fatally shot following a traffic stop in East Oakland on March 21, 2009. The field is used today for organized baseball, soccer and children’s activities. The park also has two tennis courts, a backboard, a volleyball court, and six basketball hoops. There is a children’s play structure and sand area that are located near the tennis courts.

articles.text: Piedmont Avenue Library (PAL) patrons are invited to return their neighbhood library. It is now open from Tuesdy through Saturday, 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Come to the library to browse, get a library card, and check out books with Oakland Public Library’s Express service. Five patrons at a time are allowed for now. Teachers are allowed to bring students, but the library is working with the schools to have planned programs later in the afternoon. For the time being, patrons still cannot use the computer or sit and read for an hour, but the library hopes to see those restrictions lifted soon. With OPL Express, patrons can stack books on the machine and check them out all at once. Meet new Branch Manager Leni Matthews The public is invited to come to the libraayr and meet the new Branch Manager, Leni Matthews. As a young girl in Chicago, libraries required that young patrons know how to write their names to get a library card. When the librarian discovered Leni didn’t know how to write her name very well, she took her to a table in a quiet corner and practiced with her. Leni’s name was legible, and the librarian gave Leni her first library card. She has been involved with libraries ever since. Her librarian training began with volunteering at local school libraries, tutoring as a “Teacher in the Library,” and participating in internships at Chicago Public Library, the Art Institute of Chicago, and Argonne National Laboratory. She attended library school at the University of Illinois, and her first full time job as a librarian was in Arlington, Texas as the User Experience Librarian. When her family relocated to the Bay Area, she researched Bay Area neighborhoods before making a final decision on where she wanted to work. Leni believes in involving the library with the community and developing supportive relationships. She is especially interested in finding ways the library can fill gaps in community services. Be sure to stop in and welcome Leni to Piedmont Avenue Library. HOURS & LOCATION Piedmont Avenue Branch Library is located at 80 Echo Avenue in back of Piedmont Avenue Elementary School. For more information, call 510-597-5011 or see the website: https://oaklandlibrary.org/locations/piedmont-avenue-branch. Hours of operation are 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday. Closed Sunday and Monday.

articles.text: Mollie Kinney, a longtime Piedmont resident, died peacefully in her sleep on the evening of April 20, 2021 after a long illness, with her husband by her side. Born Marie Mitchell Mulford, she was the oldest daughter of Lloyd and Adele Mulford of Piedmont. She was born in Oakland, and attended schools in Piedmont, graduating from Piedmont High school in 1949. She earned a degree from Nursing School at St. Francis Hospital in San Francisco, and though a nurse all of her life, she never practiced nursing. During her time in nurses training, she established many lasting friendships and enjoyed immensely their yearly reunions. Everyone who knew Mollie remembers her laugh, and her wonderful, positive view of life. She could look at everything with humor. Not only that but she could always sneak in a good nap. Mollie met her husband, Bill Kinney, when he was in the milMollie Kinney with her favorite cup of coffee. “Aloha” from the Islands. Mollie and Bill Kinney in Hawaii – “Five o’clock in Paradise.” itary during the Korean conflict. They corresponded for the two years and when he returned, they were married at St. Paul’s Church in Oakland on September 26, 1953. They lived in the country for a short time before moving to Piedmont, where Mollie lived the rest of her life. Mollie was a member of the Piedmont Garden Club, Hoe and Hope Garden Club, and the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. She was also a member of the Junior League of the East Bay and a longtime member of Claremont Country Club where she enjoyed playing golf, tennis and bridge. She most often could be found playing bridge somewhere. She loved the game and the friends she made playing over the years. She was also a wonderful athlete. She spent the early years of her life riding and jumping horses. When that career ended, she took up golf and tennis and was excellent at both. Additionally, she loved dogs, especially Springer Spaniels. articles.text: Sociologists have a term to describe a contemporary family dynamic that has been the norm in many cultures for centuries: intensive grandparenting. Today’s intensive grandparents provide weekly, regular childcare for grandchildren, as well as providing additional support such as housework, shopping for groceries, carpooling, and preparing meals. These care arrangements may begin with full-time care of an infant when the mother returns to work and may continue as the child ages to include after-school care and coverage for sick days. As author Paula Span writes in her NY Times article for Generation Grandparent, “When grandparents help hold it all together,” intensive grandparents are not necessarily defined by the number of hours per week they provide care, but rather by their commitment to the task longterm. It allows working parents the opportunity to rely on the grandparents in the same way they would a hired caregiver. For grandmothers in particular, there can be a strong motivation to help their adult children in this way, even when those grandmothers are still working. These working grandmothers treasure time with their grandchildren, and yet they may find themselves tapping into their employee benefits and retirement accounts prematurely. Many have aging parents to care for as well, so that being an intensive grandparent can lead to lost personal time and some of their own social support system. When grandparents embark on this kind of arrangement voluntarily, the results can be delightful. Grandparents who live close by and who are physically fit enough to provide regular childcare can make lifelong memories with their grandchildren. The rewards can be extraordinary. Many discover pleasures that they may have missed out on when they were raising their own children, and these joys can be unlike any other that they’ve experienced. One Korean study found that intensive grandchild care compared to grandparents who provide no grandchild care is associated with a reduction in depressive symptoms in older adults, particularly men. Intensive grandparenting may have different outcomes in other situations. A study in Ireland found that the emotional effects of intensive caring on grandparents is strongly affected by whether the care is provided by choice or by obligation. In families where the care is requested due to socioeconomic constraints, the grandparents may find it nearly impossible to say No. In this study, grandparents who provide high intensity care showed an increase in depressive symptoms and a decrease in their sense of well-being, particularly if they did not have a balance of social and leisure activity in their lives. Each family that employs an intensive grandparenting plan is unique, and the factors that motivate these arrangements can be vastly different across households. Social norms and national public policy initiatives relating to affordable childcare are a work in progress and one day may change the face of grandparent care. Meanwhile, if you are an intensive grandparent, consider how to make the most of your time with your family and find balance for yourself as well. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents.
