articles.text: It might be time to start thinking about being together again. Well-being is not just about exercise and nutrition, but also relationships and emotional resilience. Beyond spending time with immediate family, studies have found that people can benefit from all kinds of relationships in their lives. A decades-long Harvard University study found that close relationships spanning a lifetime can alleviate pain levels, support the nervous system, and keep the brain healthier longer. On the other hand, those who feel a prolonged sense of loneliness may have a shorter lifespan. Here are some ways to prioritize togetherness and relationships to benefit not only you but also those in your life whom you care about. 1. Make time It’s so easy to get caught up in daily tasks, the ‘to-do’ list and the ‘should ofs’ in life. “It’s easy to get isolated,” said Professor Robert Waldinger, director of the Harvard Study of Adult Development, in an interview. He suggests “investing time in relationships”. 2. Be casual Keeping up relationships isn’t about the big events of life, but the little moments. If you can get together in-person in a way that feels safe for all parties, then go out and do something meaningful together. In instances where you cannot be in the same place, send a card just because, call them up to share a story, or find a way to connect online through a shared game or activity. 3. Move past the shame of loneliness. People often feel ashamed of their feelings of loneliness. It can feel like admitting you are lonely is akin to saying you are not likeable; that you are socially deficient in some way. This feeling is actually an instinctual survival skill and is perfectly natural. But at the same time, loneliness can have negative physical consequences. Rather than being ashamed, recognize loneliness as the body signaling a biological need, just like hunger or thirst. 4. Know that age doesn’t matter. Experts agree that human connection and togetherness is important at every age and people of different ages can have essential relationships. People can make new friends throughout life by sharing a hobby, activity, or story. Beyond grandparents and grandchildren, friendships can develop across an age gap through a caregiving connection, in a work environment, or by engaging in shared interests. 5. You go first. Stop waiting for the phone to ring. If that feeling of loneliness is nagging at you, be the one to take the initiative. Try getting in touch with an old friend or make new ones by joining an in-person or online group. There are book clubs, caregiver support groups, knitting circles, and much more out there to become part of. articles.text: After a year of being cooped up, everyone I know is delighted with this beautiful spring weather we are having. Many of us are going outside and are so happy to increase our activity level to regain physical fitness. Yet, one of the discoveries we’ve made in a year of staying indoors is that there are ways to develop our inner strength and resiliency. One very popular way we’ve found to restore ourselves in the face of the unpredictable, and to enrich both the mind and soul, is through meditation and mindfulness exercises. Residents of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living community have found this to be true. Many have been practicing mindfulness exercises for years. Meghan Collins, a resident since 2012, has been a Zen practitioner for 45 years and a lay teacher for 22 years. She has been leading our meditation group since she moved to The Lake Merritt. “The residents tell me it is very calming and beneficial,” Collins says. Medical professionals concur. According to the National Institute of Health, there is a beneficial link between mindfulness meditation and measurable changes in the brain regions involved in memory, learning and emotion. Data indicates that meditation can also help improve psychological balance, coping with illness, and may enhance overall health and well-being. The Lake Merritt’s yoga instructor, Bethany Hobbs, couldn’t agree more. She offers classes of Chair Yoga, Meditation & Relaxation, and Balance Awareness for our community. Her work focuses on breathing, balance, stretching and strengthening the body, as well as the Wes Nisker and Megan Collins and lead a meditation session at The Lake Merritt in Oakland. mind, so that older adults can help keep both their minds and bodies more flexible and relaxed. The Lake Merritt’s newest resident, Wes Nisker, is a Buddhist meditation teacher, author, and performer. His books include national bestseller, Essential Crazy Wisdom, as well as Buddha’s Nature and The Big Bang, The Buddha, and the Baby Boom. Nisker has studied Buddhist meditation for over three decades with teachers in Asia and America. For the past 15 years he has been leading retreats and workshops in Buddhist insight meditation and philosophy at national and international venues. Collins and Nisker were excited to meet one another and have recently joined forces in leading the meditation group at The Lake Merritt. When asked whether they prefer to lead or participate, they are in agreement. “When you lead you are trying to experience what you are calling on others to do. You don’t let go as deeply into the experience,” says Nisker. “As a participant, you can just let go. When you lead. you have to keep track of the time and things around you. Over the years I’ve learned to do both,” adds Collins. A major benefit of mindfulness meditation is that it encourages you to pay attention to your thoughts, your actions and your body. Finding time for mindfulness in our culture, however, can be a challenge. We tend to place great value on how much we can do at once and how fast. Being more mindful is within anyone’s reach. “Over the years it seems the practice of meditation has given me a lot more equilibrium,” Collins says. Given the very turbulent times we have been through recently, it seems like meditation might be just the thing for everyone. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, 1800 Madison Street, Oakland. For more information call 510-903- 3600 or visit www.thelakemerritt. com.

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. articles.text: On May 21, Stagebridge and Asian American Storytellers in Unity will join forces to uplift the diverse cultures and heritage of the Asian American and Pacific Islander diaspora in Finding Ourselves in America: Asian American Voices. As a direct response to the recent anti-Asian attacks across the United States, this one-of-akind digital event brings together 16 nationally recognized storytellers for a stimulating and informative gathering. Through personal narratives, historical stories, folktales, art, and music, these storytellers will elevate immigration experiences, discrimination, struggles with self-identity, and cross-cultural understanding. San Francisco Bay Area storytellers Eleanor Clement Glass and Linda Yemoto will coordinate a star-studded lineup, including award-winning journalist Emil Guillermo (former host of “All Things Considered”), cultural activists Robert Kikuchi-Yngojo and Nancy Wang (Eth-Noh-Tec), and playwright and actress M.J. Kang (Noran Bang: The Yellow Room). “Yes, we are addressing the current and horrific violence against our communities, but we are leading by embracing our heritage and fostering cross-cultural understanding,” explained ClemStorytellers Robert Kikuchi-Yngojo (left), Nancy Wang and Alton Takiyama Chung are a few of the 16 nationally acclaimed artists showcased in Finding Ourselves in America: Asian American Voices. ent Glass. “The rich diversity of our Asian American and Pacific Islander identities throughout America is the message.” Other artists include Alton Takiyama Chung (Hawaii), Anne Shimojima (Illinois), Roopa Mohan (California), Motoko Dworkin (Massachusetts), Joel Ying (Florida), Bowen Lee (California), Karin Amano (Georgia), Tobey Ishii Anderson (Washington), Yasu Ishida (South Carolina) and Kuniko Yamamoto (Florida). This event will kick off Finding Ourselves in America, a Stagebridge series highlighting BIPOC voices through storytelling partnerships with artists from Oakland and beyond. “It’s inspiring to be a part of a team focused on an equitable future and committed to healing marginalized voices through storytelling and performing arts,” said Stagebridge Executive Director Shannon McDonnell. “Finding Ourselves in America is just one of the ways we are committed to doing the work at Stagebridge.” Finding Ourselves in America: Asian American Voices will be live-streamed on the Stagebridge YouTube channel for individuals who cannot access it digitally. For more information, visit www. stagebridge.org/findingourselves. To register for classes and learn about the full range of activities at Stagebridge, visit www.stagebridge.org. Located at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland (across from Whole Foods), Stagebridge is the nation’s oldest and most renowned theatre company of older adults. For information, call (510) 444-4755.

pages.text: Wednesday, May 19, 2021 29 Meditation: Food for the mind and soul By Tim Johnson After a year of being cooped up, everyone I know is delighted with this beautiful spring weather we are having. Many of us are going outside and are so happy to increase our activity level to regain physical fitness. Yet, one of the discoveries we’ve made in a year of staying indoors is that there are ways to develop our inner strength and resiliency. One very popular way we’ve found to restore ourselves in the face of the unpredictable, and to enrich both the mind and soul, is through meditation and mindfulness exercises. Residents of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living community have found this to be true. Many have been practicing mindfulness exercises for years. Meghan Collins, a resident since 2012, has been a Zen practitioner for 45 years and a lay teacher for 22 years. She has been leading our meditation group since she moved to The Lake Merritt. “The residents tell me it is very calming and beneficial,” Collins says. Medical professionals concur. According to the National Institute of Health, there is a beneficial link between mindfulness meditation and measurable changes in the brain regions involved in memory, learning and emotion. Data indicates that meditation can also help improve psychological balance, coping with illness, and may enhance overall health and well-being. The Lake Merritt’s yoga instructor, Bethany Hobbs, couldn’t agree more. She offers classes of Chair Yoga, Meditation & Relaxation, and Balance Awareness for our community. Her work focuses on breathing, balance, stretching and strengthening the body, as well as the Wes Nisker and Megan Collins and lead a meditation session at The Lake Merritt in Oakland. mind, so that older adults can help keep both their minds and bodies more flexible and relaxed. The Lake Merritt’s newest resident, Wes Nisker, is a Buddhist meditation teacher, author, and performer. His books include national bestseller, Essential Crazy Wisdom, as well as Buddha’s Nature and The Big Bang, The Buddha, and the Baby Boom. Nisker has studied Buddhist meditation for over three decades with teachers in Asia and America. For the past 15 years he has been leading retreats and workshops in Buddhist insight meditation and philosophy at national and international venues. Collins and Nisker were excited to meet one another and have recently joined forces in leading the meditation group at The Lake Merritt. When asked whether they prefer to lead or participate, they are in agreement. “When you lead you are trying to experience what you are calling on others to do. You don’t let go as deeply into the experience,” says Nisker. “As a participant, you can just let go. When you lead. you have to keep track of the time and things around you. Over the years I’ve learned to do both,” adds Collins. A major benefit of mindfulness meditation is that it encourages you to pay attention to your thoughts, your actions and your body. Finding time for mindfulness in our culture, however, can be a challenge. We tend to place great value on how much we can do at once and how fast. Being more mindful is within anyone’s reach. “Over the years it seems the practice of meditation has given me a lot more equilibrium,” Collins says. Given the very turbulent times we have been through recently, it seems like meditation might be just the thing for everyone. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, 1800 Madison Street, Oakland. For more information call 510-903- 3600 or visit www.thelakemerritt. com. Wednesday Evening Meditation Group is online The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. articles.text: An intelligent response to and prioritization of each of these overlapping and integrated considerations is what makes for successful architecture. What is occurring over time, however, is that each and every one of these three important considerations is in flux – they are always changing. Adjacent trees grow, neighboring buildings are built, and overhead utility lines are removed. Just accommodating current lifestyles, newer building methods, and improved material selections necessarily changes and advances any base architectural style initially chosen with every year that passes. A partial exception to this would be the case of strict historical renovations where exact themes and details are duplicated for historical accuracy. So, it is easy to see how all architectural styles can evolve. And with changes in the world occurring more rapidly, the style evolutions will also occur faster. Just think of the pandemic we are now in. More time spent in the house with virtual activities has created in one year a whole new set of building program criteria to which architects, designers, engineers, and their clients are already responding. Next: The Design Professions that shape our Built Environment Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. articles.text: Under the guidance of Piedmont School District, Communications Consultant Naomi Hunter conducted a survey to assess the performance of School District and School Board members during the pandemic, a period of slightly more than a year. During an April 28 school board meeting, Hunter presented her summary report and recommendations, one of which was for the district to hire a communications expert to help disseminate district communications to the community – a job commonly known as public relations. The survey which was anonymous (no names used) was on the SurveyMonkey platform and was open from February 26 to April 2, 2021. It drew responses from 1159 individuals, consisting of 972 parents, 102 teachers, 58 staff in non-teaching roles, 20 community members without students enrolled, and 7 administrators. The survey of 16 questions drew over 2,700 open-ended comments. Questions asked respondents about their trust level with the school board and Superintendent, asked for ways to improve, and general preferences about information that had been made public. For example, question 7 read: “I trust the Superintendent and Board of Education to make decisions that are in the best interest of students.” 46% of all respondents agreed or strongly agreed with the statement, 17% were indifferent and 37% “Disagreed or Strongly Disagreed” that decisions were being made for students. articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council approved at its May 3 meeting “traffic-calming” measures at the triangular intersection of Lower Grand Avenue at Grand Avenue, a major arterial within the city. The city will solicit bids for the proposed improvements, not to exceed $75,000. Grand Avenue is a key connector to Oakland on both the southern and northern borders of Piedmont. It also carries the highest traffic volume of any roadway in the city. Seven years ago, in 2014, the location was identified by the city’s Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan as one needing “additional traffic calming,” and was prioritized for improvements due to its unique geometry, explained Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. Plans for improvements were developed by Public Works staff previously, but improvements were delayed due to an East Bay Municipal Utility District [EBMUD] water pipeline project that took more than two years to be completed. City staff’s original intent was to construct a landscaped triangle in the same location as the currently painted triangle in the intersection. It would include subtle directional signage, visible bike lanes, and green infrastructure. However, staff is now considering the “less expensive, but nevertheless effective traffic calming features of painted islands and triangles with reflective bollards Staff photo The Grand Avenue and Lower Grand Avenue intersection was identified by the city’s Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan as needing improved signage for motorists. as a way of implementing more traffic calming features sooner and for less cost,” according to a city staff report. In the southbound direction, a new, small triangular-shaped “bulb-out” adjacent to the curb in front of 1608 Lower Grand will be installed, and it will have bollards around its perimeter. Arrows on Grand Avenue will be installed to indicate the direction of traffic for through traffic proceeding north on Grand Avenue. The project will include the installation of “One Way” and “Do Not Enter” pavement markings for the northbound traffic on Lower Grand Avenue adjacent to the new island, and the installation of new red curbing on the nose of the existing island. Bollards will be placed around the painted median. New striping on the north side of the new island or median will include double yellow centerlines, “Stop” signage, and a new limit line. High visibility bicycle lane striping will be added. Painted lines of bike lanes have nearly disappeared due to weather, and all lanes on Grand Avenue from Lower Grand Avenue to Rose Avenue on both sides of the street will be repainted, with buffers or bollards for the southbound bicycle at the curve on Grand Avenue just south of Lower Grand. In the past three years, three accidents have occurred at this intersection, Gonzales explained. articles.text: Editor: I believe it’s important to understand the basis of the latest attempt by the Piedmont School District to reach back to 1896 and try to bring back the by-now infamous Plessy v. Ferguson U.S. Supreme Court decision. Better known as the “separate but equal” doctrine, it legalized school discrimination under the guise of being able to provide separation of the races with equal access to instruction and facilities. Plessy was separate and very un-equal. Unanimously demolished by the 1954 Warren Court in Brown v. Board of Education, the old “separate but equal” conundrum was declared unconstitutional and opened the country to a new era for school education. The recent attempt by the Piedmont School District to bring back “Plessy” by mandating separate racial groups to provide “discussion circles” to “help interpret” the outcome of the George Floyd trial is a feeble try to reinstate the worst of the now obliterated “Plessy” doctrine, bringing torrents of comare well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. or in a scrapbook for publication in the Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken. 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmontpost.org Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Barry Eitel Allyson Aleksey Jay Russell Ed Gilligan SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: Editor: I am very concerned that the real problem with the “white student support circle” is being missed entirely by PUSD Superintendent Randy Booker, Assistant Superintendent Cheryl Wozniak, and board President Cory Smegal. As a former Piedmont student, from Havens kindergartner to PHS graduate, I experienced a chilling effect upon reading about this incident. discussion groups. Reading Wozniak’s messages and “apology,” Booker’s response, and Smegal’s commentary, I saw no recognition at the entire glaring problem with racial segregation. In fact, Wozniak attempted to justify segregating white students, saying that “[she] did not make it clear that the circle being offered ... is for those who want to be allies for BIPOC.” What Wozniak, Booker, and Smegal seem to be missing completely is that it is basically irrelevant that the call for a white student support circle was made with “best intentions” – for white students to discuss their role in improving race relations. It is imperative that these discussions are informed by Black people and POC. pages.text: 2 Wednesday, May 12, 2021 Opinion LETTERS - MAIN School District fails a basic history lesson Editor: I believe it’s important to understand the basis of the latest attempt by the Piedmont School District to reach back to 1896 and try to bring back the by-now infamous Plessy v. Ferguson U.S. Supreme Court decision. Better known as the “separate but equal” doctrine, it legalized school discrimination under the guise of being able to provide separation of the races with equal access to instruction and facilities. Plessy was separate and very un-equal. Unanimously demolished by the 1954 Warren Court in Brown v. Board of Education, the old “separate but equal” conundrum was declared unconstitutional and opened the country to a new era for school education. The recent attempt by the Piedmont School District to bring back “Plessy” by mandating separate racial groups to provide “discussion circles” to “help interpret” the outcome of the George Floyd trial is a feeble try to reinstate the worst of the now obliterated “Plessy” doctrine, bringing torrents of complaints from teachers, parents and, of course, students. There is no room in Piedmont, or anywhere else for that matter, to create such revisiting. Those days are gone. Let’s make sure the Piedmont School administration shows better judgment and avoids such lack of historical knowledge in the future. –Carlos N. No new cases of COVID-19 were reported in Piedmont in the past week, according to Alameda County Public Health Department data. The total number of Piedmont cases since the pandemic began is 181. Across Alameda County, the total caseload is 87,733 – an increase of 407 new cases weekover-week. There have been 27,300 cases recorded in Oakland and 13,612 cases in Hayward. Tragically, 13 more people have died of COVID-19 in Alameda County, bringing the total number of fatalities countywide to 1,551. On May 3, California officially adopted masking guidance that follows new recommendations from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention that said people fully vaccinated against the COVID-19 virus do not need to wear masks outdoors anymore unless they are in a crowd of strangers. People are considered fully vaccinated if it has been two weeks since either their second dose of Pfizer or Moderna vaccine or their one dose of Johnson & Johnson vaccine. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,656,967 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 61,246 deaths due to the disease statewide. The rate of positive cases of COVID-19 in California dropped to a record low of 1 percent as of Monday, May 10. The rolling seven-day positivity rate in Alameda County, now 1.2 percent, was only slightly higher. Since March 10, the county’s positivity rate has been lower than at any other point of the 14-month pandemic. Alameda County has yet to meet state benchmarks to move into a less-restrictive tier for reopening its economy, but metrics are moving in the right direction. Since March 30, Alameda County has been in the orange tier, or moderate tier, the second-least restrictive tier in California’s color-coded four-tier system. Last Tuesday, May 4, San Francisco County was moved into the least-restrictive yellow tier, or minimal tier. Yesterday, Tuesday, May 11, San Mateo County became the second Bay Area county to be moved into the yellow tier. Most indoor activities can resume, with modification, in the yellow tier. To move into the yellow tier, the positivity rate in Alameda County needs to stay below 2 percent. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to stay below 2.2 percent – it is currently 1.6 percent in Alameda County. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to be below 1 – right now there are 2.9 cases per 100,000, a drop from last week but still above the benchmark. The entire color tier system is planned to be closed in about a month. Gov. Gavin Newsom announced plans several weeks ago to lift most COVID-19 restrictions statewide on June 15. It is expected that the reopening plan will continue if hospitalizations remain low and vaccination supply is not majorly disrupted. California ranks 49th in the nation in terms of where the coronavirus is spreading the fastest, according to data from Johns Hopkins University. articles.text: Young Californians ages 12 to 15 could start receiving doses of COVID-19 vaccine as early as tomorrow, Thursday, May 13. On Monday, May 10, the Food and Drug Administration expanded the emergency use authorization offered to vaccine manufacturer Pfizer so that its vaccine can be used in children ages 12 to 15. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is scheduled to discuss this new authorization today, May 12. Additionally, the Western States Scientific Advisory Group is expected to vote today on the updated guidelines for California. Vaccines could start going into the arms of this new age group a day after approval is issued. The new authorization means all high schoolers and most middle schoolers will be eligible for vaccination. Vaccinations continue apace in Alameda County. Almost 1.6 million vaccine doses have been administered countywide, and over 52 percent of adults in Alameda County are now fully vaccinated. Piedmont is the most vaccinated municipality in the county by a large margin. The City is approaching some experts’ definitions of so-called “herd immunity,” a point when enough people are immune to a disease, either through vaccination or infection, that its spread is reduced. Initial estimates suggested that COVID-19 herd immunity would be reached when 60 to 70 percent of a population is immune, although more recent estimates suggest that immunity might need to be as high as 90 percent. Alameda County has said that its goal is to vaccinate at least 70 to 80 percent of the county. In Piedmont, 95 percent of residents ages 16 and older, some 8,112 people, have received at least one dose of vaccine, as of Monday. Over 72 percent of the City’s adults, about 6,175 people, have been fully vaccinated. Hesitancy surrounding the COVID-19 vaccine in Alameda County is about 9 percent – below national averages, according to polls released in April by the Department of Health and Human Services. Only 3.4 percent of those polled in the county said they were strongly hesitant. As a small city, vaccination will have to increase across Alameda County before herd immunity is really reached in the region. In Oakland, 70 percent of the adult population is partially vaccinated and 50 percent are fully vaccinated. Three vaccines are available in the United States, but only the Pfizer vaccine has been approved by the FDA for those age 12 and older. Pfizer and Moderna vaccines require two doses administered several weeks apart. A vaccine produced by Johnson & Johnson, which is back in use after being paused due to rare blood clotting concerns, requires only one dose. The Moderna and Johnson & Johnson vaccines are approved for adults ages 18 and older. Both Pfizer and Moderna are currently conducting vaccine trials in children as young as 6 months old. Dr. Anthony Fauci, the Chief Medical Advisor to the White House, said this week that he expected all children will be eligible for vaccination by the end of the year. On April 12, Alameda County opened COVID-19 vaccination appointments to all residents. As of press time, same-day appointments were available at several locations in Oakland and elsewhere in the county. Alameda County links to available vaccine appointments at covid-19.acgov.org/vaccines The state has administered about 32.9 million vaccine doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. The state is vaccinating an average of almost 264,000 people per day. Almost 14.5 million Californians, about 46 percent of the adult population, have been fully vaccinated. articles.text: The Piedmont community is invited to attend two upcoming Housing Advisory Committee meetings on Wednesday, May 19, and June 15. The newly formed Housing Advisory Committee was created by City Council earlier this year to provide feedback on documents prepared throughout the city’s housing programs project, and the housing element update process. The committee meets as needed and terminates upon the receipt by City Council of a draft Housing Element Update document. The committee consists of Rani Batra, June Catalano, Jane Lin, Justin Osler, and Claire Parisa. Planning Director Kevin Jackson serves as staff liaison. The meeting on May 19 will feature results of the city’s fair housing survey and pinnable map. Both were made accessible to residents on March 12, and the survey was available through April 15. The survey is one of several opportunities throughout the 18-month, city-led effort to ensure that new housing in Piedmont is feasible to develop, high in quality, and affordable. In the next Regional Housing Needs Cycle (RHNA), Piedmont is tasked with creating 587 housing units, compared to 60 units in the current RHNA cycle, representing a 979 percent increase. On March 2, city council issued a Request for Proposal [RFP] seeking a consulting firm to assist it in meeting the next RHNA planning period, which falls between 2023 and 2031. On May 3, City Council approved a proposal from Lisa Wise Consulting (LWC) to update the Housing Element of the city’s general plan. The consultant is expected to present the analysis of Piedmonters’ design preferences, understanding of housing laws, and other ideas drawn from the survey. The consulting firm will also provide recommendations for guiding principles for new tools to accelerate housing production. In addition, the first meeting will include a briefing on the Housing Element 2015 - 2022 annual progress report and a discussion of next steps and plans for a future community workshop. It will also include the election of a chair and vice chair of the committee. Agendas and instructions for participating in both Zoom meetings, which begin at 5 p.m., are posted on the city’s website at: https://piedmont.ca.gov/government/commissions___committees/housing_advisory_committee. The two meetings will be televised live on KCOM-TV, the City’s government TV station (Channel 27), and will be available through streaming video on the City’s web site: https://piedmont.ca.gov/services___departments/kcom-tv/live_content_ and_video_archive. For more information and project updates, visit the City’s website at: https://piedmont. ca.gov/, or contact Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell (pmacdonald@piedmont.ca.gov).

The meeting on May 19 will feature results of the city’s fair housing survey and pinnable map. Both were made accessible to residents on March 12, and the survey was available through April 15. The survey is one of several opportunities throughout the 18-month, city-led effort to ensure that new housing in Piedmont is feasible to develop, high in quality, and affordable. In the next Regional Housing Needs Cycle (RHNA), Piedmont is tasked with creating 587 housing units, compared to 60 units in the current RHNA cycle, representing a 979 percent increase. On March 2, city council issued a Request for Proposal [RFP] seeking a consulting firm to assist it in meeting the next RHNA planning period, which falls between 2023 and 2031. On May 3, City Council approved a proposal from Lisa Wise Consulting (LWC) to update the Housing Element of the city’s general plan. The consultant is expected to present the analysis of Piedmonters’ design preferences, understanding of housing laws, and other ideas drawn from the survey. The consulting firm will also provide recommendations for guiding principles for new tools to accelerate housing production. In addition, the first meeting will include a briefing on the Housing Element 2015 - 2022 annual progress report and a discussion of next steps and plans for a future community workshop. It will also include the election of a chair and vice chair of the committee. articles.text: Transportation is one of the two largest causes of greenhouse gas emissions in the City of Piedmont. As you may guess, this stems largely from gas powered cars. Driving is not unique to Piedmont. Transit is the largest emissions category for California and the U.S. Bay Area drivers collectively clock over 170 million miles every day. For environmental planners, emissions from driving obviously is a priority. Vehicle miles travelled, one metric used to measure usage, has been steadily climbing for years nationwide. Although 2020 has fewer VMT’s due to COVID, the larger issue still remains – people rely on driving to get around. They will continue to drive more unless something changes. How can governments convince residents to drive less? At the local government level, there are a few tools up our sleeves. One method is to change the built environment. Visit any street with lots of car traffic and you’ll notice something: the car lanes are a lot bigger than the sidewalks and bike lanes. Drivers respond to their environment. If a trip is easiest to take by driving, cars are going to be the main way people get to and from their destination. By using planning, we can make other methods of transportation more appealing, and hopefully increase those methods. Every person who takes the bus or walks means one fewer less car on the road. You can see how planning impacts commuting habits with highway construction. One common proposed way to deal with traffic has been to widen roadways. Study after study has shown that wider roadways eases traffic – but only temporarily. Five to ten years after the widening, traffic is back to its normal levels, and the road is wider, meaning more cars, and more pollutants (in economics, this phenomenon is “induced demand”). If you build it, they will come! The inverse of this is to expand oppor t u nities for non-drivers. Piedmont Public Works is always working on more sustainable solutions. Improving bike lanes and sidewalks are great examples of ways to offer alternatives that will entice people to change their habits. Other examples include “bulbouts,” which encourage cars to slow down around corners, speed bumps, improved signage, and enhanced crosswalk visibility. The list goes on. Many of these techniques have real effects on driving and walking habits. Another way to get people to change their driving habit is to make alternatives more appealing, either through cost or time savings, or having people associate alternatives with their values. In electric vehicle ads, you will often see monetary savings advertised, but there is usually environmental messaging as well. Manufacturers know that some buyers will be interested in having a smaller carbon footprint in addition to saving money. You can also change the building code to make electric vehicle charging easier for homeowners. Although encouraging people to use public transit, biking, and walking is a priority, driving will not go away overnight. The City of Piedmont tries to encourage drivers to switch to electric vehicles because they can use our carbon free electricity to charge, meaning far fewer emissions than a normal car. Ultimately, it is up to individuals how they choose to travel, but the built environment can help people make up their minds. Piedmont is hilly, but there is a lot of bike infrastructure in our little city. I encourage you to give it a try. If you have questions about electric vehicles, charging, or anything else related to sustainability, please reach out to Nate at nredinbo@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: Some alternatives to gas-powered cars

articles.text: The Bay Area “Bike to Wherever Day,” which replaces the popular “Bike to Work Day” due to the COVID-19 pandemic, will take place on Friday, May 21. Traditionally, Bike to Work Day is a celebration of cycling as a sustainable and healthy way to get to work, and serves as an opportunity for those who don’t usually bike commute to try it out. Many Piedmont residents and city staff participate in the event. Due to the prolonged pandemic, this year the event returns as Bike to Wherever Day. Make a pledge to ride and join other Bay Area residents by visiting https://bikeeastbay.org/events/bike-wherever-day-2021 before the day of the event. By signing up, you’ll receive a map of energizer stations, a digital goody bag, and suggested bicycle routes in Alameda County. You’ll receive a limited-edition tote bag at a contact-free energizer station this year. The East Bay Bike coalition also includes tips for new riders, opportunities to take free classes, and more digital resources.
articles.title: “Bike to Wherever” Day on May 21

articles.text: Sunday, May 2, was a splendid day for some service and adventure for Troop 6 Scouts. Working as the guest crew on the sailing ship SeaValor under the command of Eric Jones, the Scouts spent a beautiful day on the Bay learning and practicing seamanship skills, like piloting, setting and maintaining sails, as well as navigating the busy Bay. The Scouts also worked on their search and rescue skills, including visual search patterns as well as victim recovery. The sailing ship did numerous man-overboard drills with their certified rescue bear – a large stuffed bear fitted with a life jacket that mimics the weight and size of an overboard child. Upon arrival at Angel Island, patrols of scouts were dispatched A large group of Scouts from Troop 6 come onto land at a secluded spot on Angel Island to do some service Two Boy scouts from Piedmont’s Troop 6 test their navigational skills on the bowsprit of the SeaValor. by a Zodiac launch to a series of boat-in only beaches to collect trash and debris. During this activity, a dead gray whale was spotted floating in the shipping channel. SeaValor leaped into action, capturing the carcass and towing it to shore at a secluded beach for later review by the Marine Mammal Center. After this excitement, the SeaValor traveled to another boat-in beach for a scout-cooked lunch, waterplay, and exploration. While on the beach, more whales were spotted, but these whales were alive and active, feasting in the strong currents of the Racoon Straits between Tiburon and Angel Island. All in all, this was another memorable Troop 6 adventure.
articles.title: Troop 6 Scouts sail, work in day on the Bay

articles.text: As the world starts to open little bits at a time, it is easy to start to think that we can just go back to “the way things were.” We are starting slowly to do more things, go out more, maybe even see a few more people. My kids were able to see their grandparents who live in the Midwest for the first time in a year. And they were delighted. But it was also hard to realize how much time had passed since we had seen them. As we approach each moment that feels slightly more “normal,” I am noticing something fascinating. There is a process of grieving that is appearing for my kids and me, and I’ve heard the same thing from other parents. In experiencing things that should feel so natural, it is putting a magnifying glass on how completely weird the past year has been. If your young kids are experiencing this same cognitive dissonance of the joy of re-emerging and the realization of how strange their lived experience has been during Covid, here are a few creative ways to help kids express their feelings: 1. What colors are you feeling right now? Put out paint, crayons, markers, anything with lots of different color options and paper. Encourage your child to put on paper what color they are feeling. It can be lots of different colors or maybe Help kids use their creativity to work out their feelings. all one. But, sometimes just giving a child the opportunity to make a visual representation of what’s happening inside can allow those emotions to release. Plus, it gives you a starting point to help name the feelings or talk about them if that’s hard for your kids. 2. Story Game: What is Opposite? Laughter can sometimes be an incredible healing tool. This game will hopefully bring a smile to you and your child’s face. Person One suggests something that you do every day like, brushing your teeth. Person Two now has to come up with the complete opposite of that activity. For instance, “The opposite of brushing your teeth is eating super-duper chewy caramel.” Take turns back and forth. The idea of this game is to explore that everything in life has a flip side.

articles.text: The Piedmont Makers hosted the Annual Maker Faire on Saturday, May 8. Even with the socially-distanced event spread across the city, Piedmont’s vibrant maker community eagerly embraced a day filled with inventive DIY spirit, complete with car crashes, course changes, robotic exhibitions, and more. A Nerdy Derby racetrack was set up at Beach, Havens, and Wildwood schools. At each elementary school stop kids gravitated to tables of spare parts and decor and designed and refined their cars for speed and aesthetics. Different stops developed different themes on their own. Makers at Wildwood, as example, collected different (and ever larger) rocks to add weight and speed. A student at Beach built a jump that became a permanent track fixture. Cars did flips and occasionally landed on the other track, but almost all managed to keep going. Nerdy Derby cars were as varied as the participants. Cars featured battery-powered LED headlights, a laser-engraved car name, a banana bread body, minifigure drivers, a root beer bottle, custom-cut aerodynamic car bodies, wheels lubricated with graphite and silicone, and a balloon car. Kids and parents alike enjoyed the opportunity to exercise their creative spirit in an open, inventive, and supportive environment. At the robotics demo, people explored some of the cutting-edge maker technology that will soon populate the Piedmont Engineering Lab in the high school’s new STEAM building. The FIRST Robotics Competition (FRC) team members demoed their robots’ amazing dexterity and shooting capabilities. For those who were more comfortable maintaining distance, the Piedmont Makers organized five Maker Faire At-Home projects. Kids (and parents) built homemade Water Blasters using PVC pipes, designed Paper Circuit Cards just in time for Mother’s Day, made Glow-in-the-Dark Lava Lamps, balanced found objects into surprisingly stable sculptures, and made spinning Lego® tops. pages.text: 8 Wednesday, May 12, 2021 By Jon Schleuning The Piedmont Makers hosted the Annual Maker Faire on Saturday, May 8. Even with the socially-distanced event spread across the city, Piedmont’s vibrant maker community eagerly embraced a day filled with inventive DIY spirit, complete with car crashes, course changes, robotic exhibitions, and more. A Nerdy Derby racetrack was set up at Beach, Havens, and Wildwood schools. At each elementary school stop kids gravitated to tables of spare parts and decor and designed and refined their cars for speed and aesthetics. Different stops developed different themes on their own. Makers at Wildwood, as example, collected different (and ever larger) rocks to add weight and speed. A student at Beach 2021 Maker Faire a fantastic day of creativity built a jump that became a permanent track fixture. Cars did flips and occasionally landed on the other track, but almost all managed to keep going. Nerdy Derby cars were as varied as the participants. Cars featured battery-powered LED headlights, a laser-engraved car name, a banana bread body, minifigure drivers, a root beer bottle, custom-cut aerodynamic car bodies, wheels lubricated with graphite and silicone, and a balloon car. Kids and parents alike enjoyed the opportunity to exercise their creative spirit in an open, inventive, and supportive environment. At the robotics demo, people explored some of the cutting-edge maker technology that will soon populate the Piedmont Engineering Lab in the high school’s new STEAM building. The FIRST Robotics Competition (FRC) team members demoed their robots’ amazing dexterity and shooting capabilities. For those who were more comfortable maintaining distance, the Piedmont Makers organized five Maker Faire At-Home projects. Kids (and parents) built homemade Water Blasters using PVC pipes, designed Paper Circuit Cards just in time for Mother’s Day, made Glow-in-the-Dark Lava Lamps, balanced found objects into surprisingly stable sculptures, and made spinning Lego® tops. articles.text: Piedmont Boy Scouts JD Harrison, Alex Hilton, and Nicky Allen-Goix will attain the rank of Eagle at a National Court of Honor cereemony on May 15. Three Piedmont Boy Scouts from Troop 1 – JD Harrison, Alex Hilton, and Nicky AllenGoix – will be presented with the rank of Eagle Scout on May 15 at 3:30 p.m. in a National Court of Honor ceremony at the amphitheater behind the Piedmont Community Center. Harrison and Hilton began their scouting journey in elementary school, moving from Cub Scouts to Webelos and finally, onto Boy Scouts. Allen-Goix joined them in Troop 1 as a 7th grader and quickly became an integral part of the Troop. As they grew in age, so did their responsibilities, leadership, and service roles and experiences. They advanced through the ranks of Tenderfoot, Second Class, First Class, Star, Life, and finally, to Eagle. In addition to the 21 merit badges required to achieve the rank of Eagle, a scout must accomplish a service project which involves hours of planning, developing and leading others to help with its implementation. Often Eagle projects are chosen because of personal importance to the scout. All three dedicated their projects to students with fewer resources and opportunities. Allen-Goix created 50 backpacks filled with school supplies matching the list that first grade teachers at Cox Academy said each child needed for pandemic distant learning. The school serves a low-income population in Oakland. Harrison built three planter boxes to be used as an educational garden at the Booth Memorial Center Childcare in Oakland, which provides childcare for houseless families. Hilton built three planter boxes and a connecting bench for James Baldwin Academy, a middle school in Alameda for learning disabled children. All three Scouts are grateful for all the help they received from Troop 1 adult leaders, from their Eagle advisors, their fellow scouts and friends who helped them achieve this milestone in their scouting careers.
articles.title: Troop 1 celebrates 3 more Eagle Scouts

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council approved a contract in the amount of $118,504 with AVI SPL to enhance the city’s police department audio and visual capabilities. The contract will allow audio and visual enhancement for daily briefings, training, presentations, web conferencing and public information. Key areas that will be enhanced in the department include the briefing room, sergeants’ office, and police department public lobby. The police will outfit each of the spaces with digital video displays within an integrated system. It is expected to provide better communication and information to the public, as well as support the department’s critical work. The briefing room will be equipped with a multi-window display of content feeds, and the Sergeants’ office will be outfitted with a wall-mounted flat-panel display for web conferencing. AVI SPL was the lowest of two bidders for the contract. Community Oriented Policing Services (COPS) funds, from the 2020-2021 state budget, also will help fund the project. Dealbreaker for Mohammed bin Salman No one is doubting that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) bought Salvator Mundi via proxy. Its unveiling was expected at Louvre Abu Dhabi’s inaugural in 2018 but canceled. The exhibit Leonardo da Vinci at the Louvre the following year was expected to feature the rediscovered painting, but also was abruptly cancelled. By all accounts, Salvator Mundi hasn’t appeared in public since the November 2017 auction. Rumor has it spotted on display on bin Salman’s luxury yacht the Serene – or possibly stored on the yacht pending completion of a luxe museum in Medina, northwest Saudi Arabia. Or possibly it is in storage in Geneva. No one, and especially MBS, has any comment. A documentary film, The Savior for Sale, has the art world buzzing about why Salvator Mundi is in hiding. It describes an insider story insisting that the Louvre refused to commit to authenticating the painting as wholly Leonardo’s. The multiple restorations, it claims, make it impossible to discern how much See Americans in Paris on page 30 2005: Above shows the painting’s condition when sold to a New York City art dealer: its dimensions are 25” x 19” Continued from page 11 Carmen Bambach, a trusted Renaissance art historian wrote, “it’s a severely damaged original painting exhibiting large portions” of extensive restoration “with passages done by Leonardo himself”, meaning she disagreed with full attribution. Renaissance scholar Matthew Landrus of Oxford University said that “Leonardo produced the preparatory drawings” and “the artist is likely his pupil Bernardino Luini.” Art historian Martin Kemp rhetorically asked, “Was the National Gallery tacitly involved in a huge act of commercial promotion?” A noisy chorus of critics answered “yes,” though Kemp said, “of course not.” For the next three years the consortium pushed the pedal to the metal to sell – their costs from restoration to storage to insurance to travel – had climbed exponentially. They preferred placing the painting with a public museum in the U.S. – but an outright donation was out of the 2007: The art dealer authorized cleaning showing “Salvator Mundi” in visibly damaged condition. question. When a sale to any museum didn’t pan out, they agreed to seek a private buyer through Sotheby’s. Swiss art-broker Yves Bouvier of Singapore was interested but declined to pay the desired $150 million, and the exhausted dealers accepted $80 million. The next day, Bouvier flipped the painting to Russian billionaire Dmitry Rybolovlev for $127.5 million. Details of the deal gone awry leaked, and all parties were unhappy and filed lawsuits – still active three years later when Rybolovlev hired Christie’s to resell Salvator Mundi. Prior to 2005, two Leonardo da Vinci paintings remained unaccounted for, Leda and the Swan, a large-scale mythological allegory, and the Salvator Mundi (Savior of the World), which depicted Christ’s benediction. It was favored by private devotees and became wildly popular in this period. Disciples and followers of da Vinci created their own versions, and about 30 paintings exist today. Those attributed to da Vinci’s workshops in Florence and Milan are highly valued. articles.text: Staff Photos Kai Johnson hit the game-winning free throw to put PHS up 45-44 against Marin Catholic with 42 seconds left in the game. The girls’ basketball team remained undefeated at 7-0 after a busy week with five more victories, improving its record to 7-0 after recording five wins in the last seven days. Three were against non-league teams and two were WACC Foothill Division games. Results include a 49-44 win at Binks Rawlings Gym against Marin Catholic on Monday, May 10; a one-sided 68-28 win against San Marin on May 8 also at home; a 62-66 victory over San Leandro on the road on May 7; another rollover win, 65-25 against Alameda at home on May 5; and a surprisingly easy 62-36 over California on May 4. The most impressive win came against Marin Catholic, a perennial post-season playoff team in Piedmont’s Div. 4 North Coast Section bracket. They were the No. 3 seed in last year’s NCS playoffs. “We knew that Marin Catholic would be really tough, but our senior, Nakilah [Kai Johnson], really led us. This game was probably more fun than the others. Marin Catholic is a good Div. 4 team, and we love the competition,” said coach Bryan Gardere Each of Piedmont’s other opponents last week rank above PHS in the NCS divisions, California and San Leandro are Division 1, Alameda is Div. 2, and San Marin is Div. 3. All have larger enrollments than Piedmont, but the Highlanders’ level of talent made the difference. “We really picked it up at halftime and kept our composure. We attacked the basket and started getting points and free throws. We’re coming off a busy week and just had to focus,” said Johnson, the senior captain. 5-point win vs. Marin Catholic The 49-44 victory over the Wildcats was a defensive bout between the two Div. 4 contenders. The visitors from Kentfield held a 23-22 lead at halftime. After five lead changes, Trinity Zamora buried a 3-pointer from the top of the key to tie the game at 44-44 with 3:55 remaining. Piedmont’s defense then held Marin Catholic without a score for four minutes and limited them to 7 points in the final quarter. A Johnson free throw gave Piedmont a 45-44 lead, and freshman Natalie Martinez scored the final four points on a pair of free throws and layup on a pass from Brie Sotelo. Final stats: Zamora had 12 points, 10 rebounds, two assists, and two blocks. Johnson had 19 points and two rebounds. Martinez had nine points, three rebounds, two steals, and an assist. Maddie Hill had six points and two assists. Aniya Perine had three points. articles.text: Photos by Nancy Brahm Senior perimeter player Max Wagener had seven goals against Alameda. The Highlander boys’ water polo team has raced out to a 4-0 start of its season, no matter how short the season may be. Last Thursday, May 6, they defeated Alameda 12-8, and bowled over Encinal 12-6 on Tuesday, May 11. Both games were at the Encinal pool. The two victories give Piedmont a rare sweep of the two teams from the island of Alameda. It was a big pair of games for senior leaders Max Wagener and Spencer Stein. Wagener led the way against the Hornets with seven goals, and Stein scored four against the Jets. “Max’s length and outside shot is vital for us. With his size, Max can create shooting space from anywhere. Spencer in the hole set helps create opportunities for players like Max on the outside,” said coach John Savage. Sophomore goalie Dariush Kashani recorded 10 saves, four steals and one assist against the Hornets, and seven steals, three steals and two assists against the Jets. “Dariush is the anchor of our defense. He quarterbacks the defense and gets people in the right spot. He’s taking the next step in his development as a creator and passer,” explained Savage. Alameda win On Thursday, Piedmont and Alameda ended the first quarter in a 2-2 deadlock, but PHS bounced ahead 6-3 by halftime, and extending the lead to 10-6 by the start of the fourth quarter. They added two more in the final period. Antonio Rivera opened scoring for Piedmont after one minute of play, while Wagener scored his first of seven goals with 3:35 left in the first quarter for a 2-2 tie. After that it was all Piedmont. Rivera got his second on the board after 40 seconds in the second quarter, Wagener scored back-to-back to make it 5-2 with 2:37 left in the half, while Stein scored his second with 1:10 left in the quarter for a 6-3 lead. Wagener opened up the third quarter with a goal after one minute, while Stein made it 8-4 with Antonio Rivera had four goals against Encinal. Jake Hart had three goals against Encinal.

articles.text: The Piedmont girls’ water polo team opened the season dramatically with a 10-4 win against rival Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, May 4 at a neutral site, the Encinal pool. PHS beat the Dragons 8-6 in last year’s League Tournament. “It’s a unique season but we’re making the best of it and doing the best we can,” said senior captain Ella Wright, who led the Highlanders with five goals. “It was a game that we showed a lot of improvements and saw our team working together and communicating with each other.” Piedmont led 4-1 by the end of the first quarter, and both teams added a goal for a 5-2 score at halftime. More goals came in the third period, with the score 9-3 entering the final quarter. “We really worked as a complete unit, and it seemed to come together for that game. We only had a couple of practices prior to the game,” added Wright. Macie Gard scored the first goal of her varsity career to open the game a minute and 10 seconds into action. Wright put the Highlanders ahead 2-0 with a goal 45 seconds later, followed by Odessa Dando with her first goal in a PHS uniform. Wright scored again with 1:22 remaining. Wright got her hat trick with a third goal just prior to halftime. Gard scored to start the third quarter with after a minute of play and got attained a hat trick for herself with 1:59 remaining. Wright added her fourth and fifth goals to end the quarter. Rosie Feldman scored Piedmont’s final goal one minute into the fourth quarter. Ella Wright scored five goals in Piedmont’s season-opening 10-4 win over Bishop O’Dowd. Loss to Encinal Piedmont traveled to Alameda last night, May 11, for a game with Encinal, but lost 13-3. The Highlanders trailed 4-2 at the end of the first quarter and 7-3 at halftime but couldn’t maintain possession in the second half. Wright and Aoife Cain scored in the first quarter. It was Cain’s first goal of her high school career. Feldman scored in the second quarter. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-1) head to Berkeley tomorrow, Thursday, May 13 for a 5:00 p.m. game. The team will play at Alhambra HS in Martinez on Monday, May 17 at 4:00 p.m. Rosie Feldman scored against Bishop O’Dowd and Encinal.
articles.title: Girls Water Polo opens season with big win over O’Dowd

articles.text: Staff Photos Russell Tan had goals against Hayward and Tennyson. His goal in the game with Hayward was his first in a PHS uniform. Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team posted a pair of 5-0 shutout victories last week, beating Hayward on Tuesday, May 4 and Tennyson two days later. Both games were at their opponents’ fields. The wins bumped Piedmont’s record to 3-0-0 in a shortened 10-game season. “Both teams were quite low on their numbers,” explained PHS coach Todd Sullivan. “Tennyson didn’t have a Junior Varsity team, so I think that’s part of it. Both schools seem to be struggling a little bit.” The Highlanders are gearing up for a game with WACC rival, San Lorenzo, scheduled for this Saturday, May 16. The teams split their season series last year in a pair of scrappy, aggressive matches. PHS won 1-0 in the first meeting but lost 2-1 in the return match. The Highlanders won the 2019 Shoreline title and San Lorenzo finished second. “It’s always a fiery contest, and I expect the same again. The last time I talked to their coach, he mentioned that their numbers were affected, and they had some academic casualties as well. But all that goes out the window when facing a rival like that,” Sullivan added. 5-nil win vs. Tennyson The Highlanders thrashed Tennyson in Hayward on May 6. Piedmont led 3-0 at halftime and added two goals in the second half. “We’ve been able to make some tactical changes and get some extra players from the JV team. It’s a good opportunity for players to get minutes and extra experience this year,” explained Sullivan. Goals were scored by senior captain Connor Curtis, Russell Tan, Andre Stankiewicz, and Myles Gray. Zach Luna scored the fifth and final goal. 5-0 shutout vs. Hayward Piedmont led 1-0 after the first 15 minutes and led 2-0 by halftime with a goal from striker Aidan Woolwine on a slick through-ball from Curtis. It marked Woolwine’s first varsity goal. Curtis scored early in the second half, working the ball around the keeper, followed by Tan’s first high school goal, while Zach Luna killed the game 5-0. Tuesday vs. Encinal Piedmont traveled to Alameda on Tuesday, May 11, and came away with a satisfying 3-0 shutout of Encinal. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (4-0-0) heads to San Lorenzo on Saturday, May 15 for a 6:00 p.m. match. Connor Curtis scored goals on Hayward and Tennyson as well. Aidan Woolwine scored the first goal of his high school career against Hayward.

After the Dragons’ opened with a goal in the 3rd minute, the Highlanders tied it at 1-1 three minutes later when Zenobia Pellissier-Lloyd uncorked a hard shot on goal. The ball rebounded off the keeper directly to the feet Joyce Stern, who scored Piedmont’s only goal. PHS created some chances in the second half. Sophomore Emily Fitzgerald, last year’s leading scorer, had a shot on goal at the 44th minute. Pellissier-Lloyd had a shot attempt trail wide with 15 minutes left, and Ellie DeVan had a shot also go wide in the 76th minute. Tuesday vs. San Leandro Piedmont traveled to San Leandro last night, May 11, where they beat the Pirates 3-1. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-1-1) hosts Castro Valley tomorrow, Thursday, May 13 at 7:30 p.m. at Witter Field, then plays Berkeley on the road on Saturday evening, May 15 at 6:00 p.m. In back-to-back games at Witter Field last week, the girls’ soccer team came away with a 1-1 draw with Arroyo on Wednesday, May 5, but suffered a one-sided 5-1 loss to soccer rival Bishop O’Dowd on Thursday. The decision by the Western Alameda County Conference to schedule games on consecutive days was not widely applauded by coaches. Locally it required PHS coach Dan Chubbock to call up several players from the JV team for both matches in order to manage playing time to avoid injuries. “The league scheduled our games this year. [The game with O’Dowd was] a tough result, but we gave away some goals. We’re a young team; we’ll improve and get better. pages.text: 14 Wednesday, May 12, 2021 Highlanders post shutouts vs. Hayward, Tennyson Staff Photos Russell Tan had goals against Hayward and Tennyson. His goal in the game with Hayward was his first in a PHS uniform. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team posted a pair of 5-0 shutout victories last week, beating Hayward on Tuesday, May 4 and Tennyson two days later. Both games were at their opponents’ fields. The wins bumped Piedmont’s record to 3-0-0 in a shortened 10-game season. “Both teams were quite low on their numbers,” explained PHS coach Todd Sullivan. “Tennyson didn’t have a Junior Varsity team, so I think that’s part of it. Both schools seem to be struggling a little bit.” The Highlanders are gearing up for a game with WACC rival, San Lorenzo, scheduled for this Saturday, May 16. The teams split their season series last year in a pair of scrappy, aggressive matches. PHS won 1-0 in the first meeting but lost 2-1 in the return match. The Highlanders won the 2019 Shoreline title and San Lorenzo finished second. “It’s always a fiery contest, and I expect the same again. The last time I talked to their coach, he mentioned that their numbers were affected, and they had some academic casualties as well. But all that goes out the window when facing a rival like that,” Sullivan added. 5-nil win vs. Tennyson The Highlanders thrashed Tennyson in Hayward on May 6. Piedmont led 3-0 at halftime and added two goals in the second half. “We’ve been able to make some tactical changes and get some extra players from the JV team. It’s a good opportunity for players to get minutes and extra experience this year,” explained Sullivan. articles.text: In its first game on its home turf of Witter Field this season, Piedmont’s lacrosse team made short work of Berkeley in a 13-3 victory on Friday, May 7. “Our offense is starting to come around,” said coach Ryan Price of the 13-goal output. “Our defense has been solid, and it looked good. The team looked more balanced than the previous couple of games.” The Highlanders’ touted defense was ready on Friday, allowing just one goal in the first half and two after intermission. Piedmont continuously forced turnovers when the Yellowjackets entered its opponent’s half of the field. The PHS defense recorded six turnovers and scooped up 25 groundballs. Additionally, it killed five Berkeley penalty opportunities. “Defensively, we’ve had a lot of change but we’re chipping away getting better each game. Today was a pivotal game in trying to work cohesively as a team. We’re still not there yet, but I’m excited to see how we will look at the end of the season,” said defensive captain Alden Heske, who forced four Berkeley turnovers on the night. Piedmont led 3-0 after the first quarter and 7-1 going into halfGately, also a senior captain. The third quarter featured Dixon sending another assist to Nelson after four minutes, and Heske scoring after fielding a groundball in Piedmont’s own half and covering half the field a minute later. Biehn added Piedmont’s 10th goal with 3:35 left in the quarter. Fredericks lit up the final quarter with three goals, first with a score with 3:48 left, another quick one a minute later, then the final goal of the game with 2:01 on the clock. Final stats: Fredericks with four goals and four groundballs; Biehn with three goals, two assists, and three groundballs; Dixon with one goal, three assists, two ground balls; Nelson had a goal and groundball; Gately with one goal; and Heske with a goal, three groundballs, and four forced turnovers. See next week’s Post for game details. We did not play our best, but we showed very good glimpses– also glimpses of things we need to work on,” said Price. PHS got the show started with Luke Biehn scoring on a slick pass from J.D. Harrison two and a half minutes into the game. Jack Nelson scored after another two minutes, and Biehn scored again with 1:15 left in the first period. Piedmont tacked on four more goals in the second period, triggered by goalie Joe Hempeck running the length of the field to score after recording a save. Sophomore Soren Dixon flicked a pass to Greg Gately for a goal and a 5-0 lead with seven minutes remaining. MUSTANG (AGE 9-10) Ghosts 8, Jet Hawks 5 Aidan Shartsis shut out the Jet Hawks in two innings with 5 strikeouts. Gael Fierro took over, striking out 1, and Will Harris and Dylan Toyama finished the game, combining for 9 strikeouts. At the plate Eli Posamentier and Shartsis combined for 5 RBIs. Dylan Jerez hit a triple, driving in 2 runs. The Jet Hawks’ Travers Kemp held the Ghosts to just 1 run in 2 innings. The Jet Hawks offense came alive late in the game, scoring 3 runs in the 4th inning and 2 more in the fifth inning on hits by Cyrus Emanuelson and Charlie Myers. Emanuelson shut down the Ghosts in the 6th with 3 strikeouts. Emanuelson, the catcher, threw out 2 runners on the basepaths. PINTO (Age 7-8) Pirates 12, Padres 6 In the last game of the regular season on Sunday, May 9, the Pirates had a big 4th inning with their first maximum 5-run inning of the season. The offense was led by Finn Holder (driving the ball to the left side), Slammin’ Sammy Sohn (a 3rd-base-curling double), “Moonshot” Max, Jonah Kerr, and Zubin Sen. The Padres rallied to score six runs, including a triple by Theo Thomas that he nearly stretched into a homer with some riveting cat-andmouse base running. SOFTBALL — 8 & UNDER Night Wolves 5, Green Missiles 0 Behind the strong pitching of Isabel Martinez, Madi Farboud, and Eisa DeAvila, the 8U Night Wolves kept the score close for the first 3 innings until the bats came alive. Mailey Small scored the Wolves first run on a bases-loaded single by Gaby Chase. The Wolves broke the game open in the 4th inning, scoring 4 runs on consecutive two-out singles by Isabel Martinez, Vivi Nisenbaum, Dahlia Quintero, Bailey Gregovich, Abby Gregovich, Sophie Shartsis, and Audrey Lew. Night Wolves 9, Emerald Elephants 0 With strong pitching, great defense and big hits, the 8U Night Wolves continued their strong season with a shutout victory on May 8. Rookie pitcher Ashley Oh got the Night Wolves started with a 1-2-3 first inning, throwing all three hitters out at 1st base. In the bottom of the 1st, the Wolves got consecutive singles by Sophie Shartsis, Bailey Gregovich and Ashley Oh. Abby Gregovich then smashed a deep drive down the left field line for a grand slam home run. In the 2nd inning, the bats stayed hot with more hits by Evelyn MacMichael, Mailey Small, Isabel Martinez and Madi Farboud. Eisa DeAvila doubled, and Catriona Mactaggart capped the scoring with a booming 3-run triple.

articles.text: A group of five Piedmont artists, all of whom were featured at the annual Art Walk recently, will have an exhibit at the Piedmont Center for the Arts from May 21 through June 6. articles.text: This is the last weekend to visit the 7th annual Juried Art Show at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. It will be open on Saturday and Sunday May 15-16 from 12 p.m. to 2 p.m. A total of 35 pieces of art were selected by two guest jurors from a record-high 500 submissions. The artwork appearing in the exhibition, the first public event PCA has held this year, was selected by Rene de Guzman, Senior Curator of Art at Oakland Museum of California, and Danielle Fox, Principal of Slate Gallery in Oakland. Artists from nine counties in the greater Bay Area were invited to enter the competition, resulting in an eclectic range of artwork, including oil on canvas, pigment prints, and photography, The Juried Art show debuted in November 2013, PCA Board Member Valerie Corvin explained. The annual event is made possible through the John P. Thornborrow Memorial Fund, which was created to support local artists and is distributed as a cash prize to three selected artists. Thornborrow was a Bay Area artist who created hundreds of artwork across a variety of mediums. In 2008, Thornborrow’s work was selected for the Pro Arts Juried Annual, which was juried by Laura Hoptman, Senior Curator of the New Museum in New York. He continued to produce artwork until his death in 2011; his print, “Fake Flowers,” hangs as part of the Juried Art Show exhibit. “Every year, the Juried Art Staff photo The 7th annual Juried Art Show ends this Sunday at the Center for the Arts. show aims to give emerging artists from the Bay Area an opportunity to gain exposure with top curators and gallerists and the general public,” explained Corvin. “Thanks to the John P. Thornborrow Memorial Endowment Fund, total cash awards of $4,000 [are] allocated to juror-designated award winners. First place winner Pep Ventosa was awarded $2,500 for “Watching the Night Sky.” Second place for $1,000 went to Tamara Avery for “#114 Justice?,” and See C Oh took third place and $500 for “Tranquility.” Three honorable mentions were also awarded: Brian Molyneaux’s photo on a metal sheet, “Moon, Neferttiti, Barry”; Nelson Loskamp’s “Cay on the Beach;” and Daniel San Souci’s “Flight of the Monarchs.” Honorable mentions received ribbons. Corvin said that the selections this year produced the “best Juried Art Show yet” in the event’s seven-year existence at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. “The art is a high level, and it feels like you are in a downtown art gallery, it’s very exciting,” she added. Visitors should sign up in advance for a time slot at https:// bit.ly/3mwWuwT. Gallery viewers will be asked to sanitize hands upon entry, wear face masks, and observe social distancing. For more information, see www.piedmontcenterforthearts. org. Napoleon Bonaparte Ludwig van Beethoven Niccolo Paganini had the talent of genius and the morals of an ape. Another apocryphal story tells us that Napoleon tried to play the cello. The most famous cellist of the time had just completed a command performance. After the cellist finished his performance, Napoleon asked to try to play the same cello himself. The story goes that his spurs put some gauges in the cello. Wouldn’t you know it… That cello became the most expensive Stradivarius in the world. The great musical liberator Beethoven was so inspired by Napoleon that he dedicated his colossal Third Symphony to the Frenchman. When Napoleon crowned himself Emperor, Beethoven obliterated the name of Napoleon from the title page. His rage was so furious that he made a hole in the paper. Up until then, Beethoven had faith that Napoleon would be the great leader for all of mankind. Paganini‘s connection with Napoleon is somewhat oblique. He was hired to be the violin soloist to Napoleon’s sister. During his employ, he dedicated at least two of his most important compositions to the emperor. One was the “Napoleon Sonata” which caused a sensation because it was played entirely on one string. No violinist had ever done this before. The other famous composition also caused a sensation. It is known today as Duetto Amoroso. Even though it was written as a birthday present for Napoleon, Paganini really intended it as a love letter to his employer. As you can guess, Paganini was more interested in love than in politics. All of these three great men knew that music has the greatest effect on the emotions. Napoleon spoke for all when he said: “music is the soul of love, the sweetness of life, the consolation for sorrow, and the companion of innocence.“ That’s about all that needs to be said. And now for present times After such a long time, concert life is showing signs of rejuvenation. My wife and I attended a concert in Saint Mary’s Cathedral on Sunday as performed by the “Quantum Quintet.” Traffic over the bridge to San Francisco was miserable, but the concert was a delight. We missed the first number on the program but we did enjoy Dvorak’s superb Piano Quintet. The musicians were pianist Jeanette Wilkin Tieze, violinists Wendy Loder and Odin Mitaine, violist Meg Eldridge, and cellist Joel Cohen. Throughout the performance, the musicians were ever-alert to the musical exigencies of the spirit of the music. The expressive second movement was particularly heartfelt. The fast scherzo movement was taken at a conservative tempo, proving that it is not necessary to play fast and loud to be effective. This type of playing should serve as a good example to other performers who seem to think that the faster and louder they play the greater will be the ovation. Napoleon’s advice should be the guideline: Music is the soul of love.

articles.text: By Joseph Gold There are a few numbers which have meaning to all of us. If I say G8, you know what I am talking about. In psychology, there is the big five. CURRENTLY ON VIEW The 7th Annual Juried Art Show continues at the Center for the Arts through May 16. Gallery hours are 12:00 to 2:00 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays. From a record-high 500 submissions of original art created within the past year, 35 works of art were selected by guest jurors René de Guzman, Senior Curator of Art at Oakland Museum of California, and Danielle Fox, Principal of Slate Gallery in Oakland. Through an endowment by the family of John P. Thornborrow, cash awards of $4,000 will be awarded to the top award winners, with an emphasis on honoring emerging artists in the Bay Area. All guests must wear masks, observe social distancing and use hand santizers upon entering. The exhibition will be limited to a maximum of 25 visitors at a time. No food or drink is permitted. The artists exhibitng their work are Valerie Corvin, Mike Welch, Paula Valenzuela, Jon Schleuning and photographr Brian Molyneaux. Artists from nine counties in the greater Bay Area were invited to enter the competition, resulting in an eclectic range of artwork, including oil on canvas, pigment prints, and photography, The Juried Art show debuted in November 2013, PCA Board Member Valerie Corvin explained. The annual event is made possible through the John P. Thornborrow Memorial Fund, which was created to support local artists and is distributed as a cash prize to three selected artists. Thornborrow was a Bay Area artist who created hundreds of artwork across a variety of mediums. In 2008, Thornborrow’s work was selected for the Pro Arts Juried Annual, which was juried by Laura Hoptman, Senior Curator of the New Museum in New York. First place winner Pep Ventosa was awarded $2,500 for “Watching the Night Sky.” Second place for $1,000 went to Tamara Avery for “#114 Justice?,” and See C Oh took third place and $500 for “Tranquility.” Three honorable mentions were also awarded: Brian Molyneaux’s photo on a metal sheet, “Moon, Neferttiti, Barry”; Nelson Loskamp’s “Cay on the Beach;” and Daniel San Souci’s “Flight of the Monarchs.” Honorable mentions received ribbons.
