For more information, see www.piedmontcenterforthearts. org. The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet Can you name the Big Three? By Joseph Gold There are a few numbers which have meaning to all of us. If I say G8, you know what I am talking about. In psychology, there is the big five. The four Horsemen of the Apocalypse figure prominently in religion. The big three are the victors of World War I or World War II. But in world culture, the big three could be only Napoleon, Beethoven, and Paganini. Napoleon was the catalyst in this group, and as such, he inspired the great musical liberators who were Beethoven and Paganini. The connection of these three giants is fascinating. Taken as a group, they are a mighty Trinity. Napoleon was the catalyst in many ways. However, he gets a bad rap. His death almost exactly 200 years ago requires a reevaluation of his deeds. Everyone knows the famous oration of Mark Anthony in Shakespeare’s play Julius Caesar. He could have been writing about Napoleon when he said: “The evil men do lives after them. The good is oft interred with their bones.” The victors at Waterloo made sure that Napoleon’s good deeds were besmirched. The English referred to Napoleon as ”the little corporal”, though he was never a corporal. He started his military career as a captain of artillery. As for being little, he was 5-feetsix, which was certainly not short in his era. Paganini was always considered a tall man, yet he was 5-feet-five. Napoleon always loved music. Some music critics commented that his voice was not very good, but what he accomplished has enriched the world ever since. The great Paris Conservatory had been closed for many years. Napoleon reopened it, financed it richly, and saw to it that it continued in glory. Napoleon supported the arts financially and made sure that everyone knew he was in attendance at the performances. He always tried to sit next to the most famous musicians of the time. He went to the opera and to the ballet. Some of Napoleon‘s favorite composers were the Italian opera composer Paisiello and the French composer Mehul. As an aside, one of Paisiello’s contemporaries said that Napoleon Napoleon Bonaparte Ludwig van Beethoven Niccolo Paganini had the talent of genius and the morals of an ape. Another apocryphal story tells us that Napoleon tried to play the cello. The most famous cellist of the time had just completed a command performance. After the cellist finished his performance, Napoleon asked to try to play the same cello himself. The story goes that his spurs put some gauges in the cello. Wouldn’t you know it… That cello became the most expensive Stradivarius in the world. The great musical liberator Beethoven was so inspired by Napoleon that he dedicated his colossal Third Symphony to the Frenchman. When Napoleon crowned himself Emperor, Beethoven obliterated the name of Napoleon from the title page. His rage was so furious that he made a hole in the paper. Up until then, Beethoven had faith that Napoleon would be the great leader for all of mankind. Paganini‘s connection with Napoleon is somewhat oblique. He was hired to be the violin soloist to Napoleon’s sister. During his employ, he dedicated at least two of his most important compositions to the emperor. One was the “Napoleon Sonata” which caused a sensation because it was played entirely on one string. No violinist had ever done this before. The other famous composition also caused a sensation. It is known today as Duetto Amoroso. Even though it was written as a birthday present for Napoleon, Paganini really intended it as a love letter to his employer. As you can guess, Paganini was more interested in love than in politics. All of these three great men knew that music has the greatest effect on the emotions. Napoleon spoke for all when he said: “music is the soul of love, the sweetness of life, the consolation for sorrow, and the companion of innocence.“ That’s about all that needs to be said. And now for present times After such a long time, concert life is showing signs of rejuvenation. My wife and I attended a concert in Saint Mary’s Cathedral on Sunday as performed by the “Quantum Quintet.” Traffic over the bridge to San Francisco was miserable, but the concert was a delight. We missed the first number on the program but we did enjoy Dvorak’s superb Piano Quintet. The musicians were pianist Jeanette Wilkin Tieze, violinists Wendy Loder and Odin Mitaine, violist Meg Eldridge, and cellist Joel Cohen. Throughout the performance, the musicians were ever-alert to the musical exigencies of the spirit of the music. The expressive second movement was particularly heartfelt. The fast scherzo movement was taken at a conservative tempo, proving that it is not necessary to play fast and loud to be effective. This type of playing should serve as a good example to other performers who seem to think that the faster and louder they play the greater will be the ovation. Napoleon’s advice should be the guideline: Music is the soul of love.

articles.text: Soprano Vanessa Becerra will be featured in Opera San Jose’s recital program on May 14, Opera San Jose, in partnership with Los Angeles Opera, has created a recital program featuring Latina composers. The program was prepared with the assistance of Indiana University’s Latin American Music Center and will stream on Facebook and YouTube on May 14, after which it will be available on-demand. The program is curated by Los Angeles Opera Artist in Residence Russell Thomas, and features Opera San Jose resident company members. It will include songs by Maria Luisa Escobar, Consuelo Velazquez, Modesta Bor, and Angela Peralta. Four contemporary composers, Gabriela Lena Frank, Tania Leon, Mariela Rodriguez, and Irma Urteaga, will be represented. The featured performers in the Latina Composers recital are soprano Vanessa Becerra, tenor Enrique Santelli, and baritone Efrain Solis. Becerra and Santelli are both alumni of Los Angeles Opera’s Domingo-Colburn-Stein Young Artist Program. “The songs celebrate an incredibly rich and diverse range of musical works created by Latinas over the past two centuries throughout the Americas,” said Thomas. “Their music will transport audiences to Mexico, Venezuela, Argentina, Cuba, and Peru, all while honoring the women who wrote each piece. It was fantastic to partner with the incredible team at Opera San Jose on this gorgeous new project.” You can sign up for the livestream by visiting: https://www. operasj.org/latina-composers-recital/.
articles.title: Opera San Jose recital program to feature Latina composers May 14

articles.text: This is the last weekend to watch San Francisco Opera’s production of The Barber of Seville, the company’s first live production since the health pandemic closed venues last year. The new, 90-minute adaptation of Rossini’s romantic comedy is sung in English. This performance will feature Lucas Meachem as Figaro, Daniela Mack as Rosina, Alek Shrader as Almaviva and Philip Skinner as Doctor Bartolo, with music performed by the San Francisco Opera Orchestra. “The Barber” is an opera buffa in two acts, and is widely regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of comedy within music. The play follows the story of a cunning barber who helps a young ward escape from the custody of her guardian, and into the arms of a noble suitor. The opera is directed by Matthew Ozawa. The final performances are Friday and Saturday, May 14 and 15. Both performances will be drive-in productions held at Marin Center in San Rafael. To purchase tickets, visit: https://sfopera.com/on-stage/ barber/?gclid=Cj0KCQjwl9GCBh DvA R IsA Fu n hsl-mpHzLjDH-jrSuLjWBFKDQfyzvdUGzz8yUltPUWy954eqM1ctonsaAnCZEALw_wcB.
articles.title: Last chance this weekend to see SF Opera’s Barber of Seville

articles.text: Cast members rehearse for Youth Musical Theater Company’s production of 13 the Musical opening May 22 in Berkeley. Youth Musical Theater Company (YMTC) presents 13 the Musical for six performances from May 22–30. It will be the third Covid-compliant musical the company has produced during the pandemic. After their March 2020 production of The Music Man was shut down mid-run, YMTC asked their donors to help raise funds to build an outdoor stage at its Aquatic Park rehearsal space in order to continue offering in-person programming. In October 2020, they produced The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee with a small audience of family members on the stage. This February, they produced a concert version of Sondheim’s Merrily We Roll Along with a slightly larger audience sitting on newly built outdoor bleachers. Now, using updated state and county Covid requirements and with a teenage cast that is half-vaccinated and a creative team and crew that is fully vaccinated, they are highlighting 13 young artists in this delightful and funny musical. Jason Robert Brown’s jazzy pop-rock score tells the classic story of coming-of-age against all odds. Professional directors, designers and technicians work alongside the student both onstage and off as part of the Theater Arts Apprentice Program (TAAP). The six piece band features professional Bay Area musicians, led by music director Jon Gallo, and includes Piedmont High freshman Miranda Long on guitar. “It is always especially exciting when we can produce a musical that places teenagers at the center of its story. It is surprising how few musicals do this, given the popularity of musical theater among young people,” said YMTC Artistic Director Jennifer Boesing. Due to the limited audience size and social distancing requirements, all shows are now sold out. YMTC will return in July with Light in the Piazza. For more information, visit: ymtcbayarea.org.
articles.title: YMTC brings live theater back to Berkeley

articles.text: Aurora Theatre Company is presenting an audio play adaption of Toni Morrison’s novel, The Bluest Eye, available to stream now through May 21. Morrison’s debut novel comes to the Aurora stage in an adaption by playwright Lydia Diamond, and follows young protagonist Pecola Breedlove. The novel is told from Claudia MacTeer’s perspective, the daughter of Pecola’s foster parents. Pecola dreams of having blue eyes like the young actress Shirley Temple, believing that blue eyes would make her more accepted and beautiful. Morrison is a Pulitzer and Nobel Prize-winning writer whose works are praised for addressing the harsh realities and consequences of racism in the United States. The audio drama cast Michael Asberry as Chilly, Sam Jackson as Frieda, Cathleen Riddley as Mama, Jeunee Simon as Claudia and Jasmine Williams as the protagonist Pecola. Diamond is a nationally recognized award-winning playwright and currently Cathleen Riddley is Mama in Aurora Theatre’s audio adaption of Toni Morrison’s novel, The Bluest Eye. serves on the faculty at Boston University. She has taught playwriting at Columbia College, DePaul University and Loyola University in Chicago. Her other credits include The Gift Horse, Stick Fly, The Inside, and Voyeurs de Venus. To listen to the audio drama any time from now through May 21, visit https://www.auroratheatre.org/thebluesteye.
articles.title: Aurora Theatre presents The Bluest Eye as audio play

articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir will present its annual Spring Recital on May 8. The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choirs’ youngest choral groups, the Kinder and Training departments, presented their 2021 Spring Recital on Saturday, May 8. The concert showcased the departments’ progress in choral training, and featured virtual choir performances from the six ensembles within both departments. The concert is live-streaming on YouTube. The kinder choir consists of students age five and six. Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir introduces intermediate music skills to students grades one and up in the training department, the second echelon of the three-department program. After graduating from the kinder department, students move on to the training department, where they deepen their understanding of dictation, music theory, and beginning stage presence. They also expand their musical literacy and begin to learn how to sight-read. Many other basic skills are solidified here, such as ear training, breath control, and vowel formation. These skills are necessary as young students’ voices begin to mature. The kinder and training departments will join the older performing department on June 5 Piedmont Choirs’ annual Spring Sing. Over 200 singers from all 10 of the organization’s departments will present this special choral performance. Both events are free to watch; because of the generosity of patrons, Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir is able to offer its entire 2020 - 2021 “Discovering our Voices” virtual concert season free to the public via YouTube. Donations in any amount toward normal ticket prices offset production costs. For more information, and to register on Eventbrite for the event, visit https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/ event-calendar.
articles.title: Entire PEBCC student body to perform on June 5

articles.text: Gold Coast Chamber Players’ season finale, “Dvorak’s America,” will conclude their collection of virtual concerts on Saturday, May 15. Streaming access has been extended one week and will include a pre-concert talk by noted musicologist Kai Christiansen. “Dvorak’s America” explores the impact that Spirituals and Native American music had on Czech composer Antonin Dvorak during his time in America. The project, three years in the making, highlights the interconnectedness of these cultures. The program will feature the composer’s Sting Quintet, op. 97, and the Lento from his String Quartet op. 96, both of which are known as “the American.” Original music performed on heart of American music,” and the genre serves as perhaps the greatest Western influence on the composer. Spirituals, sung by soprano Michele Kennedy, include “Swing Low Sweet Chariot,” “By an’ By,” and “My Lord What a Morning.” Concluding the program will be “Goin’ Home,” from the composer’s New World Symphony. Alexander String Quartet will lead the ensemble, marking one of the first performances with their new violist, David Samuel. Violist Pamela Freund-Striplen, founder of Gold Coast Chamber Players, and a frequent collaborator with the Quartet, will join its members for “Dvorak’s America.” The event will be available through May 15. Viewers will learn that the algorithms designed to capture your attention are also profoundly affecting your brains and beliefs in ways that directly threaten democracy. An internal Facebook report by sociologist Monica Lee states, “64% of the people who joined extremist groups on Facebook did so because the algorithms steered them there.” Other documentaries have raised concerns about the impact of social media on privacy and even democracy. This film’s advantage is that the speakers in The Social Dilemma include top executives from Twitter, Instagram, Pinterest, Facebook, and others. articles.text: Free Solo follows Alex Honnold as he climbs El Capitan in Yosemite National Park. Free Solo is a National Geographic documentary film, directed by award-winning filmmaker Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and shot by world-renowned photographer and mountaineer Jimmy Chin. It is a stunning and unflinching portrait of professional mountain climber Alex Honnold and focuses primarily on his obsessive preparation to fulfill a lifelong dream. His goal is to climb the face of the world famous 3,200-foot El Capitan in Yosemite National Park without safety gear. What “free” means is that such a climb surpasses all definitions of extreme sports, existing in a realm that defies all explication and enters into the mystical, a silent meditation on life – or death. To climb El Capitan solo and survive is one of the greatest athletic feats of any kind. There is nothing else in sports that compares. The actual filming of such an attempt is also breathtaking in its beauty and sustained sense of risk (and vertigo). It’s beautiful. There is also a sense of controlled and disciplined panic on the part not only of Honnold but of Chin and the film crew. It is quietly gripping, conveyed with each harrowing pitch on the ascent up the granite face. To climb solo at such heights is to exist in the zone of the unblemished, beyond anything that can be imagined. To attempt such a climb is to celebrate life intensely, risking all you so profoundly love and hold dear. How could Free Solo be anything less than exhausting not only for Honnold, but equally for the photographers and director, who, as the film shows, are deeply conflicted by recording and enabling what could so easily be a wrenching tragedy. The film does attempt to explore the “why?” and pushes Honnold, not the most emotive of persons, for explanations that he is either unable or unwilling to share. He says simply that he is doing what he loves to do and is fortunate to be able to support what he acknowledges is his passion. Inherent in his choice, he admits, is the impact it has on those who care about him, especially his partner Sanni McCandless. It is her tears at the end of the film that are parenthetical to a reality she can’t bear to contemplate. It is an emotion that haunts this compelling, most amazing film. Free Solo. Documentary. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG-13. View on VUDU, Prime Video. Alex Honnold in Free Solo.

articles.text: Berkeley Art Museum’s Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) is streaming a new documentary that profiles eight Bay Area artists. The film, Tell Them We Were Here, was created by Gallery 16 founder Griff Williams and filmmaker Keelan Williams, and made its worldwide debut in the virtual cinema of the BAMPFA. The film features local curators from BAMPFA, Oakland Museum and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SF MOMA). It includes an appearance by filmmaker Eleanor Coppola, and Matt Gonzalez, chief attorney of the San Francisco Public Defender’s office, who is also an artist. The eight Bay Area artists highlighted in the documentary are Amy Franceschini, Sadie Barnette, Alicia McCarthy, Jim Goldberg, Tucker Nichols, Lynne Hershman Leeson, Nigel Poor, and Michael Swaine. The collection of art is a mix of photography, sculpting, podcasting, graffiti, and street art. The artists’ work spans decades and are considered to have made an emotional or cultural impact in the Bay Area. The film’s run time is 87 minutes, and has been available to stream since May 7 through BAMPFA’s virtual cinema. For streaming information, visit: https://bampfa.org/about/aboutbampfa.

articles.text: A scene from The Mitchells vs The Machines. Review by Chris Honoré Hollywood Writers have gotten a lot of mileage out of the dysfunctional family road trip, one that relies on a familiar trope: what can go wrong will go wrong, resulting, for the audience, in headshaking chuckles to outright laughter. At the center of The Mitchells vs The Machines is Katie Mitchell (Abbi Jacobson), a teen who loves movies, yearns to be a filmmaker, and dreams of moving to California, heartland of the fantasy industry. She lives with her mom, Linda (Maya Rudolph), maker of grotesquely charming cupcakes; a mutt named Monchi; her little brother Aaron (Mike Rianda), obsessed with dinosaurs; and her dad, Rick (Danny McBride), a hulking outdoors Mr. fix-it guy with whom she doesn’t quite feel at ease. But then he’s the kind of guy who gives you a non-slip screwdriver as a birthday gift, loves to build stuff, and worries that Katie’s dream of making movies will likely end in failure. He wonders where his little girl (who believed he could do anything) has gone, causing him to ask: who is this budding, newbie teenstranger called Katie? Inspired, Rick decides that what the family should do is not say goodbye to Katie at the airport as she heads off to college, but cancel her ticket and take a family road trip, giving them all a chance to reconnect. Katie is not so sure and is a little mortified at the thought of arriving at her new college with (gasp) her parents. Nevertheless, so begins a series of really “wide-eyed”, “good grief” misadventures from food poisoning to a visit to a seedy dinosaur theme park, and way more, all punctuated with minor family squabbles. Let’s just say that there is a lot going on, much of it hyper-manic, reactions that gives new meaning to the term “bug-eyed.” Act three, unexpectedly, involves techie stuff, involving a hoodie-wearing IT guy named Mark Bowman (Eric André), a billionaire who has invented countless bots, and smart phones implanted with the ubiquitous voice of PAL (Olivia Colman). Of course, the bots are deemed benign and created to serve their master… sure thing. As it turns out the bots have a scheme to send all the humans into outer space and then create a bot-machine utopia. And so, it’s up to the Mitchells to save the world and undermine the bot plan and thereby avoid an impending apocalypse. The animation dazzles, the plot is a media-mix of cacophony and wonderfully stylized, engaging, audacious lunacy. But still, at the center of all the chaos is the Katie-Dad relationship wherein they team up to save the world, and in the process affectionately realize the talents they each possess. Kids will be wonderfully engaged with this charming, animated film. The Mitchells vs The Machines. Animation. Directed by Mike Rivanda and Jeff Rowe. Voices of Abbi Jacobson. Danny McBride, and Maya Rudolph. 1 hr., 54 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: Take the kids to see The Mitchells vs The Machines

articles.text: Mustang is a delight, stitched together with threads of melancholy. Directed and co-written by Deniz Erguven, a French-Turkish filmmaker and writer in her debut film, it’s in Turkish with an ensemble of five captivating actresses that enchant from the opening scenes. Each is remarkable. They portray sisters all in their early to mid teens – with the exception of Lale (Gunes Sensoy), who is perhaps 11 or 12. Each is brimming with youthful vitality and together they form a collective of willful sweetness that illustrates their bond as well as their rebelliousness. Each is coltish with rich, streaming hair, the intensity of their emotions palpable and wonderful. What is done to one is done to all, and though they argue and disagree, when faced with an impenetrable force like their grandmother (Nihal Koldas), they immediately form a united front. Orphaned when young, they are now being raised by their grandmother and uncle Erol (Aybeck Pekan). Though they vary in age, all, with the exception Lale, are on the cusp of young womanhood. Their youthful innocence is self-evident, their connection to one another unbreakable. The story takes place in a small town in northern Turkey on the Black Sea. It is the last day of school and summer stretches before them. Excited, filled with anticipation, they walk home with a group of boys along the shoreline of the ocean and end up splashing in the water, their uniforms drenched, some sitting on the shoulders of the boys as they try to push each other into the water. A neighbor sees them laughing and playing like young seals and reports their behavior to their grandmother who is scandalized and angry. She accuses them of pleasuring themselves while sitting on the shoulders of the boys – an idea completely foreign to the sisters. And so, the grandmother begins a campaign of cloistering the sisters as if they were nuns, having taken vows of chastity. With the uncle’s support, the grandmother begins to fashion their two-story house into a fortress, buttressing the walls, attempting to prevent every avenue of escape the girls might use to slip out into the night (or day). As well, she undertakes a program of preparing the girls for matrimony – cooking lessons, cleaning, sewing – an idea that shocks and even repels the sisters. Of course, both the uncle and grandmother are dealing with a collective life force, a blossoming sexuality that is culturally forbidden as a topic for discussion and behavior to be repressed at all cost. And so, what Lale regards as a “wife factory” is set in motion with the grandmother orchestrating arranged marriages for the older girls. In contrast, Lale can only think about escaping the fate that has descended on her muchloved sisters. She plots and plans her freedom, struggling with the cultural imperatives that confront every young Turkish woman. She begins a pitched, subversive battle to find an alternative for herself. She knows intuitively that she is facing a rigid (even violent), patriarchal future and rejects a life in which she has no choices. Mustang is a moving and engaging window into a culture far removed from the West. To the film’s credit, it avoids expository judgment; instead it allows circumstances and contrasts to carry and display a chasm of cultural differences in what proves to be a beautifully crafted and remarkable narrative. As an aside, Mustang was selected in 2015 as Best Foreign Language Film by the Academy of Motion Pictures. It is that good. Mustang. In Turkish with subtitles. Directed by Deniz Gamze Ergüven. Starring Gunes Senjoy, Tugba Sunguroglu, and Elit Iscan. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG-13. A scene from Mustang.
articles.title: Mustang a beautiful, moving film from Turkey

Bodies were buried very close to each other, sometimes on top of each other. There was no room for plantings and no temptation to linger. was filled. Oakland officials moved the cemetery an additional 10 blocks away to Webster and 17th Streets, near today’s Snow Park. At that time, it was well out of town. Bodies were reinterred in the new Oakland Cemetery. Record keeping was poor and not all of the bodies were reinterred. When Mountain View Cemetery was established, these bodies were moved again. Oakland continued to grow, and by 1863 this second cemetery was nearly full. It was no longer out of town. It was blocking civic expansion and posing a health hazard. Dr. Samuel Merritt formed a board of trustees of twelve Oakland leaders for yet a new cemetery. Trustee Isaac Brayton owned 200 acres of land two miles out of town – so far from downtown Oakland that development would never encroach on this land. In February of 1864, the Mountain View Cemetery trustees bought the land for $13,000 and began looking for someone to develop it as an attractive rural cemetery. Fortunately, Frederick Law Olmsted was in California. He was already famous for designing Central Park in New York City and had travelled to Mariposa in 1863 to manage a gold mining operation. In 1864, Olmsted met with the Mountain View Cemetery trustees and said he’d take a look at the land. The bare hills intrigued him, and he saw the land as a palette for some of his landscaping ideas. In September of 1864, Olmsted signed an agreement with the Mountain View Cemetery trustees. It was his first independent commission and the only cemetery Olmsted designed. Olmsted’s design of Mountain View Cemetery followed the principles of the Rural Cemetery Movement, which began in the 1830s in Boston, Philadelphia, and New York. Cemeteries were no longer barren and desolate. They were designed to be sanctuaries — a place of solitude, quiet, and beauty. Cemeteries were planted with trees, shrubs, and flowers, and families could leave the city, picnic on the cemetery grounds, and take long walks among the trees in peaceful settings. Frederick Law Olmsted took one look at the surveyor’s topographical map of the Mountain View Cemetery site and saw the best design for the cemetery. He traced his finger in a straight line from the entrance up the center of the land toward the top of the hill. The bare hills intrigued Olmsted who saw them as a palette for his landscaping ideas. He divided this central avenue into several parts with circles he called “rond points” where pathways radiated. In the flatter portion of land, the pathways were straight and defined diamond-shaped plots. In the hillier portions, the pathways followed the contours of the land and formed the boundaries for cemetery plots. Olmsted’s plan included trees and shrubbery, like a park. He recommended that the trustees line the central avenue with cypress trees, and that they plant hedges around the plots. He also urged the trustees to plant large trees of simple form and compatibility and listed five specific trees for the cemetery. To the native California live oak and Monterey cypress, he added Italian cypress, Olmsted’s original 1864 plan for Mountain View Cemetery with its Main Avenue up the center and “rond points” with radiating paths. Olmsted designed the Main Avenue as a straight line through the cemetery.

Dr. Samuel Merritt formed a board of trustees of twelve Oakland leaders for yet a new cemetery. articles.text: Facing a large remodel, whether several rooms or a whole house, it can be hard to imagine bringing a whole team together from the start. But I can tell you, having completed several homes like this where we — designer, architect, and contractor — meet regularly with each other and the client from the beginning, rather than the client hiring us in stages or working with us separately, the results are absolutely worth it. Recently my firm completed a fabulous whole house remodel in Marin County. The original structure was built in 1920 and had been added onto and revised repeatedly over the decades to become a spacious 4-bedroom, 5-bathroom estate. The new homeowners, Ken and Pam Hirsch, felt the flaws in the layout immediately, particularly in the kitchen, and wanted to improve their forever home before moving in. So, they hired architect Debbi Peterson. She describes the challenges we faced with the house: “It had this great presence, the lot and the landscaping and the approach. But once you were inside the home, that broke down. There was no real symmetry. It had been remodeled many times with many different aesthetics. There was this feeling of not knowing who the house was. The main living spaces had really great access, but everything was not symmetrical. The biggest challenge was the kitchen. It was basically a walk-through to the back hall. We made it a destination. We regained the symmetry and created a balanced, calm, The new layout offers improved workspace, flow, and beauty, plus ample seating around the island and in the cozy breakfast nook. View from the new formal dining room through the living room to the kitchen shows how all of the rooms are connected, balanced, and open while also maintaining a feeling of intimacy in each space.
articles.title: Architects, designers, and contractors are better together

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had its monthly Zoom book discussion on May 3, with 13 members in attendance to discuss Homegoing, a best seller. Participating were Mike Bandrowski, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Laura Goldman, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Margie Blodgett, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Maggie Blodgett, Karin Fetherston, Sally Arney, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. Homegoing is Gha naian-American author Yaa Gyasi’s debut historical fiction novel published in 2016. The book’s title comes from an African-American belief that death allows an enslaved person’s spirit to travel back to Africa. Each chapter of the book follows a different descendant of an African Asante woman, starting with her two daughters. One marries the British governor in charge of the Cape Coast Castle, one of about 40 “slave castle” commercial forts that were built on the Gold Coast of West Africa by European slave traders. The other sister is held captive in the castle’s dungeons below and shipped off to America as a slave. The book follows seven generations of their children and covers 300 years. The 14 characters’ often tragic histories include Anglo-Asante wars in Ghana, and slavery and segregation in America. It was reported that Gyasi received a book advance of more than $1,000,000, enabling her to spend seven years researching the broad range of the book. It was selected in 2016 for the National heartaches, as well as the progress to the current day. Homegoing helped readers feel the emotions that these people experienced and better understand hard parts of our nation’s history as it relates to the treatment of African-Americans. The book, however, did not satisfy everyone. Some readers found the novel’s structure with alternating chapters of African and American characters difficult to follow, as well as to emotionally engage with the different characters. Some readers wanted to better understand them and know what happened in their lives after their chapters in the novel ended. This work of historical fiction has compressed nine generations and almost 300 years of African-American experiences in 320 pages – no mean feat. One reader said she liked the concept of the book more than the book itself. There was, however, agreement that Homegoing is an important book; it provides a set of human stories that give readers a more complete understanding of our racial past and the current state in which we live today. articles.text: If you have children or grandchildren, you may already be somewhat familiar with the 529 plan, a popular education savings vehicle. But you may not have kept up with some recent changes in the plan’s capabilities and in the educational environment in which the plan might be used. Let’s start with the learning environment. During the COVID- 19 pandemic, colleges and universities switched to online classes, or at least to a hybrid of in-person and online. And even before the pandemic, many schools offered remote classes, though obviously not to the same extent. But after COVID-19 subsides, it’s likely that the online component will remain an important part of higher education. What does this “new world” mean for you when you’re saving for college? Will a 529 plan still be relevant? In a word, yes. First of all, a 529 plan can offer tax advantages. Earnings in a 529 plan are federally tax-free, provided the money is used for qualified educational expenses. And if you invest in your own state’s 529 plan, your contributions may be tax deductible. (Withdrawals used for expenses other than qualified education expenses may be subject to federal and state taxes as well as a 10% penalty.) Because tax issues for 529 plans can be complex, you’ll want to consult with your tax advisor before investing. Online learning costs are eligible for a 529 plan’s tax benefits just as much as those incurred from in-person classes. Tuition, textbooks, supplies, computers and services – all of these should qualify, assuming the school meets certain criteria. Also, students enrolled half-time or more don’t have to live in a dorm for room and board expenses to be covered by a 529 plan – they can live in off-campus housing. However, these room-and-board costs typically must equal the cost of living on campus. Some schools identify a specific cost for “commuters” or “at-home students,” so you will need to contact the college directly to determine qualified room-and-board costs. Now, let’s take a quick look at what some changes in the rules governing 529 plans over the past few years might mean for you. Eligible expenses from your 529 plan include the following: • K-12 expenses – Parents can withdraw up to $10,000 per student, per year, from their 529 plan to pay for tuition expenses at elementary and secondary schools. So, if you intend to send your children to a private school, this use of a 529 plan might interest you. • Apprenticeships – 529 plans can be used to pay for fees, textbooks, equipment and other supplies connected to apprenticeship programs registered with the Department of Labor. These programs, typically offered at a community college, combine classroom instruction with on-the-job training. • Student loans – Families can withdraw funds from a 529 plan to repay the principal and interest for qualified education loans, including federal and most private student loans. There’s a lifetime limit of $10,000 for student loan repayments per each 529 plan beneficiary and another $10,000 for each of the beneficiary’s siblings. All of these newer uses of 529 plans may contain additional guidelines and exceptions, and state tax treatment varies, so you’ll want to consult with your tax advisor before taking money from your account. But it’s valuable for you to know the different ways you can put a 529 plan to work. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. T.J. articles.text: Registration for University of California, Berkeley’s Osher Lifelong Learning Institute (OLLI) summer courses is now open. OLLI is a learning community for audiences of age 50 and up. Taught by Cal faculty and other experts and scholars, OLLI provides a year-round lineup of lectures, workshops, discussion groups, clubs and activities. The upcoming term will consist of two sessions. A live, interactive summer session will be held June 1 through July 1, and a second session will take place from July 12 through August 27. Pre-recorded courses include two live-streamed conversations with OLLI faculty. All classes are $120. RSVP to the event before this Friday by visiting https:// olli.berkeley.edu /programs/ courses. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. articles.text: Ann Reynolds, a longtime Piedmont leader and educator, died peacefully on May 1st in her Piedmont home surrounded by her family after a valiant fight with pancreatic cancer. Born on January 8, 1935, she had a full, happy, and productive life and enjoyed every minute of it. With a smile that lit up a room, Ann was an adoring wife of 62 years, a loving mother and grandmother, a devoted daughter, and a joyful sister to her immediate family. As the glue to an extended family that included four generations of Reynolds and Seulbergers, she was the absolute center of the family universe, and a steward to so many more. She was seen as a champion in warmth, intelligence, humor, humanity, authenticity and certainly bravery right to the end. Ann lived a life of great purpose as she transformed her many passions into lasting contributions to her family, friends and community. Her infectious zest for life and the people in it became the fuel that changed the world in so many ways. Music, flowers, education and people were her love as she danced her way through life. As a curious and consummate learner, Ann was committed to not only her own education, but that of others. She studied at both Wellesley College and the University of California at Berkeley. She earned a masters of Science degree in Educational Psychology with a specialty in learning and a California school of counseling credential. Ann’s fervent commitment to education was the seed for several scholarships, and she delighted in interviewing amazing young people who not only loved learning but loved giving back. Ann’s dedication to Piedmont’s students, residents and causes reached far and wide. It began in 1959 as a math teacher at Piedmont High School, and later as a counselor and math teacher at Piedmont Middle School. When she moved to Piedmont with her husband Jon in 1974, Piedmont and education also as the co-founder of A Beautiful Night Housing in 2002, a non-profit committed to building a working farm for young adults with mental illness. Most recently, in July 2019 Ann co-founded LookUp.live with her daughter, Susan Reynolds, a non-profit venture to counter the impact of digital addiction and social isolation on youth mental health. She was integral to the successful launch of LookUp with an inaugural student-led campaign at Piedmont High and Millennium High, where students and adults alike took breaks from their phones for better tech-life balance. Ann had a deep love of flowers that began early with her father, J. Fred Seulberger, of Seulberger’s Flowers. She carried on his tradition through wildflower walks with her grandchildren and community members, sharing her Piedmont home on garden tours and as a board member of the Piedmont Garden Club and UC Botanical Garden. She was also an active member and avid supporter of the Piedmont Beautification Foundation and Piedmont Historical Society. Other things that brought joy to Ann’s life were golf, bridge, skiing, music and swing dancing. She brought passion and enthusiasm to all of her pursuits, and she shared them with family, friends and her community, including skiing with her grandchildren well into her 80’s. Ann is survived by her husband Jon Reynolds, her sister Jane Woodson, her three children, Susan Reynolds, Kassie Thomas (Bill), Jake Reynolds (Robin) and six grandchildren, Brittany Cappetta, Olivia Cappetta, Joseph Thomas, Sophie Reynolds, Annie Reynolds, and Zach Reynolds, and an extensive extended family. A small family service was held with plans for a Celebration of Ann’s life when Covid relents. Donations in Ann’s honor can be made to the Ann Reynolds Legacy Fund at www.LookUp.live, P.O. Box 1571, Concord, MA, 01742, or a charity of choice. This project is full of “wow factors” and at the same time, the overall feeling is of understated elegance. Pam and Ken understand and appreciate the value of artisan touches, and the value of pieces having story — where it comes from, how it is made and acquired. As longtime readers of my column know, experiencing the hand of the maker, honoring quality materials and craftsmanship, the histories that pieces represent, all of that are part of my core values. The results? Our clients are thrilled. Pam says, “It was amazing to me, I originally described my wishes for the house in generalities, words like light and bright, cohesive, and calming. And Laura was able to figure out my style and keep my husband and me on track in our selections. I’m still in wonder and awe at how Debbi and Laura were able to put that all together. The house feels very peaceful and serene. It was exactly what I was looking for. The result honored some of the more traditional aspects of the architecture of the home while updating it. All of our wishes came true.” Laura Martin Bovard is the principal at LMB Interiors, located in downtown Oakland. Since 2002 she has helped clients create beautiful, joyful, and functional homes. The firm has garnered numerous awards and recognition as one of the Bay Area’s most sought after interior design agencies. articles.text: The city of Piedmont is seeking volunteers to serve on the newly established Community Pool Advisory Committee (PAC). The deadline to apply is today, May 5. Interested residents may download the “Application for Appointive Vacancy” from the city’s website and apply online at https:// piedmont.ca.gov. Applications are due at City Hall by Wednesday, May 5 at 5 p.m. Interviews with the City Council for these positions will be scheduled for the evening of Monday, May 10. No appointments will be made without a city council interview. Committee members will offer advice throughout the design process, as well as serve as a conduit for the community’s needs in the design refinement and construction of the pool. The committee will not be responsible for managing or directing project activities; instead, the committee is expected to use the experience and expertise of its members to provide support and insight to staff and city council members for the $19 million project. Main responsibilities of PAC members will include: ensuring the project meets community expectations, communicating project progress to residents, and making recommendations to staff on how to best balance any conflicting priorities with budget resources and community expectations. The PAC will consist of five to seven residents. Recruitment for the committee takes place separately from recruitment that has taken place for other commissions and committees. City staff will announce the recruitment period on the city website and social media channels, as well as with a press release. After receiving applications from interested residents, city council will then conduct interviews of qualified candidates. The council will appoint a Chair of the committee and its members. Residents with questions should contact City Clerk John Tulloch at (510) 420-3040.

articles.text: The first Tuesday in May is National Teacher Appreciation Day, and it marks the start of Teacher Appreciation Week. To honor the little-known holiday the Post checked in with some Piedmont teachers to open a window into the classroom, so to speak. Among the district’s many outstanding teachers, Ted Sherman (6th grade), Marna Chamberlain (Honors Physics), and Aaron Barlin (English, ASB Advisor) have met the crises head on to embody the high school’s motto, “Achieve the Honorable.” Two years ago the high school started the year without a Physics teacher. Last year, 2019-2020, Marna Chamberlain volunteered to teach the course for the first time, though she wasn’t sure how or where she would find the extra time that would be required. When schools closed in March 2020 she found herself teaching new material in a format completely foreign to nearly everyone – distance learning. “Between gallery walks, posters and whiteboards, that’s how I would usually run my classroom for feedback. It is called formative assessment, which are not graded but I get to see where students are,” Chamberlain explained. In the first months of the pandemic teachers were not even allowed to make kits to send home to do projects at home. Chamberlain ended up videotaping labs performed in her kitchen and constantly tried to keep the material fresh by using different mediums and applications. “You think about what works best, and you change it – and you keep changing it. If you do the same thing every day kids will say, ughh,” she said. 60 hours a week, every single week.” she said. As a hands-on teacher, the switch to screenbased learning was not easy, and eventually she experienced a case of vertigo from the stress of staring at a monitor for hours and hours. Students have taken notice of their teachers’ efforts throughout the school district. Ted Scherman (6th grade), Flint Christensen (Computer Sceince) and Doyle O’Regan (Math) showed up to work every day throughout the pandemic and broadcast their lessons from their classrooms, providing a semblance of normalcy. English teacher Aaron Barlin has gotten the notice of his students, including Millennium senior Ang Lee. “He drove all the way from SF to come with us to this allday event and we spent hours going to different seminars and learning about all sorts of things. With his help we were able to meet tons of Bay Area leaders working on projects like educational equity and student affinity leadership,” explained Lee. “His commitment to social justice is unquestionable. I don’t know many teachers who would have given their Saturday to learn alongside their students.” And so, during Teacher Appreciation Week, what better time to tell a teacher, thank you. -Marna Chamberlain Physics teacher, Piedmont High School Then came the summer, normally a time for teachers and students to recharge. But that was not the case last summer for Chamberlain. “I spent probably 40 plus hours every week during the summer working; my husband was not pleased. But every teacher I know spent their entire summer getting ready for fall,” Chamberlain explained. “The first semester this year was horrible. I easily worked over

articles.text: Editor: 95.1 – Percentage of Piedmonters age 16 and up who have had at least one dose of the vaccine against COVID-19. It’s the highest percentage in Alameda County. 5130 – Lost number of minutes of in-person learning due to Piedmont School District’s failure to open in hybrid mode on November 3, 2020 as previously directed by its trustees. Because PUSD failed to meet the dates, it was not until Feb 2, 2021 that the youngest learners stepped foot onto campus. 8505 – Maximum number of minutes of in-person instruction the youngest students will complete this school year under the current hybrid model. This declines by 135 minutes per increasing elementary grade in accordance with the phased role out. The minimum number of minutes of in-person learning for elementary students for the year is 7695 for 5th grade. 12,240 – Lost number of additional minutes of in-person learning had elementary hybrid learners been expanded to full time in-person learning at the end of March, [based upon] how San Rafael and other school districts in Marin County did. 25,200 – The number of in-person instructional minutes Piedmont elementary students should have received this year. This could have been accomplished with hybrid schedules starting in November and extended to full time in-person learning when teachers were fully vaccinated at the end of March. –Amy Vallerie
articles.title: Let’s take a look at the numbers and see how we’re doing (not too good)

articles.text: As 2020 drew to a close, America was left overwhelmed by the sheer panic created by the deaths of Breanna Taylor, George Floyd, and countless others. With police brutality on the rise, I met with Officer David Cutler of the Piedmont Police Department. Together, we discussed the future of policing in America and what would be needed to relieve ageold tensions between the African American community and the police. “Trust runs downhill,” said Officer Cutler when referring to community relations. In a sense, policing procedures would need to change by creating stronger relationships between everyday citizens and officers. Officer Cutler stated that “maintaining an open dialogue” would garner a solution to widespread police brutality and open them up to become more transparent in the future. He explained that officer training varies from state to state. Unlike many other states, California requires de-escalation training every two years as well as other requirements yearly to maintain a level of commitment and determination for their job. Under our current administration, the path towards safer policing seems bleak as VP Kamala Harris has in the past received criticism when she was Alameda County District Attorney. Even as I write this article, more innocent lives have been gunned down, including Daunte Wright, who was shot after an officer mistook their firearm for a taser. The gross negligence caused by this lack of proper safety has fueled an era of systematic racism that cannot go unnoticed. articles.text: Over 95 percent of adult Piedmonters – some 7,900 people – have received at least one dose of COVID-19 vaccine as of Sunday, May 2, according to Alameda County Public Health Department. In addition, more than 66 percent of Piedmonters are now fully vaccinated, representing over 5,500 people. The sky-high rates of vaccination amongst City residents begs the question – will Piedmont soon be fully vaccinated? While 100 percent vaccination might not be reached, it remains a distinct possibility. Hesitancy surrounding the COVID-19 vaccine in Alameda County is about 9 percent – well below national averages, according to polls released last month by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. Only 3.4 percent of those polled in the county said they were strongly hesitant. Alameda County has said that its goal is to vaccinate at least 70 to 80 percent of the county. This mirrors goals from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to reach “herd immunity” nationwide – a situation where enough people are immune to COVID-19 to control its spread. Piedmont is quickly closing in on that goal. The City’s high vaccination rate is likely due to several factors. Data from across the country has shown that wealthier areas have the highest vaccination rates, and Piedmont is one of the wealthiest communities in California. The Census estimates that about 21 percent of the City’s population is age 65 years or older, a group receiving priority for vaccine. Piedmont also has many people considered essential front-line workers, such as doctors and nurses. Vaccination rates are rising countywide, and appointments seem to be more available than in recent weeks. Over 1.45 million doses have been administered in Alameda County as of press time, and more than 45 percent of the whole county has been fully vaccinated. In Oakland, 44 percent of the population has been fully vaccinated. Three vaccines are available in the county. Options from Pfizer and Moderna require two doses administered several weeks apart. A vaccine produced by Johnson & Johnson, which is back in use in the county after being paused due to rare blood clotting concerns, requires only one dose. Alameda County began using the Johnson & Johnson vaccine last week after the CDC recommended its use be paused for 10 days. A small number of blood clotting cases connected to the vaccine were investigated, and it was found that the benefits of a third vaccine supplier outweighed the exceedingly small risk of blood clots. The CDC has confirmed 17 cases of a blood clotting disorder out of some 8 million people who have received the Johnson & Johnson COVID-19 vaccine. There have been three reported deaths due to the blood clots. Most of the blood clot cases were in women between the ages of 18 and 48. Symptoms typically occurred 6 to 13 days after vaccination. Even though the blood clot disorder appears to be extremely rare, people who receive the Johnson & Johnson vaccine are encouraged to monitor themselves for symptoms, like severe headache, abdominal pain, leg pain or shortness of breath within three weeks after vaccination. Anyone experiencing these symptoms should contact their health care provider immediately. On April 12, Alameda County opened COVID-19 vaccination appointments to all residents ages 16 and older. The Moderna and Johnson & Johnson vaccines are approved for people ages 18 and older. Pfizer vaccines are currently approved for teenagers as young as 16, and the pharmaceutical company will likely soon get authorization for their vaccine for children ages 12 to 15. Alameda County has a form to receive notifications about available appointments at covid-19. acgov.org/vaccines As of May 4, same-day appointments were available at several locations in Oakland and elsewhere in the county. The state has administered about 30.7 million vaccine doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. The state is vaccinating an average of almost 264,000 people per day. Almost 13 million Californians, about 41 percent of the adult population, have been fully vaccinated. articles.text: Even though the number of new COVID-19 cases is trending downward in Alameda County, it is not yet meeting the benchmarks to move into the least restrictive tier for reopening its economy as of yesterday, Tuesday, May 4. The state did move San Francisco County into the least-restrictive yellow tier, or minimal tier, this week. The looser restrictions will become effective this Friday, May 7. San Francisco is the only county in the Bay Area that has been moved into the yellow tier. Most other counties, including Alameda County, are in the orange, or moderate, tier, the second-least restrictive tier. Solano County is the only Bay Area county in the more restrictive red tier, or substantial tier. Alameda County moved out of the red tier on March 30. The positivity rate for Alameda County is 1.2 percent as of yesterday, a slight decrease from last week. The positivity rate has not been above 2 percent since February 25. Across Alameda County, the total caseload is 87,326 – an increase of 1,643 new cases week-over-week. There have been 27,179 cases recorded in Oakland and 13,555 cases in Hayward. Another 47 people have died of COVID-19 in Alameda County, bringing the total number of fatalities countywide to 1,538. The county has met orange tier metrics for several weeks but has not yet met benchmarks to move into the yellow tier. To move up into the yellow tier, the positivity rate needs to stay below 2 percent. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to be below 1 – right now there are 3.7 cases per 100,000. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to stay below 2.2 percent – it is currently 2 percent in Alameda County. In the yellow tier, most indoor operations are allowed with modifications. Indoor gyms, bars, museums, and family entertainment centers can all increase capacity. The entire color tier system is scheduled to be discontinued next month. Gov. Gavin Newsom announced plans several weeks ago to lift most COVID-19 restrictions statewide on June 15. It is expected that the reopening plan will continue if hospitalizations remain low and vaccination supply is not majorly disrupted. A mask mandate for indoor activities and crowded outdoor spaces will likely remain in place until further notice. Five new cases of COVID- 19 have been reported in Piedmont across the past seven days, according to Alameda County Public Health Department data. The total number of Piedmont cases since the pandemic began is 181. “The ideal solution would be for the Post Office to run the IRS, and Dude to run the Post Office.

articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will host a virtual town hall with California Assembly member Buffy Wicks today, Wednesday, May 5, at 5 p.m. Wicks, Piedmont’s elected representative in the 15th Assembly District, also represents Berkeley, Albany, Emeryville, Richmond, and parts of Oakland. She was elected to the State Assembly in November 2018. Wicks’ 2021 legislative prioritizes long-standing challenges in the district, now exacerbated by the pandemic. She has introduced and authored assembly bills that combat homelessness, support gun violence prevention, and target the debt settlement industry. She gained national attention last year when she brought her month-old baby to the state capitol and voted on the floor with her newborn in her arms, described by the New York Times as “an image of moms who do it all.” Click on http://tiny.cc/WicksTownHall2021 to sign up for the May 5 meeting. Questions may be posted in prior to the discussion on tinyurl.com/429k24yv. Buffy Wicks is Piedmont’s elected representative in the State Assembly.

articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters is hosting a public discussion with Alameda County District Attorney Nancy O’Malley tomorrow, Thursday, May 6 starting at 4 p.m. The event is free and open to all community members. To register for the Zoom event, visit https:// www.lwvpiedmont.org/content. a spx?page_id= 40 02&club_ id=601389&item_id=1256825. It will be recorded and posted on the League of Women Voters of Piedmont website for those who cannot join live. O’Malley will describe the work by her department with abused and homeless women, helping them move beyond trauma into a positive future. She will also address the many challenges COVID-19 has posed, and the ways in which the current lack of civility in politics is impeding the pace and scale of progress for women who suffer from violence. Passage of the Violence Against Women Act was held up due to politics, and funding for the Victims Crime Act, which provides resources to states for victims of crime, was also reduced. O’Malley is a nationally recognized expert on issues involving violence against women, violence against persons with disabilities, and interpersonal violence including sexual assault, domestic violence, elder abuse, child abuse, stalking, and human exploitation and trafficking. She serves in the office that dates to a time when Earl Warren was the Alameda County D.A. before becoming United States Supreme Court Chief Justice. O’Malley is the first woman to serve as the County’s District Attorney.
articles.title: LWV discussion tomorrow with D.A. O’Malley

articles.text: At a May 3 meeting, Piedmont’s City Council approved a proposal from Lisa Wise Consulting to prepare updates to the city’s Housing Element. The state has announced it will require the construction of 587 new housing units in Piedmont by the end of the next Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) cycle in 2031. The City’s current Housing Element of the General Plan was adopted in 2011 and outlines the city’s housing goals from 2015 to 2023. The city is close to meeting, and surpassing, the amount of housing units mandated by the RHNA 2015-2023 cycle, according to a 2020 annual progress report. Piedmont has issued building permits for the construction of 73 new units out of a mandated 60 units by the end of next year, 2022. The State of California requires that each jurisdiction’s housing element be updated every eight years and certified by the State. While most portions of a General Plan are updated every 20 to 25 years, State law requires that the Housing Element be updated every eight years. Housing Element planning periods are referred to as “cycles.” The 6th RHNA cycle will require 587 housing units, compared to 60 units in the current cycle, representing a 979% increase. The expected allocation includes 163 very low-income units, 94 low-income units, 92 moderate income units, and 238 above moderate-income units. On March 2, the city council issued a Request for Proposal [RFP] seeking a consulting firm to assist it in meeting the next RHNA planning period, which falls between 2023 and 2031. Lisa Wise Consulting, Inc. (LWC) submitted the only proposal received. The cost of the next Housing Element policy document that the firm will prepare is estimated at $691,000, with $172,000 earmarked for public engagement and outreach. “With approval of LWC as the lead housing consultant, the City moves forward with planning to meet the mandates set by the State of California, starting with meetings of the new Piedmont Housing Advisory Committee on May19 and June 15,” Planning Director Kevin Jackson wrote. “We are confident that the Piedmont community will come together to share ideas and expertise to solve the region’s housing crisis.” Housing Advisory Committee meetings this month and next will highlight results of the citywide fair housing survey and “pinnable” map tools, both of which closed for public comment in April and were funded through a $160,000 grant awarded to Piedmont by California Senate Bill (SB) 2 planning grant program, explained Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell. LWC is expected to present their analysis of Piedmonters’ design preferences, understanding of housing laws, and other ideas drawn from the survey. The consulting firm will also provide recommendations for guiding principles for new tools to accelerate housing production. Interested residents are invited to participate in these meetings. The agenda and instructions for participating in the meeting, which start at 5 p.m., will be posted on the city website: https:// piedmont.ca.gov/government/ commissions_ _ _committees/ housing_advisory_committee. Housing Advisory Committee meetings will be televised live on KCOM, the city’s television station, and will be available through streaming video on the city’s website at https://piedmont.ca.gov/services___departments/kcom-tv/ live_content_and_video_archive. with Piedmont because historically Berkeley and Piedmont Fire Departments have worked closely together. Brannigan admitted that the difference in department’s sizes did take some time getting used to, though. “There are seven stations [in Berkeley] versus one in Piedmont. So, my first week on the job was a big shift. We’re similar in that both departments provide ambulance transport, which is unusual in the fire service. How was his first week on the job in Piedmont? “I spent my first week just listening and learning,” he said with a smile. Brannigan’s formal appointment was approved by City Council following a rigorous recruitment process and a field of over 30 candidates. Mayor Teddy Gray King praised Brannigan for his extensive experience in the fire service. “I know he will be a tremendous assist to the Piedmont community. The fact that Chief Brannigan knows Alameda County so well will is a great asset,” she said.

articles.text: The Oakland Center of the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, directed by Piedmont resident, Dr. Steve Sidney, currently has job postings for a 35-year follow-up exam of study participants who were first examined in 1985-1986. The CARDIA study, funded by the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute, is a longitudinal study of black and white men and women who were 18-30 years old at the beginning of the study and who have been followed for the development of heart disease risk factors and disease. More than 900 published scientific articles have resulted from the CARDIA study thus far. This will be the 10th examination for study participants who were initially recruited from four centers around the country, including Kaiser Permanente (KP) Health Plan members from the Berkeley-Oakland area. The examination will be conducted by the KP Northern California Division of Research at its research clinic located in the Mosswood Building, 3505 Broadway in Oakland. Positions are available for scheduling examinations, conducting exam interviews and study procedures, data management, and managing the mailing of equipment and supplies for aspects of the study conducted at the homes of participants. These positions will start in May or June of this year and end during the summer of 2022. Training will be provided. If you would like more information, please contact Dr. Sidney at steve.sidney@kp.org. With Extended hours to Fit Your Busy Schedule Dr. Gutlaizer and Ellen and Liza Konnert
articles.title: Job opportunities for local Medical Research study

Brannigan is working with the City Arborist and the Public Works Department to identify shrubs and dried foliage that could pose a fire risk. He did confirm that a herd of goats likely will be brought back to the city this year to reduce fire danger on the hills above the Corporation Yard. It is not unusual for new hires to have no prior relationship with the city of Piedmont - a small, semi-suburban city of about 10,000 engulfed by the city of Oakland. pages.text: Wednesday, May 5, 2021 5 Town hall meeting with Buffy Wicks today By Allyson Aleksey The Piedmont League of Women Voters will host a virtual town hall with California Assembly member Buffy Wicks today, Wednesday, May 5, at 5 p.m. Wicks, Piedmont’s elected representative in the 15th Assembly District, also represents Berkeley, Albany, Emeryville, Richmond, and parts of Oakland. She was elected to the State Assembly in November 2018. Wicks’ 2021 legislative prioritizes long-standing challenges in the district, now exacerbated by the pandemic. She has introduced and authored assembly bills that combat homelessness, support gun violence prevention, and target the debt settlement industry. She gained national attention last year when she brought her month-old baby to the state capitol and voted on the floor with her newborn in her arms, described by the New York Times as “an image of moms who do it all.” Click on http://tiny.cc/WicksTownHall2021 to sign up for the May 5 meeting. Questions may be posted in prior to the discussion on tinyurl.com/429k24yv. Buffy Wicks is Piedmont’s elected representative in the State Assembly. City planning for 587 new housing units City Council approves proposal from consulting firm By Allyson Aleksey At a May 3 meeting, Piedmont’s City Council approved a proposal from Lisa Wise Consulting to prepare updates to the city’s Housing Element. The state has announced it will require the construction of 587 new housing units in Piedmont by the end of the next Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) cycle in 2031. The City’s current Housing Element of the General Plan was adopted in 2011 and outlines the city’s housing goals from 2015 to 2023. The city is close to meeting, and surpassing, the amount of housing units mandated by the RHNA 2015-2023 cycle, according to a 2020 annual progress report. Piedmont has issued building permits for the construction of 73 new units out of a mandated 60 units by the end of next year, 2022. The State of California requires that each jurisdiction’s housing element be updated every eight years and certified by the State. While most portions of a General Plan are updated every 20 to 25 years, State law requires that the Housing Element be updated every eight years. Housing Element planning periods are referred to as “cycles.” The 6th RHNA cycle will require 587 housing units, compared to 60 units in the current cycle, representing a 979% increase. The expected allocation includes 163 very low-income units, 94 low-income units, 92 moderate income units, and 238 above moderate-income units. On March 2, the city council issued a Request for Proposal [RFP] seeking a consulting firm to assist it in meeting the next RHNA planning period, which falls between 2023 and 2031. Lisa Wise Consulting, Inc. (LWC) submitted the only proposal received. The cost of the next Housing Element policy document that the firm will prepare is estimated at $691,000, with $172,000 earmarked for public engagement and outreach. “With approval of LWC as the lead housing consultant, the City moves forward with planning to meet the mandates set by the State of California, starting with meetings of the new Piedmont Housing Advisory Committee on May19 and June 15,” Planning Director Kevin Jackson wrote. “We are confident that the Piedmont community will come together to share ideas and expertise to solve the region’s housing crisis.” Housing Advisory Committee meetings this month and next will highlight results of the citywide fair housing survey and “pinnable” map tools, both of which closed for public comment in April and were funded through a $160,000 grant awarded to Piedmont by California Senate Bill (SB) 2 planning grant program, explained Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell. LWC is expected to present their analysis of Piedmonters’ design preferences, understanding of housing laws, and other ideas drawn from the survey. The consulting firm will also provide recommendations for guiding principles for new tools to accelerate housing production. Interested residents are invited to participate in these meetings. The agenda and instructions for participating in the meeting, which start at 5 p.m., will be posted on the city website: https:// piedmont.ca.gov/government/ commissions_ _ _committees/ housing_advisory_committee. Housing Advisory Committee meetings will be televised live on KCOM, the city’s television station, and will be available through streaming video on the city’s website at https://piedmont.ca.gov/services___departments/kcom-tv/ live_content_and_video_archive. Dave Brannigan Continued from page 1 concern throughout Piedmont, including Blair Park, the Corporation Yard hillside, and the dense ground covering in Piedmont Park. Brannigan is working with the City Arborist and the Public Works Department to identify shrubs and dried foliage that could pose a fire risk. He did confirm that a herd of goats likely will be brought back to the city this year to reduce fire danger on the hills above the Corporation Yard. It is not unusual for new hires to have no prior relationship with the city of Piedmont - a small, semi-suburban city of about 10,000 engulfed by the city of Oakland. Brannigan, however, is very familiar with Piedmont. He lives nearby and his kids participated in Piedmont Recreation Department programs over the years. He is a former youth soccer referee for games with Piedmont Soccer Club. “For me the decision to join Piedmont’s Fire Department was largely personal. Like many others, this past year was a time to reflect on my priorities and decisions. The success I had in Berkeley was very fulfilling, but it also came at the expense of time with my family,” he explained. “When [former Fire Chief] Bret Black told me he was leaving, I wasn’t looking for another job and wasn’t interested working anywhere other than Berkeley.” Still, he decided to “throw his hat in the ring.” “The city’s small department in comparison to Berkeley’s was one major draw,” he said. “I get to work face-to-face in the same room as the firefighters,” Brannigan said. “While I spent time at the stations [in Berkeley], I wasn’t working alongside firefighters very often. To be able to have that direct connection to the career I fell in love with was a really big appeal. It brings a lot of satisfaction to me in terms of my career.” “Another plus is the very short commute,” Brannigan said with a smile. He and his family currently reside a short distance from city lines, near the Morcom Rose Garden in Oakland. Piedmont’s will be only the second department where he has worked. He is also familiar with Piedmont because historically Berkeley and Piedmont Fire Departments have worked closely together. He explained that he arrived at his new job here with a clear understanding of Piedmont and its departments’ needs. Brannigan admitted that the difference in department’s sizes did take some time getting used to, though. “There are seven stations [in Berkeley] versus one in Piedmont. So, my first week on the job was a big shift. We’re similar in that both departments provide ambulance transport, which is unusual in the fire service. How was his first week on the job in Piedmont? “I spent my first week just listening and learning,” he said with a smile. Brannigan’s formal appointment was approved by City Council following a rigorous recruitment process and a field of over 30 candidates. O’Malley The Piedmont League of Women Voters is hosting a public discussion with Alameda County District Attorney Nancy O’Malley tomorrow, Thursday, May 6 starting at 4 p.m. The event is free and open to all community members. To register for the Zoom event, visit https:// www.lwvpiedmont.org/content. a spx?page_id= 40 02&club_ id=601389&item_id=1256825. It will be recorded and posted on the League of Women Voters of Piedmont website for those who cannot join live. O’Malley will describe the work by her department with abused and homeless women, helping them move beyond trauma into a positive future. She will also address the many challenges COVID-19 has posed, and the ways in which the current lack of civility in politics is impeding the pace and scale of progress for women who suffer from violence. Passage of the Violence Against Women Act was held up due to politics, and funding for the Victims Crime Act, which provides resources to states for victims of crime, was also reduced. O’Malley is a nationally recognized expert on issues involving violence against women, violence against persons with disabilities, and interpersonal violence including sexual assault, domestic violence, elder abuse, child abuse, stalking, and human exploitation and trafficking. Job opportunities for local Medical Research study The Oakland Center of the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, directed by Piedmont resident, Dr. Steve Sidney, currently has job postings for a 35-year follow-up exam of study participants who were first examined in 1985-1986. The CARDIA study, funded by the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute, is a longitudinal study of black and white men and women who were 18-30 years old at the beginning of the study and who have been followed for the development of heart disease risk factors and disease. More than 900 published scientific articles have resulted from the CARDIA study thus far. This will be the 10th examination for study participants who were initially recruited from four centers around the country, including Kaiser Permanente (KP) Health Plan members from the Berkeley-Oakland area. The examination will be conducted by the KP Northern California Division of Research at its research clinic located in the Mosswood Building, 3505 Broadway in Oakland. Positions are available for scheduling examinations, conducting exam interviews and study procedures, data management, and managing the mailing of equipment and supplies for aspects of the study conducted at the homes of participants. These positions will start in May or June of this year and end during the summer of 2022. Training will be provided. If you would like more information, please contact Dr. Sidney at steve.sidney@kp.org.
