articles.text: As I was scrolling through my news feed several weeks ago, ironically enough, I came across an article about a “No-Tech” contest. Yes, it’s true. Reviews.com was looking for a lucky “I can’t live without tech” individual to go without technology for 24 hours. That the contest was for 24 hours only was in itself startling to me. They went on to clarify that applicants need not apply unless the thought of no technology for 24 hours induced a panic attack. To support the contestant, a lock box safe to store each of the tech culprits and a $200 gift card to build a survival kit would be provided. The contest prompted me to think about our use of, and dependency on, technology over the past year and its influence on every aspect of occupation. The American Occupational Therapy Association identifies 8 areas of occupation: • Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) • Instrumental Activities of Daily Living (IADLs) • Education • Work • Play • Leisure • Social Participation • Rest and Sleep Technology has been interwoven in all 8 occupations of life in one way or another as a result of the global pandemic. Don’t get me wrong, I am thankful for technology. It helped all of us make it through the past 15 months. However, as counties shift to less restrictive tiers and we begin to return to a way of life that is less dependent on technology, can we Are your kids spending too much time on tech devices? – especially our students – wean away from screens and willingly engage in daily life activities that do not involve technology? I decided to find out. As part of a handwriting exercise for my students (yes, a paper and pencil task), I asked them to respond to the writing prompt, “If I went without tech for 24 hours, I would want/need the following in my No Tech survival kit.” To my pleasant surprise (and frankly, relief), the question was not met with gasps or “I don’t know.” Students listed all that is music to an occupational therapist’s ears. Their lists were rich in areas of play, leisure and socialization. Examples of items in their kits and activities included: family, friends, pets, reading books, board and card games, baking supplies, crafts and hobbies, hiking, camping, fishing, golf, and basketball. We have not lost them. So as the school year is quickly coming to an end, now is the time to make plans about the role of technology for the summer and set expectations about screen use. As a family, build your own “No Tech” survival kit. How about a “No Tech Tuesday” for each Tuesday of the summer? A weekend No Tech survival kit? Demonstrate that you too can engage in “occupations of life” without technology. On a final note, there happened to be one student whose initial response to my assignment of no technology was “this would be impossible for me.” He went on to consider the challenge and came up with the reply, “I would just rest.” How amazingly insightful. So don’t delay. Make your summertime survival kit and enjoy occupations of play, leisure, social participation and of course rest and sleep. Have a wonderful less-tech summer! Kimberly Bonacum is an occupational therapist for Piedmont Unified School District and owner of Mindful Fidgets, LLC www.mindfulfidgets.com. For additional questions, she can be contacted at mindfulfidgets@ gmail.com.

articles.text: Piedmont Scouts in Troop 6 love a good service project. Recently they had the opportunity to help out at Oakland’s Elizabeth House (www.oakehouse. org), which offers a residence to women with children who have experienced the poverty of homelessness, violence, and addiction. The facility supports women and children in their transition to independence by empowering them with the tools to rebuild their lives. The House’s yards needed some TLC, and Troop 6 was up for the challenge. The first phase of the project was weeding and removing unusable garden beds as well as repairing bikes. A total of 20 Scouts, seven adults, and several of the children of the house pitched in to make fast work of the project. Three green bins and over 20 garden bags later, the space was transformed. The next phase of the project will involve building and planting new garden beds, and if funds can be raised, installing a stone patio which will enable the residents to more fully enjoy their outdoor space. articles.text: Q-ZAR 2295 Willow Pass Rd, Concord, 521-9663 Q-ZAR.com Laser Tag and Arcade After 386 Days of closure Q-ZAR Laser Tag is back. The laser tag arena has been a kid favorite for decades and is now open on weekends from noon to 8 p.m. for walk in Laser Tag games. Private sessions may be booked for weekdays by appointment only. Waiver forms must be submitted online and a printed receipt must be brought in with you in order to play. No waiver forms may be filled out in store. Q-ZAR also has dozens of retro and modern video games everyone in the family will get a kick out of. Set the blasters to stun and prepare for fun. MONTCLAIR GOLF COURSE 2477 Monterey Blvd, Oakland, 482-0422 www.montclairgc.com Driving Range & 9-hole short course Practice your swing on their spacious, double-decker driving range. The top deck on the range is equipped with 19 stalls, plenty of sunshine during the day, and bright lighting in the evenings. The bottom deck, with 17 stalls, provides plenty of shade and is just steps away from the bar counter, with the best root beer in the Bay Area. Try your luck at the challenging, tranquil 9-hole course – perfect for kids having their first day on the course. TILDEN PARK MERRY GO-ROUND Central Park Drive & Lake Anza Rd, Berkeley 559-1004 tildenmerrygoround.org Merry Go-Round and cafe Tilden Park’s famous merry go-round reopened to the public on April 17. Take the kids for rides on a merry-goround that was constructed 110 years ago – in 1911. Hours of operation are Saturdays and Sundays from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Reservations are recommended, but walkups are welcome. Starting May 14, the hours of operation will extend to include Fridays. The little lads and lassies will love riding their favorite ceramic horses and the other hand-carved animals. Stay for a full afternoon of fun, by taking a ride on the park’s equally famous miniature train. Kids can also try Tilden’s golf driving range. The cafe serves ice cream, hot dogs, beverages & snacks to refuel a day of fun. OAKLAND ZOO 9777 Golf Links Rd, Oakland 632-9525 oaklandzoo.org Zoo There’s no better time to go to the Oakland Zoo. The California Wilds Playgrounds just reopened, where kids can slide, spin, soar, and build in the five play zones inspired by the different native habitats of the California Trail animals. The zoo also just introduced a new exhibit, “Taking Action Against the Illegal Wildlife Trade.” Other previously closed areas like the petting zoo will be opening in the near future. Fifty cents of every ticket purchase goes to conservation efforts of chimps, elephants, the California Condor, the yellow-legged frog and more. Advance ticketing is required at oaklandzoo.org.

articles.text: For over a year the taken part of the population has been separated. For long-distance lovers, it’s your average Tuesday. For those couples it’s harder, because they have to adjust to being far away from their girlfriend or boyfriend. If you are married, it’s a whole other story. To survive this quarantine, they needed the holy trinity: unlimited wine, trashy Netflix films, and an occasional escape from each other. Let’s say t here a re 2,000,000,000 couples worldwide, excluding long distance and married couples. The let’s thrust a global pandemic on loving couples. From my deductions I believe that the number has halved. Maybe one in the pair has finally realized that he or she deserves something better than the other, something as basic as hating how they chew when they eat, or they are incredibly messy. everyone actually thinks they will get married. These couples lasted throughout the entire quarantine phase because they put in the effort. They were persistent about being safe while still trying to be with each other. They would go on socially-distant picnics and walks. When these couples got into a bubble, they could finally be within hugging range of one another. When the pandemic is finally over, they will probably stick together because they have persevered together. Everyone’s always rooting for the high school sweethearts. Type three: The germaphobe couple. This is the couple who somehow confessed their feelings to each other, but there’s no bubble for them. Even when they get within 50-yards of one another, they wish they had a hazmat suit on because one can never be too careful. This couple also spends most of their time on their phones calling one another because going outside is just too risky. This couple will go on a hike as a date, but the twist is this hike will be nowhere near civilization. Another date night idea would be to go to a romantic drive-in movie theatre. But once again the plot twist is that they will be in separate cars, on the complete opposite side of the lot, and need megaphones to talk to each other. Type four: The couple that never talks to each other but somehow is still together. This is the couple where both people forgot they were in a relationship until someone reminded them. It’s not that they don’t feel affection towards one another, it’s just they are both antisocial, spend most of their time listening to music, and prefer the company of cats. Lord knows how they even got together in the first place. This couple will last only because they rarely ever talk to each other, therefore can’t start any arguments. Type five: Married couples. They are the one who have the worst luck in quarantine. Not only is there no escape from one another, they most likely have kids who need to be homeschooled. The spouse is always there, whether you want it or not. And there are no distractions, like eating in restaurants or spending time with other couples. What if you don’t like the way your significant other eats? You have to watch this three times a day, seven days a week. And you can’t even go on vacation. Props to the ones who put up with everything. As a single person (OK, a student) who is also an extrovert, my quarantine has been dull and irritating. I have had to deal with my sister’s relationship, which is annoyingly Type two, the true high school love. While she is off galivanting with Prince Charming, I’m stuck here with my crush on Harry Styles and Corbyn Besson. In other words, I am suffocatingly lonely. And to make matters worse, my friend has a boyfriend she acquired during quarantine. I honestly don’t understand how. What black magic did she use to find him? Not only that but my standards are ridiculously high, like Burj Khalifa high (the Burj Khalifa is the tallest building in the world). So, any chance of me finding someone I would date is gone. I have honestly forgotten how to deal with real people during this pandemic. For those who somehow are still dating. may the force be with you, ‘cause you are going to need it. But there is always light at the end of the tunnel (unless it’s nighttime; then it’s dark). To all the couples who have made it this far, I hope that you all eventually get married because you can obviously conquer the world. And if you are married, don’t go looking for a divorce attorney as soon as the California Lockdown ends. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont student with a keen eye and the ability to be in several places at one time. Now let’s look at the types of quarantine relationships. Type one: the super clinging, attention-grabbing couple. This is the couple that literally can’t keep their hands off each other (and not in a good way). They make everyone uncomfortable because they are all over each other in the hallways during the first period. When quarantine hit, they were devastated because they wouldn’t get their daily dose of attention. They will last probably between 3-4 months then grow tired of each other because they can’t flaunt their relationship in public. Type two: High school sweethearts. articles.title: City’s first Arbor Day video celebrates Piedmont’s urban forest

articles.text: Sue Herrick and Cameron Wolfe Jim Horner The City of Piedmont opted for a virtual Arbor Day celebration this year in light of the COVID-19 pandemic, which is still prohibiting events with large gatherings. A 20-minute video, created by KCOM, the city’s TV station, and produced by Park Commission Chair Patty Dunlap, celebrates the city’s diverse urban forest by highlighting all 19 Heritage Trees throughout Piedmont. The tree, or group of trees, should exhibit three qualities. The tree should be an integral part of an architectural theme, or play an important role in framing or screening a building or other civic feature. It should be recognized as part of a memorial or is an outstanding remnant of early civic plantings, and it should represent an outstanding example of the species, in its age, size and form, is unique to the City, or is an outstanding example of California flora. The Arbor Day celebration spans four years of nominations, from 2018, when the Heritage Tree policy began, through this year. In the video, community members introduce the trees they have nominated. When the original nominator was unavailable, a stand-in resident introduced the tree, explained Patty Dunlap. Piedmont resident Zack Parisa served as the guest speaker. The video also included submissions from a chalk drawing contest in which the city’s young artists depicted their favorite city trees using colored chalks. The video was shot and edited by KCOM’s Jason Liao. “[The video] turned out beautifully and is a great educational piece. The Park Commission is really excited to present it,” Dunlap said. Formal portraits of this year’s five designated Heritage Trees will be taken by Park Commissioner Brian Mahany and should be available next week. With the final portraits, the city will be able to populate an interactive map of all Heritage Trees. “With the interactive map, people will be able to click coordinates and get exact locations where the Heritage Tree or cluster of trees is located,” Dunlap said. It is a long-standing tradition to plant a tree on Arbor Day. This year, the city will be planting a tree honoring the life of Ralston Louie, a Piedmont graduate who passed away unexpectedly this year. The commemorative tree, a Yulan Magnolia, will be planted in Dracena Park. The video can be viewed on Youtube or on the City’s website by visiting https://piedmont. ca.gov/government/city_news___ notifications/arbor_day_2021. You can also visit www.piedmont. ca.gov to learn more about the heritage trees; featured trees are listed below. Coast Redwood, nominated by Cameron Wolfe and Susan Herrick Residents Cameron Wolfe and Susan Herrick, independently of each other, nominated the first Heritage Tree for the city of Piedmont. It is the large Coast Redwood in Piedmont Park; the tree first served as a community “holiday greeting tree” in the early 1970s, Wolfe explained. “[It] is appropriate [as a Heritage tree] because it is a Sequoia Sempervirens, probably the most significant tree in California, better known as the coastal, or California Redwood,” said Wolfe. “This tree really has a remarkable history. Many, many generations of children, and now adults, have come here to celebrate the holiday season and light the lights on this beautiful tree, and Cameron and I both felt it had such a significance in the history of our beautiful city,” Herrick said. Highland Poplars, nominated by Jim Horner Park Commissioner Jim Horner nominated a cluster of Highland Poplar trees forming the backdrop of the Exedra at Highland and Magnolia. “They are really an important aesthetic contribution to the city. And I think it’s amusing - that there are Highland Poplars right on Highland Avenue,” he said. “They provide a wonderful winter scrim of lacework branches, and in the summertime, billowing green leaves.” Grove of Dawn Redwoods, nominated by Lyle Gordon Resident Lyle Gordon nominated a grove of Dawn Redwoods in 2018. “I thought they were really interesting as one of the three types of conifers that lose their needles in the fall, and then get them back in the Spring,” he said. Southern Magnolia, nominated by Betsy Goodman Park Commissioner Betsy Goodman nominated a Southern Magnolia four years ago when the Heritage Tree program began. “I asked [former Public Works Supervisor] Dave Frankel, what is the most beautiful tree in PiedBetsey Goodman mont? pages.text: 10 Wednesday, May 5, 2021 Sue Herrick and Cameron Wolfe Jim Horner City’s first Arbor Day video celebrates Piedmont’s urban forest Residents participate by presenting Heritage Tree nominations By Allyson Aleksey The City of Piedmont opted for a virtual Arbor Day celebration this year in light of the COVID-19 pandemic, which is still prohibiting events with large gatherings. A 20-minute video, created by KCOM, the city’s TV station, and produced by Park Commission Chair Patty Dunlap, celebrates the city’s diverse urban forest by highlighting all 19 Heritage Trees throughout Piedmont. The tree, or group of trees, should exhibit three qualities. The tree should be an integral part of an architectural theme, or play an important role in framing or screening a building or other civic feature. It should be recognized as part of a memorial or is an outstanding remnant of early civic plantings, and it should represent an outstanding example of the species, in its age, size and form, is unique to the City, or is an outstanding example of California flora. The Arbor Day celebration spans four years of nominations, from 2018, when the Heritage Tree policy began, through this year. In the video, community members introduce the trees they have nominated. When the original nominator was unavailable, a stand-in resident introduced the tree, explained Patty Dunlap. Piedmont resident Zack Parisa served as the guest speaker. The video also included submissions from a chalk drawing contest in which the city’s young artists depicted their favorite city trees using colored chalks. The video was shot and edited by KCOM’s Jason Liao. “[The video] turned out beautifully and is a great educational piece. The Park Commission is really excited to present it,” Dunlap said. Formal portraits of this year’s five designated Heritage Trees will be taken by Park Commissioner Brian Mahany and should be available next week. With the final portraits, the city will be able to populate an interactive map of all Heritage Trees. “With the interactive map, people will be able to click coordinates and get exact locations where the Heritage Tree or cluster of trees is located,” Dunlap said. It is a long-standing tradition to plant a tree on Arbor Day. This year, the city will be planting a tree honoring the life of Ralston Louie, a Piedmont graduate who passed away unexpectedly this year. The commemorative tree, a Yulan Magnolia, will be planted in Dracena Park. The video can be viewed on Youtube or on the City’s website by visiting https://piedmont. ca.gov/government/city_news___ notifications/arbor_day_2021. articles.text: In a strong pair of games, Piedmont’s basketball team opened league play in the Foothill Division of Western Alameda County Conference with victories over former State champion St. Joseph, 78-66, on April 28 and an 86-77 win against Castro Valley on Friday, April 30. “4-1 overall and 2-0 in the league feels great right now. It feels great to go into St. Joe and win. I’m not from the Bay Area, but we knew on the East Coast about Jason Kidd. Castro Valley had a strong team, the best they’ve been since I’ve been at Piedmont. We weathered the storm and bounced back,” said coach Ben Spencer of both games. The two games featured Piedmont’s main scorers, JoJo Murphy and Luke Harris, who recorded career highs. Murphy put up 32 points against St. Joseph, and Harris scored 35 points against Castro Valley. “We just want to get through league with all wins,” said Murphy. PHS vs. St. Joseph St. Joseph enters its first season in the WACC’s Foothill Division as a storied basketball program in Alameda. Coach Don Lippi’s teams have won four State and seven NCS titles since 2003. The Pilots opened with a 20-18 advantage by the end of the first quarter, but a monster 30-point second quarter gave the Highlanders a 48-34 lead at halftime. The gap narrowed to 62-53 at the end of the third quarter but PHS closed out the victory at 78-66. Staff Photos JoJo Murphy had 32 points against St. Joes and 25 against Castro Valley. The Highlanders had 72 points from three players: Murphy’s 32, Harris had 24, and A.J. Harris scored 16. In Piedmont’s breakout second quarter, A.J. Luke Harris had 35 points against Castro Valley, a career high. with a 3-pointer to put his team ahead 21-20, a lead the Highlanders never relinquished. Murphy scored 15 points in the quarter with three 3-pointers, showing off his refined repertoire of shooting and creating space. “My teammates have been really supportive. I’ve been working on all the shots all year; it wasn’t an overnight process. I’ve been working on my pickups and footwork. I know those are things colleges pay attention to,” said Murphy. After trailing 23-21, Piedmont stormed back to take a 43-41 lead at halftime, and 62-59 at the end of the third. They closed out strong to win 86-77. It showed the Trojans’ improvement after finishing with a 7-17 record last season. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team is 3-0 after winning two more games, both on the road. They beat St. Joseph 70-43 on Thursday, April 29, and overpowered Hayward 69-28 the next day. “The game with St. Joe went back and forth. But in the second half, we were hustling and diving on the floor. That stuff is contagious,” said coach Bryan Gardere with a grin. Senior Kai Johnson had 27 points against Hayward and 20 against St. Joe. She is the only senior on this year’s young, talented team. “I was training non-stop during quarantine. I feel like I’ve gotten stronger and my game has improved,” Johnson said. “I’ve been here for four years. It’s hard, but it’s fun because [my teammates] are my little young ones,” she added with a laugh. 70-43 win vs. St. Joseph St. Joseph is starting its first season in the Foothill Division of the WACC after going 24-8 last season. PHS ended the first quarter tied 13-13 and went into halftime with a 29-25 lead, and then the Highlanders exploded. They held the Pilots to four points in the third quarter and took a commanding 52-29 lead entering the fourth quarter. PHS added 18 in the fourth for the 70-43 final. The Pilots relied heavily on Makena Mastora, who scored 15 points in the first half on 3-pointers. Piedmont defenders held her to three points in the third quarter and nine in the fourth. “The help-defense was always there; we had her locked up,” said Johnson. Trinity Zamora was red hot with 30 points, 12 rebounds, and three assists, while sophomore Maddie Hill added seven points. Freshman Natalia Martinez had eight points. “My shots weren’t falling, so I knew I had to do what I can on defense like diving on the floor and looking for Kai and Tri [TrinTrinity Zamora had 30 points and 12 rebounds against St. Joe, while having 13 points and 15 rebounds against Hayward. Natalia Martinez had eight points and 15 points in two games last week. Staff Photos Kai Johnson scored 27 points against Hayward and 20 points in a win with St. Joseph. On defense, she locked up the Plots’ Makena Mastora. ity],” said Martinez. Maya Leggett scored six points with a pair of 3-pointers in the fourth quarter. Brie Sotelo had two points. Blowout win vs. Hayward The Highlanders tilled up the Hayward Farmers after leading 18-2 after the first quarter, 45-10 at halftime, 63-14 at the end of the third, on the way to a 69-28 rout. Johnson led with 27 points, 12 rebounds, and three steals. Zamora also had a double-double with 13 points and 15 rebounds, plus seven assists. Martinez had 15 points, six rebounds and four steals. Aniya Perine and Luisa Murray each had three pointers, and forward Sotela had 6 rebounds and two blocked shots. articles.text: Piedmonts’ lacrosse team returned to the field last week with one win and one loss. The Piedmont High boys’ lacrosse team returned to the field on Wednesday, April 28 for its opening of a short 13-game schedule in 2021. Playing in Hayward, thy made light work of Moreau Catholic with a 17-0 shutout victory. But against California HS in San Ramon, the Highlanders struggled, losing 13-4 to the Div. 1 opponent. Seven players scored against Moreau, led by five-goal performances by Nate Guzdar and Soren Dixon. Goals against California were scored by Guzdar, Greg Gately and J.D. Harrison. In the 17-0 drubbing the Highlanders rarely let the fledgling Moreau team near the net, allowing just three shots and requiring just two saves on the night. “We have a very strong and experienced defense that will hold teams below 10 goals a game. We knew California would be tough; we’re playing some of the best teams in the East Bay this season, so we’ll continue to be tested,” said coach Ryan Price. Moreau shut out The Highlanders scored eight goals in the first quarter against Moreau, then added three goals each in the second, third, and fourth period. Aside from Dixon and Guzdar’s five-goal games, Luke Beihn scored two goals and logged an assist, and Gately, Harrison, Alden Heske, and Nash had individual goals. Goalies Joe Hempeck and Ryan Roos were rarely tested on the night thanks to Piedmont’s stout backline defense. Hempeck had one save in the first quarter, and Roos had one in the third. articles.text: Staff Photos Zach Luna’s goal in the 30th minute came after quickly winning the ball off Alameda in its own 18-yard box. Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team opened their season with a 1-0 shutout of Alameda at Thompson Field on Thursday, April 29. Zach Luna scored the lone goal in the 30th minute in quick pressing fashion, while Alameda had few scoring chances. “On a horrible field, we were playing in a particular way that will differ from when we get back to Witter,” said PHS coach Todd Sullivan of Alameda’s patchy surface. “With the players we have, I’m expecting to play more possession-based soccer.” The two schools had a solid rivalry in 2019-2020. The Highlanders beat Alameda 3-0 early in the season but lost 4-0 in the final week of the 2020 season. Alameda went on to win the league title. “It’s always a good game with Alameda, you have to come ready to play. It’s a good first game to have,” added Sullivan. Thursday’s game featured the Highlanders playing a high defensive line in the first half, resulting in the Hornets often struggling to get the ball past midfield. The press enabled Luna to score the eventual game-winner after taking the ball in front of the net and rolling it past Alameda’s keeper. “I think the boys noticed that they weren’t very strong good in the back. We nicked the ball high up the field and that’s how we got the goal. We put Zach in the middle of the midfield; he’s a bit older and wiser, and he did quite well in that central role. He got right in behind Aiden [Woolwine], won the ball in a great area and got the goal,” he explained. Piedmont had another chance to score earlier after striker Aiden Woolwine won a set piece, leading to Connor Curtis launching a curling pass to the feet of Ian Work, who forced a diving save by the Hornets’ keeper. Soon after, in the 24th minute, Alameda had its best chance to score after their striker chipped the ball over a charging PHS goalkeeper Daniel Malecki. Waiting on the goal line in front of the empty net was centerback Sawyer Collins, who easily cleared the ball. In the second half, the Hornets did well to keep possession for the majority of the 40 minutes, but never challenged Malecki with any shots. Tuesday night shutout vs. Hayward The Highlanders hosted Hayward last night, Tuesday, May 4 at Witter Field, and posted an impressive 5-0 shutout victory. details. articles.title: Piedmont opens season with 1-0 shutout of Alameda

articles.text: Traveling to San Lorenzo for their first game of the season, Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team produced a 1-0 victory on Thursday, April 29. “We have really good energy on the team right now,’ said veteran coach Dan Chubbock. “Arroyo has improved over the years and they were without a couple of their best players. They are definitely a school we can’t overlook.” The Highlanders will play a return match with Arroyo tonight at Witter Field, then play longtime soccer rival Bishop O’Dowd on Thursday, May 6. The two games in two days is a schedule created by the league and frowned upon by coaches. “The league scheduled all the games for us this year, I definitely didn’t like that draw when the WACC released schedules,” confirmed Chubbock. The shutout of Arroyo came with plenty of help from the defense, and sophomore goalkeeper Morgan Hunt was rarely challenged. Piedmont’s goal was scored by Zenobia Pellissier-Lloyd 20 minutes into the game after receiving a pass from Zoe Wolfers. After receiving the ball around midfield, Wolfers played a perfectly driven through-ball to Pellissier-Lloyd as she made a run behind Arroyo’s back line. On her way to the goal, Pellissier-Lloyd shrugged off the Don’s centerback, who fell to the ground as the Piedmont attacker sent a left-footed shot past the charging keeper for the score. “It was a nice through-ball from Zoe into Zenobia, who had a nice finish with her left foot,” said Chubbock. “We only had a few practices before the game, so we’re still really building our chemistry,” SAID described Pellissier-Lloyd. “But we were able to build the ball up from the back, and Zoe played a ball through and I was able to get by the defender,” Piedmont played in a 4-4-2 diamond formation, allowing Chubbock to load the midfield with four central midfielders including Emily Fitzgerald as an attacking midfielder behind the striker, Pellissier-Lloyd. “We’re finding the right role for Emily to utilize her strengths. She’s definitely an attacking player,” said Chubbock of last year’s team leading scorer. The Highlanders will use the same formation against Arroyo tonight, according to Chubbock. Some adjustments will be made in the game with O’Dowd to prevent BOD runners charging down the wing. “We’re going to stick with this system because it allows us to adapt during the game defensively. That obviously will change for some opponents.” With today’s game against Arroyo and Thursday’s Bishop O’Dowd match exactly 24-hours apart, Piedmont is expected to enlist several J.V. players against tonight in order to conserve some energy for Thursday’s match with the Dragons. “We will likely have five JV players for Wednesday’s game. We want to do well with integrating players from J.V. this year, especially with no NCS playoffs.” added Chubbock. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-0) hosts Arroyo tonight, Wednesday, May 5 at 7:30 p.m. The game tomorrow, Thursday, May 6, with O’Dowd is also at Witter Field at the same time. Emily Fitzgerald played the central Attacking Midfield role in the season-opener. Zoe Wolfers (30) finds Zenobia Pellissier-Lloyd for Piedmont’s goal against Arroyo.

articles.text: The Piedmont High Mountain Bike Team is back in action with races at Sigma Six Ranch in Lower Lake on consecutive Sundays, April 25 and May 2. The 6.2-mile course had an estimated 700 feet of elevation gain. The squad brought 15 student-athletes to compete in multiple categories, including Varsity Boys, JV Boys, Sophomore Boys, Sophomore Girls and Freshman Boys. The races were hosted by the National Interscholastic Cycling Association’s NorCal Cycling League, in which PHS riders compete with students from Bishop O’Dowd, Head-Royce, San Ramon Valley, Berkeley, Oakland Tech, El Cerrito, Clayton Valley Charter, and local clubs including Oakland Composite, Hayward Composite, and Castro Valley MBT. Will Shields placed 2nd overall in the varsity races on both dates. Shields describes the differences between this years’ time trial runs, compared to races with mass starts in previous years. “Normally we’d do a mass start with four laps of racing against other people, which requires some tactics in sitting behind people, drafting, and being focused on what other people are doing. This year, it’s all about yourself, trying to keep a fast pace and finish under 40 minutes,” he said. But time trials require careful planning. “In a race with a mass start, you want to conserve energy without letting people pass you, plan your attack and respond to people who are attacking. With a time trial, it’s kind of the opposite. You have to use full power as much as possible,” he said. This year the number of riders is greatly reduced because the 2020 season had only one preseason race before the season was canceled due to Covid. Typically, racers must qualify for the varsity division through JV races. “Qualification for varsity is usually done through the previous year’s race results, but because there were so few races last year, the varsity field this year is even smaller,” explained coach Sally Aldridge. Race results For the JV Boys, sophomore Artun Duransoy finished 9th of 34 in Sunday’s race with a time of 42:23.3, and placed 6th in the first race. Junior Kurt Wilson was right behind Duransoy in 10th (43:50) in Sunday’s race and 12th in the earlier. Nathan Willson placed 14th on Sunday in 45:07. Piedmont’s Mt. Bike team entered three girls in the sophomore race. Julia Caputo finished 9th of 12 in 1:07:20 on Sunday and 8th in the first race. Heather Stoneman clocked a 1:15:08, and Lilly Kaltner finished in 1:35:29. Three competed in the Sophomore Boys categories as well; Andres Roberts finished 7th of 33 in 44:23, Aleksi Valkonen was Will Shields placed 2nd in a race May 2 at Sigma Six Ranch. on May 2. was 15th. The win last night was very much a “team win” as Piedmont was without senior captain Spencer Stein, who days earlier had a hat trick against James Logan. Shane Miller stepped in to the hole set position, and Max Wagener chewed up the scorebook with six goals from the wing position – five of which came in the third quarter. “We were a little nervous because we were without Spencer Stein, so we had to have bench players step up,” said coach John Savage. “The real key has been the offensive development of Max Wagener. He’ now 6-foot-4, and any time there’s open water in front of him, he [is] a scoring threat.” The games demonstrated the strong work of sophomore goalie Dariush Kashani, who was the Post’s Freshman of the Year in 2020. He recorded 10 saves and four assists against O’Dowd and another 15 saves against James Logan with two steals and two assists on quick plays out of the defensive end. “Dariush played well. articles.text: De Young Museum on Golden Gate Park. The “Calder-Picasso” exhibit will be on view at San Francisco’s de Young Museum from now through May 23. The museum re-opened in March with the U.S. debut of the Calder-Picasso exhibit, which includes over 100 paintings, sculptures, drawings, and photographs that explore the relationship between Alexander Calder and Pablo Picasso, widely regarded as two of the most influential artists of the twentieth century. Additionally, the exhibition “Uncanny Valley: Being Human in the Age of AI” has been extended through June 27 and is available with a general-admission ticket. The museum is open Tuesday through Sundays from 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m. The Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, which include both the de Young in Golden Gate Park and the Legion of Honor, is maintaining rigorous health and safety measures based on county guidelines. Visitor capacity is reduced to 25 percent, and timed tickets are required. To obtain tickets, visit https:// deyoung.famsf.org/exhibitions.
articles.title: Calder-Picasso exhibit at De Young until May 23

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet will stream Helgi Tomasson’s production of Romeo & Juliet starting tomorrow, May 6, and will continue through May 26. The multi-capture, cinematic production was performed on-stage at the San Francisco War Memorial Opera House and was the last work that the company performed on tour prior to 2020 COVID-19 closures. It was last performed in the fall of 2019 at The Royal Danish Opera House in Copenhagen, Denmark, where it was noted for its “color rich” set design and interpretation of the classic Shakespeare story. The production, which premiered during SF Ballet’s 1994 Repertory Season, is considered a signature work of SF Ballet and has been performed worldwide. It is performed under the baton of SF Ballet music director Martin West and includes former prinA scene from San Francisco Ballet’s production of Romeo & Juliet. cipal dancers Maria Kochetkova and Davit Karapetyan in the title roles. Pascal Molat, now a faculty member at SF Ballet School, is cast as Mercutio. The opulent set is designed by Jens-Jacob Worsaae, with lighting design by Thomas Skelton. This was Worsaae’s final collaboration with Tomasson before he passed away shortly after the ballet’s premiere. “I think it was the most beautiful work he had ever done, and yet he did not see it,” Tomasson said. “That’s one reason why this production is very, very special to me.” To purchase tickets to the streaming production, visit https://www.sfballet.org/productions/digital-program-06/.
articles.title: SF Ballet streams Romeo & Juliet tomorrow to May 26

articles.text: The Bang on a Can All-Stars ensemble will perform tomorrow, May 6, as part of the “Cal Performances at Home” series. The performance will be available for live-streaming at 7 p.m. The New York-based group was formed in 1992 by parent organization Bang on a Can to take on touring and recording projects. In 2005, the All-Stars were named “Ensemble of the Year” by the Musical America International Directory of the Performing Arts. The ensemble was also praised as “the country’s most important vehicle for contemporary music” by the San Francisco Chronicle. For tomorrow’s performance, the group will perform “Still Hammer,” an acclaimed oratorio by Bang on a Can co-founder Julia Wolfe, winner of a Pulitzer Prize. She has created a musical amalgamation of the folk tale “John Henry,” complete with the sounds and stories of the Appalachia region. The music combines folk and rhythm with a layered compositional style, and is performed by three female vocalists and a chamber ensemble with hammered dulcimer, mouth harp, bones, clogs, banjo, and metal percussion. A premiere watch party will begin promptly at 7 p.m. tomorrow, and the performance will be available on-demand through August 4. To purchase tickets, visit https://secure.calperformances.org/15200/15821. Bang on a Can All-Stars
articles.title: Cal Performances features Bang on a Can All-Stars performance tomorrow

articles.text: Ruth Bancroft Garden in Walnut Creek. Ruth Bancroft Garden, located in Walnut Creek, will host an Ikebana workshop on Saturday, May 22. Ikebana is the Japanese art of flower arrangements, a tradition that dates back centuries. The workshop will be led by Sharon Suimei Doi, a regular Bancroft Garden exhibitor. She will offer an Ikebana lesson using succulents. Doi will also demonstrate basic Japanese floral arrangement concepts with branches and plant materials that would be found in a dry climate similar to Walnut Creek. Bancroft Garden is known for its extensive succulent and cactus displays. Students will get to work on their own arrangements with the assistance of an instructor. Class fees include a ceramic container, pin frog and plant materials. Students will need to bring their own garden clippers. All COVID-19 protocols will be in effect. Regardless of vaccination status, students will be asked to wear a face mask and create social distancing. Hand sanitizers will be provided. The class will be held from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. on Saturday, May 22. Registration closes on May 19. To obtain tickets, visit: https://www.ruthbancroftgarden. org/event/ikebana-japanese-floral-art-workshop/.
articles.title: Bancroft Garden to host Japanese floral art workshop May 22

articles.text: Carlos Aguirre Aurora Theatre explores the intersection between art and activism in a recent panel discussion with Bay Area activists. In this latest episode of “Aurora Connects,” guests Carlos Aguirre, Shannon Davis, and Steven Flores join theatre staff to discuss the unique challenges and opportunities that face indigenous artists. Aguirre has performed both as a hip-hop actor and artists in the Bay Area for over 19 years. He has performed with well-known groups and artists like The Roots, Eryka Badu, Black Eyed Peas, Mary J. Blige, Jam Master Jay, and George Clinton. A Bay Area native, Davis has performed with American Conservatory Theatre, American Indian Community House, the American Repertory Theatre, Oregon Shakespeare Festival, and Berkeley Reparatory Theatre. Flores is a multidisciplinary artist, whose crafts include dancing, acting, and painting. “Aurora Connects” is Aurora Theatre Company’s bi-weekly live broadcast, an “online salon and virtual happy hour.” A broadcast will go live every other Thursday at 5 p.m. on the theatre company’s YouTube channel. Each episode is hosted by theatre Artistic Director Josh Costello and Associate Artistic Director Dawn Monique Williams. Costello was appointed artistic director in 2019 following a national search. At Aurora, he has directed, among others, Exit Strategy, The Importance of Being Earnest, Detroit, and the award-winning world premiere of Jonathan Spector’s Eureka Day. Williams has been Aurora’s Associate Artistic Director since August 2019. An Oakland-native, she was Artistic Associate and a resident artist at the Oregon Shakespeare Festival for six seasons. To watch the panel discussion, visit https://www.auroratheatre. org/auroraconnects.
articles.title: Aurora Theatre panel discussion on arts and activism

articles.text: The Horszowski Trio will perform at the Kohl Mansion in a live-streaming performance on Sunday, May 9 at 7 p.m., and again Thursday, May 13, at 6 p.m. The trio has been described by The New Yorker as “the most compelling American group to come on the scene.” The Horszowski Trio has been widely regarded in the international chamber music world since their debut in 2011. The trio is comprised of violinist Jesse Mills, pianist Rieko Aizawa, and cellist Ole Akahoshi, who replaced founding cellist Raman Ramakrishnan this season when he retired from the trio after nine years. “I have been admiring the trio for many years,” said Akahoshi. “I have had the pleasure of performing with Rieko and Jesse The Horszowski Trio – violinist Jesse Mills, pianist Rieko Aizawa, and cellist Ole Akahoshi – will perform at the Kohl Mansion on May 9 separately on numerous occasions. Being on stage with them has always been a tremendously invigorating, inspiring, and highly gratifying experience for me. I hope to continue Raman’s inspiring tradition.” Music at Kohl Mansion, located in Burlingame, is the longest-running chamber-music-only presenter on the San Francisco Peninsula. Live-streaming performances will take place on Sunday, May 9 at 7 p.m., and again Thursday, May 13, at 6 p.m. To obtain tickets, visit https://musicatkohl.org/ horszowski-trio-3/.
articles.title: Horszowski Trio to perform at Kohl Mansion, May 9 & 13

articles.text: Louise M. Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco San Francisco Symphony has announced the return of live concerts at Davies Hall beginning tomorrow, May 6. Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen leads the symphony in live performances for medical professionals in concerts on May 6 and May 7, and tickets will go on sale tomorrow for seven additional concerts. The list of guest conductors includes: Jeremy Denk, International Concert Pianist James Gaffigan, Trondheim Symphony Orchestra & Opera (Norway) Ken-David Masur, Milwaukee Symphony Orchestra Joseph Young, Berkeley Symphony Joshua Weilerstein, Chamber Orchestra of Lausanne (Switzerland) “A friend recently told me that we need to just start,” said Salonen. “I feel joy and relief at finally being able to do just that with the San Francisco Symphony. We go into these concerts having worked as a unit to bring music into homes in unique and meaningful ways this year. We now welcome audiences into our home – something we didn’t realize we had taken for granted.” After nearly a year of vacancy, Davies Hall will be packed with performances from tomorrow through June 25. Program highlights for the first two concerts include Jean Sibelius’ Rakastava, George Walker’s Lyric for Strings, Carl Nielsen’s Little Suite for Strings, Caroline Shaw’s Entr’acte, and Edvard Grieg’s From Holberg’s Time Suite. All concerts will be approximately 75 minutes in length and will be performed without intermissions. Instrumentation and orchestra size is planned in accordance with city guidelines and will vary. All San Francisco Symphony performances will require proof of vaccination or a negative COVID-19 test as well as mask-wearing. To comply with current health restrictions, there will be significantly reduced concert hall capacity, contactless tickets, assigned seats, and increased ventilation. You can visit sfsymphony.org/safety. “I want to thank every member of the San Francisco Symphony family – from our Orchestra colleagues and COVID Health and Safety task force, to our incredibly supportive Board leadership – for working creatively together to make these concerts happen so quickly,” said SF Symphony CEO Mark Hanson. “There is nothing that compares to experiencing music together in a physical space. After 14 months without sharing these human connections with each other, we simply cannot wait to resume performing for our community on the stage of Davies Symphony Hall.” To obtain tickets and to view a full list of programming, visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/.
articles.title: Tickets available for performances through June 25

articles.text: You can watch a performance by San Francisco Opera’s resident artists, the 2021 Adler Fellows, at the Marin Center for a unique drive-in concert of classic arias, duets, and ensembles. Named for Kurt Herbert Adler, San Francisco Opera’s former general director, the fellowship program is a multi-year performance-oriented residency for opera’s promising young artists and performers. It was founded in 1977 and is now considered one of the world’s most prestigious programs for advanced training. A short list of fellowship alumni includes sopranos Leah Crocetto, Heidi Melton, Patricia Racette, Ruth Ann Swenson, and Zheng Cao. Two performances will take place, one tomorrow, Thursday, May 6, and the other on May 13, both at 8 p.m. Both performances will take place at the Marin Center in San Rafael, and will showcase “the power of music to heal and offer hope even in the darkest of times.” The performances will be directed for the stage by Jose Maria Condemi. Running time is approximately 70 minutes, with no intermission. To purchase tickets, visit: https://sfopera.com/on-stage/theadlers-live-at-the-drive-in/. SF Opera performances will be held at the Marin Center in San Rafael. Tuck Andress and Patti Cathcart
articles.title: SF Opera – Adler Fellows live tomorrow and May 13

articles.text: The Living Jazz arts organization will present a call-and-response discussion with the veteran musical duo Tuck and Patti on May 16 at 4 p.m. Tuck & Patti, the husband-wife duo of Tuck and Patti Andress, have a signature musical style that combines jazz, folk, and R&B. For 40 years the pair has performed for audiences around the world with a penchant for re-imagined jazz classics and pop-music billboard charters. Their albums have themselves regularly appeared on top 10 Billboard Contemporary Jazz charts, and their SF Jazz performances are highly anticipated. Living Jazz created the calland-response series in 2020 in response to the current health pandemic and subsequent venue closures. The unique series of intimate conversations features some of the world’s most iconic jazz musicians in an effort to provide exposure to meaningful, in-depth conversation by jazz luminaries. The musicians are considered jazz legends, and will speak candidly about the inspiration behind their music, struggles and victories. Audience members will be invited to ask questions and actively participate in an open question-and-answer session. To reserve your spot for the discussion, visit https://www. sfarts.org/event/living-jazz-presents-call--response-tuck--patti-2TGo2vUeVpjFhgr6wJenP5.

pages.text: Wednesday, May 5, 2021 19 Horszowski Trio to perform at Kohl Mansion, May 9 & 13 By Allyson Aleksey The Horszowski Trio will perform at the Kohl Mansion in a live-streaming performance on Sunday, May 9 at 7 p.m., and again Thursday, May 13, at 6 p.m. The trio has been described by The New Yorker as “the most compelling American group to come on the scene.” The Horszowski Trio has been widely regarded in the international chamber music world since their debut in 2011. The trio is comprised of violinist Jesse Mills, pianist Rieko Aizawa, and cellist Ole Akahoshi, who replaced founding cellist Raman Ramakrishnan this season when he retired from the trio after nine years. “I have been admiring the trio for many years,” said Akahoshi. “I have had the pleasure of performing with Rieko and Jesse The Horszowski Trio – violinist Jesse Mills, pianist Rieko Aizawa, and cellist Ole Akahoshi – will perform at the Kohl Mansion on May 9 separately on numerous occasions. Being on stage with them has always been a tremendously invigorating, inspiring, and highly gratifying experience for me. I hope to continue Raman’s inspiring tradition.” Music at Kohl Mansion, located in Burlingame, is the longest-running chamber-music-only presenter on the San Francisco Peninsula. Live-streaming performances will take place on Sunday, May 9 at 7 p.m., and again Thursday, May 13, at 6 p.m. To obtain tickets, visit https://musicatkohl.org/ horszowski-trio-3/. SF Opera – Adler Fellows live tomorrow and May 13 By Allyson Aleksey You can watch a performance by San Francisco Opera’s resident artists, the 2021 Adler Fellows, at the Marin Center for a unique drive-in concert of classic arias, duets, and ensembles. Named for Kurt Herbert Adler, San Francisco Opera’s former general director, the fellowship program is a multi-year performance-oriented residency for opera’s promising young artists and performers. It was founded in 1977 and is now considered one of the world’s most prestigious programs for advanced training. A short list of fellowship alumni includes sopranos Leah Crocetto, Heidi Melton, Patricia Racette, Ruth Ann Swenson, and Zheng Cao. Two performances will take place, one tomorrow, Thursday, May 6, and the other on May 13, both at 8 p.m. Both performances will take place at the Marin Center in San Rafael, and will showcase “the power of music to heal and offer hope even in the darkest of times.” The performances will be directed for the stage by Jose Maria Condemi. Running time is approximately 70 minutes, with no intermission. To purchase tickets, visit: https://sfopera.com/on-stage/theadlers-live-at-the-drive-in/. SF Opera performances will be held at the Marin Center in San Rafael. Tuck Andress and Patti Cathcart Living Jazz presents Tuck & Patti in discussion May 16 By Allyson Aleksey The Living Jazz arts organization will present a call-and-response discussion with the veteran musical duo Tuck and Patti on May 16 at 4 p.m. Tuck & Patti, the husband-wife duo of Tuck and Patti Andress, have a signature musical style that combines jazz, folk, and R&B. For 40 years the pair has performed for audiences around the world with a penchant for re-imagined jazz classics and pop-music billboard charters. Their albums have themselves regularly appeared on top 10 Billboard Contemporary Jazz charts, and their SF Jazz performances are highly anticipated. Living Jazz created the calland-response series in 2020 in response to the current health pandemic and subsequent venue closures. The unique series of intimate conversations features some of the world’s most iconic jazz musicians in an effort to provide exposure to meaningful, in-depth conversation by jazz luminaries. The musicians are considered jazz legends, and will speak candidly about the inspiration behind their music, struggles and victories. Audience members will be invited to ask questions and actively participate in an open question-and-answer session. To reserve your spot for the discussion, visit https://www. sfarts.org/event/living-jazz-presents-call--response-tuck--patti-2TGo2vUeVpjFhgr6wJenP5. SF Symphony live performances begin this week Tickets available for performances through June 25 Louise M. Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Symphony has announced the return of live concerts at Davies Hall beginning tomorrow, May 6. Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen leads the symphony in live performances for medical professionals in concerts on May 6 and May 7, and tickets will go on sale tomorrow for seven additional concerts. The list of guest conductors includes: Jeremy Denk, International Concert Pianist James Gaffigan, Trondheim Symphony Orchestra & Opera (Norway) Ken-David Masur, Milwaukee Symphony Orchestra Joseph Young, Berkeley Symphony Joshua Weilerstein, Chamber Orchestra of Lausanne (Switzerland) “A friend recently told me that we need to just start,” said Salonen. “I feel joy and relief at finally being able to do just that with the San Francisco Symphony. We go into these concerts having worked as a unit to bring music into homes in unique and meaningful ways this year. We now welcome audiences into our home – something we didn’t realize we had taken for granted.” After nearly a year of vacancy, Davies Hall will be packed with performances from tomorrow through June 25. Program highlights for the first two concerts include Jean Sibelius’ Rakastava, George Walker’s Lyric for Strings, Carl Nielsen’s Little Suite for Strings, Caroline Shaw’s Entr’acte, and Edvard Grieg’s From Holberg’s Time Suite. All concerts will be approximately 75 minutes in length and will be performed without intermissions. Instrumentation and orchestra size is planned in accordance with city guidelines and will vary. All San Francisco Symphony performances will require proof of vaccination or a negative COVID-19 test as well as mask-wearing. To comply with current health restrictions, there will be significantly reduced concert hall capacity, contactless tickets, assigned seats, and increased ventilation. You can visit sfsymphony.org/safety. “I want to thank every member of the San Francisco Symphony family – from our Orchestra colleagues and COVID Health and Safety task force, to our incredibly supportive Board leadership – for working creatively together to make these concerts happen so quickly,” said SF Symphony CEO Mark Hanson. “There is nothing that compares to experiencing music together in a physical space. After 14 months without sharing these human connections with each other, we simply cannot wait to resume performing for our community on the stage of Davies Symphony Hall.” To obtain tickets and to view a full list of programming, visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/.

articles.text: In many ways the well-made and superbly acted Eye in the Sky is reassuring. But it also can be chillingly disconcerting. It begins as a straightforward surveillance of a militant group associated with the East Africa terrorist organization Al Shabab. Then unexpectedly it morphs into something far more serious and morally hazardous. What is initially being watched – from 20,000 feet by an unseen, eerily quiet drone – is a house in Nairobi, Kenya, where a meeting is taking place between highly placed Shabab leaders, to include a woman, a British citizen, who has aligned herself with the organization. The original plan is to raid the house and capture those inside. But using a cyborg beetle, an agent (Barkhad Abdi), is sitting outside on the street and using a control no larger than a cell phone. He positions the small beetle with a miniaturized camera inside the house where it reveals that in another room several suicide bombers are preparing to put on explosive vests. The stakes for all concerned – Col. Katherine Powell (Helen Mirren), located in Surrey England, and Lt. General Frank Benson (Alan Rickman), who is in London with several British officials and politicians – have suddenly changed. What was a “capture” is now suddenly reframed as a “kill.” The only question, both legal and moral, is what collateral damage within the circumference of the explosion will be sustained once the drone Helen Mirren stars in “Eye in the Sky.” releases its missile? Complicating that question is the presence of a small girl, seated just outside the house at a table selling her mother’s homemade flatbread to passing locals. She is clearly within the kill zone. The pilot of the drone (Aaron Paul) is in Nevada. When he spots the girl, he asks for a review of all facets of the operation, to include legal and ethical concerns. And so, the tension continually increases. Powell and Benson argue that to delay could mean that the suicide bombers will leave and ultimately appear in a shopping mall where perhaps hundreds of innocents will be maimed or killed. This reality is weighed against the life of that one little girl. Others argue for delay as the decision is “referred up.” No civilian in the room with the Gen. Benson wants to take final responsibility. Across four continents, involving ministers and secretaries of state, the “kill” decision is incrementally postponed. The reality that confronts those involved, to include the pilot of the drone, is the proverbial rock and the hard place. The debate is both agonizing and complex and riveting. Collateral damage is a euphemism that laden with horrible, unintended consequences. And to make the moment even more dreadful is that it has a video game quality to it – warfare at its most detached. This is an intense and rare military meditation on war that focuses not on the battle but on the choices that we ask our military leaders to make as they conduct this most lethal form of warfare. To its credit the film avoids becoming a melodrama, while still examining very effectively the moral quandary that we can only hope our soldiers and officials consider with each “kill” order. Eye in the Sky is taut and well-constructed and highly recommended. Eye in the Sky. Directed by Gavin Hood. Starring Helen Mirren, Aaron Paul, and Alan Rickman. 1 hr., 42 min. Rated R. articles.text: Come join your friends at the Piedmont Center as it begins to reopen for public events after a year of closure due to COVID-19. CURRENTLY ON VIEW The 7th Annual Juried Art Show returns to the Center for an exhibition through May 16. Gallery hours are 12:00 to 2:00 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays. From a record-high 500 submissions of original art created within the past year, 35 works of art were selected by guest jurors René de Guzman, Senior Curator of Art at Oakland Museum of California, and Danielle Fox, Principal of Slate Gallery in Oakland. Through an endowment by the family of John P. Thornborrow, cash awards of $4,000 will be awarded to the top award winners, with an emphasis on honoring emerging artists in the Bay Area. All visitors must sign up in advance for their visit. An email-based online system will be established where visitors may sign up for their choice of day. A health screening form will be emailed to visitors with their confirmation, also listing all health requirements. The exhibition will be limited to a maximum of 20 visitors at a time. Masks and social distancing will be observed. Visitors may view the art in a one-way direction to prevent clustering. No food or drink will be permitted. To sign up for a time to view the show, visit: https://bit. ly/3mwWuwT. For more information, see the website: piedmontcenterforthearts.org. articles.text: Piedmont’s long-running Appreciating Diversity Film Series will present Jeff Orlowski’s award-winning documentary, The Social Dilemma, on Thursday, May 13, from 5:00-6:00 p.m. The film will be followed by a Question & Answer session with UC Berkeley Law Professor Rebecca Wexler. The film is free by registering at diversityfilmseries.org, and clicking on the “Register for The Social Dilemma button”. The film documents the hidden practices that underlie the business of social media. Viewers will learn that the algorithms designed to capture your attention are also profoundly affecting your brains and beliefs in ways that directly threaten democracy. An internal Facebook report by sociologist Monica Lee states, “64% of the people who joined extremist groups on Facebook did so because the algorithms steered them there.” Other documentaries have raised concerns about the impact of social media on privacy and even democracy. This film’s advantage is that the speakers in The Social Dilemma include top executives from Twitter, Instagram, Pinterest, Facebook, and others. The experts assure us their intentions were good – even the one whose job title at Facebook was head of “monetization”. Yet all are deeply concerned about what they’ve created, and one confesses that he worked all day on making his site irresistibly seductive and then found himself unable to resist the very algorithmic tricks he helped to create when he went home at night. The most important lesson from the film is that people should question everything they read online, especially if it is presented in a way that reflects a detailed understanding of personal inclinations and preferences. Viewers should learn to resist the “attention extraction model” that makes social media seem friendly and reinforcing. As the New York Times has advised, “Unplug and run”. After viewing The Social Dilemma, join the Diversity Film Series audience for Q & A discussion with Rebecca Wexler, Assistant Professor of Law at UC Berkeley Law, and Co-Director of the Berkeley Center for Law & Technology. Wexler teaches, researches, and writes on issues concerning data, technology, and criminal justice. Sign up at www.diversityfilmseries.org for the Diversity Film viewing on Thursday, May 13, from 5:00-6:00 p.m. The Appreciating Diversity Film Series is co-sponsored by the City of Piedmont, Piedmont League of Women Voters and Piedmont School District.

articles.text: Sunday was a sparkling day. The 2nd Annual Piedmont Art Walk brought out people in droves. Many of them stopped by the Piedmont Center for the Arts to view the current Juried Art Show. One was a violinist who just happened to have his violin with him. Well… You know how performers are. The violinist saw a ready audience, so he took his violin out and played a brief concert and then departed. It was a nice touch and added a lot to the festivities. That’s the way music is. That brings me to page 2. I listened to President Biden’s recent speech with great interest; especially the part about early education. OK. At least this is a start. We need to realize that we are losing ground educationally, and this is of great concern. But the solution is obscure. Politicians and “educational czars“ do a lot of talking. They are good at that. Somehow, they fail in the history department. Education and art were valued by some enlightened civilizations of the past. Foremost in this pantheon of education was Greece in the Classic era. Anyone who has been to Greece has been awestruck by the architecture and the statues. But ancient Greece was far more than architecture and statues. Its culture valued a lively interchange of ideas. They respected intellectual and divergent opinions. It was the ancient Greeks who popularized the epic poem. The plays of Euripides and other authors are studied to this day. Those plays formed the basis of modern European opera, an art form regarded as the epitome because it combines literature, graphic art, dancing, singing, and instrumental music. As a former teacher I have thought a lot about education. In the United States we have 12 years of public school education. In Italy they have 13. Why can’t we add just one more year to public school education? While we’re at it, let’s give kids a good start by welcoming them one year before kindergarten. I use the word “welcoming” for good reason. Education should be fun. While some may regard education as a competitive sport, it should always by enjoyable and fun. I see competitive sports the same way. This was the philosophy of the ancient Greeks. It was good then and it is good now. Everything about education these days is so serious. Our education “leaders” wring their hands and lament that some segments of the population are falling behind. What they fail to recognize is that kids will want to learn if the experience is fun. We now have a problem of subject matter. The same education leaders stress science, and mathematics, and mathematics and science. But the glory that was ancient Greece combined science and mathematics with physical education and music. If we started school kids with music at an early age, they would have a better attitude toward every aspect of education. If people enjoy what they are doing, they will want to continue. Music makes us feel good psychologically. Along the way, musicians learn mathematics, good listening skills, individual initiative in combination with teamwork, and logical thinking among many other things. It is also important to recognize that music is the easiest written language. When I was teaching in public schools, I taught all my students how to read music… It took about five minutes. All of these things are then carried over into other aspects of education. We had great music educators in the past. When my mother was a youngster, her teachers brought their radios into the classroom. They listened to the concerts for kids by great musicians and music educators like Walter Damrosch. Leonard Bernstein continued where Damrosch left off. Why can’t we do that now? The cost is absolutely nothing, and maybe that’s the problem, because the politicians and the education bureaucrats want to throw money at our problems thinking that will solve them. Singing, after all, costs nothing. We see all too frequently the dumbing down of education. I was in a shop recently. They had the radio on, and I listened to the music with great interest. The song consisted of a repetitive drum track and a monotone singer singing these lyrics: “Duhduh, Duhduh, Duhduhduh, DUH?” Is this the example we want to present in education?
articles.title: Piedmont Art Walk: Merging music, art, and education

articles.text: The stop-motion, animated feature Coraline is a tour de force of imagination. Though made to be shown in stereoscopic 3-D, even in 2-D it is vivid and rich with a panoply of colors and strange, interesting characters. But for all of its technical wonder and labor-intensive filming – the characters are three-dimensional figures that are moved ever so slightly, a single frame at a time, it’s hard to enthusiastically recommend this film for children. Caroline is a dark and sinister narrative which takes a young girl’s fantasy and turns it into a gothic nightmare. Of course, all fairytales have a distinctly dark side to them. Dorothy follows the yellow brick road only to meet the Wicked Witch. Alice falls down the rabbit hole. And certainly Harry Potter, for all of his deft ability with magic, encounters evil that takes many forms and threatens his very existence. And so it is with Coraline, who recently moved from Michigan to Ashland, Oregon. She and her parents are living in a Victorian rooming house called The Pink Palace filled with eccentric boarders. Feeling lonely and bored, and finding her parents distracted and cranky as they work intensely on a gardening catalogue, she explores the house and soon discovers a hidden door in her room that opens into a narrow tunnel (a rabbit hole?) and a parallel world. In this mirror universe, however, her new parents are attentive to her every need, and her room is wonderfully inviting. The only disconcerting aspect is that everyone she meets has buttons instead of eyes – something she is willing to overlook. So seductive is this new world, where flowers bloom in the moonlight, where all is a kaleidoscope of colors, she begins to find it harder and harder to return to her real life and her real parents. And, of course, her newly discovered mother encourages her to remain forever. It all seems so perfect. But as a talking cat suggests, perhaps there is more to this parallel world than first meets the eye (or button). And perhaps all of this goodwill and attention is a bit suspicious. What child doesn’t fantasize about a world in which they are the center of attention, a world in which they feel powerful and have more than a modicum of control over their own lives. Or a world suddenly absent parents who draw boundaries and make rules and all seems so arbitrary. The culmination of this fantasy was captured perfectly in the film Home Alone, when Kevin wakes up in his house and discovers everyone is gone. He wished them gone, and suddenly his wish has come true. He quickly sets out to create a life in which he rules. It’s a rush until it isn’t. Like Kevin, Coraline is soon confronted with more than she can handle. What was a thrill becomes deeply frightening. Will she be able to find her way back to her real world and once again be able to embrace her parents? Nothing is certain. What is surprising about Coraline is that none of the characters are particularly attractive. Even Coraline herself is feisty and a bit ill-tempered. That’s not to say that she should be more like Cinderella; but there has to be an emotional bridge built between the young audience and Coraline. Not even a young neighbor, Wybie, who wants to befriend Coraline, is terribly endearing. In return, she accuses him of being a stalker. Young children ever so easily blur the lines between what is real and what is fantasy and might find the last half of Coraline too intense. The strength of this film is that it is so wonderfully imagined. Based on Neil Gaiman’s book of the same name, which has sold over a million copies worldwide, there clearly is something about the story that resonates with kids. No doubt, all kids love to be scared – a little. Call it the jeepers creepers effect. On the larger-than-life screen, however, its impact may be more than some youngsters can handle. Coraline. Stop-motion animation. Starring the voices of Dakota Fanning, Teri Hatcher, Directed by Henry Selick. Rated PG.
articles.title: Coraline a scary story for older kids

Stop-motion animation. Starring the voices of Dakota Fanning, Teri Hatcher, Directed by Henry Selick. Rated PG. Piedmont Art Walk: Merging music, art, and education By Joseph Gold Sunday was a sparkling day. The 2nd Annual Piedmont Art Walk brought out people in droves. Many of them stopped by the Piedmont Center for the Arts to view the current Juried Art Show. One was a violinist who just happened to have his violin with him. Well… You know how performers are. The violinist saw a ready audience, so he took his violin out and played a brief concert and then departed. It was a nice touch and added a lot to the festivities. That’s the way music is. That brings me to page 2. I listened to President Biden’s recent speech with great interest; especially the part about early education. OK. At least this is a start. We need to realize that we are losing ground educationally, and this is of great concern. But the solution is obscure. Politicians and “educational czars“ do a lot of talking. They are good at that. Somehow, they fail in the history department. Education and art were valued by some enlightened civilizations of the past. Foremost in this pantheon of education was Greece in the Classic era. Anyone who has been to Greece has been awestruck by the architecture and the statues. But ancient Greece was far more than architecture and statues. Its culture valued a lively interchange of ideas. They respected intellectual and divergent opinions. It was the ancient Greeks who popularized the epic poem. The plays of Euripides and other authors are studied to this day. Those plays formed the basis of modern European opera, an art form regarded as the epitome because it combines literature, graphic art, dancing, singing, and instrumental music. As a former teacher I have thought a lot about education. In the United States we have 12 years of public school education. In Italy they have 13. Why can’t we add just one more year to public school education? While we’re at it, let’s give kids a good start by welcoming them one year before kindergarten. I use the word “welcoming” for good reason. Education should be fun. While some may regard education as a competitive sport, it should always by enjoyable and fun. I see competitive sports the same way. This was the philosophy of the ancient Greeks. It was good then and it is good now. Everything about education these days is so serious. Our education “leaders” wring their hands and lament that some segments of the population are falling behind. What they fail to recognize is that kids will want to learn if the experience is fun. We now have a problem of subject matter. The same education leaders stress science, and mathematics, and mathematics and science. But the glory that was ancient Greece combined science and mathematics with physical education and music. If we started school kids with music at an early age, they would have a better attitude toward every aspect of education. If people enjoy what they are doing, they will want to continue. Music makes us feel good psychologically. Along the way, musicians learn mathematics, good listening skills, individual initiative in combination with teamwork, and logical thinking among many other things. It is also important to recognize that music is the easiest written language. When I was teaching in public schools, I taught all my students how to read music… It took about five minutes. All of these things are then carried over into other aspects of education. We had great music educators in the past. When my mother was a youngster, her teachers brought their radios into the classroom. They listened to the concerts for kids by great musicians and music educators like Walter Damrosch. Leonard Bernstein continued where Damrosch left off. Why can’t we do that now? The cost is absolutely nothing, and maybe that’s the problem, because the politicians and the education bureaucrats want to throw money at our problems thinking that will solve them. Singing, after all, costs nothing. We see all too frequently the dumbing down of education. I was in a shop recently. They had the radio on, and I listened to the music with great interest. The song consisted of a repetitive drum track and a monotone singer singing these lyrics: “Duhduh, Duhduh, Duhduhduh, DUH?” Is this the example we want to present in education?

articles.text: If you are like me, the differences between all those buildings with prominent columns on them has always been a little unclear. Maybe today we can begin to sort it out. First, we go back to the Greeks. Their architecture was simpler, characterized by closely spaced columns because their era did not have the spanning capability of the arch. Along came the Romans, who in addition to borrowing heavily from the Greeks, were beneficiaries of the invention of concrete which allowed vaults, domes and arches, leading to a different, more developed architecture. Although the Greek and Roman civilizations were about 1000 years apart at their peaks, in our era the architecture they produced has been conventionally lumped together as Classical Architecture. This Classical Architecture was, and indeed is, pretty amazing. Well thought out with mathematically calculated proportions that are pleasing to the eye and mind, they seem to form a natural part of the universal order. Certainly they have endured over the centuries, having been “revived” numerous times. That is because they utilize the classical characteristics of large porticos (covered, columned entries), tall columns and classical orders (note the Ionic and Corinthian columns). At that time there was a Classical Revival in vogue in Europe. It appeared on this side of the pond as well, and was the start of our Colonial Architecture style. Fast forward 100 years of style preference upswings and downswings to the Centennial Exhibition of 1876 in Chicago – America’s first World’s Fair. With 10 million visitors viewing the pervasive Classical style architecture of the fair developed principally by the architect Daniel Burnham, America was exposed and reawakened to the architecture of antiquity and its colonial past, which we knew principally through our Colonial Architecture. Colonial Revival was born, and was immensely popular, flourishing for decades throughout the country, including California. So, Classical and Colonial Revival styles are stylistically linked, although there are many variants out there. Generally, the “purer” Classical Revival (or Neoclassical) style is more formal and monumental, occurring in larger institutional and civic buildings such as city and state capitals. articles.text: Like most of the world’s great wine regions, the prices of great Riojas have risen quite a bit in the last decade. So, I was happy to come across some true bargains from CUNE, Spain’s iconic Rioja producer. The name is an acronym for Compania Vinicola del Norte de Espagna and it is one of the oldest producers in Rioja, founded in 1879. Their topflight wines can demand near $100 a bottle, but they are also known for their value offerings like these. If your wine drinking is pretty much limited to California, I highly recommend trying some of the wines of Rioja. One characteristic of the region is they generally hold their wines longer in the barrel and release them with some age, so they are ready to drink when released. The tradition in the area is to use American oak. not French, so the wines often have a scent of sweet vanilla provided by the American oak. The following wines would be a great introduction to the Rioja region and are remarkable bargains. • 2019 CUNE Rioja, $15 This is made from 100% Tempranillo grapes grown organically. It boasts a medium ruby/ garnet color as well as a big, sweet nose of leather, currants and earth. A hint of toasty oak is also apparent in this ripe, medium bodied wine. It is soft and smooth on the finish and would be a great partner to roasted meats or hearty stews. 2019 CUNE Rioja 2020 CUNE Monopole Blanco Seco
