articles.text: Many may be unfamiliar with kumquats, a petite jewel of the citrus family, where the entire fruit is consumed in one delicious bite, sweet and tart. About the size of a grape, the entire kumquat is eaten, including the skin, which is actually the sweeter part of the fruit. A visit with my mom, who lives in Roseville, included picking a sizeable harvest of kumquats from her backyard tree. Since I had too many to eat at their peak of freshness, I knew I was going to be in for at least a couple of baking projects. Advance tip: Dates, and many dried fruits, will stick together when chopped. To help with an even distribution throughout the tea cake, I spread out the chopped pieces on a plate. When ready to add to the batter, I sprinkle them in and gently fold into the batter so they stay separated. Kumquat Tea Cake Adapted from Nicole Coudal’s My Delicious Blog INGREDIENTS • 1/2 cup unsalted butter, softened • 3/4 cup granulated sugar • 1/2 cup sour cream, room temperature • 1/2 cup kumquat puree • 4 tablespoons freshly squeezed orange juice • 2 extra-large eggs • 1/2 teaspoon vanilla extract • 1-1/2 cup all-purpose flour • 3/4 teaspoon baking powder • 1/2 teaspoon baking soda • 1/2 teaspoon sea salt • 1 cup walnuts, coarsely chopped • 1/2 cup dates, coarsely chopped INSTRUCTIONS To puree the kumquats, slice in half crosswise and remove any seeds. Then blitz in a mini-food processor or small blender until nearly smooth. I prefer having a few bits of identifiable rind. Position an oven rack at the lower third position. Preheat oven to 350˚ F. Line an 8.5 x 4.5-inch loaf pan with parchment paper crosswise, then generously butter the exposed ends. Set aside. Combine the flour, baking powder, baking soda, and salt in a medium bowl and whisk to combine well. Set aside. In a large mixing bowl, use an electric mixer to cream the softened butter until light and fluffy. Gradually add the sugar and continue beating until sugar is dissolved. Add the eggs, beating to incorporate well, then add the kumquat puree, orange juice and vanilla extract. The mixture will look curdled, but that’s OK. Add one-third of the flour mixture on low speed, then alternate one-half of the sour cream, another one-third of the flour mixture, the remaining sour cream, and end with the flour mixture. Take care to not overmix, using a spatula to complete the incorporation of the flour mixture into the batter. Add the chopped walnuts and dates. Take care to separate the dates, as they are sticky and will tend to clump together. You will want an even distribution of dates and walnuts throughout the batter. Pour the batter into the prepared loaf pan and bake for about 1 hour, until a toothpick inserted in the middle of the loaf comes out clean. Cool in the pan for about 10 minutes, then remove from the pan and transfer to a wire rack to complete cooling. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com.
articles.title: A sweet surprise for May: Kumquat Tea Cake

articles.text: 2018 Dry Creek Vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon Dry Creek Vineyards, in the eponymous region of Sonoma County, is a pioneer winery that has been operating there for nearly 50 years. I have admired their well-made Zinfandels for many years, but this was my first exposure to their Cabernet Sauvignon. It hails from a vineyard on the terraced hillsides of the western slope of the valley. It is 79% Cabernet Sauvignon with the remainder coming from the major Bordeaux grapes Merlot, Malbec, Cabernet Franc and Petite Verdot. The wine has a dense purple color and a wonderful, sweet, Bordeaux-like nose of licorice, currants, cedar and spice. Medium to full-bodied, elegant but authoritatively flavored, the wine is delicious now but should improve for up to two decades. Would be great partnered with grilled meats or hearty stews.

This wine shows floral notes, melon and mineral flavors inform the nose of this tasty, lively, impeccably balanced wine. This lengthy effort is an outstanding value for drinking over the next 3-4 years. 2016 CUNE Monopole Classico • 2016 CUNE Monopole Classico, $30 This wine has an interesting backstory. articles.text: Stephen Payne a 1955 graduate of Piedmont High School passed away on March 24, 2021 in Reno, Nevada. Born Stephen Ross Payne in Baltimore, Maryland, he was the son of Eugene Bennet Payne and Margaret Grace Adams Payne. He grew up in Montclair and moved to Piedmont in 1952, graduating from Piedmont High School in 1955. While in high school he played football and ran track. After high school he served in the Navy, and then studied business at Menlo College and San Francisco City College. He was a self-employed realtor in the East Bay and Sacramento. He loved tennis and shared this love with his daughters and grandchildren. Stephen Payne is survived by his wife, Judy Payne, four daughStephen Payne passed away on March 24. ters and eight grandchildren. He is also survived by a sister, Joan Payne Getz of Fairfax, CA.

articles.text: Photo by Harriette Louie Members of Walking on Wednesdays had a group photo taken while visiting Davie Tennis Stadium on the Piedmont-Oakland border. Pictured are: Albert Chen (left), Jim Kao, Pat McSwain, Sue Shepardson, Dick Carter, Melba Yee, Sherry Jacobs, Kathy Gustafson, and Bob Gustafson. Not shown: Andree and Mark Greenberg. On a beautiful, spring Piedmont day on April 28, the Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group gathered for their third week of walks since Covid restrictions were lifted. Thirteen walkers were on hand, including Andree Greenberg, Mark Greenberg, Kathy Gustafson, Bob Gustafson, Harriette Louie, Nancy Henn, Sherry Jacobs, Jim Kuo, Albert Chen, Melba Yee, Dick Carter, and firsttime walkers Sue Shepardson and Pat McSwain. The day before their walk the CDC had issued new guidelines for small groups to walk outdoors without masks, but the group agreed that they would continue to wear masks. The previous week the group walked to Dracena Park, a former rock quarry, so they decided to continue their exploration of quarry sites that have become recreation parks. The decision was to visit Davie Tennis Stadium on the Piedmont/Oakland border. The site was the former Piedmont Paving Company quarry and was given to the City of Oakland in 1931 by John L Davie, a former mayor and lawyer. The stadium includes five courts and a clubhouse mainly within the Piedmont city limits. After meeting at the Exedra, the group walked behind the Community Hall up to Guilford Avenue and then down a short path to Hazel Lane. They viewed the historic, huge redwood tree in the road just before Requa Road. This tree marked the entrance to Piedmont’s first school, the Ransom-Bridges School, which opened in 1913 on land that is now the Hazel Lane loop. The group went down Requa Road, past the home of Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi, who has provided so much Piedmont history that the walkers have enjoyed. They also noted an impressive gazebo in a backyard perched high above the street on large steel beams. After crossing Wildwood Avenue they went down Prospect Avenue to Oakmont Avenue and then into the tennis stadium. Looking up at the steep rock walls, they saw the slope that was created by the quarry digging decades ago. Players were on the courts, but the historic clubhouse with its collection of vintage racquets and pictures of local tennis greats was closed because of the pandemic. The morning was going by quickly and it was time to head back. The group walked up to Park Lane, over to Lakeshore Avenue and up Harvard Road and back to Prospect. The walkers made their way back to the Exedra by going through Piedmont. They were pleased with its shade provided by the park and pleased to see that water was still flowing in Bushy Dell Creek. The walkers emerged from the park after a leisurely, enjoyable two-mile walk in 90 minutes. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at 10:30 a.m. at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues). Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge and new walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required by contacting John Wilk at jwilk@piedmont. ca.gov. Walking on Wednesday Walking on Wednesdays group discovers Davie Tennis Stadium Photo by Harriette Louie Members of Walking on Wednesdays had a group photo taken while visiting Davie Tennis Stadium on the Piedmont-Oakland border. Pictured are: Albert Chen (left), Jim Kao, Pat McSwain, Sue Shepardson, Dick Carter, Melba Yee, Sherry Jacobs, Kathy Gustafson, and Bob Gustafson. Not shown: Andree and Mark Greenberg. By Dick Carter On a beautiful, spring Piedmont day on April 28, the Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group gathered for their third week of walks since Covid restrictions were lifted. Thirteen walkers were on hand, including Andree Greenberg, Mark Greenberg, Kathy Gustafson, Bob Gustafson, Harriette Louie, Nancy Henn, Sherry Jacobs, Jim Kuo, Albert Chen, Melba Yee, Dick Carter, and firsttime walkers Sue Shepardson and Pat McSwain. The day before their walk the CDC had issued new guidelines for small groups to walk outdoors without masks, but the group agreed that they would continue to wear masks. The previous week the group walked to Dracena Park, a former rock quarry, so they decided to continue their exploration of quarry sites that have become recreation parks. The decision was to visit Davie Tennis Stadium on the Piedmont/Oakland border. The site was the former Piedmont Paving Company quarry and was given to the City of Oakland in 1931 by John L Davie, a former mayor and lawyer. The stadium includes five courts and a clubhouse mainly within the Piedmont city limits. After meeting at the Exedra, the group walked behind the Community Hall up to Guilford Avenue and then down a short path to Hazel Lane. They viewed the historic, huge redwood tree in the road just before Requa Road. This tree marked the entrance to Piedmont’s first school, the Ransom-Bridges School, which opened in 1913 on land that is now the Hazel Lane loop. The group went down Requa Road, past the home of Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi, who has provided so much Piedmont history that the walkers have enjoyed. They also noted an impressive gazebo in a backyard perched high above the street on large steel beams. After crossing Wildwood Avenue they went down Prospect Avenue to Oakmont Avenue and then into the tennis stadium. Looking up at the steep rock walls, they saw the slope that was created by the quarry digging decades ago. Players were on the courts, but the historic clubhouse with its collection of vintage racquets and pictures of local tennis greats was closed because of the pandemic. The morning was going by quickly and it was time to head back. The group walked up to Park Lane, over to Lakeshore Avenue and up Harvard Road and back to Prospect. The walkers made their way back to the Exedra by going through Piedmont. They were pleased with its shade provided by the park and pleased to see that water was still flowing in Bushy Dell Creek. The walkers emerged from the park after a leisurely, enjoyable two-mile walk in 90 minutes. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at 10:30 a.m. at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues). Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge and new walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required by contacting John Wilk at jwilk@piedmont. ca.gov. The swing pictured is 18 feet tall. $4,911, which would include a couple of truckloads of dirt, a couple of shovels, and a second-hand swing set. However, safety-conscious Piedmonters may consider “Airborne Teens” way too dangerous. A small handful of community members rallied around the idea on April 1, but it was April Fool’s Day, so no one took them seriously. In dog years that’s 119 – truly a wonderful life. –Abby Dear Abby: We were up at Sibley Park eating a picnic lunch and a sizable dog smelled the food and made a beeline for us. I moved our lunch in the nick of time and fortunately the dog was friendly and listened to his owner to leave us alone and continue onward. But it seems everyone has been sharing stories with me that don’t end quite as happily. Are dogs allowed off-leash up there? –Serena, a hiker, dog lover (but no dogs yet) Dear Serena: Dogs are permitted to be off leash in Sibley and other East Bay Regional Parks, although each park has specific rules which are posted at the entrances. The East Bay Regional Park District has heard your concerns and is running a “Be a Pup Pro” campaign right now. It’s never easy to react when a big dog comes over sniffing for food. Essentially the District’s campaign has three basic themes: 1. Bag it and Bin it. Don’t leave your dog deposits on the side of a path for other dog walkers to pick up on their way out. Just slip it in a bag and carry it until you see a trash can. 2. Leash your dog in designated areas like the parking lot, trailheads, picnic areas, paved trails or by the public bathrooms. Again, each park posts specific signs on where a dog needs to be leashed which will prevent unnecessary accidents. 3. Actively keep your dog safe. Don’t permit your dog to mingle with cattle or horses that might be grazing on the grasslands. Definitely watch out for rattlesnakes and even wild rabbits which can bite a dog and infect them. And though it might be a bit inconvenient, carry water. As the weather heats up, our furry friends can dehydrate quickly. You can find an array of inexpensive, lightweight, compact bowls at local pet food shops or online that can squeeze into a pocket and water can be carried in a small container. Remember pavement and rocks can get very hot in the sun which can be hard on even the toughest paws. Right now, brilliant silver-blue lupine, bunches of hot yellow mustard, Scotch broom golds and the gorgeous orange of the California poppies are covering the hillsides, not to mention the shades of green. Recently we even stumbled on a glade of wild cherry blossoms. This year seems to be particularly gorgeous and since you can’t get on a plane to hike in Switzerland right now. Just drive 10 minutes to Skyline and pretend. It’s pawsome. –Abby E-mail your comments, ideas and dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston at MSJ312@ aol.com. articles.text: On the weekend of April 10-11 Piedmont Scouts from Troop 15 had their first overnight campout since the start of COVID more than one year ago. They went to Camp Tamarancho, a BSA campsite in Marin County. To comply with Marin COVID restrictions, the troop split up into patrols and stayed in their patrols throughout the weekend. All of the Scouts were excited to get back to nature and into tents. Everyone arrived on Saturday morning. A formal flag ceremony was followed by a big troop cheer. Scouts hiked to four campsites nestled in the woods with the peak of Mt Tamalpais off in the distance. Scouts unpacked their camping gear and split into their patrols for advancement activities. There were three advancement stations – knife safety, knots and lashings, and First Aid. Ten new Scouts attended knife safety training, which allows them to carry a pocket knife. Older Scouts worked on knots, lashings and first aid. Each patrol cooked its own meals. After dinner the Troop gathered at the Tamarancho fire ring and amphitheater for a traditional campfire where the patrols put HS ninth grader Romi Bhatia teaches sixth-graders Callum Louch and Thalay Visessonchoke how to interlock their hands and wrists to form a seat to carry an injured person With Trenton Downing on his back, Gabriel Barbosa-Topete practices carrying an injured victim to safety. Avi Maidenberg and Thalay Visessonchoke chop carrots under the watchful eye of Patrol Leader Corbin Breeden. Piedmont Scouts from Troop 15 hike to their campsite at Tamarancho in Marin County. 6th grade Platypus Patrol members receive instruction on lighting a camp stove from Patrol Leader Nathan Fredericks. on skits. Master of Ceremonies was Senior Patrol Leader Jack Gross-Whitaker. There were a lot of funny skits, and all the new Scouts were laughing and having a great time. On Sunday the troop broke down their campsites and went on a short hike on a trail where they saw the wreckage of a B-17 bomber from a plane crash on November 2, 1941. After that it was time to hike to the parking lot for rides back home. Troop 15 Scouts are looking forward to a trip to Camp Tamarancho on May 22-23, when they will be hiking 5 miles to the campsites, bringing everything they will need in backpacks.

articles.text: The Number 10 streetcar on Highland Avenue at Park Way in Piedmont in 1943. In 1939, this Piedmont Avenue Station at 41st Street in Oakland replaced the original station. The canopy was demolished in 1961, but the clock tower remains. or token. Upon entering the car, passengers could ask the conductor for a transfer, which allowed them to change to other streetcars for a limited time. Electric streetcars were powered by an overhead electrical wire. A pole on the car contacted the wire and drew power to the traction motors. Each wheel had a traction motor which drove the car. Metal wheels on the metal tracks grounded the cars. Piedmont’s Streetcar Lines Two of the three streetcar lines in Piedmont carried passengers to the small shingled Key Route Station on Piedmont Avenue near 41st Street. There, passengers could stay on the Number 10 car and continue to downtown Oakland. They could also transfer to a streetcar to the ferry terminal on a 16,000-foot pier at the end of Yerba Buena Street in Oakland. There, they would board a ferry to San Francisco. Hugh Craig noted that on a good day it took him 1½ hours to get from his home in Piedmont to his office in San Francisco. Passengers could also transfer to other streetcars at the Piedmont Avenue Station to go to other neighborhoods. At its height, the Key System had over 66 miles of track, and served East Bay residents from Albany to San Leandro. articles.text: Alameda County announced on Friday, April 23 it would begin administering a COVID-19 vaccine produced by Johnson & Johnson again after investigating its connection to a small number of blood clot cases. The county joined other Bay Area counties in following guidance from the Centers of Disease Control and Prevention and the Food and Drug Administration released that day. The county said it would make more information about the rare blood clotting risks widely available. The CDC recommended that health agencies pause the use of the Johnson & Johnson vaccine on April 13 “out of an abundance of caution” due to reports of severe blood clotting issues in a handful of cases. The Alameda County Public Health Department followed this guidance. As of last week, the CDC has confirmed 17 cases of a blood clotting disorder out of some 8 million people who have received the Johnson & Johnson COVID- 19 vaccine. There have been three reported deaths due to the blood clots. Most of the blood clot cases were in women between the ages of 18 and 48. Symptoms typically occurred 6 to 13 days after vaccination. Due to the exceedingly low rate of blood clots, the CDC found the benefits of the Johnson & Johnson vaccine outweighed the risks and announced that health providers should begin providing it again after a 10-day pause. Alameda County announced it would begin using up its small supply of Johnson & Johnson vaccine as soon as possible. Even though the blood clot disorder appears to be extremely rare, people who receive the Johnson & Johnson vaccine are encouraged to monitor themselves for symptoms, like severe headache, abdominal pain, leg pain or shortness of breath within three weeks after vaccination. Anyone experiencing these symptoms should contact their health care provider immediately. “The public is strongly urged to get vaccinated as soon as possible,” health officers from all Bay Area counties said in a joint statement released Sunday, April 25. “All vaccines are proven to be highly effective at preventing hospitalization or death from COVID-19, and people who are fully vaccinated are also much less likely to be contagious or transmit the virus to someone else. The longer you wait to get vaccinated, the greater the risk of contracting COVID-19, and infecting a friend, loved one or coworker.” Even with the pause on the Johnson & Johnson vaccine, vaccination in Alameda County has continued on a brisk pace. Because the Johnson & Johnson vaccine only requires one shot compared to the two-dose vaccines available from Pfizer and Moderna, health officials hope its reintroduction to the county’s supply will accelerate vaccination even more. In Piedmont, 92 percent of the adult population, about 7,650 people, have received at least one dose of vaccine as of last week. Almost 61 percent of Piedmonters, about 5,000 residents, are now fully vaccinated, the highest percentage in the county. Alameda County has administered over 1.35 million doses of vaccine since December, and over 41 percent of the county’s population is now fully vaccinated. In Oakland, almost 65 percent of the population has received at least one dose and about 41 percent of Oaklanders are fully vaccinated. Overall, the county is hoping to vaccinate at least 70 to 80 percent of the population. On April 12, Alameda County opened COVID-19 vaccination appointments to all residents ages 16 and older. The Moderna and Johnson & Johnson vaccines are approved for people ages 18 and older. Pfizer vaccines are currently approved for teenagers as young as 16, and the pharmaceutical company is in the process of seeking authorization for their vaccine for children ages 12 to 15. Alameda County has a form to receive notifications about available appointments at covid-19. acgov.org/vaccines Californians are also encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, employer or the county to receive a vaccination appointment. The state asks residents to utilize the digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn.ca.gov to determine their vaccine eligibility and schedule appointments. ACPHD said that appointments are prioritized for people who are most at risk for COVID- 19 exposure or severe symptoms. “Vaccine distribution is being prioritized for persons who are most at risk for hospitalization or death due to COVID-19, as well persons who are at high risk for occupational exposure,” ACPHD said on its website. “We expect to have more vaccine supply in the coming months.” The state has administered about 28.7 million vaccine doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. The state is vaccinating an average of over 340,000 people per day. Almost 12 million Californians, about 37 percent of the adult population, have been fully vaccinated. door dining, without a mask. articles.text: These beautiful Piedmont homes are of the Colonial Revival style. Less monumental, they are asymmetrical and exhibit many classical motifs including the balustrades (fancy guardrails) and dentils (the small repetitive protrusions at the cornice). The Colonial Revival giveaway is the use of paired columns, not employed in earlier eras, something I think adds an incredible richness to the design. The arches (but not the solar panels) are a Roman contribution. A variant of the Colonial Revival is the Georgian style from England. It is restrained in classical ornamentation but wonderfully proportioned and balanced over the entire symmetrical facade. The Gambrel (double sloped) roof with dormers, and curved eave on this fine home is a characteristic of the Dutch influence, another subcategory of the Colonial Revival genre.

articles.text: On April 21 Piedmont School District Curriculum Director and Assistant Superintendent Cheryl Wozniak sent a series of three messages to the entire Piedmont High School and Millennium High School student body and all high school staff announcing that meetings for student discussions of the Derek Chauvin trial verdict were being scheduled. One message was for “Black students,” another was for “BIPOC students” and the final message was for “White students.” The “White students” message created an immediate backlash. Wozniak later issued an apology, and the following day Supt. Randy Booker sent a message to the high school community. A Piedmont junior was outraged by the segregation and tone-deafness of the email announcement and proceeded to create a TikTok video discussing the email while displaying the text of the email in the background. He implored viewers of the video to make the video go viral, and it has. As of press-time the social media video had over 76,000 likes, 5,000 comments and 232,000 views. “Look at what my school sent out [...] Like, what? I don’t get it. Let’s make this go viral,” he said. tiktok.com/@sueyd_/ video/6954438540075732230. Piedmont School District Curriculum Director Cheryl Wozniak. articles.text: The city of Piedmont is seeking volunteers to serve on the newly established Community Pool Advisory Committee (PAC). Residents have until Wednesday, May 5 to apply. Committee members will offer advice throughout the design process, as well as serve as a conduit for the community’s needs in the design refinement and construction of the pool. The committee will not be responsible for managing or directing project activities; instead, the committee is expected to use the experience and expertise of its members to provide support and insight to staff and city council members for the $19 million project. Main responsibilities of PAC members will include: ensuring the project meets community expectations, communicating project progress to residents, and making recommendations to staff on how to best balance any conflicting priorities with budget resources and community expectations. The PAC will consist of five to seven residents. Recruitment for the committee takes place separately from recruitment that has taken place for other commissions and committees. City staff will announce the recruitment period on the city website and social media channels, as well as with a press release. After receiving applications from interested residents, city council will then conduct interviews of qualified candidates. The council will appoint a Chair of the committee and its members. Interested residents may download the “Application for Appointive Vacancy” from the city’s website and apply online at https:// piedmont.ca.gov. Applications are due at City Hall by Wednesday, May 5 at 5 p.m. Interviews with the City Council for these positions will be scheduled for the evening of Monday, May 10. No appointments will be made without a city council interview. Residents with questions may contact City Clerk John Tulloch at (510) 420-3040.

Wozniak will also present results from the survey on social and emotional health of PUSD students. articles.text: Nate Redinbo joined Piedmont through an AmeriCorps CivicSpark fellowship in September 2020. In his eight months with the City, he has helped orchestrate and organize the city’s major sustainability programs and events, despite the hurdles of the COVID pandemic. CivicSpark fellows serve the needs of community members by building public sector capacity to address emerging issues, and by fostering authentic community engagement. Each year, AmeriCorps CivicSpark recruits 90 recent college graduates to help local communities with sustainability projects. articles.text: Editor: I was saddened to read Shirley Hooi’s letter more or less admonishing PUSD to stay in their lane as it concerns race relations and history including current events. I would suggest that her letter is exactly the reason the schools need to talk about race. Her most memorable anecdotal stories from her childhood 35 years ago were being asked if she spoke English by PPD and being jumped by two black youth. Using a modern lens, I would say the African American youth from her attack should be considered “a one off, a bad apple; the whole barrel isn’t rotten, just a few bad seeds.” We have extended that identical courtesy to every single officer involved in shootings of unarmed black people. Until [recently], most police officers involved in murdering unarmed black folks have kept both their pension and freedom. I want to scream for every mother, myself included, who wonders if today is the day some jumpy cop is going to kill my son. Is today the day that some racist neighbor is going to murder my son for wearing a hoodie? Is today the day my son will be executed by white men for running in the wrong neighborhood? Will my other son be lynched for looking at a white woman? The three black men in this household have multiple negative anecdotal stories because they have had the audacity to drive, bike, walk, ride the elevator, and shop in a department store all the while being black men. My husband went to a tworoom, segregated school specifically for “coloreds” 10 years after Brown v. Board of Education. The subhuman and racist treatment of people of color, specifically black men, in my immediate family spans decades. If Ms. Hooi’s letter is any indication, even some educated parents in this town aren’t talking about race with their kids other than to shut down uncomfortable conversation with terse responses. It would seem counter intuitive, given Ms. Hooi’s selfproclaimed blunt answers to her children, that she would have an in-depth conversation about race being that she herself trotted out a rather tone-deaf response. It’s not enough in 2021 to “not be a racist” The easiest way to obliterate white guilt is to be an ally to people of color. You cannot be an ally if you don’t listen, if you don’t acknowledge and if you don’t converse. Please keep race relations, current and historic in this country as part of the PUSD curriculum. To do otherwise is a tragedy we cannot afford to repeat. –Sydney Proctor
articles.title: Becoming an ally by listening

articles.text: “I am a voice crying in the wilderness, Make the Lord’s path straight.” John the Baptist stood proudly in the tradition of the biblical prophets. He stood in the tradition of Moses who led the people to freedom and toward an understanding of what it meant to be the people of God. He stood in the tradition of Elijah who knew what it was like to face hostility, to feel alone and afraid, even as God’s words poured from his mouth. He stood in the tradition of Jeremiah who strove to counter the self-serving lies of the religious and political establishments. Consider John’s use of the words voice, cry and wilderness. pages.text: 2 Wednesday, April 28, 2021 Opinion Becoming an ally by listening Editor: I was saddened to read Shirley Hooi’s letter more or less admonishing PUSD to stay in their lane as it concerns race relations and history including current events. I would suggest that her letter is exactly the reason the schools need to talk about race. Her most memorable anecdotal stories from her childhood 35 years ago were being asked if she spoke English by PPD and being jumped by two black youth. Using a modern lens, I would say the African American youth from her attack should be considered “a one off, a bad apple; the whole barrel isn’t rotten, just a few bad seeds.” We have extended that identical courtesy to every single officer involved in shootings of unarmed black people. Until [recently], most police officers involved in murdering unarmed black folks have kept both their pension and freedom. I want to scream for every mother, myself included, who wonders if today is the day some jumpy cop is going to kill my son. Is today the day that some racist neighbor is going to murder my son for wearing a hoodie? Is today the day my son will be executed by white men for running in the wrong neighborhood? Will my other son be lynched for looking at a white woman? The three black men in this household have multiple negative anecdotal stories because they have had the audacity to drive, bike, walk, ride the elevator, and shop in a department store all the while being black men. My husband went to a tworoom, segregated school specifically for “coloreds” 10 years after Brown v. Board of Education. The subhuman and racist treatment of people of color, specifically black men, in my immediate family spans decades. If Ms. Hooi’s letter is any indication, even some educated parents in this town aren’t talking about race with their kids other than to shut down uncomfortable conversation with terse responses. It would seem counter intuitive, given Ms. Hooi’s selfproclaimed blunt answers to her children, that she would have an in-depth conversation about race being that she herself trotted out a rather tone-deaf response. It’s not enough in 2021 to “not be a racist” The easiest way to obliterate white guilt is to be an ally to people of color. You cannot be an ally if you don’t listen, if you don’t acknowledge and if you don’t converse. Please keep race relations, current and historic in this country as part of the PUSD curriculum. To do otherwise is a tragedy we cannot afford to repeat. –Sydney Proctor Originally printed in the Piedmont Post on March 17, 2021 Piedmont Post at your door and online The Piedmont Post remains available online to all subscribers, no matter where they live. articles.text: The East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD), will hold a public hearing on proposed rate increases to water and wastewater service charges. The virtual meeting will be held on Tuesday, June 8 at 1:15 p.m. A notice was mailed to customers in Alameda, Albany, Berkeley, El Cerrito, Emeryville, Kensington, Oakland, and Piedmont last week. EBMUD is proposing to increase the rates for both its water and wastewater service charges based on its most recent rate models and cost of service studies. Rates would increase over a two-year period, by approximately 4 percent overall on July 1, 2021, followed by another 4 percent increase the next year, July 1, 2022. This is an approximate increase. Individual bills may increase by slightly more or less that amount depending on the specific rates and charges that apply to you and how much water you use. The notice mailed to residents provides an example of an average single family residence which could expect a water rate increase of $5.19 per month, and a wastewater increase of $1.87 per month. A temporary “Drought Surcharge” may be assessed on all potable water use during a declared drought or water shortage. EBMUD has not yet declared a drought. Drought surcharges are calculated to recover costs of providing supplemental water, cost of water-shortage related customer service, and losses of revenue. How to participate in the hearing The board of directors will hold the public hearing on June 8, which will be conducted via Zoom. The public may participate in the hearing virtual or by telephone. The Zoom Meeting ID is 958-6681-4531, and the passcode is 810650. You must enter both numbers to participate in the meeting telephonically (by calling 1-699-900-6833) or virtually (by visiting www.edmud.com/ rates.) Written comments may be mailed before the hearing date to EBMUD, MS 218, PO Box 24055, Oakland, CA 94623-1055. The first event focused on the City’s Climate Action Plan, a document approved by Council that sets emissions goals for the City. Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman and Americorps Fellow Nate Redinbo led participants through a brief overview of the Plan and highlighted actions staff had taken over the last 12 months to meet the CAP goals. Highlights included the February passage of energy reach codes through council, and a continued focus on transportation and solid waste management. Staff then asked participants to offer suggestions and thoughts on actions to take next. In the evening, staff held a panel discussion with new Fire Chief David Brannigan, Fire Captain Scott Barringer, and wildland fire scientist Dr. Sasha Berleman on the film Rebuilding Paradise and Piedmont’s fire management practices. Audience members asked questions ranging from the fire safety of various native species to evacuation plans. Dr. Berleman described controlled burns and the future of firefighting measures. Piedmont firefighters highlighted steps residents can take to be fire safe. articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will host a virtual town hall with California Assembly member Buffy Wicks on Wednesday, May 5, at 5 p.m. Wicks, Piedmont’s elected representative in the 15th Assembly District, also represents Berkeley, Albany, Emeryville, Richmond, and parts of Oakland. She was elected to the State Assembly in November 2018. Wicks’ 2021 legislation prioritizes long-standing challenges in the district, now exacerbated by the pandemic. She has introduced and authored assembly bills that combat homelessness, support gun violence prevention, and target the debt settlement industry. She gained national attention last year when she brought her month-old baby to the state capitol and voted on the floor with her Assemblywoman Buffy Wicks newborn in her arms, described by the New York Times as “an image of moms who do it all.” Click on http://tiny.cc/WicksTownHall2021 to sign up for the May 5 meeting. Questions may be posted prior to the discussion on tinyurl.com/429k24yv.

articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters is hosting a public discussion with Alameda County District Attorney Nancy O’Malley on Thursday, May 6 starting at 4 p.m. She will describe the work by her department with abused and homeless women, helping them move beyond trauma into a positive future. O’Malley will address the many challenges COVID-19 has posed. She will explain the ways in which the current lack of civility in politics is impeding the pace and scale of progress for women who suffer from violence. For example, passage of the Violence Against Women Act was held up due to politics, and funding for the Victims Crime Act, which provides resources to states for victims of crime, was also reduced. O’Malley is a nationally recognized expert on issues involving violence against women, violence against persons with disabilities, and interpersonal violence including sexual assault, domestic violence, elder abuse, child abuse, stalking, and human exploitation and trafficking. She serves in the office that dates to a time when Earl Warren was the Alameda County D.A. before becoming United States Supreme Court Chief Justice. O’Malley is the first woman to serve as the County’s District Attorney. The event is free and open to all community members. To register for the Zoom event, visit https:// www.lwvpiedmont.org/content. a spx?page_id= 40 02&club_ id=601389&item_id=1256825. It will be recorded and posted on the League of Women Voters of Piedmont website for those who cannot join live.

articles.text: On Tuesday, April 27, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention updated its guidance on masking, announcing that people fully vaccinated against the COVID-19 virus do not need to wear masks outdoors unless they are in a crowd of strangers. Soon after the CDC announcement, California Governor Gavin Newsom said that he would update California’s mask mandate to match the new guidance. “After reviewing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s masking recommendations, and with science and data as our guide, we are moving to align California’s guidance with these common-sense updates,” Newsom said in a statement. People are considered fully vaccinated if it has been two weeks since either their second dose of Pfizer or Moderna vaccine or their one dose of Johnson & Johnson vaccine. The CDC said that fully vaccinated people can participate in most outdoor activities, like small outdoor gatherings or outdoor dining, without a mask. However, masks are recommended in crowded outdoor settings and venues, like packed stadiums and large concerts. “We will continue to recommend this until widespread vaccination is achieved,” CDC Director Dr. Rochelle Walensky said in a White House briefing yesterday. The number of new COVID- 19 cases has remained low in California, Alameda County and Piedmont this week, with California now having some of the lowest positivity rates in the nation. No new cases of COVID- 19 have been reported in Piedmont across the past seven days, according to Alameda County Public Health Department data. The total number of Piedmont cases since the pandemic began is 176. The positivity rate for the county is 1.4 percent as of Monday, April 26, a slight decrease from last week. The positivity rate has not been above 2 percent since February 25. Across Alameda County, the total caseload is 85,683 – an increase of only 215 new cases week-over-week, a large decrease compared to recent weeks. There have been 26,664 cases recorded in Oakland and 13,333 cases in Hayward. Tragically, another 14 people have died of COVID-19 in Alameda County, bringing the total number of fatalities countywide to 1,491. In terms of reopening businesses and activities, Alameda County moved into the orange tier on March 30. The orange tier, or moderate tier, is the second-least restrictive tier in California’s color-coded four-tier reopening protocol. The county has met orange tier metrics for several weeks but has not yet met benchmarks to move into the least-restrictive yellow tier, or minimal tier. To move up into the yellow tier, the positivity rate needs to stay below 2 percent. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to be below 1 – right now there are 3.6 cases per 100,000. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to stay below 2.2 percent – it is currently 2.4 percent in Alameda County. Only four of California’s 58 counties are in the yellow tier. All Bay Area counties are in the orange tier besides Solano County, which is in the more-restrictive red tier. If San Francisco and Marin counties continue to meet yellow tier metrics, they could move into the least-restrictive tier next week. In the yellow tier, most indoor operations are allowed with modifications.
articles.title: COVID NEWS California to follow new CDC guidance on use of masks outdoors for the vaccinated

articles.text: PHS senior Jake Ochoa He’s not yet old enough to get one on his body, but 17-year-old Jake Ochoa has tattoos on his mind. For this visual artist, it’s mainly about the self-expression that tattoos represent. “I saw a YouTube video about tattoos, and this tattoo artist said, basically, that we don’t get to choose the body that we’re born with, but we can choose how we decorate it,” said the Piedmont High School student. “That really resonated with me. It’s decorating in the purest sense.” Ochoa’s interest in tattoos started three years ago when he was a freshman. He is now concentrating on tattoo imagery and culture for his Advanced Placement Art class project. “There are a lot of different styles,” he said. “[Tattooing]’s a window into different cultures, different lifestyles.” A fan of the uniformity of traditional Japanese tattoos, Ochoa also appreciates the unorthodox art of Neo-traditional tattoos. “I’m really getting into Polynesian and Filipino tattoos,” he said. “The imagery is always fascinating. There’s a flow; they fit onto the body really well. I find that composition really appealing.” Ochoa will display his tattoo-influenced designs on small paper items, like prints or bookmarks, at this year’s Piedmont Art Walk. But some day, with a lot of training and financial security, he might start inking his designs onto the skin of paying customers. “There’s a lot of merit to doing it; it’s creatively stimulating,” “8Dragon” by Jake Ochoa he said. “It’s stressful, because you’re marking someone’s skin. But I think it’d be a fun adventure. Tattooing is something I’d like to do in the future – when I have free time, and when I’m old enough to get the machines.” Ochoa plans to study graphic design at college next year.
articles.title: ARTIST PROFILE Teen artist finds inspiration in tattoo culture

articles.text: I spent a few hours last week talking to a mom who was wracked with guilt. The problem was her son, she explained, who was struggling in school. His grades had dropped in a few classes and she was beside herself with self-recrimination. I should have done this, she said. Or that. Or maybe I should have done something completely different. It took me a while to follow her logic, but it went something like this: if she had just known more, done more, and helped more, then her child wouldn’t be suffering. This is a trap many parents fall into these days, especially in the midst of COVID. You believe that it is your job to prevent your child’s suffering, and because so many kids are suffering in COVID, it means you’re doing a terrible job, or even worse, that you’ve failed as parents. The mom I spoke with certainly believed this, and it was making her life miserable. Parents: raise your hands if, at some point during this disastrous year, you have worried that you aren’t doing enough for your kids. I’m assuming that’s all of you, so I have a few words of advice. The best thing you can do for Forgiveness leads to healing. your kids right now is to forgive yourself, unconditionally, for every misstep you’ve made this year, no matter how big. And I mean it: forgive yourself for everything. Here’s why: your concern about your own shortcomings weighs you down, and it leaves you less able to attend to all of the important things in your life, such as your child’s suffering. Because while it’s futile to focus on preventing suffering – something that is impossible – it is helpful to focus on soothing the suffering, which is quite a different matter. You can begin this process by soothing yourself, forgiving yourself, having a good cry, and recognizing that this has been a horrible year. Forget about silver linings for the moment. Focus on being tender and kind to yourself, in your role as a parent, and recognize that the best next step is to forgive your child too. It’s been an awful time, and it’s not over yet, but we can ease our pain by not second-guessing, criticizing, or punishing ourselves for not being perfect. Dr. Susan Eva Porter is the Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. articles.title: A time for forgiveness

articles.text: Double Play, the independent robotics team of Eva and Mikey Swei and neighbor Jasper Schuetz, qualified for the 2021 VEX World Championship by receiving the Design Award at the VEX California State Championship in April for their robot designed to put basketballs through hoops. The Swei siblings got their start in robotics by learning about VEX competitions from their older cousins who competed for Head Royce Robotics. Mikey started competing as a 4th grader. As a 5th grader last year, he competed in the VEX High School Division with sister Eva, then a PHS freshman. They recruited Schuetz for more support in building, designing, and programming. VEX has over 200,000 teams from 50 countries competing worldwide. Every year, a new challenge is revealed with aspects of driving, shooting, lifting, stacking and other tasks in a tournament format. At tournaments, teams are required to pair up in alliances and compete with two other teams. In this year’s challenge, Double Play engineered a robot that can pick up and score balls in goals, similar to basketball. Over the course of a year, the team has spent over 400 hours building, designing, and programming the robot. You can watch their robot reveal here:yout ube.com / watch?v=mPFmXM4kCZo or search “8OOO1B Double Play” on Youtube. For more information about VEX and this year’s challenge, see vexrobotics.com/v5/competition
articles.title: Vex Robotics team advances to Worlds

Wozniak apology “Subject: Apology and Clarification for Support Circles Dear PUSD Students and Staff, I apologize for the harm my previous communication where I used the language “support circle for white students” has caused the students of color in our community. I did not make it clear that the circle being offered by Ms. Ina and Ms. Jean is for those who want to be allies for BIPOC, and, consequently, I have learned that the impact on our students of color has left them feeling hurt and disrespected by district administration. I sincerely apologize for the lack of sensitivity in my communication and invite anyone who has been impacted to reach out to me directly so I can repair the harm I have caused. Kindly, Cheryl L. Wozniak, Ed.D. Assistant Superintendent, Educational Services District Title IX Coordinator and Complaint Officer Among the senior district staff, her role has been marked by being non-responsive to phone and e-mail inquiries from the Post. She is now listed as Assistant Superintendent, second only to Supt. Booker. Her salary in 2018 was shown as $190,125. Thinking Outside The Classroom A time for forgiveness By Susan Eva Porter, Ph.D. I spent a few hours last week talking to a mom who was wracked with guilt. The problem was her son, she explained, who was struggling in school. His grades had dropped in a few classes and she was beside herself with self-recrimination. I should have done this, she said. Or that. Or maybe I should have done something completely different. It took me a while to follow her logic, but it went something like this: if she had just known more, done more, and helped more, then her child wouldn’t be suffering. This is a trap many parents fall into these days, especially in the midst of COVID. You believe that it is your job to prevent your child’s suffering, and because so many kids are suffering in COVID, it means you’re doing a terrible job, or even worse, that you’ve failed as parents. The mom I spoke with certainly believed this, and it was making her life miserable. Parents: raise your hands if, at some point during this disastrous year, you have worried that you aren’t doing enough for your kids. I’m assuming that’s all of you, so I have a few words of advice. The best thing you can do for Forgiveness leads to healing. your kids right now is to forgive yourself, unconditionally, for every misstep you’ve made this year, no matter how big. And I mean it: forgive yourself for everything. Here’s why: your concern about your own shortcomings weighs you down, and it leaves you less able to attend to all of the important things in your life, such as your child’s suffering. Because while it’s futile to focus on preventing suffering – something that is impossible – it is helpful to focus on soothing the suffering, which is quite a different matter. You can begin this process by soothing yourself, forgiving yourself, having a good cry, and recognizing that this has been a horrible year. Forget about silver linings for the moment. Focus on being tender and kind to yourself, in your role as a parent, and recognize that the best next step is to forgive your child too. It’s been an awful time, and it’s not over yet, but we can ease our pain by not second-guessing, criticizing, or punishing ourselves for not being perfect. Dr. Susan Eva Porter is the Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. She can be reached at sue@orindaacademy.org. Vex Robotics team advances to Worlds Double Play, the independent robotics team of Eva and Mikey Swei and neighbor Jasper Schuetz, qualified for the 2021 VEX World Championship by receiving the Design Award at the VEX California State Championship in April for their robot designed to put basketballs through hoops. A brainchild of Troop 6 (also originators of the Scout Tree Lot in the 1950’s), the first ever Troop 6 Plant Sale was hosted with great success the weekend of April 24-25 on the black top at Corpus Christi School. In an effort to earn their Gardening and Salesmanship badges, Troop 6 Scouts raised, from seed over 1,000 plants, 20 varieties of tomatoes, 15 varieties of peppers, plus squash, zucchini, cucumber, beans, eggplant, beets, carrots, and herbs. Over half of the vegetables and fruits were sold, with plans to sell the rest at a local farmer’s market. Sales were steady all weekend with Scout families, Piedmont garden clubs and friends coming out to support the Plant Sale. Proceeds will be used to help offset the cost of summer camp, an annual and much-anticipated rite of passage. But Holy Mole, why so many peppers? Answer: Troop 6 Scouts love to cook and keep it hot. Some of the peppers they had for sale included Arapaho, Bulgarian Carrots, Cozumel, Early Jalapeno, Hungarian Sweet, Neapolitan, and of course, Siracha. Daniel Certa waters plants during the Troop 6 Plant Sale. Troop 6 sold 500 plants and have more to sell. They are going to extend the sale to next Saturday, May 1 from 10am - 1pm on Jordan Rd off of Redwood Rd/35th Ave - Avenue Terrace Park.

articles.text: Consumer Affairs Reporter PG&E customers in Alameda County recently received a letter informing them that PG&E would be switching them to a time of use (TOU) plan on May 1. The letter is part of a large initiative to switch all customers in Northern and Central California to TOU by March 2022. If your reaction is “What does this mean?”, “How will this affect my bill?”, or simply “Huh”?, you are not alone. Paraphrasing the Bible, “It is easier for a camel to fit through the eye of a needle than for a normal person to comprehend PG&E rates.” PG&E offers two broad types of rate plans – TOU and Tiered. In TOU plans, when you use electricity, it determines the rate you pay, while Tiered is based upon how much you use as the basis for the rate. Tiered plans work a lot like marginal income tax brackets. You start with a low rate, but when you pass certain usage points, you move into higher rates on the excess. If you don’t use a lot of electricity, the Tiered Plan might be best, especially if you want to use electricity during peak hours. The Time of Use Plan to which PG&E is switching customers has only two rates: Peak, which is 4-9 PM every day, and Off-Peak, which is everything else. So, if you use a lot of electricity but are generally able to avoid those peak hours, you could buy most of your electricity at the lower rate. What activities use the most electricity? Electric appliances such as clothes dryers and ovens are examples, but the big energy hogs are air conditioners and electric vehicle recharging. While not a lot of Piedmont residents have air conditioning, many of us do have electric vehicles, which gets very expensive on a Tiered Plan. EV owners almost always do best on a TOU Plan by setting up their charging for off peak hours (we set ours to start at midnight, and it is done by 7 a.m.). And if you do have an air conditioner and need to use it, you would want to cool down your house earlier in the day and turn it off at 4 p.m. to avoid a shock when you view you next bill. So, with these choices – and there are several TOU Plans, including a special one for EVs – how do you choose? PG&E actually provides a pretty neat tool for you: 1. Log on to your account at pge.com 2. Choose “Rate Plans” 3. Choose “Time of Use Rate Plans” 4. Click the orange box marked “Compare Rates” PG&E will show you all of your options, along with your expected annual electric cost based on your most recent twelve months of usage. It will let you switch to any plan you want, but only once a year. As an incentive to get customers to accept the default switch to the new TOU Plan on May 1, PG&E is giving you what amounts to a money back guarantee. If, after a year, you end up paying more on the new plan than you would have under your existing plan, PG&E with refund you the difference. At that point you can continue on the TOU plan or switch to another that makes more sense. So, for most of us, doing nothing and accepting the switch will probably work out fine. However, it’s always a good idea to be an informed consumer, so go online and look at your options. You might find a more cost-effective option for your particular situation. Paris, the city of sidewalk cafes is hollowed out and packed away. Social interaction and street noises have simply vanished. President Emmanuel Macron declared a national emergency on March 10 and has instituted massive state intervention to manage the crisis. articles.text: Bryan Gardere’s girls’ basketball team burst into their new season on Wednesday, April 21 with a commanding 83-49 victory over Clayton Valley Charter in Concord. Leading 15-9 after the first quarter, they exploded for 29 points in the second quarter to lead 44-20 at halftime. The Highlanders poured in 24 points in the third, 68-38, then added 15 more in the last quarter. Leading all scorers was senior Kai Johnson with 33 points, 14 rebounds, eight steals, and six assists. “Kai does it all. She plays outstanding defense and has really improved as a shooter,” said Gardere after the blowout win. With Trinity Zamora and Maddie Hill out for the opener, it enabled freshman guard Natalia Martinez to step into the limelight with 26 points, six rebounds, six assists, and two steals. Hannah Govert had five points, five assists, and five rebounds. Piedmont plays St. Joseph today at 5:30 p.m. then play against tomorrow at Hayward High. The home-opener is set for Tuesday, May 4 against Cal High, 7 p.m. Staff Photos Kai Johnson had 33 points, 14 rebounds, eight steals, and six assists in the season-opening victory over Clayton Valley. “Natalia is one of the players we are most excited about. This girl is a real-deal Hooper,” he exclaimed with a broad grin. “She’s probably the fastest player on the team and is a great finisher.” Also making her varsity debut was junior Aniya Perine, who scored 10 points, and had eight rebounds and two assists. “Aniya did well in all phases. She scored the first bucket of the 2021 season,” said Gardere with a smile. Piedmont also shot well from beyond the arch, knocking down eight 3-pointers spread among six players. In addition to Johnson, the only returning player from last season is Hannah Govert, a key role player. She had a triple five: five points, five boards and five assists. The game also featured freshman Mai Leggett and Luisa Murray making their varsity debuts. Leggett hit a 3-pointer, while Murray landed a pair. “Hannah is an important player for us. She played great defense on Wednesday. Mai and Luisa are great natural shooters and we want to get them minutes. They hit back-to-back threes in the second quarter,” said Gardere about Govert, Leggett, and Murray. Final stats: Johnson scored 33 points, 14 rebounds, six assists, and eight steals. Martinez had 26 points, six rebounds, six assists, two steals. Perine had 10 points, eight boards, two steals. Govert had five points, five rebounds, five assists. Murray had six, Leggett had three. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-0) plays St. Joseph in Alameda today, April 28, at 5:30 p.m., and tomorrow, April 29 at Hayward at 6:30 p.m. The league season opens at home on Tuesday, May 4 against Cal High at 7:00 p.m.
articles.title: Highlanders dominate Clayton Valley in season-opener

articles.text: Staff Photos In Piedmont’s opening three games, senior guard Luke Harris scored 35 points against Northgate, 14 at Campolindo, and 25 against San Ramon Valley. four assists. Luke Harris was back on track with 25 points, four rebounds, and four steals. A.J. Harris had 11 points, seven boards, three assists, and three steals. Parker Terrill had four points, Holmes had two, and Mason Kimball had three. Loss to Campo Arguably the best of the three opponents last week was Campolindo, among the top teams in the North Coast Section. The game was deadlocked 16-16 going into the second quarter, but a stout Cougars’ defense helped build the score to 38-26 by halftime. It was extended to 55-44 by the fourth, and the Highlanders couldn’t get closer. Murphy led with 23 points, A.J. Harris had 15 points, and his older brother was held to 14 points. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-1) head to St. Joseph in Alameda today, Wednesday, April 28 for a 7:00 p.m. game. The Highlanders play again on Friday, April 30 at Castro Valley at 7:00 p.m. In a strong opening week, Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team beat Northgate by six points on Tuesday, April 20, and edged San Ramon Valley by five points on Saturday, April 24. At midweek they lost 68-53 to Campolindo. All games were played at home in Binks Rawling Gym. All three opponents are Division 2 teams in the North Coast Section. Piedmont will play its first season in Division 3 after getting promoted from Div. 4 after winning last year’s North Coast Section Championship. “These games get us ready for league play with teams like O’Dowd, Alameda, and St. Joe. It’s a great test to see where we are. You circle games like Campolindo on your calendar. We’re excited to play,” said coach Ben Spencer. The games featured team leaders Luke Harris and JoJo Murphy, who put up points by the carload. The pair combined for 155 points in three games. “Bringing back those two is just tremendous. Their work ethic rubs off on the younger players. They definitely lead by example,” added Spencer. But this year will see largely a brand-new team – Harris and Murphy plus 11 new faces on varsity. Sophomore forward A.J. Harris, younger brother of Luke Harris, is a new starter. “We have two really good returners in Luke and JoJo. I’ve just been working on getting open looks for 3s and complement their games,” he said. ”Luke and I have been playing 1-on-1 since we were really little; he usually wins, but it’s close. We have a lot of brotherly love; I’ll push him around a little. though,” said A.J. with a laugh. Season opener: 88-82 win vs. Northgate Pied mont’s 88-82 victory over Northgate saw the Highlanders with a 20-13 lead in the first quarter and never relinquishing the advantage over the Broncos. PHS held a narrow 41-37 lead at halftime, and stretched the lead to 10 points, 65-55, after three quarters. Luke Harris put up 35 points, topping his career high at PHS by two points, including 14 points in the last quarter. His counterpart in the backcourt, Murphy, scored 27 points, including four 3-pointers. A.J. Harris had 14 points, Raydan Holmes scored eight, and Justice Hartford had three. 5-point win over San Ramon Piedmont topped San Ramon Valley 76-71 on Saturday. Similar to its win against Northgate, PHS ended the first quarter with a 27-17 advantage and never surrendered the lead. The gap narrowed to 38-31 at halftime, but the deficit remained at seven points going into the fourth, 58-51. Piedmont’s defense got the job done with 13 steals on the night. Murphy led the charge with a career high of 31 points, to go along with eight rebounds and JoJo Murphy scored 27 points against Northgate, 23 against Campolindo, and a career-high 31 points against San Ramon Valley.

articles.text: Photos by Todd Marshburn The girls’ lacrosse team celebrated its five seniors on April 20. Pictured are: Maya Galbreth (left), Bella Kjellen, coach Carlton Chan, Caroline Devine, Sadie Tschider, and Heidi Helm. Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team ended its 2021 season in thrilling fashion, beating league rival Bishop O’Dowd and North Coast Section rival University. Both victories were by a single goal and were played at Witter Field. On Tuesday, April 20, the Highlanders topped league opponent O’Dowd 16-15. Four days later, on Saturday night, they nicked the Red Devils 14-13. Piedmont ended its season with a 6-4 overall record, and undefeated at 5-0 in league. A typical season is 20 or more games. On Tuesday PHS players celebrated their five seniors and family members, including Sadie Tschider, Caroline Devine, Maya Galbreth, Bella Kjellen, and Heidi Helm. “A crazy way to end the season. It was also a bittersweet victory knowing that this was the last game for our five seniors,” said coach Carlton Chan, whose teams have beaten O’Dowd four times. Devine, the team’s top scorer, poured in eight goals and added four assists in another monster game. Katherine Kinne, meanwhile, had a team-high five goals against University while Tschider had five assists and four goals. Piedmont 16, Bishop O’Dowd 15 The Highlanders’ 16-15 win came one day after a 13-11 victory over the Dragons at the Daognns’ home field. The Highlanders trailed at halftime, 7-5. Elizabeth Ethington opened up the scoring in the second half with a goal within the first minute, followed by Devine bagging her third goal to tie it at 7-7. After a BOD goal, Tschider tied it 8-8. Three minutes later the Highlanders pulled ahead 11-9 with backto-back goals from Devine, and one from Tschider. With 11 minutes left, the Dragons narrowed to 12-11 with 11 minutes left but PHS extended the advantage to 15-12 with five minutes left. O’Dowd stormed back to force a tie, 15-15 with two minutes on the clock. articles.text: Piedmont’s softball team closed its shortened season with a narrow 1-0 loss to El Cerrito at Witter Field, finishing with a 6-4 overall record and 5-3 against league competition in the WACC’s Shoreline Division. The team has no seniors, so the 10 returning players are eager for a full season next spring “We hope everyone comes back and that we can build a junior varsity roster,” said coach Gene Dennard. That is very important to us. It’s my understanding that a JV team hasn’t happened here in some time.” PHS was held to three hits. The Gauchos scored the winning run in the top of the second. Pitcher Izzy Epstein struck out eight batters and allowed five hits. The run scored was unearned. Leah Bell led off the third inning with a single and stole second and third base. She attempted to steal home on a hit and run play, but was tagged out. In the bottom of the fourth, Chiarra Lundin advanced to third base with one out but was picked Staff Photos PHS softball finished its 10-game season with a 6-4 record. off by El Cerrito’s catcher. Piedmont’s last chance came in the bottom of the seventh when Morgan Hunt led off with a single and got to second base on a sacrifice bunt by Gretchen Gerhardy. She was caught stealing third, again by the Gauchos’ talented catcher. Lundin led the team during the season with a .469 batting average three home runs, 11 RBIs, and 16 runs scored. Bell, the talented sophomore, had her second consecutive big season, with a .462 average, one home run, three triples, four doubles, 11 runs scored, and four RBIs. Hunt finished at .300 with two homers and a team-leading 14 RBIs. Epstein had a .414 batting average with eight RBIs and 14 runs scored. On the mound, she finishes with 49 innings pitched, a 4-4 overall record with 66 strikeouts and a 3.71 earned run average.

articles.text: Piedmont concluded its 16-game season with an 8-2 victory over Miramonte on Tuesday, April 20 at Humphries Diamond. Earlier it lost 4-1 to North Coast rival St. Mary’s on Saturday, April 24. PHS finished the shortened 2021 season with a 12-4 overall record and remained undefeated at 8-0 against WACC Shoreline Division teams. In a yar of Covid, no league playoffs were held and no championship declared. The team was led by senior pitchers Cal Barna, Ben Levinson, Julian Scherman, pitcher/ first baseman Garren Riley, pitcher/third baseman Lars Derr, and outfielder Aidan Mitchell. “Obviously we’re going to miss everyone. Ben, Lars, and Julian were four-year players. They unfortunately lost a full year and this year was structured differently. I would have loved to see them all compete fully for the year,” said coach Eric Olson. The team was able to call back two players from 2019-2020 for the final two games with seniors Brian Cain and Alex Hilton after they finished the football season. 8-2 win over Miramonte The Highlanders dominated the Matadors 8-2 on Tuesday, April 20, extending their winning streak to six games. Piedmont led 4-2 after the bottom of the second inning and tacked on another four runs in the bottom of the sixth. The win featured Levinson, in his Michael Aikawa stands at second base after smacking a double. He finished the year with an impressive .547 on-base percentage. Ben Levinson was masterful this season. He had nine strikeouts against Miramonte and finished the 16-game season with a 0.8 earned run average. final appearance in a Piedmont jersey, throwing six innings for nine strikeouts, one earned run, and three walks. He finished the season with a 2-0 record in five appearances, striking out 40 in 26 innings with a glistening 0.8 earned run average, allowing just three earned runs, eight walks, and 17 hits. Sophomore second baseman Michael Aikawa had a breakout year, with another big game at the plate with 3 hits with a double and two RBIs. He finished the season with a .396 batting average, and led with a .625 slugging percentage, .547 on-base percentage. He had two home runs, 20 runs scored and 13 RBIs. Final stats: Derr went 2-for-4. Barna had one hit, a run scored, and an RBI. Nico Defazio had a hit, run scored, and RBI. Riley had a hit, run scored, RBI, and drew three walks. Brian Cain drew two walks, scored a run, and gained an RBI. St. Mary’s season-finale Playing in Berkeley on Saturday, April 24, Piedmont lost 4-1 to longtime North Coast Section and former league rivel St. Mary’s. The Panthers led 4-0 by the end of the third inning. Defazio went 2-for-3 and drove in Levinson in the top of the fourth for Piedmont’s only run. Barna threw five innings, striking out seven and allowed three hits. Riley pitched one inning of relief with one strikeout.

articles.text: Piedmont High athletes competed at the Dublin Distance Fiesta at Dublin High School on Saturday, April 24, with runners from 83 schools in distance events ranging from the half mile to ow-mile runs. Junior standout runner Jack Stein did well to create two more personal records in 1600- and 3200-meter events. In the 3200, Stein set a PR by 10 seconds with a time of 9:46. He finished 44th of 212 runners in Dublin. He also placed 39th of 410 runners in the 1600 with a time of 4:36.14. Seamus Chamberlain-Carr placed 86th in a field of 212 runners in the 3200 with a time of 10:15, and Alex Ware was 114th with a time of 10:36.3. In the 1600, Christian Taylor was 94th out of 410 in a time of 4:48.79. Cooper Downing was 105th in 4:50.2, Ware placed 155th in 4:58.6. Julien Lee and Rowen Connelly had nearly identical times of 5:07. Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai, Piedmont’s only runner in the 800, placing 68th in a field of 234 runners with a time of 2:11.78. She also placed 65th of 242 athletes in the 1600-meter run in 5:42.1, a 10-second improvement in her previous top time. Molly McWeeny was 128th and Kristen DeBella 129th in the 800-meters with near identical times of f2:50.57 and 2:50.72. Aya Troyer finished 99th in the 1600 in 5:54.3, McWeeny was 111th in 5:59, and Mara Lovric 173rd in 6:28. articles.text: The second phase of a Spring sports season begins with both the boy’s and girls’ basketball teams getting back in action this week. At the same time, both the girl’s and boys’ soccer teams will begin their season, as well as boys’ and girls’ water polo. The boys’ lacrosse team opens its season with three games on the road, starting tomorrow night, Wednesday, April 28, at Moreau Catholic in Hayward at 7 p.m. Boys Lacrosse The PHS lacrosse team is the Div. 2 North Coast Section defending champions from 2019. Despite missing a year of development, coach Ryan Price is eager to see his senior-heavy team back on the field. “We have a very balanced, senior-heavy team this year. We should see scoring from multiple players. We’ll have a strong, experienced defense and should Photo by Todd Marshburn Connor Curtis, am attacking midfielder, was last year’s leading scorer as a sophomore. Photos by Sam Deaner Piedmont’s defense will be led by senior captain Alden Heske. be able to hold teams below 10 goals a game,” he predicted. Price keyed on defensive senior captain Alden Heske, who he called a “rock” throughout the offseason as a leader and “anchor” of their back line. Senior midfielder Greg Gately and sophomore attack Soren Dixon are expected to be big contributors. “We have an athletic midfield and a balanced attack unit who should jell together to become a potent offense,” added Price. articles.text: Piedmont’s second annual Art Walk will take place this Sunday, May 2, from 12 p.m. to 5 p.m., and will include artworks from more than 40 Piedmont artists. Last year’s event was “born out of necessity,” explained co-organizer Jon Schleuning, when shelter-in-place guidelines had obliterated live events and decimated the arts industry in the process. “Last year, many artists’ open studios were cancelled [due to COVID-19], so artists were looking at a decrease in sales and didn’t have a place to show. The idea was to create a purposely de-centralized art walk that allows artists to showcase and sell their work, with 20 percent of proceeds going to art programs in the schools,” he explained. Schleuning and Larraine Seiden came up with the idea, with help from featured artists Valerie Corvin and Paula Valenzuela, and in May 2020, a group of about 20 Piedmont artists opened their “home studios” for the city’s first organized Art Walk. This year, artist participation has doubled in size. “The Piedmont community believes strongly in the arts, and there’s a real commitment to fostering arts and culture in the schools. It’s one of the benefits of living here,” said Schleuning. “The Art Walk is unique, in that you actually get to see your neighbors’ and community members’ works. It’s wonderful [to discover] that your neighbor may be an amazing photographer or a phenomenal potter.” Similar to last year’s event, artwork will be displayed in front of the artists’ homes and social distancing guidelines will be observed. All featured artists have agreed to guidelines that require a six-foot distance from one another, wearing face coverings, and engaging in no physical contact. Participants also agree to disinfect and wipe down sites as necessary and will make hand sanitizer or other effective disinfectants available. Artwork on display will range from a variety of mediums, including paintings, ceramics, mixed media, sculpture, photography, quilts, and textile art. In addition, the Piedmont Art Fund’s “Things that Matter” community art quilt will be displayed at an “Pistachio Collection” by Bob Dinetz LMBInteriors.com 510.531.8438

articles.text: A still from the documentary, The Social Dilemma. Piedmont’s long-running Appreciating Diversity Film Series will present Jeff Orlowski’s award-winning documentary, The Social Dilemma, on Thursday, May 13, from 5:00-6:00 p.m. The film will be followed by a Question & Answer session with UC Berkeley Law Professor Rebecca Wexler. The film is free by registering at diversityfilmseries.org, and clicking on the “Register for The Social Dilemma button”. The film documents the hidden practices that underlie the business of social media. Viewers will learn that the algorithms designed to capture your attention are also profoundly affecting your brains and beliefs in ways that directly threaten democracy. An internal Facebook report by sociologist Monica Lee states, “64% of the people who joined extremist groups on Facebook did so because the algorithms steered them there.” Other documentaries have raised concerns about the impact of social media on privacy and even democracy. This film’s advantage is that the speakers in The Social Dilemma include top executives from Twitter, Instagram, Pinterest, Facebook, and others. The experts assure us their intentions were good -- even the one whose job title at Facebook was head of “monetization”. Yet all are deeply concerned about what they’ve created, and one confesses that he worked all day on making his site irresistibly seductive and then found himself unable to resist the very algorithmic tricks he helped to create when he went home at night. The most important lesson from the film is that people should question everything they read online, especially if it is presented in a way that reflects a detailed understanding of personal inclinations and preferences. Viewers should learn to resist the “attention extraction model” that makes social media seem friendly and reinforcing. As the New York Times has advised, “Unplug and run”. After viewing The Social Dilemma, join the Diversity Film Series audience for Q & A discussion with Rebecca Wexler, Assistant Professor of Law at UC Berkeley Law, and Co-Director of the Berkeley Center for Law & Technology. Wexler teaches, researches, and writes on issues concerning data, technology, and criminal justice. Sign up at www.diversityfilmseries.org for the Diversity Film viewing on Thursday, May 13, from 5:00-6:00 p.m. The Appreciating Diversity Film Series is co-sponsored by the City of Piedmont, Piedmont League of Women Voters and Piedmont School District.
articles.title: Diversity Film Series to present The Social Dilemma May 13
