articles.text: The prospect of a new concert tour lured me to Southern California. But the reward wasn’t musical. My sister, a former Deputy Attorney General, is a graduate of the CIA boot camp. But it’s not the CIA you are thinking about. This CIA is the Culinary Institute of America. They offer a wide range of classes and you can put your learning to good use immediately. During my recent visit, the first breakfast I had was one of my favorites – popovers. I told my sister that I had purchased readymade packages of popovers. She responded that popovers are so easy to make, you really don’t need a package. The basic recipe has a total of five ingredients – a cup of all-purpose flour, a little salt, 1 tablespoon of butter, a cup of milk and two eggs. That’s it. You can enjoy them as they come out of the oven or serve them with your favorite jam or fruit. The second memorable meal was a braised veal roast with carrots and boiled potatoes. My sister decided to splurge. She bought the veal roast from the kosher butcher. When she told me that the meat cost $70, I was a bit surprised. However, considering that the quality was much better than the meat from a supermarket, the cost was warranted. Another consideration was that it served eight people and the bones were enjoyed by the dog. Thus, the cost was less than $10 per person. The next memorable meal was actually rather easy. My sister prepared a basic crêpe mix which can be used to make a manicotti An elegant breakfast with delicious crêpes – very easy to make. at the same time as the veal roast.
articles.title: Elegant dining – the easy way

articles.text: Piedmont author Kelly Corrigan released a children’s book, Hello World! on April 20. A New York Times bestselling author, Corrigan wrote this book in honor of her father and his endless enthusiasm. Hello World! celebrates the people in everyone’s life and the meaningful connections that come from asking each other questions. Hello World! reminds readers that the journeys we take through life are all about the people along the way. With her trademark inspirational messages, Corrigan’s book is for kids about to embark on new adventures. Illustrator Stacy Ebert brings the 44-page story to life with vivid artwork. The book is primarily for children age three to seven. The book is published by Flamingo Books and is available at bookstores. For more information, go to Kellycorrigan.com. Kelly Corrigan’s newest book is a story for children, Hello, World!
articles.title: Corrigan releases kids’ book, Hello World!

articles.text: Piedmont resident Shanti Brien published a new book on March 2, 2021 about criminal justice, titled Almost Innocent: From Searching to Saved in America’s Criminal Justice System. The book is her insider account as a lawyer of the messy, tragic, and often unjust legal system in America. From defunding the police to the college admissions scandal, from the national rise in crime to seditious mobs escaping prosecution, Brien tackles some of the most urgent criminal justice topics of today. Part memoir, part political commentary, Almost Innocent details the stories of nine legal cases. It goes behind the headlines to break down and challenge the dichotomies our country grapples with – us versus them, good versus bad, guilt versus innocence, and Black versus white. Weaving stories of the obviously guilty to the surprisingly innocent, the book is a love letter to the author’s clients. Though their profiles are as individual as their sentences – the teenage gang member whose gun never fired, the victim of the world’s most vindictive HOA, the soft-spoken three-strikes rapist, and the getaway driver – all touched Shanti Brien’s life in surprising ways. Almost Innocent is an intimate portrait of the criminal justice system, offering suggestions for how it can be more fair, more humane, and more just. “Almost Innocent” is published by Amplify Publishing, Ingram, Baker & Taylor, and American West. It is available at most bookstores and outlets. For more information go to www. ShantiBrien.com
articles.title: Shanti Brien publishes book about criminal justice system

Note that manicotti in America is the same as cannoli in Italy. You can go to a supermarket and buy a package of ready-made dried cannoli, but you will be much happier if you make your own crêpes rather than use packaged cannoli. The ingredients for the cannoli-manicotti are exactly the same as for the popovers. You will need a lightweight, nonstick skillet. Make enough crepes for both the dinner and breakfast the next day. The filling for the manicotti can be a mixture of cheese combined with any green vegetable or ground meat. You can top the manicotti with a prepared Italian red sauce or make your own. For breakfast the next morning, use the same crêpes that you made for the manicotti and fill them with fruit, jam, sweetened ricotta cheese or even chocolate – basically anything that pleases you. Be sure to use some colorful plates and pretend that you are in a romantic location, like Paris or Rome. Recipes for all of these delicacies are easily available in cookbooks and on the Internet. Elegant dining – the easy way By Joseph Gold The prospect of a new concert tour lured me to Southern California. But the reward wasn’t musical. My sister, a former Deputy Attorney General, is a graduate of the CIA boot camp. But it’s not the CIA you are thinking about. This CIA is the Culinary Institute of America. They offer a wide range of classes and you can put your learning to good use immediately. During my recent visit, the first breakfast I had was one of my favorites – popovers. I told my sister that I had purchased readymade packages of popovers. She responded that popovers are so easy to make, you really don’t need a package. The basic recipe has a total of five ingredients – a cup of all-purpose flour, a little salt, 1 tablespoon of butter, a cup of milk and two eggs. That’s it. You can enjoy them as they come out of the oven or serve them with your favorite jam or fruit. The second memorable meal was a braised veal roast with carrots and boiled potatoes. My sister decided to splurge. She bought the veal roast from the kosher butcher. When she told me that the meat cost $70, I was a bit surprised. However, considering that the quality was much better than the meat from a supermarket, the cost was warranted. Another consideration was that it served eight people and the bones were enjoyed by the dog. Thus, the cost was less than $10 per person. The next memorable meal was actually rather easy. Piedmont author Kelly Corrigan released a children’s book, Hello World! on April 20. A New York Times bestselling author, Corrigan wrote this book in honor of her father and his endless enthusiasm. Hello World! celebrates the people in everyone’s life and the meaningful connections that come from asking each other questions. Hello World! reminds readers that the journeys we take through life are all about the people along the way. With her trademark inspirational messages, Corrigan’s book is for kids about to embark on new adventures. Illustrator Stacy Ebert brings the 44-page story to life with vivid artwork. The book is primarily for children age three to seven. The book is published by Flamingo Books and is available at bookstores. For more information, go to Kellycorrigan.com. Shanti Brien publishes book about criminal justice system Piedmont resident Shanti Brien published a new book on March 2, 2021 about criminal justice, titled Almost Innocent: From Searching to Saved in America’s Criminal Justice System. The book is her insider account as a lawyer of the messy, tragic, and often unjust legal system in America. From defunding the police to the college admissions scandal, from the national rise in crime to seditious mobs escaping prosecution, Brien tackles some of the most urgent criminal justice topics of today. Part memoir, part political commentary, Almost Innocent details the stories of nine legal cases. It goes behind the headlines to break down and challenge the dichotomies our country grapples with – us versus them, good versus bad, guilt versus innocence, and Black versus white. Weaving stories of the obviously guilty to the surprisingly innocent, the book is a love letter to the author’s clients. Though their profiles are as individual as their sentences – the teenage gang member whose gun never fired, An elegant breakfast with delicious crêpes – very easy to make. Almost Innocent is an intimate portrait of the criminal justice system, offering suggestions for how it can be more fair, more humane, and more just. “Almost Innocent” is published by Amplify Publishing, Ingram, Baker & Taylor, and American West. articles.text: San Francisco’s Legion of Honor museum. The Legion of Honor, part of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, is re-opening with special member preview days beginning May 6. The Legion of Honor will require timed tickets for every visitor, including general admission to its current exhibition,” Tickets will be released in 60-day increments to ensure social distancing. Health guidelines have reduced the capacity at any one time to less than 25 percent of the museum’s capacity. Pompeii Exhibit The “Last Summer in Pompeii” exhibition examines the fiery eruption of Mount Vesuvius, which left Pompeii and nearby villages and farms buried under pumice and hot ash. “Pompeii” brings audiences back to this world prior to the devastation, with a focus on everyday life, culture, and the food and drink of Pompeii. Pots, pans, and other household items for the preparation and serving of food is displayed, as well as works of art that reveal the luxury of wealthy Romans who called the oasis home. To learn more about the exhibition, and to secure timed reservations, visit https://legionof honor.famsf.org/exhibitions/ pompeii. To learn about the extra safety precautions Legion of Honor is taking when re-opening, visit https://legionofhonor.famsf.org/ legion/visiting/museum-policies. Ongoing digital programs In addition, a new partnership between the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco (the de Young and Legion of Honor) and the “SeeBlackWomxn” collective has launched a five-part series focused on the contemporary Black Arts scene. The collective was founded by artists and activists Tahirah Rasheed, Angela Hennessy, Dana King, and Jamani Montague, and celebrates the lineage and legacy of Black women in contemporary arts. SeeBlackWomxn serves as a collective narrative of artists and writers who contribute to Black feminist theory. The platform emphasizes self-representation and aims to stray from the stereotypical tropes assigned to Black women and identifying women. The series is programmed through the museums’ “Virtual Wednesdays” and Local Voices podcast, which aims to explore the impact of public art on the Bay Area community. This year, notable artists who contributed to the podcast include Lava Thomas, Catherine Wagner, and Alison Saar, musical duo Mercury Soul, Fredrika Newton of the Dr. Huey P. Newton Foundation, the #SayHerName Movement, Susan Cervantes of the Precita Eyes Muralists, artist duo Rue Bainbridge, artist and composer Gryphon Rue, and artist Peter Simensky. Visit https://www.youtube. com/watch?v=Yk9TV4-GA78 to watch the conversation, and visit https://www.seeblackwomxn. com to learn more about the collective.

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet will stream Helgi Tomasson’s Romeo & Juliet from May 6 through May 26. The multi-capture, cinematic production was performed at the San Francisco’s War Memorial Opera House. It was SF Ballet’s last production prior to 2020 COVID-19 closures. It was last performed in 2019 at the Royal Danish Opera House in Copenhagen. The production premiered during SF Ballet’s 1994 Repertory season and is considered a signature work of the San Francisco Ballet company, which has performed it worldwide. Tomasson’s Romeo and Juliet is performed with music under the direction of Martin West. The production includes former principal dancers Maria Kochetkova and Davit Karapetyan in the title roles. Pascal Molat, now on faculty at SF Ballet School, is cast as Mercutio. The opulent set is designed by Jens-Jacob Worsaae, with lighting design by Thomas Skelton. This was Worsaae’s final collaboration with Tomasson before he died shortly after the ballet’s premiere. “I think it was the most beautiful work he’d ever done, and yet he did not see it. That’s one reason why this production is very, very special to me,” Tomasson said. To purchase tickets to the streaming production, visit https://www.sfballet.org/productions/digital-program-06/.
articles.title: SF Ballet to stream Romeo & Juliet beginning May 6

articles.text: A scene from Diablo Ballet’s production of Once Upon a Time. Tickets are now on sale for Diablo Ballet’s production of Once Upon a Time, which will premiere on May 7. The performance will be available on demand from Friday through Sunday, May 7-9, and the following weekend, May 14-16. Diablo Ballet, located in Walnut Creek, is an award-winning professional dance company founded in 1993. Dancers perform a collection of classical and contemporary works, and have performed throughout the United States, Europe, and South America. Once Upon a Time is the story of a young man who accidentally finds himself as the male lead in favorite classic fairytales like Cinderella, Snow White, Alice in Wonderland, and Little Red Riding Hood. The unconventional ballet relies on the age-old narrative of “happily-ever-after,” with the music of George Gershwin and Benjamin Britten, and choreography by Julia Adam. Purchasing a virtual ticket will allow you to view the performance either weekend. Ticket holders can watch the on-demand performance multiple times throughout that weekend. To purchase tickets call (925) 943-7467, or visit: https://diabloballet.org/ onceuponatime/.
articles.title: Diablo Ballet presents Once Upon A Time

articles.text: Conductor Donato Cabrera Donato Cabrera will conduct the San Francisco Conservatory of Music Orchestra on Saturday, May 1 in a live-stream performance at 7:30 p.m. Cabrera is the current Music Director of the California Symphony as well as the Las Vegas Philharmonic. He has a long history in the Bay Area music industry, leading up to his position as the resident conductor of the San Francisco Symphony. Cabrera joined the San Francisco Opera in the 2005-2006 season as Associate Conductor and made his debut in May 2006 for the company’s well-attended “Opera in the Gardens” concert. Cabrera made his debut with the Berkeley Opera company, conducting a production of “L’elisir d’amore.” Since Cabrera’s appointment in 2013 to the California Symphony, the organization has implemented innovative programming that commits to presenting music by women and people of color. The conductor also oversees the selection process of the California Symphony’s celebrated Young American Composer-in-Residence program. On the program for May 1, audiences will hear Hannah Kendall’s Verdala, Igor Stravinsky’s Suite No. 1 and No. 2, and Ludwig van Beethoven’s Symphony No. 7 in A Major. The live-stream will begin promptly at 7:30 p.m. Reservations can be made by visiting https://sfcm. edu/performance-calendar/event/ sfcm-orchestra-conducted-donato-cabrera?utm_source=SFC V& ut m _ me d iu m=Ext e rnal&utm_campaign=SFArtsMonthly%22%3E.
articles.title: SF Conservatory Orchestra and Donato Cabrera on May 1

articles.text: Gold Coast Chamber Players’ season finale, “Dvorak’s America”, takes place this Saturday, May 1 at 7 p.m. “Dvorak’s America” explores the impact that Spirituals and Native American music had on Czech composer Antonin Dvorak during his time in America. The project, three years in the making, highlights the interconnectedness of these cultures. The program will feature the composer’s String Quintet, op. 97, and the Lento from his String Quartet op. 96, both of which are nicknamed “the American.” Original music by Mary Youngblood for Native American flute, “Within My Heart” and “Beneath the Raven Moon,” as well as her arrangement of “Amazing Grace”, represent what Dvorak heard during his stay in America. Dvorak proclaimed that African American Spirituals are “the heart of American music,” and the genre serves as perhaps the greatest Western influence on the composer. Spirituals that will be performed in this program include “Swing Low Sweet Chariot,” “By an’ By,” and “My Lord What a Morning.” ConcludAlexander String Quartet: Zakarias Grafilo and Frederick Lifsitz, violins, Sandy Wilson, cello and violist David Samuel, a recent addition. ing the program will be “Goin’ Home,” from the composer’s New World Symphony. Alexander String Quartet will lead the ensemble, marking one of the first performances with their new violist, David Samuel. Violist Pamela Freund-Striplen, founder of Gold Coast Players and a frequent collaborated with the Quartet, will join its members for “Dvorak’s America.” The event will be livestreamed via YouTube at 7 p.m. on Saturday, May 1. For more information and to obtain tickets, visit www.gccpmusic.com, or call (925) 283-3728.
articles.title: Concert will feature Alexander String Quartet

articles.text: Aurora Theatre Company is presenting an audio play adaption of Toni Morrison’s novel The Bluest Eye, available to stream now through May 21. Morrison’s debut novel comes to the Aurora stage in an adaption by playwright Lydia Diamond, and follows young protagonist Pecola Breedlove. The story is told from the perspective of Claudia MacTeer, the daughter of Pecola’s foster parents. Pecola dreams of having blue eyes like the young actress Shirley Temple, believing that blue eyes would make her more accepted and beautiful. The play adaption deals with themes of racism, incest, and child molestation. Morrison is a Pulitzer and Nobel Prize-winning writer whose works are praised for addressing the harsh realities and consequences of racism in the United States. The audio drama has Michael Asberry as Chilly, Sam Jackson as Frieda, Cathleen Riddley as Mama, Jeunee Simon as Claudia and Jasmine Williams as the protagonist Pecola. Diamond is a nationally recognized and award-winning playwright, and Lydia Diamond’s audio play The Bluest Eye is an adaption of Toni Morrison’s debut novel of the same name. currently serves as an assistant professor at Boston University. She has also taught playwriting at Columbia College, and at DePaul University and Loyola University in Chicago. Her other playwright credits include The Gift Horse, Stick Fly, The Inside, and Voyeurs de Venus. To listen to the audio drama any time from now through May 21, visit https://www.auroratheatre.org/thebluesteye.
articles.title: Aurora Theatre presents audio play, The Bluest Eye

articles.text: The 7th Annual Juried Art show, which opened April 17 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, will be open for gallery hours from 12:00 to 2:00 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays through May 16. The exhibition will be limited to a maximum of 20 visitors at a time. Visitors will be asked to sanitize hands upon entry, wear face masks, and observe social distancing. To view the exhibit, sign up at: https://bit.ly/3mwWuwT. A total of 35 pieces of art were selected among a record-high 500 submissions. The artwork that appeared in the exhibition, the first public event PCA has held this year, was selected by Piedmont native Rene de Guzman, Senior Curator of Art at Oakland Museum of California, and Danielle Fox. Principal of Slate FIRST PLACE: Pep Ventosa’s “Watching the Night Watch” Gallery in Oakland. Artists came from nine counties in the Bay Area, from Alameda to Santa Clara to Sonoma. Submissions represented an eclectic range, including oil on canvas, pigment prints, and photography. The selections this year have produced the “best Juried Art Show yet” in the event’s seven-year existence,” according to Valerie Corvin, who curated the show. “The art is a high level, and it feels like you are in a downtown art gallery,” she added. SECOND PLACE: Tamara Avery’s “#114 Justice?” THIRD PLACE: See C Oh’s “Tranquility”
articles.title: Annual Juried Art Show continues to May 16

articles.text: Come join your friends at the Piedmont Center as it begins to reopen for public events after a year of closure due to COVID-19. CURRENTLY ON VIEW The 7th Annual Juried Art Show returns to the Center for an exhibition now on view through May 16. Gallery hours are 12:00 to 2:00 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays. From a record-high 500 submissions of original art created within the past year, 35 works of art were selected by guest jurors René de Guzman, Senior Curator of Art at Oakland Museum of California, and Danielle Fox, Principal of Slate Gallery in Oakland. Through an endowment by the family of John P. Thornborrow, cash awards of $4,000 will be awarded to the top award winners, with an emphasis on honoring emerging artists in the Bay Area. The following COVID protocols will be in place: All visitors must sign up in advance for their visit. An email-based online system will be established where visitors may sign up for their choice of day. A health screening form will be emailed to visitors with their confirmation, also listing all health requirements. The exhibition will be limited to a maximum of 20 visitors at a time. Staff will be seated at the entrance, maintaining a roster of visitors correlating to time to facilitate any needed contact tracing, performing temperature checks, and collecting health screening forms. Masks and social distancing will be observed while guests visit the exhibition and while waiting to enter, Visitors will be asked to sanitize hands on entry and to circle the exhibition in a one-way direction to prevent clustering. No food or drink will be permitted. To sign up for a time to view the show, visit: https://bit. ly/3mwWuwT. For more information, see the website: piedmontcenterforthearts.org. To view a sampling of past exhibits and performances, click on https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d3q9otV5emI
articles.title: Celebrating Spring at the Center For The Arts

articles.text: Photos by Steve Goodall Tsavo (left), a male giraffe from Fresno Chaffee Zoo, enjoys a snack with female giraffe Kijiji at The Oakland Zoo’s African Savanna. The Oakland Zoo proudly announced that Tsavo, a fouryear-old male reticulated giraffe, arrived in Oakland from the Fresno Zoo on April 22. Earlier in the week another young male giraffe came to Oakland from San Diego Zoo. Oakland Zoo’s animal care team had been seeking compatible additions to the herd after suffering the loss of four giraffes to age in recent years. The need to cultivate a new herd comparable in number to those in the wild is critical to the social structure and well-being of giraffes. Giraffes are highly social animals that in the wild maintain relationships with many individuals. Tsavo’s presence will provide the giraffe herd at Oakland Zoo with a more robust and needed social structure, bringing the herd to a healthy six in number. “Animal welfare goes beyond the daily care and dedicated attention our animal residents receive from our animal care staff. Planning for their futures and strengthening their social structures also play a vital role in our animals’ lives,” explained newly named Oakland Zoo Director Nik Dehejia. Tsavo’s arrival follows months of planning between Fresno Zoo and Oakland Zoo. Before his departure, the animal care team at Fresno Chaffee Zoo used positive reinforcement training to help persuade him to complete new behaviors voluntarily which were needed for his transport, such as walking through specific areas of the giraffe night house. “We are excited for our newest giraffe additions to join our giraffe herd,” said Colleen Kinzley, VP of Animal Care at Oakland Zoo. “The diversity of ages and mixture of males and females in this herd will be similar to the social dynamics that giraffe experience in the wild. This addition reinforces the importance of animal welfare at the Zoo.” The young male giraffe from the San Diego Zoo is still unnamed. The zoo is currently having their Homeward Bound Silent Auction and one of the auction items is the right to name him. Over the past 15 years, giraffes in Africa have faced a “silent extinction” with a 40 percent decline in their population. Both the Oakland and Fresno zoos partner with the Reticulated Giraffe Project in Kenya, a conservation organization dedicated to working with local communities in Africa to help reduce human-wildlife conflict and habitat loss to preserve endangered giraffe populations in the wild. For more information, go to Oaklandzoo.org. Tsavo and a male adolescent giraffe from San Diego Zoo explore their new habitat at The Oakland Zoo.

pages.text: Wednesday, April 28, 2021 23 Features your Oakland Zoo welcomes two new giraffes Look at your financial situation holistically What’s the biggest financial mistake you can make? Choosing the wrong investments? Waiting too long to save for retirement? Underestimating the costs of retirement? All these are reasonable answers, but the biggest mistake you might make is not looking at your financial picture holistically – that is, not bringing into the picture all the elements of yourself. Let’s consider some of them: • Your views on helping your family Your decisions about helping your family are clearly going to be a major part of your financial strategy – and this is true at virtually all stages of your life. When your children are young, you’ll need to decide if you’re going to put away money for their college education, and, if so, how much, and in what investment vehicles. When they’re young adults, you may also need to decide how much financial support you’re willing to provide for things such as the down payment on a new home. And when you’re drawing up your estate plans, you’ll need to consider how to distribute assets to your children, grandchildren or other family members. • Your personal beliefs As someone with civic, ethical and moral concerns, you want to positively affect the world around you. And that’s why you may feel compelled to make charitable gifts throughout your life and then make philanthropy part of your legacy. To accomplish these objectives, you’ll want to include gifting techniques in your financial strategy today and your estate plans for tomorrow. Of course, for the estate planning component, you’ll need to work with your tax and legal advisors. • Your purpose in life when you retire When you retire, you may be stepping off a career path, but you’re also entering a world of possibilities. How will you define, and live out, your new sense of purpose at this stage of your life? Do you seek to broaden your horizons by traveling around the world? Do you want to give back more to the community by volunteering? Can you spend more time pursuing the hobbies you enjoy? Each of these choices will carry different financial implications for how much you’ll need to accumulate for retirement and how much you will need to take out each year from your retirement accounts, such as your IRA and 401(k). • Your health Your physical and mental health can play big roles in your financial plans and outlook. On the most basic level, the healthier you are, and the better you take care of yourself, the lower your health care bills will likely be during retirement, which will affect the amount you need to put away for health care. And you also may need to prepare for the costs of long-term care, which can be enormous – in fact, a private room in a nursing home can easily cost $100,000 per year, according to the insurance company Genworth. It can be challenging to weave all these elements into a single, unified vision, so you may want to get some help from a financial professional. But, in any case, be prepared to look at your situation holistically – because, when putting together a lifetime’s financial strategy, every part of your life matters. articles.text: Chris Thayer, a former teacher at Piedmont Middle School and distance running coach at Piedmont High School, for many years, died at his home in Concord on March 25, 2021. He was 52. Born Christopher Paul Thayer in Silver Spring, Maryland on April 29, 1968, he grew up in San Rafael and graduated from Terra Linda High School in 1986. He earned a B.A. in International Relations at the University of California at Davis in 1992. He served in the U.S. Air Force Reserves for four years, with two years of active duty in the U.S. and overseas. Following his time in the service, he obtained his teaching credential from Dominican College and began his teaching career at Piedmont Middle School in 2002. Chris taught in Piedmont and in other schools in the East Bay for nearly 20 years. “Chris was a committed, inspirational teacher who dedicated himself to teaching, his colleagues, and his students,” said Piedmont Middle School colleague Ted Scherman. “He had boundless energy and enthusiasm. Beyond the classroom, I remember Chris’s devotion to his cross-country teams and the pride he felt watching his athletes compete and improve. “Above all, I will remember Chris as a father. He loved his sons deeply and was immensely proud of their development,” Scherman added. His love of competitive running led him into coaching. He was an inspirational coach to high school runners in Piedmont and San Rafael, routinely leading athletes to the State Cross-Country championships. Piedmont High School track & field coach Chris Smith offered some insight into the impact Thayer had on the runners he coached. “Chris had the ability to Chris Thayer, a former Piedmont Middle School teacher and high school distance running coach, died on March 25, 2021. He was 52. develop and maintain a positive and productive relationship with the athletes that was tempered with fairness He had a genuine passion for coaching and running. He was very even-keeled emotionally and made a conscious effort to spend time with every student who chose to participate, regardless of ability,” said Smith. Running was a part of Chris’ life; he really enjoyed sharing his love for the sport with the kids, often going on workout runs with them. Additionally, Chris added something extra. On warm days he would end training runs at Yogofina, a frozen yogurt shop on Lakeshore Avenue, and on one occasion we wound up at Lake Temescal with a swim. Chris is survived by his former wife, Denelle Thayer, and his three sons, Dylan (20), Trevor (17), and Jax (11), all of Piedmont. He is also survived by parents Joan and John Thayer, and a brother and sister-in-law, Kevin and Carol Thayer. This Saturday morning, May 1, set your alarms and check your internet connection, because the annual White Elephant Sale, held at Oakland Museum of California (OMCA), opens as an on-line shop at 8 a.m. sharp. This being OMCA’s first virtual event, a list of “pro-tips” have been provided by OMCA Woman’s Board volunteers, the group that organizes the event each year. These tips can also be found on the organization’s website by visiting https://www. whiteelephantsale.org/home/ pro-tips. ▪ You can “Shop By Department” or browse among the collections listed on our home page. Then you can browse page by page or narrow your choices by Category, Color, or Size. Or you can go straight to “Search” to find items that might be in one of several departments. ▪ Want to see some of our most wonderful, unusual, and odd things the sale is known for? Do a search for Vintage or Unique. ▪ If you think you’ll be shopping a few times during the sale, select a pickup date toward the end of May, so you can collect all your treasures in one trip. ▪ Plan to shop a few times during the sale. We’re not adding more items but there’s over 6000 items on hand. Keep looking: who knows what kind of treasures you’ll find! ▪ Do you really need to know if that dress has a belt, or if the badminton set comes with extra birdies? Sure, you can ask us, but someone else may snatch up the item before we can reply. Better to buy and hope for the best. ▪ Even after you put your items in your cart, it’s not yours until you pay for it. Keep in mind that someone else can still buy it before you have a chance to. ▪ This year, it’s really easy to buy complementary things across departments. Found a Thai table runner? Match it with that Thai terra cotta vase or a Thai cookbook. Found some nice jewelry? With one click you’ll find a jewelry box and a second click gets you a book on fine jewels. ▪ When you come to pick up your items, bring your mask. Bring bungee cords and ropes if you’re collecting large or bulky things. We can help with some heavy lifting but you will be the one to secure your items in your vehicle. ▪ Not sure if it will fit? Buy it. If you don’t like it, donate it to the 2022 White Elephant Sale. It all benefits the Oakland Museum of California. ▪ Everything is one of a kind. At these prices, there’s no wrong purchase. Caveat emptor Note that while you can shop from home, no shipping or delivery of items will be available. All items purchased must be picked up curbside at the warehouse, located at 333 Lancaster Street in Oakland. For a full list of frequently asked questions, visit https://www.whiteelephantsale. org/online. The sale will close on Sunday, May 23, at 6 p.m. There will be over 6,000 items for sale, all available on a first-come, firstserve basis. You’ll find these unique salt and pepper shakers in the “Bric-a-Brac” department. The once-popular “Troll” dolls will be available as part of the 2021 online White Elephant Sale.

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.
articles.title: Wednesday Evening Meditation Group is online

articles.text: Members of the Walking on Wednesday group stopped for a photo in Upper Dracena Park on April 21. Pictured are: Mark Greenberg (left), Andree Greenberg, Albert Chen, Nancy DeRoche and dog Chili, Brenda Ferrero, Kathy Gustafson, Harriette Louie, Jim Kao, and Bob Gustafson. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group assembled last Wednesday, April 21, for its second weekly walk of the year. After a year of no activity due to Covid-19, last week’s gathering was a “Goldilocks” walk in the park. A total of 22 people had registered for the walk, and ten were on hand for the day’s activity: Nancy DeRoche with her K-9 best friend Chili, Brenda Ferrero, Andree Greenberg, Mark Greenberg, Kathy Gustafson, Bob Gustafson, Harriette Louie, Jim Kuo, Dick Carter, and first-time walker Albert Chen. Over the years Dracena Park has become one of Piedmont’s best recreational spots because of the City and Piedmont Beautification Foundation’s work and investment. This is an eight-acre park woven into the surrounding neighborhood. Its boundaries are Dracena, Blair, El Cerrito, Artuna Avenues and Park Way. It was a rock quarry in the early 20th century that supplied material for local streets and other construction. The area has been transformed since then into a beautiful park. The City recently reworked the park’s upper grass area. About two years ago the walkers were “sidewalk superintends” for the removal of a set of huge eucalyptus trees that threatened nearby homes. The walkers set off going down Magnolia Avenue past Piedmont High School, where they admired the new STEAM classroom building and the construction going on for the school’s new theater and offices. Some stories were told by walkers about the original, classically designed Piedmont High School that was built in 1921 and the buildings that replaced it in the 1970s, which were largely demolished recently in order to build the new structures. The group then went up Hillside Avenue, across Oakland Avenue to Blair Avenue, and down Blair to Dracena Avenue, passing lovely homes and front yards along the way. Rhododendrons had started to explode with color and the beautiful white dogwood flowers were still in bloom. The walkers entered the park on Dracena Avenue at the large lawn at the top of the park, then down the dog path shaded by redwood trees past Storyteller Bridge that was rebuilt in 2014. They came to the popular children’s playground at the park’s base with its climbing wall, cement slide, and play structure. Kids were enjoying them and also chasing soap bubbles on the nearby lawn. The group walked the loop at the base of the former rock quarry, and emerged on Artuna Ricardo Avenue. They went up Ricardo to Arroyo Avenue, down to York Drive to Cambridge Way, and up to Latham, Piedmont’s only roadway with street in its name. The walkers went up Latham and noted a long, narrow home that was built in the 1950s on land created after the Key System train line closed and sold its right-of-way land for house development. The group crossed Oakland Avenue and went up to San Carlos Avenue, a split-level street, where they walked on both the upper and lower portion of the street. Rounding the corner onto el Cerrito Avenue, Dick Carter pointed out his childhood home and a classic Piedmont sycamore tree in front that has a noticeably wider trunk that the surrounding trees. Dick told the group this tree’s trunk is much larger than the others because his father watered the grass car strip in front of their home constantly during his over 50 years living there. The walkers went down El Cerrito to Magnolia Avenue and back up it to the Exedra with additional personal and local history stories being told along the way. The 90-minute, three-mile walk made for a “Goldilocks” morning with a beautiful park, great streets, sites, stories, and friends. Everyone agreed it had been just right. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge, and new walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required. Sign up at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu, or contact John Wilk at the Piedmont Recreation Department (jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov) for more information. pages.text: Wednesday, April 28, 2021 25 Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers back in action Members of the Walking on Wednesday group stopped for a photo in Upper Dracena Park on April 21. Pictured are: Mark Greenberg (left), Andree Greenberg, Albert Chen, Nancy DeRoche and dog Chili, Brenda Ferrero, Kathy Gustafson, Harriette Louie, Jim Kao, and Bob Gustafson. By Dick Carter The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group assembled last Wednesday, April 21, for its second weekly walk of the year. After a year of no activity due to Covid-19, last week’s gathering was a “Goldilocks” walk in the park. A total of 22 people had registered for the walk, and ten were on hand for the day’s activity: Nancy DeRoche with her K-9 best friend Chili, Brenda Ferrero, Andree Greenberg, Mark Greenberg, Kathy Gustafson, Bob Gustafson, Harriette Louie, Jim Kuo, Dick Carter, and first-time walker Albert Chen. Over the years Dracena Park has become one of Piedmont’s best recreational spots because of the City and Piedmont Beautification Foundation’s work and investment. This is an eight-acre park woven into the surrounding neighborhood. Its boundaries are Dracena, Blair, El Cerrito, Artuna Avenues and Park Way. It was a rock quarry in the early 20th century that supplied material for local streets and other construction. The area has been transformed since then into a beautiful park. The City recently reworked the park’s upper grass area. About two years ago the walkers were “sidewalk superintends” for the removal of a set of huge eucalyptus trees that threatened nearby homes. The walkers set off going down Magnolia Avenue past Piedmont High School, where they admired the new STEAM classroom building and the construction going on for the school’s new theater and offices. Some stories were told by walkers about the original, classically designed Piedmont High School that was built in 1921 and the buildings that replaced it in the 1970s, which were largely demolished recently in order to build the new structures. The group then went up Hillside Avenue, across Oakland Avenue to Blair Avenue, and down Blair to Dracena Avenue, passing lovely homes and front yards along the way. Rhododendrons had started to explode with color and the beautiful white dogwood flowers were still in bloom. The walkers entered the park on Dracena Avenue at the large lawn at the top of the park, then down the dog path shaded by redwood trees past Storyteller Bridge that was rebuilt in 2014. They came to the popular children’s playground at the park’s base with its climbing wall, cement slide, and play structure. Kids were enjoying them and also chasing soap bubbles on the nearby lawn. The group walked the loop at the base of the former rock quarry, and emerged on Artuna Ricardo Avenue. They went up Ricardo to Arroyo Avenue, down to York Drive to Cambridge Way, and up to Latham, Piedmont’s only roadway with street in its name. The walkers went up Latham and noted a long, narrow home that was built in the 1950s on land created after the Key System train line closed and sold its right-of-way land for house development. The group crossed Oakland Avenue and went up to San Carlos Avenue, a split-level street, where they walked on both the upper and lower portion of the street. Rounding the corner onto el Cerrito Avenue, Dick Carter pointed out his childhood home and a classic Piedmont sycamore tree in front that has a noticeably wider trunk that the surrounding trees. Dick told the group this tree’s trunk is much larger than the others because his father watered the grass car strip in front of their home constantly during his over 50 years living there. The walkers went down El Cerrito to Magnolia Avenue and back up it to the Exedra with additional personal and local history stories being told along the way. The 90-minute, three-mile walk made for a “Goldilocks” morning with a beautiful park, great streets, sites, stories, and friends. Everyone agreed it had been just right. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge, and new walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required. Sign up at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu, or contact John Wilk at the Piedmont Recreation Department (jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov) for more information. You know he’s a stickler for a clean house, orange juice with no pulp, and the thermostat at 67°. We’ll know that, too. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. articles.text: windows and stand on balconies to acknowledge their gratitude for fellow citizens sacrificing their own health to help the sick during a pandemic and to thank city maintenance workers, military and peace officers for keeping the city in order, safe, and sanitary. Paris, our world-famous city, is certainly emotionally displaced by the coronavirus and has been economically pushed into extraordinary hibernation. Yet, people are hopeful. To ensure one’s sanity, it’s best to stay busy and productive (however it’s defined). We are reminded daily to keep the faith and believe that there will be an end to this. Despite the pandemic, Parisians still complain often and seriously about the chilly, rainy weather and gray skies that seem to plague every otherwise nice day. To escape the chill and the Paris lockdown, the fortunate are headed to their country places or to the south of France, especially Nice and Aix-Provence. Such is the irony that the coronavirus weather is balmy and sunny with a forecast of the temperature reaching the mid-70s most days this week. Gazing from our open windows, lovely as that is, we literally have no place to go. articles.text: Garden Club members Agnès Kang and Janine McAuliffe came up with a creative way to brighten a quiet spring morning in Piedmont. On April 21, early morning joggers and people driving to work were treated to an unusual sight. The Piedmont Police Department’s speed trailer, parked in front of the station, was festooned with bright spring flowers. On the back was an orange umbrella shaped like a flower flanked by tall branches of pink dogwood and lime-green viburnum. The day before, Kang and McAuliffe journeyed to the San Francisco Flower Market at 5 a.m. to prepare for their flower pop-up. Kang explained that the project was inspired by New Yorkbased florist Lewis Miller, who started the “Flower Flash” craze. “A ‘flash’ is exactly that: an unexpected burst of colorful flowers in the most unexpected places, and for a short period of time,” Kang said. “You will see [Lewis’] amazing flower flashes in street garbage cans, construction sites, chain link fences, phone booths, hot dog carts, and bus stops. My favorites are the ones with flowers set against walls covered with graffiti. What I find so appealing, as a former New Yorker, is his guerrilla-style street art using the city’s grit, grime and graffiti as props for his flashes,” Kang said. “This year I saw the speed trailer parked in front of the police station and thought, why not? I wrote to Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, who approved our project and assigned Capt. Chris Monahan to assist us,” Kang explained. Kang and McAuliffe asked Monahan if he could change the speed trailer’s electronic sign to show the message, “April Showers Bring May...” The pair thought it would be clever to omit the word “flowers,” because the trailer would be fashioned with a big arrangement of them. Staff photos “Chris [Monahan] was less sure, thinking that he would be getting calls from residents complaining that the message was incomplete,” she said. As the two stood near the newly decorated speed trailer, they were greeted with car-honks and passerby-shouts of approval. The finishing touches were put on just as the sun rose that morning. “The smiles and positive comments that we received made the whole project worthwhile,” Kang said.
articles.title: Flower Flash comes to Piedmont

articles.text: Piedmont officers observed a white Chevrolet Malibu fail to stop at a stop sign at Wildwood and Nova on Monday morning, April 19. A records check revealed that the vehicle had been stolen out of Hayward. The male driver was detained on scene, but he refused to provide his name. A records check identified him as Anthony White, 29, who was on probation for Domestic Violence and was listed as a possible suspect in the theft of the car. White was arrested for possession of a stolen vehicle and probation violations. He was transported to Santa Rita jail, but was refused at the jail for a medical reason and was transported to John George psychiatric hospital in San Leandro. White was later released from the hospital after being issued a citation and a notice to appear in court.
articles.title: Car thief refuses to provide name; refused entry at Santa Rita Jail

articles.text: Piedmont Police officers were alerted that two stolen vehicles had entered the city on Tuesday afternoon, April 20. Officers found a 2007 white Chevy Trailblazer stolen from San Francisco towing a stolen 1997 silver GMC Sonoma with a rope at Olive and Oakland Avenues. Officers conducted a “high risk” stop at Fairview and Grand Ave. When the suspects spotted the police, the person in the vehicle being towed jumped out of the SUV and into the GMC and the suspect fled at high speed. Officers recovered the Chevy Trailblazer and had it towed. The vehicle was missing the front license plate and its interior had been stripped.
articles.title: More car thieves stopped in Piedmont

articles.text: Piedmont Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue The matter of a city-owned building leased to a non-profit arts organization has caused a strange schism in Piedmont, a fact acknowledged by all city council members at an April 19 meeting. The city council was asked to vote on what customarily would be a routine approval of an extension on an existing 10-year lease. Since its approval of the lease in November in a first reading, the council was asked to make decisions on a number of significant changes to the terms of the lease. On Monday night, the council decided not to move forward with the heavily modified lease proposal for the non-profit Piedmont Center for the Arts, which created the city’s first cultural arts center 10 years ago and has operated it since then at no cost to the city. Among the changes the council wanted was an increase in rent from $1 a year to $800 a month, a 30-day termination clause, and requirements to include non-arts related rentals as deemed appropriate by the city. These modifications were added following an approved first reading and a lengthy discussion with the prior council led by former mayor Bob McBain. The question Monday night instead became whether or not the city should become the “gatekeeper” of programs at 801 Magnolia Avenue, and if so, should there be a lease agreement at all? “A local, nonprofit group is not the best entity to be managing a city facility,” claimed Vice Mayor Tim Rood. “The way we approach our other [city-owned] rentals would apply here,” council member Jen Cavenaugh said. “Not once did anyone in PCA tell me that their goal was to manage a facility. I question whether the proposed lease agreement plays to the strengths of each party,” council member Conna McCarthy said. The first reading was approved on a 3 to 2 vote on November 16, 2020. Since that first reading, the organization has offered several amendments to the proposed agreement, at city council’s request. The city changed terms of the lease to include rental payment, designated city use on weekday mornings, an early lease termination clause, the addition of an emergency circumstance clause, and requirements for nonarts related rentals. The proposed amendments to the lease stated that the PCA would pay the city $800 a month, with a 3% per-year escalation. The city would have more use and control over the premises, and would take over responsibility for maintaining the interior of the building. Since its inception, the Center for the Arts has been responsible for all upkeep, maintenance, repairs, and renovations. The ensuing discussion, which lasted nearly two hours, began to oscillate. The first reading was approved in November with Cavenaugh and Rood dissenting. Again, they were unwavering in their opposition of a lease renewal. articles.text: Guilty. Yesterday afternoon, April 20, ex-Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin was convicted of the second-degree unintentional murder, third-degree murder and second-degree manslaughter of George Floyd. In Piedmont a message of remembrance and support for Floyd was displayed at the Exedra: “Hold George Floyd in your heart today.” The five signs were spread out over the entire exedra facade, just as events on May 25, 2020 swept across the entire nation. “The conclusion of one of the most consequential trials in our country’s recent history undoubtedly leaves us all with many emotions and an understanding that while one step towards justice has been made, much work remains,” said Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. “The Piedmont Police Department is committed to continuing in this work together, with our community, through openness, professionalism, dignity and respect.” The trial began March 8, and testimony was heard from 45 witnesses, including bystanders, police officials and medical experts. In closing statements on April 19, Prosecutor Jerry Blackwell said, “There is a 46th witness... that witness is common sense.” A jury of seven women and five men deliberated for 10 hours before pronouncing Chauvin guilt on all accounts. Mr. Chauvin had been free on bail since October, but was put in handcuffs yesterday and ordered into custody by judge Peter Cahill. Minnesota’s sentencing guidelines recommend 12.5 years in prison for each murder charge and four years for the manslaughter. The state has asked for a tougher sentence than the recommendations provide. Chauvin’s sentencing will be in eight weeks.
articles.title: Justice for the murder of George Floyd

articles.text: The city is close to meeting, and surpassing, the amount of housing units mandated by the RHNA (Regional Housing Needs Allocation) 2015-2023 cycle, according to a 2020 annual progress report. Piedmont has issued building permits for the construction of 73 new units out of a mandated 60 units by the end of next year, 2022. With changes in state legislation, however, it will “be challenging for the city to show that sufficient low and very low-income housing” is being produced, according to the report. That’s because most of the units that have received planning entitlements since the beginning of 2017 are allowed to be rented at market rates. To date, 12 very low income, 17 low income, 17 moderate, and 27 above moderate income level accessory dwelling units, or ADUs, have or are being constructed, for a total of 73 units. The current RHNA cycle mandates that 24 very low units be constructed - so Piedmont will still need to produce 12 “very low income” living units by the end of the cycle in 2022. “City staff has prepared a survey of local rents based on similar floor areas and amenities to substantiate the expected rents for moderate, low, and very low ADUs,” Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell told council members at Monday night’s City Council meeting, April 19. The survey found that average rents in Piedmont in 2020 total $2,590 a month, less than that reported for Oakland - which averaged at $2,705 for an approximately 780-square foot unit, or $3.47 per square foot. According to the state Department of Housing and Community Development, the allowable rents for very low-income units is between $1,143 for a studio, $1,305 for a one-bedroom, and $1,469 for a two-bedroom. In addition, Piedmont expects an RHNA 6th cycle of approximately 587 housing units, compared to 60 units in the current RHNA 5th cycle, representing a 979 percent increase. The expected allocation includes: 163 very low-income units, 94 low income units, 92 moderate income units, and 238 above moderate income units. The newly-minted Housing Advisory Committee held their first meeting last night, April 20. The purpose of the committee is to consider housing and equity issues in Piedmont, including the upcoming draft RHNA and the next housing element. To ensure that the city meets its housing needs assessment, it will seek a consulting firm; contractor Barry Miller, FAICP, prepared the city’s 3rd, 4th, and 5th RHNA, but has advised the city that he does not have the capacity to be the prime contractor on the city’s 6th cycle, given the significant increase in the RHNA, and need for a multi-disciplinary team to complete the work. Submission of the next cycle’s adopted Housing Element is due to The California Department of Housing and Community Development by January 2023. To meet this requirement, the city is listing Summer 2021 as a tentative due date for any RHNA appeals, and the first review of the draft housing element to take place in Summer 2022.
articles.title: State requires “very low income” units

articles.text: Editor: How does a parent answer a child who asks, “does my life matter?” Or asks, “is Daddy racist?” With the Black Lives Matter and “woke” culture being ever-present in our everyday lives, this has created concerning issues in my household. As a Chinese mother raising children who are half White, I am asked on a continual basis those questions. My children are torn that being White in America means they are assumed to be racist while being Chinese means that they will face some form of discrimination or hate. There is no “middle” for my children. After recent conversations with fellow Piedmonters there was agreement that racial discrimination will always be present in society. I cannot count the number of times that I have either been shunned, ridiculed, physically or verbally attacked because of my race. My two most memorable experiences were being “jumped” by two Black kids on the outskirts of Oakland Chinatown when I was in elementary school; and being asked by a Piedmont police officer in the late 1980’s “do you speak English?” I hold no anger towards these individuals because those were my life experiences and I have persevered. Although I applaud Piedmont Unified School District for exposing students to the racial and economic inequalities that Black Americans experience, these teachings have created a profusion of “white guilt” for my children while they struggle to discern their Chinese side (especially during this period of increased Asian hate attacks). past and present-day race issues under the rug, but there should be limitations of these teachings by PUSD. I thank PUSD for acknowledging the many issues that we face today, but I believe PUSD should yield to families the in-depth discussion of race issues, along with political viewpoints, due to unrestrained and undue influences. So, to bluntly answer my child’s questions: “Yes, your life matters along with everyone’s life” and “No, just because your father is White does not mean he is racist.” –Shirley Hooi For 22 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. Wishing I could honestly say “I would love to but I have a previous commitment,” but unable to do so, I agreed to be there. When the meeting started there were brief introductions, short preliminary statements and I was introduced as the one who would manage the heart of the meeting. articles.text: With COVID-19 vaccine eligibility open to all adults, Piedmont is closing in on total vaccination and leads Alameda County with more than 86 percent of its residents having received at least one dose of vaccine. Even though the use of a vaccine manufactured by Johnson & Johnson has been on pause since last week over blood clot concerns, vaccination in Alameda County has continued at a brisk pace. The Johnson & Johnson vaccine, which requires only one shot compared to the two-dose vaccines from Moderna and Pfizer, should return to circulation by this Friday, April 23, according to comments over the weekend from Dr. Anthony Fauci, the director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommended that health agencies pause the use of the Johnson & Johnson vaccine last Tuesday, April 13 “out of an abundance of caution” due to reports of blood clotting issues in a handful of cases. The Alameda County Public Health Department announced the same day that it would stop administering Johnson & Johnson vaccines until further investigation. Almost 7 million doses of Johnson & Johnson vaccine have been administered in the United States. Six cases of the rare blood clot reaction have been recorded nationwide, and one death has been reported. The six cases of blood clots all occurred in women between the ages of 18 and 48. Symptoms occurred 6 to 13 days after vaccination. Even though the blood clots appear to be exceedingly rare, people who received the Johnson & Johnson vaccine before the pause occurred are encouraged to monitor themselves for symptoms, like severe headache, abdominal pain, leg pain or shortness of breath within three weeks after vaccination. Anyone experiencing these symptoms should contact their health care provider immediately. Although one of the three vaccines approved by the Food and Drug Administration has been halted, daily vaccination rates have remained high countywide. articles.text: Join the City of Piedmont in celebrating the 51st anniversary of Earth Day. This Thursday, April 22, the City will be holding virtual events featuring a presentation and community discussion about Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan and a discussion of the documentary Rebuilding Paradise with a panel of local fire experts, including the City’s new Fire Chief. The City will also announce the winners of this year’s Piedmont Climate Challenge. Visit the City’s Earth Day page to find additional information about the events including a list of regional celebrations and resources. Also, community members are encouraged to sign up for the free induction cooktop loaning program offered by the City. This program allows you to test out electrifying your kitchen by lending out induction cooktop kits. Induction is becoming more and more popular among chefs and has a number of advantages over gas cooking. APRIL 22, 12-1 pm: City Climate Updates. Bring your lunch and hear about Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan and Climate Challenge. The conversation will include information on what has been accomplished and potential climate measures and the road ahead. There will be an open discussion format to voice your questions, ideas, and concerns. You can register here: https://piedmont-ca-gov.zoom.us/meeting/register/tZEucOmsrjsiGtecfF2vvYI1C6U4Sgmx67vm APRIL 22, 7-8 pm: Movie Discussion & Panel. In the evening, join us for a discussion of the documentary film Rebuilding Paradise and a talk with local fire management experts. Panelists include Piedmont’s new Fire Chief David Brannigan, Fire Captain Scott Barringer, and wildland fire specialist Dr. Sasha Berleman. The event will also include a special announcement on the winners of the Climate Challenge. articles.text: The Oakland Center of the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, directed by Piedmont resident, Dr. Steve Sidney, currently has job postings for a 35-year follow-up exam of study participants who were first examined in 1985-1986. The CARDIA study, funded by the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute, is a longitudinal study of black and white men and women who were 18-30 years old at the beginning of the study and who have been followed for the development of heart disease risk factors and disease. More than 900 published scientific articles have resulted from the CARDIA study thus far. This will be the 10th examination for study participants who were initially recruited from four centers around the country, including Kaiser Permanente (KP) Health Plan members from the Berkeley-Oakland area. The examination will be conducted by the KP Northern California Division of Research at its research clinic located in the Mosswood Building, 3505 Broadway in Oakland. Positions are available for scheduling examinations, conducting exam interviews and study procedures, data management, and managing the mailing of equipment and supplies for aspects of the study conducted at the homes of participants. These positions will start in May or June of this year and end during the summer of 2022. Training will be provided. If you would like more information, please contact Dr. Sidney at steve.sidney@kp.org.
articles.title: Job opportunities for local Medical Research study

articles.text: Photo by Dick Carter Members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesday group stopped on Sea View Avenue on April 14 for a group photo of some colorful tulips. Pictured are Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Sherry Jacobs, Nancy Henn, Brenda Ferrero, Bob and Kathy Gustafson, Harriette Louie, and Adrienne Hamlin. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group is back roaming the streets of Piedmont. On April 14th members of the group assembled at the Exedra for the first time in over a year. The pandemic made the group stop their walks over a year ago, but when Alameda County went to the Red/Tier 2 level on March 9th, the Recreation Department began the process of restarting the activity. A new set of safety protocols were developed that require registration, as well as social distancing, the use of masks, limited physical contact, and small size pods during the walks. The walk on April 14th marked the third anniversary of the group’s first walk in 2018. A total of 17 walkers had registered, but due to some schedule conflicts, 11 walkers were at the Exedra on Wednesday morning at 10 a.m. ready to reconnect with old friends and make some new ones. Participating were Nancy Henn, Bob Gustafson, Harriette Louie, Brenda Ferrero, Adrienne Hamlin, Nancy DeRoche, Dick Carter, and first time walkers Kathy Gustafson and Andree and Mark Greenberg. Dick Carter welcomed everyone. During its first two years almost 150 people had participated in the walks. He acknowledged that the weekly walks have provided not only physical activity but also a community for older adults where lasting friendships have been formed. April 14th was a beautiful spring morning with spring flowers in bloom, especially the fragrant cherry blossoms in full bloom in Piedmont Park. Dividing themselves into two groups (pods) they agreed on a route the walkers would take them to Sea View Avenue, one of their favorite destinations. But first, a Walk in the Park Before beginning Wednesday’s walk, the group walked through Piedmont Park, seeing the flowering cherry trees, the Japanese Tea House and the historical plaques. The group agreed this spot is a Piedmont treasure. The walkers went on Sierra Avenue to Sheridan and then to Wildwood, stopping to admire the profusion of flowers at the Davis house at the corner of Wildwood and Sheridan. Crossing the street, they went through the Hall Fenway, past Crocker Park and up to Sea View Avenue. They stopped for some photos of a front yard filled with colorful tulips before heading down Mountain Avenue. On Mountain they noticed a larger-than-life statue of a distinguished gentleman in the front yard of a home, something no one had noticed on previous walks on the street. To return to the Exedra, they took the somewhat hidden path connecting Mountain with Piedmont Court – and more cherry trees. Nancy DeRoche pointed out a home where she first lived in Piedmont. The house now has a birdhouse that matches the actual house and a metal sculpture of a bagpiper in its front yard. It was the first time on Piedmont Court for many of the walkers. The group finished their 2-1/2 mile walk in 90 minutes, a typical outing for the weekly walks. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues). Next Wednesday, April 28, they will meet at 10:15 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge, and new walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required. To sign up, click on https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu, or contact John Wilk at jwilk@ piedmont.ca.gov, for more information. articles.text: The State Bar Board of Trustees has appointed Piedmont resident Stella Ngai to serve as the 2021 Chair of the Judicial Nominees Evaluation Commission. The Commission of the State Bar of California assists the Governor in the judicial selection process, promoting a California judiciary of quality and integrity by providing independent, comprehensive, accurate and fair evaluations of candidates for judicial appointment and nomination. Ngai was first appointed to the Commission in 2018. Her term as chair begins on April 26, 2021. She works in the office of the General Counsel of the Regents of the University of California at the UC Office of the President in Oakland. An expert in privacy, public disclosure laws, and education affairs, she advises senior Stella Ngai management, staff, and faculty at the 10 UC campuses. Previously, she was an Assistant District Attorney for the City and County of San Francisco, and also practiced law at the highly regarded San Francisco firm of Minami Tamaki.
articles.title: Stella Ngai named Chair of Judicial Evaluation Commission

Next Wednesday, April 28, they will meet at 10:15 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge, and new walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. The CARDIA study, funded by the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute, is a longitudinal study of black and white men and women who were 18-30 years old at the beginning of the study and who have been followed for the development of heart disease risk factors and disease. More than 900 published scientific articles have resulted from the CARDIA study thus far. This will be the 10th examination for study participants who were initially recruited from four centers around the country, including Kaiser Permanente (KP) Health Plan members from the Berkeley-Oakland area. The examination will be conducted by the KP Northern California Division of Research at its research clinic located in the Mosswood Building, 3505 Broadway in Oakland. Positions are available for scheduling examinations, conducting exam interviews and study procedures, data management, and managing the mailing of equipment and supplies for aspects of the study conducted at the homes of participants. These positions will start in May or June of this year and end during the summer of 2022. Training will be provided. If you would like more information, please contact Dr. Sidney at steve.sidney@kp.org. Stella Ngai named Chair of Judicial Evaluation Commission The State Bar Board of Trustees has appointed Piedmont resident Stella Ngai to serve as the 2021 Chair of the Judicial Nominees Evaluation Commission. The Commission of the State Bar of California assists the Governor in the judicial selection process, promoting a California judiciary of quality and integrity by providing independent, comprehensive, accurate and fair evaluations of candidates for judicial appointment and nomination. Ngai was first appointed to the Commission in 2018. Her term as chair begins on April 26, 2021. She works in the office of the General Counsel of the Regents of the University of California at the UC Office of the President in Oakland. An expert in privacy, public disclosure laws, and education affairs, she advises senior Stella Ngai management, staff, and faculty at the 10 UC campuses. Previously, she was an Assistant District Attorney for the City and County of San Francisco, and also practiced law at the highly regarded San Francisco firm of Minami Tamaki.

articles.text: In the last part of its phased reopening, Children’s Fairyland in Oakland will resume live entertainment this weekend, beginning Saturday, April 24. The park’s famed Blue Fairy will kick off the re-opening of live events. The Blue Fairy (Jacquelyn Lynaugh) is a longtime park favorite, equipped with her guitar, the aptly named “Prince Charming.” The Blue Fairy will share stories and perform wellknown folk songs for young audiences. Shows will take place on the Festival Stage behind Aesop’s Playhouse, and will include four sessions each day: two morning sessions at 10 a.m. and 11:15 a.m., and two afternoon sessions at 2 p.m. and 3:15 p.m. Guests are advised to bring a blanket and sunscreen, as seating will be on the lawn for all festival stage performances. This weekend completes Fairyland’s phased reopening of live events. Puppet shows began on April 14, last week. Toddler Storytimes are still temporarily on pause, but Fairyland is offering digital toddler storytime, which you can view at https:// www.fairylandsmagictree.org/ toddlerstorytime. Two puppet shows are currently running at Fairyland, “The Three Dinosaurs Gruff,” playing at the open-air Storybook Puppet Theatre, and “Fantasy on Strings,” playing on the festival stage behind Aesop’s Playhouse. Each will show twice per session, both in the mornings and afternoons, a total of four times a day each on two different stages. Morning sessions take place at 10 a.m. and 11:15 a.m., and afternoon sessions are at 2 p.m. and 3:15 p.m. Puppet shows are included in the cost of your park ticket. Come for the rides Rides are back at Fairyland with reduced capacity. Young visitors will love riding on the colorful Jolly Trolly, taking a trip on the Wonder-go-Round, and exploring Ansansi’s Magic Web, a mini-Ferris wheel that resembles a spider’s web. Visitors to the 10-acre storybook theme park must adhere to social distancing and mask-wearing guidelines. The cafe is open with a limited menu, and indoor retail spaces are open as well. Visitors will be allowed to enter retail spaces one “social bubble” at a time. To secure tickets, visit: https:// fairyland.org/visit-us/admissions/. Every show that takes place in Fairyland’s Storybook Puppet Theater is a completely original production, and all scripts, costumes, music and sets are designed by the park’s puppeteers. Pictured are puppets for Fairyland’s production of the Velveteen Rabbit. Jacquelyn Lynaugh will resume her role as Fairyland’s Blue Fairy with special live performances this weekend. The Jolly Trolly is open at reduced capacity.
