articles.text: Beginning next Tuesday, April 27, high schools and middle school students will have the same class schedule. It consists of eight hours and 45 minutes of class time per week. High schoolers are on this schedule this week, while middle schoolers are on a “step-in” schedule this week of four to five hours of class. Piedmont elementary school students were the first in the city to return to in-class instruction in February. Since then, they have been on a schedule with nine hours of classroom instruction per week (two hours and 15 minutes, Tuesday through Friday). Though it represents less than one-third of a normal 28-30 hour-school week, getting to this schedule has been exhausting for everyone involved. Here is a chronological recap of Piedmont schools reopening. March 13, 2020: Piedmont School District close all schools as the first cases of COVID-19 are detected in the Bay Area. The initial shutdown plan is only for two weeks, March 16-27, and Piedmont is first school in Alameda County to announce closure. March 16: Class assignments move online to Schoology for grades 6-12; elementary students receive assignments on Google Docs. There is no minimum online “classtime” requirement or required attendance. Chromebooks are given out to all students in grades 6-12. March 25: Alameda County Office of Education requires all schools to stay closed through May 1. The State Department of Education drops the requirement of 180- day instructional day minimum. Piedmont has no plans of extending school year for lost days of instruction. March 31: California State Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond announces schools in California will not reopen until fall 2020. May 14: Tony Thurmond announces that the decision of when and how to reopen public schools will be left to each school district. May 29: PHS holds in-person, masked and distanced graduation ceremonies in groups of 50-60 students at Witter Field; each student is allowed two guests from their household. No students give speeches. June 4: Piedmont’s School Reopening Task Force holds its first meeting with nearly 100 participants including 11 students, 20 parents, 12 classified community members, 46 certificated educators, 13 administrators, and two board members. June 26: “Piedmont Partners” starts a petition to reopen schools in the fall. 740 parents, students and community members sign the petition in four days. June 30: The School Board votes for a hybrid learning model for 2020-21 school year. The board approves in-person classes four or five days per week. July 13: The School Board directs the superintendent to start the school year online, Sixth graders Maya Sears (left) and Ruby Yasar create “automata” in a Makers Class by building a camshaft to twist and make their figures move. citing increases in Bay Area COVID cases. July 17: Governor Newsom decrees public schools cannot open if their county is on the COVID “Watch-List,” (now equivalent to the purple tier). Alameda County was put on the list July 12. August 17: The first day of school begins with online classes, with mandatory attendance and scheduled screen time. August 26: The district reaches a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with its teacher’s union solely for Distance Learning. Teachers receive a guarantee that in-person learning for TK-5th grade will not start before October 1. September 9: Piedmont teachers and the school district strike a tentative agreement for in-person learning based on a hybrid model. Cohort student sizes are limited to 15. The agreement would be activated if the County is in the red tier, and is not in a waiver of the K-5 plan. September 22: Alameda County moves to the red tier. Schools will have the green light to open after two weeks in the red tier. September 23: With a 3-2 vote, the School Board agrees to file a waiver with the county to allow TK-5th grade students back in school, regardless of COVID tier. The waiver program is later nullified by Alameda County. October 6: Piedmont’s School Board approves a school reopening plan. TK-2 students plan to return November 3 and grades 3-5 on November 10. October 23: Elementary school reopening is delayed from November 3 until December 1. Eleven days before the planned school reopening, Supt. Booker announces the district is unable to create a master schedule. November 9: Alameda County allows secondary schools to reopen with protocols in place. November 12: Ms. Cowan’s SPED Learning Center welcomes back five students to Wildwood Elementary School. November 13: Millennium High School welcomes small cohorts of students on campus. November 16: Piedmont’s reopening plan for elementary schools on December 1 is canceled. Alameda County enters the purple tier due to a spike in COVID-19 cases. Schools that have not started by November 17 are not allowed to open. Schools that are already in session may continue. November 17: Nine Transitional Kindergarten (TK) students have their first day of School. December 1: A survey sent to parents to choose in-person or distance learning sparks many complaints. The distance learning option includes an undiscussed or consented to movement to an online “Edgenuity” program. Parent disapproval leads Booker to cancel the plan and the survey. December 30: Newsom introduces “Safe Schools For All” plan with financial incentives for elementary schools that open in February or March. Restrictions are lessened on reopening. To reopen a school’s county need only be under 25 new COVID cases per day instead of seven. January 27, 2021: Teachers and PUSD reach a tentative agreement on reopening. January 31: Booker submits the required COVID Safety Plan to the state and county. February 2: COVID case rates drop to 23.1 new cases per day, opening the door for Alameda County elementary schools to reopen. February 8: Teachers become eligible for COVID-19 vaccine. February 9-11: Grades K-2 return to school for two hours and fifteen minutes per day, four days a week (Tuesday through Friday). February 23: 6th graders return to class for two and a half hours of class per week. February 24: A group of Piedmont parents in an online Reopening Advocacy group conduct a survey of 406 families about their likeliness to stay in the school district. The group asks for a guarantee from PUSD that schools will be fully open in the fall. February 23-25: Grades 3-5 return to school for two hours and fifteen minutes per day Tu-F. March 9: Alameda County enters the red tier of Covid restrictions. Secondary schools can reopen March 10. March 9: The Reopening Advocates distribute over 400 lawn signs reading “OPEN OUR SCHOOLS.” March 16: Exactly one year after closing, grades 9-10 return for eight hours 45 minutes of class every other week (average of four hours 22.5 minutes per week). March 16-19: Grades 7-8 return for two periods of class per week (two and a half hours). March 23: 11th and 12th graders return to school (average of four hours, 22.5 minutes per week). March 25: PUSD commits to opening school full time in fall. A joint statement is signed by Booker, School Board members and representatives of the Piedmont unions

articles.text: Oakland Zoo 9777 Golf Links Rd, Oakland 632-9525 oaklandzoo.org Zoo- Open There’s no better time to go to the Oakland Zoo, as the children’s California Wilds Playground just reopened. In the expansive outdoor space, children can slide, spin, soar, and build in the five play zones inspired by the different native habitats of the California Trail animals. The zoo also just introduced a new exhibit, “Taking Action Against the Illegal Wildlife Trade.” Other previously closed areas like the petting zoo will be opening up in the near future too. Come by for safe and depopulated visits to support the zoo and its conservation efforts. 50 cents of every ticket purchase goes to conservation efforts of chimps, elephants, the California Condor, the yellow-legged frog and more. Advanced ticketing is required. Children’s Fairyland 699 Bellevue Avenue, Oakland 452-2259 Fairyland.org Theme Park - Open The rides at Fairyland opened April 7, the puppet shows started on April 14, and live theater performances returns this weekend on April 24. Fairyland has also expanded its schedule to five days a week W-Su. Toddlers, Tiddlywinks, little guys and gals have a new adventure place open to them. The whole acreage is open to guest and over 50 storybook sets are fully open. Many have just received fresh layers of paint, meaning Fairyland looks better than ever. Get tickets online now. Lindsay Wildlife Center- Summer Camps 3701 Treat Blvd., Concord (925) 935-1978 Lindsaywildlife.org/special-events Registration is now open for Lindsay’s Wildlife Experience Summer Camps which will get your budding naturalists and wildlife conservationists out into nature. The day camps start Monday, June 7. Lindsay offers two-week camps for kids to meet some of Lindsay’s animal ambassadors, and study local wildlife. Camps will also be academic and educational; kids will participate in games, crafts and STEM building challenges. Camps are located at Lime Ridge Open Space and Newhall Community Park in Concord. Each camp runs from 8:30 a.m. – 1:00 p.m. M-F; all sessions are entirely outdoors and have a maximum size of 12 children. Camps are for 4-6 year-olds or 7-10 year-olds. Lawrence Hall of Science- Summer Camps 1 Centennial Drive, Berkeley (510) 642-5132 Lawrencehallofscience.org In-person summer camps are available for children in grades TK-12, in topics ranging from dinosaurs and slime to astronomy and coding. Camps will take place at The Lawrence Hall from June 7 to August 6. Make a Rube Goldberg machine, or enter the Hall’s Maker space for engineering fun. Safety precautions will be put in place for these 3-week summer camps including separating campers into pods. Some sessions for younger scientists are already booked up, but waitlists are open, and all sessions for older kids are still fully open. for administrators, classified staff, teachers. April 20: PHS students begin their new “checkerboard” schedule, which doubles their time in class. High school students attend class Tu-F each week instead of alternating weeks on campus and then off. articles.text: The Piedmont Avenue Branch Library reopened to the public yesterday, April 20. It also welcomed its new Branch Manager, Leni Matthews, who is both a librarian and a teacher. Hours of operation are 10:00 am to 1:00 pm, Tuesday through Saturday. Visitors will be required to wear masks, get screened for a temperature at the door, and maintain social distancing. Capacity will be limited, and there will be no seating inside. The library will continue to quarantine returned materials for 24 hours before putting them back on the shelves. Digital offerings, including movies, and eBooks, plus virtual programs, are still available online at www.oaklandlibrary.org. The Oakland Public Library has reopened 16 locations including indoor Express services. Library users will be able to access modified library services including limited browsing, checkout of materials, and computer use. The following in-person services will be available: • Library card registration and renewal • Browsing the collection • Wi-Fi access and mobile device charging Visitor guidelines • Wear a face mask covering nose and mouth, for all patrons over two years old. • Maintain a physical distance of 6-feet apart • Self-screen for COVID-19 symptoms. • Wash or sanitize hands frequently. The library will continue to offer 24/7 access to digital offerings including e-books, audiobooks and streaming movies, in addition to virtual programs, including storytimes, book clubs and author talks. For more information contact the Piedmont Ave. Branch Library, located at 80 Echo Avenue in Oakland, at (510) 597-5011 (www.oaklandlibrary.org)
articles.title: Piedmont Ave. Library now open to public

articles.text: A new partnership between Chabot Space & Science Center in Oakland and NASA’s Ames Research Center in Mountain View now underway. Anchoring the partnership is a new visitor center called “The NASA Experience” and opening at Chabot in November this year. Under the terms of a 5-year Space Act Agreement, the organizations are beginning a longterm collaboration to create accessible STEAM (science, technology, engineering, art, and math) community engagement and education opportunities in Oakland and beyond. “We are delighted to have this opportunity to bring a deeper NASA experience into our surrounding communities,” said Eugene Tu, director of Ames. “It’s one of NASA’s founding functions to share our work as widely as possible, and this partnership for a new visitor’s center will allow us to reach more broadly than we’d ever be able to do with our existing resources and location in the South Bay.” NASA and Chabot have identified three main areas for immediate collaboration that will use the strengths of NASA’s research and Chabot’s long-standing programs. “We are so excited to share the fascinating science, extraordinary people and groundbreaking research of NASA’s Ames Research Center right here in Oakland,” said Adam Tobin, Executive Director at Chabot Space & Science Center, “Bringing together NASA Ames’ long legacy of innovation and Chabot’s 137-year history in STEM education creates a powerful opportunity to inspire the next generation of future scientists, engineers and astronomers.” “The NASA Experience” creates an immersive, dynamic, STEAM lear ning environment that puts the visitor into the role of a NASA researcher. Hands-on STEAM studios highlight the current science at NASA through interactive challenges, models, artifacts, and more. The visitor center brings to life the challenging and inspiring process of scientific discovery by showcasing the real stories and people at NASA’s Ames Research Center. The two groups will create an interconnected network of STEAM education experiences throughout the city that deepens Chabot’s existing “Learning Everywhere” initiative. Building on existing connections with Oakland’s schools, libraries, and local organizations, this partnership will create programs that engage learners in current NASA research. The partnership will create tangible STEAM career pathways by developing connections between NASA’s career opportunities and Chabot’s youth development programs. NASA will provide speakers, field trips, and independent study on the missions and technology associated with work happening at NASA Ames in collaboration with Chabot’s Galaxy Explorers program, first established in 2000. Chabot Space & Science Center is a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth. NASA’s Ames Research Center, one of 10 NASA field centers across the country, is located in the heart of California’s Silicon Valley. Since 1939, Ames has led NASA in conducting world-class research and development in aeronautics, exploration technology, and science aligned with the center’s core capabilities.

articles.text: Starting in the fall semester, first-year students accepted to University of California in Berkeley will have the option of beginning classes on Cal’s campus or Mills College, a women’s liberal arts college in Oakland. The “UC Berkeley Changemaker in Oakland” program, initiated for the 2021-22 academic year, will accept 200 first-year students for a yearlong residential college experience offered by Cal. Ramu Nagappan, assistant dean of UC Berkeley Extension, explained that the program addition compliments the university’s longstanding Fall Program for Freshman (FPF), which since 1983 has offered one-semester opportunities in Berkeley for 750 incoming students to take core classes together. UC Berkeley Extension runs the FPF and will operate the new program at Mills College. “We’re building on the Fall Program for Freshman, [which] has a good legacy. The FPF is a small, collaborative learning community for incoming students in the College of Letters and Science that refers to itself as a small liberal arts college, with the resources and opportunities of a large research university,” Nagappan said. She added that, results from students who complete FPF semesters demonstrate “small, but measurable differences in academic outcomes - their GPAs [grade point average] are slightly higher, their time to graduate is a little faster than College of Letters and Science students who start on the main campus.” The “UC Berkeley Changemaker in Oakland” program application calls on students who “find [themselves] questioning the status quo, seek to make things better for [their] community, and want to build a lasting connection and dream of making a meaningful difference.” Program highlights include living in a single-occupancy room on the pastoral campus of Mills College. Students accepted to the program will be able to take classes with smaller groups of students, and participate in co-curricular events that highlight arts, culture, activism, history and innovation in Oakland. Students will also receive dedicated academic advising and will be able to choose internships that bring a final “changemaker project to life.” Chinyere Oparah, the Mills College Dean of Faculty, said that Mills is an ideal location for Berkeley’s new freshman program. “Oakland is a vibrant cultural hub and a community with a deep history of social activism, and Mills’ faculty and students see ourselves as being in partnership with Oakland, and specifically with educators, artists, practitioners, people doing real change work in the community,” Oparah said. Last month, Mills College announced that it will no longer be enrolling first-year undergraduate students after the upcoming fall 2021 semester. The college cited economic pressures brought on by the COVID-19 pandemic as well as declining enrollment as reasons for closure. Mills, founded in 1852, offered bachelor’s degrees to women and general nonbinary students as the oldest undergraduate college for women in the Western United States - the UC Berkeley program will accept male, female, and gender nonbinary students. The new coalition with UC Berkeley has the added benefit of keeping incoming students in smaller cohorts, advised by the Center for Disease Control (CDC) as an effective way of controlling the COVID-19 virus. “By creating this cohort program at Mills, we will be able to educate 200 freshmen for a year, without overtaxing the main campus. The impact is lighter for sophomore year [students],” Cal Vice Chancellor for Undergraduate Education Rick Russo said. Russo added that the new program at Mill College is ideal for “a family that wants their students on a campus with less density, for a student who wants a single room instead of a double at the same cost, for a student who hoped to attend a liberal arts college but wasn’t offered admission to it, and a student who is really interested in Berkeley Changemaker curriculum, which is meant to connect with many majors [across Cal offerings].”
articles.title: Program for 200 first-year students in small cohorts

articles.text: “If you look good, you feel good. If you feel good, you play good. If you play good, they pay good,” stated Football Hall of Fame player Deion Sanders While academic and athletic achievement certainly differ, the premise behind this saying can be applied to test taking, speeches and schoolwork in general. In some respects, taking a test is no different than a sporting match. A game or match is the big stage. It’s the time to play “good” to get paid “good.” In school the games are tests, and the payments are A’s, a G.P.A, and scores of 100. In 2003, Dan Bonin, then a Geometry teacher at Piedmont High, preached the same philosophy on test day. He even offered bonus points to students who dressed up for midterms and finals. Why? It’s all about confidence. –Football Hall of Fame player Deion Sanders It is well known that test scores do not necessarily reflect a student’s comprehension or mastery of course material. This is why the SAT and class grades are not the only factors on college applications. Extra circular activities and essay writing on topics outside of class material can be just as important as numeric scores. Even with comparable understanding of class materials, some students seem to be “good test takers,” or the opposite, kids who “just don’t test well.” Becoming a good test taker is not something you are born with – it is a learned skill. It can be as simple as confidence, demeanor and patience. Looking sharp in an ironed shirt, and tie or in a sophisticated ensemble can be just the edge a B student needs to ace the exam. It’s not about hiding a flash card on the underside of a tie; it is a small investment in self-respect There is something to be said about the effectiveness of school uniforms. Choosing to look snazzy on test day can help your score. and looking the part that can be a major boon on test day. “Look your best” is not an old wives’ tale. It is rooted in psychology and is a tried and true method. I encourage every student to just give it a try on their next big test. Merely taking yourself and the task at hand seriously sets the stage for success. When you look good, you feel good. When you feel good, you are more confident. A tough question early on in an exam has less of a chance to derail your train of thought. Some of the enemies when taking a test include: 1) test material 2) distractions 3) your own mind Some tests require patience to prevent you from breaking concentration which can cause students to miss questions they actually know, or fail to make educated guesses. Another sports mantra, “practice like you play,” can be applied when studing, doing homework, and taking practice tests. In golf, that means going through your normal routine on the driving range before every shot and always picking a target. If a test is going to be timed, time yourself at home. If a test is without the use of a calculator, then attempt to solve problems the same way. A simple thing like wearing polished dress shoes or lucky socks has nothing to do with your feet scoring points on the test. The practice may seem like a superstition but goes beyond that into the realm of the psyche. A picture is worth a thousand words, so look picture- perfect and see what you get in return. Jay Russell has over 10 years of experience as a tutor; he specializes in essay writing and algebra. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Immediately, the new city was beset with problems. Some residents still wanted to be part of Oakland. Varney Gaskill resigned as President of the Board of Trustees three months later. The Board then elected Hugh Craig as President, and he served for seven years, guiding the city through its early years. The issue of incorporation continued to stir controversy in the community. Commuters discussed it on the streetcars and ferries. Residents discussed it at dinner parties and teas. Just four and a half months after Piedmont residents voted to incorporate as a city, a new faction of Piedmonters led by Edward Engs filed a petition for another election. They felt the question of cityhood should go before the voters again. Hugh Craig’s original house on Vernal Avenue (now Highland Avenue) with a water tower and barn, 1879-1912. New Zealand Insurance Company and opened an office in San Francisco where he worked in the fire and marine insurance business from 1875 until his death in 1919. Hugh Craig married Inez Gilcrest in 1875, and they raised six children in Piedmont: Evelyn, Roy, Margery, Jessie, Colin, and Eric. In 1954, Evelyn Craig Pattiani published her memoir, Queen of the Hills, about growing up in Piedmont. Craig hired Samuel Bugbee in 1879 to build a house on his acreage on Vernal Avenue (now Highland Avenue) for $5,000. Architect Bugbee designed the house as a Stick Italianate. It is completely built of redwood with square window bays, vertical siding, and tall narrow windows. Until 1912, the house faced Vernal Avenue and was surrounded by lawns, flower beds, and fruit trees – peach, apricot, plum, and cherry. The water tower had a windmill that pumped the water 50-feet up to the tank to provide water pressure for the house. There was a stable for horses, a barn for cows, and pens for chickens, turkeys, and pigs. It was essentially a self-sustaining farm, as were all the houses in Piedmont in the 1880s. Craig commuted to his insurance office in San Francisco by horsecar and ferry. He said that on a good day, it took 1½ hours to get to the office. The ferry rides On September 5, 1907, Piedmonters again voted on whether to remain a city or to dis-incorporate and become part of Oakland. This time, as a municipality, the vote to dis-incorporate required a two-thirds vote. Of the 154 voters, 92 voted to dis-incorporate, and 62 voted against. Despite the majority vote, those voting to dis-incorporate failed to carry the required two-thirds majority. Piedmont continued as a municipality. A vote of 102 to dis-incorporate would have carried the measure. Just 10 votes made the difference between Piedmont remaining a city or becoming part of Oakland. In those early years, the new city of Piedmont had many issues to solve. The city needed a City Hall, street maintenance, sewer systems, water service, and police and fire protection. How to fund these services? Prior to incorporating, residents paid just one small tax to the County. Owners of city-sized lots paid the same tax as those who owned large acreage. To fund city services, Craig instituted a tax based on the size of the property. The large landowners were not happy with their increased taxes and complained bitterly to Mayor Craig. The taxes remained, but Craig was not re-elected in 1914. Mayor Craig was also a victim of the increased tax basis. He owned six acres and his house was in the middle of his land. In 1912, he moved his house and sub-divided his land. The house was put on log rollers and slowly moved by horses to the corner of Craig’s property where it is now, at 55 Craig Avenue at the corner of Mountain Avenue. Craig then created Craig Avenue with residential lots on both sides of the street. Who was Hugh Craig? Hugh Craig was born in Sydney, Australia in 1841 to Scottish parents. He grew up in New Zealand before moving to Oakland. articles.text: You can thank Hugh Craig if you like living in Piedmont and not in Oakland. The San Francisco earthquake and fire in 1906 left most San Franciscans homeless. They fled to Oakland and the East Bay by ferry, and many decided to stay and build their homes here. To accommodate the earthquake refugees, Oakland began annexing as much land as possible. Oakland Mayor Mott spoke to Piedmont residents extolling the advantages of becoming part of “Greater Oakland.” He promised better sewers and roads, improved water supply, and police and fire protection. Oakland politicians thought that annexing the beauty of the Piedmont hills would be a great asset for Oakland. Taxes on the Piedmont land would swell the Oakland coffers. But a group of far-sighted Piedmont residents realized that if they did not do something, they would become part of Oakland. In a race between annexation and incorporation, Piedmont had to move quickly. To incorporate, the city had to have boundaries. With no time for a survey, Hugh Craig and others accepted the northern edge of Oakland as the southern boundary of Piedmont, and the eastern edge of Oakland as the western boundary of Piedmont. With this Seal of Incorporation, Piedmont became an official municipality on January 31, 1907. Hugh Craig was Mayor of Piedmont from 1907 to 1914. The north and east boundaries of the already existing Piedmont Sanitary District completed Piedmont’s boundaries. (This hastily drawn map explains why some Piedmont houses straddle the city lines.) pages.text: 10 Wednesday, April 21, 2021 The History of Piedmont Hugh Craig – and how Piedmont became a City By Gail Lombardi You can thank Hugh Craig if you like living in Piedmont and not in Oakland. The San Francisco earthquake and fire in 1906 left most San Franciscans homeless. They fled to Oakland and the East Bay by ferry, and many decided to stay and build their homes here. To accommodate the earthquake refugees, Oakland began annexing as much land as possible. Oakland Mayor Mott spoke to Piedmont residents extolling the advantages of becoming part of “Greater Oakland.” He promised better sewers and roads, improved water supply, and police and fire protection. Oakland politicians thought that annexing the beauty of the Piedmont hills would be a great asset for Oakland. Taxes on the Piedmont land would swell the Oakland coffers. But a group of far-sighted Piedmont residents realized that if they did not do something, they would become part of Oakland. In a race between annexation and incorporation, Piedmont had to move quickly. To incorporate, the city had to have boundaries. With no time for a survey, Hugh Craig and others accepted the northern edge of Oakland as the southern boundary of Piedmont, and the eastern edge of Oakland as the western boundary of Piedmont. Immediately, the new city was beset with problems. Some residents still wanted to be part of Oakland. Varney Gaskill resigned as President of the Board of Trustees three months later. The Board then elected Hugh Craig as President, and he served for seven years, guiding the city through its early years. The issue of incorporation continued to stir controversy in the community. Commuters discussed it on the streetcars and ferries. Residents discussed it at dinner parties and teas. Just four and a half months after Piedmont residents voted to incorporate as a city, a new faction of Piedmonters led by Edward Engs filed a petition for another election. They felt the question of cityhood should go before the voters again. With this Seal of Incorporation, Piedmont became an official municipality on January 31, 1907. Hugh Craig was Mayor of Piedmont from 1907 to 1914. The north and east boundaries of the already existing Piedmont Sanitary District completed Piedmont’s boundaries. (This hastily drawn map explains why some Piedmont houses straddle the city lines.) On January 7, 1907, Hugh Craig and James Ballentine raced to Sacramento to file the map of Piedmont, and on Saturday, January 26, 1907, Piedmonters voted to incorporate as a municipality. The Oakland Tribune reported that 117 votes were cast: 79 Piedmont men voted for incorporation, and 38 men voted against. (Women would not be able to vote until 1920.) James Ballentine was elected as Piedmont’s first City Clerk, and five trustees were elected: George Armstrong, Henry Butters, Hugh Craig, Varney Gaskill, and Miles Standish. The trustees surprisingly elected Varney Gaskill as President of the Board of Trustees over Hugh Craig who had led the movement to incorporate. On January 31, 1907, the State of California stamped the documents making Piedmont an official municipal corporation. “Just 10 votes made the difference between Piedmont remaining a city or becoming part of Oakland.” Hugh Craig’s original house on Vernal Avenue (now Highland Avenue) with a water tower and barn, 1879-1912. New Zealand Insurance Company and opened an office in San Francisco where he worked in the fire and marine insurance business from 1875 until his death in 1919. Hugh Craig married Inez Gilcrest in 1875, and they raised six children in Piedmont: Evelyn, Roy, Margery, Jessie, Colin, and Eric. In 1954, Evelyn Craig Pattiani published her memoir, Queen of the Hills, about growing up in Piedmont. Craig hired Samuel Bugbee in 1879 to build a house on his acreage on Vernal Avenue (now Highland Avenue) for $5,000. Architect Bugbee designed the house as a Stick Italianate. It is completely built of redwood with square window bays, vertical siding, and tall narrow windows. Until 1912, the house faced Vernal Avenue and was surrounded by lawns, flower beds, and fruit trees – peach, apricot, plum, and cherry. The water tower had a windmill that pumped the water 50-feet up to the tank to provide water pressure for the house. There was a stable for horses, a barn for cows, and pens for chickens, turkeys, and pigs. It was essentially a self-sustaining farm, as were all the houses in Piedmont in the 1880s. Craig commuted to his insurance office in San Francisco by horsecar and ferry. He said that on a good day, it took 1½ hours to get to the office. The ferry rides On September 5, 1907, Piedmonters again voted on whether to remain a city or to dis-incorporate and become part of Oakland. This time, as a municipality, the vote to dis-incorporate required a two-thirds vote. Of the 154 voters, 92 voted to dis-incorporate, and 62 voted against. Despite the majority vote, those voting to dis-incorporate failed to carry the required two-thirds majority. Piedmont continued as a municipality. A vote of 102 to dis-incorporate would have carried the measure. Just 10 votes made the difference between Piedmont remaining a city or becoming part of Oakland. In those early years, the new city of Piedmont had many issues to solve. The city needed a City Hall, street maintenance, sewer systems, water service, and police and fire protection. How to fund these services? Prior to incorporating, residents paid just one small tax to the County. Owners of city-sized lots paid the same tax as those who owned large acreage. To fund city services, Craig instituted a tax based on the size of the property. The large landowners were not happy with their increased taxes and complained bitterly to Mayor Craig. The taxes remained, but Craig was not re-elected in 1914. Mayor Craig was also a victim of the increased tax basis. He owned six acres and his house was in the middle of his land. In 1912, he moved his house and sub-divided his land. The house was put on log rollers and slowly moved by horses to the corner of Craig’s property where it is now, at 55 Craig Avenue at the corner of Mountain Avenue. Craig then created Craig Avenue with residential lots on both sides of the street. Who was Hugh Craig? Hugh Craig was born in Sydney, Australia in 1841 to Scottish parents. He grew up in New Zealand before moving to Oakland. In 1874, he began working for the Inez Gilcrest Craig was Hugh Craig’s wife and the mother of their six children. were a great opportunity for businessmen to catch up on the news and to network with one another. Hugh and Inez Craig lived in Piedmont until his death in 1919. She died the following year. Family members continued to live in the Craig house until 1938. articles.text: Piedmont’s 2nd annual Art Walk, scheduled for Sunday, May 2 between 12:00-5:00 p.m. will feature the work of more than 40 local artists. Paintings, ceramics, mixed media, sculpture, photography, quilts, and textile art will be displayed by the artists in front of their homes. Community members are invited to enjoy this outdoor event and fundraiser hosted by Piedmont artists and the Piedmont Arts Fund. The Art Walk is generously supported by The Grubb Company and Muller-Nicholls Builders. The event benefits the arts in the community, and 20 percent of proceeds will be donated to the Piedmont Arts Fund to support art in the schools. Featuring a Who’s Who of Piedmont artists, the popular event brings together live art, artists, and community members while following Alameda County’s COVID-19 guidelines to keep everyone safe. The event is spread out over Piedmont to avoid crowds and ensure social distancing. When the COVID quarantine took effect in last March, the Piedmont Arts Fund (formerly PAINTS and CHIME) had to cancel its spring fundraisers. articles.text: The Piedmont’s boys’ and girls’ tennis teams traveled to Alameda High for the WACC singles and doubles championship on Friday and Saturday, April 16-17. Makenna Thiel, receiving the No. 1 seed and first-round bye, dominated with three victories on her way to the singles title. Seeded No. 2 in doubles, Audrey Edel and Anne Jumper placed 3rd. There was no award ceremony this year due to the COVID pandemic. The boys’ team brought Charlie Lambert, Sajan Srivastava, and Luke Hawkins for singles, while listing doubles teams Akash Kothari with Linus Lee, and Jake Cota and Justin Katter. Thiel, a nationally ranked player, never lost more than one game in any of her three matches. She defeated Bishop O’Dowd’s Marianne Taner 6-0, 6-1 on Friday, shut out Berkeley’s Estelle Handa 6-0, 6-0 in Saturday’s semifinals, and beating Kyra Yee of Alameda 6-0, 6-1 in the finals. “I felt great about all the matches I played in this year. It was really fun just to be able to play,” said Thiel after beating Yee for the third time this year. “The Thiel tradition continues; another league championship, said coach Neil Rothenberg, referring to Makenna’s older sister, Kaelli, who won two consecutive North Coast Section titles while at Piedmont. In doubles, Edel and Jumper, first-time doubles partners, beat Alameda’s Adia Jallali/Angeline Yi 6-4, 6-2 in the second round but lost to O’Dowd’s Ava Daniel/ Alexa Allred in a tense two-set match in the semifinals, 7-5, 7-6 (7-3). But Edel and Jumper found their stroke in the third-round match against Berkeley’s Andrea Morales-Mendoza/Lydia Schrag to win in straight sets, 6-4, 6-1. Jumper provided some strong Anne Jumper (left) and Audrey Edel, shown with coaches Neil Rothenberg (back left), Corey Reich, and Jim Landes, earned third place in doubles at the league championship tournament. No. 3 Charlie Lambert lost in the second round in 3 sets, 2-6, 7-5, 13-11.

Competing in the League championships on Saturday, April 17 at Hayward High, Piedmont’s track & field team was led by Jack Stein, who won the 3200 with a record time of 9:56.10, Jasmine Ghaderi, who placed first in the pole vault with a height of 9 feet, 6 inches, and freshman Jamie Schwarz who placed 2nd in the 800 meters in 2:34.25. It has been a breakout season for Stein, a junior. In addition to winning the 3200, he improved his fastest time by 18 seconds. On Saturday, he also placed 5th in the 1600 in 4:37.7. “That was awesome to achieve. Doing a sub-10 [minute] was one of my goals,” said Stein of his record time in the 3200. “The credit goes to our team,” Stein added. “We have a really strong group of guys who show up to practice every day and push each other in every single run and workout. I think that’s a lot of the reason why the Piedmont boys have found success this year.” Seamus Chamberlain-Carr, also a junior, placed 5th of 35 runner in the 3200 in 10:15, his fastest time by nine seconds. Freshman Christian Taylor finished 9th in 10:28.34, and sophomore Alex Ware was 11th in 10:35.52. In the 1600, Taylor placed 10th in 4:42.6, with teammate Cooper Downing was right behind in 11th place in 4:44.5. Ghaderi won the pole vault at 9-feet, 6-inches, the best of seven vaulters. PHS freshman Spencer Sorensen-Wald placed 2nd in the pole vault at 9-feet, 6-inches, less than an inch below the winner from Berkeley, Alfonso Quilatan. articles.text: It was a classic barnburner between Piedmont and Bishop O’Dowd’s girls’ lacrosse team on Monday, April 19 at the Dragons’ home field, with the Highlanders coming away victorious in a heated one-goal decision, 12-11. It marked the closest time the Dragons came to unseating the Highlanders in Foothill Division rivalry since BOD won the WACC Championship 10-9 on May 5, 2017. “It’s a fun rivalry. We’re coming off of Spring Break and many girls didn’t pick up a stick for over a week. It was really reaching down and being really gutsy,” said Piedmont coach Carlton Chan. Since Chan took over as head coach in 2019, Piedmont has dominated the series of games with their primary rival. Piedmont has a six-game winning streak against the Dragons dating back to the 2017 WACC title game with former coach Emily Hook. “It was [O’Dowd’s] senior night. They had some loud fans here and their boys’ team heckling us from the side. It’s really a mental game against O’Dowd,” added senior captain Sadie Tschider. Monday came down to the very last possession, with BOD looking to score with 16 seconds left. With four seconds on the clock, O’Dowd’s Lily Yu earned a penalty in the 12-meter area. The space allowed Piedmont’s defense of Maya Galbreth, Charlotte Theut, and Tschider to collapse on her, forcing a loose ball in the process. “We had to make some big substitutions. I don’t normally play defense and I had to get in there at Caroline Devine works to reel off a shot against O’Dowd’s physical defense. She scored four goals against the Dragons. Staff Photos Piedmont’s 12-11 win over O’Dowd came down to the last possession. Pictured are Sadie Tschider (24), Maya Galbreth (left) and Charlotte Theut forcing a groundball against the Dragons. the end. We just knew we weren’t going to allow a shot off in those 16 seconds,” explained Tschider. The Highlanders’ defense came through in the clutch. Goalie Lindsay Kottle recorded four critical saves in the second half, including one that led to a quick pass to Tschider at midfield which led to a goal. “That last clear by Lindsay when she nailed Sadie downfield on a 30-yard clear, that burned the clock. That clear gave us a lot of yards,” said Chan of Kottle’s big play. Piedmont opened the game with a 3-0 lead, but trailed by a goal, 6-5, at halftime. The Dragons’ high press was able to force several quick turnovers at midfield to enable their comeback. But the Highlanders answered quickly in the second half, tying the game after one minute with a field-length run by Caroline Devine for one of her four goals. PHS scored the go-ahead goal after forcing a quick turnover, resulting in Katherine Kinne sending a quick pass to Tschider for a 7-6 lead after five minutes. The Highlanders maintained the lead and expanded it to a 12-9 lead on back-to-back goals by Kinne, Devine, Tschider, and another goal by Devine. But O’Dowd stormed back, closing the score to 12-11 before time ran out for them. Final stats: Tschider, Kinne, and Devine finishes with four goals apiece. Kinne and Tschider each had two assists. Elizabeth Ethington also had an assist. Firsthalf GK Sophia Ethington also had six saves to her credit. Rematch with O’Dowd yesterday The Highlanders hosted the Dragons for their series finale on Tuesday, April 20. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (4-4) hosts its season finale tomorrow night, Thursday, April 22 with Newark Memorial at Witter Field at 7:00 p.m. Goalie Lindsay Kottle had four critical saves in the second half. Her pass to Sadie Tschider led to a goal.

articles.text: It’s a big week for Piedmont High sports with two of its most popular teams returning to Binks Rawlings Gym for a basketball season long delayed by the coronavirus epidemic. The boys’ team takes the court as the defending North Coast Section Div. 4 champion, and with sights set strongly on returning to the title game. Their championship last year was the first in school history. The girls’ team returns with talented sophomores Trinity Zamora and Maddie Hill, led by team captain Kai Johnson, a senior. “The energy is off the charts,” exclaimed boys’ coach Ben Spencer. “We went not having basketball from the middle of February and now being able to schedule up to 18 games. We’ve been eager to pick up where we left off. articles.text: The Piedmont Center for the Arts opened its 7th Annual Juried Art show last weekend on April 17. Three winners and three honorable mention works of art have been announced. A total of 35 pieces of art were selected among a record-high 500 submissions. The artwork that appeared in the exhibition, the first public event PCA has held this year, was selected by Piedmont native Rene de Guzman, Senior Curator of Art at Oakland Museum of California, and Danielle Fox, Principal of Slate Gallery in Oakland. Artists came from nine counties in the Bay Area, from Alameda to Santa Clara to Sonoma. Submissions represented an eclectic range, including oil on canvas, pigment prints, and photography. The Juried Art show debuted in November 2013, explained Valerie Corvin, the Juried Art Show curator since its founding. The annual event is made possible through an endowment created by the family of the late John P. Thornborrow. Cash prizes totaling $4,000 are awarded to the top three artists. John Thornborrow was a Bay Area artist who created hundreds of artworks across a variety of mediums. In 2008, his work was selected for the Pro Arts Juried Annual, which was juried by Laura Hoptman, Senior Curator of the New Museum in New York. He continued to produce artwork until his death in 2011. His print, “Fake Flowers,” is on permanent display at the annual show in Piedmont. John Thornborrow Every year, the Juried Art show aims to give emerging artists from the Bay Area an opportunity to gain exposure with top curators and gallerists and the general public,” Corvin said. 2021 Award Winners • First place winner Pep Ventosa was awarded $2,500 for “Watching the Night Sky” • Second place: $1,000 to Tamara Avery for “#114 Justice?” • Third place: See C Oh, $500 for “Tranquility” Honorable Mention Four honorable mentions were also awarded: • Brian Molyneaux’s photograph displayed on metal, “Moon, Neferttiti, Barry” • Nelson Loskamp’s “Cay on the Beach” • Daniel San Souci’s “Flight of the Monarchs.” • Hadi Aghaee’s “Chaos Before The Storm” Honorable mention winners receive ribbons. Corvin said that the selections this year have produced the “best Juried Art Show yet” in the event’s seven-year existence. “The art is a high level, and it feels like you are in a downtown art gallery. It’s very exciting,” added Corvin. The exhibition will be on view at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, at 801 Magnolia Avenue, on Saturdays and Sundays through May 16. Gallery hours are 12:00 to 2:00 p.m. each day. Visitors need to sign up before their visit, and the exhibition will be limited to a maximum of 20 visitors at a time. Visitors will be asked to sanitize hands upon entry, wear face masks, and observe social distancing. To view the exhibit, register at: https://bit.ly/3mwWuwT. FIRST PLACE: Pep Ventosa’s “Watching the Night Sky”

articles.text: Come join your friends at the Piedmont Center as it begins to reopen for public events after a year of closure due to COVID-19. CURRENTLY ON VIEW The 7th Annual Juried Art Show returns to the Center for an exhibition from April 17 through May 16.Gallery hours are 12:00 to 2:00 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays. From a record-high 500 submissions of original art created within the past year, 35 works of art were selected by guest jurors René de Guzman, Senior Curator of Art at Oakland Museum of California, and Danielle Fox, Principal of Slate Gallery in Oakland. Through an endowment by the family of John P. Thornborrow, cash awards of $4,000 will be awarded to the top award winners, with an emphasis on honoring emerging artists in the Bay Area. The following COVID protocols will be in place: All visitors must sign up in advance for their visit. An email-based online system will be established where visitors may sign up for their choice of day. A health screening form will be emailed to visitors with their confirmation, also listing all health requirements. The exhibition will be limited to a maximum of 20 visitors at a time. Staff will be seated at the entrance, maintaining a roster of visitors correlating to time to facilitate any needed contact tracing, performing temperature checks, and collecting health screening forms. Masks and social distancing will be observed while guests visit the exhibition and while waiting to enter. Visitors will be asked to sanitize hands on entry and to circle the exhibition in a one-way direction to prevent clustering. No food or drink will be permitted. To sign up for a time to view the show, visit: https://bit. ly/3mwWuwT. For more information, see the website: piedmontcenterforthearts.org. pages.text: 16 Wednesday, April 21, 2021 Arts & Entertainment Celebrating Spring at the Center For The Arts Come join your friends at the Piedmont Center as it begins to reopen for public events after a year of closure due to COVID-19. CURRENTLY ON VIEW The 7th Annual Juried Art Show returns to the Center for an exhibition from April 17 through May 16.Gallery hours are 12:00 to 2:00 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays. From a record-high 500 submissions of original art created within the past year, 35 works of art were selected by guest jurors René de Guzman, Senior Curator of Art at Oakland Museum of California, and Danielle Fox, Principal of Slate Gallery in Oakland. Through an endowment by the family of John P. Thornborrow, cash awards of $4,000 will be awarded to the top award winners, with an emphasis on honoring emerging artists in the Bay Area. The following COVID protocols will be in place: All visitors must sign up in advance for their visit. An email-based online system will be established where visitors may sign up for their choice of day. A health screening form will be emailed to visitors with their confirmation, also listing all health requirements. The exhibition will be limited to a maximum of 20 visitors at a time. Staff will be seated at the entrance, maintaining a roster of visitors correlating to time to facilitate any needed contact tracing, performing temperature checks, and collecting health screening forms. Masks and social distancing will be observed while guests visit the exhibition and while waiting to enter. Visitors will be asked to sanitize hands on entry and to circle the exhibition in a one-way direction to prevent clustering. No food or drink will be permitted. To sign up for a time to view the show, visit: https://bit. ly/3mwWuwT. For more information, see the website: piedmontcenterforthearts.org. Annual Juried Art Show winners announced By Allyson Aleksey The Piedmont Center for the Arts opened its 7th Annual Juried Art show last weekend on April 17. Three winners and three honorable mention works of art have been announced. A total of 35 pieces of art were selected among a record-high 500 submissions. The artwork that appeared in the exhibition, the first public event PCA has held this year, was selected by Piedmont native Rene de Guzman, Senior Curator of Art at Oakland Museum of California, and Danielle Fox, Principal of Slate Gallery in Oakland. Artists came from nine counties in the Bay Area, from Alameda to Santa Clara to Sonoma. Submissions represented an eclectic range, including oil on canvas, pigment prints, and photography. The Juried Art show debuted in November 2013, explained Valerie Corvin, the Juried Art Show curator since its founding. The annual event is made possible through an endowment created by the family of the late John P. Thornborrow. Cash prizes totaling $4,000 are awarded to the top three artists. John Thornborrow was a Bay Area artist who created hundreds of artworks across a variety of mediums. In 2008, his work was selected for the Pro Arts Juried Annual, which was juried by Laura Hoptman, Senior Curator of the New Museum in New York. He continued to produce artwork until his death in 2011. His print, “Fake Flowers,” is on permanent display at the annual show in Piedmont. John Thornborrow Every year, the Juried Art show aims to give emerging artists from the Bay Area an opportunity to gain exposure with top curators and gallerists and the general public,” Corvin said. 2021 Award Winners • First place winner Pep Ventosa was awarded $2,500 for “Watching the Night Sky” • Second place: $1,000 to Tamara Avery for “#114 Justice?” • Third place: See C Oh, $500 for “Tranquility” Honorable Mention Four honorable mentions were also awarded: • Brian Molyneaux’s photograph displayed on metal, “Moon, Neferttiti, Barry” • Nelson Loskamp’s “Cay on the Beach” • Daniel San Souci’s “Flight of the Monarchs.” • Hadi Aghaee’s “Chaos Before The Storm” Honorable mention winners receive ribbons. Corvin said that the selections this year have produced the “best Juried Art Show yet” in the event’s seven-year existence. “The art is a high level, and it feels like you are in a downtown art gallery. It’s very exciting,” added Corvin. The exhibition will be on view at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, at 801 Magnolia Avenue, on Saturdays and Sundays through May 16. Gallery hours are 12:00 to 2:00 p.m. each day. Visitors need to sign up before their visit, and the exhibition will be limited to a maximum of 20 visitors at a time. Visitors will be asked to sanitize hands upon entry, wear face masks, and observe social distancing. To view the exhibit, register at: https://bit.ly/3mwWuwT. articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Crip Camp: A Disability Revolution, is a film nominated for an Oscar for Best Documentary feature and is co-directed by Nicole Newnham, a nearby Oakland resident. The film opens with a long introduction to a unique summer camp called Jened, located in the Catskills a few hours north of New York City. From the 1950s through the 1970s, Crip Camp was a place for teens with a spectrum of disabilities (from polio to cerebral palsy), its purpose was to create an embracing community in which the campers no longer existed on the fringes of society as an invisible minority, but were welcomed, and viewed as far more than one dimensional individuals. The mantra was that everyone mattered, the intent being to offer the quintessential camp experience of dances, baseball games, flirtations, messy bunks, and accessibility to all. You can almost hear their voices calling out, “Yahoooo!” Using archival footage from Camp Jened, shot in the 70s by the People’s Video Theater, this compelling film reminds us that prior to the late 1970s, Americans with disabilities were excluded from schools, public places that were ill-equipped to receive them, and many were denied jobs for which they were qualified. Crip Camp is actually two narratives: The first focuses on a cohort of disabled teens who, in the early 1970s, came to Jened and formed a summer community, days rife with joy and mutual respect, crafting connections that would endure well beyond camp. For many, the Jened experience was revelatory, life changIn 1971 Camp Jened sparked the disability rights movement in America. Documentary filmmakers Nicole Newnham and Jim LeBrecht. ing, a place where they were seen not as one-dimensional individuals who had to confront the assumptions and prejudices of the greater society, but where their disabilities were treated with a shrug, telling them that their handicaps were challenging but not disqualifying. Camp Crip is an extraordinary look at the power of a life experience that throws into relief the contrasting differences between how life was for the disabled and how it could be. And it is that “could be” which represents a dramatic shift in the point of view of Crip Camp, for the campers and the audience. The second part of the film shows the alumni of Jened taking the essence and spirit of Jened to Berkeley, where they form a radical disability movement, a second community of activists and organizers who insisted that legislators see them – really see them – for the first time. Setting up a base in Berkeley’s Center for Independent Living, they worked to find services, jobs, and housing for the disabled, led by Crip Camp alumna Judy Heumann. They also made the strategic decision in 1977 to occupy for 28 days the federal building that housed the Health, Education and Welfare offices. It was a classic protest, and, to their surprise, the occupiers received the support of churches, unions, and advocacy groups including the Black Panthers, some offering supplies and meals. Soon politicians, local and national, began to listen, and, remarkably, change began to take hold. Life for the disabled was reimagined, and equality demanded. This was in reality a civil rights journey for the Jened revolutionaries. Change comes about slowly, but the final result did arrive two decades later with the Americans With Disabilities Act (1999), which proved to be transformative. A f inal comment: Jim Albrecht, who wrote and directed Crip Camp: A Disability Revolution, along with Nicole Newnham, was born with spina bifida. He attended Camp Jened as a teenager where he found he was treated like an ordinary teen, absent even a hint of reflexive discomfort or condescension. “What we saw at that camp,” he said, “was that our lives could be better. You don’t have anything to strive for, if you don’t know it exists.” The 93rd Academy Awards ceremony will be held on April 25 and will include films released between January 1, 2020 and February 28, 2021. There will be no in-person attendance. Crip Camp: A Disability Revolution (2020). Documentary. Written and directed by Jim LeBrecht, Nicole Newnham. 1 hr., 47 min. Rated R.

articles.text: Alicia Vikander as Ava in Ex Machina. Review by Chris Honoré Be prepared to be captivated (or puzzled or creepily moved) by a stylish film that not only constructs a compelling glimpse into the future but asks some big questions along the way. What does it mean to be fully human? Can edgy, idiosyncratic computer geeks/engineers ever create A.I. machines (call them animatronics) that possess a brain that doesn’t just store information, no matter how sophisticated, but can respond to questions posed with a startling self-awareness? Ex Machina opens with Caleb (Domhall Gleeson), an employee of a Google-like company, flying in a helicopter to the remote, mountainous retreat of the company’s owner, Nathan (Oscar Isaac). He will spend a week involved in what is called a “Turing test.” Upon his arrival – the home is constructed of steel and concrete and glass, beautiful yet stark, built into a mountain – he is briefed by Nathan about his mission. Caleb will be conducting a series of interviews with a robot named Ava (Alicia Vikander). She has a human form, her body transparent, revealing her inner circuitry, and possesses a gorgeous face and a soft, seductive voice. Caleb is tasked with determining whether Ava can cross that boundary that differentiates man from machine. Is she conscious of the difference between Caleb and herself? He sits in a glass walled room, Ava on one side of a window of sorts and Caleb on the other. Nathan is watching and recording the interactions. It is a fascinating series of conversations and it soon becomes clear that Caleb is drawn to Ava. Her humanity, so to speak, attracts him. Her preternatural responses are enigmatic, varied, demonstrating a curiosity about him that he finds appealing and surprising. The above doesn’t begin to describe how strangely creative this film is, how remarkably different. The characters, to include Ava, are remote, bright, inaccessible, yet maddeningly flawed and revealing. Nathan delivers a fraternal, let’s be bros patter with an embedded menace that makes Caleb feel relaxed, at least initially, and then increasingly uneasy as each day passes. The setting is simultaneously austere and yet welcoming, the trees seeming to be part of the house’s modern and sparse interior. There is a sense of bonhomie and beauty layered with a chilling detachment (Ex Machina was filmed in a mountainous region of Norway). There is also a question woven into the narrative: how do we define our own humanity? What makes us unique, as distinguished from other life forms on the planet? We know there are those among us who seem to have flatlined, as if they had been in retreat all of their lives. And yet there are those who, in the alternative, burn with a life force and possess a certain spark. Many glow with a humanity that can astonish when they engage. They possess qualities that can seem indefinable. Whatever it is, we know it when we encounter it. And it is that experience with Ava that gives Caleb pause while he marvels at what Nathan has achieved. Clearly her intelligence exceeds his. And yet, he also feels surrounded by a sense of corruption, that much of what he is told is a distortion and that he is being manipulated. The question is, by whom? Ex Machina. Directed by Alex Garland. Starring Domhall Gleeson, Oscar Isaac and Alicia Vikander. 1 hr., 47 min. Rated R. Domhall Gleeson and Oscar Isaac in a scene from Ex Machina.
articles.title: Ex Machina a riveting story of artificial intelligence

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Frozen II, released in 2019, was the sequel to Disney’s hugely popular Frozen from six years earlier. It was an Oscar-winning animated film featuring not only a compelling story of sister empowerment, but songs that still stand alone. Sequels are often a gamble for any studio and the bar had been set high with the first Frozen. But the sequel proved to be family-friendly, and again sought out and found the target audience (young girls, especially), while incorporating not only strong role model relationships, but a touch of romance, comedy and adventure, all blended with new songs that fit the narrative. The challenge for the creators of Two was to tell a new story that, while relying on the first Frozen, would be fresh and engaging, with elements found in the extraordinary work of Japanese animator Hayao Miyazaki of Studio Ghibli. The story opens in that familiar terrain of the original Frozen. Queen Elsa (Idina Menzei), has regained her magical powers, and now rules over the peaceful kingdom of Arendelle. Her sister, Princess Anna (Kristen Bell), offers advice and encouragement. The two have an unbreakable bond. And there is ice-cutter Kristoff (Jonathan Groffer) who is planning to ask for Anna’s hand in marriage, though he can’t seem to get the proposal right. Meanwhile, Snowman Olaf (Josh Gad), immune to melting, offers continual comic relief. Though Arendelle is tranquil, dark forces are gathering, emanating from an enchanted and mysterious forest. Queen Elsa must penetrate the shroud of misty fog that surrounds the woods, subdue the power therein, and reveal the secret that threatens the kingdom. Frozen II is reliant on superb CGI animation and imagery, with crisp colors that are stunningly realistic, bringing the vistas and the characters into dramatic relief. Musically, the new material mirrors the original, and the songs, which fit nicely into the narrative. Frozen II. Disney Animation. Directed by Chris Buck & Jennifer Lee. With the voices of Kristen Bell, Idina Menzei, Josh Gad and Jonathan Groff. 1 hr., 43 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: Frozen II a lovely sequel to the Oscar Award-winning original

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré If you have some youngsters hanging around the house and you haven’t taken them to see A Wrinkle in Time, pile them in the car and insist they see it on the big screen. It’s a gorgeous film, a solid adventure, and while the kids will easily access their sense of wonder, well, reach for yours as well. As an adult I acknowledge that the most interesting part of the story for me was act one when Meg Murray (Storm Reid) is introduced. She’s a 13-year-old middle schooler who has developed an attitude that gets her either picked on by her school’s Mean Girls or results in a visit to the principle’s office. In truth Meg has been grieving for the last four years due to the baffling disappearance of her beloved father, Dr. Alex Murray (Chris Pine), a physicist. Meg is clearly gifted, though she suffers from a damaged self-image and sense of self-worth. Her mother (Gugu MbathaRaw), also a physicist, is equally devastated by the loss of her husband, and is upset with Meg. It’s only Meg’s brother, Charles Wallace (Deric McCabe), who has made some friends who he is convinced can assist them in finding their father. As it turns out, Calvin, from Storm Reid stars in A Wrinkle in Time. Meg’s school, shows up one day and is around when Charles’ new acquaintances reveal themselves: think of them as the three Missus – Mrs. Which (Oprah Winfrey), Mrs. Whatsit (Reese Witherspoon) and Mrs. Who (Mindy Kaling). They are celestial, ephemeral beings that agree to help Meg and Charles Wallace and Calvin find Dr. Murray. And so off they go, into the farthest parts of the universe. It’s quite a journey and one that first introduces kids to a planet of light. It’s there they confront the IT, which represents the dark side of life – a threatening essence that the three must face alone and likely has Meg’s father. Mrs. Which tells them that IT is spreading through the universe and to be careful. Remember – this is a kids’ movie and therefore has as its premise a complete suspension of disbelief. An example is the word “tessering,” meaning a wrinkle in time and the way that the three Mrs. and Meg, et al. travel across the universe. It proves to be a great trip (and back) filled with lessons for all of them. Kids of all ages will enjoy A Wrinkle in Time, but especially tweens and younger. A Wrinkle in Time. Starring Storm Reid, Chris Pine and Oprah Winfrey. Directed by Ava DuVernay. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated PG. Reese Witherspoon, Oprah Winfrey, and Mindy Kaling as the three Muses in A Wrinkle in Time.
articles.title: A Wrinkle in Time – pure delight for kids & teens

articles.text: University of California Botanical Garden in Berkeley. University of California, Berkeley’s Botanical Garden has an impressive display of Southern African flora and fauna now in bloom. Thousands of vividly colored flowers – in hues of yellow, purple, orange, fuchsia and white – cover the hillsides of the botanical garden. This spring is an excellent time to see the floral display in the designated Southern African area of the gardens. Annuals, succulents, and geophytes, or plants that grow from bulbs, are now blooming in abundance in the botanical garden’s Karoo beds. South African plants include natives of South Africa, Lesotho, Swaziland, Botswana and Namibia. The plants of this region of the African continent are famous for their diversity of fauna, owing to the diverse typography and climate. The blooms have also attracted a variety of pollinators. Garden staff have noted two bird species, Hooded Orioles and Bushtits, have gravitated to the floral beds, and can be seen sipping nectar from their preferred candelabra aloe. Visitors have just two weeks to see these blooms in full force. Many of the featured spring bulbs and annuals bloom mostly in February and May. Advance ticketing is required. Modified hours are observed, although the garden is open daily. Members-only hour is 10 a.m. to 11 a.m., and general admission is available from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Note that there will be path disruptions throughout the garden, as staff manages visitation flow as per Center for Disease Control guidelines. Glasshouses and water fountains are temporarily closed. To obtain tickets, visit: https:// botanicalgarden.berkeley.edu/ covid-reopen.
articles.title: UC Botanical Garden’s Southern African collection now on display

articles.text: The San Jose Museum of Art (SJMA) is open to the public three days a week, Friday through Sunday. Two new exhibitions will be on view: Do Ho Suh’s “Karma” and Pae White’s “Noisy Blushes.” April 22 is the last day to see “Barring Freedom”, an exhibit co-organized by UC Santa Cruz Institute of the Arts and Sciences and the museum. The exhibition confronts the historical and structural racism that is embedded in the United States’ criminal justice and mass incarceration systems. It has been on display since the museum’s reopening last month. White’s “Noisy Blushes” (2020) serves as a meditation on movement and time, light and color; as well as actual material presence and form. The artwork was commissioned by the San Jose Museum of Art and fills the building’s 30-foot-tall atrium to transform the entrance for visitors. Do Ho Suh’s “Karma,” a 23-foot tower of bronze male figures stacked on top of one another perched on top of each other’s shoulders, will be on display through January 30, 2022. The museum has exhibits for youth as well. The Koret Gallery and Art Learning Lab is a dedicated exhibition space inspired San Jose Museum of Art by sensory learning and promotes creative exploration in children aged 12 and younger. The museum’s multi-award-winning STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Art and Math) education program features a diverse selection of artworks from the permanent collection. Through interactive play, young visitors are encouraged to draw their own connections between individual creative exploration using various tools and mediums. “We have been hard at work investing in a better SJMA for a stronger post-pandemic Museum,” said Executive Director Sayre Batton. The museum is restricting large groups and has temporarily cancelled group tours. Individuals, and small cohorts of visitors, are welcome to watch exhibitions and artist highlights made by SJMA docents and educators that are on gallery walls. All volunteers, docents, staff, and visitors must wear a mask or face covering at all times and acknowledge physical distancing guidelines. The museum reopened March 12 on weekends 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., with the first hour dedicated to seniors, SJMA offers free individual admission for youth, college students, and teachers. To obtain tickets, visit https:// sjmusart.org/visit.
articles.title: On view: Do Ho Suh’s “Karma” and Pae White’s “Noisy Blushes”

articles.text: Photo by Cory Weaver Daniela Mack sings the role of Rosina in San Francisco Opera’s production of The Barber of Seville Beginning this Friday, April 23, live, drive-in performances of Rossini’s The Barber of Seveille will be performed at the Marin Center in San Rafael. They will be performed in English with no intermission. Running time is approximately 90 minutes. The performances will feature Lucas Meachem as Figaro, Daniela Mack as Rosina, Alek Shrader as Almaviva and Philip Skinner as Doctor Bartolo, with music performed by the San Francisco Opera Orchestra. Barber of Seville is an opera buffa in two acts, and is widely regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of comedy within music. The play follows the story of a cunning barber who helps a young ward escape from the custody of her guardian, and into the arms of a noble suitor. To purchase tickets, visit: https://sfopera.com/on-stage/ barber/?gclid=Cj0KCQjwl9GCBhDvARIsAFunhsl-mpHzLjDH-jrSuLjWBFKDQfyzvdUGzz8yUltPUWy954eqM1ctonsaAnCZEALw_wcB. In addition to its spring season, San Francisco Opera has announced it will be offering more digital content, including its “Opera is On” archive streaming series. The Opera will launch a series called “In Song” of 10-minute video profiles of six singers well-known to San Francisco audiences. Another series planned, “Atrium Sessions,” will have art songs and arias recorded in performance at the Atrium Theater. A new behind-thescenes podcast will compliment at digital offerings at the San Francisco Opera.
articles.title: SF Opera’s Barber of Seville on-stage, drive-in now through May 15

articles.text: San Francisco’s Cutting Ball Theatre is presenting the film Phantasmagoria in collaboration with Bay Area Theatre Cypher and Mugwumpin. The collaborative film will be premiered on Thursday, April 29, and will be available until May 23. The brand-new, stream-fromhome “theatre oddity” is part Horror fantasia, part psychedelic. True to the avant-garde nature of Cutting Ball Theatre, this production is described as an “other-world rumination on how we return as our world calls us back from isolation.” “Phantasmagoria” combines collaged classic texts by Lewis Carroll, as well as brand-new music by Bay Area Theatre Cypher and non-stop visuals from Mugwumpin, which creates art that aims to ignite radical collaboration. The theatre experiments routinely with theatrical form, beyond naturalism and conventionalism, to “tell relevant stories that embolden and engage audiences.” You can stream “Phantasmagoria” starting April 29 through Vimeo.com, a leading professional video platform. Once you purchase streaming access, you will have seven days to watch. You will need a Vimeo account to stream the production. For more information on how to watch, visit https://cuttingball.com/productions/phantasmagoria.
articles.title: Cutting Ball Theatre presents “Phantasmagoria” April 29 - May 23

articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir will present its annual spring recital on May 8. The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choirs’ youngest choral groups, the Kinder and Training departments, will present their 2021 spring recital on Saturday, May 8. This recital will showcase the departments’ progress in their choral training, and also will feature virtual choir performances from the six ensembles within both departments. The concert will live-stream via YouTube at 4 p.m. The kinder choir consists of students ages five and six. Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir introduces intermediate music skills to students grades one and up in the training department, the second echelon of the three-department program. After graduating from the kinder department, students move on to the training department, where they deepen their understanding of dictation, music theory, and beginning stage presence. They also expand their musical literacy and begin to learn how to sight read. Many other basic skills are solidified here, such as ear training, breath control, and vowel formation. These skills are necessary as young students’ voices begin to mature. The kinder and training departments will join the older performing department on June 5 for the annual “Spring Sing!” Over 200 singers from all ten of the organizations’ departments will present this special choral performance. Both events are free to watch; because of the generosity of patrons, Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir is able to offer its entire 2020-21 “Discovering our Voices” virtual concert season free to the public via YouTube. Donations are gratefully received to help offset production costs. For more information, and to register on Eventbrite for the event, visit https://www.piedmontchoirs. org/event-calendar.
articles.title: All PEBCC vocalists in finale concert on June 5

articles.text: Gold Coast Chamber Players’ season finale, “Dvorak’s America” on Saturday, May 1, will conclude their collection of virtual concerts. “Dvorak’s America” explores the impact that Spirituals and Native American music had on Czech composer Antonin Dvorak during his time in America. The project, three years in the making, highlights the interconnectedness of these cultures. The program will feature the composer’s Sting Quintet, op. 97, and the Lento from his String Quartet op. 96, both of which are nicknamed “the American.” Original music by Mary Youngblood for Native American flute, “Within My Heart” and “Beneath the Raven Moon,” as well as her arrangement of “Amazing Grace”, represent what Dvorak heard during his stay in America. Dvorak proclaimed that African American Spirituals are “the heart of American music,” and the genre serves as perhaps the greatest Western influence on the composer. Spirituals that will be performed in this program include “Swing Low Sweet Chariot,” “By an’ By,” and “My Lord What a Morning.” ConcludAlexander String Quartet: Zakarias Grafilo and Frederick Lifsitz, violins, Sandy Wilson, cello and violist David Samuel, a recent addition. ing the program will be “Goin’ Home,” from the composer’s New World Symphony. Alexander String Quartet will lead the ensemble, marking one of the first performances with their new violist, David Samuel. Violist Pamela Freund-Striplen, founder of Gold Coast Players and a frequent collaborated with the Quartet, will join its members for “Dvorak’s America.” The event will be livestreamed via YouTube at 7 p.m. on Saturday, May 1. For more information and to obtain tickets, visit www.gccpmusic.com, or call (925) 283-3728.
articles.title: Concert will feature Alexander String Quartet

articles.text: The highly-anticipated annual White Elephant Sale, sponsored by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board, will operate this spring as an on-line shop, with sales beginning on May 1. All items for sale will be on a firstcome, first-served basis, and virtual shoppers can expect many unique treasures that can only be found at a sale like this – everything from antique items, vintage furniture, costume jewelry, art, and more. The sale traditionally is held in early March for one weekend and attracts thousands of shoppers from the Bay Area and beyond. Last year, hundreds of thousands of items were up for sale - but this year’s virtual sale will be scaled back. There are still thousands of items for sale at the same discounted prices shoppers have come to expect. All merchandise sold at the White Elephant Sale has been donated and is sold as-is. Through the annual sale, members of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board have raised more than $27 million in 62 years to support the museum’s art acquisitions and education programs, exhibitions, educational programs, capital improvements, and more. Since the Board’s inception Oakland Museum’s first-ever online White Elephant Sale will begin on May 1 and continue through the month. in 1959, it has contributed over $23 million to the Museum. The White Elephant Sale, touted as Northern California’s largest rummage sale, garners a significant amount of funding for the museum. The Sale also boasts many volunteers from Piedmont, a number of whom are members of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. While you can shop from home, no shipping or delivery of items will be available. All items purchased must be picked up curbside at the warehouse located at 333 Lancaster Street in Oakland. articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters is hosting a public discussion with Alameda County District Attorney Nancy O’Malley on May 6 starting at 4 p.m. She will describe the work by her department with abused and homeless women, helping them move beyond trauma into a positive future. O’Malley will address the many challenges COVID-19 has posed. She will explain the ways in which the current lack of civility in politics is impeding the pace and scale of progress for women who suffer from violence. For example, passage of the Violence Against Women Act was held up due to politics, and funding for the Victims Crime Act, which provides resources to states for victims of crime, was also reduced. O’Malley is a nationally recognized expert on issues involving violence against women, violence against persons with disabilities, and interpersonal violence including sexual assault, domestic violence, elder abuse, child abuse, stalking, and human exploitation and trafficking. She serves in the office that dates to a time when Earl Warren was the Alameda County D.A. before becoming United States Supreme Court Chief Justice. O’Malley is the first woman to serve as the County’s District Attorney. The event is free and open to all community members to register for the Zoom event, visit https:// www.lwvpiedmont.org/content. a spx?page_id= 40 02&club_ id=601389&item_id=1256825. It will be recorded and posted on the League of Women Voters of Piedmont website for those who cannot join live.
articles.title: LWV discussion May 6 features County D.A., Nancy O’Malley
