articles.text: • • It’s become a mantra. If you want to have a close relationship with your grandchildren and their parents, just zip your lip and open your wallet. I challenge you to find one book, article, or expert who does not advocate this as a first line approach to becoming a new grandparent. When you think about it, who wouldn’t adore you if you never said a word, just smiled lovingly, and supplied them with unlimited funds? No one! But is this really what constitutes a satisfying grandparent-adult child relationship? Satisfying for whom? When the lip is zipped, not only is all the unsolicited advice and criticism silenced, but so too are the accolades, the support, the encouragement, and the loving praise. New parents are learning their role on the job, and they seek information and reassurance from trusted sources all around them. Websites with information and advice about every developmental stage, countless parent advice blogs, baby tracking apps, sleep training books, and their friends and colleagues with children are all constantly being polled. Reviews of every baby and child product are scoured before a purchase is made. And once polled, decisions about their children are made with confidence. Once these choices and decisions are made, then what? It’s normal to look for affirmation that you’re doing a good job at something that you care about. Perhaps a grandparent unzipping the lip is just what new parents need? Sometimes finding just the right words can be difficult. But with authentic intention, and not mere flattery, specific feedback is almost always welcome. Examples: • When the baby was appearing inconsolable and screaming this morning, I watched you soothe him calmly and confidently. This allowed his big sister to continue playing without interruption or distraction. • You walked in the door yesterday after a rough day of work, and immediately and joyfully engaged with your daughter and began to play with her. She is learning that she is always the most important part of your day. The meals that you plan for your children every day are balanced and healthy. These meals keep the kids really well satisfied and it’s clear that they are not hyped up on sugar or additives. You have a reliable bedtime ritual for the children that is relaxing and predictable for them. I can see that it helps them to prepare for going to bed and I bet it’s why they sleep so well through the night. Do young parents really want silent grandparents? Of course, they don’t. What they want and need is support, reassurance, and positive feedback. They want the freedom to raise their children in the manner that feels right to them. They don’t want to be judged by yesterday’s standards when they live in a world that is almost unrecognizable to the older generation. They need grandparental support, and yes, sometimes the support they need is financial. But more than anything else, they need their parents’ love and acknowledgement that they themselves are doing a great job at being parents. It’s their turn, after all. Piedmont resident Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides, counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Cynthia can be reached at cynthia@ itstheirturn.com.
articles.title: How Grandparents can move beyond “Zip-the-Lip”

articles.text: The other day I saw the U.S. Surgeon General, Vivek H. Murthy interviewed on television. Though he stressed the need to continue following CDC guidelines, he was happy to point out that because of the COVID vaccination successes, “we are seeing the light at the end of the tunnel getting brighter and brighter.” Talk like this gets me excited to think about life getting back to “normal,” though this looks quite different now than it did only a year ago. I know many people are wondering if senior living communities, including assisted living and independent living, are safe to explore again in this “new normal?” Early data appears to show that the highest quality senior living communities adapted quickly and responsibly to COVID-19. They spent the last year implementing prevention measures and determining what healthy socialization looks like for their residents. Some of these plans included new opportunities for indoor exercise and dining, special learning activities, integrating entertainment and providing innovative ways for face-to-face engagement for residents and staff. If you’re not certain that now is the right time to consider a community, ask yourself what has this past year been like for you and those you love? Many older adults have become more isolated because of the necessary precautions that were put in place to prevent the spread of COVID-19. Today, more active older Eleanor, Karma and Gloria enjoy a conversation during a Residents’ Happy Hour at The Lake Merritt Independent Senior Living. adults are making the move to senior living communities as a lifestyle choice. They want to be active in their retirement, relinquish daily tasks and home maintenance, and want to take advantage of the social aspects, custom services, amenities and opportunities created just for them. Researchers have found that older adults who report the highest levels of well-being and happiness are those who socialize, work or volunteer and exercise with others. If you visit an independent living community or an assisted living community, you’ll find residents participating in many different activities, programs and committees. You’ll also find that each community’s culture is shaped by the residents who live there. Diane Broch, the Community Relations Director at The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living community has been getting a lot of calls from people who tell her they have been feeling isolated and are more curious than ever about community living. “We are able to reassure them that our residents interact with each other on a daily basis and are fully vaccinated as are all newcomers to the community,” she explained. “It is a much healthier lifestyle to have a community of fellow residents and staff you can engage with, versus being alone in your home. We follow the CDC guidelines as they are released and really care about each other. Our residents are happy that they can engage with everyone here.” With the light at the end of the tunnel getting brighter, all of us will have an opportunity to reassess our many options for what’s next. As for me, I know I am joined by our residents who are thrilled to be fully vaccinated and who can plan for a more active and involved future. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, at 1800 Madison Street in Oakland. For further information call 510- 903-3600 or visit www.thelakemerritt.com.
articles.title: The light at the end of the tunnel

articles.text: Two extraordinary artists return to Oakland-based arts education company Stagebridge for a session filled with opportunities for elders to take back their stories. With classes starting next week, April 26, Masankho Banda and Sheila Arnold are two incredible instructors sparking creativity in the Performing Arts Institute (PAI) session this Spring “The fact that we have so many returning instructors for Spring 2021 session is a real tribute to our students,” PAI program director Lily Nguyen said. “I’m so happy we can have incredible instructors tapping deeper into everyone’s creativity.” In “Dynamic & Effective Storytelling,” African storyteller Banda teaches an introductory class welcoming everyone interested in turning their memories and experiences into stories for all. The Malawi-born InterPlay Leader tours the world telling stories and teaching the craft of storytelling. He is also a member of the National Association of Black Storytellers (NABS) and the National Storytelling Network (NSN). Concurrently, performer and storytelling instructor Arnold will be teaching “Fairytales, Folklore & Social Justice.” This discussion-based class encourages students to utilize stories to address social issues including poverty, immigration, race reconciliation, PTSD, and more. “…with encouragement and instruction from Sheila Arnold and support of my classmates, I worked at it, saw the light, and wrote my very first fairytale, ‘King LeRoy and Alia,’” student Eleanor Levine said. “I am proud of the way I was able to weave magical twists into my morality tale [about] ending the death penalty.” With this wave of instructors exploring the depths of storytelling, Stagebridge has also offered Storyteller and performer Sheila Arnold leads “Fairytales, Folklore & Social Justice” for Stagebridge’s Spring 2021 Online Performing Arts Institute session. more and more scholarships and one-on-one Zoom coaching for new students, ensuring online classes are accessible to all new students. “Everyone has the ability to be touched by performing arts,” Executive Director Shannon McDonnell said. “And we are always trying to break down all barriers to accessing the magic and joy in our classes.” To register for classes and learn about the full range of activities at Stagebridge, visit www.stagebridge.org. Located at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland (across from Whole Foods), Stagebridge is the nation’s oldest and most renowned theatre company of older adults. For information, call (510) 444-4755.
articles.title: Storytelling masters lead online classes for Oakland elders

Concurrently, performer and storytelling instructor Arnold will be teaching “Fairytales, Folklore & Social Justice.” This discussion-based class encourages students to utilize stories to address social issues including poverty, immigration, race reconciliation, PTSD, and more. “…with encouragement and instruction from Sheila Arnold and support of my classmates, I worked at it, saw the light, and wrote my very first fairytale, ‘King LeRoy and Alia,’” student Eleanor Levine said. “I am proud of the way I was able to weave magical twists into my morality tale [about] ending the death penalty.” With this wave of instructors exploring the depths of storytelling, Stagebridge has also offered Storyteller and performer Sheila Arnold leads “Fairytales, Folklore & Social Justice” for Stagebridge’s Spring 2021 Online Performing Arts Institute session. more and more scholarships and one-on-one Zoom coaching for new students, ensuring online classes are accessible to all new students. “Everyone has the ability to be touched by performing arts,” Executive Director Shannon McDonnell said. “And we are always trying to break down all barriers to accessing the magic and joy in our classes.” To register for classes and learn about the full range of activities at Stagebridge, visit www.stagebridge.org. articles.text: Well-meaning family members and friends often give an enthusiastic “Yes!” when someone asks for a little help at home due to age, illness, or other life change that leaves them in need of support. It feels good to help someone and make them happier, after all. However, this temporary commitment can soon expand into something that requires more than they can handle in terms of time, physical strength, or emotional stamina. Injured on the “Job” A family member may offer to help someone simply to step safely out of the tub, and then find themselves with a back injury. There are proper techniques for lifting someone from a chair or bed, or assisting them in the bathroom, which professional caregivers receive training for. A possible solution is to determine which aspects of care seem the riskiest for the person who is helping out, then hire a caregiver to step in for those specific tasks instead. This might mean just an hour or two per day, giving the family member a little break and keeping them safe as well. What’s Burnout? The definition of burnout is “fatigue, frustration, or apathy resulting from prolonged stress, overwork, or intense activity.” When an untrained family member or friend attempts to be a caregiver, while possibly balancing work or family responsibilities, they can burn out. It’s impossible to keep adding more and more to your plate, especially when you don’t really know what to do, or what’s coming next… Eventually the plate comes crashing down. Establishing boundaries is important for family caregivers so that they don’t experience burnout. If they’re not careful other issues can develop while caring for an elder loved one, such as stress at work or with children in the home. Consider asking other friends or family to share the responsibilities of caregiving or hire someone to be part of your care team. Feelings do matter Caregivers can feel resentful, and it’s perfectly natural, especially if they give too much of themselves without much in return. Ideally, a care relationship can involve both give and take so that resentment doesn’t develop. Finding others who are having similar experiences can be helpful for negative feelings affecting a caregiver. There are all kinds of support groups, both online and in person, in which family caregivers can vent, learn, and share. Support groups might be for caregiving in general or for a specific type of caregiving such as for someone who is living with dementia or Parkinson’s disease. These groups may be an offshoot of an organization such as the Alzheimer’s Association or a local church. When a family member or friend begins to experience some of the possible challenges of caregiving, a professional caregiver can step in to ease the burden. articles.text: Recently the staff at Stagebridge was alerted to a new scam targeting senior and their bank information. Some have reported receiving phone calls from scammers posing as bank officials to obtain account information. Remember to always ensure the identity of individuals looking for this information. Release banking and financial and other personal details only to known individuals. Here are some tips to protect yourself: • Attempt to recognize scam attempts and end all communication with the perpetrator. • Search online for the contact information (name, email, phone number, addresses) and the proposed offer. Other people have likely posted information online about individuals and businesses trying to run scams. • Resist the pressure to act quickly. Scammers create a sense of urgency to produce fear and lure victims into immediate action. Call the police immediately if you feel there is a danger to yourself or a loved one. • Be cautious of unsolicited phone calls, mailings, and door-todoor services offers. • Make sure all computer anti-virus and security software and malware protections are up to date. Use reputable anti-virus software and firewalls.

The first part recorded the video you were viewing (you’ve got exceptional taste ha-ha) and the next part recorded your webcam (Yep t’s you doing nasty things!) What should you do? Well, I believe $4900 is a fair price for our little secret! Don’t waste your time or mine replying to this email, this is not a negotiation. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: On the beautiful spring afternoon of Sunday, April 18, a quickly organized but lovely gathering formed to grieve, recall, and honor Susan Dutcher of Piedmont. The memorial gathering on her front lawn was put together by her many local friends and adoring neighbors. Also in attendance were Susan’s only two West Coast relatives who came from Reno. The attendance of about 30 included people of all ages. The crowd was addressed casually, informally, and from the heart by about 15 speakers. Everyone wore a mask, even though Piedmonters have the highest vaccination rate in the state. It was heartwarming to hear reminiscences and anecdotes and thereby learn more about Susan and her varied life over about 76 years. Her closest neighbors talked about the many, many nice things she did for them, unasked, appearing like a genie when suitcases, packages, or groceries needed to be carried. Although it was wryly observed that Susan didn’t much waste time cleaning her own house, she would materialize when she could help others. She was also known among neighbors for using her own traffic cones or her battered old truck to save parking spots right in front of neighbors’ houses when they were returning from a trip. When boulevard median strips around town became either overgrown or barren, Susan would appear fearlessly near traffic to garden and plant. She baby-sat local kids for parents who were called away, tutored some kids and read to others, and filled in at games when another playmate was needed to even up teams. She taught math in East Palo Alto for many years as a career. She sponsored her best learners in their continuing education, like personal scholarships. She took it upon herself to provide extra tutoring for those students who needed it. “Quirky” but beloved were adjectives used frequently at the memorial gathering. It was overwhelming to see how strongly she was appreciated by all her neighbors and friends. She knew all the neighbors and their kids, and kept an eye out for them as a block guardian. She knew which college every kid on the block had gone off to and greeted them to inquire about their studies and their college life when they came back home for holidays. Every holiday she received invitations to family meals and celebrations, like everyone’s favorite aunt. Her cause of death is currently unknown. A neighbor reported that she looked peaceful and pain-free when found inside her home. Several Piedmonters wish to honor her by contributing to the several charities she did volunteer work for. She generously helped: Mexican & Guatemalan poor village communities; her school in East Palo Alto; and locally, Bambino, a thrift shop in Oakland run by a nonprofit charity for children., for whom she took care of all the books donated and sold. Susan walked every day to Mulberry’s Market, Piedmont’s only grocery store and central gathering point, for coffee and to chat with others. It was revealed that every Christmas, Susan gave every Mulberry’s employee a $50 bill and sometimes a $100 bill. The owners of Mulberry’s Market are going to put up a plaque honoring Susan’s friendship. Among the 15 speakers at the memorial gathering were about five women who had been friends with Susan since kindergarten, including Piedmont historian Gail Lombardi. A message sent from out of state by old friend Pam Arlett Garzini was read by Nancy DeRoche. Dave DeRoche explained that everyone should realize that Susan Dutcher was one of the world’s top two dozen or so experts on the Maya people, their art, civilization, architecture, written language, and ruins. This ancient culture was one of the world’s greatest and biggest, circa AD 300–900, with a calendar, a writing system, irrigation, and pyramids. Susan explored a large number of Maya ruins in Mexico’s and Guatemala’s steamy jungles, apparently never slowed by the heat and humidity. Susan was an extremely dedicated assistant to, and researcher with, the legendary Mayanist author, photographer, scholar, philanthropist and foundation director Merle Greene Robertson. Susan travelled with Merle on more than 20 trips to Mexico and Guatemala. Greene, said, “My mom was a wonderful person and scholar, but she was so passionate about Mayan research and so energetic (even well into her 80s and 90s) that she could be demanding to work with and hard to travel with. Susan Dutcher got along better with my mother than anyone else on earth. I think this was because of three reasons: they tolerated each other’s quirkiness 100%; they had a mutual admiration society; and Susan would talk to my mother all day long and my mother was deaf as a post.” The Mexican government awarded Merle Greene a Gold Eagle award as a great citizen who did so much for Mexico. It was the equivalent of an honorary Nobel Prize and citizenship. For decades, Merle was considered one of the top ten persons leading Mayan research, conservation, and knowledge. Always alongside was Susan Dutcher as Merle’s volunteer helper, administrative assistant, expedition-planner, conference and lecture-planner, and supportive friend. confirmed that Piedmont currently does not have staff that can coordinate arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue. Andersen added that the building, with no kitchen, is not capable of serving hot food, that parking is a challenge in the vicinity, and that the building has immediate next-door neighbors unlike the Veterans Hall and Community Hall. “It’s not apples-to-apples with our other rental spaces. There are significant limitations on use,” she said. City staff will now be tasked with bringing a further-amended Memorandum of Understanding (MOU), or lease agreement, in the near future. At City Attorney Michelle Kenyon’s suggestion, staff will explore new alternatives for 801 Magnolia Avenue. Some questions for staff now will be: who will delegate programming in the building? What Piedmont groups will be given precedence over others – and what will the “litmus test” for precedence be? Will the cost of rental space be affordable for all Bay Area residents, or will rental fees be dependent on Piedmont city residency status, as they are now? And, what does the loss of the Piedmont Center for the Arts mean to non-residents? The city is earnest in its mission to open its borders to the greater Bay Area, a Bay Area that has long seen Piedmont as being “exclusive.” What message will it send if the city becomes the “gatekeeper” of a venue that has drawn, for nearly a decade, crowds from throughout the greater Bay Area to one, small building, in the name of artistic expression?
articles.title: Mayanist scholar, generous researcher of Pre-Columbian art and culture

articles.text: Three Yulan Magnolia trees will be planted on Arbor Day in memory of Ralston Louie. The City of Piedmont’s annual Arbor Day celebration will take place on Friday, April 30, and will be virtual. It will include youth-focused activities, a video that highlights selections of Heritage Trees, and the traditional tree-planting. This year, for the first time, celebrations will include a sidewalk chalk-drawing contest for Piedmont’s younger residents. Children will be encouraged to select their favorite street tree or park tree next to a sidewalk, write the name of the tree in chalk, and then decorate the sidewalk with chalk art to celebrate the tree. Parents can take a photo of the artwork and submit it to Parks Projects Manager Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmint.ca.gov. Prizes will be awarded for the most creative tree art. A 30-minute video is being created with footage of each designated Heritage Tree in Piedmont, including the most recent winners. Heritage Trees will be introduced by the person or the family that nominated them. Zack Parisa will be featured in the video as Arbor Day speaker. Parisa, a Piedmont resident, is the co-founder and CEO of SilviaTerra. SilviaTerra uses Natural Capital Exchange (NCAPX) to provide a marketplace for forest carbon payments. Recently, SilviaTerra collaborated with Microsoft to create “Basemap,” the first high-resolution forest inventory of the United States. The video will be shown live via KCOM on April 30 and will be available to view on the city’s website after then. This year’s traditional Arbor Day tree planting will be the planting of three Yulan Magnolia trees in honor of Ralston Louie, the son of Park Commissioner Robin Wu.
articles.title: Piedmont Arbor Day virtual celebration on April 30

articles.text: Bill Hosler has served as Chair of the city’s Budget and Financial Planning Committee since its inception in 2011. His recent departure from the committee (terming out) marked more than 20 years of unparalleled civic volunteer work with Piedmont. Among Hosler’s long list of achievements, perhaps the most important was the formation of the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee, but his involvement in advising city councils on budget-related issues began as far back as 2003, then as a member of the Municipal Tax Review Committee. That committee, which met only every four years, provided the city with a diverse range of financial recommendations, including controlling pension costs and re-investing in the city’s facilities. –Former Piedmont Mayor Bob McBain In 2011, after serving eight years on that committee, Hosler recommended that the city council form a separate advisory and planning committee. Led by Mayor John Chiang, the committee was formed by the city council. articles.text: The City of Piedmont has announced the selection of David Brannigan as Piedmont’s new Fire Chief yesterday, April 13. Brannigan was chosen unanimously by the City Council in a pool of more than 30 candidates. His formal appointment is expected to take place at the city council meeting on April 19. The selection follows a rigorous recruitment process and interviews of highly qualified finalists, according to City Clerk John Tulloch. Finalists were interviewed by a panel of staff and residents, and then separately by City Administrator Sara Lillevand. Two finalists were then interviewed by City Council members. articles.text: The Piedmont City Council will review and consider an application on behalf of Gulf South Towers (GST) to construct a 95-foot-tall telecommunications tower in the city’s Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue. The review will take place on April 19, following Planning Commission approval on March 8. The tower would improve wireless cell phone coverage in Moraga Canyon and its surrounding neighborhoods. GST has applied to use a portion of the city’s Corporation Yard, where a 30-foot wireless pole already exists. The existing installation is not capable of accommodating new technology equipment, such as 5G, and it is not capable of providing service for multiple carriers. Currently, the tower is servicing T-Mobile. City Planner Kevin Jackson noted that city staff had recognized the current facility’s lease had expired and that it was underserving the area. “We looked for a provider who might build a tower that would co-locate with other carriers, because that’s something that the [city code] requires,” he said. “Co-locating with other carriers will also eliminate the number of cell towers needed in the city,” he added. During its March 8 Planning Commission meeting, residents of Moraga Canyon and its surrounding neighborhoods questioned whether the tower would have impacts on property value, and views. Piedmont Center for the Arts Also on the April 19 City Council agenda is the second reading of a proposed extension of the city’s current 10-year lease with the non-profit Piedmont Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue. Council approved terms of the lease extension at a first reading on November 16. Since that time, city staff has recommended some major changes, including rent payment, reducing the time of occupancy by the Center, an early termination clause, and prior written consent for non-arts related rentals.
articles.title: 2nd reading of proposed lease extension of PCA

GST has applied to use a portion of the city’s Corporation Yard, where a 30-foot wireless pole already exists. The existing installation is not capable of accommodating new technology equipment, such as 5G, and it is not capable of providing service for multiple carriers. Currently, the tower is servicing T-Mobile. City Planner Kevin Jackson noted that city staff had recognized the current facility’s lease had expired and that it was underserving the area. “We looked for a provider who might build a tower that would co-locate with other carriers, because that’s something that the [city code] requires,” he said. “Co-locating with other carriers will also eliminate the number of cell towers needed in the city,” he added. During its March 8 Planning Commission meeting, residents of Moraga Canyon and its surrounding neighborhoods questioned whether the tower would have impacts on property value, and views. Piedmont Center for the Arts Also on the April 19 City Council agenda is the second reading of a proposed extension of the city’s current 10-year lease with the non-profit Piedmont Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue. Council approved terms of the lease extension at a first reading on November 16. Since that time, city staff has recommended some major changes, including rent payment, reducing the time of occupancy by the Center, an early termination clause, and prior written consent for non-arts related rentals.

articles.text: Something in our nature inspires humans to collect religious trinkets—talismans and relics that remind us of life’s transcendent mysteries, or icons through which we glimpse the divine. I’ve got dozens of such pious knickknacks – everything from a small collection of large Bibles to a cross necklace – but I suspect the most important of my faith-based souvenirs is a plastic dashboard Jesus figurine that sits up on the back of my stove beside an empty bottle of Calvin beer from Geneva, my daughter’s Albert Einstein action figure and a miniature Moses, which bends like Gumby. My dashboard Jesus is like just about any other dashboard Jesus: the Son of Man sits on a spring with a goofy molded smile and his hands lifted up as if to invoke some kind of blessing. This is Jesus Junk writ large. I should be quick to point out that the importance of my dashboard Jesus lies not in its sentimental value or in its intrinsic worth. They hardly broke the mold when they made this version of the Jeez; one just like mine can be had for less than $10 on eBay. I won’t shed any tears if the little guy catches fire while I’m flambéing mushroom sauce, but I will replace my dashboard Jesus should any ill befall him, because he represents an important spiritual truth: those of us who take our religion seriously should never lose the ability to laugh at our piety. This is not to say that we should mock God or ridicule what is sacred; rather, it is ourselves and our zealous posturing that needs an occasional palliative guffaw. When people lose a sense of humor, they are inspired by faith to engage in all sorts of heinous tomfoolery. I think of Christians who oppose marriage equality on the faulty assumption that one person’s beliefs can dictate another person’s love life; or I think of people killing one another in the name of God in places like Gaza, Syria, Myanmar, and heaven-knows-where else. articles.text: Alameda County opened COVID-19 vaccination appointments to all adult residents age 16 and older on Monday, April 12. Vaccines manufactured by Moderna are approved for people ages 18 and older. Pfizer vaccines are currently approved for teenagers as young as 16. Alameda County has a form to receive notifications about available appointments at covid-19. acgov.org/vaccines Californians are also encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, employer or the county to receive a vaccination appointment. The state asks residents to utilize the digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn. ca.gov to determine their vaccine eligibility and schedule appointments. The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) said that appointments are prioritized for people who are most at risk for COVID-19 exposure or severe symptoms. “Vaccine distribution is being prioritized for persons who are most at risk for hospitalization or death due to COVID-19, as well as persons who are at high risk for occupational exposure,” ACPHD said on its website. “We expect to have more vaccine supply in the coming months. Eligibility criteria will continue to be updated based on capacity and vaccine availability.” People who work in Alameda County in certain sectors, like janitorial, food service, transportation and education, are also eligible for appointments. The county opened appointments to all adults a few days earlier than the state’s mandate to expand eligibility to everyone aged 16 on April 15. The county expanded eligibility to everyone aged 50 and older on April 1. Before that, vaccination was open to senior citizens, people with underlying health conditions and workers in certain industries that increase their exposure risk to COVID-19. Vaccines from Moderna and Pfizer require two doses injected several weeks apart. The Johnson & Johnson vaccine, a viral vector-type vaccine, requires only one dose, but the county stated yesterday, April 13, that it is pausing distribution of the Johnson & Johnson vaccine, following new federal recommendations. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said yesterday that “out of an abundance of caution” it recommended that health agencies suspend administering the Johnson & Johnson vaccine due to concerns about rare blood clots. To date, 6.8 million doses of Johnson & Johnson vaccine have been administered in the United States. Six cases of the rare blood clot reaction have been recorded nationwide, and one death has been reported. The six cases of blood clots all occurred in women between the ages of 18 and 48. Symptoms occurred 6 to 13 days after vaccination. Even though the blood clots appear to be exceedingly rare, people who have received the Johnson & Johnson vaccine are encouraged to monitor themselves for symptoms, like severe headache, abdominal pain, leg pain or shortness of breath within three weeks after vaccination. Anyone experiencing these symptoms should contact their health care provider immediately. Alameda County said it will cancel all existing Johnson & Johnson vaccine appointments or reschedule them for other vaccine options based on supply. “Per state and federal recommendations, Alameda County will suspend administration of the Johnson & Johnson vaccine until state and federal authorities determine it is safe to begin administering the vaccine again,” said Neetu Balram, the spokesperson for the Alameda County Public Health Department, in a statement. 4200 Piedmont residents vaccinated Over half of Piedmont’s adult population, roughly 4,200 people, have been fully vaccinated as of Monday, April 12, according to ACPHD data. The health department reports that 6,410 Piedmonters have received at least one dose, which amounts to 77 percent of the City. Piedmont is the most vaccinated municipality in the county by a large margin, but other cities are catching up. Alameda County has administered over 1 million doses of vaccine since December, and 33 percent of the county’s population is now fully vaccinated. In Oakland, almost 52 percent of the population has received at least one dose and 33 percent of Oaklanders are fully vaccinated. Even as all adult residents become eligible for vaccination, the state expects it will take several months for everyone who wants a vaccine to get one. This week, the county announced that the mass vaccination site at the Oakland Coliseum will remain open. Up to 6,000 vaccine doses are expected to be administered every day at the site. Half of the doses will be supplied by the state and the other half will be provided by Alameda and Contra Costa counties. The “megasite” also sends out mobile vaccine clinics. Overall, the county is hoping to vaccinate at least 70 to 80 percent of the population. The state has administered almost 23 million vaccine doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. The state is vaccinating an average of over 366,000 people per day, an increase compared to last week.

articles.text: Puppet shows are returning to Oakland’s Fairyland starting today, Wednesday, April 14. It’s another step forward in the County’s loosening of restrictions of entertainment events. Since 1956, Fairyland’s famed puppet shows have captivated audiences of all ages. Storybook Puppet Theater is considered the oldest continuously operating puppet theater in the United States. Every show that takes place is a completely original production, and all scripts, costumes, music and sets are designed by the park’s puppeteers. Luman Coad, Frank and Dorothy Hayward, Tony Urbano, and Mike and Frances Oznowicz, all wellknown in the world of puppeteering, have contributed to the stage’s legacy. The current theater director, Randal Metz, has an impressive career of his own. Mentored by the legendary puppeteer Lewis Mahlman, Fairyland’s first puppeteer, Metz was honored by the city of Oakland in 2016 for nearly 50 years of artistic work at Fairyland. pages.text: 4 Wednesday, April 14, 2021 Local Items Once Upon a Time at Fairyland Puppet Shows are back today at Fairyland By Allyson Aleksey Puppet shows are returning to Oakland’s Fairyland starting today, Wednesday, April 14. It’s another step forward in the County’s loosening of restrictions of entertainment events. Since 1956, Fairyland’s famed puppet shows have captivated audiences of all ages. Storybook Puppet Theater is considered the oldest continuously operating puppet theater in the United States. Every show that takes place is a completely original production, and all scripts, costumes, music and sets are designed by the park’s puppeteers. Luman Coad, Frank and Dorothy Hayward, Tony Urbano, and Mike and Frances Oznowicz, all wellknown in the world of puppeteering, have contributed to the stage’s legacy. The current theater director, Randal Metz, has an impressive career of his own. Mentored by the legendary puppeteer Lewis Mahlman, Fairyland’s first puppeteer, Metz was honored by the city of Oakland in 2016 for nearly 50 years of artistic work at Fairyland. Two shows will be performed on April 14, “The Three Dinosaurs Gruff,” a hand puppet show, and “Fantasy on Strings,” a marionette show. Each performance will be shown twice per morning and twice in the afternoon on two different stages. Morning sessions take place at 10 a.m. and 11:15 a.m., and afternoon sessions are at 2 p.m. and 3:15 p.m. Puppet shows are included in the cost of admission to the park. “The Three Dinosaurs Gruff” is based on the well-known Grimms Brothers tale of “The Three Billy Goats Gruff,” but this adaption tells the story of three dinosaurs - a Stegosaurus, a Triceratops, and a Ceratosaurus, who love to cross a tree bridge to eat greens and play in the sun. Three-foot tall, articulated marionettes present puppetry in one of its most exciting forms. The cabaret puppet shows allow audiences to see the puppeteer dance and perform with the marionette in front of a curtained stage. Children will meet a disco-dancing duck, a tap-dancing skeleton, and other fantastical characters. Make sure to pack a blanket and sunscreen, as seating for the shows is on Fairyland’s grassy lawn. articles.text: The Oakland Center of the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, directed by Piedmont resident, Dr. Steve Sidney, currently has job postings for a 35-year follow-up exam of study participants who were first examined in 1985-1986. The CARDIA study, funded by the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute, is a longitudinal study of black and white men and women who were 18-30 years old at the beginning of the study and who have been followed for the development of heart disease risk factors and disease. More than 900 published scientific articles have resulted from the CARDIA study thus far. This will be the 10th examination for study participants who were initially recruited from four centers around the country, including Kaiser Permanente (KP) Health Plan members from the Berkeley-Oakland area. The examination will be conducted by the KP Northern California Division of Research at its research clinic located in the Mosswood Building, 3505 Broadway in Oakland. Positions are available for scheduling examinations, conducting exam interviews and study procedures, data management, and managing the mailing of equipment and supplies for aspects of the study conducted at the homes of participants. These positions will start in May or June of this year and end during the summer of 2022. Training will be provided. If you would like more information, please contact Dr. Sidney at steve.sidney@kp.org. articles.text: Piedmont students in grades 6-12 will receive additional time in classrooms starting April 27. All students in Piedmont and Millennium High and Piedmont Middle School will be on the same schedule (see chart). They will have 8 hours and 45 minutes per week of classroom time. After continuing pressure from parents insisting on more classroom time, the school board unanimously confirmed at a special board meeting on April 7 that Piedmont’s teachers’ union voted to approve a revised Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) adopting the expanded classroom hours. “My overwhelming feeling is relief for our secondary students,” said School Board President Cory Smegal. Piedmont Middle School students previously attended school for 2.5 hours of class per week (two periods). The increase to eight hours and forty-five minutes is still only a fraction of a normal 28-30 hour school week. The middle school will institute a “Step-In Week” schedule starting the week of April 20, in which 6th graders will attend three class periods of 1 hour, 15 minutes each, while 7th and 8th graders will attend four class periods in the week. The new schedule effectively doubles the time of instruction for high school students. Prior to the agreement, 9th graders and 10th graders were on campus one week for 8.5 hours, and 11th and 12th graders went to school on alternating weeks. Under the new schedule, cohorts will not be combined and class rosters will not change. Teachers will be responsible for processing students’ daily health screener information. This task was previously delegated to other school staff seated in front of schools prior to class. The change was made in order to get the increased number of students The new “checkerboard schedule” will be the same for all students at Piedmont and Millennium High, and the middle school. on-campus every day to their classes in a timely manner. In exchange, full-time teachers not on leave will receive a one-time $1,000 stipend. Smegal explained the financials. “On March 5, the Governor signed AB 86 COVID-19 Relief Package that includes an in-person instruction grant for schools that reopen. Piedmont qualifies for $715,145 under this grant. A portion of this grant will be used for the stipend.” “There are 205 APT members as of April 8, but they are not all full-time and a few are on leave, so the final number will be between $188,000 and $205,000,” she explained. School board meetings have been unusually long for the last 13 months, often lasting for up to five hours. They also have nearly doubled in frequency. Parent comments at meetings have consistently sent a message to open schools, increase class time, and guarantee full-time in-person class in the fall. Alissa Welch, the parent of two children, said, “It is immensely gratifying and exciting to see the middle school schedule that was developed last summer by the task force finally come to fruition.” “This expansion represents the hard work and coming-together of everyone in the community in the best interests of our secondary students. I’ve always loved this schedule for its daily touchpoints,” she added. Welch was a member of the reopening task force comprising over 100 students, parents, teachers, and administrators. To view the full text of the new agreement between teachers and PUSD, go to https://agendaonline. net/public/Meeting/Attachments/ DisplayAttachment.aspx?AttachmentID=1290213&IsArchive=0.

articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is sponsoring its second annual essay contest, open to all Piedmont high school juniors and seniors. The essay should answer the question, “Given the fragility of democracy as evidenced by the insurrection of January 6, 2021, how can your generation work to ensure that democracy in the United States is strengthened for future generations?” Contest entrants may, but are not required to, rely on outside sources that are properly cited within the text and in a bibliography. A specific format for citations or bibliography is not required, but there must be enough information to allow the judges to easily verify your sources. Citations do not count toward your total number of words. Remember that this essay is not solely a research paper and should draw on the writer’s personal experiences and insights. Essays will be judged on originality, clarity of expression, vocabulary and style, proper grammar, punctuation and spelling. Students are encouraged to have a teacher, parent or mentor review the essay prior to submission keeping in mind that all work must be the student’s own. The essay must be 250 to 500 words, excluding citations. At the top of the essay include the following information: the title, your first and last name, city of residence (must be Piedmont), name of your school, and your current grade. Essays must be typed and double-spaced and submitted in a .pdf format. All entries are to be submitted to lwvpiedmont@gmail.com. The deadline is this Saturday, April 17. Winners will be announced on May 1.
articles.title: Deadline to enter League of Women Voters contest is April 17

articles.text: Faith Zirkelbach-Ngai, a 2020 Piedmont High graduate, was named to the University of California, Davis College of Engineering Dean’s List for the Fall 2020 quarter. To earn Dean’s List recognition, students must have achieved a GPA equal to or higher than the minimum GPA attained by the upper 16 percent of students registered in the same class level and college during that quarter. UC Davis is ranked as the fifth-best public university in the United States, per the Wall Street Journal’s 2021 Higher Education Rankings. Nine subject areas at UC Davis have captured top 50 international rankings, including Biological Science and Economics. Recently, UC Davis’ “Healthy Davis Together” initiative won national acclaim as an innovative city­ -campus partnership serving the public good. Under that initiative, the campus expanded its own COVID-19 program to the entire city of Davis. The school provided free rapid testing, contact tracing, isolation housing and masks to Davis residents, and successfully slowed the spread of COVID-19 in the town by identifying and containing infection before it could spread.
articles.title: COLLEGE NEWS Faith Zirkelbach-Ngai named to UC Davis Dean’s List

articles.text: Alameda County teachers have been eligible for COVID-19 vaccines since February 8, when Phase 1B prioritized persons in the education field. But since vaccination history is confidential, the number of Piedmont teachers who have chosen to be vaccinated is not publicly available. California employers have the ability to require employees to get vaccinated, however they run the risk of violating the Americans with Disability Act when asking questions about medical history. In the March 24 School Board Meeting Superintendent Booker said he did not want to risk issuing even an informal survey on vaccination status to teachers. Approximately 4,200 Piedmont adults were fully vaccinated as of April 12, representing more than half of the adult population. Alameda County’s Public Health Department reports that 6,410 Piedmonters have received at least one dose, or 77% of residents, the highest in the county. Piedmont teachers are not required to be vaccinated and no clauses in the school reopening agreements stipulated that teachers would return to classes only after being vaccinated. The district applied to the county to obtain vaccination supplies and offer injections to teachers via school nurses but were not granted any. With no district-wide vaccination plan, teachers independently networked with each other to find vaccination sites and make appointments. “When appointments were first available, people got on it quickly. School nurses and Superintendent Booker were sending out emails with lots of updates,” said PHS science teacher John Savage. “We know that many teachers were offered codes for vaccinations and anecdotal reports among the community suggest that many people were vaccinated at the Oakland Coliseum and received whatever vaccine was being offered at the time,” said Piedmont school nurse Amy Goldfarb. “Much like people in the community are sharing leads, sharing strategies, and actually doing the ‘refresh, refresh, refresh’ legwork, teachers supported each other too,” said PHS science teacher Auban Willats. Piedmont parents have frequently called into the school board meetings trying to find out how many teachers have been vaccinated. Some parents feel that knowing the data is crucial to public health for not only the safety of teachers and students, but also for their family members at home.
articles.title: PUSD teachers and their vaccinations

articles.text: “He is not talking because his brother speaks for him.” “She is not talking because her sister interprets for her.” These are common comments I hear when parents are calling about their second- or third-born child, as parents wonder if this will result in the younger sibling’s language being slower to develop. Is this really a phenomenon with families who have talkative older siblings? Is there a difference in the language development of later born children? If the later born child seems language delayed, will she “grow out of it”? Parents often report that their first-born children knew and understood more words than their later born children and hypothesize that later born children do not get the same amount of attention or one-to-one interaction with a parent as the eldest child does, causing the younger sibling to speak later. The impact of birth order on language development has been studied. The research shows that while some differences emerge between first and later born children’s language development, later born children are not delayed in their language development and first-borns do not have better language skills than their siblings. Some interesting differences that emerge in the research show patterns regarding sibling language development, suggesting Siblings share more with each other than love. that perhaps the differences parents see in the early language development of their first vs second born children may be influenced by the different language environments that each child is exposed to by virtue of who is in the family and the kind of interactions they have. For example, first born children tend to reach the 50-word milestone earlier than later born children (although the later born children catch up by the 100-word milestone and there are no lasting differences in vocabulary). Perhaps this is due to the first-born’s language learning environment in which parent child interactions are often centered around direct vocabulary expansion? While first-born children show strengths in vocabulary and grammar, later-born children show strengths in conversational skills. Second-born children also show particularly advanced use of pronouns such as my, mine, you and yours. Perhaps this is
articles.title: Am I my brother’s keeper?

articles.text: due to the second- or third-born’s environment in which language is often centered around overheard conversations, communication between siblings, and interactions such as sharing? Neither of these environments are detrimental to language development and there are no lasting developmental differences between first and later born siblings. In fact, studies show older siblings can have a positive impact on the development of their younger siblings’ language development. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. pages.text: Wednesday, April 14, 2021 7 Thinking Outside The Classroom Am I my brother’s keeper? E v e n t C a l e n d a r By Katie Pengilly “He is not talking because his brother speaks for him.” “She is not talking because her sister interprets for her.” These are common comments I hear when parents are calling about their second- or third-born child, as parents wonder if this will result in the younger sibling’s language being slower to develop. Is this really a phenomenon with families who have talkative older siblings? Is there a difference in the language development of later born children? If the later born child seems language delayed, will she “grow out of it”? Parents often report that their first-born children knew and understood more words than their later born children and hypothesize that later born children do not get the same amount of attention or one-to-one interaction with a parent as the eldest child does, causing the younger sibling to speak later. The impact of birth order on language development has been studied. The research shows that while some differences emerge between first and later born children’s language development, later born children are not delayed in their language development and first-borns do not have better language skills than their siblings. Some interesting differences that emerge in the research show patterns regarding sibling language development, suggesting Siblings share more with each other than love. that perhaps the differences parents see in the early language development of their first vs second born children may be influenced by the different language environments that each child is exposed to by virtue of who is in the family and the kind of interactions they have. For example, first born children tend to reach the 50-word milestone earlier than later born children (although the later born children catch up by the 100-word milestone and there are no lasting differences in vocabulary). Perhaps this is due to the first-born’s language learning environment in which parent child interactions are often centered around direct vocabulary expansion? While first-born children show strengths in vocabulary and grammar, later-born children show strengths in conversational skills. Second-born children also show particularly advanced use of pronouns such as my, mine, you and yours. Perhaps this is due to the second- or third-born’s environment in which language is often centered around overheard conversations, communication between siblings, and interactions such as sharing? Neither of these environments are detrimental to language development and there are no lasting developmental differences between first and later born siblings. In fact, studies show older siblings can have a positive impact on the development of their younger siblings’ language development. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C . articles.text: Piedmont will celebrate its first virtual Arbor Day on Friday, April 30. It will include youth-focused activities, a video that highlights the Heritage Tree selections this year, and a traditional tree-planting. “As a commission, we are trying to include every community member possible in this celebration, beginning with children,” said Park Commission Chair Patty Dunlap. For the first time, the celebration will include a sidewalk chalk-drawing contest for Piedmont’s younger residents. Children will be encouraged to select their favorite street tree or park tree, write the name of the tree in chalk, and then decorate the sidewalk with chalk to celebrate the tree. Parents can take a photo of the artwork and submit it to Parks Projects Manager Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmint.ca.gov. Prizes will be awarded for the most creative tree art. A 30-minute video is being created to feature footage of each designated Heritage Tree in Piedmont, including the most recent winners. Heritage Trees will be introduced by the person or the family that nominated them. KCOM technician Jason Liao assisted with the filming and production. “Jason has been all over Piedmont, capturing the beauty of not only the trees, but also the surrounding settings,” Dunlap said. Zack Parisa, a Piedmont Three Yulan Magnolia trees will be planted as part of Piedmont’s Arbor Day celebration on April 30. resident and co-founder of SilviaTerra, will be the Arbor Day guest speaker. SilviaTerra uses Natural Capital Exchange (NCAPX) to provide a marketplace for forest carbon payments. Recently, SilviaTerra collaborated Yulan Magnolia flowers appear on bare branches in April. with Microsoft to create “Basemap,” the first high-resolution forest inventory of the United States. The video will be shown live on KCOM (Channel 27) on April 30 and will be available to view on the city’s website after that. Arbor Day’s tradition in Piedmont includes the planting of a tree. This year three Yulan Magnolia trees will be planted in honor of Ralston Louie who passed on January 31. He was the son of Park Commissioner Robin Wu. This species of magnolia has been cultivated in Chinese Buddhist temple gardens for centuries and was regarded as a symbol of purity in the Tang Dynasty. “It’s regarded as one of the most beautiful magnolias – a deciduous, small tree with beautiful ivory-colored flowers that bloom on bare branches before the leaves come out in the spring,” Dunlap said. A memorial bench in Dracena Park near Ralston’s family home also will be installed. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

France keeps people employed But through it all, more than 3.6 million French workers are on paid furlough during lockdown, according to the New York Times. By squelching a tidal wave of unemployment, the country stays ready to ramp up the economy on a day’s notice, when the data shows Covid-19 is under control. A lesson learned from the 2008 Recession for France is not taking aggressive enough steps to arrest unemployment that ballooned in 2008 to 10 percent and drove the economy into a dive bomb. It took five years to recover. In the U.S. where a $2.2 trillion relief package provides jobless benefits, the problem may prove to be that sporadic onetime checks create inadequate welfare safety nets. France disperses directly to employers, which includes reimbursement of 80% of paychecks to full-time employees. Many companies pay the remaining 20% to keep employees’ pay whole and keep people employed. Families can pay their rent and feed the children, and the economy – while not exactly zinging – is showing very little downturn in the pandemic. Most businesses are not in collapse. Furloughed employees want to get back to work and are ready tomorrow, but in America, such a sentiment appears to be a debatable issue among its electorate. Coronavirus has drained millions of families’ resources due to millions of employee layoffs and small business closures. Among European nations, the paradigm for close to full employment within the safety net is showing positive results. Patricia Forsyth and Michael Mathews decamped to Paris in September 2019 and bide our time for pandemic’s end – and for Paris to be Paris again. The beautiful Carnavalet, all about the history of Paris, is preserved in two conjoined city houses in the 4th arrondissement. It has remained closed for more than four years of renovation, and now awaits a grand reopening this year. All Paris museums remained closed during the lockdowns. articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team is red hot on a three-game winning streak after beating Encinal in Alameda 10-6 on Wednesday, April 7, edging past the Jets 6-5 on Friday, April 9, and bashing Castro Valley 8-2 at Humphries Diamond on Saturday, April 10. The two-game series between Piedmont and Encinal re-visited the Western Alameda County Conference’s classic rivalry in the Shoreline Division. They last played in the 2019 league championship, which the Jets won 3-1. The Highlanders won the 2018 championship against Encinal 4-2 in extra innings. Piedmont’s two wins over Encinal makes them the top team in the Shoreline Division, undefeated in six games and 9-3 overall. No league championship is planned with this year’s shortened season. Piedmont’s 6-5 victory against Encinal marked its fifth win by fewer than two runs this season, all with game-winning hits in the last two innings. “Even when we’re down, we know that we can go off at any second and bring ourselves back in the game no matter what. It brings the best out in us,” said junior infielder Nico Defazio. The game featured sophomore leadoff hitter Michael Aikawa cracking his second homer this year. He currently carries a .378 batting average with 14 hits, two HRs, 10 RBIs and 14 runs scored. Photos by Mark Aikawa Nico Defazio (8) scores the winning run against Encinal in their 6-5 win last Friday. He also hit two doubles against Castro Valley. “We were watching [their pitcher] in the bullpen and everything seemed off-speed, but he threw me a fastball and I was waiting back on it,” said Aikawa. 10-6 win vs. Encinal In last Wednesday’s game, Piedmont led 9-0 in the top of the fifth before Encinal scored its first runs. The Highlanders used three pitchers; Cal Barna got the win after four innings and nine strikeouts. Will Sprague pitched two innings, two strikeouts. Julian Scherman entered for the last inning, striking out two. Lars Derr went 2-for-5 with three RBIs and one run scored. Barna went 2-for-5 with two RBIs. Aikawa had two walks, one RBI, two runs scored. Sprague had one hit and scored two runs. 6-5 comeback win in sweep of Encinal The Comeback Kids prevailed on Friday. Trailing Encinal 5-4 going into the bottom of the sixth inning. Garren Riley got on base on a hit-by-pitch (he was plunked three times in Friday’s game). Riley stole second and Defazio drew a walk with two outs. Derr, the cleanup hitter, smacked a hard groundball through the gap between second and shortstop to score Riley and Defazio, for a 6-5 lead and his second game-winning hit of the year. Piedmont opened with four runs in the first inning, sparked Michael Aikawa with a leadoff homerun against Encinal in Friday’s 6-5 win. Ben Levinson pitched a complete game against Castro Valley; seven innings with six strikeouts.

articles.text: The Annual PCA Juried Art Show returns this weekend to Piedmont Center for the Arts for its 7th year and will be open to the public starting at noon on Saturday, April 17. The show includes 35 pieces selected by guest jurors René de Guzman, Senior Curator of Art at Oakland Museum of California, and Danielle Fox, Principal of Slate Gallery in Oakland. The art was selected from more than 500 submissions. The exhibition will be open to the public for five weekends on Saturdays and Sundays, April 17 through May 16, from 12:00 noon to 2:00 p.m. each day. Thanks to a generous gift from the family of John P. Thornborrow, cash awards totaling $4,000 are allocated annually to the top award winners, with an emphasis on honoring emerging artists in the Bay Area. All visitors must register in advance. An email-based online system allows visitors to sign up for their choice of day and time slot. A health screening form listing all health protocols will be emailed to visitors with their confirmation. Register for your visit at https://bit.ly/3mwWuwT. The Art Show will be limited to a maximum of 20 visitors at Pages from my journal: I give thanks, by Elizabeth Bennett, 37x40, collage on wood panel any one time. Guests are asked to check in at the entrance at the start of their reserved time to be temperature-checked and to turn in health screening forms. Social distancing norms will be observed while guests visit the exhibition and while waiting to enter. Masks are to be worn at all times. Visitors must sanitize hands upon entry and will view the art in one direction to prevent clustering. No food or drink will be permitted. Entry to the exhibition will be through the front doors facing Magnolia Avenue, and visitors will exit through the east side door to Magnolia, avoiding twoway traffic through doorways. For more information, visit the Center for the Arts website at: piedmontcenterforthearts.org. articles.text: SF Jazz will present an online concert featuring Afro-Cuban jazz artist Dayme Arocena this Friday, April 16, at 5 p.m. The concert is part of SF Jazz’s “Fridays at Five” archival, online concert series. Arocena appears on National Public Radio’s (NPR) list of 50 favorite albums of 2015 with her album “Nueva Era.” She has been described as a cross between Celia Cruz and Aretha Franklin and has won international recognition for her unique approach to jazz. Originally from Havana, she has now become one of the most widely-recognized artists in Latin American jazz in recent years. In describing her musical influences, Arocena describes herself as an onward-looking artist with a deep understanding of where she comes from. “We don’t have this native culture [in Cuba]. We don’t have indigenous people like Maya Dayme Arocena or Quechua,” she said. “They made a country with people from everywhere. That’s what make’s Cuban culture so different.” For more information on how to watch the performance on Friday, visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ watch/.
articles.title: SF Jazz presents Dayme Arocena concert on April 16

articles.text: San Francisco Opera will stream an archival capture of Don Carlo on Saturday and Sunday, April 17-18. The production will be available for viewing through the weekend. This 2016 revival of Giuseppe Verdi’s Don Carlo utilizes the composer’s 1886 five-act version of the score. Michael Fabiano stars as Carlo, both son and heir to the king of Spain. Carlo’s love for the princess Elisabetta, played by soprano Ana Maria Martinez, is dashed when his father instead claims her as his bride. The story follows a “web of courtly intrigue and machinations,” and forces Carlo to make a fatal choice. The international, all-star cast includes German bass Rene Pape, who returns to San Francisco Opera in this production as King Philip II, Carlo’s father. Polish baritone Mariusz Kwiecien is Carlo’s friend and confidant Rodrigo, and Bulgarian mezzo-soprano Nadia Krasteva makes her company debut as Princess Eboli. The impressive set is designed by Zack Brown with lighting by Gary Marder. The opera is led by former San Francisco Opera Music Director Nicola Luisotti. The opera is sung in Italian with English subtitles available, and has a run time of approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes. This opera, and other streaming archival captures, are made available through San Francisco Opera’s “Opera is On,” an at-home digital streaming service. For more information on how to watch Don Carlo, visit https://sfopera.com/opera-is-on/ streaming/.
articles.title: SF Opera streaming Don Carlo April 17 and 18

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet’s “Rubies” is part of Jewels, a trilogy by George Balanchine. You can now stream George Balanchine’s full-length trilogy Jewels performed by San Francisco Ballet through April 21. The ballet told in three parts – “Emeralds,” “Rubies,” and “Diamonds” – is inspired by the ornate displays at New York City jeweler Van Cleef & Arpels. “Emeralds,” the first in the trilogy, is set to the music of Gabriel Faure. It evokes forest-green meditation in long, Romantic-era style skirts and costumes. Emeralds is influence by the French style of ballet - restrained and pristine. “Rubies” follows. and is set to music by Igor Stravinsky. Vibrant, hot hues are reminiscent of Times Square at midnight. A touch of jazz in the choreography mimics rushing crowds and pedestrians. The finale, “Diamonds,” is set to the music of Peter Tchaikovsky. It is a glittering homage to Imperial Russia, and specifically, to the style of Marius Petipa who is considered the father of classical ballet. Balanchine is also considered one of the most famous and prolific choreographers of the 20th century. Both “Rubies” and “Diamonds” are from SF Ballet’s archives. Streaming access became available last week and will be available until April 21. To obtain streaming access. visit https://www.sfballet.org/productions/digital-program-04/.
articles.title: SF Ballet’s Jewels now available through April 21

articles.text: Violinist Owen Dalby will lead a chamber music master class, hosted by the San Francisco Conservatory of Music, on Saturday, April 17. Dalby is an acclaimed soloist and chamber musician internationally and a member of the St. Lawrence String Quartet. Founded in 1989, the Canadian string quartet is one of the country’s premier chamber ensembles. The quartet has served residencies at the Julliard School, Yale University, the University of Toronto, Stanford University and the Hartt School. His recent projects include timore Symphony Orchestra. In 2010, Dalby completed a threeyear tenure with the Ensemble Connect, a fellowship at Carnegie Hall and the Juilliard School that links performers with advanced training. Dalby’s master class will begin at 7:30 p.m. and will be performed from Sol Joseph Recital Hall in SF Conservatory. articles.text: Gold Coast Chamber Players’ season finale, “Dvorak’s America,” will conclude their collection of virtual concerts on Saturday, May 1. “Dvorak’s America” explores the impact that spirituals and Native American music had on Czech composer Antonin Dvorak during his time in America. The project, three years in the making, highlights the interconnectedness of these cultures. The program will feature the composer’s String Quintet, op. 97, and the Lento from his String Quartet op. 96, both of which are nicknamed “the American.” Original music “Within My Heart” and “Beneath the Raven Moon” by Mary Youngblood is for Native American flute. Her arrangement of “Amazing Grace” represents what Dvorak heard during his stay in America. Dvorak proclaimed that African American Spirituals are “the heart of American music,” and the genre served as perhaps the greatest Western influence on Dvorak. Spirituals that will be performed in this program include “Swing Low Sweet Chariot,” “By an’ By,” and “My Lord What a Morning.” Concluding the program will be “Goin’ Home,” from the composer’s New World Symphony. Alexander String Quartet will lead the ensemble, marking one of the first performances since their unofficial retirement and addition of their new violist, David Samuel. Violist Pamela Freund-Striplen, a frequent collaborator with the Quartet, will Gold Coast Chamber Players founder, violist Pamela FreundStriplen. join its members for Dvorak’s America. The event will be livestreamed via YouTube at 7 p.m. on Saturday, May 1. For more information and to obtain tickets, visit www.gccpmusic.com, or call (925) 283-3728.
articles.title: Gold Coast Chamber Players presents Dvorak’s America streaming on May 1

It is a glittering homage to Imperial Russia, and specifically, to the style of Marius Petipa who is considered the father of classical ballet. Balanchine is also considered one of the most famous and prolific choreographers of the 20th century. Both “Rubies” and “Diamonds” are from SF Ballet’s archives. Streaming access became available last week and will be available until April 21. To obtain streaming access. visit https://www.sfballet.org/productions/digital-program-04/.

Piedmont realized this about 10 years ago when it established the Piedmont Center for the Arts which is an all-encompassing arts venue. The city also has its own chamber Orchestra. The future looks bright. Every hopeful project needs someone to initiate it. Every artistic endeavor begins this way. The community then unites, and the project is finished to the betterment of the entire community. These days, unfortunately, there is usually someone lurking in the shadows who has an ax to grind. The result is stagnation. San Francisco was fortunate to have had an organizational genius. He was the Oakland-born Sir Henry Heyman. It did not hurt that Sir Henry was one of San Francisco’s most colorful characters. He was like a musical Emperor Norton, but unlike Emperor Norton, Sir Henry was the real deal, not a fictitious character. He was born to a Jewish family in Oakland in 1855. His talent was recognized early and it was acknowledged that he was a child prodigy on the violin. The family decided to send him to Europe where he was enrolled at the illustrious Leipzig Conservatory. He graduated in 1871 with highest honors after having studied with the most famous musicians in Germany. Before returning to the U.S., he traveled the length and breadth of Europe making important and lasting friendships. In addition to being an extraordinary musician, Sir Henry was a diplomatic genius. Upon return to San Francisco, Sir Henry established the first important chamber music society. In 1881 he was selected to be the concertmaster of the newly formed San Francisco Philharmonic. He received glowing reviews in the newspapers for everything he did. Under his guidance he was helpful in organizing the musical activities of the Pan Pacific Exhibition in San Francisco in 1915. Sir Henry’s influence formed the exhibition’s orchestra. He brought in some of his world-famous friends, including Camille St. Saens and Ignacy Jan Paderewski. And this was only the beginning. In contrast, Sir Henry Heyman’s health failed him and he died in Paso Robles in 1924. The entire Bay Area mourned his passing. Sir Henry had a very good sense of humor. articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA)’s annual Art Bash fundraiser is underway, with a live “thank you” event and auction to take place tonight, Wednesday, April 14 at 6 p.m. The Art Bash began on Monday, April 12, as a virtual and free event. articles.text: Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) located on the University of California campus, has announced that it will reopen to the public following a 13-month closure due to the COVID pandemic. The museum will open on May 2 and will operate on a three-day weekly schedule thereafter. A comprehensive safety plan and protocol, developed in consultation with public health authorities, is now in place, with limited attendance, advance ticketing required, and social distancing and mask-wearing. The museum will be limited to 25% of its full capacity at any one time. Reservations are available at BAMPFA.org beginning April 21 for members, and April 22 for the general public. The museum will waive admission fees for all visitors on opening day and will offer a reduced $10 general admission fee that can be used for future admission. A free preview day will be held for BAMPFA members and UC Berkeley faculty and students. A free preview day will take place on Saturday, May 1, for essential workers. BAMPFA will reopen with the exhibition “Rosie Lee Tompkins: A Retrospective,” which opened in February 2020 and was on view for less than a month before the museum closed. The exhibition is the largest retrospective to date of the work of Tompkins, who is considered one of the most celebrated quilt makers of the twentieth century. Her work was newly re-discovered following a bequest to BAMPFA of nearly 3,000 quilts by African American artists. The exhibition has been extended through July 18 this year. In addition, three major new exhibitions will be on view: “Ulrike Ottinger / MATRIX 276,” “Beyond Boundaries: Buddhist Art of Gandhara,” and “Present Tense: Five Centuries of Colonialism in Latin American and Caribbean Art.” “As BAMPFA begins the process of safely reopening this spring, we’ll be doing so with an enormous sense of appreciation for the dedicated community of art and film lovers who have stayed connected with the museum throughout this tumultuous year,” said BAMPFA Director Julie Rodrigues Widholm. “We believe that art can provide respite during uncertain times, and in that spirit, we’re looking forward to offering our audiences a space for joy and reflection.” Visit the museum’s website (BAMPFA.org) for more re-opening information, and to reserve tickets.
articles.title: On display: “Rosie Lee Tompkins: A Retrospective”
