articles.text: It was July 16, 1942, and a defining moment for the French people. On that day, that singular day, some 13,000 French Jews were rounded up and taken to the Velodrome d’Hiver, a sports stadium, where they were kept in unspeakable conditions for days, absent water and food and sanitation. They were then transported to Beaune-la-Rolande, a transit camp, where families were separated, children from parents, wives from husbands. Their ultimate destination was Auschwitz. Most were never heard from again. What is generally not known is that the French police and the French government collaborated with the Germans in the roundup. It is an astonishing and incontrovertible fact that went unspoken for decades in France. Sarah’s Key tells the story of one family, most especially Sarah (Melusine Mayance), 10-yearsold, who, with her mother and younger brother, hear a loud knock on the door in the dark of night. Two French policemen, examining their identification papers, tell them to pack; they will be leaving immediately. On impulse, gripped by fear, Sarah takes Thomas, only fouryears-old, and locks him in their bedroom cupboard, promising to return shortly; he must not make any noise and he must remain hidden. And with the cupboard key clutched in her hand, she follows her mother and father out onto the street. They are taken to the Vel d’Hiv, as it was called. Sarah, ever mindful of the key and her promise, is frantic to return for Thomas. And so, the journey of Sarah Starzynski begins. Her story is woven together with that of Julia Jarmon (Kristin Scott Thomas), a journalist, who is writing a story in 2002 for the 60th anniversary of the Vel d’Hiv roundup. Julia begins to research the events surrounding that infamous day and soon discovers more truth than she ever contemplated. Her quest to unravel the story of Sarah grows ever more painful and disturbing, haunted by the question: how could this have happened? How could the French have been complicit in such an atrocity? Julia interviews a man who is charged with chronicling the events and he remarks to her that he is committed to putting a face to each person lost and he rejects any attempt to express what occurred in terms of numbers. And it is when he hands her a photo of Sarah and Thomas, yellow stars sewn to their coats, that she becomes profoundly moved and disturbed and committed to Sarah’s story. What makes the film ever more powerful and moving is that it is, in great part, told from the point of view of Sarah. Her journey took her into the heart of darkness, devastating and horrible, is inexplicable to those who bore witness. It would change Sarah’s life forever, as it changed Julia’s. Ultimately the key becomes a metaphor, holding the promise of opening the cupboard door. But also, Julia concludes, that key holds the promise of unlocking memories, no matter the pain inherent in their revelation. Sarah’s Key. Directed by Gilles Paquet-Brenner, Starring Kristin Scott Thomas, Mélusine Mayance, Aidan Quinn and Frédéric Pierrot, 1 hr., 51 min. Rated PG-13. articles.text: “Patience is a virtue” is being taken to a whole new level in our lives, at this time as we pivot toward the next phase of the global pandemic. Readers of this column know that I am a proponent of SLOW as a hallmark of quality and beauty and soulfulness. Especially when we are talking about high-quality, handmade, consciously, and thoughtfully sourced materials. And you might guess, in my industry as an interior designer, I already navigate through the tricky territory of educating clients to calibrate their expectations. These days, because of the pandemic and its consequences, there is a new normal: even slower delivery times. Sheltering in place over this past year has created an increased demand for home services, especially interior design. And this awareness of the importance of home is not likely to leave us. Many people are not going back to work in person, even after restrictions lift. We like our homes, we like being at home, and now we want to love them, beautify them. We nourish ourselves by beautifying our spaces. What has happened globally is that the supply chain has slowed. This affects the availability and cost of raw materials as well as finished products. Even when materials are locally sourced, the international market has an impact on supply. Labor has been affected also as businesses shuttered their doors, workers fell ill, or lost family members. The human family is having this experience of loss and we are realizing how we are all interconnected. Even with somebody on the other side of the world, their loss impacts us locally. With all of the interruptions, delays, and increases in demand in our industry, we are seeing that items that used to have an 8–10- week lead time are now taking 20 weeks; 16-week lead times now are going to 24 weeks. articles.text: Organic waste includes many types of materials, but the most common one stemming from households is food waste. Organic waste in landfills accounts for 20% of methane generated in California and is also the most common material type to end up in landfills. Reducing organic waste in landfills can reduce greenhouse gas emissions, create jobs, and produce compost, all while feeding more people. California Senate Bill (SB) 1383 has plans to address all of these issues. The bill aims to reduce waste sent to landfills while getting food to people who need it. This is a win for both the environment and people. First passed in 2016 by the California Legislature, SB 1383 mandates methane reduction targets statewide. Food waste emits a lot of methane, which means that less food waste will produce less methane. articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will host a public discussion with Alameda County District Attorney Nancy O’Malley on May 6 starting at 4 p.m. She will describe the work by her department with abused and homeless women, helping them move beyond trauma into a positive future. O’Malley will address the many challenges COVID-19 has posed. She will explain the ways in which the current lack of civility in politics is impeding the pace and scale of progress for women who suffer from violence. For example, passage of the Violence Against Women Act was held up due to politics, and funding for the Victims Crime Act, which provides resources to states for victims of crime, was also reduced. O’Malley is a nationally recognized expert on issues involving violence against women, violence against persons with disabilities, and interpersonal violence including sexual assault, domestic violence, elder abuse, child abuse, stalking, and human exploitation and trafficking. She serves in the office that dates to a time when Earl Warren was the Alameda County D.A. before becoming United States Supreme Court Chief Justice. O’Malley is the first woman to serve as the County’s District Attorney. The event is free and open to all community members to register for the Zoom event, visit https:// www.lwvpiedmont.org/content. a spx?page_id= 40 02&club_ id=601389&item_id=1256825. It will be recorded and posted on the League of Women Voters of Piedmont website for those who cannot join live.

How SB 1383 will affect Piedmont By Nate Redinbo Organic waste includes many types of materials, but the most common one stemming from households is food waste. Organic waste in landfills accounts for 20% of methane generated in California and is also the most common material type to end up in landfills. Reducing organic waste in landfills can reduce greenhouse gas emissions, create jobs, and produce compost, all while feeding more people. California Senate Bill (SB) 1383 has plans to address all of these issues. The bill aims to reduce waste sent to landfills while getting food to people who need it. This is a win for both the environment and people. First passed in 2016 by the California Legislature, SB 1383 mandates methane reduction targets statewide. Food waste emits a lot of methane, which means that less food waste will produce less methane. This effort is especially important because methane traps far more heat than carbon dioxide and can have a larger impact on climate change. The overarching goal of SB 1383 is to help California meet its 2045 carbon neutrality goal. Interestingly, this bill doesn’t target individual jurisdictions, but the state as a whole. Certain jurisdictions will have to implement many more changes than others. As a leader in waste management, Piedmont is largely compliant already, and SB 1383 should not radically change how waste is managed in the City. articles.text: Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had its monthly book discussion on April 5 via Zoom. Thirteen readers were on the call to discuss this month’s selection, The Splendid and the Vile, a detailed story of Winston Churchill by best-selling author Erik Larson. Participating in the discussion were Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Laura Goldman, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Albert Chen, Margie Blodgett, Bella Almanzan, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Jamie Forsythe, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. The Splendid and the Vile is Larson’s 600 plus page account of Churchill’s first year as prime minister of the United Kingdom at the start of World War II. The story begins on May 10, 1940, the day Germany invaded Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands. Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain had resigned, and King George VI appointed Churchill to replace him. The king was not enthusiastic about the choice of Churchill. Some people thought he was “flamboyant, electric, and wholly unpredictable,” as well as “capricious and meddlesome, and inclined toward dynamic action in every direction at once.” Churchill also had several personal problems. He was deeply in debt, as was his son, Randolph, who spent money freely and had lost a lot of it gambling. However, the British public came to appreciate Churchill quickly, in large part because of his powerful oratory. A prime example of this was one month later, in June 1940, in which he proclaimed, “We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills; we shall never surrender.” Larson writes that Churchill then turned to a colleague and said, under his breath, “And ... we will fight them with the butt end of broken bottles, because that’s bloody well all we’ve got.” Churchill realized that the British needed the United States’ industrial and military power to defeat Germany. Larson details Churchill’s efforts to persuade President Franklin Delano Roosevelt to help the Allies, and was overjoyed when Roosevelt signed the Lend-Lease Act into law that provided the assistance that Great Britain desperately needed. Larson focuses on Churchill and his family, but also provides a vivid account of the Blitz, the horrific German bombing of Great Britain that had the British people living in danger for many months. Larson relates Churchill’s fearless reaction to the bombings, but also the intimate experiences of a wide group of people including many ordinary Brits. Larson also profiles Churchill’s family, aides, and colleagues, providing readers with a deeper understanding of him. Larson also paints a vivid portrait of Churchill’s personality, which was intense and erratic, and, for some readers, comical. The book was generally well received by the Monday Reading group, with some exceptions. Everyone agreed that Larson and his team did a remarkable job of researching and documenting Churchill and the first year of Great Britain’s war with Germany. Readers also enjoyed Larson’s writing style. The book reads like a novel. The Splendid and the Vile has so much detail and so many personal stories that the reader not only has a full understanding of the events, but also an emotional appreciation of what life was actually like during this harrowing period for the English people. The readers found this book complementary to a previous book selection, No Ordinary Time, by American historian Doris Kearns Goodwin, which told the story of Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt during World War II. The Splendid and the Vile, however, was not everyone’s cup of tea. Some members of the group found all the information and details overwhelming. They had to struggle through it, but they did find the personal stories of Churchill’s daughter Mary, his son’s wife, Pamela, and others engaging. Additionally, the effects on English children from the German Blitz were an important facet of the history for some readers. With their book discussion complete, the group discussed future books to read. Homegoing, an historical novel by Yaa Gyasi, was selected as the group’s May read, and former President Obama’s new memoir, A Promised Land, will be the book selection for June. The selection for July will be Chinatown by Charles Yu. The group is looking forward to the time when they will be able to meet again in Person. Their next book discussion will be on Zoom on Monday, May 3rd, at 1:30 PM. New members are always welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration with the Recreation Department is required by contacting John Wilk at jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: The Oakland Public Library (OPL) will open 16 locations including the Piedmont Avenue Branch for indoor Express services starting April 19. Library users will be able to access modified library services including limited browsing, checkout of materials, and computer use. Gathering and play spaces will remain closed, but patrons can expect welcoming staff available to help them navigate OPL Express services and safety protocols. The Asian Branch Library and the Oakland Tool Lending Library will continue to offer Sidewalk Service due to ongoing facility improvements. During visiting hours, the following in-person services will be available: • Library card registration and renewal • Browsing the collection • Computer use (excluding Lakeview, Montclair and Piedmont Ave.) • Print, scan and faxing services (at available locations) • Laptop and Wi-Fi hotspot checkout (at available locations) • Wi-Fi access and mobile device charging Visitor guidelines • Wear a face mask covering nose and mouth, for all patrons over two years old. • Maintain a physical distance of 6-feet apart • Self-screen for COVID-19 symptoms. • Wash or sanitize hands frequently. • Eating and drinking will not be permitted during OPL Express. Oakland Library is providing the following to protect the safety of patrons and staff: • Limiting occupancy inside each location • Providing self-checkout stations at all locations • Piloting a new mobile checkout service • Quarantining items for at least 24 hours before returning to circulation • Disinfecting high-touch surfaces regularly The library will continue to offer 24/7 access to digital offerings including e-books, audiobooks and streaming movies, in addition to virtual programs, including storytimes, book clubs and author talks. For more information contact the Piedmont Ave. Branch Library, located at 80 Echo Avenue in Oakland, at (510) 597-5011 (www.oaklandlibrary.org)
articles.title: Oakland Public Libraries to open indoors April 19

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department has announced that the Walking on Wednesdays group, sidelined for one year due to the coronavirus, will be back in action starting this morning, Wednesday, April 14. This restart marks three years since the group’s first weekly walk on April 18, 2018. Some new protocols will help keep walkers as COVID-safe as possible. Before the pandemic, many people enjoyed the weekly Wednesday morning walks on Piedmont’s beautiful streets. “Members of the group have remained in contact during the pandemic. “Being able to be with members of the group again will be great,” said coordinator Dick Carter. Since last week, March 30, Alameda County has been at the Orange Tier level within the state’s Blueprint for Safer Economy Opening Plan. The Orange Tier allows for many outdoor group activities to be conducted. Individuals planning on participating in the weekly walks need to register on the Recreation Department’s CommunityPass site. Walkers will be placed in a pod and each pod of walkers will have a different start time at 15-minute intervals starting at 10:00 a.m. every Wednesday at the Exedra Plaza at Magnolia and Highland Avenues. Walkers in each pod will be defined and set until pandemic activity restrictions are removed or modified by the County or City. Participants will not be allowed to move within pods, or walk with other pods, after the pods have been defined. Participants will be required to wear masks during, and after their walks, and maintain six feet of separation from non-family member participants. There are no fees to participate in Walking on Wednesdays activities. Those interested in walking with the group should register at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. For more information, contact the Piedmont Recreation Department at 510 420-3070.

articles.text: California Coffeeberry The Piedmont Garden Club has donated $5,000 to the city to plant native California plant species as part of the Highland-Guilford Steps and Handrail project connecting the Community Hall area with Guilford Road. Former Piedmont Mayor Valerie Matzger presented the donation on behalf of the Piedmont Garden Club to the Piedmont Park Commission on April 7. “Piedmont Garden Club’s conservation focus this year has been the importance of California native plants in supporting pollinators, and other wildlife,” Matzger said. “There has been a catastrophic decline in insect and bird populations, due to several factors, among them, a loss of habitat, climate change, and pesticide use.” “If we use native plants that have evolved with these creatures, we can support our ecosystem and reverse these population declines,” she said. The plants will be grown adjacent to the project near the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. An existing path entry on Highland Avenue will be replaced by a new entry plaza. New light posts and benches will be placed along the walkway. “We used to design our gardens to be beautiful, to be just ‘eye-candy.’ Now, something much more important has come up, it impacts the natural world and us,” Matzger added. California Native Plant Week The California Native Plant Society (CNPS) has deemed April 17 through April 24 as California Native Plant Week. CNPS is a volunteer organization dedicated to the preservation and celebration of California’s native flora, founded in Berkeley in 1965. In its more than 40 year-history, the volunteer group has garnered an impressive group of volunteers, including Ansel Adams, Chief Justice Earl Warren, Linus PaulRed-flowering currant (Ribes Sanguineum) ing, Philip Munz, and Lester Rowntree. CNPS encourages Californians to explore hyperlocal gardening with native plants. Similar in scope to the Piedmont Garden Club’s plans for the Guilford project, local gardening creates “urban habitats” for local wildlife, created by native plants. Suggestions from the Piedmont Garden Club included Coffeeberry, red-flowering currant, and Manzanita. For those interested in including native foliage in their gardens, the UC Berkeley Botanical Garden has expanded its plant offerings to celebrate California Native Plant week. Plants available to purchase include California lilacs, Bush Mallows, Bush Anemone, Red Willow, and others. All can be purchased at the Garden Shop. To learn more about California Native Plant Week, and the host of gardening workshops being offered by CNPS, visit https:// www.cnps.org/california-native-plant-week. articles.text: Staff Photos Pitcher Izzy Epstein had a no-hitter in Piedmont’s 12-0 victory over the Encinal Jets. The Piedmont Highlander softball team walked into Spring Break on a high note after shutting out the Encinal Jets 12-0 in Alameda on Friday, April 9. It marks the fourth win by more than 10 runs. The team has won its last two games by a total of 32-0 after beating San Lorenzo 20-0 on April 5. Piedmont’s record improves to 6-2 overall with two games remaining. Their only losses were to Mt Eden, the defending League champion. No league playoff series or championship game is planned this year. “It’s unfortunate to have a short year with this team, but the future is bright. We have a strong program with a lot of young talent,” said coach Gene Dennard. The Highlanders led 10-0 after the top of the fourth inning with four runs in the second inning, three in the third, another three runs in the fourth, and two more in the fifth and final inning for the 12-0 shutout. Pitcher Izzy Epstein hurled a no-hitter with four strikeouts and one walk. Junior Ginger Gardner hit her first high school home run in the top of the second, and power hitter Chiarra Lundin snacked her third home run of the year in the fourth inning. Final Stats: Gardner went 2-for-4 with two RBIs and two runs scored. Lundin had her homer, two RBIs, two runs scored. Castronovo went 2-for-4, two RBIs, and a run scored. Ronen went 2-for-3, two runs, one RBI. Gerhardy had a double, one RBI and one run scored. Bell had one double, one RBI, one walk drawn. NEXT UP Piedmont (6-2) plays its final home game on Tuesday, April 20 with Hayward at 3:30 p.m. PHS then plays Alameda on Thursday, April 22 at 4:00 p.m. Ginger Gardner cracked an inside the park home run against Encinal, the first of her high school career. Chiarra Lundin hit her third home run of the year against the Jets.

articles.text: The Piedmont girls’ tennis team suffered an 8-1 loss to Campolindo in Moraga on Tuesday, April 6. “There were some close matches that could have gone either way, but it just wasn’t our best day. We committed too many double faults which put us behind the 8 ball all the time,” said coach Jim Landes. The Highlanders now look ahead to the Western Alameda County Conference Individual Singles & Doubles Tournament this weekend on Friday and Saturday, April 16-17 to be held at Alameda High School. The following week the team will play a final match with Castro Valley on Saturday, April 24. The Trojans missed nearly the entire season after being without a coaching staff. In the match with Campolindo, the Highlanders were without singles starters Makenna Thiel and Audrey Edel. The only winner on the day was Michaela Bini at No. 3 singles in a dominant victory, 6-2, 6-2. “Michaela hit a lot of strong forehands and volleys that were too much for her opponent,” explained Landes. Bridgette McEfee appeared at No. 1 singles and played to a three-set loss, 3-6, 6-3, 10-1. “Bridgette cruised in the first set, but had some double faults in the next two,” said Landes. Losses at singles include Anne Jumper at the No. 2 spot, 6-4, 6-3. Audrey Mahany battled at No. 4 singles in a 6-1, 6-3 loss. At No. 5 singles, Amanda Becker lost 6-3, 6-3, and Mara LaForte at No. 6 lost 6-4, 6-3. At No. 1 doubles, Rosie Siemers and Kate Dorman had the best match of the day in a three-set battle, ultimately losing 5-7, 6-4, 10-7. “Our top team of Kate Dorman and Rosie Siemers played well with some beautiful ground strokes and volleys. Their opponents out-served them and ended up beating us in the super breaker,” said Landes. Also at doubles was Audrey Frankel and Sofia Ferraro at No. 2, losing 6-1, 6-1. Talia Blumberg and Ava Hersch lost 6-2, 6-1 at No. 3. WACC Tournament Preview The Highlanders look ahead to the league’s most prestigious tournament, the Singles and Doubles championships, to be played this weekend at Alameda HS. Landes has scheduled Makenna Thiel and Bridgette McEfee for singles in the 12-entrant ladder. Thiel will be the top-seed. Audrey Edel, who played No. 1 and No.2 singles during the season, will be paired with rising star Anne Jumper as a doubled team, and Mara LaForte and Kate Dorman will make their first doubles appearance in the league championship tournament. NEXT UP Piedmont brings six players to the WACC Individual Tournament on Friday and Saturday, April 16-17 at Alameda High. Matches start 10:00 a.m. The season’s final match will be played in Castro Valley on Saturday, April 24. Michaela Bini was dominant in her match at No. 3 singles against Campolindo, winning in straight sets, 6-2, 6-2. Playing No. 1 singles, Bridgette McEfee took her opponent to three-sets, 3-6, 6-3, 10-1, before losing to Campo. She will compete in singles at the league tournament.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ cross-country team placed first and the boys’ team came in 3rd at this year’s Western Alameda County Conference Championship, held on Saturday, April 10 at Hayward High. The girls finished first among seven schools, edging Alameda by three points, and led by junior Ellie Black who won the overall met with a time of 19:26.4 on the 3-mile double loop trail. The boys’ team placed 3rd of nine schools, led by junior Jack Stein who was third in a field of 58 runners with a time of 15:58.53. “We were so thrilled to see everyone race hard on the course. We feel many made a name for themselves in this strange pandemic year. All the hard work is paying off,” said coach Jeanine Holmlund. Saturday’s meet was the first league championship for the girls’ team since 2017. The PHS boys’ and girls’ teams placed second in the WACC Final in November 2019. The WACC meet capped a brief season of only four meets. The distance running team is coupled with track and field for the 2021 school year and returns to Hayward High for its WACC Championship on April 17. Track will continue competing in multiple events through May. Girls’ Results Black had a huge lead on the field, beating second place Sophia Carpenter of Alameda by 19 seconds. It marked her third league victory of the shortened season. She placed 14th of 37 runners at the Dublin Invitational on February 27. Competing concurrently with the track team, she also has won three 1600-meter races, two 3200- meter races and once in the 400. Senior Aya Troyer finishing fifth of 46 runners with a time of 20:41.26. Junior classmates Mara Lovric and Juliette Palacios ran side by side for 11th and 12th place finishes with times of 21:18.51 and 21.19.77. Freshman Jamie Schwarz was close behind 21:26.25 and placed 14th. She also runs the half mile on the track team and has won four 800-meter races this spring Boys Results Junior Jack Stein missed winning the League meet by four seconds and placed third with a time of 15:58.53. Stein has been a breakout performer this season placing first in two league meets. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team came up short in a match with North Coast Section power University in San Francisco, 5-2, on a windy afternoon on April 7. Unlike the PHS girls’ team, they were able to compete in Golden Gate Park’s recently renovated Goldman Tennis Complex. “We lost to our nemesis again,” said coach Jim Landes. “The wind wreaked havoc at times, but University has a very strong singles lineup, but we took two of three at doubles,” The Piedmont-University rivalry in North Coast Section has been building since 2017 when PHS last won the Dib. 2 NCS Team Championship with a 5-2 win over the Red Devils. University followed with a 4-3 win over Piedmont in the 2018 Finals, then the San Francisco school beat PHS 4-3 in the 2019 Semifinals. In Wednesday’s match, wins were recorded by the No. 2 doubles team of freshman Monte Imburg and senior Akash Kothari, 6-3, 6-3. The No. 3 pairing of Oliver Maxwell and Ethan Pham won their fourth match as a tandem, 6-1, 7-5. “We had some good matches. Oliver and Ethan jumped to a quick lead, had some hiccups in the second set, but won in straights with great volleying and smart movement on the court,” said Landes. Charlie Olcott and Kai Baudendistel lost at No. 1 doubles, 6-1, 6-4. In singles, Sajan Srivastava lost narrowly in straight sets, going to a first-set tiebreaker and nearly forcing another tiebreaker in the second, 7-6 (7-4), 7-5. “It was a high-quality match,” said Landes. “Sajan hit his signature big serves and added some Charlie Olcott (front) and Kai Baudendistel played No. 1 doubles against University.

articles.text: for everyone – a resetting of the expectations that we are all experiencing. We are recalibrating after so many years of being given to instantaneously, being promised we could have all this beauty at the click of a button. In this time, my favorite word has become Pivot! The challenges we are experiencing have made us more resilient as humans. As a designer, it is my job to help my clients through the process, to create beauty, and to manage the project, the budget, and the expectations. It is not all bad news. Sometimes I get to deliver the good news, about a solution we’ve discovered, or about items arriving on time. The over-arching good news is that we’ve reset ourselves to be more patient and resilient – as people and as a community. This moment in our culture is an opportunity to practice gratitude. To acknowledge that we who get to order new, high-quality, handmade furniture, and who get to hire a designer to help make our homes beautiful, are lucky. And when we beautify our spaces, when we nourish ourselves with beauty and quality, we feel filled up, safe, and content. We are empowered to give our gifts, be the good people we are, and contribute to those around us. We are all prone to feeling beleaguered by delays, slowness, the things we cannot control. I am feeling it too. I am excited to move on to a fresh, new chapter. I love momentum. I love to start a project, get it done, and move on. But here we all are, practicing our Buddha natures. Engaging with patience, acceptance, and gratitude. If items do come in on time, we all celebrate together. If they don’t, that’s all part of the new normal. One takeaway: Hire a designer you love, because they are going to be in your life for a good long while. When the workers are gone and you are showering in your brand-new shower for the first time, and sleeping in your new primary bedroom, you will know it will all have been worth it. And it wouldn’t have been nearly as lovely if you hadn’t hired quality professionals to help. and that all good things are truly worth the wait. Laura Martin Bovard is the principal at LMB Interiors, located in downtown Oakland. Since 2002 she has helped clients create beautiful, joyful, and functional homes. The firm has garnered numerous awards and recognition as one of the Bay Area’s most sought after interior design agencies. For information see laura@lmbinteriors. com

articles.text: The popular annual Piedmont Art Walk, now in its 2nd year, has more than 40 local artists signed up to display their art outside on Sunday, May 2 between 12:00- 5:00 p.m. Paintings, ceramics, mixed media, sculpture, and photography will be displayed and shown by local artists in front of their homes. The community is invited to enjoy this outdoor art event and fundraiser hosted by local Piedmont artists and the Piedmont Arts Fund. Purchases support artists in town, and 20 percent of proceeds will be donated to the Laura LImpias, a painter and portraitist, works primarily in oil and pencil. Piedmont Arts Fund to support art in the schools. This fundraising event brings together live art, artists, and community members while following Alameda County’s COVID-19 guidelines to keep everyone safe. The event is spread out over Piedmont to avoid crowds and ensure social distancing. When the COVID quarantine took effect in last March, the Piedmont Arts Fund (formerly PAINTS and CHIME) had to cancel their spring fundraisers. The diminished school budget outlook for next school year makes this year’s fundraising critical for maintaining robust art programs in Piedmont schools. The Art Walk features a Who’s Who of Piedmont artists, and residents and students may not realize how many accomGary Laymon’s abstract landscapes, still life compositions and story illustrations, utilize bright colors, strong geometry.
articles.title: Piedmont artists gearing up for annual Art Walk on May 2

articles.text: In April David Olson ran the London Marathon, his final accomplishment in completing the six major world marathons, which included Boston, New York, Chicago, Tokyo and Berlin. In London to cheer him on were Dana and John Kirby, Emily and Bill Brizendine, daughter in law Nadja Olson, granddaughter Sydney Olson and David’s wife, Gail. Sydney gets credit for remembering to bring the Piedmont Post for a quick peek at the news back home. Previously published in the Piedmont Post on June 13, 2018. articles.text: The Association of Piedmont Teachers has until today, Wednesday, April 7, at 4:00 p.m., to vote on changes to its Memo of Understanding with the School District. At stake is an increase of in-person class time for middle and high school students. The school board has scheduled a Special Board Meeting tonight, at 7 p.m. via Zoom, Currently, Piedmont Middle School students have the fewest hours of classroom instruction – 2 hours, 30 minutes per week. High schooler students taking a full load of seven periods of classes receive 4 hours, 22 minutes of instruction in classrooms per week. The details of a new schedule have not been publicly released. “This is not just a Piedmont policy. Virtually every district in the state does not bargain in public,” said Board President Cory Smegal. On March 31 Superintendent Randy Booker indicated one of the district’s goals was to have Middle and High Schoolers on the same schedule. The schedules at the elementary schools will not change based on this agreement. Elementary school students will continue to have 2 hours, 15 minutes of class-time instruction per day from Tuesday through Friday, a total of nine hours a week. Negotiations for an increase in class time between the school district and teachers began on March 24. By law, the teachers’ union is given three days to vote. The Special Board meeting tonight will not be broadcast on KCOM, but only via Zoom zoom. us/j/97224679919. If an agreement is approved by the teachers, a copy of the Tentative Agreement will be posted today for the Board to ratify. The School Board has given every indication that it will ratify the new Memorandum of Understanding Addendum with the increased schedule, if given the chance. “We will see, fingers crossed,” Smegal said. The earliest a new schedule could go into effect would be April 20, after Spring Break.
articles.title: Teachers to vote today on increasing class time at PHS, PMS – or not

articles.text: Dr. Joel Parrott, head of Oakland Zoo for the past 37 years, was honored at a lively retirement ceremony at the zoo’s California Trail hilltop banquet facility on Friday April 27 Forty years ago, in 1981, Parrott began working at the Oakland Zoo as a veterinarian. Three years later he was promoted to the top, as Director of the zoo. Since then, he has helped build Oakland Zoo into a thriving zoo, well-known and well respected throughout the world. In as grand of a send-off as the zoo could muster with COVID protocols, Dr. Parrott – affectionately called Doc – said his goodbyes on a beautiful sunny afternoon Thursday, April 1. Arrivals were staggered for the outdoor and masked event high atop the zoo overlooking the glassy waters of the bay. Parrott spoke with eloquence and conveyed his profound gratitude to the crowd of family, friends and colleagues. He also formally introduced and enthusiastically ushered in the new CEO, Nik Dehejia, a veteran of 14 years as Parrot’s right-hand man. Piedmonters have long been associated with the Oakland Zoo, dating back to Joseph R. Knowland I, who secured the purchase of the land in 1948 to be used for a state park and zoo. Numerous

articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council has agreed to provide child-care at no cost for full-time, in-class Piedmont School District teachers with a need for such service for the remainder of the academic year. “Of the many challenges facing our community during the course of the COVID-19 pandemic, the closure of schools to in-person learning has been one of the hardest,” explained City Administrator Sara Lillevand in a city report. “While many obstacles are beyond our control, [city] staff has examined possible mechanisms the city might undertake to support the [school] district’s efforts to expand in-person learning hours.” Lillevand added that availability and cost of childcare can provide a barrier for educators and staff to return to campuses, and that the city should be able to assist. “The Recreation Department,” she said, “has managed to provide childcare throughout the pandemic and subsequent lockdowns, all in a safe manner and while following guidance directed from the Alameda County Health Department.” The Recreation Department oversees all city childcare programs, including the popular Schoolmates program. The motion, approved unanimously at an April 5 council meeting, authorizes Recreation Director Chelle Putzer to waive childcare fees for employees of the school district who will teach in-person classes for the rest of the 2020 - 21 academic year and a 2021 summer school if it is scheduled. The council will also authorize Putzer to make and enforce rules regarding fee waivers, and requests that the district provide the city with a list of employees who are currently providing on-campus learning and have a need for child care. “Without a full understanding of the needs of Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) employees, the city cannot commit to the feasibility of creating space for all, but it can commit to a good faith effort to expand offerings to meet those needs and to offering programs at no cost,” Lillevand said. Currently, five school district employees have children in Camp Smart Start, the COVID-equivalent of Schoolmates, and have collectively paid $10,000 thus far for the service. The city will commit to supporting this effort without tapping into its general fund, Lillevand explained. A city staff report confirmed that the Schoolmates reserve fund has a current balance of $236,000 and a projected year-end balance of $150,000-$200,000. City staff also expect funds from the American Rescue Plan to be distributed in coming months, which could likely bring one to two million dollars for the city. Support for educators and school staff to return to in-person learning is expected to be an approved expenditure for the funds received.
articles.title: City to provide free childcare for Piedmont teachers

articles.text: The following letter was sent to Piedmont School District and the Piedmont School Board. We are writing on behalf of the more than 250 parents in the Advocates for Full-Time, In-Person Piedmont Schools group, as well as the students in the Piedmont Unified School District who have been suffering as a result of distance learning over the past 365+ days. First, we would like to express our sincere gratitude for the many extra hours that all of you have put into our schools throughout this unprecedented year. COVID- 19 has been hard on all of us, but we recognize and appreciate that as educators and administrators, you have experienced a level of stress and exhaustion that many of us cannot fully comprehend. We hear you when you say you are exhausted and burned out. We write to you today because of our respect for what you have taken on, and because of our shared commitment to the students in our district. We are grateful that most Piedmont students now have an opportunity for some in-person instruction. We are also grateful that the district and our local teachers’ union (APT) have reached tentative agreements for expanding secondary in-person class time. We look forward to hearing the details about those new schedules soon. Our remaining concern is the current elementary schedule, which the district and APT have not yet reached an agreement for expanding. As the graph above shows, at 9 hours per week, our elementary students are receiving less in-person education than many of their peers in surrounding districts, despite PUSD’s modest size and sizable resources. It is not clear why our elementary students are spending a full school day out of the classroom on Mondays when they could significantly increase their in-person time with little-to-no disruption of classes and cohorts. Consequently, we would like to propose the following in-person expansion for grades K-5: convert distance learning Mondays to hybrid for a total of 11 hours in-person instruction per week. articles.text: In a series of lectures on the history of human rights, “Rights of Man, Great Thinkers and Great Movements,” Professor Paul Gorden Lauren summarizes Christianity as follows: Christianity was founded 2,000 years ago with the example, deeds, and teachings of Jesus of Nazareth. Although his ministry lasted only a few years, his influence has been such that Christianity claims more adherents today than any other religion in the world. A. His teachings centered on two principles: that God possesses an overwhelming love for all men, women, and children, and that we, in turn, have a responsibility to receive this love and then let it flow outward to God and to others. B. Jesus thus emphasized the value of all human life and sought to break down ethnic, gender, and class divisions. He instructed his followers to show love and compassion for “the least of these,” the powerless, the outcasts, the weak, the abused and oppressed, the sick, the hungry, the naked, the meek, and those who suffer. This is why he told the parable of the good Samaritan and instructed his followers to “Go For 22 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send us photos still on your camera or in a scrapbook for publication in the Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. Otherwise we are left to ask, “Where in the World Are They?” Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmontpost.org, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.

pages.text: 2 Wednesday, April 7, 2021 Opinion Parents offer plan for more classroom time this spring The following letter was sent to Piedmont School District and the Piedmont School Board. We are writing on behalf of the more than 250 parents in the Advocates for Full-Time, In-Person Piedmont Schools group, as well as the students in the Piedmont Unified School District who have been suffering as a result of distance learning over the past 365+ days. First, we would like to express our sincere gratitude for the many extra hours that all of you have put into our schools throughout this unprecedented year. COVID- 19 has been hard on all of us, but we recognize and appreciate that as educators and administrators, you have experienced a level of stress and exhaustion that many of us cannot fully comprehend. We hear you when you say you are exhausted and burned out. We write to you today because of our respect for what you have taken on, and because of our shared commitment to the students in our district. We are grateful that most Piedmont students now have an opportunity for some in-person instruction. We are also grateful that the district and our local teachers’ union (APT) have reached tentative agreements for expanding secondary in-person class time. We look forward to hearing the details about those new schedules soon. Our remaining concern is the current elementary schedule, which the district and APT have not yet reached an agreement for expanding. As the graph above shows, at 9 hours per week, our elementary students are receiving less in-person education than many of their peers in surrounding districts, despite PUSD’s modest size and sizable resources. It is not clear why our elementary students are spending a full school day out of the classroom on Mondays when they could significantly increase their in-person time with little-to-no disruption of classes and cohorts. Consequently, we would like to propose the following in-person expansion for grades K-5: convert distance learning Mondays to hybrid for a total of 11 hours in-person instruction per week. articles.text: California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced yesterday, Tuesday, April 6, that the state plans to lift most restrictions due to the COVID-19 pandemic on June 15. While a mask mandate will stay in place until further notice, Newsom said most restrictions will end if hospitalizations remain low and vaccinations continue apace. “We can confidently say by June 15 that we can start to open up as business as usual, subject to ongoing mask-wearing and ongoing vigilance,” Newsom said at a press conference. “This is a big day,” he added. According to the new plan, California’s “Blueprint for a Safer Economy” – the state’s four-tiered color-coded protocol for reopening activities and sectors – will be abolished on June 15. Instead of focusing on specific sectors and industries, the state will focus mostly on masks and vaccinations. Dr. Mark Ghaly, the California Director of Health Services, joined Newsom at the announcement and said there was no timeline for ending the statewide face mask mandate. “We still see masking as a key protective feature,” Ghaly said. Last Tuesday, March 30, the state moved Alameda County into the orange tier, or moderate tier, the second-least restrictive tier for reopening. As part of the orange tier, the capacity for indoor dining increased to 50 percent and outdoor bars reopened. Gyms and fitness centers reopened at 25 percent capacity, while some indoor offices reopened with modification. Indoor capacity limits for retail were removed. Indoor gatherings are strongly discouraged by the state but are allowed in the orange tier. Only three households can gather at a time with face masks and social distancing. Museums, zoos and family entertainment centers all now have greater indoor capacity. Outdoor live events were permitted beginning Thursday, April 1 with many modifications. Last Friday, April 2, the state announced indoor concerts, performances and other events will be allowed starting next Thursday, April 15. On March 9, Alameda County was moved into the red tier, or substantial tier, the second-most restrictive tier. Before that, the county was in the most-restrictive purple tier, or widespread tier, for several months. The county must meet orange tier benchmarks for at least three weeks before moving into the least-restrictive yellow tier, or minimal tier. Accordingly, the soonest the county could move up tiers is April 20. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in Alameda County remained at 1.4 percent as of Monday, April 5. This rate will need to stay below 4.9 percent for the county to remain in the orange tier. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to stay below 3.9 – right now there are 3.5 cases per 100,000. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to stay below 5.2 percent – it is currently 2.1 percent in Alameda County. To move into the yellow tier, the cases per day need to be below 1 per 100,000 and the positivity rate needs to be below 2 percent. The positivity rate in low-income census tracts needs to be below 2.2 percent. Two new cases of COVID-19 were reported in Piedmont over the past seven days. In total, there have been 172 COVID-19 cases reported in Piedmont. Across Alameda County, the total caseload for the county is 83,979, an increase of 681 new cases week-over-week. There have been 26,074 cases recorded in Oakland and 13,158 cases in Hayward. There have been 1,432 deaths caused by COVID-19 countywide, an increase of 31 in the past seven days. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,583,830 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 58,541 deaths due to the disease statewide. In his remarks, Newsom noted that infections are decreasing and that California has “the lowest case rates, positivity rates in America.” You may now subscribe online at:

articles.text: California opened COVID- 19 vaccination eligibility last Thursday, April 1 to all people age 50 and over, although vaccination appointments remain in extremely high demand in Alameda County. Expecting an influx of vaccine supply, the state announced last month plans to expand eligibility to all Californians over the age of 16 next Thursday, April 15. Alameda County’s website lists people ages 50 and over as eligible for the vaccine but requests that residents “please complete our notification form to hear when appointments are available.” The notification form is available at covid-19.acgov.org/vaccines 28.5 percent of the county’s population is now fully vaccinated. In Oakland, over 45 percent of the population has received at least one dose and 28 percent of Oaklanders are fully vaccinated. Even as all adult residents become eligible for vaccination next week, the state expects it will take several months for everyone who wants a vaccine to get one. Last month, Alameda County opened vaccine eligibility to people aged 16 to 64 years old “who are deemed to be at the very highest risk due to complex health conditions,” the county stated. The severe health conditions include cancer, kidney disease, down syndrome, pregnancy, sickle cell disease, heart conditions, severe obesity and several other comorbidities. Furthermore, people aged 65 years and older have been eligible for weeks. Essential workers in healthcare, food, agriculture, education, childcare, emergency services, public transportation and air travel are eligible. Additionally, those working or living in congregate living facilities, including people experiencing homelessness, are eligible. This week, the county announced that the mass vaccination site at the Oakland Coliseum will remain open even though its contract with FEMA is scheduled to end on Sunday, April 11. The county is still dealing with a demand for vaccine that outstrips supply, although new shipments of doses should mitigate the issue in the coming weeks. The county is hoping to vaccinate at least 70 percent of the population. The state has administered about 20.3 million vaccine doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. The state is vaccinating an average of over 360,360 people per day, a significant increase compared to last week. Californians are also encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, employer or the county to receive a vaccination appointment. The state asks residents to utilize the digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn.ca.gov to determine their vaccine eligibility and schedule appointments. Three different COVID-19 vaccines are currently being administered in Alameda County. Vaccines from Moderna and Pfizer, mRNA vaccines that were both first approved last year, require two doses injected several weeks apart. A vaccine manufactured by Johnson and Johnson, a viral vector-type vaccine, requires only one dose. County health experts encourage residents to take the vaccine that is available to them the soonest. “While the Johnson and Johnson vaccine has slightly lower effectiveness against all COVID- 19 symptoms, all three vaccines are 100 percent effective against death and hospitalization,” the Alameda County Public Health Department states. Over 45 percent of Piedmont’s adult population, some 3,746 people, have been fully vaccinated as of Sunday, April 4, according to ACPHD data. The health department reports that 5,693 Piedmonters have received at least one dose, which amounts to almost 69 percent of the City. Piedmont is the most vaccinated municipality in the county by a wide margin, but other cities are catching up. A pamphlet detailing the project was mailed to Piedmont residents last week. The existing path entry on Highland Avenue will be replaced by a new entry plaza, with light poles and benches placed along the walkway. articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will host a public discussion with Alameda County District Attorney Nancy O’Malley on May 6 starting at 4 p.m. She will describe the work by her department with abused and homeless women, helping them move beyond trauma into a positive future. O’Malley will address the many challenges COVID-19 has posed. She will explain the ways in which the current lack of civility in politics is impeding the pace and scale of progress for women who suffer from violence. For example, passage of the Violence Against Women Act was held up due to politics, and funding for the Victims Crime Act, which provides resources to states for victims of crime, was also reduced. O’Malley is a nationally recognized expert on issues involving violence against women, violence against persons with disabilities, and interpersonal violence including sexual assault, domestic violence, elder abuse, child abuse, stalking, and human exploitation and trafficking. She serves in the office that dates to a time when Earl Warren was the Alameda County D.A. before becoming United States Supreme Court Chief Justice. O’Malley is the first woman to serve as the County’s District Attorney. The event is free and open to all community members, to register for the Zoom event, visit https:// www.lwvpiedmont.org/content. a spx?page_id= 40 02&club_ id=601389&item_id=1256825. It will be recorded and posted on the League of Women Voters of Piedmont website for those who cannot join live.

articles.text: If you own real property in California, you must pay property taxes twice a year. The second installment of property taxes is normally due on April 10. However, since this year that date falls on a Saturday, the due date is the next business day, or April 12. Missing the deadline is a very expensive mistake, since the penalty is 10% plus a $10 fee. If you don’t pay by June 30th, things start to get worse very quickly. You can send a check, along with your 2nd payment voucher, or pay by phone. However, most people find it more convenient to pay online. The Alameda County Tax Collector’s URL for making payments is: http://co.alameda.ca.us/propertytax/ If you want to use a credit card and get those frequent flyer miles, you can do so, but you pay a 2.5% processing fee (the money does not go to the county). A direct debit to your bank account does not incur any additional charges. Finally, if you have incurred a financial hardship due to the Covid pandemic and are unable to pay your taxes, do not simply ignore the deadline. The Tax Collector has an online form (see the above URL) you can fill out to avoid penalties, although you are still responsible for the taxes themselves.

articles.text: MS, OTR/L Are you beginning to think that handwriting is obsolete? This is certainly a valid thought given our students’ dependency over the last year due to the pandemic on keyboarding assignments instead of handwriting them. Keyboarding is always legible and who doesn’t like spell check? At a recent IEP (Individualized Education Plan) meeting for a student that I serve, the topic of handwriting versus keyboarding was raised. Lists can be made on phones, letters sent by email and essays written using Google documents. In short, is handwriting even necessary? To this question, the answer is a resounding Yes. Recent research, comparing handwriting to keyboarding, found handwriting improves memory/recall, comprehension, and even test scores. Handwriting remains an essential skill for both younger and older students, including those in college. Three recent studies noted the following: • Preschool students were taught to copy letters of the alphabet by hand or by typing them. After three weeks of learning, letter recognition tests were completed. The older preschool students in the handwriting instruction/ practice group demonstrated better letter recognition - a fundamental skill for learning letter sounds and reading (Longcamp et al, 2005). • One study compared methods of note taking, handwritten or typed, and the recall and understanding of children 10–11 years old. Using a multiple-choice question (MCQ) format, factual recall and understanding of a history and a biology lesson were assessed. MCQ tests were carried out both immediately after each lesson and one week later. Factual recall was not affected by the note-takStudies show there are many benefits to handwriting, so don’t give up your pencil yet. • ing mode, but those students who wrote their notes by hand had greater conceptual understanding one week after their lesson compared to those who typed notes (Horbury & Edmonds, 2021). Eighty college students were included in a study to compare taking notes or a quiz by hand or on their laptop. Those who took notes by hand performed better on quizzes overall and with conceptual questions than students who took notes on their laptop, suggesting that handwritten notes may improve how students encode and store material. (Crumb et al, 2020). The cognitive benefits of handwriting compared to keyboarding as noted above are just one facet. There are many other benefits from handwriting. Some examples include: • Handwriting helps students to slow down and gather their thoughts. • Handwriting benefits creative writing by removing the urge to immediately edit as one writes thereby allowing thoughts to flow more freely and less fragmented. • Handwriting supports writing outlines and brainstorming ideas. A blank page has no restrictions - add side notes or circle important points to link thoughts. So even though lists can be made on phones, letters sent in an email and essays written on the computer, at a minimum, encourage your student to put down their laptops and take handwritten notes in class, as they read a chapter or make index cards for studying with a nicely sharpened pencil. If your student is a naysayer, share the evidence-based research with them. They may come to realize that they’d prefer an A on that quiz instead of the ease of spell check. Kimberly Bonacum is an occupational therapist for Piedmont Unified School District and owner of Mindful Fidgets, LLC www.mindfulfidgets.com. For additional questions, she can be contacted at mindfulfidgets@ gmail.com.
articles.title: Is keyboarding making handwriting obsolete?

articles.text: The Piedmont Council BSA’s 100th Annual Recognition Dinner last month included many awards for volunteers who make the program a success. Included in the honorees is one award presented to a youth who demonstrates outstanding youth leadership and service to the Council. Bridget Bentley, president of the Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) was presented with the annual William R. Peterson Award for Leadership by Youth. Established in 1999, it honors William R. Peterson, a lifelong Scouter who died in 1998. The award recognizes a Piedmont Council youth, who demonstrates the benefits of being a member of the youth-run organization, and who has demonstrated outstanding youth leadership. Bentley led a team of nine vice-presidents, organized and presided over monthly crew meetings, and dedicated time to welcome all new members. In the past, she was VP of Fundraising, VP of Administration, served on the Rebuilding Together Oakland house renovation project planning team, and led the planning for a summer backpacking trip. She attended the 6-day National Youth Leadership Training (NYLT) course and served on its staff the following year. She is a co-founder of Camp Crew which took over the operation of Piedmont’s Cub Scout Day Camp. She served as Camp Crew President last year when the council had to change camp plans to a virtual camp due to COVID-19. After joining the Venturing program’s High Adventure Crew as a high school freshman, she discovered that she loved backpacking. She is presently a co-VP of the Crew and an essential reason for that crew’s ongoing success. Bridget has also been involved in the Piedmont BSA Council Board of Directors as a youth member of the Marketing Committee. Bridget Bentley, the president of the Piedmont Community Service Crew, was named the recipient of the Piedmont Scout Council’s annual William Peterson Youth Leadership Award.
articles.title: Bridget Bentley earns Peterson Leadership Award

articles.text: Piedmont High School alums (Class of 2017) Sebastian Mueller and Madison Pehanick have been named to the Honor Roll at Oregon State University. A total of 8,150 students earned at least a 3.5 GPA to qualify for the Scholastic Honor Roll. Mueller, a senior, is majoring in Environmental Sciences. Pehanick, also a senior, is a Digital Communication Arts major. Located principally in Corvallis, Oregon State is one of only two universities in the nation designated as a land, sea, space and sun grant. The school serves the world by working on today’s most pressing issues. Its 31,000 students come from across the globe. The school receives more research funding than all of the state’s comprehensive public universities combined. Its campuses are in Corvallis, Bend and marine research facility in Newport.
articles.title: Piedmont students on Oregon State Honor Roll

articles.text: Last Sunday, April 4th, was Easter. Just like the entire last year, it’s been anything but normal. No churches promoting their traditional Easter egg hunts, no big gatherings, and no major festivities. But that didn’t stop families from celebrating together. As I began my day on Sunday, I saw Easter eggs in front of houses and kids running around frantically trying to collect the eggs ahead of their younger siblings. I saw houses decked out in Easter décor, with bunny paraphernalia, big plastic eggs in the yards, and streamers in spring colors. There was a sense of holiday, after all. I have always loved Easter, but as I get older, I find myself reflecting on some holiday concepts. In addition to Easter as a major religious event, its celebrations involve having eggs with candy in them being placed in yards. But if there are eggs, why is a bunny the mascot and not a chicken? I mean, a bunny is certainly more friendly than a chicken, but I would love to know why, Easter bunnies? This year the city didn’t have its annual egg hunt in the park, and I don’t understand why. Sure, we’re still in the pandemic, but Alameda Country is in the orange tier, and the age of kids participating in the hunt is usually under 10 – the lowest risk group. OK, occasionally a group of teenagers who have nothing better to do will join in. But it’s quite easy to be socially distant while egg hunting. I remember that I once did an Easter egg hunt when I was in kindergarten and I was so excited because I had the most eggs out of the entire class. But when I went to open my collection, I discovered that they were real eggs. I was hoping for jelly beans, but instead was faced with egg yolks. I have had trust issues ever since that day. When I was younger, I always had Easter celebrations with my friends. We would dye eggs with beautiful colors or draw cute designs on them. I remember one time when I was coloring eggs with my grandma, my hand let go of the egg I was holding, and the dye splashed everywhere. Let’s just say that my grandma wasn’t happy, because who likes to be doused with vibrant purple dye? But she cooled off quickly, and before long we were decorating our special Easter cakes. We dip them in icing and cover them in sprinkles. It’s one of my favorite traditions. For all struggling parents, I know that you definitely didn’t hold back on making yourself another mimosa when your toddler asked you for the fifth time to get an egg that was too high or when you heard a crash and an oops and knew it was the vase your mother got you as a wedding gift. I do know that Easter used to be a day when parents invited their friends over to socialize while the kids searched frantically outside for the eggs. Now some parents just sit on a lawn chair with a pair of shades over their eyes and pretend they’re asleep so the kids will leave them alone. Hopefully, next year there will be more normalcy and Easter can go back to its full potential. I can’t wait to dye eggs, create my own egg hunts, and eat way too much chocolate. To the parents, I hope that your Easter went well without too many broken vases. If I were you, I would book tickets next year to the Maldives so your mind can be put to rest. To grandparents, I hope you get vaccinated soon, so that you can reunite with your grandkids who may or may not douse you in purple dye. And for now, I hope everyone had an enjoyable Easter. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont student with a keen eye and the ability to be in several places at one time.
articles.title: The last Covid Easter – and the meaning of trust

articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is sponsoring its second annual essay contest, open to all Piedmont high school juniors and seniors. The essay should answer the question, “Given the fragility of democracy as evidenced by the insurrection of January 6, 2021, how can your generation work to ensure that democracy in the United States is strengthened for future generations?” Contest entrants may, but are not required to, rely on outside sources that are properly cited within the text and in a bibliography. A specific format for citations or bibliography is not required, but there must be enough information to allow the judges to easily verify your sources. Citations do not count toward your total number of words. Remember that this essay is not solely a research paper and should draw on the writer’s personal experiences and insights. Essays will be judged on originality, clarity of expression, vocabulary and style, proper grammar, punctuation and spelling. Students are encouraged to have a teacher, parent or mentor review the essay prior to submission keeping in mind that all work must be the student’s own. The essay must be 250 to 500 words, excluding citations. At the top of the essay include the following information: the title, your first and last name, city of residence (must be Piedmont), name of your school, and your current grade. Essays must be typed and double-spaced and submitted in a .pdf format. All entries are to be submitted to lwvpiedmont@gmail.com. The deadline is April 17. Winners will be announced on May 1. The list included former Piedmont mayors Skip Rhodes and Michael Bruck, George Zimmer, John Protopappas, Jon and Ann Reynolds, Joyce Hicks and Eric Behrens, Dana Sack, Carolyn Bruck, and Carla Betts. Also on hand was Oakland Mayor Libby Schaff with a proclamation honoring Parrot. “I thought the zoo did an excellent job,’ said Rhodes. “They honored Joel in a number of ways. His successor, Nik Dehejia, gave a very nice tribute to him and Mayor Schaff’s proclamation from the City Council of ‘Joel Parrott Day’ was a fitting touch. Everyone there let Joel know what a tremendous job he did,” Zimmer, a longtime benefactor of the Zoo, funded the creation of the Oakland Zoo Education Center. “It was a fun event; everyone was very happy,” said Bruck, a current Representative of Docents on the zoo’s board. The docents added Parrot as an honorary docent and presented him with a docent shirt to be displayed at the zoo. During the event the zoo also unveiled its new exhibit, “Taking Action Against the Illegal Wildlife Trade,” an exclamation mark on Dr. Parrott illustrious tenure, and his strong support of wildlife preservation causes. pages.text: Wednesday, April 7, 2021 11 Inching closer to May 2 Art Walk More than 40 local artists sign up for 2nd annual event The popular Piedmont Art Walk, now in its 2nd year, is benefitting from last year’s success. More than 40 local artists have signed up so far to show their art outside on Sunday, May 2 between 12:00- 5:00 p.m. Paintings, ceramics, mixed media, sculpture, photography, quilts, and textile art will be displayed and shown by local artists in front of their homes The community is invited to enjoy this outdoor art event and fundraiser hosted by local Piedmont artists and the Piedmont Arts Fund. The event is generously supported by Grubb Company owner DJ Grubb and MN Builders owner Steve Nicholls. Purchases support artists in town and 20 percent of proBeach Umbrellas by Pam Murray. Mixed media, torn paper collage. Yendo al laburo, oil on canvas, by Raul Jorcino. ceeds will be donated to the Piedmont Arts Fund to support art in the schools. The Art Walk features a Who’s Who of Piedmont artists. Residents and students may not realize how many accomplished artists live in Piedmont. The event brings together live art, artists, and community members while following Alameda County’s COVID- 19 guidelines to keep everyone safe. The event is spread out over Piedmont to avoid crowds and ensure social distancing. When the COVID quarantine took effect in last March, the Piedmont Arts Fund (formerly PAINTS and CHIME) had to cancel their spring fundraisers. The diminished school budget outlook for next school year makes this year’s fundraising critical for mainMoon Jar. Ceramic. By Roberta Gross. taining robust art programs in Piedmont schools. Plan now to take a walk on Sunday afternoon, May 2 to visit the artists during the second Annual Piedmont Art Walk. Who knows? You may find a new art piece that brightens your day and supports art in the schools. For an online map and to see a gallery of artists, visit https://piedmontartsfund.org/ piedmont-art-walk-2021. articles.text: Piedmont’s tennis team traveled to Alameda for a rematch with the Hornets, but on Saturday, Apri 3, the results were the same as their match on March 13. The Highlanders skipped home with their second 7-0 shutout of Alameda. It was the team’s sixth straight victory. Their only loss has been to Miramonte on March 2. Their final match of the regular season is today, Wednesday, April 7 against University at Golden Gate Park. They’ll return to Alameda for the Western Alameda County Conference’s singles and doubles championships on Friday and Saturday, April 16-17. “We swept Alameda for the second time this season, but that’s not to say it was easy. Everyone played really well. We had some close points, and our No. 1 singles starter, Charlie Lambert, went to a third-set super breaker against a good opponent,” said coach Jim Landes. Lambert’s results with Mason Conlin were 6-4, 4-6, 10-5. He beat Conlin in an earlier meeting this season, 7-6 (7-5), 6-2. “Charlie was pushed to a super breaker and played superbly. He lost his second set after becoming a bit too conservative trying to close it out, and got pushed around the court by Conlin, who can pop some big forehands. In the breaker, Charlie took control with his own forehands,” said Landes of Lambert’s day. Other than No. 1 singles, it was a complete day of straight sets for the rest of the roster. Sajan Srivastava had a 6-3, 6-3 win at No. 2 singles, freshman Ben Breber had a 6-4, 6-0 win at No. 3 singles, while senior Luke Charlie Lambert won a grueling 3-set victory over Alameda’s Mason Conlin, 6-4, 4-6, 10-5. Freshman Ben Breber won 6-4, 6-0 at No. 3 singles.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team pulled out a big 6-1 win over league opponent Alameda on Saturday, April 3 at the Corey Reich Tennis Center. The team’s two seniors, Makenna Thiel and Audrey Edel were celebrated by teammates on Senior Day. Prior to the match, coaches Jim Landes and Neil Rothenberg recalled watching both players grow up before their eyes, as Piedmont players presented flowers to seniors on both teams. “She used to be in the clinics Anne Jumper had Piedmont’s clinching victory against Alameda. It was her first win of the season. The first win of the day came from the No. 2 doubles’ team of Audrey Mahany (front) and Mara LaForte. I taught at the Hampton Courts back when she was five- or six-years old,” said Landes in describing Edel. “It’s been a long, long time.” Rothenberg recalled his time as head coach with her older sister, Kaelli, meeting up to hit with a growing Makenna. Rothenberg, in particular, came out of retirement to help out with both girls’ and boys’ programs for 2021. “I’ve known Makenna since Kaelli was a freshman, so when she was around seven- or eightyears old – since she was kneehigh,” said Rothenberg. Saturday’s win against the Hornets brought Piedmont’s record to 4-3 with two nonleague matches remaining prior to the Western Alameda County Conference on Friday and Saturday, April 16-17 at Alameda High. Their win avenges a 4-3 loss to the Hornets on March 13. It was a big afternoon for Anne Jumper at No. 4 singles, who reeled in Piedmont’s fourth victory to guarantee a team win in a best-of-seven matches. Her 6-4, 6-4 win was her first victory of the season. She rallied after trailing 0-4 in the second set, snapping off six straight games to win it for the Highlanders. “I got a lot less nervous as the match went on and grew confidence in my line-calls, so I started taking more risks,” Jumper said. “I started hitting more angles, but a big part has been just shaking the nerves. I’ve had some problems throughout the season just collecting myself and not getting nervous. The big thing for me was just going out there with confidence,” said Jumper, with an ear-to-ear smile underneath her mask. Piedmont’s first win came from the No. 2 doubles combination of sophomore Mara LaForte and junior Audrey Mahany in straight sets 6-4, 6-2; playing with dominant forehands from Mahany out of the back and several smashes from LaForte in front of the net. Sooner after, No. 3 singles starter Bridgette McEfee won in straight sets 6-2, 6-3, followed by Amanda Becker and Michaela Bini dominating to a 6-3, 6-3 win at No. 1 doubles. After Jumper’s clinching victory, No. 1 singles starter Thiel powered through Kyra Yee, 6-2, 6-1. It was the first time she allowed an opponent to win a game in four appearances. Rosie Siemers and Kate Dorman, meanwhile, won 7-6 (7-0), Staff Photos Piedmont’s tennis team celebrated its two seniors on Senior Day: Audrey Edel (left) and Makenna Thiel. 6-1 at No. 3 doubles. Audrey Edel at No. 2 lost 6-0, 7-5. Loss against Campolindo The Highlanders traveled to Moraga to play Campolindo for a non-league match on Tuesday, April 6 and lost in a one-sided defeat, 8-1. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (4-4) heads to Miramonte for a non-league match with Miramonte on Thursday, April 8 for the regular season finale at 3:30 p.m. The league will host its individual league championship tournament at Alameda High on Friday and Saturday, April 16-17.

articles.text: Piedmont’s track team brought 12 athletes to Pittsburg for the Pirates Steel City Invitational on Saturday, April 3, competing in 11 events in a meet with 14 schools. The most active event was the 100-meter dash, where junior Luke Alban placed sixth with a time of 11.76. Also in the event, Matthew Riordan had a time of 12.23. PHS fielded teams in two boys’ relay events. The 4x100 team of Quincy Munyan, Matthew Riordan, Parker Terrill, and Luke Alban placed 3rd in a time of 48.60 seconds. The same group ran in the 4x200, placing 4th with a time of 1:40.3. Jack Zirkelbach had a time of 5:23.45 in the 1600. Jasmine Ghaderi placed 2nd of seven in the pole vault, clearing a height of 8- feet, 6-inches. In other field events, Gavin Horne and Aaron Valva threw the shot 29 feet, 10 inches and 28 feet, 4.5 inches respectively. In the discus, Valva had a throw of 81-feet, 2 inches, Munyan threw 68-feet, 2-inches; and Kai Lambert had 65-feet, 3-inches. Parker Terrill was 2nd of four in the high jump after clearing a height of 5-feet, 8-inches, Horne was 3rd at 5-6. As for the long jump, Horne was also 3rd in the long jump with a leap of 18-feet, 8.5 inches. Terrill was close behind at 17-feet, 11-inches. In his third event, Horne leaped 33-feet, 3.5-inches in the triple jump. Connor Kim placed 3rd in the Pole Vault at 8-feet, 6-inches, tied with freshman Spencer SorensenWald. Lambert had a height of 6-0. NEXT UP Piedmont competes in the NorCal 1-day Multi-Event at Alhambra HS in Martinez today, Wednesday, April 7 at 7:30 a.m. Photos by Steve Zirkelbach Connor Kim vaulted 8-feet, 6-inches at the Steel City Invitational, to place 3rd.
