articles.text: Caroline Devine scored seven goals and had four assists against Monte Vista. Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team went toe-to-toe with Monte Vista in Danville before losing 13-12 to the Division 1 North Coast Section opponent. As a reminder, PHS plays in Division 2 and were the 2019 champions. With a shortened season and just five games remaining, and no playoffs planned, coach Carlton Chan was committed to scheduling some solid competition. The Highlanders were well within grasp of a victory, but some confusion on the field took place and mistakenly Monte Vista was awarded an extra possession. The Western Alameda County Conference has new rules for teams with the removal of the draw (faceoff) circle. “We knew we’d play some tough teams. It was a tough loss against Monte Vista. We were doing alternate possessions because of the WACC’s rules against taking draws [faceoffs] and the Mustangs were inadvertently given an extra possession. I can’t blame them because it gets a little confusing with these new rules, but in a 1-score loss, it was critical,” explained Chan. The game was deadlocked at 6-6 going into halftime, and extended to the very last Monte Vista possession for the game-winner. Katherine Kinne got the day started for the Purple and White with a goal in the first 30 seconds, but MV’s Allison Devane followed up with a score of their own after a couple of minutes. Kinne added her second goal to put PHS ahead 2-1, but the Mustangs tied again. “Monte Vista had a couple of strong players, Allison Devane Katherine Kinne (13) scored a hat trick against Monte Vista. was a tough lefty. Who drove well and kicked the ball out perfectly. She always occupied two defenders,” mentioned Chan. The game went back and forth with goals from Caroline Devine, while Sadie Tschider landed a goal on a pass from Devine. While at 4-4, Kinne got her hat trick with 13 minutes left in the half 5-4, but the Mustangs galloped back once again after a minute and a half. Tschider added Piedmont’s sixth goal with around 11 minutes left in the half, but they couldn’t get back on the board with stout defense from both sides. MV’s Devane scored with 6:11 left in the first half and the score remained 6-6 until halftime. The Highlanders jumped into a 2-goal lead right after halftime with scores by Devine and Tschider within five minutes. Some costly turnovers opened the door for the Mustangs to come back. MV got back on the board to make it 8-7 with 20 minutes left, but Devine stretched it back to 9-7—she had the next four scores for PHS, but it unfortunately wasn’t enough. After a Mustang score, Devine scored with 15:20 left in the game on another slick pass from Tschider. The Highlanders held an 11-9 lead with another score from Devine with 11:27 left in the game, but MV stormed back with six goals in the last 10 minutes, and two in the last 30 seconds. Devine scored, once again, with 7:07 on the clock to make it 12-11 and PHS went up 13-11 with slightly over 6 minutes left. But from there, MV’s Jaiden Wire netted their 12th with 3:30 left and the tying goal with 25 seconds on the clock, following a quick turnover at midfield, MV scored the winner. But Devine had one last chance, drawing a foul at the 12-yard line and peeling off an angled shot with 1.2 seconds left after driving past two defenders. Devine, who drew contact within the shooting area, wasn’t given a free-space penalty on the play. “For whatever reason, the refs did not award her free possession and instead placed her on the 12. Even still, she battled through two defenders and the goalie made the save with 1.2 seconds left,” added Chan. Final stats include: Devine with seven goals, four assists. Tschider had three goals, four assists. Kinne scored three goals. Goalie Sophia Ethington recorded three saves in the first half. Lindsay Kottle entered in the second half, recording five saves. Piedmont girls take Monte Vista to the wire By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team went toe-to-toe with Monte Vista in Danville before losing 13-12 to the Division 1 North Coast Section opponent. As a reminder, PHS plays in Division 2 and were the 2019 champions. With a shortened season and just five games remaining, and no playoffs planned, coach Carlton Chan was committed to scheduling some solid competition. The Highlanders were well within grasp of a victory, but some confusion on the field took place and mistakenly Monte Vista was awarded an extra possession. The Western Alameda County Conference has new rules for teams with the removal of the draw (faceoff) circle. “We knew we’d play some tough teams. It was a tough loss against Monte Vista. We were doing alternate possessions because of the WACC’s rules against taking draws [faceoffs] and the Mustangs were inadvertently given an extra possession. I can’t blame them because it gets a little confusing with these new rules, but in a 1-score loss, it was critical,” explained Chan. The game was deadlocked at 6-6 going into halftime, and extended to the very last Monte Vista possession for the game-winner. Katherine Kinne got the day started for the Purple and White with a goal in the first 30 seconds, but MV’s Allison Devane followed up with a score of their own after a couple of minutes. Kinne added her second goal to put PHS ahead 2-1, but the Mustangs tied again. “Monte Vista had a couple of strong players, Allison Devane Katherine Kinne (13) scored a hat trick against Monte Vista. was a tough lefty. Who drove well and kicked the ball out perfectly. She always occupied two defenders,” mentioned Chan. The game went back and forth with goals from Caroline Devine, while Sadie Tschider landed a goal on a pass from Devine. While at 4-4, Kinne got her hat trick with 13 minutes left in the half 5-4, but the Mustangs galloped back once again after a minute and a half. Tschider added Piedmont’s sixth goal with around 11 minutes left in the half, but they couldn’t get back on the board with stout defense from both sides. MV’s Devane scored with 6:11 left in the first half and the score remained 6-6 until halftime. The Highlanders jumped into a 2-goal lead right after halftime with scores by Devine and Tschider within five minutes. Some costly turnovers opened the door for the Mustangs to come back. MV got back on the board to make it 8-7 with 20 minutes left, but Devine stretched it back to 9-7—she had the next four scores for PHS, but it unfortunately wasn’t enough. After a Mustang score, Devine scored with 15:20 left in the game on another slick pass from Tschider. The Highlanders held an 11-9 lead with another score from Devine with 11:27 left in the game, but MV stormed back with six goals in the last 10 minutes, and two in the last 30 seconds. Devine scored, once again, with 7:07 on the clock to make it 12-11 and PHS went up 13-11 with slightly over 6 minutes left. But from there, MV’s Jaiden Wire netted their 12th with 3:30 left and the tying goal with 25 seconds on the clock, following a quick turnover at midfield, MV scored the winner. But Devine had one last chance, drawing a foul at the 12-yard line and peeling off an angled shot with 1.2 seconds left after driving past two defenders. Devine, who drew contact within the shooting area, wasn’t given a free-space penalty on the play. “For whatever reason, the refs did not award her free possession and instead placed her on the 12. Even still, she battled through two defenders and the goalie made the save with 1.2 seconds left,” added Chan. Final stats include: Devine with seven goals, four assists. Tschider had three goals, four assists. Kinne scored three goals. Goalie Sophia Ethington recorded three saves in the first half. Lindsay Kottle entered in the second half, recording five saves. articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team split its two games last week, falling to Berkeley 4-0 on the road on Tuesday, March 30, and winning dramatically, 6-5, in a late inning comeback against St. Joseph of Alameda on Saturday, April 3. Sophomore second baseman Michael Aikawa slugged a tworun homerun in the bottom of the sixth to win it for the Highlanders. “All my teammates say that all they saw were fastballs, I think he threw just one off-speed. I was looking for a fastball. I saw a low fastball, inside and low, and turned on it,” explained Aikawa. Aikawa is building quite a resume for his heroics this year. It is his second game-winning hit after smacking an RBI double in an earlier game against Oakland Tech in the bottom of the fifth. But it’s not just Aikawa getting the job done in high-intensity situations. You can label coach Eric Olson’s team the “Clutch Kids.” They have won four of their games by fewer than two runs, and game-winning hits have come in the final two innings. “Unfortunately, we’ve gotten down in some games, but these kids have resolve and a ‘Never Say Die’ attitude,” Olson said. “Give credit to the quality of St. Joe. We’ve come back against some teams who aren’t as good as these guys. It’s one of the best wins I’ve seen here at this diamond,” said Olson after the win at Witter Field. The fire started for Piedmont when down 5-1 entering the bottom of the third inning. They scored progressive runs in the third, fourth, and fifth innings to make it 5-4 St. Joseph. And then Aikawa stepped to the plate in the bottom of the sixth to end it. In the bottom of the third, Aikawa drew a one-out walk and advanced to third base on two wild pitches, scoring on a single by Nico Defazio. Their run in the bottom fourth came after Evan McConathy came around to score after Will Sprague struck a hard line drive to the left fielder to cause a costly error and a 5-3 score. In the bottom of the fifth, Lars Derr reached on an error and came all the way around to score on a hard-hit ball through the infield by Cal Barna, recording a double to bring it within one run, 5-4. He describes having some background with St. Joseph’s pitcher, Emmitt Phinney. “The pitcher is a good friend of me. I knew he’d go fastball with runners on, so I just sat back and ripped it. It was a good at bat; it was fun,” said Barna, who also entered the game as the closing Staff Photo Nico Defazio got the comeback started with an RBI single in the bottom of the third. Staff Photo Cal Barna, who gained the save against St. Joseph, also hit an RBI double in part of PHS’ comeback victory. Photo by Mark Aikawa Michael Aikawa (16) heads to his jubilant teammates at home after hitting a two-run game-winning home run against Berkeley in the bottom of the sixth. pitcher in the top of the seventh. In the critical bottom of the sixth, Sprague drew a two-out walk to bring up Aikawa. With a 0-1 count, Aikawa turned on a low fastball to smack the ball over the high left field fence. Starting on the mound was Ben Levinson, where it’s worth mentioning St. Joseph’s five runs scored were all unearned. After the first two innings, Levinson allowed just two base runners, one hit, and finished with 10 strikeouts. In relief, Julian Scherman gained the win with two strikeouts in one inning of work. Barna gained the save as the closer, striking out one. Final stats include Aikawa went 1-for-3 with his home run, two RBIs, three runs scored, and a walk. Defazio went 2-for-3, one RBI. Barna went 1-for-2, an RBI, and a walk. Loss to Berkeley Piedmont was shut out by Berkeley 4-0 on March 30, snapping its five-game winning streak. Stats include Derr recording a double, while individual hits went to Aikawa, Aidan Mitchell, and Evan McConathy. Piedmont loses to El Cerrito The Highlanders’ played El Cerrito yesterday, Tuesday, April 6 on the road, and came away with a 10-2 loss. See next week’s Post for game details. NEXT UP Piedmont (6-3) heads to Encinal in Alameda today, Wednesday, April 7 for a 4:00 p.m. game, and then hosts Encinal at Humphries Diamond on Friday, April 9, 4:00 p.m. They will also host Castro Valley on Saturday, April 10 at 2:00 p.m.

articles.text: She’s “art teacher” to 280 students at Wildwood Elementary School and “mom” to two students at Piedmont Middle School. But Piedmont resident Larraine Seiden is also a working artist whose ability to adapt kept her creating throughout the COVID- 19 pandemic. “I try to harness interruption,” said Seiden, whose work has been seen throughout the Bay Area and across the country. “My time was still the same. I was still teaching the whole time. My kids were here the whole time. I just harnessed that even more — to keep working.” Seiden took inspiration from the new reality that came with the March 2020 shutdown to create several new pieces of art. When the pandemic also forced cancellations of her scheduled art shows and events, she adapted again — and worked with other Piedmont artists to create the 2020 Art Walk. “Everybody here was walking every day,” she said. “I thought, what if we just do an art walk here in town and give people something to see?” “Crowded Room” by Larraine Seiden. Photo by Kristen Hatcher Larraine Seiden in her studio with a work of art from her series “The Vanishing Points Suite.” The concept of artists’ open studio was moved out of doors for almost 20 local artists, who donated a portion of their sales to support arts programs in the local schools. As one of this year’s Piedmont Art Walk participants, Seiden hopes the event will again raise needed funding. “The teachers of the arts really depend on that money and it was harder to get this year,” Seiden said. “We actually had to spend more this year because we had to buy kits for art at home. I had to buy [art supplies] for every student.” Seiden is still managing distance-learning with her Wildwood students and is making plans to exhibit her work over the coming months. Whatever changes the pandemic brings, she will continue to teach and create. “Interruption is just a part of my life,” she said. “I used to fight that, and I just don’t anymore. My art has grown into those interruptions of time.” This year’s Art Walk will take place on Sundey, May 2, from 12 noon to 5 p.m. Kristen Hatcher is a member of the Piedmont Arts Fund, which supports visual and performing arts programs for students in Piedmont schools.

articles.text: California Sister butterfly The UC Berkeley Botanical Garden staff will host a virtual butterfly walk and presentation this Sunday, April 11 at 11 a.m. Join resident botanists Sal Levinson and Sarab Seth for this monthly presentation, held via Zoom, and learn about the garden’s butterflies as well as some species rarely seen in the garden. Some of the more common species sighted in the gardens are West Coast Ladies, Painted Ladies, Common Buckeyes, Fiery Skippers, and Red Admirals. Resident propagators will Photo by Sarab Seth describe what makes these species unique. Those who tune in will also learn about the butterflies’ life cycles, preferred host plants, and how to “de-code” butterfly wing color. This event is suitable for all ages and will feature an illustrated slideshow. The event is free, but donations will benefit the garden’s education programs. articles.text: The 7th Annual Juried Art Show, presented by the Piedmont Center for the Arts, returns to the Center for a juried art exhibition selected from submissions, highlighting a large variety of contemporary 2-dimensional works by Bay Area artists. From a record-high 500 submissions of original art created within the past year, 35 pieces were selected by guest jurors René de Guzman, Senior Curator of Art at Oakland Museum of California, and Danielle Fox, Principal of Slate Gallery in Oakland. Thanks to an endowment by the family of John P. Thornborrow, cash awards of $4,000 are allocated annually to the top award winners, with an emphasis on honoring emerging artists in the Bay Area. René de Guzman, a Piedmont native and Senior Curator of Art at Oakland Museum of California, is one of two guest jurors of the 7th Annual Juried Art Show at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. articles.text: Woodminster Summer Musicals may be able to return to Woodminster Amphitheater in the Oakland Hills this summer. The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) and the California Department of Industrial Relations (CAL OSHA) released updated guidance for the safe operation of outdoor, seated, live events and performances. The joint guidance was released on March 26 and went into effect on April 1. According to the guidelines, venues can open for live audiences with a maximum of 33% capacity. Venues may increase attendance capacity to 67% if all guests show a negative test result within 72 hours prior to attendance or show proof of full vaccination. Performers, athletes, and workers who participate in routine, weekly testing are not counted toward any occupancy capacity limit. Only California spectators are to be allowed for outdoor live performances. At the time of ticket purchase, the operator of the venue must obtain verification that the ticket holder lives in California. Only advanced ticket reservations are permissible. These restrictions are in addition to all Center for Disease Control (CDC) sanitation recommendations and employee protocol and training. The 18-page guidance released by the state includes information for various, essential departments in live entertainment, such as casting, set design, scenery, sounds, props, costume and wardrobe and hair and makeup. Performers who “cannot feasibly perform or work with a face covering” (i.e. horn players in music groups) are not required to do so, as long as they are at least six feet from other performers and are routinely tested at least twice weekly for COVID-19. Performers may rehearse indoors. For the purpose of the guidance, a “permissible outdoor venue” is a permanent, fixed facility, either open to the sky with no roof or at least 50% of the perimeter open. It should be designed in a way that provides operators the ability to control the ingress and egress of all visitors; and there must be permanent or added barriers to create at least 12-feet of space between performers and audience members. The guest or ticket holder’s “block” of seat reservations should contain no more than one household, and advance ticketing is required. were released, Alameda County had already moved into the less restrictive Orange Tier, which made more indoor and outdoor business operations possible. Specifically, the guidance provides a loosening of restrictions for live performances, both indoor and outdoor. Nearby outdoor venues Some examples of venues that fit the description are Woodminster Amphitheater, home of the Summer Musical Theatre in Joaquin Miller Park in Oakland, and California Shakespeare Festival, whose summer productions are held at Bruns Amphitheater in the hills near Orinda. Other popular Bay Area music venues such as the Greek Theatre in Berkeley, the Shoreline Amphiteatre in Mountain View, and the Concord Pavilion, would qualify to re-open for outdoor, live events under the new guidance. Woodminster theatre holds 1,200 attendees, and the Bruns Amphitheater holds 545. At 33% capacity, as suggested by state guidelines, Woodminster could hold 396 attendees, and Bruns Amphitheater could hold 179. Woodminster Summer Musicals has not planned for fullstaged performances this summer, but Harriet Schlader, who, with her late husband James Schlader, founded Woodminster Summer Musicals in 1967, said that the company is looking at shows with small casts. Instead of a full orchestra, they will plan to have just a few musicians. Some possible musicals that will grace the stage this summer season include “Mirette,” “I Do, I Do,” “Blood Brothers,” and “Always…Patsy Cline.” Definitive details should be announced soon. Originally scheduled for last summer, 2020, Woodminster will produce An American in Paris, On Your Feet!, and Something Rotten for next year in July, August, and September 2022, respectively.
articles.title: State releases guidance, reduced restrictions, effective April 1

articles.text: You can now see George Balanchine’s full-length trilogy “Jewels” performed by the San Francisco Ballet and streaming through April 21. Told in three parts ­ – Emeralds, Rubies, and Diamonds – is inspired by the ornate displays at New York City jeweler Van Cleef & Arpels. Emeralds, the first in the trilogy, is set to music by Gabriel Faure. It evokes forest-green meditation in long, Romantic-era style skirts and costumes, and is influenced by the French style of ballet - restrained and pristine. Rubies follows next, set to the music of Igor Stravinsky. Vibrant, hot hues are reminiscent of Times Square at midnight. A touch of jazz in the choreography mimics rushing crowds and pedestrians. The finale, Diamonds, is set to the music of Tchaikovsky, and is a glittering homage to Imperial Russia, specifically to the style of Marius Petipa, the father of classical ballet. Balanchine is one of the most famous and prolific choreographers of the 20th century. Both Rubies and Diamonds will be archival captures. Streaming access will be available until April 21. For access, visit https:// www.sf ballet.org/productions/ digital-program-04/.
articles.title: SF Ballet’s Jewels streaming through April 21

articles.text: In the latest episode of “Aurora Connects,” a panel of industry leaders and casting directors discuss their experiences in the local and national theatre scene. Special guests include Jeffrey Lo, Casting Director at TheatreWorks Silicon Valley; Chicago-based theater director Lavina Jadhwani; and Bay Area casting director and instructor Dena Martinez. “Aurora Connects” is Aurora Theatre Company’s bi-weekly live broadcast, described as an “online salon and virtual happy hour.” A broadcast goes live every other Thursday at 5 p.m. on the theatre company’s YouTube channel. Each episode is hosted by Aurora Artistic Director Josh Costello and Associate Artistic Director Dawn Monique Williams. the Emerging Artist Laureate by Arts Council Silicon Valley and Theatre Bay Area Director’s TITAN Award. Jadhwani is a Chicago-based theatre director with nearly 15 years of facilitation experience. As a theatre director, her works have been featured at the Guthrie, Oregon Shakespeare Festival, Asolo Rep and others. The three guests discuss pitfalls and best practices of casting, and also examine casting through a racial justice lens. Martinez has over 30 years of national professional acting experience to her credits, and has toured nationally with the San Francisco Mime Troupe, Culture Clash, and the acclaimed El Teatro Campesino. To watch the discussion, visit https://www.auroratheatre.org/ auroraconnects. Theater Director Lavina Jadhwani is a special guest in the most recent episode of “Aurora Connects.” Lo is a Filipino-American playwright and director based in the Bay Area. He is the recipient of numerous accolades in the industry, including the Leigh Weimers Emerging Artist Award,
articles.title: Aurora Theatre roundtable discussion with casting directors

articles.text: Aspects of the fabulous career of the Hungarian firebrand violinist Edouard Remenyi. Note the announcement of his final concert in the Orpheum Theater and his notorious “bow of death.” Ever dream a life of romantic adventure? That was the introduction to one of the great radio dramas of the past. They should have done a program on the Hungarian violinist Edouard Remenyi. No one in the entire history of music led a more adventurous life than did Remenyi. He was a firebrand revolutionary in the 1848 Hungarian revolution. He fled Europe under penalty of death, came to the United States when our country was really wild, and played in the gold mining towns. Every music lover knows Brahms‘ Hungarian dances. So, let me ask you; who wrote Brahms’ Hungarian dances? Wrong. It was not Brahms at all. He plagiarized them… all of them. You need to remember that Brahms was a cocktail lounge piano player from the north of Germany; very far removed musically and culturally from the Hungarian gypsies. The composer was none other than Edouard Remenyi, that Hungarian firebrand. But now to return to our story. Remenyi was born in Hungary and had the usual musical education in Vienna. He was a child prodigy. And now the story gets really interesting. 1848 was the year of revolution everywhere. The Hungarians revolted against the young Austro-Hungarian Emperor Franz Joseph. General Kossuth, the leader of the Hungarians in revolt, chose Remenyi to be the psychological leader of the revolution. The young violinist played his violin in every military camp, drumming up enthusiasm. After Emperor Franz Joseph put down the revolution, he placed a bounty on Remenyi – “wanted dead or alive.“ Remenyi fled for his life as far from Europe as he could go. He came all the way to America and became an instant success. He traveled throughout the entire country playing concerts in formal concert halls as well as in saloons in the Wild West. Sometimes the miners were so enthusiastic that they threw gold nuggets onto the stage. On another occasion, Remenyi was so fatigued, he could not play the numerous encores the audience wanted. The rough audience became enraged and smashed all the furniture. Soon after, Queen Victoria sent a message to Remenyi that he was to be her court violinist in London. That’s when Austro-Hungarian Emperor Franz Joseph changed his mind. You guessed it. Franz Josef wanted Remenyi to be his private violinist in Vienna. It seems that all was forgiven. It was during this time that Remenyi’s friendship with Brahms disintegrated. But it wasn’t because of Brahms’ plagiarism; it was because of a woman. At about this same time he scampered to the top of the great pyramid in Egypt with his violin and played to the great nothingness of the Egyptian desert. The worldwide press later announced that he had drowned in a disaster at sea. He survived and announced that the news of his death was greatly exaggerated. Remenyi returned to America where he continued to enjoy great musical success. He became wealthy and possessed a large collection of expensive violins and expensive paintings. In retirement, his fortunes changed. The Orpheum vaudeville circuit lured him out of retirement and engaged him at what was announced as a “fabulous contract.” Remenyi traveled from New York across the country to San Francisco for his first engage-
articles.title: Concerts in the Wild West: The bow of death

articles.text: The Telegraph Quartet will give a virtual performance on Sunday, April 18, presented by Crowden Music Center as part of its “Sundays at Four” concert series. The quartet is comprised of Eric Chin and Joseph Maile (violins), Pei-Ling Lin (viola), and Jeremiah Shaw (cello). The performance will feature Britten’s Three Divertimenti; Beethoven’s String Quartet No. 1 in F Major, Op. 18 No. 1; and Brahms’ String Quartet No. 2 in A minor, Op. 51 No. 2. The concert will be performed and streamed live and is free to watch online with advance reservations; it will also be available for on-demand viewing for one week following the livestream on April 18. “All three of these works represent each composer’s first public foray into the string quartet medium,” explained Maile. “Benjamin Britten’s spirited Three Divertimenti were some of the young composer’s first professional works. Beethoven’s Op. 18 No. 1 is his ambitious, if slightly delayed, entry into the quartet medium as the vanguard of his set of six quartets. And Brahms’ wistful second string quartet is one of his two final products, of numerous discarded attempts – most likely with Beethoven metaphorically looking over his shoulder.” The concert will begin at 4 p.m. To reserve tickets, visit https://www.crowden.org/telegraph-quartet.
articles.title: Telegraph Quartet in concert April 18

articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC) will have its first concert of spring this Saturday, April 10, featuring with the concert choirs, Ensemble, Ecco, and Ancora groups performing. PEBCC’s most advanced choral ensembles will sing stories of the earth in the concert titled “Making History – Singing the Earth.” The concert, in partnership with the Stanford Chamber Chorale, will also include the world premiere of Kerry Andrew’s Wake Up! – a meditation on the climate crisis as seen through the eyes of young climate activists. Piedmont Choirs singers will also collaborate with Finnish youth choir Vox Aurea and medieval ensemble Yr Awen. The program will also include Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir rarely heard partsongs by the Black English composer Samuel Coleridge-Taylor. The concert begins at 4 p.m. PEBCC is able to offer the 2020- 2021 virtual concert season for free because of the generosity of patrons. To reserve a spot and make a donation for the April 10 performance, visit https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/event-calendar.
articles.title: Piedmont Choirs “Singing the Earth” concert on Saturday

Note the announcement of his final concert in the Orpheum Theater and his notorious “bow of death.” By Joseph Gold Ever dream a life of romantic adventure? That was the introduction to one of the great radio dramas of the past. They should have done a program on the Hungarian violinist Edouard Remenyi. No one in the entire history of music led a more adventurous life than did Remenyi. He was a firebrand revolutionary in the 1848 Hungarian revolution. He fled Europe under penalty of death, came to the United States when our country was really wild, and played in the gold mining towns. Every music lover knows Brahms‘ Hungarian dances. So, let me ask you; who wrote Brahms’ Hungarian dances? Wrong. It was not Brahms at all. He plagiarized them… all of them. You need to remember that Brahms was a cocktail lounge piano player from the north of Germany; very far removed musically and culturally from the Hungarian gypsies. The composer was none other than Edouard Remenyi, that Hungarian firebrand. But now to return to our story. Remenyi was born in Hungary and had the usual musical education in Vienna. He was a child prodigy. And now the story gets really interesting. 1848 was the year of revolution everywhere. The Hungarians revolted against the young Austro-Hungarian Emperor Franz Joseph. General Kossuth, the leader of the Hungarians in revolt, chose Remenyi to be the psychological leader of the revolution. The young violinist played his violin in every military camp, drumming up enthusiasm. After Emperor Franz Joseph put down the revolution, he placed a bounty on Remenyi – “wanted dead or alive.“ Remenyi fled for his life as far from Europe as he could go. He came all the way to America and became an instant success. He traveled throughout the entire country playing concerts in formal concert halls as well as in saloons in the Wild West. Sometimes the miners were so enthusiastic that they threw gold nuggets onto the stage. On another occasion, Remenyi was so fatigued, he could not play the numerous encores the audience wanted. The rough audience became enraged and smashed all the furniture. Soon after, Queen Victoria sent a message to Remenyi that he was to be her court violinist in London. That’s when Austro-Hungarian Emperor Franz Joseph changed his mind. You guessed it. Franz Josef wanted Remenyi to be his private violinist in Vienna. It seems that all was forgiven. It was during this time that Remenyi’s friendship with Brahms disintegrated. But it wasn’t because of Brahms’ plagiarism; it was because of a woman. At about this same time he scampered to the top of the great pyramid in Egypt with his violin and played to the great nothingness of the Egyptian desert. The worldwide press later announced that he had drowned in a disaster at sea. He survived and announced that the news of his death was greatly exaggerated. Remenyi returned to America where he continued to enjoy great musical success. He became wealthy and possessed a large collection of expensive violins and expensive paintings. In retirement, his fortunes changed. The Orpheum vaudeville circuit lured him out of retirement and engaged him at what was announced as a “fabulous contract.” Remenyi traveled from New York across the country to San Francisco for his first engageSee Musical Gourmet on page 30

articles.text: Mary Elizabeth Winstead and John Goodman in 10 Cloverfield Lane. Review by Chris Honore’ If you move in the right creepy-movie circles, you may have seen the 2008 film Cloverfield, a found camcorder style movie about a monster rampaging through Manhattan. But if you didn’t, no worries. 10 Cloverfield Lane is not a sequel, but a standalone taut psychological thriller that does have a high creep factor, but is far more subtle though unsettling than its distant cousin. The use of “Cloverfield” in the title is just good marketing. If there is a fragile thread that connects the two, it runs through J. J. Abrams (“The Force Awakens”), a guy who knows a good story when he finds one. This is indeed a sinister tale that makes superb use of what might be referred to as the “terror-trope.” If all of this is beginning to feel like I’m avoiding even hinting at the plot, you’d be right. The less you know about what to expect from 10 Cloverfield Lane, the better. Try not to watch the trailer. What you will experience going in is a master class in pacing and ambience, using those enjoyably uncomfortable yet familiar emotions such as claustrophobia and paranoia. Meanwhile you will be doing your own check regarding what is real and what are the demented delusions of a wacked-out survivalist. That would be the talented John Goodman as a guy named Howard. Without giving too much away, this is what you might call a container film – a hothouse of riveting tension, created by the fact that the situation is inescapable. This story takes place in an underground bunker that offers as many amenities as can be created, all predicated on not going topside for one to two years. Whatever’s up there, Howard insists, he doesn’t want to experience. The three actors are excellent, led by a solid and nuanced performance by Goodman and buttressed by a convincing, resourceful, McGuyver-like damsel-in-distress portrayal by Mary Elizabeth Winstead as Michelle. The third corner of the triangle is John Gallagher Jr., a local handyman called Emmett, who talked his way into the bunker. Winstead didn’t. Whether you agree with the film’s ending or not will be a personal judgment. It may satisfy or it may be simply too predictable. Admittedly, the writers do get themselves into a bit of a jam, though the story possess that wonderful, chilling, sustained sense of dread. Which is exactly the emotion – call it that affective thriller sweet spot – that films of this genre aim for. Nailed. 10 Cloverfield Lane. Directed by Dan Trachtenberg. Starring John Goodman, Mary Elizabeth Winstead and John Gallagher. 1 hr., 43 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Free State of Jones brings to the screen a little-known moment taken from the pages of America’s Civil War. The year is 1863. A poor southern Mississippi farmer, Newton Knight (Matthew McConaughey), having deserted his post as a front-line nurse, brings the body of his nephew back to Jones County for burial. He is told repeatedly by his neighbors that Confederate agents are confiscating farmers’ livestock, grain and goods for the war effort. Hearing these stories Newton has an epiphany: what he and his brethren are fighting for is the right of the rich plantation owners to continue to grow cotton and own slaves (of which he has neither). And thus begins the first stirring of what will soon grow into an armed rebellion of runaway slaves and a band of Confederate deserters who soon are fighting a war within a war, deciding they’d prefer to cast their lot with the Union. Writer/director Gary Ross (Sea Biscuit, Hunger Games) wades into this chapter in our history knowing that it is a labyrinth of complexity and nuance. It is a project he had contemplated for almost a decade. He shows remarkable restraint when demonstrating that while the poor whites of Mississippi do not bear the weight and cruelty of racism, they are, like the slaves of the south, disenfranchised. And so, Newton and his ragtag company of slaves and runaway Confederate soldiers begin a guerilla campaign against the soldiers of the South, against its privileged aristocracy, establishing what came to be known as the Free State of Jones, a piece of geography they managed to hold until the end of the war. Free State of Jones represents the nexus of economic and racial oppression. The film is a stark reminder of the inhumanity and profound cruelty of an institution that still astonishes and ripples through our society. Before the Civil War was a time when black lives mattered for their free labor. The value of slaves was solely an economic process, never a human one. But this film is not about a “white savior” helping the oppressed. Newton joins forces not just with those white men who’ve deserted, but he finds a boon companion in Moses Washington (Mahershala Ali), a runaway slave who displays as deep well of intelligence and courage as does Newton. He is also helped by and attracted to Rachel (Gugu Mbatha-Raw), a household slave, who joins him in purpose and in emotional attachment. This band of black brothers and sisters is as essential to Newton’s victory as are the white soldiers who, especially after Vicksburg, decide to take up arms against the South. Free State of Jones is not a perfect film. Ross wanted to tell a story that easily could have been Jones plus a sequel, one in which he dealt with Jim Crow and Plessy v, Ferguson. The Civil War did not end racial prejudice; it just altered its posture. Regardless of the criticism that Free State of Jones is too long, what Ross has accomplished with this story is remarkable, a tale of courage and rebellion and one that we should never forget. Free State of Jones. Starring Matthew McConaughey, Gugu Mbatha-Raw and Mahershala Ali. Directed by Gary Ross. 2 hrs., 19 min. Rated R.

articles.text: The San Francisco International Film Festival opens this Friday, April 9, with a Fort Mason drive-in screening of Lost Landscapes of Oakland, set to a live performance by Grammy-winner Fantastic Negrito. This year’s festival will be split partially between online premieres and drive-ins sponsored by Fort Mason Flix, located at 2 Marina Boulevard in San Francisco. Over 100 films from 41 countries, including 42 features, 56 shorts, and five mid-length films will be available throughout the festival. More than 50 programs are available to stream from home; through April 18. Festival streaming passes are $75 to the general public and $50 for members. Online individual tickets are $12 general and $8 for members. Drive-in screenings are $70 per car general admission, and $55 for members. The cost on opening night is $100 and $75 respectively. For online offerings, visit https://sffilm.org/2021-festival-streaming-programs/. For a full schedule of drive-in offerings, visit https://sffilm.org/2021-sections-spotlights/drive-ins/.

articles.text: A scene from Disney-Pixar’s Onward. Onward is a release by Pixar-Disney in which they once again bring to bear what is a marvelous engine of imagination that creates, with each film, a special world that beckons kids of all ages to enter and enjoy. The world created in Onward is one of blue-toned elves who live in toadstool houses, a place of dragons, unicorns, magic spells, and not to forget some engaging wizardry. From the outset the story is carried by two brothers, Ian (Tom Holland), who has just turned 16, and Barley (Chris Pratt), older and just a tad different and rebellious. They are the Lightfoot bros, and a study in contrast. They discover a birthday gift left for Ian by his deceased dad: it’s a wizard’s staff along with a letter of instructions that will allow their dad to return for just one day. Ian, with Barley’s help, makes a valiant attempt, but only manages to get halfway through the spell, resulting in dad ending up as a pair of pants, socks and shoes. What is needed is a new gemstone to replace the one that fizzled. Barley is certain he knows where to find one. And so, the adventure begins. The brothers set out on a quest that will take them from place to place, each fraught with perilous moments. The part of this hunt that is unusual is that they take half their dad along, hooked up to a doggy leash so he can’t wander off. Dad, after all, can’t speak or see hence is high maintenance. Their mode of transportation is Barley’s well-used van, outfitted with some amazing stuff, like blasting air conditioning. The boys bicker about directions and the ability of Ian to use the staff to create critical magic when needed – like a magical bridge. What is surprising is that there is a tone of sadness to the story. Both the brothers are grieving for their dad. Ian never knew his father, since he was born shortly after dad died. Barley, however, does have small kid memories and yearns for more. They are convinced that once they locate the special stone they can complete their dad’s final transformation and have that one conversation. And so, onward. The film is essentially episodic and situational, and there are lots of speed bumps along the way. And for good measure, mom Laurel (Julia Louis-Dreyfus) is right behind the pair, desperate to find them, certain they are in danger. It’s all in the Pixar wheelhouse, and kids, say six and seven, will enjoy the journey and the cast of characters, including Colt-Bronco, a police officer centaur (Mel Rodriquez), and a Manticore restaurant with a Manticore (Octavia Spencer). It’s where they find a needed map to get them from point A to point B. It’s all a trip to be enjoyed, especially if you’re a kid and relish quality time in elf-land. Onward. Directed by Dan Scanlon. Animated. With voices of Chris Pratt, Tom Holland, Octavia Spencer and Julia Louis-Dreyfus. 1 hr., 54 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: Onward a journey in the land of elves

articles.text: It’s been some 25 years since the first Jurassic Park was released, directed by Steven Spielberg, based on the Michael Crichton book, the central idea being that cretaceous creatures, most especially the high-rise dinosaurs with those signature reptilian eyes, could be reproduced using engineered DNA. It was a massive hit that combined all the ingredients of horror and action filmmaking for a breathtaking experience. As well, there is a through line from, say, a film like Jaws to the Jurassic series where a predator is loose and humans, no matter how resilient or well-defended, are ultimately helpless. A sense of overwhelming vulnerability represents the genius of these stories. After all, teethfilled jaws come in all sizes and the image of a person’s torso dangling part way out of a raptor’s mouth will cause viewers to pay attention. Each of the movies that have followed, in the aggregate, have created what has been a durable franchise, while giving audiences a rush of adrenalin as computer generated raptors, scarily smart, manage to get free and overcome all best efforts to contain them. Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom, is the second in what will be a trilogy that began with Jurassic World. The set-up is fairly straightforward. The island of Isla Nublar was devastated when the dinos got loose. What made World riveting was that the island is now a popular amusement park, all revolving around the reptiles. The dinos, now free, devastate the park and the tourists, who run for their lives. Finally the island is abandoned to the animals. What has now occurred in Fallen Kingdom is that a once dormant volcano is on the cusp of erupting and Claire (Bryce Dallas Howard) and Owen (Chris Pratt) are recruited by a long-ago benefactor, Benjamin Lockwood (James Cromwell), to rescue the remaining dinos and transport them to another island absent tourists and rides. But, as is explained, the plan, born of avarice, is orchestrated by a nefarious Lockwood assistant unbeknownst to Lockwood. The plan is to put the captured dinos on the market to the highest bidder. So, instead of a pristine island, they are sent to the Lockwood compound, a massive, 19th century manor house. Claire, Owen, and their two aids, Zia (Daniella Pineadad) and Franklin (Justice Smith), manage to sneak onto a boat along with the animals. The exit from the island entails scenes of the island exploding as well as a harrowing trip to the Lockwood home, a darkly gothic warren of spaces with a basement filled with cages where the dinos are kept until auctioned off. Assume that at the manor what can go wrong will go wrong, only the location is no longer an island, but a dark, atmospheric, three-story house with a firstfloor entry replete with museum quality dioramas of dinos in their prehistoric habitats. The dilemma facing Claire, Owen, and sidekicks, is how to rescue the dinos, thus preventing them from falling into the commercial hands of potential buyers. Think raptors weaponized. Things, however, go from dicey to very bad. What has always been a strength of this franchise is that there have been tweens or teens woven into the plot. And Kingdom is no exception. Lockwood, so it seems, has a teenage granddaughter, Maisie (Isabella Sermon), who is terrified. One of the best scenes that kids will definitely relate to is when Maisie, hiding under her covers with an Indoraptor (a designer raptor) standing over her bed, a long claw tapping the tile floor. It’s a chilling moment. When I screen any of the Jurassic films, I remind myself that the audience is made up of youngsters. They show up to be scared and the challenge is always how to go about creating that creepy, terrifying feeling in all its variations. Discussing this point in an email exchange with Piedmont native and co-writer, Colin Trevorrow, the director of Jurassic World, he wrote: “We have a responsibility to appeal to everyone around the world. These movies don’t belong to America, they’re global, and they need to incorporate universal themes that can connect with a hugely diverse audience. It’s not just about age. It’s diversity of experience, of context. Many movies have the luxury of appealing to one group. We have to think about everybody.” Kingdom is a bridge movie and the second in the Jurassic World trilogy. Much of what takes place is leading to the final film. As Trevorrow wrote, “We can’t get to where we’re going without this…. The dynamic between the characters has completely shifted by the end of this story. The equilibrium of the planet has been altered. Nothing will ever be the same for them, or the world they live in.” The challenge, of course, will be how to make the third story fresh and compelling. But then the films that followed Jurassic Park were never about the big reveal. As mentioned, it’s about exploring the dimensions of vulnerability. Recall in Jaws the young woman taking a late-night swim while just below is the ultimate predator, pacing her in what she assumes are benign waters. And there was, of course, that brilliant, memorable soundtrack. Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom. Directed by J.A. Bayona. Written by Colin Trevorrow and Derek Connelly. Starring Chris Pratt, Bryce Dallas Howard and Rafe Spall. 2 hrs., 9 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom another scary film by Trevorrow

It’s a chilling moment. When I screen any of the Jurassic films, I remind myself that the audience is made up of youngsters. They show up to be scared and the challenge is always how to go about creating that creepy, terrifying feeling in all its variations. Discussing this point in an email exchange with Piedmont native and co-writer, Colin Trevorrow, the director of Jurassic World, he wrote: “We have a responsibility to appeal to everyone around the world. These movies don’t belong to America, they’re global, and they need to incorporate universal themes that can connect with a hugely diverse audience. It’s not just about age. It’s diversity of experience, of context. Many movies have the luxury of appealing to one group. We have to think about everybody.” Kingdom is a bridge movie and the second in the Jurassic World trilogy. Much of what takes place is leading to the final film. As Trevorrow wrote, “We can’t get to where we’re going without this…. The dynamic between the characters has completely shifted by the end of this story. The equilibrium of the planet has been altered. Nothing will ever be the same for them, or the world they live in.” The challenge, of course, will be how to make the third story fresh and compelling. But then the films that followed Jurassic Park were never about the big reveal. As mentioned, it’s about exploring the dimensions of vulnerability. Recall in Jaws the young woman taking a late-night swim while just below is the ultimate predator, pacing her in what she assumes are benign waters. And there was, of course, that brilliant, memorable soundtrack. Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom. Directed by J.A. Bayona. Written by Colin Trevorrow and Derek Connelly. Starring Chris Pratt, Bryce Dallas Howard and Rafe Spall. 2 hrs., 9 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: If people know of Marsala wine at all, it is likely they remember buying a bottle for five bucks about 10 years ago to make chicken Marsala, and the bottle still sits in the cupboard. Let me give you a little historical background before we talk about the wine itself. Marsala is a fortified wine, dry or sweet, produced in the region surrounding the city of Marsala in Sicily. It was probably first popularized outside Sicily by the English trader John Woodhouse. In 1773, he landed at the port of Marsala and discovered the local wine produced in the region, which was aged in wooden casks and tasted similar to Spanish and Portuguese fortified wines then popular in England. Fortified Marsala was, and is, made using a process called in perpetuum, which is similar to the solera system used to produce Sherry in Jerez, Spain. Woodhouse recognized that the in perpetuum process raised the alcohol level and alcoholic taste of this wine while also preserving these characteristics during long-distance sea travel. Woodhouse further believed that fortified Marsala would be popular in England. The wine indeed proved so successful that Woodhouse returned to Sicily and, in 1796, began its mass production and commercialization. Popularity grew over the years. Slightly less than 200 years later, in 1969, Marsala received its DOC status as a protected name from the European Union. Marsala wine is frequently used in cooking and is especially prevalent in Italian food. Dry Marsala is used in savory cooking. A typical savory Marsala sauce, for example, involves reducing the wine almost to a syrup with onions or shallots, then adding mushrooms and herbs. The ever-popular dinner of Chicken Marsala is flour-coated pounded chicken breast halves braised in a mixture of Marsala, butter, olive oil, mushrooms and spices. Sweet Marsala is used to produce rich Italian desserts such as zabaglione and tiramisu. The following wines are excellent examples of both dry and sweet styles of Marsala. • 2015 Cantina Florio Vecchiflorio Marsala Superiore Dry This delicious Sicilian wine is amber colored with aromas and notes of toffee, nuts, raisins and other dried fruits. It is rich and yet not ponderous or cloying with good acid and structure. It can be served chilled as an aperitif or sipped at room temperature after dinner. 2015 Cantina Florio Vecchiflorio Marsala Superiore Dry. • 2017 Cantina Florio Vecchioflorio Marsala Superiore Sweet This sweet Marsala is aged 24 months in oak casks and is mellow as can be. It has a dark amber color with an intense aroma with hints of dates and peaches. On the palate it is deep and rich with a long satisfying finish. An excellent post-prandial dram. Pierre’s Cocktail – an Extra Bonus In addition to being a wine man, at times I dabble a bit in mixology. So these two wines inspired me to see if I could come up with a cocktail that did these hedonistic wines justice. So here it is. DUMONT’S DOWNFALL • 1 oz. Cantina Florio Dry Marsala • 1 oz. Cantina Florio Sweet Marsala • 1 oz. Dry Curacao • 2 dash Angostura Bitters Stir gently with ice then pour over ice into an old-fashioned glass. Garnish with a slice of orange. DuMont’s Downfall – a cocktail combining both dry and sweet Marsala.

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department has announced that the Walking on Wednesdays group, sidelined for one year due to the coronavirus, will be back in action next Wednesday, April 14. This restart marks three years since the group’s first weekly walk on April 18, 2018. Some new protocols will help keep walkers as COVID-safe as possible. Before the pandemic, many people enjoyed the weekly Wednesday morning walks on Piedmont’s beautiful streets. “Members of the group have remained in contact during the pandemic. Being able to be with members of the group again will be great,” said coordinator Dick Carter. Since last week, March 30, Alameda County has been at the Orange Tier level within the state’s Blueprint for Safer Economy Opening Plan. The Orange Tier allows for many outdoor group activities to be conducted. Individuals planning on participating in the weekly walks need to register on the Recreation Department’s CommunityPass site. Walkers will be placed in a pod and each pod of walkers will have a different start time at 15-minute intervals starting at 10:00 a.m. every Wednesday at the Exedra Plaza at Magnolia and Highland Avenues. Walkers in each pod will be defined and set until pandemic activity restrictions are removed or modified by the County or City. Participants will not be allowed to move within pods, or walk with other pods, after the pods have been defined. Participants will be required to wear masks during, and after their walks, and maintain six feet of separation from non-family member participants. There are no fees to participate in Walking on Wednesdays activities. Those interested in walking with the group should register at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. For more information, contact the Piedmont Recreation Department at 510-420-3070.
articles.title: Walking on Wednesday group returns – Live on April 14

Post your ad in the Call (510) 626-2468 nancy@cmc-ads.com Photo by Deborah Quok Strawberry Kale Salad with Lemon-Mint Dressing For a taste of Springtime, try Strawberry Kale Salad By Deborah Quok Every spring I eagerly anticipate the arrival of strawberries at my favorite farmers market vendors. It takes a lot of restraint to skip them the first couple of weeks when they look under ripe with white shoulders and ruby tips. Perhaps the farmers are as eager as the rest of us to see a new season dawning for fruit varieties. But by early April I dive in. Our younger son always requests Strawberry Shortcake for his early-April birthday dessert. So, no matter their ripeness, I’m heading home with two or three baskets. They always look delicious, but it’s clear their flavor has not quite caught up to peak strawberry-liciousness. Adding them to a salad does not disappoint though. The additional ingredients and dressing help to amplify the strawberry flavor, and they are still stunning to the eye. I chose kale as the primary green as we always seem to have a bunch of kale ready to go. This springtime salad is a perfect use, but any leafy green such as spinach, arugula, or lettuce will be tasty too. A few notes: If the kale is a bit tough, you may have to massage it with a small amount of the dressing to help soften it. Even though I chose a curly red for the photos, I often use lacinato kale as it is often more tender. Slicing the kale thinly, across the ribs, helps too. This recipe is adaptable in many ways. Add in cheese, avocado, switch out the pecans for toasted sliced almonds. Go with what you like. Side note: Omit the honey in the dressing and try it on steamed new potatoes with snap peas. INGREDIENTS • 1 bunch kale, either torn or sliced into 1/2-inch wide strips • 1 pint fresh strawberries, sliced lengthwise in halves or thirds, depending on size • 1/2 small red onion, sliced thinly and crosswise to create rings • 1/2 cup pecan pieces, lightly toasted • 3 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil • 2 tablespoons freshly squeezed lemon juice, use sweeter Meyer lemons if available • 1/4 cup loosely packed, fresh mint leaves, finely minced • 1 teaspoon honey, optional, to taste • Salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste INSTRUCTIONS Make the dressing: Measure the lemon juice into a small, deep bowl. Add honey, if using. Slowly drizzle in the olive oil, whisking continuously to maximize emulsification. Add minced mint leaves, salt, and pepper to taste. Set aside. Rinse the leaves of kale to remove any dirt and dry well. Either tear into bite-sized pieces, or slice into 1/ 2”-wide strips. Place into a large salad bowl. Pour about half of the prepared dressing over the kale and mix well to begin softening the kale. Add the sliced red onion, toss to mix, then drizzle in additional dressing to taste – taking care to avoid drowning the salad with too much. Add the sliced strawberries and gently combine. Finally, sprinkle on the toasted pecan pieces and serve. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com. articles.text: The Oakland Public Library (OPL) will open 16 locations including the Piedmont Avenue Branch for indoor Express services starting April 19. Library users will be able to access modified library services including limited browsing, checkout of materials, and computer use. Gathering and play spaces will remain closed, but patrons can expect welcoming staff available to help them navigate OPL Express services and safety protocols. The Asian Branch Library and the Oakland Tool Lending Library will continue to offer Sidewalk Service due to ongoing facility improvements. During visiting hours, the following in-person services will be available: • Library card registration and renewal • Browsing the collection • Computer use (excluding Lakeview, Montclair and Piedmont Ave.) • Print, scan and faxing services (at available locations) • Laptop and Wi-Fi hotspot checkout (at available locations) • Wi-Fi access and mobile device charging Visitor guidelines • Wear a face mask covering nose and mouth, for all patrons over two years old. • Maintain a physical distance of 6-feet apart • Self-screen for COVID-19 symptoms. • Wash or sanitize hands frequently. • Eating and drinking will not be permitted during OPL Express. Oakland Library is providing the following to protect the safety of patrons and staff: • Limiting occupancy inside each location • Providing self-checkout stations at all locations • Piloting a new mobile checkout service • Quarantining items for at least 24 hours before returning to circulation • Disinfecting high-touch surfaces regularly The library will continue to offer 24/7 access to digital offerings including e-books, audiobooks and streaming movies, in addition to virtual programs, including storytimes, book clubs and author talks. For more information contact the Piedmont Ave. Branch Library, located at 80 Echo Avenue in Oakland, at (510) 597-5011 (www.oaklandlibrary.org)
articles.title: Oakland Public Libraries to open indoors April 19

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: In previous columns, I have written about Wallace Alexander, Piedmont’s benefactor. In 1913, he gathered several successful Piedmont businessmen to purchase land opposite Piedmont Park, and hired Albert Farr to design the Piedmont Commercial Center, the first stores in Piedmont. Alexander also saved Piedmont Park from development in 1921 by purchasing the land (when the city had no funds) and selling it back to the city the following year. After the 1906 earthquake and fire, many San Franciscan residents fled to Oakland and the Piedmont hills and built new homes. By the 1910s, Piedmont’s population was expanding rapidly. Just as these residents needed a grocery store, they were also outgrowing Mowbray Hall, the 1908 Sunday School, and needed a church. When Wallace Alexander led a group of residents to purchase land for the commercial center, he also purchased an adjacent 1-1/2 acres and offered that land for a church. Alexander then hired Albert Farr to design it and construction began in 1916. Piedmont residents who contributed to the construction of the facility came from all faiths, and interdenominational services would be held in the new church. Albert Farr called his design “Mission” or “Spanish Colonial” and credited Junipero Serra and Jose Churriguera as his inspirations. He designed the church around a courtyard with a central fountain and an outdoor pulpit (now gone). Farr claimed the tiered fountain was an exact replica of an old Spanish fountain at the Santa Barbara Mission. The courtyard was to be planted with shrubs and was designed to be a resting place for all during the week. Farr designed the sanctuary with a domed ceiling, seating for 300, antique lamps, decorative screens to conceal the mechanisms of the organ, and elaborately carved Churrigueresque doors. He designed the south side The Piedmont Interdenominational Church sanctuary in 1918 with its dome, beamed ceiling and antique lamps. One of the Churrigueresque doors is on the right. ❏ New Membership

articles.text: Photos by Kate Fratar The doorway to City of London Distillery sits below the steeple of St. Bride’s Church, known as the church of the media and press, and just off Fleet Street, once home to a bustling newspaper scene. Aboard the Flying Scotsman – a train, lest the name suggest otherwise – I’m bound for Edinburgh and the second stop on this summer’s spirits trail. The primary focus of this adventure will be on whisky tasting and studying the subtleties of peat and esters. The kickoff to this hard-nosing jaunt came in London, where the emphasis was on gins. Because, well, when in Rome, as they say. Tucked away on an easily missed side alley of Fleet Street is the City of London Distillery. Founded in 2012, the urban upstart is bringing back the tradition of gin distillation to the City of London after a nearly 200-year absence. During the eighteenth century, gin distilleries sprouted in this area, originally the site of a fortified Roman settlement at Londonium, as citrus fruits became available through London’s port. Among the distillery’s gins, The Square Mile is a nod to the two square miles that establishes the City of London as a separate entity, complete with its own mayor and independent police force, within the jurisdiction of Greater London. Its doorway sits beneath the steeple of St. Bride’s Church, known as the church of the media and the press. Down the narrow wooden stairs is the bottle shop, bar, tasting room, and fireproofed, glassed-walled distillery. The cozy setup, complete with dark green paint and plush leather chairs, echoes an era when cigarette smoke might have lingered overhead and the din of clacking typewriters would have overridden conversation (perhaps of the latest news tip?). It’s one-part speakeasy to two-parts journalist hideaway. Jake meets me to host a tour – including the botanicals room, where guests can tinker with their own blends of spices and take the concoction home – and a tasting. The four pillars of the City of London production line are all in the classic London Dry style, with varying levels of citrus. There are also gins infused with rhubarb, lemon and mandarin, respectively, made more as experiments to play within market trends. pages.text: Wednesday, April 7, 2021 29 TRAVELS WITH KATE Gin and the City Photos by Kate Fratar The doorway to City of London Distillery sits below the steeple of St. Bride’s Church, known as the church of the media and press, and just off Fleet Street, once home to a bustling newspaper scene. By Kate Fratar Aboard the Flying Scotsman – a train, lest the name suggest otherwise – I’m bound for Edinburgh and the second stop on this summer’s spirits trail. The primary focus of this adventure will be on whisky tasting and studying the subtleties of peat and esters. The kickoff to this hard-nosing jaunt came in London, where the emphasis was on gins. Because, well, when in Rome, as they say. Tucked away on an easily missed side alley of Fleet Street is the City of London Distillery. Founded in 2012, the urban upstart is bringing back the tradition of gin distillation to the City of London after a nearly 200-year absence. During the eighteenth century, gin distilleries sprouted in this area, originally the site of a fortified Roman settlement at Londonium, as citrus fruits became available through London’s port. Among the distillery’s gins, The Square Mile is a nod to the two square miles that establishes the City of London as a separate entity, complete with its own mayor and independent police force, within the jurisdiction of Greater London. Its doorway sits beneath the steeple of St. Bride’s Church, known as the church of the media and the press. Down the narrow wooden stairs is the bottle shop, bar, tasting room, and fireproofed, glassed-walled distillery. The cozy setup, complete with dark green paint and plush leather chairs, echoes an era when cigarette smoke might have lingered overhead and the din of clacking typewriters would have overridden conversation (perhaps of the latest news tip?). It’s one-part speakeasy to two-parts journalist hideaway. Jake meets me to host a tour – including the botanicals room, where guests can tinker with their own blends of spices and take the concoction home – and a tasting. The four pillars of the City of London production line are all in the classic London Dry style, with varying levels of citrus. There are also gins infused with rhubarb, lemon and mandarin, respectively, made more as experiments to play within market trends. The City of London Authentic gin won a Double-Gold Award at the San Francisco World Spirits Competition in 2017. The recognition is when the distillery decided to stop any further finessing of the recipe, Jake noted. In 2016, the Christopher Wren, named for the architect of St. Paul’s Cathedral, the more recognizable church-top to overlook the distillery, took home the same award. Where the Christopher Wren carries more undertones of orange, the citrus lacing the Old Tom is primarily lemon zest. The garnishes of orange twist with Christopher Wren and lemon with hibiscus for the Old Tom, along with the choice of tonic, bring variation to the standard G&T on the bar menu. It was a different classic gin cocktail that I wanted to see sampled, however. After a day spent walking to get the rhythm and beat of London’s different neighborhoods, I returned to City of London Distillery for a Negroni. The Florentine invention turns 100 years old this year. In 2018, it was the second-most ordered cocktail worldwide, according to a poll conducted by the magazine Drinks International of more than 100 bars. Perhaps it is due to the pure simplicity of the Negroni that great diversification can be found. Essentially equal parts gin, sweet vermouth, and Campari, variations in any of these ingredients can lead to marked differences. Within the stratosphere of The bar at City of London Distillery, founded in 2012, is well supplied with its gins, which have taken top honors at the San Francisco World Competition. gins, the qualifying factor, by and large, is having some sort quantity of juniper. (Note that gin is not distilled from juniper berries. It is typically grain-based, but it can be made from any fermented base. Locally, Oakland Spirits Company produces gins distilled from grapes.) Today’s gin makers are having fun with the open field allowed to them, leading to more options for consumers. Speaking for myself, I would pull from the Christopher Wren of the City of London Distillery lineup to mirror the orange peel garnish of a Negroni. On to Bar Termini For a real study in the portrait of the Negroni, the place to go is Bar Termini in Soho. Named for Rome’s train station, the place bustles with all the organized frenzy of a terminal, as white-jacketed waiters zip from bar to table carrying trays of coffee and cocktails. American jazz, with Ella Fitzgerald and Frank Sinatra crooning Cole Porter, tries to make itself heard over the hubbub that bubbles out of any proper pub. On the menu are four separate house Negroni options. Classico lives up to its name. The Rosato has a trace of rose petal, the Superiore adds green peppercorn that amazingly doesn’t overpower but adds bite on the aftertaste to the juniper, and the Robusto is aged, doing what aging does. The vibrancy and rougher edges to a Negroni’s bitterness are softened and rounded off, being replaced with deeper, more mature flavors. All four are prepared sous vide, the water bath style of cooking in vacuumed, sealed containers that is known for delivering consistency and integrated flavors. Dry essences are used as part of the mixture in place of fresh garnish. The Negroni is poured tableside from a bottle and served in a chilled glass in a smaller portion that the standard three ounces, without an ice cube that would add dilution. Paired with the burrata, which is topped with a basil leaf to mirror the bitterness of the cocktail, with the acidity of the sun-dried tomatoes to add a touch of tang, and the creaminess of the cheese to undercut it all, the experience is as the near sun-drenched hillsides of Tuscany as one could find in the Old Smoke. Reservations are highly recommended at this small joint, which has been listed to The World’s 50 Best Bars three years running. While it’s possible to be Bar Termini, named for the train station in Rome, has been included on The World’s Top 50 Best Bars for three years running. Its four house Negronis are the perfect blend of Italian flair with honest-to-goodness London Dry gin. accommodated without a reservation, guests were seated with the friendly caveat that the table would need to be free in 10 or 15 minutes. Even advance reservations are limited to an hour and half. As I settled into my booth seat at 5:00, I was grateful for the ticket that allowed me to sit back and enjoy the scene and tastes before me. Then, at 6:15, like a well-timed conductor, a waiter, with all due courtesy, asked if there was anything else I would like. My ride was coming to its stop. Kate Fratar is a certified sommelier and the founder and editor of ChasingWine.org, a website dedicated to travel, history, and a study of the world’s varietals. articles.text: The Oakland Center of the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, directed by Piedmont resident, Dr. Steve Sidney, currently has job postings for a 35-year follow-up exam of study participants who were first examined in 1985-1986. The CARDIA study, funded by the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute, is a longitudinal study of black and white men and women who were 18-30 years old at the beginning of the study and who have been followed for the development of heart disease risk factors and disease. More than 900 published scientific articles have resulted from the CARDIA study thus far. This will be the 10th examination for study participants who were initially recruited from four centers around the country, including Kaiser Permanente (KP) Health Plan members from the Berkeley-Oakland area. The examination will be conducted by the KP Northern California Division of Research at its research clinic located in the Mosswood Building, 3505 Broadway in Oakland. Positions are available for scheduling examinations, conducting exam interviews and study procedures, data management, and managing the mailing of equipment and supplies for aspects of the study conducted at the homes of participants. These positions will start in May or June of this year and end during the summer of 2022. Training will be provided. If you would like more information, please contact Dr. Sidney at steve.sidney@kp.org.

She has also directed six local families to the Alameda County Youth and Family Services department. During her tenure, Piedmont Police Department provided Casalnuovo with 12 hours of adolescent mental health training, 40 hours of crisis intervention training, 10 hours of implicit bias training, and 40 hours of parent project facilitator training, among other resources. Police Chief Jeremey Bowers, who presented information on the position to council members, noted that Casalnuovo was integral in solidifying relationships between the school community and the department. “The value of the juvenile officer [includes] building relationships so a feedback loop can exist. Officer Casalnuovo has done a great job of that. The [PUSD] administration has her cell phone number. [They] know how to get hold of her and give her feedback,” Bowers said. “Continuing the juvenile officer program by applying for this grant will enable us to dedicate a resource specifically for youth-related issues in our community.” Bowers admitted that continuous feedback was derailed during COVID, but said that “as we go forward, we absolutely look to be thoughtful about different ways to get more formal feedback and data from parents and teachers on the success of the program,” to include surveys or other public outreach. Bowers recognized also, however, that Casalnuovo may not continue in the position if the grant is accepted. “Obviously, we can’t keep her forever [in this position]. She has other goals, so she will probably move on to a team to function as an active watch commander more frequently,” he said. Bowers confirmed that a new juvenile officer has already been identified. “He has substantial experience working with youth, mentoring youth, and brings real-world experience of dealing with a very diverse student population,” he said.

articles.text: The Cherry trees in the main area of Piedmont Park are now in full bloom. These cherry trees typically begin budding in late winter and blossom in spring, over a season that usually lasts several weeks. Renovations to include cherry trees that line the entrances and walkways of Piedmont Park were supported by the Piedmont Beautification Foundation 40 years ago. From the 1980s to 1994, foundation members assisted in restoration of the park, which included landscaping the Highland Avenue entrance. In addition to cherry trees, the foundation also funded the planting of oaks and ferns. Since 1980, Piedmont Beautification Foundation members assisted with major pruning of Piedmont Park’s planted trees. Traditionally, Piedmont celebrates Arbor Day with an afternoon of ceremonial tree planting, garden talks, and honors for local garden clubs and the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. A highlight was the planting of a Yoshino cherry sapling that was a gift of the Japanese Embassy in 2012. Piedmont was one of only several communities in the U.S that was selected for the cereCherry tree flower. Staff Photo monial planting, which marked the centennial of Tokyo’s gift of 3,000 cherry trees to Washington, D.C in March 1912. A sprinkling of Akebono Cherry trees along “Cherry Walk” was nominated for heritage tree status by resident Nancy McHugh in 2020. articles.text: Six juveniles in a stolen vehicle with a concealed handgun were arrested and sent to Juvenile Hall on Saturday, March 27 by Piedmont Police officers. At 7:26 p.m. the Automatic License Plate Reader recorded a hit on a stolen blue 1999 Lexus RX300 SUV heading north on Estates Drive near Park Boulevard. The vehicle was reported stolen and had been used in a carjacking in Oakland three days earlier. Piedmont Officers responded to the scene, located the vehicle at a dead-end near Sunnyhills Road and Downey Place, and initiated a vehicle stop. Four juveniles were initially detained in the front and rear seats of the car. A search of the vehicle found two more juveniles laying down in the back trunk portion of the SUV. A further search of the vehicle revealed credit cards and ID cards in names of other people, and a 9mm semi-automatic handgun. With the assistance of Oakland Police, Piedmont officers arrested all six individuals and transported them to the Police station. The juveniles were booked into Juvenile Hall without incident on charges of Stolen Vehicle, Armed Carjacking, Possession of Stolen Property, and Possession of a Concealed Firearm. One suspect also had an active warrant for his arrest.
articles.title: Police arrest 6 juveniles for carjacking, concealed weapons
